## 9. Pāpavagga
## 1. Cūḷekasāṭaka Brāhmaṇa Vatthu
(The Story of the Brahmin Cūḷekasāṭaka)

"Abhittharetha kalyāṇe..." The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning the Brahmin Cūḷekasāṭaka.

## The Brahmin Couple with Only One Upper Garment
In the time of the Buddha Vipassī, there was a man known as the Brahmin Mahāekasāṭaka. This same Brahmin, in the present time of the Buddha, is known as the Brahmin Cūḷekasāṭaka in the city of Sāvatthī. The reason he was called Ekasāṭaka (One-Cloth) was that he had only one cloth to wear around his waist, and his wife also had only one. For both of them, there was only a single upper garment (outer cloth). When going outside, either the Brahmin or his wife would wear that single upper garment.

Then one day, when the announcement for listening to the Dhamma at the monastery was made, the Brahmin said, "My dear, the Dhamma preaching has been announced. How shall it be? Will you go to hear the Dhamma during the day, or will you go at night? Since we lack an upper garment, it is not possible for us to go together at the same time."

The Brahmin's wife replied, "My lord, I shall go during the day," and she went wearing the upper garment.
2:
## Considering the Offering of the Single Upper Garment
The Brahmin spent the day at home and went at night, sitting before the Buddha to listen to the Dhamma. At that time, fivefold joy (pīti) arose, permeating his entire body. The Brahmin, desiring to make an offering to the Blessed One, thought, "If I give this upper garment, there will be no outer cloth for my wife or for me."

Then, a thousand thoughts of stinginess (macchera) arose within him. Again, a single thought of faith (saddhā) arose. Overpowering that thought of faith, a thousand thoughts of stinginess arose once more. Thus, his powerful stinginess seemed to bind and seize him, obstructing his thought of faith. While he was thinking, "I shall give, I shall not give," the first watch of the night passed. Even when the middle watch arrived, he was unable to give. When the last watch arrived, the Brahmin thought, "While I have been fighting between the thought of faith and the thought of stinginess, two watches have already passed. If this stinginess of mine continues to increase, it will not allow me to lift my head from the four woeful states (apāya). I shall give this upper garment!"

Having suppressed the thousand thoughts of stinginess and making the thought of faith his forerunner, the Brahmin took the cloth, placed it at the feet of the Blessed One, and shouted loudly three times, "I have won! I have won!"

## The King Rewards the Brahmin
King Pasenadi of Kosala, who was also listening to the Dhamma, heard that sound and said, "Ask him, what is it that he has won?" When the King's men questioned him, the Brahmin explained the matter. Hearing this, the King said, "The Brahmin has done a deed that is difficult to do (dukkaraṃ). I shall show him favor," and he ordered a pair of cloths to be given to him. The Brahmin gave that pair of cloths also to the Tathāgata. Again, the King doubled the gift, giving two, four, eight, and sixteen pairs. The Brahmin gave all those pairs to the Tathāgata as well. Then the King ordered thirty-two pairs of cloths to be given to him.

To avoid being criticized for giving away everything he received without keeping anything for himself, the Brahmin took two pairs from those thirty-two—one for himself and one for his wife—and gave the remaining thirty pairs to the Tathāgata. Even after the King had rewarded the Brahmin a hundred times, he still wished to give more.

The King said to his attendants, "Friends, the Brahmin has done a deed that is difficult to do. Bring my two blankets (kambala) from the palace." They did as the King commanded. The King then presented the two blankets, worth a hundred thousand each. The Brahmin thought, "These blankets are not suitable for use on my body; they are only worthy of the Buddha's Sasana." He hung one blanket as a canopy over the Blessed One's bed inside the Gandhakuti (Perfumed Chamber), and the other he hung as a canopy in his own house at the place where the monk who regularly received alms there would eat.
3:
## Receiving the Reward of Fourfold Everything for Offering a Ceiling Cloth

When King Pasenadi of Kosala went to the presence of the Blessed One in the evening, he recognized that blanket and asked, ‘Venerable Sir, who performed this offering?’ When the Buddha replied, ‘The Brahmin Ekasāᅡaka performed the offering,’ the King thought, ‘This Brahmin has faith in the same place where I have faith.’ He then ordered the reward known as the ‘Fourfold Everything’ (Sabba-catukka) to be given to the Brahmin, consisting of four elephants, four horses, four thousand coins, four women, four female slaves, four male servants, and four great villages—giving four of each for these seven items.

The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: ‘Oh, how wonderful is the deed of Cũᄵekasāᅡaka! In just a moment, he received the Fourfold Everything. The wholesome deed performed just now has given its fruit this very day.’ The Buddha came and asked, ‘Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?’ When they replied, ‘For such and such a discussion, Venerable Sir,’ he said, ‘Monks, if this Brahmin Ekasāᅡaka had been able to give to me in the first watch, he would have received the Sixteenfold Everything (Sabba-soᄵasaka). If he had been able in the middle watch, he would have received the Eightfold Everything (Sabba-aᅡᅡhaka). But because he gave in the last watch after much time had passed, he received the Fourfold Everything. One who wishes to perform a wholesome deed should do so that very moment without letting the arising thought diminish. Merit performed slowly, though it gives wealth and happiness, gives its fruit only slowly. Therefore, a wholesome deed should be performed immediately after the thought arises.’ Connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse to preach the Dhamma:

## The Teaching

(116) Abhittharetha kalyāᅅe, pāpā cittaᅁ nivāraye.
Dandhaᅁ hi karoto puaᅁ, pāpasmiᅁ ramati mano.

Puaᅁ: wholesome merit. Dandhaᅁ: slowly. Karoto: of one who performs. Mano: the mind. Pāpasmiᅁ: in evil. Hi-yasmā: because. Ramati: delights. Tasmā: therefore. Kalyāᅅe: in wholesome deeds. Abhittharetha: one should hasten to perform. Pāpā: from evil. Cittaᅁ: the mind. Nivāraye: one should restrain.
4:
## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the verse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The Story of the Brahmin Cũᄵekasāᅡaka is finished.

## The Teaching

(117) Pāpace puriso kayirā, na naᅁ kayirā punappunaᅁ.
Na tamhi chandaᅁ kayirātha, dukkho pāpassa uccayo.

Puriso: a man. Pāpaᅁ: evil. Ce kayirā: if he should do even once. Naᅁ: that evil. Punappunaᅁ: again and again. Na kayirā: he should not do. Tamhi: in that evil. Chandaᅁ: the desire to do. Vinodetvā: having dispelled. Na kayirātha: he should not do. Kiᅁ kāraᅅā: for what reason? Pāpassa: of evil. Uccayo: the accumulation. Dukkhā: leads to suffering.

## 2. The Story of Elder Seyyasaka

The Buddha, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with ‘Pāpace puriso’ concerning the Elder Seyyasaka.

## Evil Only Leads to Bad Results

That Seyyasaka was a co-resident (saddhivihārika) pupil of Elder Lāᄵudāyĩ. Having informed Lāᄵudāyĩ of his dissatisfaction with the holy life, Lāᄵudāyĩ encouraged him in an act that would constitute a first Saᅁghādisesa offense. Thus, whenever dissatisfaction arose, he would perform that act leading to a first Saᅁghādisesa offense. When the Blessed One heard about the behavior of the monk Seyyasaka, he had him summoned and asked, ‘Is it true, as they say, that you act in this way?’ When he replied, ‘It is true, Blessed One,’ the Buddha rebuked him in various ways, saying, ‘Why have you committed such a grave act? Vain man, it is not suitable...’ After prescribing the training rule (sikkhāpada), he said, ‘Such an evil deed leads only to suffering both in this life and in the life to come.’ Connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse to preach the Dhamma.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The Story of Elder Seyyasaka is finished.

## 3. The Story of the Goddess Lājā
(Lājādevadhītā Vatthu)
The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Puññañce," while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, concerning the Goddess Lājā. The story originated in Rājagaha.

## The Country Girl Who Offered Puffed Rice
While the Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pipphali Cave, he entered into a meditative absorption. On the seventh day, having emerged from that absorption, he surveyed the place for alms-round with his divine eye. He saw a woman guarding a large paddy field, taking ears of rice and roasting them into puffed rice. He reflected, "Does she have faith or not?" Knowing she had faith, he further considered, "Will she be able to support me or not?" Realizing, "This young woman will fearlessly and bravely support me, and having done so, she will attain great wealth," he put on his robes, took his bowl, and stood near the paddy field. As soon as the young woman saw the Elder, her heart was filled with devotion, and her body was suffused with the five kinds of joy. She said, "Please wait, Bhante," took the puffed rice, went quickly, and poured it into the Elder's bowl. Having paid homage with the fivefold prostration, she made a wish: "Bhante, may I be a partaker of the Dhamma that you have realized." Venerable Mahākassapa gave his blessing, saying, "May it be as you have wished."

## Dying from a Snake Bite and Rebirth in Heaven
That young woman, having paid homage to the Elder, returned while reflecting on the gift she had given. On the path along the dike of that field, a highly poisonous snake lay in a hole. That snake was unable to bite the calf of the Venerable Mahākassapa, which was covered by his saffron robe. As the young woman returned, reflecting on her offering, she reached that spot. The snake came out of the hole, bit her, and caused her to fall right there on the dike. With a heart full of devotion, that field-guarding girl passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

She appeared in a golden mansion thirty leagues in size, as if waking from sleep, with a body three gāvutas in height, adorned with all kinds of ornaments. Wearing one divine cloth twelve leagues long and wrapped in another, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, she stood at the door of the mansion, which was decorated with golden vessels filled with golden puffed rice hanging in clusters, to manifest her past good deed. Looking at her own wealth, she reflected with her divine eye, "What good deed did I perform to obtain this wealth?" and realized, "I obtained it as a result of the puffed rice offered to my noble lord, the Venerable Mahākassapa."

## Performing Merit to Make Heavenly Wealth Permanent
The goddess thought, "Having obtained such wealth through such a small merit, it is not proper for me to be negligent now. Therefore, I will perform major and minor duties for my noble lord to make this wealth permanent." Thinking thus, early in the morning, she took a golden broom and a basket for disposing of rubbish, swept the precinct of the Venerable Mahākassapa's monastery, and set out drinking water and water for use. When the Elder saw this, he noted, "Some young monk or novice must have performed these duties." On the second day, the goddess did the same, and the Elder noted it in the same way.
6:
## Forbidding the Goddess Lājā from Coming
On the third day, the Elder heard the sound of the goddess sweeping and saw the radiance of her body entering through the gaps in the palm leaves and other openings. He opened the door and asked, "Who is this sweeping?" She replied, "Bhante, I am your attendant, the Goddess Lājā." He said, "Is it not the case that I have no such attendant by that name?" She explained, "Bhante, while I was guarding the paddy field, I offered puffed rice and returned with a devoted heart. I was bitten by a snake and died, and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. I obtained this wealth because of you, noble sir. I have come with the intention of performing major and minor duties for you, Bhante, to make my wealth permanent." He asked again, "Did you sweep this place yesterday and the day before as well? Did you set out the drinking water and water for use?" She replied, "Yes, Bhante." The Elder said, "Go away, Goddess. Let the duties you have performed remain as they are. From now on, do not come to this place."

## To Avoid Blame from Dhamma Preachers
"Bhante, do not destroy my merit. Please give me the opportunity to perform duties for you and make my wealth stable," she pleaded. "Goddess, go away. Do not let it be said by Dhamma preachers in the future, who sit holding ornate fans, 'It is said that a goddess used to come to the Great Elder Mahākassapa, performing major and minor duties and setting out drinking water and water for use.' From this day on, do not come here; depart and go away." The goddess pleaded repeatedly, "Bhante, do not destroy my merit." The Elder thought, "This goddess does not listen to my words," and snapped his fingers, saying, "You, goddess, do not know your limits."

(When words are not enough, it is customary to snap fingers. When Arahants snap their fingers, no deity can remain; they must depart.)

The goddess, unable to remain in that place, flew up into the sky. With her hands joined in reverence, she stood in the air, weeping and lamenting, "Bhante, do not destroy the wealth I have obtained; please give me the opportunity to make it permanent."

## To Each Their Own Responsibility
The Buddha, while staying in the Gandhakuti, heard the goddess's weeping. He emitted a radiance and, as if sitting in front of the goddess, spoke to her: "Goddess, to practice restraint and prohibition is the duty of my son Kassapa. But for those who desire merit, it is their duty to recognize 'This is our benefit' and perform merit. Indeed, performing merit brings happiness both in this world and in the world hereafter." Having thus connected the sequence, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:
7:
## The Teaching

(118) If a man should perform merit, let him do it again and again.
Let him find pleasure and exert effort in that merit.
For what reason? Because the accumulation of merit brings happiness.

If a man should perform merit, he should do it repeatedly. He should find delight and effort in that merit. For what reason? Because the increase of merit leads to the attainment of happiness.

"Performing merit with the awareness that 'This merit is beneficial to us' is the duty of those who desire merit. The performance of merit is the cause of happiness in both the present life and the life hereafter." Wishing to preach the Dhamma by connecting the sequence of the discourse, the Buddha spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the goddess, while standing in the sky at a height of forty-five yojanas, attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The story of Lājā the Goddess ends.

## 4. The Story of Anāthapiṇḍika the Treasurer

(Anāthapiṇḍika-seṭṭhi-vatthu)

While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Pāpopi passatī bhadraṃ," concerning the great treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika.

## The Financial Ruin of Anāthapiṇḍika the Treasurer

With the great Jetavana monastery in mind, the great treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika spent fifty-four koṭis of wealth on the Buddha's Dispensation. While the Buddha resided at the Jetavana monastery, he went to pay his respects three times daily. Whenever he went, he never went empty-handed, thinking, "The novices or young monks might look at my hands and wonder what I have brought."

1. When going early in the morning, he went only after having rice gruel (yāgu) taken along.
2. After breakfast, he took medicines such as ghee, fresh butter, and so on.
3. In the evening, he went to the monastery taking flowers, perfumes, scented ointments, garments, and so on.

In this manner, he constantly gave alms every single day and observed the precepts (sīla). Later on, his wealth reached a state of exhaustion and ruin. Those who lived by trade also borrowed a debt of eighteen koṭis of wealth from the hand of that great treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika. Furthermore, eighteen koṭis of gold belonging to his family lineage, which had been buried and kept on the riverbank, were all swept into the ocean when the bank collapsed due to the water.

In this way, the great treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika gradually reached the exhaustion of his possessions. Even though this happened, the treasurer continued to give alms to the community of monks (Saṅgha) as usual. However, he was no longer able to provide excellent and refined offerings. One day, when the Buddha asked,

"Householder, is alms still being given in your house?"

He replied, "Venerable Sir, alms is being given; however, that alms consists of broken rice with sour gruel (bilanga) as the second dish."
8:
## There is No Such Thing as a Meager Gift

Then the Buddha said to the treasurer, "Householder, do not think, 'I am giving a meager gift.' When the mind is noble, there is no such thing as a meager gift given to the Buddhas and others. In fact, householder, you have given alms to the eight types of Noble Persons (ariya-puggala). When I was the Brahmin Velāma, although I performed a great distribution of alms (Mahādāna) throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa, making it free from the plow, I did not find even a single person who had taken refuge in the Triple Gem. Those who are worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya) are indeed difficult to find in this way. Therefore, do not think, 'My gift is very meager.'" Having said this, He preached the Velāma Sutta to the treasurer.

## The Plan of the Gatekeeper Deity

At that time, the deity residing in the main gatehouse of the treasurer's mansion was unable to remain steady due to the majesty and power of the Buddha and His disciples whenever they entered the house. Thinking, "I will cause a rift for the treasurer so that these people cannot enter this house," she wished to speak to the treasurer but was unable to say anything during the time he was a powerful master of wealth. Now, however, she thought, "This treasurer has become poor. He will surely listen to my words." During the night, she entered the treasurer's auspicious chamber and stood in the air.

## The Treasurer Expels the Deity

Then, upon seeing the deity, he asked, "Who are you?"

"O great treasurer, I am the deity residing in your fourth gatehouse. I have come to give you advice," she replied. He then requested, "If that is so, please speak, O deity."

"Treasurer, without looking to the future, you have scattered much wealth in the Dispensation of the ascetic Gotama. Even now, having become a poor man, you still do not let go of that scattering. If this continues, in just a few days, you will not even have enough for food and clothing. What benefit is there for you in the ascetic Gotama? Refrain from excessive giving, exert yourself in trade, farming, and other works, and re-establish your wealth properly," she advised.

When he asked, "Is this the advice you, O deity, are giving me?", she replied, "Yes, treasurer."

"Go away! I am one who cannot be shaken even by a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand of those like you. You have spoken what is improper. What is the use of you living in my house? Leave my house immediately!" he said.

Yadā ca paccatī pāpaṃ, atha pāpo pāpāni passati.

"There is no benefit in you staying in my house; leave my house as quickly as possible!" thus he expelled her.

## The Expelled Deity Seeks Help from the City Guardian

When that deity heard the words of the Noble Disciple, a student of the Buddha who was a Sotāpanna, she could no longer stay and had to leave, taking her young sons and daughters with her. Even after leaving, she could not find a place to stay elsewhere. Thinking, "I will make the Great Treasurer forgive me and live in his house again," she approached the deity who guarded the city. After explaining the offense she had committed, she pleaded, "Please come, take me to the Great Treasurer, make him forgive me, and let him give me a place to stay (make him take me back)." That city-guarding deity said, "You have spoken improper words. I do not dare go to that Great Treasurer's house," and rejected the deity's request.

## Sakka's Advice

The deity then went to the Four Great Kings, and when they also rejected her, she approached Sakka, the King of Gods. After explaining the matter, she pleaded earnestly, "O King, having no place to stay, I am wandering helplessly, holding my young sons and daughters by their hands. Please help me get my dwelling place back." Then Sakka said to that deity, "I too am unable to speak to the Great Treasurer on your account. However, I will tell you one way." The deity pleaded, "Very well, my Lord, please tell me." Sakka instructed, "Go—disguise yourself as the Great Treasurer's steward or accountant. Recover the eighteen crores of wealth taken by those who live by trade, which was recorded in the ledgers from the Treasurer's hand, by using your own power. Fill the empty treasury rooms. There are also eighteen crores of wealth that entered the great ocean, and another eighteen crores of ownerless wealth in such-and-such a place. By collecting all of that and filling the Treasurer's empty treasury rooms, perform this as a penalty and ask for his forgiveness."

## Apologizing to the Great Treasurer

The deity agreed, saying, "Very well, Lord Sakka," and after doing everything as instructed, she once again illuminated the Great Treasurer's auspicious chamber with her radiance. Standing in the air, when asked, "Who is this?", she replied, "I am the very foolish and deluded deity who guarded your four...

## The Teaching
(121) Do not think lightly of evil, saying, 'It will not come to me.' Even a water jar is filled by the falling of drops of water. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.
'Mandaṃ' means an unwholesome deed performed in a small measure. 'Na āgamissati' means it will not come by way of producing its result. 'Iti'—thus. 'Pāpassa'—evil. 'Mā vamaññetha'—one should not underestimate or look down upon. Just as 'udakumbho'—a large water jar—'pūrati'—is gradually filled—'udabindunipātena'—by the falling of drops of water, so too 'bālo'—the foolish person—'pūrati'—is filled—'pāpassa'—with evil, when he makes an effort to increase even 'thokaṃ thokaṃ'—very small amounts—of unwholesome deeds.
'I have no concern for these requisites to be destroyed, nor do I have any mindfulness,' he said, speaking with the same disregard as before. Then the Blessed One said to that monk, 'Monks, it is not proper to act in this way. One should not underestimate evil, thinking it is small. Even if a vessel with an open mouth placed in an open space does not fill with a single drop when it rains, it will certainly overflow if it rains repeatedly. Likewise, a person who commits evil is said to perform a great mass of evil gradually.' Having thus connected the sequence, he spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Blessed One also prescribed a training rule for the monk who, having spread out bedding in an open space, did not put it back as it was: 'He commits such and such an offense.'
The Story of the Monk with Unrestrained Requisites is finished.
## 6. The Story of Bilālapādaka the Treasurer
(Bilālapādaka Seṭṭhi Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Mā vamaññetha puññassa,' concerning Bilālapādaka the Treasurer.
## Four Types of Givers and Four Types of Results
On one occasion, the citizens of Sāvatthī, having formed groups, offered alms to the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at their head.
Then one day, while the Buddha was giving the words of appreciation (anumodanā), he said: 'Lay followers, in this Dispensation, some people give alms only by themselves. They do not urge or encourage others. Such a person, in whatever life they are reborn, obtains the perfection of wealth but not the perfection of followers. Some people do not give alms themselves but urge and encourage others.'
12:
'...Such a person, in whatever life they are reborn, obtains the perfection of followers but not the perfection of wealth. Some people neither give alms themselves nor urge or encourage others. Such a person, in whatever life they are reborn, obtains neither the perfection of wealth nor the perfection of followers; they wander about as a poor person eating scraps. Some people both give alms themselves and urge and encourage others. Such a person, in whatever life they are reborn, obtains both the perfection of wealth and the perfection of followers.'
## One who Gives Personally and Urges Others
At that time, a wise man, having heard that Dhamma teaching, thought, 'Oh, how wonderful this is! I will now perform a wholesome deed that leads to both types of perfection.' Having stood up as the Teacher was departing, he said, 'Venerable Sir, please accept our alms tomorrow.' When asked, 'How many monks do you require?' he replied, 'Venerable Sir, I require all the monks.' The Buddha consented. That wise man then entered the village and went about proclaiming, 'O mothers and fathers, I have invited the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at their head for the sake of merit tomorrow. Whoever is able to give for however many monks, please give rice and so forth for the sake of rice gruel and other offerings for that many monks. We shall have it cooked in one place and offer the alms.'
## How the Great Treasurer came to be named Bilālapādaka
Then, a treasurer, seeing the announcer arrive at the door of his shop, became angry and said, 'This man, instead of inviting only as many monks as he himself can afford, goes about urging the whole village!' He then said, 'Bring the vessel you have brought,' and taking a small amount of rice with three fingers, he gave it. He gave green gram and black gram in the same way. From that day on, that treasurer became known by the name Bilālapādaka (Bilāla + pādaka = cat + footprint; because when he took the rice with three fingers, it left a mark like a cat's footprint). Even when giving ghee, molasses, and so forth, he put them in a small basket, tilted it to one corner, and let it drip through a hole, giving only a tiny amount. The lay announcer took the offerings given by the others and put them together, but he took the offerings given by this Treasurer Bilālapādaka separately.
## Bilālapādaka's Malicious Intent
When that Treasurer Bilālapādaka saw the actions of the wise announcer, he thought, 'Why does this man take the offerings I gave separately?' He then sent a trusted young servant to follow the announcer, saying, 'Go and find out what this man does.' That announcer, as he went, made the mental aspiration, 'May the treasurer have great fruit,' and he distributed the one or two grains of rice into all the food for the sake of the rice gruel, rice, and cakes, and he also put the drops of green gram, black gram, oil, and molasses into all the food. The trusted servant returned and told the treasurer. Hearing those words, the treasurer thought, 'If that announcer speaks of my discredit in the midst of the assembly...'
13:
## The Teaching
(122) Think not lightly of merit, saying, 'It will not come to me.'
Even a water-pot is filled by the falling of water-drops.
Likewise, the wise man, gathering it little by little, fills himself with merit.

'Mandaṃ' means merit performed in small measure. 'Na āgamissati' means it will not come by way of producing results. Thus, 'mā vamaññetha puññassa' means one should not underestimate merit. Just as a large water-pot is filled by the falling of water-drops, so too the wise man (dhīro), by making an effort to increase merit even in small amounts (thokaṃ thokaṃpi), becomes full of merit.

Thinking, "If he mentions my name, I will strike and kill that alms-organizer right then and there," the treasurer hid a knife within his garments and went the next morning to the place where the meal was being served.

## The Noble Intention of the Alms-Organizer
After serving the meal to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, that wise alms-organizer addressed the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, I have offered this gift by encouraging many people to participate. In this offering, the people who were encouraged have contributed rice and other items, some much and some little, according to their own means. May all of them receive great and noble fruits of this merit."

## The Apology of Bilālapādaka
Upon hearing these words, the treasurer Bilālapādaka thought: "I came here with the intention, 'If he mentions my name, saying this person gave rice and such by taking it with only three fingers, I will kill him.' However, this alms-organizer, acting with universal inclusion, says, 'May all those who gave by measuring with a peck-measure and those who gave by taking with three fingers receive great and noble fruits.' If I do not ask for forgiveness from such a virtuous person, a divine punishment will surely fall upon my head." Feeling distressed, the treasurer prostrated at the feet of the alms-organizer and said, "Sir, please forgive me." When the lay devotee (the organizer) asked, "What is the meaning of this?", the treasurer related the whole story.

## Merit is Never Small
Seeing this incident, the Buddha asked the alms-organizer who had performed the great and small tasks of the offering, "What is this about?"

The alms-organizer then related the entire sequence of events starting from the previous day. Then the Buddha asked the treasurer, "Lay disciple, is it true as he says?" When the treasurer replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, it is true," the Buddha said, "Lay disciple, one should not think of merit as 'only a little.' Wise people, while performing merit, fill themselves with merit gradually, just as an open vessel is filled with water." Having thus connected the sequence, the Buddha spoke this verse to teach the Dhamma:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, the treasurer Bilālapādaka attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The story of the treasurer Bilālapādaka ends.
14:
## 7. The Story of Mahādhana the Merchant
(Mahādhana-vāṇija-vatthu)

The Buddha told this Dhamma teaching starting with "Vāṇijova" while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, concerning a merchant named Mahādhana.

## Inviting the Saṅgha on a Trading Journey
Five hundred robbers were seeking an opportunity at the house of that merchant but found none. On another occasion, the merchant filled five hundred carts with goods and sent word to the monks: "Venerable sirs, I am going to such-and-such a place for trade. Those noble ones who wish to go to that place, please set forth; you will not suffer for lack of alms-food on the journey." Hearing this, five hundred monks set out on the journey together with the merchant. The robbers, hearing that the merchant had departed, went and waited in the forest. The merchant also traveled and, staying at a village at the entrance of the forest, spent two or three days preparing the bullock carts and other equipment. He continuously offered alms-food to those monks. As the merchant stayed there for a long time, the robbers sent one man, saying, "Go, find out the day of his departure and return."

## Robbers Spying on the Merchant's Route
When that robber reached the village, he asked a friend, "When will the merchant depart?" The friend replied, "He will depart after two or three days have passed," and asked in return, "For what purpose do you ask?" Then the robber told his friend, "We are five hundred robbers waiting in the forest for the sake of that merchant." The village friend said, "If that is so, go quickly; he will be departing soon."

After sending him away, the friend thought, "Should I stop the robbers, or should I stop the merchant? What benefit do I have from the robbers? Five hundred monks are living depending on the merchant; I will give a sign to the merchant." With this thought, the village friend went to the merchant and asked, "On which day will you depart?" When the merchant replied, "We will depart on the third day," the friend warned him, "Please follow my words; five hundred robbers are waiting in the forest for your arrival. Do not go in haste."
15:
## The Teaching

(123) Just as a merchant with few companions and great wealth avoids a dangerous path, and as one who loves life avoids poison, so should one avoid evil deeds.

Appasattho: one who has few merchant companions. Mahaddhano: one who has great wealth. Vāṇijo: the merchant. Bhayaṃ: dangerous. Maggaṃ: the path. Parivajjeti iva: just as he avoids. Jīvitukāmo: one who loves life. Visaṃ: deadly poison. Parivajjeti iva: just as he avoids. Paṇḍito bhikkhu: the wise monk. Pāpāni: even slight evil deeds. Parivajjaye: should avoid.

## The Villager's Information on the Robbers' Plot

When asked, "How do you know this?" the villager replied, "I have a friend among those five hundred robbers; I know this from the words spoken by that robber friend." The merchant then said, "If that is the case, what benefit is there for me to go to this place? I shall only return home."

After some time had passed, the man sent by the robbers came again and questioned his friend in the village. Upon hearing the news, he said, "He will surely return home," and went back to tell the robbers. Hearing this, the robbers left that forest and stayed on another path. After more time passed, those five hundred robbers again sent someone to the friend. When the friend learned that the robbers were waiting on that path, he informed the merchant once more. The merchant thought, "I have no lack of anything in this village; since there is no lack, I will not go to that place or this place. I will stay right here."

Then the merchant went to the monks and said, "Venerable sirs, the robbers are waiting on the path with the intent to plunder. Hearing that I would return, they are now waiting on another path. I will not go to that place or this place yet, but will stay here for a while. If you, venerable sirs, wish to stay here, please do so; if you wish to go, please do as you please."

## The Buddha's Admonition to the Monks Using the Merchant as a Simile

The monks replied, "In that case, we shall return," and after taking leave of the merchant, they returned to Sāvatthī, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat down. When the Buddha asked, "Monks, did you not go with the merchant Mahādhana?" they replied, "Venerable Sir, it is true we did not go. Robbers were obstructing both paths to plunder the merchant Mahādhana. Because the merchant stayed there, we have returned."

The Buddha said, "Monks, the merchant Mahādhana avoided the path because of the presence of robbers. Just as a man who loves life avoids deadly poison, a monk should avoid evil, knowing that 'the three realms of existence are like a path infested by robbers.'" Having thus connected the sequence, he spoke this verse in teaching the Dhamma:

## The Monks Attain Arahantship

At the end of the teaching, those monks attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude who had gathered.

The story of the merchant Mahādhana ends.

## 8. The Story of Kukkuṭamitta the Hunter

(Kukkuṭamittanesāda Vatthu)

While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Pāṇimhi ce," concerning a hunter named Kukkuṭamitta.
16:
## The Beginning of the Life of the Merchant's Daughter and the Hunter

In the city of Rājagaha, there was a merchant's daughter who, upon reaching marriageable age, was provided with a young maidservant for protection and was cared for in a beautiful chamber atop a seven-storied palace. One day, in the evening, while looking out at the main street through a window, she saw a hunter named Kukkuṭamitta. He made his living by killing deer, carrying five hundred snares and five hundred stakes. Having killed five hundred deer, he had filled a large cart with their meat and was entering the city to sell it, sitting at the front of the cart.

Seeing him, she fell in love with the hunter. She gave a letter to her maidservant and sent her, saying, "Go, give this letter to that hunter, find out the time he will return, and then come back."

The maid went, gave the letter to the hunter, and asked him. When he said, "Today I will sell the meat and return early tomorrow morning through such-and-such a gate," the maid returned and told the merchant's daughter what the hunter had said.

## The Merchant's Daughter Follows in Disguise

The merchant's daughter prepared her clothes and ornaments, and early the next morning, she put on a soiled garment, carried a water pot on her head, and left as if going to the watering place with her maids. She went to that spot and waited, watching for the hunter's arrival. The hunter also came out early, driving his cart. The merchant's daughter followed behind him.

## Fortune Arriving Voluntarily Should Not Be Rejected

When the hunter saw her, he asked, "Sister, whose daughter are you?" and said, "I do not know you as the daughter of such-and-such a person. Do not follow me."

She replied, "Lord, you did not call me. I have come of my own accord. Please remain silent and just drive your cart."

Even though the hunter repeatedly forbade her, she said to him, "Noble son, when what is called 'Siri' (fortune/auspiciousness) comes to one's presence, it is not proper to reject it."

## The Birth of Seven Sons

When the hunter became free of doubt regarding her and learned the reason for her coming, he took her onto the cart and departed. When her mother and father searched here and there and could not find her, they thought, "She must be dead," and performed the funeral rites (matakabhatta) for the deceased.

The merchant's daughter, living together with the hunter, gave birth to seven sons in succession. When those sons reached marriageable age, she bound them in marriage.

One day, at dawn, as the Buddha was surveying the world, he saw Kukkuṭamitta along with his sons and daughters-in-law enter into his net of knowledge. While considering, "What is this?" he saw that all fifteen of them possessed the supporting conditions for the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). Early in the morning, taking his bowl and robes, he went to the place where the hunter set his traps.
17:
## The Buddha's Footprint Near the Snare

Then one day, at dawn, when the Buddha surveyed the world, he saw Kukkutamitta along with his seven sons entering the net of his knowledge. Considering "What is the reason for this?", he saw their potential (upanissaya) for attaining the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), all fifteen of them. Therefore, early in the morning, taking his bowl and robes, he went to the place where the hunter had set his snares. On that day, not even a single deer was caught in the snare. The Buddha displayed his golden footprint near the hunter's snare and sat down in the shade under a bush ahead. Kukkutamitta, taking his bow early in the morning, went to the place of the snares. Looking at the snares from the beginning, he did not see even one deer caught, but he saw the golden footprint of the Buddha.

## The Intent to Shoot the Buddha with an Arrow

Then the hunter thought, "Who has gone about releasing the deer I have trapped?" The hunter, harboring malice toward the owner of the footprint, went along and saw the Buddha sitting under the bush. Thinking, "This person must have released my deer; I will kill him," he drew his bow. The Buddha allowed him to draw the bow but did not allow him to release it. The hunter, unable to release the arrow or lower it, stood there as if his ribs were breaking, with saliva trickling from his mouth, looking exhausted. Then the hunter's sons went home and said, "Our father is taking a long time; what could be the reason?" Sent by their mother saying, "Go, dear sons, to your father," the seven sons each took their bows and went. Seeing their father standing there with his ribs almost breaking, holding his bow with saliva trickling down, they thought, "This person must be our father's enemy." The seven sons also drew their bows, and by the Buddha's psychic power, they stood exactly as their father was standing.

## The Hunter and His Family Attaining Stream-entry

Then the mother of the sons thought, "My sons are taking a long time; what is the reason?" She went along with her seven daughters-in-law and saw those eight people standing in that manner. Looking to see at whom they were standing with bows drawn to shoot, she saw the Buddha. Raising her arms, she cried out loudly, "Do not kill my father! Do not kill my father!" When Kukkutamitta the hunter heard that voice, he thought, "I am truly ruined! This is my father-in-law (spiritual father), it seems. Oh, what a heavy deed I have committed!" His sons also thought, "This is our grandfather, it seems. Oh, what a heavy deed we have committed!" Kukkutamitta developed a mind of loving-kindness, thinking, "This is my father-in-law." His sons also developed a mind of loving-kindness, thinking, "This is our grandfather." Then their mother, the treasurer's daughter, said, "Quickly discard your bows and ask my father for forgiveness." The Buddha, knowing their minds had become supple, allowed them to lower their bows. They all paid homage to the Buddha, asked for forgiveness saying, "Venerable Sir, please forgive us," and sat in a suitable place. Then the Buddha gave them a graduated discourse. At the end of the discourse, Kukkutamitta the hunter, together with his seven sons and seven daughters-in-law, himself being the fifteenth, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).
18:
## The Teaching

(124) If there is no wound on the palm, one may carry poison with the hand. Poison does not follow a hand without a wound. There is no evil for one who does not do [evil] (due to lack of intention).

## Attaining Stream-entry While Still at Her Parents' House

The Buddha, having wandered for alms, returned to the monastery after the meal. Then the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, where did you go?" "Ānanda, I went to the hunter Kukkutamitta," he replied. "Venerable Sir, have you made him one who does not commit the act of taking life?" he asked. "Yes, Ānanda, he, being the fifteenth, has established himself in unshakable faith, and having no doubt in the Three Jewels, has become one who does not commit the act of taking life." Then the monks asked, "Venerable Sir, does that hunter not have a wife?" "Yes, monks, he does. That wife attained the Fruit of Stream-entry while she was still a young girl in her parents' house." Then the monks started a discussion: "It is said that Kukkutamitta's wife attained the Fruit of Stream-entry while still a young girl, then went to the hunter's house and had seven sons. For all this time, when told by her husband, 'Bring the bow, bring the arrows, bring the spear, bring the javelin, bring the net,' she gave them."

## Unwholesome Result Only When There Is Intention to Kill

"The hunter, taking those things given by her, went and committed the taking of life. How is it? Do Stream-enters also commit the taking of life?" Thus they started the conversation. The Buddha came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion, Venerable Sir," he said, "Monks, those who are Stream-enters do not commit the taking of life. That woman did so thinking, 'I am following my husband's words.' She had no such thought as, 'Taking these, let this hunter go and commit the taking of life.' If there is no wound on the palm of the hand, the poison cannot burn the person who holds it. In the same way, for one who does not wish to do evil because of the absence of unwholesome intention (akusala-cetanā), even if they bring out and give bows and so on, it is not called evil." Having thus connected the sequence, he spoke this verse to preach the Dhamma.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so on.

## The Past Merits of the Hunter's Family

At another time, the monks started a discussion: "What was the supporting condition (upanissaya) for Kukkutamitta the hunter, along with his sons and daughters-in-law, to attain the Path of Stream-entry? For what reason were they born in a hunter's family?" The Buddha came and asked, "For what [discussion] are you [gathered]..."
19:
“For what reason was he born into a hunter’s family?” they discussed. The Buddha approached and asked, “Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?” When they replied, “We are discussing such and such a matter, Venerable Sir,” He said, “Monks, in the past, while the relic stupa of Kassapa the Ten-Powered One was being constructed, people spoke thus: ‘What shall be the mortar for this stupa? What shall be the water?’ Then this thought occurred to them: ‘Realgar and orpiment shall be the mortar, and sesame oil shall be the water.’ Having ground the realgar and orpiment, they mixed them with sesame oil, joined them with bricks, and decorated them with gold, building the interior. On the exterior surface, however, there were only solid gold bricks. Each brick was worth one hundred thousand.

When the stupa was completed up to the point of enshrining the relics, they desired a great amount of wealth and thought, ‘Whom shall we appoint as the leader?’ Then a village treasurer thought, ‘I shall be the leader,’ and contributed ten million (one koṭi) at the enshrinement of the relics. Seeing this, the townspeople complained, ‘This city treasurer only knows how to accumulate wealth; he is unable to be the leader for such a stupa. But the village treasurer, by contributing ten million, has become the leader.’ Hearing their words, the city treasurer gave twenty million, thinking, ‘I shall be the leader.’ The village treasurer gave thirty million, thinking, ‘I alone shall be the leader.’ Increasing the amount in this way, the city treasurer eventually gave eighty million.

The village treasurer had only ninety million in his house, while the city treasurer had four hundred million. Therefore, the village treasurer thought, ‘If I say I will give ninety million, he will say he will give a hundred million, and then my lack of wealth will become apparent.’ Thus, the village treasurer said: ‘I will give this much wealth, and together with my wife and children, I shall become a servant of the stupa.’ He then took his seven sons, seven daughters-in-law, and his wife, and together with himself, dedicated them to the stupa.

The townspeople said, ‘Wealth can indeed be produced, but this village treasurer has dedicated himself along with his wife and children. Let this man alone be the leader,’ and they made him the leader. Thus, all sixteen of them became servants of the stupa. The townspeople, however, made them free men (not servants). Even so, they continued to attend to and maintain the stupa for the rest of their lives. When they passed away from that existence, they were reborn in the deva world. Having lived in the deva world for the interval between two Buddhas, when our Buddha appeared in the world, the wife passed away from that deva world and was reborn as the daughter of a treasurer in the city of Rājagaha. Even as a young maiden, she attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The rebirth of one who has not yet seen the Four Noble Truths is indeed burdensome. Therefore, that maiden’s husband, wandering through the rounds of rebirth, was born into a hunter’s family. As soon as she saw that hunter, the daughter of the treasurer was overwhelmed by ancient affection. Therefore, this verse was spoken:”
20:
“Through previous association,
Or by present benefit;
Thus is that love born,
As a lotus is in water.”

Whether it be the Uppala lotus or other types of lotuses like the Paduma, when they are born in the water, they are born because of two causes: water and silt. In the same way, when that love is born, it arises due to these two causes: through having lived together happily in a past life, or through performing many beneficial services for one's welfare in the present life. (This verse from the Sāketa Jātaka of the Duka Nipāta was also mentioned in the story of Sāmāvatī in the Appamāda Vagga of the Dhammapada Commentary. If the stem has no thorns, it is called Uppala; if it has thorns, it is called Paduma.)

Due to that ancient affection, the treasurer’s daughter went to the hunter’s house. Her sons, having passed away from the deva world, took conception in the womb of that very treasurer’s daughter. Her daughters-in-law were also born in various places, and upon reaching maturity, they also came to that very house. Thus, all of them, because they had maintained the stupa of Kassapa Buddha at that time, attained the Fruit of Stream-entry through the power of that merit.

The story of Kukkuṭamitta the Hunter is finished.

## 9. The Story of Koka the Dog-Hunter
(Koka-sunakha-luddaka Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Yo appaduṭṭhassa,” concerning a dog-hunter named Koka.

## The One Who Set Dogs on a Monk
One day in the morning, that hunter, carrying his bow and surrounded by a pack of dogs, was going to the forest. When he saw a monk entering for alms on the way, he became angry and thought, “I have seen an ill-omen (kāḷakaṇṇi); today I will not get anything,” and he went away. The Elder, having wandered for alms in the village and finished his meal, was returning to the monastery. The hunter, having wandered in the forest and obtained nothing, was returning when he saw the Elder again. He thought, “Today, because I saw this ill-omen, I got nothing when I went to the forest. Now he has appeared before me again. I will have the dogs bite him.” He gave a signal and released the dogs. The Elder pleaded, “Lay follower, do not do this.” The hunter replied, “Today, because you appeared before me, I obtained nothing. Now you have come before me again; I will certainly have them bite you,” and he released the dogs.
21:
The Elder quickly climbed a tree and stayed at a height of one fathom. The dogs surrounded the tree and stayed there. The hunter followed and said, "Even if you climb a tree, there is no escape from death for you," and he stabbed the monk's soles with a sharp arrow-tip. The Elder pleaded with the hunter, "Do not do this." The hunter, disregarding his plea, stabbed him repeatedly.

## The Hunter's Dogs Eating the Hunter's Flesh
When the hunter stabbed one sole, the Elder lifted that foot and let the second foot hang down; when that foot was stabbed, he lifted it as well. In this way, the hunter, disregarding the monk's plea, stabbed both soles. The Elder's whole body felt as if it were being consumed by fire. Being overcome by painful feelings, he was unable to maintain mindfulness and did not even notice his robe slipping off. The falling robe dropped down, completely enveloping the hunter named Koka from his head downwards. The dogs, thinking "The Elder has fallen," entered inside the robe, dragged out their own master, the hunter, and ate him until only the bones remained. The dogs came out from the robe and stood outside. Then the Elder broke off a dry twig and threw it at the dogs. When the dogs saw the Elder, they realized, "We have bitten and eaten our own master," and fled into the forest. The Elder felt remorse, thinking, "This hunter died because he entered my robe; is my virtue still untainted?" He descended from the tree, went to the Buddha, and reported the whole matter from the beginning. "Venerable Sir, because of my robe, that lay devotee has perished. Do I still possess the status of a monk?" he asked.

## Destruction by Harming the Innocent
Hearing the monk's words, the Buddha said, "Monk, your virtue is untainted; you still possess the status of a monk. That hunter met his destruction because he offended one who was harmless. Not only now, but in the past too, he met destruction by offending the harmless." Having said this, the Buddha brought forth the past to illustrate the matter.

## One Who Was Wicked in a Past Life
In the past, a physician wandered through a village looking for work. Finding none and being hungry, he saw children playing at the village gate. He thought, "If I have these children bitten by a snake and then treat them, I will get food."
22:
## The Teaching
(125) Whoever harms a harmless man, one who is pure and faultless, the evil recoils upon that fool, like fine dust thrown against the wind.

*Yo*: Whoever (the foolish person). *Appaduṭṭhassa*: One who does not harm anyone. *Suddhassa*: Pure and free from fault. *Anangaṇassa*: Free from the defilements of passion. *Posassa*: Worthy of being nurtured. *Narassa*: A being. *Dussati*: Harms by striking, etc. *Tam eva bālaṃ*: To that very fool. *Pāpaṃ*: That evil deed of harming. *Paṭivātaṃ*: Against the wind. *Khitto*: Thrown. *Sukhumo rajo iva*: Like fine dust. *Pacceti*: Recoils as an evil result.

He showed them a snake sleeping with its head out of a tree hollow and said, "O boys, this bird is a young starling; catch it." Then one boy grabbed the snake firmly by the neck. Realizing it was a snake, he cried out and threw it onto the head of the physician standing nearby. The snake coiled around the physician's shoulder and bit him severely, causing his death right there. "In this way, this hunter Koka met destruction in the past as well by harming the harmless." The Buddha, connecting the past and present, spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, that monk was established in the Fruit of Arahantship. The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of Koka the Hunter and the Dogs ends.

## 10. The Story of Tissa the Elder Who Frequented the Jeweler's House
(Maṇikārakulūpaka-tissatthera-vatthu)
The Buddha, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, gave this teaching starting with "Gabbham eke," concerning Tissa the Elder, the teacher of a jeweler.

## The Ruby Disappears and the Elder is Accused
That Elder Tissa had taken his meals at the house of a jeweler for twelve years. The husband and wife treated him like their own parents and looked after him. One day, the jeweler was sitting in front of the Elder, cutting meat. At that moment, King Pasenadi of Kosala sent a ruby, saying, "Clean and pierce this gem and send it back."
23:
The jeweler, with blood-stained hands, took the gem and placed it on top of a basket, then went inside to wash his hands. In that house, there was a pet crane. Smelling the blood and thinking it was meat, the crane swallowed the gem right before the Elder's eyes. When the jeweler returned and did not see the gem, he asked his wife and sons in order, "Who took the gem?" When they replied, "We did not take it," he thought, "The Elder must have taken it," and consulted with his wife.

## Bound with Rope and Beaten with a Stick
"My lord, do not say such a thing. In all this time, I have never seen any fault in the Elder. He would not take the gem," she said. The jeweler then asked the Elder, "Venerable Sir, did you take the gem that was placed here?" "Lay follower, I did not take it," he replied. "Venerable Sir, there is no one else here; only you could have taken it. Give me the gem," he accused and demanded. When the Elder did not admit to it, the jeweler said to his wife again, "The Elder took the gem; I will question him by torturing him." "My lord, do not ruin us. It would be better for us to become slaves. It is not right to speak such things to an Elder like this," she said. The jeweler replied, "Even if all of us become slaves, we would not equal the price of the gem." He then took a rope, bound the Elder's head, and beat him with a stick.

## Recovering the Gem from the Crane's Belly
Blood flowed from the Elder's head, ears, and nose. His eyes reached a state as if they were about to pop out. The Elder, experiencing such agonizing pain, fell to the ground. The crane, drawn by the smell of blood, came and drank it. At that moment, the jeweler, in a fit of rage toward the Elder, said, "You foolish bird, what are you doing?" and kicked it away. With that single blow, the crane died and lay on its back. Seeing the crane lying there, the Elder said, "Lay follower, first loosen the rope bound around my head and see whether this crane is dead or not." The jeweler replied, "You shall die just like this crane." "Lay follower, this crane swallowed the gem. Therefore, if this crane had not died, I would not have told you about the gem even if I were dying," the Elder said. When the jeweler cut open the belly of the dead crane, he saw the gem. Then, with a terrified heart, he prostrated at the Elder's feet and said, "Venerable Sir, please forgive me. I did this out of ignorance." "Lay follower, there is no fault in you, nor in me. This is only the fault of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). I forgive you," the Elder said. "Venerable Sir, if you forgive me,

"Food is cooked for the sage, a little in each house. I will wander for alms; I have the strength in my legs."

*Munino*: for the sake of the monk. *Thokaṃ thokaṃ*: a little, a little. *Bhattaṃ*: alms-food. *Kule kule*: in every house. *Paccati*: is ready and cooked. *Piṇḍikāya*: for the sake of alms. *Carissāmi*: I shall wander. *Mamaṃ*: for me. *Jaṅghabalaṃ*: the strength of the legs. *Atthi*: there is.

## The Teaching
(126) Some are born in a womb; evil-doers go to hell. The righteous go to heaven; those without taints attain Parinibbāna.
