"please sit and receive alms in my house as before," he pleaded.

## The Parinibbāna of Elder Tissa
"Lay follower, from today on, I shall no longer enter inside the roof of another's house," he said. "This fault occurs only to one who enters a house. From this day forth, while my legs can still carry me, I will receive alms only by standing at the house door." Having said this and undertaking the piṇḍapāta dhutaṅga, he recited this verse.

After saying these words, the Elder passed away into Parinibbāna not long after due to that injury. The crane took rebirth in the womb of the jeweler's wife. The jeweler, after passing away, was reborn in hell. The jeweler's wife, because of her tender and clear heart toward the Elder, passed away and was reborn in heaven. The monks asked the Teacher about their future destination. The Teacher said, "Monks, in this world, some are born in a mother's womb. Some, being evil-doers, are born in hell. Some, having performed meritorious deeds, are born in heaven. Those who are free from taints (anāsava), the Arahants, attain Parinibbāna." Connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse to teach the Dhamma.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The story of Elder Tissa, the associate of the jeweler's family, ends.

## 11. Tayojana Vatthu
(The Story of Three People)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Na antalikkhe" concerning three people.

## The Crow that Died with a Ring of Fire around its Neck
While the All-Knowing Buddha was residing at Jetavana Monastery, many monks, coming to see the Buddha, entered a village for alms. The villagers took their bowls, seated them in the alms-hall, offered gruel and snacks, and while waiting for the time for the main meal, sat listening to the Dhamma.
25:
At that moment, while a certain woman was cooking curry after having cooked rice, a flame rose from her pot and caught the roof. From that rising flame, a bundle of grass in the shape of a ring rose up and flew into the sky while burning. At that moment, a crow flying through the sky put its neck into that burning grass ring, and being entangled by the grass-vines, it was burnt and fell in the middle of the village. When the monks saw that crow, they thought, "Oh, what a heavy deed! Friends, look at the calamity the crow has met. Who else but the Buddha would know the deed done by this crow? Let us ask the Blessed One about the past evil kamma of this crow," and they departed.

## The One Thrown into the Ocean with a Sand-pot Tied to the Neck

Other monks were also traveling by boat to see the Buddha when the boat became motionless in the middle of the ocean. They thought, "There must be an unlucky person (kāḷakaṇṇī) among those on this boat," and they distributed lots. The boat captain's wife, who was in her first stage of life, was beautiful and pleasant to look at. The lot fell to the captain's wife. Saying, "Distribute the lots again," they did so up to three times. For all three times, it fell only to that woman. The people looked at the captain's face, asking, "Master, what shall we do?" The captain said, "It is not right for many people to perish for the sake of this one woman. Throw her into the water." When they seized her to throw her into the water, she cried out loudly, being terrified by the fear of death. Hearing her cries, the captain said, "What is the use of these ornaments of hers being destroyed? Take off all her ornaments, clothe her in a piece of rag, and discard her. As for me, I cannot bear to see this woman floating on the surface of the water. Therefore, so that I may not see her, tie a pot of sand to her neck and throw her into the ocean." The people did as the captain said. In the very place where she fell, fish and turtles tore her apart and ate her. When the monks learned of that event, they thought, "Except for the Blessed One, who else will know the deed done by this woman? Let us ask the Blessed One about her kamma," and upon reaching their destination, they disembarked from the boat and departed.

## Seven Monks Trapped in a Cave

Furthermore, seven other monks, while traveling to see the Buddha, entered a monastery in the evening and asked for a place to stay. In a certain cave, there were seven couches. Having obtained that very place and lying down there, during the night, a large rock the size of a peaked house rolled down and blocked the entrance of the cave. The resident monks thought, "We have given this cave as a dwelling to the visiting monks. This large rock has now stood blocking the cave entrance. Let us remove it." They gathered people from the seven surrounding villages and made an effort, but they were unable to move it from its place. The monks inside the cave also made an effort. Although they tried in this way, they were unable to move the large rock for seven whole days. Those visiting monks reached a state of hunger and thirst for seven days and experienced great suffering. On the seventh day, the large rock rolled away on its own.
26:
The monks also came out and, thinking, "Who else but the Omniscient Buddha can know our misfortune? Let us ask the Buddha," they departed. Those seven monks met with the previous monks on the way, and all together they approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. Since the Blessed One had exchanged friendly greetings with them, they asked in order about the causes they themselves had seen and experienced. The Blessed One also answered them in order as they asked:

## The Past Evil Deed of the Crow

Monks, first of all, that crow experienced only the result of the deed he himself had done. In the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a farmer, while taming his ox, was unable to tame it. That ox of his would go a little way and then lie down. Even when beaten and made to get up, it would go only a little way and lie down again as before. That farmer, being unable to tame it despite his efforts, was overcome by intense anger and saying, "From now on, you shall sleep comfortably," he wrapped the ox's neck with straw, making it like a bundle of straw, and set it on fire. The ox burned right there and died.

"Monks, at that time, that farmer committed that evil deed. As a result of that unwholesome kamma, after suffering in hell for a long time, by the power of the remaining result, he was reborn in the species of crows seven times and died in this very way, being burned in the sky. Thus, he experienced the result of the deed he himself had done."

## The Past of the Ship-Captain's Wife

Monks, that woman also experienced only the result of the deed she herself had done. In the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, she was the wife of a householder and performed all the household duties such as fetching water, pounding and husking rice, and cooking with her own hands. A dog of hers used to sit watching that woman as she performed all the duties in the house. When she carried food to the field or went to the forest for the sake of wood or leaves, it went along with her. Seeing them going together, young men mocked her, saying, "Friends, the dog-hunter has gone out; today we shall eat with meat." Because of their mockery, she became embarrassed and tried to drive the dog away by hitting it with stones, sticks, and so on. The dog, however, turned back and followed her again.

(That dog, it is said, had been her husband in his third previous existence. Therefore, he could not break the affection. In the beginningless Saṃsāra, there is indeed no one who has not been a wife or a husband before. Even so, an excessive affection arises towards relatives in a recent existence. Therefore, that dog could not give up the affection he had for that woman.)

That woman, being very angry with the dog, while carrying rice gruel to the field for her husband, went with a rope hidden in her garment. The dog also followed along with her. After giving the gruel to her husband, she took an empty pot and went to a place where there was water. She filled the pot with sand and, while the dog stood nearby watching, she made a sound. The dog, thinking, "After a long time, I have received sweet words today," approached her wagging its tail. That woman grabbed the dog firmly by the neck, tied the pot to one end of the rope and tied the other end of the rope to the dog's neck, and rolled the pot towards the water. The dog, following the pot, fell into the water and died right there. As a result of that unwholesome kamma, after suffering in hell for a long time, by the power of the remaining result, in a hundred existences, she died by being thrown into the water with a sand-pot tied to her neck. Thus, she experienced the result of the kamma she herself had done.
27:
## The Past of the Seven Monks Trapped in the Cave

Monks, you seven also experienced only the result of the deed you yourselves had done. In the past, seven cowherd boys living in Vārāṇasī, while wandering and tending cows in a certain forest area for seven-day shifts, one day, while returning after counting the cows, saw a large monitor lizard and chased it. The monitor lizard fled and entered a termite mound. There were seven holes in that termite mound. The boys said, "We cannot catch it today; let's come and catch it tomorrow." Each boy took a handful of broken branches, and all seven of them blocked the seven holes and went away.

The next morning, those cowherds did not remember that monitor lizard. After tending the cows in another place, on the seventh day, while going with the cows, they saw that termite mound and regained their memory. Thinking, "What has happened to that monitor lizard?" they opened the holes they themselves had blocked. The monitor lizard, having no hope for its life, came out trembling, being only skin and bones.

When the cowherds saw that monitor lizard, they felt compassion and said, "Do not kill this monitor lizard; it has been without food for seven days." They stroked its back and released it, saying, "Go in peace." Because they did not kill the monitor lizard, they did not suffer in hell. However, those seven boys, being together, were without food for seven days in fourteen existences. "Monks, at that time, you were those seven cowherds and did that unwholesome deed. Thus, you have experienced the result of the deed you yourselves have done." In this way, the Blessed One answered the questions asked by those monks.
28:
## The Verse
(127) Not in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a mountain cave;
There is no place on earth where one, remaining there, might escape from an evil deed.

Antalikkhe: in the sky. To one who flies away: there is no escape from the consequences of evil. Samuddamajjhe: in the midst of the ocean. Or, to one who goes into the midst of the ocean: there is no escape from the consequences of evil. Pabbatanāṃ vivaraṃ pavissa: to one who enters and dwells in a mountain cave: there is no escape from the consequences of evil. Yattha jagatippadese: in whatever part of the earth, such as the eastern direction. Ṭhito: one who remains. Pāpakammā: from the consequences of evil deeds. Mucceyya: might be liberated. So jagatippadeso: that part of the earth, such as the eastern direction. Na vijjati: does not exist.

At that time, a certain monk said to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, how is it? For one who has committed an evil deed, is there no such thing as escape, whether he flies into the sky, goes into the ocean, or enters a mountain cave?" The Buddha replied, "Monks, it is just as this monk says. Even in the sky and so forth, there is not even a single spot where one, remaining there, could be liberated from the consequences of an evil deed." Having thus connected the sequence of the discourse, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, those monks attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude of people who had gathered.
The Story of the Three Groups (Tayojana-vatthu) ends.

## 12. The Story of Suppabuddha the Sakyan
(Suppabuddha-sakya-vatthu)
While residing at Nigrodhārāma Monastery, the Blessed One spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Na antalikkhe," concerning the Sakyan King named Suppabuddha, the ruler of Devadaha City.

## Suppabuddha's Offense against the Buddha
That Sakyan King Suppabuddha held a grudge against the Blessed One for two reasons: "This Prince Siddhattha abandoned my daughter Yasodharā-Bimbā to go forth into the forest," and "He ordained my son Devadatta and stands as my son's enemy." One day, thinking, "I will not allow this All-Knowing Buddha to go and eat at the place where he is invited," he blocked the path and sat in the middle of the road drinking liquor. When the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, arrived at that place, they informed King Suppabuddha, "The Blessed One has arrived."

Upon hearing this, King Suppabuddha said, "Go ahead and tell that Gotama: This Gotama is not older than I am. Therefore, I cannot give way to that Gotama." Even though he was asked repeatedly, he remained there just as before. Since the Blessed One did not receive the path from his uncle, he had to turn back from that place.

(When King Sīhahanu, the son of King Jayasena, was wedded to Princess Kañcanā of Devadaha, they had five sons and two daughters: Suddhodana, Dhotodana, Sakkodana, Sukkodana, Amitodana, and the sisters Amitā and Pālitā—seven in total. When Princess Yasodharā, daughter of King Jayasena, was wedded to Prince Añjana of Devadaha, they had two daughters and two sons: Mahāmāyā, Pajāpati Gotamī, and the brothers Daṇḍapāṇi and Suppabuddha—four in total. From Suppabuddha and Amitā, two siblings were born: Bhaddakañcanā, also known as Yasodharā, and Devadatta.)

## The Prediction of Being Swallowed by the Earth
Suppabuddha then sent a spy, saying, "Go, listen to the words of that Gotama and then return." When the Blessed One returned, he smiled. Venerable Ānanda, seeing this, asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the cause for manifesting a smile?" The Blessed One asked, "Ānanda, did you see Suppabuddha?" "Venerable Sir, I saw him," he replied. "Suppabuddha has committed a grave deed by not giving way to a Buddha like me. On the seventh day from today, at the foot of the stairs below his palace, he will be swallowed by the earth," the Buddha declared. The spy, having heard these words, went to King Suppabuddha. When asked, "What did my nephew Gotama say?" he reported the words exactly as he had heard them.
29:
They reported it. He said, “Tell him to go ahead; he is not older than I, and I will not give way to him.” Even though he was told repeatedly, he spoke in the same way and remained sitting. The Teacher, not receiving a path from his maternal uncle, turned back from there. He (Suppabuddha) also sent a spy, saying, “Go, listen to what he says and come back.” As the Teacher was returning, he smiled. When asked by the Elder Ānanda, “Venerable Sir, what is the cause for the manifestation of a smile?” he said, “Ānanda, do you see Suppabuddha?” “I see him, Venerable Sir.” “He has committed a grave deed by not giving way to a Buddha like me; on the seventh day from now, he will enter the earth at the foot of the stairs on the ground floor of his palace.” The spy, having heard those words, went to Suppabuddha and, when asked, “What did my nephew say as he turned back?” reported exactly what he had heard. Hearing those words, he said, “Now, there is no fault in my nephew's speech; certainly, what he says happens just so. Even so, I will now refute him for speaking a falsehood. For he did not say indefinitely that I would enter the earth on the seventh day, but said specifically that I would enter the earth at the foot of the stairs on the ground floor of the palace. From now on, I will not go to that place; and if I do not enter the earth at that place, I shall refute that Gautama Buddha for his falsehood.” Then, he had all his belongings moved to the top of his seven-storied palace, had the stairs removed, the doors closed, and placed two wrestlers at each door, saying, “If I should wish to descend out of forgetfulness, restrain me,” and he stayed in the auspicious chamber on the seventh floor of the palace. When the All-Knowing Buddha heard of this matter, he said, “Bhikkhus, whether King Suppabuddha stays only on the palace floor, or flies into the sky and sits in the air, or enters the ocean by boat, or enters a mountain cave, there is no such thing as duality in the words spoken by the Buddhas; he will enter the earth exactly at the place I have mentioned.” Connecting the sequence and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(128) Na antalikkhe na samuddamajjhe, na pabbatānaṃ vivaraṃ pavissa.
Na vijjati so jagatippadeso, yatthaṭṭhitaṃ nappasaheyya maccu.

Whether sitting in the sky (antalikkhe), one is not free from death. Whether crossing into the midst of the ocean (samuddamajjhe), one is not free from death. Whether entering and staying in a mountain cave (pabbatānaṃ vivaraṃ), one is not free from death. There is no such part of the earth (jagatippadeso) where, staying there, death (maccu) cannot overcome or oppress one.

(How did the Elder Ānanda, who followed behind, know the Buddha smiled? He sensed it by seeing the white rays of light emanating from the front of the Buddha. These white rays emanated from his white teeth. That the rays could pass through the closely closed lips was because the lips were slightly relaxed. He sensed it by inferring that the relaxation of the lips was due to a slight smile. He [Suppabuddha] was born of Amitodana.)

## Living to Avoid Being Swallowed by the Earth

When King Suppabuddha heard the report of the spy, he thought, “As of now, there is no fault yet in the words spoken by my nephew Gautama Buddha. Whatever words that Gautama Buddha speaks, let them happen without fail as spoken. Even so, I will now suppress and speak against that Monk Gautama for his falsehood. That Gautama did not speak generally that I would be swallowed by the earth on the seventh day, but spoke with a specific location that I would enter the earth at the foot of the stairs under the palace. Now, from this day forth, I shall live without going to that place. If I live without going there, because I do not enter the earth at that stairway location, I shall be able to suppress that Gautama Buddha for his falsehood.” Having said this, King Suppabuddha had all his belongings taken to the top of the seven-storied palace, had the staircases dismantled and removed, and had the doors shut, placing two wrestlers at each and every door, saying, “If I should desire to descend because of forgetfulness, you all must stop me,” and he lived in the auspicious chamber on the seventh floor of the palace. When the All-Knowing Buddha heard that news, he said, “Bhikkhus, whether King Suppabuddha stays merely on the palace floor, or flies up into the sky and stays in the air, or enters the ocean by boat, or enters a mountain cave or tunnel, there is no such thing as duality in the words uttered by the Buddhas.”
30:
"King Suppabuddha will be swallowed by the earth only at the place I have designated," the Buddha said, and wishing to preach the Dhamma by connecting the sequence of events, he uttered this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

## Swallowed by the Earth on the Seventh Day
On the seventh day, at the time when the path for the Buddha's alms-round was blocked, King Suppabuddha's auspicious state horse became terrified and kicked the walls here and there. While sitting on the upper floor of the palace, King Suppabuddha heard the horse's neighing and asked, "What is this sound?" They informed him that the auspicious horse was terrified.

(That horse would only become calm upon seeing King Suppabuddha.)

Then, King Suppabuddha, wishing to catch or stroke the horse, rose from his seat and headed towards the door. The doors opened by themselves. The staircase, which had been removed, returned to its original place. The wrestlers standing at the door seized King Suppabuddha by the neck and threw him downwards. In this manner, on all seven floors of the palace, the doors opened by themselves and the staircases remained in their places. At each level, the wrestlers seized King Suppabuddha by the neck and threw him downwards. Then, as soon as he reached the foot of the stairs at the bottom of the palace, the great earth opened up, cracked, and received the Sakyan King Suppabuddha. King Suppabuddha fell through and was reborn in Avīci Hell.

The Story of Suppabuddha the Sakyan ends.
The Chapter on Evil ends.
Ninth Chapter.
31:
## 10. Daṇḍavagga
## 1. The Story of the Group-of-Six Monks
(Chabbaggiya Bhikkhu Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Sabbe tasanti," concerning the group-of-six monks.

(Cha + vaggiya = a group of six monks. This refers to the disciples of the six senior monks: Paṇḍuka, Lohitaka, Mettiya, Bhummajaka, Assaji, and Punabbasukka, who were residents of Sāvatthī.)

## Offense for Hitting
On one occasion, while the group-of-seventeen monks were cleaning and preparing the lodgings and monastery, the group-of-six monks said, "We are more senior in years of monkhood than you. This monastery belongs to us." When the group-of-seventeen monks replied, "We cannot give it to you. We were the ones who cleaned and prepared it first," the group-of-six monks struck and beat them. The group-of-seventeen monks, terrified by the fear of death, cried out with a loud lamentation. When the Buddha heard the sound of those group-of-seventeen monks, he asked, "What is this sound?" and was informed, "It is such-and-such a sound, Venerable Sir." He then said, "Monks, from now on, a monk must not do this. Whoever does so commits such-and-such an offense." Having prescribed the Paharādāna training rule (the rule on striking) which entails a Pācittiya offense, he said, "Monks, a monk should realize, 'Just as I do, others also tremble at punishment and fear death,' and with such wisdom and understanding, one should not strike or kill others." Wishing to connect the sequence of events and preach the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:

## The Teaching
(129) Sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti maccuno.
Attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā, na haneyya na ghātaye.

All tremble at punishment; all fear death.
Comparing others with oneself, one should not strike or kill.

## Notes on the Teaching
1. Noble elephants. 2. Noble horses. 3. Noble bulls. 4. Arahants. It should be understood that except for these four, all others tremble with fear. Among these four, Arahants do not fear because they have abandoned self-illusion (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and do not see a being that can die.
32:
The other three do not fear because their self-illusion is very strong, and they do not see any being who would dare to oppose or resist them.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of the Group-of-Six Monks ends.

## The Teaching
(130) Sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbesaṃ jīvitaṃ piyaṃ.
Attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā, na haneyya na ghātaye.

All (except Arahants) tremble at punishment; life is dear to all (except Arahants).
Comparing others with oneself, one should not strike or kill.

## 2. The Story of the Group-of-Six Monks
(Chabbaggiya Bhikkhu Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Sabbe tasanti," concerning the group-of-six monks.

## Offense for Raising a Hand to Hit
On another occasion, for the same reason regarding the monastery, the group-of-six monks struck and beat the group-of-seventeen monks as in the previous training rule. For that same reason, they raised their palms (threatened) against those group-of-seventeen monks. In this case also, when the Buddha heard the sound of those group-of-seventeen monks and asked, "What is this sound?" and was informed, "It is such-and-such a sound, Venerable Sir," he said, "Monks, from now on, a monk must not do this. Whoever does so commits such-and-such an offense." Having prescribed the Talasattika training rule (the rule on raising a hand to strike) which entails a Pācittiya offense, he said, "Monks, a monk should realize, 'Just as I do, others also tremble at punishment; just as my life is dear to me, so is their life dear to them,' and with such wisdom and understanding, one should not strike or kill others." Wishing to connect the sequence of events and preach the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

(Among the group-of-six monks, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, along with their disciples, were virtuous. They traveled with the Buddha. They tended to initiate matters for which rules had not yet been prescribed, but they did not habitually violate rules that had already been prescribed. They lived permanently in Sāvatthī. Mettiya and Bhummajaka lived permanently in Rājagaha. Assaji and Punabbasukka lived permanently in the Kīṭāgiri region and were of bad character. When the seventeen youths, such as the youth Upāli, were ordained, they were called the group-of-seventeen monks. Because they ordained children, the children would wake up early and cry, "Give us food!" They also soiled their beds. From that time on, the training rule was prescribed that "one should not ordain anyone under twenty years of age." However, those seventeen who had already been ordained were not removed from the monkhood.)

The Story of the Group-of-Six Monks (Second) ends.
33:
## The Teaching
(131) All beings desire happiness. He who, seeking his own happiness, harms with a stick other beings who also desire happiness, will not find happiness after death.
(132) All beings desire happiness. He who, seeking his own happiness, does not harm with a stick other beings who also desire happiness, will find happiness after death.

Whosoever, seeking his own happiness, harms with a stick or weapon living beings who desire happiness just as he does, that person will not obtain happiness in the life hereafter.

Whosoever, seeking his own happiness, does not harm with a stick or weapon living beings who desire happiness just as he does, that person will obtain happiness in the life hereafter.

## 3. The Story of Many Young Boys
(Sambahulakumāraka Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with 'Sukhakāmāni bhūtāni', concerning many young boys.

## One Should Not Harm Others for One's Own Happiness
On one occasion, while the Buddha was entering the city of Sāvatthī for alms, he saw many young boys along the way hitting a non-venomous house-snake with a stick. He asked, 'Young boys, what are you doing?' When they replied, 'Venerable Sir, we are hitting a snake with a stick,' he asked again, 'For what reason?' They replied, 'Venerable Sir, because we are afraid of being bitten.' The Buddha then said, 'If you hit this snake thinking "we will make ourselves happy," you will not obtain happiness in the various places of rebirth. It is not proper to hit another while desiring one's own happiness.' Having thus connected the sequence, he spoke these verses to teach the Dhamma.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, those five hundred young boys were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and other stages.

The Story of Many Young Boys ends.

## 4. The Story of Elder Koṇḍadhāna
(Koṇḍadhānatthera Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with 'Māvocca pharusaṃ kañci', concerning the Elder named Koṇḍadhāna.
34:
## The Woman Following the Elder
From the day Elder Koṇḍadhāna was ordained, the form of a woman was seen following and wandering about with the Elder. The Elder himself did not see this woman, but the multitude of people saw her. Even when he went into the village for alms, people would give him a spoonful of alms-food and say, 'Venerable Sir, let this be for you; and let this second portion be for your female companion,' thus offering a second spoonful of food.

## The Elder's Actions in the Past
What was the cause of this monk's past unwholesome kamma? In the time of Kassapa Buddha, two monks who were friends were as harmonious as if they had come from the same mother's womb. During the era of long-lived Buddhas, monks would gather for the purpose of the Uposatha once a year or once every six months. Therefore, those two monks also left their dwelling place to go to the Uposatha hall. A certain deity (deva) born in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven saw those two monks and thought, 'These monks are extremely harmonious. Would I be able to cause a split between them?' Having thought this, due to his own foolishness and delusion, he arrived immediately after his thought. When one of the two monks said, 'Friend, please wait a moment; I have a need to relieve myself,' that deity created the form of a human woman. When the Elder entered a thicket and was coming back out, the deity appeared behind him, adjusting her hair with one hand and her lower garment with the other, as if making herself tidy. The monk who had relieved himself did not see the woman, but the monk who was waiting in front turned back to look and saw the woman coming out, adjusting herself in the manner described. When the deity knew that the monk had seen her, she vanished.

## The Breaking of Harmony Between the Two Monks
When the monk who had been relieving himself returned to his companion, the waiting monk said, 'Friend, your virtue (sīla) is broken.' When the other replied, 'Friend, I have no such breaking of virtue,' the first monk asked, 'Just now, I saw a young woman coming out from behind you, doing such-and-such a thing. Why do you say to me, "I have no such breaking of virtue"?' The accused monk, as if struck by a thunderbolt on his head, said, 'Friend, do not destroy me; I have no such breaking of virtue.' The waiting monk replied, 'I saw it with my own eyes. Why should I believe you?' and then, like a stick breaking in two, he split away and departed.
35:
## The Deva's Apology
In the Uposatha hall, he also remained with the thought, "I will not perform the Uposatha together with this monk." The accused monk said to the monks, "Venerable sirs, there is not even a speck of blackness [impurity] in my virtue." The other monk replied, "I saw it myself."

When the deva saw that the objecting monk did not wish to perform the Uposatha together with the monk who had been cleaning himself, he thought, "The deed I have done is very heavy indeed." He then said, "Venerable sir, there is no breach of virtue in my lord. I did this through the power of testing. Please perform the Uposatha together with that monk."

That objecting monk, believing the words of the deva who spoke while standing in the air, performed the Uposatha. Even though he did so, his heart was not as soft toward the Elder as it was before. Such was the extent of the deva's past bad kamma. At the end of their lives, those Elders were reborn in the celestial worlds according to their merit.

## The Result of Past Karma in the Present Life as a Monk
The deva was reborn in the Avīci hell and, after being cooked in that Avīci for the interval between two Buddhas, was reborn in Sāvatthī when this Buddha Gotama appeared. Following his growth, he went forth in the Dispensation and attained higher ordination. From the day of his going forth, the image of that woman appeared just as before. Therefore, they named that Elder "Koṇḍadhāna Thera."

(Koṇḍa + dhāna = the one with the phantom woman + Elder Dhāna. His original childhood name was Dhāna; "Koṇḍa" was added after he became a monk, thus Koṇḍadhāna. In the Aṅguttara Commentary, it is written as Kuṇḍadhāna.)

Seeing the Elder Koṇḍadhāna wandering about in that manner, the monks said to the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, "Great merchant, expel this immoral monk from your monastery. Because of this immoral monk, ill-repute will arise for the rest of the monks." When he asked, "Venerable sirs, is the Blessed One not in the monastery?" they replied, "He is there, lay follower." Then he said, "Venerable sirs, if that is so, the Blessed One alone will know." The monks went and spoke to Visākhā in the same way. She also gave them the same reply.

## King Kosala's Plan to Catch the Elder
Because Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā did not accept their words, the monks informed King Kosala, saying, "Great King, the Elder named Koṇḍadhāna wanders about taking a woman with him, causing ill-repute for all the monks. Please expel him from your kingdom."

When asked, "Venerable sirs, where does that Elder live?" they said, "In the great monastery, Great King." When asked, "In which lodging does he stay?" they said, "In such-and-such a lodging." Saying, "If that is so, please go ahead; I will catch that monk," King Kosala went to the great monastery in the evening, had the lodging surrounded by men, and went towards the Elder's dwelling place.
36:
## The Illusory Woman who Appears and Disappears

When the Elder heard the sound of many people, he came out of the monastery and stood at the entrance. King Pasenadi of Kosala saw the phantom woman standing behind the Elder. Knowing that King Pasenadi had arrived, the Elder went up into the monastery and remained there. King Pasenadi did not pay homage to the Elder, nor did he see the woman. When the King looked between the doors and under the couch and did not see her, he asked the Elder, "Venerable Sir, a woman was seen in this place. Where is she?"

When the Elder replied, "Great King, I do not see her," the King said, "Just now, I saw her standing behind you, Venerable Sir." Even though the Elder repeated, "Great King, I do not see her," the King thought, "What could this matter be?" and then said, "Venerable Sir, please first come out from this place."

When the Elder came out and stood at the entrance of the monastery, the woman again appeared standing behind him. King Pasenadi saw the woman and again went up to the upper level. Knowing the King was coming, the Elder sat down. Again, the King looked in all directions for the woman but did not see her, so he asked the Elder once more, "Venerable Sir, where is that woman?"

When the Elder said, "Great King, I do not see her," the King replied, "Venerable Sir, what are you saying? I saw her behind you just now."

The Elder said, "Great King, the multitude also says that a woman follows behind me. But as for me, I do not see her." Then King Pasenadi noted, "It must be an illusory phantom." He then said to the Elder again, "Venerable Sir, please first stand up from this place." When the Elder descended and stood at the entrance of the monastery, the King again saw the woman standing behind the monk and went back up to the upper level. Again, he did not see her.

When King Pasenadi asked the Elder once more and the Elder replied, "King, I do not see her," the King came to the conclusion, "That woman is indeed only an illusory phantom." He then addressed the Elder: "Venerable Sir, while such a stain on the Dispensation follows behind you, no one else will offer you alms-food. Please enter my palace regularly. I alone will support you with the four requisites." After inviting the Elder, he departed.

## The Buddha's Admonition to Elder Koṇḍadhāna

The monks complained, saying, "Friends, look at the conduct of the wicked King. Although he was told to expel this monk Koṇḍadhāna from the monastery, he came, invited him with the four requisites, and left." They also said to the Elder, "Hey, you immoral monk! Now King Pasenadi has become a fool like you."

In the past, that Elder Koṇḍadhāna was unable to say anything to the monks, but now he said, "It is you who are immoral! It is you who are fools! It is you who wander around taking women with you!"

Those monks who were insulted went and reported it to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, when we spoke to Elder Koṇḍadhāna, he abused us by calling us 'immoral' and so on."

The Blessed One had Elder Koṇḍadhāna summoned and asked, "Is it true, monk, as I have heard, that you spoke thus to the monks?" When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Buddha asked, "For what reason?" He replied, "Because of the way they spoke to me, Venerable Sir."

The Blessed One then asked, "Monks, why did you speak thus with this Koṇḍadhāna?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, because we saw a woman following behind this Elder Koṇḍadhāna."

The Buddha said, "These monks spoke because they saw a woman following you. But why did you speak to these monks when you did not see her as they did? Was it not because of your own evil view in a past life that this situation has arisen? Why do you now hold an evil view again?"

The monks asked, "Venerable Sir, what was the evil deed committed by this monk in a past life?" Then the Blessed One told them of Elder Koṇḍadhāna's past evil deed and said, "Monk, because of this evil deed, you have come to this state of distress. It is not proper for you to hold such an evil view again. Do not say anything to the monks again. Be silent like a bronze gong with its rim broken off."
37:
## The Teaching

(133) Speak not harshly to anyone; those spoken to might answer back.
Harsh speech is painful indeed; retaliation may touch you.

(134) If you keep yourself as still as a broken gong,
You have reached Nibbāna; no contention is found in you.

*Kiñci*: to anyone at all. *Pharusaṃ*: harsh words. *Mā avoca*: do not speak. *Vutto*: those who are spoken to. *Taṃ*: to you. *Paṭivadeyyuṃ*: might speak in return. *Hi*: indeed, that is true. *Sārambhakathā*: speech made in contention or rivalry. *Dukkhā*: is a cause of suffering. *Paṭidaṇḍā*: retaliation in the form of physical punishment and so on.

"If you act in this way, you will be one who has reached Nibbāna." Having said this, the Buddha, wishing to connect the discourse and teach the Dhamma, admonished the monk with these verses:

Retaliatory punishments will reach you. *Upahato*: with the rim cut off. *Kaṃso yathā*: like a bronze gong (meaning, as a bronze gong makes no sound). *Attānaṃ*: oneself. *Sace nereisi* (na īresi): if you are able to make yourself unshakable. *Evaṃ sati*: if you are able to do so. *Esa tvaṃ*: you who are thus able. *Nibbānaṃ*: Nibbāna. *Patto*: though not yet reached, you are called one who has reached it. *Asi*: you are. *Te*: for you. *Sārambho*: contention. *Na vijjati*: does not exist, or will not occur.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so on. Elder Koṇḍadhāna, established in the advice given by the Blessed One, attained Arahantship. Not long after, he flew into the air and was the first to receive the food-ticket (salāka).

(Note: When food-tickets were being distributed for the invitation by Mahāsubhaddā of Ugga City, with the condition that 'only Ariyas shall go,' Venerable Ānanda did not give one to him. Later, when the Buddha said, 'Give to whoever takes it,' he stood in the air and took the ticket. The Buddha declared him the foremost (Etadagga) among those who are the first to receive tickets. — Aṅguttara Nikāya.)

The Story of Elder Koṇḍadhāna ends.

## 5. The Story of the Laywomen Observing the Uposatha
(Uposathika-itthīnaṃ Vatthu)

While residing at the Pubbārāma monastery, the Blessed One spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yathā daṇḍena," concerning the observance of the Uposatha by Visākhā and other laywomen.
38:
## The Teaching
(135) Just as a cowherd with a staff drives the cattle to the pasture,
So do aging and death drive the life of living beings.

## The Intentions of the Women Observing the Uposatha
In the city of Sāvatthī, on a certain great Uposatha day, about five hundred women, having undertaken the Uposatha precepts, went to the monastery. The great lay devotee Visākhā approached the elderly women among those five hundred and asked, "O grandmothers, for what benefit do you observe the Uposatha?" When they replied, "We observe it wishing for celestial glory and bliss," she then asked the middle-aged women. When they replied, "We observe it for the sake of being freed from living with co-wives," she asked the young women. When they replied, "We observe it for the sake of obtaining a son in our first pregnancy," she asked the maidens. When they replied, "We observe it for the sake of going to a husband's house of a good family while we are still young," she heard all their words and, taking them with her, went to the presence of the Teacher and reported the matter in due order.

Upon hearing this, the Blessed One said, "Visākhā, within these beings, things such as birth (jāti) are like a cowherd holding a staff. Birth sends them to the presence of aging (jarā), aging to the presence of sickness (byādhi), and sickness to the presence of death (maraṇa); and death cuts off life as if cutting with an axe. Even though this is so, there are none who aspire for Nibbāna, the escape from the cycle; they only aspire for the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa) itself." Having thus connected the sequence, he spoke this verse while preaching the Dhamma:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.
The Story of the Women Observing the Uposatha, the fifth, is finished.
39:
## 6. The Story of the Python Ghost
(Ajagara Peta Vatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Atha pāpāni kammāni," concerning a python ghost.

## The Great Python Ghost Engulfed in Flames
On one occasion, the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, while descending from Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa) together with the Venerable Lakkhaṇa, saw with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) a python ghost twenty-five leagues in length. Flames of fire rose from the head of that python ghost and went to its tail; flames rose from the tail and went to its head; and flames rose from both ends and met in the middle. Upon seeing that python ghost, the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna manifested a smile.

When asked by the Venerable Lakkhaṇa about the reason for his smile, he said, "Friend Lakkhaṇa, it is not the time to answer this question; ask me in the presence of the Teacher." After wandering for alms in Rājagaha and arriving in the presence of the Teacher, being asked again by the Venerable Lakkhaṇa, he replied, "Friend Lakkhaṇa, I saw a python ghost on that Vulture Peak. Such was the state of its existence (attabhāva). Seeing it, I smiled, thinking, 'Indeed, I have never seen such a state of existence before.'"

The Teacher, saying, "Monks, my disciples indeed live with vision," and so forth, confirmed the Elder's words and said, "Monks, I too saw that ghost while sitting at the Bodhi tree. However, I did not speak of it then, thinking that if there were those who did not believe my words, it would be to their disadvantage. Now, having Moggallāna as a witness, I speak." When asked by the monks about the past evil deeds of that python ghost, he explained:

## The Monastery Burns and the Donor Claps His Hands
In the time of Kassapa Buddha, a great treasurer named Sumangala covered the ground with golden bricks and had a monastery built on a site twenty usabhas in length, spending an equal amount of wealth on the construction and the same amount again on the dedication ceremony of the monastery. One day, while going early in the morning to the presence of Kassapa Buddha, he saw a thief sleeping near a rest-house by the city gate, covering his head with a dyed cloth and having feet covered in mud. He remarked, "This man has feet covered in mud; he must be someone who has been wandering about at night and is now sleeping during the day."

The thief, uncovering his face and seeing the treasurer, harbored a grudge, thinking, "Let it be as you say; I shall know what must be done to you." He then set fire to the treasurer's fields seven times, cut off the feet of the cattle in the cow-pen seven times, and set fire to his house seven times. Even with all this, being unable to quench his anger, he befriended the treasurer's young attendant and asked, "What is it that your master loves and cherishes most?" When told, "There is nothing he loves and cherishes more than the Fragrant Cell (Gandhakuṭi)," the thief thought, "Let it be so; I shall quench my anger only after setting fire to the Fragrant Cell." While the Buddha was entering for alms, the thief broke the water jars for drinking and washing and set fire to the great Gandhakuṭi monastery. When the treasurer heard that the Gandhakuṭi was on fire, he arrived just as it was being consumed. Looking at the burning Gandhakuṭi, he did not feel even a hair's breadth of displeasure; instead, he folded his left arm and clapped his right hand against it in a great gesture of joy.
40:
## Joy Enough to Snap Fingers

Then, those standing near the Great Merchant asked, "Lord Merchant, why do you snap your fingers in joy when the great Gandhakuṭi, built by relinquishing so much wealth, is being consumed by fire?"

The Merchant replied, "Friends, by performing such a meritorious deed, I have buried and stored wealth in the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana), which is not shared with fire and other enemies. Once again, I shall have the opportunity to build a Gandhakuṭi for the sake of the Buddha by relinquishing this much wealth." Thus, with a heart full of delight and joy, he said, "That is why I snap my fingers, friends."

That Great Merchant Sumangala, after relinquishing that same amount of wealth again, had a Gandhakuṭi built and offered a donation to the Buddha Kassapa, who was surrounded by a retinue of twenty thousand monks.

## Sharing Merit with the Enemy

When the thief saw the Merchant acting in this way, he thought: "I will not be able to make this Merchant lose face unless I kill him. Let it be; I shall kill him." Planning thus, he tied a small knife within the folds of his lower garment and wandered about the monastery for seven days, but he found no opportunity. 

The Great Merchant, after giving a great donation for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, paid homage to the Buddha and said: "Venerable Sir, a certain man has burned my fields seven times; he has cut off the feet of the cattle in their pens seven times; he has burned my house seven times. Now, the Gandhakuṭi must have been burned by that same man. Venerable Sir, I share the first portion of the merit of this donation with that man."

## The Thief's Apology

When the thief heard those words spoken by the Merchant, he thought: "The deed I have done is indeed heavy! This Merchant has not even a slight amount of anger toward me who has wronged him so; instead, he shares the first portion of merit from this donation with me alone. I have done wrong to such a man. If I do not ask for forgiveness from a man of such nature, a divine punishment, a thunderbolt, might fall upon my head." 

Saying this, he prostrated at the Merchant's feet and said, "Lord Merchant, please forgive me."

When asked, "What is this about?", he replied, "Lord Merchant, I have committed such and such improper deeds. Therefore, please forgive me."

Then the Merchant asked him about everything: "Did you do this and that to me?" When the thief replied, "It is true, I did it," the Merchant asked again, "I have never seen you before. Why were you angry with me and did such things?"

The thief reminded him of the words spoken by the Merchant as he was leaving the city one day and said, "For this reason, anger was aroused in me."

The Merchant, remembering his own words, said, "Friend, oh... it is true."
41:
I did say that; please forgive me for that fault." After asking the thief for forgiveness, he said, "Rise, friend, I forgive you. Go, friend."

"Lord Merchant, if you truly forgive me, please take me and my wife and children as slaves in your house," the thief said. 

"Friend, when I said only that much, you committed such destruction. If you were to live in my house, it would not be possible to say anything to you. I have no need for you living in my house. I forgive you. Go, friend."

Because of having committed that deed, when the thief died, he was reborn in the Avīci Hell. After being cooked in that Avīci Hell for a long time, due to the remaining result of his karma, he is now suffering pain, being cooked by fire on Mount Gijjhakūṭa.

Thus, the Teacher told the past deed of that python-ghost (ajagara-peta) and said, "Monks, those who are fools do not realize it while they are performing evil deeds. But later, being burned by the deeds they themselves have done, they are like those burned by their own forest fire." Connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:

## The Teaching

(136) Atha pāpāni kammāni, karaṃ bālo na bujjhati.
Sehi kammehi dummedho, aggidaddho va tappati.

When a fool performs evil deeds, he does not realize it. 
The man of poor wisdom is tormented by his own deeds, 
As if burned by fire in hell.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of the Python-Ghost is finished.

## 7. The Story of Elder Mahāmoggallāna

(Mahāmoggallānatthera-vatthu)

The Teacher, while staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yo daṇḍena," concerning the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.

## The Plot to Assassinate Mahāmoggallāna

On one occasion, the heretics (titthiyas) assembled and discussed: "Friends, do you know for what reason the gain and honor of the ascetic Gotama have become so great?" When they were asked in return, "We do not know; do you know?", they replied, "Oh... we know. It is because of an Elder named Mahāmoggallāna. That Mahāmoggallāna goes to the celestial realms and asks about the meritorious deeds performed by the deities..."
42:
[He] returned and told the people, "By performing such and such wholesome deeds, they enjoy such prosperity." Having also asked about the unwholesome deeds of those reborn in hell, he returned and told the people, "By performing such and such unwholesome deeds, they suffer such pain." When the people heard the words of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, they brought great gain and honor to him. [The heretics] plotted, "If we are able to kill this Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, that gain and honor will come to us." Those heretics, being of one mind that "this is the way," said, "Let us kill the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna by any means." They urged their supporters, and upon receiving a thousand kahāpaṇas, they summoned bandits who lived by murder and said, "The Elder named Mahāmoggallāna lives at the place called Kāḷasilā (this is the black rock on the side of Mount Isigili near Rājagaha). Go there and kill that Elder." They gave the money to the bandits.

## The Parinibbāna of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna
The bandits, out of greed for wealth, agreed, saying, "We will kill the Elder," and went to surround the Elder's dwelling. When the Elder knew he was surrounded by the bandits, he went out through the keyhole and departed. The bandits, not seeing the Elder that day, went and surrounded it again the next day. The Elder, knowing this, broke through the roof peak and flew into the sky. Thus, in the first month and the middle month, the bandits were unable to catch the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. When the final month arrived, the Great Elder, knowing the pulling force of the unwholesome karma he had committed, did not depart but remained. 

The bandits went and caught the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and they broke his bones until they were like broken rice grains. Then, thinking "He is dead," they threw him behind a bush and left. The Great Elder thought, "I will attain Parinibbāna only after seeing the Blessed One." He strengthened his body by wrapping it in the power of jhāna, went to the Blessed One through the air, paid homage to the Buddha, and said, "Venerable Sir, I will attain Parinibbāna." When asked, "Dear Moggallāna, are you going to attain Parinibbāna?" he replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir." When asked, "Where will you go to attain Parinibbāna?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, I will go to the place called Kāḷasilā." The Buddha said, "Dear Moggallāna, if so, preach the Dhamma to me before you go. For there will be no more seeing a disciple like you." The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied, "Venerable Sir, I will do as you say." He paid homage to the Buddha, flew into the sky, and just as the Venerable Sāriputta had done on the day of his Parinibbāna, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna performed various kinds of miracles, preached the Dhamma, paid homage to the Buddha, went to the forest of Kāḷasilā, and attained Parinibbāna.
43:
## Burning the Assassins and Heretics
The news that "the bandits have killed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna" spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. King Ajātasattu sent out spies to search for the bandits. While those bandits were drinking liquor in a tavern, one man struck another on the back. The man who was struck rebuked the one who struck him, saying, "Hey, you ill-disciplined scoundrel! Why did you strike me on the back?" The other replied, "Hey, you wretched bandit! What of it? Did you not strike the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna first?" The first replied, "What of it? Do you not know that I struck him?" Hearing the words of the bandits saying, "I struck him, I struck him," the spies arrested all those bandits and reported to King Ajātasattu. 

King Ajātasattu summoned the bandits and interrogated them, "Did you kill the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna?" When they replied, "Your Majesty, we did," he asked further, "Who urged and commissioned you?" When they replied, "Your Majesty, the naked Acelaka heretics urged and commissioned us," King Ajātasattu had the five hundred heretics arrested. Together with the five hundred bandits, he had them buried up to their navels in pits in the royal courtyard, covered them with straw, and set them on fire. Then, knowing that the heretics and bandits were burnt, he had them plowed over with iron plows and cut into pieces.

[The monks began a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna met a death that was quite unworthy of him." The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, Moggallāna met a death that was unworthy of this current existence, but it was a death entirely worthy of the karma he committed in the past." When asked, "Venerable Sir, what was his past karma?" he told the story in detail:]

It is said that in the past, a certain young man of good family living in Bārāṇasī looked after his parents, performing tasks such as pounding [grain] and cooking by himself.
