Though he refused, saying, "Mother and Father, I have no need for such a thing. As long as you live, I will serve you with my own hands," they asked him again and again and brought a young woman. After serving them for only a few days, she later did not even want to see them. Complaining, "It is impossible to live in the same place with your parents," [she...]
44:
## Ten Punishments for Harming the Innocent
(137) He who harms with a weapon those who are harmless and innocent, quickly reaches one of ten states.
(138) He may experience severe pain, loss of wealth, bodily injury, heavy illness, or madness.
(139) Or trouble from the king, harsh slander, loss of relatives, or destruction of wealth.
(140) Or indeed, fire may burn down his houses. Upon the dissolution of the body, that unwise one is reborn in hell.

He who (yo), harms (dussati) by giving physical punishment and so forth (daṇḍena), those persons who are free from physical punishment and the like (adaṇḍesu) and who do no harm to anyone (appaduṭṭhesu). That person (so), quickly indeed (khīppam eva), reaches (nigacchati) one of (aññataraṃ) the ten states (dasannaṃ ṭhānānaṃ) that are causes of suffering.

He may reach (pāpuṇe) severe (pharusaṃ) painful sensations such as headaches (vedanaṃ); or the loss of wealth (ဇာနိံ - jāniṃ) obtained with difficulty; or the destruction (bhedanaṃ vā) of the body (sarīrassa) such as hands and feet; or a heavy (garukaṃ) affliction (ābadhāṃ vāpi) such as paralysis or blindness; or madness (cittakkhepaṃ vā) due to a distracted mind.

He may reach (pāpuṇe) danger (upasaggaṃ vā) from the king (rājato) such as loss of property or demotion from office; or harsh (dāruṇaṃ) slander (abbhakkhānaṃ vā) being falsely accused; or the exhaustion and ruin (parikkhayaṃ vā) of relatives (ñātīnaṃ) on whom one relies; or the destruction (pabhaṅgunaṃ vā) of wealth and property (bhogānaṃ).

Furthermore (atha), the fire (aggi vā) of a natural conflagration or lightning, or a fire (pāvako) that arises spontaneously, burns (ḍahati) the houses (agārāni) of that person (assa). That unwise person (duppañño so), having already suffered one of these ten punishments, upon the dissolution (bhedā) of the body (kāyassa), is reborn (upapajjati) in hell (nirayaṃ).

The monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "The Elder Mahāmoggallāna met with a death that was truly unsuitable for him." The Buddha arrived and asked, "Dear monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit gathered here now that I have arrived?" When they informed Him, "We are gathered with this conversation, Venerable Sir," He said, "Monks, Moggallāna has met with a death that is unsuitable for this present existence, but it is a death well-suited to the evil deed he committed in a past life." When asked, "Venerable Sir, what was that evil deed committed by the Elder Moggallāna in the past?" He related the story in detail.

## Mahāmoggallāna's Past Karma
In the past, a certain young man of good family living in Vārāṇasī personally performed tasks such as pounding grain and cooking rice to serve his mother and father. Then his parents said to him, "Dear son, you are exhausted by doing all the work alone both in the house and in the forest. We shall bring a young woman for you." The young man replied, "Mother and father, I have no desire for such a married life. As long as you both live, I will serve you with my own hands." Despite his refusal, they repeatedly entreated him and eventually brought a young woman and married them. For only two or three days, that young woman served the parents well, but later she did not even wish to see them. She spoke sarcastically, saying, "I cannot live in the same place as your parents." When the young man did not heed her words, she took scraps of hemp and rice-scum while he was away and scattered them here and there. When the young man returned and asked, "What is this?" she replied, "This is the work of these blind old people; they wander about making the whole house filthy. I cannot live in the same place as these blind old people." As she said this to him repeatedly, even a being like this young man of good family, who had fulfilled the perfections of a Chief Disciple, had his bond of love and affection for his parents broken.
45:
## The Killing of the Parents
The young man thought, "Let it be so; I shall find out what must be done to these blind old people." After feeding his parents, he said, "Mother and father, your relatives in such-and-such a place desire your arrival. Let us go there." He placed his parents on a carriage and led them away. When they reached the middle of a forest, he said, "Father, take the reins; the oxen will go by the sign of the goad. Bandits live in this place; I will get down." Giving the reins into his father's hand, he got down and, while walking, changed his voice and made a noise like bandits rising up. When the elderly, sightless parents heard the sound, thinking that bandits had risen, they said, "Dear son, we are old; you must save yourself." Even though his mother and father lamented in such a manner, the young man, making the sound of bandits, beat and struck them to death, discarded them in the forest, and then returned.

The Buddha, having related that past deed of the Elder Moggallāna, said, "Monks, because Moggallāna committed such an unwholesome deed, he was cooked in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. Due to the remaining result, in a hundred existences, he met death in this very way, being beaten and crushed to pieces. Thus, Moggallāna met with a death that was well-suited to his own karma. The five hundred bandits and the five hundred ascetics also met with a death that was well-suited to them because they harmed my son Moggallāna, who was harmless. Indeed, one who harms the harmless or the innocent reaches ruin and destruction through ten causes." Having thus connected the sequence, He spoke these verses while teaching the Dhamma:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.
The story of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna ends.

## 8. The Story of the Monk with Many Possessions
(Bahubhaṇḍika-bhikkhu-vatthu)
The Buddha, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Na naggacariyā," concerning a monk who had many possessions.
46:
## The Wealthy Monk Who Cast Off His Robe in Defiance

A certain wealthy man living in Sāvatthī, it is said, became a monk after the death of his wife. When he wished to ordain, he had a monastery precinct, a fire-hall, and a storehouse built for himself. Having filled the entire storehouse with ghee, honey, oil, and so forth, he ordained. After ordaining, he would summon his own servants and have them cook food according to his desire and then eat. He possessed many goods and many requisites. He had one set of robes for the night and another for the day. During the day, he lived in a secluded monastery on the outskirts. One day, while he was drying his robes and bedding in the sun, some monks wandering through the lodgings saw them and asked, "Friends, whose robes and bedding are these?" When he replied, "They are mine," they said, "Friend, the Blessed One has allowed only three robes. You have ordained in the Dispensation of the Buddha, who teaches fewness of wishes, yet you possess such many requisites." They took that monk with many possessions to the presence of the Teacher and reported, "Venerable Sir, this monk has an excessive amount of goods." The Teacher asked, "Is it true, monk?" and when he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, why is it that while I have taught the Dhamma for the sake of fewness of wishes, you have come to possess such many goods?" That monk, becoming angry at just that much, said, "Now I shall live in this manner!" and casting off his upper robe, he stood in the midst of the assembly wearing only one robe. Then the Teacher, supporting him, said, "Monk, in the past you were a seeker of shame and fear (hiri-ottappa). Even when you were a water-demon, you sought shame and fear and lived for twelve years. Why is it that now, having ordained in the noble Dispensation of the Buddha, you stand in the midst of the fourfold assembly having cast off your robe and abandoned shame and fear?" Hearing the Teacher's words, he regained his sense of shame and fear, put on that robe, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down at a respectful distance. The monks requested the Blessed One to clarify the matter. The Blessed One brought forth the past and spoke:

## The Three Princes Leaving the Kingdom

In the past, it is said, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. On the day of his naming, they gave him the name Prince Mahisa. His younger brother was named Prince Canda. When their mother passed away, the King appointed another young queen to the position of chief queen. She also gave birth to a son, and they named him Prince Suriya. Upon seeing Prince Suriya, the King was delighted and said, "I shall grant a boon for your son." The queen replied, "Great King, I shall take it at a time I desire." When the prince reached maturity, she said to the King, "Great King, you granted a boon at the time of my son's birth. Now, please grant the kingdom to my son."
47:
The King refused, saying, "My two sons are like great masses of fire, shining as they go about. I cannot give the kingdom to Prince Suriya." However, seeing that she asked repeatedly, he thought, "This queen might even do harm to my elder sons." He summoned his sons and said, "My dear sons, I granted a boon at the time of Prince Suriya's birth. Now his mother asks for the kingdom. I do not wish to give it to him, but his mother might do you harm. Go, live in the forest, and after my passing, return and take the kingdom." Saying this, he sent them away.

Those princes paid homage to their father and descended from the palace. Prince Suriya, who was playing in the royal courtyard, saw them and, upon learning the reason, left together with his elder brothers. When they entered the Himalayas, the Bodhisatta stepped off the path and sat at the foot of a certain tree, saying to Prince Suriya, "Dear younger brother, go to this pond, bathe and drink, and bring us some water in lotus leaves."

## The Water-Demon Catching the Princes

That pond was a place granted by King Vessavaṇa to a certain water-demon. King Vessavaṇa had told the demon, "Except for those who know the Divine Virtues (Devadhamma), you may eat any others who descend into this pond." From then on, the demon would ask those who descended into the pond about the Divine Virtues and eat those who did not know them. Prince Suriya also descended into the pond without investigating or reflecting. When the demon asked, "Do you know the Divine Virtues?", he replied, "The Divine Virtues are the Moon and the Sun." Then the demon said, "You do not know the Divine Virtues," and pulling him into the water, kept him in his abode. The Bodhisatta, Prince Mahisa, seeing that Prince Suriya was taking a long time, sent his brother Prince Canda. When the demon asked him, "Do you know the Divine Virtues?", he replied, "The Divine Virtues are the four directions." The water-demon pulled Prince Canda into the water and kept him there in the same way. When Prince Canda also took a long time, the Bodhisatta thought, "There must be some danger," and went there himself. Seeing only the footprints of his two younger brothers descending, he realized, "This pond is possessed by a demon," and stood there girding his sword and holding his bow. When the demon saw that Prince Mahisa did not descend, he approached in the guise of a forest worker and said, "O man, you are weary from your journey. Why do you not descend into this pond, bathe and drink, eat lotus stalks and roots, and go on wearing flowers?" As soon as the Bodhisatta saw that man, he knew, "This is the demon," and asked, "Have you captured my brothers?" When the demon replied, "Yes, I have captured them," the Bodhisatta asked, "For what reason?" The demon said, "I get to keep those who descend into this pond." The Bodhisatta asked again, "What? Do you get to keep everyone?"
48:
Those endowed with shame and fear of sin, established in bright states, peaceful and virtuous people in the world, are called 'divine-natured' (Devadhamma).

"Those endowed with shame and fear of sin" (Hiri-ottappa-sampannā). "Established in bright states" (Sukka-dhamma-samāhitā). "Peaceful" (Santo), meaning those whose physical actions and so forth are tranquil. "Virtuous people" (Sappurisā). "In the world" (Loke), meaning in the three worlds. "Are called 'divine-natured'" (Devadhamma-ti vuccare).

When the Ogre said, "I take everyone except those who know the Devadhamma," the Bodhisatta asked, "Do you wish to know the Devadhamma?" When the Ogre replied, "Yes, I do," the Bodhisatta said, "I shall teach them to you." "If so, please teach," the Ogre said. The Bodhisatta then said, "I cannot teach with a soiled body."

## The Divine States (Devadhamma)

The Ogre then bathed the Bodhisatta, gave him water to drink, adorned him, and placed him on a throne in the center of a decorated pavilion, while he himself sat at the Bodhisatta's feet. Then the Bodhisatta said to the Ogre, "Listen respectfully," and recited this verse:

## Discussion between the Bodhisatta and the Ogre

Upon hearing this Dhamma teaching, the Ogre was greatly pleased and said to the Bodhisatta, "Wise Sage, I am very pleased with you. I will give back one of your brothers. Which one shall I bring?" When the Bodhisatta replied, "Bring the youngest, Prince Suriya," the Ogre said, "Wise Sage, you merely know the Devadhamma, but you do not practice them." "For what reason?" the Bodhisatta asked. "Because by leaving the elder brother and asking for the younger, you do not perform the act of honoring the eldest," the Ogre replied.

"O Water-Ogre, I do know the Devadhamma, and I also practice them," the Bodhisatta said. "It is because of this younger brother that we entered this forest. For his sake, his mother asked our father for the kingdom. Our father, not granting that wish and to protect us, allowed us to live in the forest. This young prince followed us without turning back. If I were to say, 'An ogre ate him in the forest,' no one would believe me. Therefore, fearing the blame of others, I ask for that younger prince to be brought back."

The Ogre was again pleased with the Bodhisatta and said, "Excellent, Wise Sage! You alone truly know the Devadhamma." He then brought both brothers and gave them back. Then the Bodhisatta taught the Ogre the danger of being an ogre and established him in the Five Precepts.

## Honoring the Ogre upon becoming King

Prince Mahimsā, having the protection arranged by that Ogre, lived in that forest until his father passed away. He then took the Ogre and went to the city of Bārāṇasī, where he took possession of the kingdom. He appointed Prince Canda as the Viceroy and Prince Suriya as the Commander-in-Chief. He had a pleasant shrine built for the Ogre and ensured that he reached the pinnacle of receiving offerings and honor.
49:
## The Teaching

(141) Neither nakedness, nor matted hair, nor mud, nor fasting, nor lying on the ground, nor dust and dirt, nor striving in a squatting posture, can purify a mortal who has not overcome doubt.

"Who has not overcome doubt" (Avitiṇṇakaṅkhaṃ), meaning a being who still has doubts that cannot be crossed over. "Nakedness" (Naggacariyā), the practice of going without clothes, "cannot purify" (Na sodhenti). "Matted hair" (Jaṭā) cannot purify. "Mud" (Paṅkā), the practice of smearing oneself with mud, cannot purify. "Fasting" (Anāsakā), the practice of starving by cutting off food, cannot purify. "Lying on the ground" (Thaṇḍilasaāyikā vā) cannot purify. "Dust and dirt" (Rajojallaṃ), the grime and dust smeared in such a manner, cannot purify. "Striving in a squatting posture" (Ukkuṭikappadhānaṃ), the effort made by remaining in a squatting position, cannot purify. (This means these are false practices that only lead to physical exhaustion.)

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Ogre was the monk with many possessions (Bahubhaṇḍika). Prince Suriya was Ānanda. Prince Canda was Sāriputta. Prince Mahimsā was I, the Buddha."

Thus the Teacher, having told this Jātaka (Devadhamma Jātaka, No. 6 in the Apaṇṇaka Vagga of the Ekanipāta), said, "Dear monk, in the past you wandered seeking the Devadhamma, endowed with shame and fear of sin. Now, standing in the midst of the fourfold assembly in this manner, claiming 'I am one of few wishes' before me, you have done what is improper. One does not become a recluse (samaṇa) merely by rejecting robes and such," and connecting the sequence to teach the Dhamma, he uttered this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The story of the monk with many possessions ends.

## 9. The Story of the Minister Santati
(Santatimahāmatta Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Alaṅkato cepi," concerning the Minister Santati.

## Predicting Arahatship for a Drunkard

At one time, that Minister Santati returned after suppressing a rebellion in a border village of King Pasenadi of Kosala. The King, being pleased with the minister, gave him the kingdom for seven days and also gave him a woman skilled in dancing and singing.
50:
That great minister, having been intoxicated with liquor for seven days, on the seventh day, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, was going to the bathing ghat while seated on the back of a noble elephant. When he saw the Blessed One entering for alms at the gateway, while still remaining on the back of the noble elephant, he bowed by nodding his head and proceeded on his way. Because the Blessed One smiled, the Elder Ānanda asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the cause for your smile?" The Blessed One, wishing to explain the reason for his smile, said, "Behold, Ānanda, the great minister Santati. This very day, adorned with all his ornaments, he will come to my presence, and at the end of a four-line verse, he will attain Arahantship. Then, seated in the air at a height of seven palm trees, he will attain Parinibbāna."

## The Intentions of the Wrong-viewers and Right-viewers

The multitude heard the words of the Blessed One as he spoke with the Elder Ānanda. Among that multitude, those with wrong views thought, "Behold the conduct of the ascetic Gotama; he speaks only what comes to his lips. He says that today this minister Santati, while intoxicated and adorned as he is, will hear the Dhamma in his presence and attain Parinibbāna. This very day, we shall catch him in a lie."

Those with right views thought, "Oh, how great is the power of the Buddhas! Today we shall have the opportunity to see the glory of the Buddha and the glory of the great minister Santati."

## The Great Minister Santati Encounters Suffering

The great minister Santati also spent the day playing in the water at the bathing ghat, then went to the park and sat at the place of drinking. That dancing woman also entered the middle of the stage and began to perform her dance and song. Because she had taken little food for seven days in order to display the grace of her body, as she was performing her dance and song that day, sharp pains like small knives (wind-ailments) arose within her womb and cut through her heart. That dancing girl died at that very moment with her mouth and eyes wide open.

When the great minister Santati said, "Examine her," and was told, "Master, she is dead," he was immediately overcome by intense grief. At that moment, the liquor he had drunk for seven days vanished and dried up like a drop of water falling on a hot pan. The minister thought, "No one other than the Tathāgata will be able to quench this grief of mine." Surrounded by his army, he went to the Blessed One in the evening, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, such grief has arisen in me. I have come thinking that you, the Exalted One, will be able to quench that grief for me. Please be my refuge."

## The Great Minister Santati Becomes an Arahant and Performs Miracles

Then the Blessed One said to the minister, "You have indeed come to the presence of one who is able to quench your grief."
51:
"In this very manner, the tears you have shed while weeping at the time of this woman's death throughout your past lives are more than the water in the four great oceans." Having said this, he spoke this verse:

"What is past, let it be dried up; let there be nothing for you in the future. If you do not grasp at the middle (the present), you will wander at peace."

(Pubbe: in the past. Yaṃ kiñcanaṃ: whatever worry or anxiety there is. Taṃ kiñcanaṃ: that worry. Visodhehi: dry it up or cut it off. Te: for you. Pacchā: in the future. Kiñcanaṃ: worry or anxiety. Mā ahu: let it not be. Majjhe: in the middle, which is the present. No ce gahessasi: if you do not grasp. Upasanto: being at peace. Carissasi: you will wander.)

At the end of the verse, the great minister Santati attained Arahantship. As he reviewed his own life-span (āyusaṅkhāra) and realized its brevity—or rather, that it would not continue further—he said to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, please permit my Parinibbāna."

Although the Blessed One knew the meritorious deeds performed by the minister, he reflected, "The wrong-viewers who have gathered to catch me in a lie will not get the chance, and the right-viewers who have gathered to see the glory of the Buddha and the glory of the great minister Santati will hear of the meritorious deeds performed by this minister and will develop respect for meritorious acts." Therefore, he said, "If that is so, recount to me the meritorious deeds you have performed. And when you recount them, do not do so while standing on the ground, but recount them while standing in the air at the height of seven palm trees."

The minister replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir." He paid homage to the Blessed One, rose to the height of one palm tree, descended, and after paying homage to the Blessed One again, he rose and sat cross-legged in the air at the height of seven palm trees in succession. He said, "Venerable Sir, please listen to my past deeds."

## Recounting Past Meritorious Deeds

Ninety-one aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, when the Blessed One Vipassī appeared in the world, I was born into a certain family in the city of Bandhumatī. I thought, "What kind of work is it that does not cause harm or oppression to others?" While thinking thus and investigating, I saw the work of a Dhamma-announcer. From then on, performing that work, I encouraged the multitude and performed meritorious deeds. I went about proclaiming, "Observe the Uposatha on Uposatha days! Give alms! Listen to the Dhamma! There is nothing equal to the Buddha-gem and the others; pay honor to the Triple Gem!"

Having heard my voice, the father of the Buddha, the Great King Bandhumatī, summoned me and asked, "Dear son, what are you doing as you go about?" When I replied, "O King, I go about proclaiming the virtues of the Triple Gem and encouraging the multitude in meritorious deeds," he asked me, "Where do you sit as you go about?" When I said, "On foot, O King," he said, "Dear son, you should not go about like that. Wear this flower garland and go about while seated on the back of a horse." He gave me a flower garland like a string of pearls and a trained horse. Then, with the honors given by the king, in that very manner...
52:
## The Teaching

(142) Alaṅkato cepi samaṃ careyya,
Santo danto niyato brahmacārī.
Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ,
So brāhmaṇo so samaṇo sa bhikkhu.

"I traveled about proclaiming, 'There is no other so-called jewel; perform offerings and honors to the Triple Gem.' Hearing my voice, King Bandhumatī, the father of the Buddha, summoned me and asked, 'Dear man, what are you doing as you travel about?' When I replied, 'Great King, I travel about making known the virtues of the Triple Gem and establishing the multitude in meritorious deeds,' he asked me again, 'In what manner do you travel?' When I replied, 'Great King, I travel only on foot,' he said, 'Dear man, it is not fitting for you to travel in this way. Travel while wearing this flower garland and sitting on the back of a horse.' He gave me a flower garland like a string of pearls and a well-trained horse.

Then, when the King saw me traveling and proclaiming in that same manner with the items he had given, he summoned me again and asked, 'Dear man, what are you doing as you travel?' When I replied, 'Great King, I am doing that same work,' he said, 'A horse is also not yet suitable for you; travel while sitting in this chariot.' He gave me a chariot yoked with four Sindh horses. Even for a third time, upon hearing my voice, the King summoned me and asked, 'Dear man, what are you doing as you travel?' When I replied, 'Great King, I am doing that same work,' he said, 'Dear man, a chariot is also not yet suitable for you.' He then gave me a great mass of wealth and noble ornaments, and also gave me an elephant.

Adorned with all the ornaments and sitting on the back of the elephant, I performed the work of a Dhamma-proclaimer for eighty thousand years. For such a long time, the scent of sandalwood has wafted from my body, and the scent of blue lotus has wafted from my mouth. This is the good deed I have performed," he reported.

## The Great Minister Santati's Entry into Nibbāna

Having thus recounted his own past deeds, while still remaining in the air, the Great Minister Santati entered the Tejo-kasiṇa Jhāna and attained Parinibbāna. Flames arose from his body and consumed his flesh and blood. Relics like jasmine flowers remained. The Blessed One spread out a clean cloth, and the relics fell upon it. He placed those relics in a bowl and had a stupa built at a crossroads, saying, "The great multitude, having worshipped it, will share in the merit."

The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, the Great Minister Santati attained Arahatship at the end of the verse and, while still adorned in finery, attained Parinibbāna in the air. How is it? Is it proper to call him a 'Samaṇa' or is it proper to call him a 'Brāhmaṇa'?" The Teacher, having arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" and being told, "For such a discussion," said, "Monks, it is proper to call my son a 'Samaṇa', and it is also proper to call him a 'Brāhmaṇa'." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

Yo, whichever person. Alaṅkato pi, even if adorned. Samaṃ, in harmony of body, speech, and mind. Ce careyya, if he should practice. Santo, is calmed by the stilling of passion and so forth. Danto, tames the faculties. Niyato, is firm through the fourfold Path-certainty. Brahmacārī, is one who habitually practices the noble life. Sabbesu bhūtesu, towards all living beings.
53:
Daṇḍaṃ, bodily punishment and so forth. Nidhāya, because of having laid down. So, that person. Brāhmaṇo, is called a Brahmin because of having barred evil. So, that person. Samaṇo, is called a Samaṇa because of having stilled evil. Sa so, that person. Bhikkhu, is called a Bhikkhu because of having broken the mass of defilements. Vattabbo, should be so called.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the Great Minister Santati ends.

## 10. The Story of Elder Pilotikatissa

(Pilotikatissattheravatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Hirīnisedho" regarding Elder Pilotika.

## Taking Old Rags as a Teacher

On another occasion, when Venerable Ānanda saw a boy wearing a piece of worn-out cloth and carrying a bowl, wandering for food, he said, "How is it? Is it not much better for you to become a novice than to live by wandering like this?" When the boy replied, "Venerable Sir, who will ordain me?", Ānanda said, "I will ordain you," and took the boy away.

After washing him with his own hands and giving him a meditation subject, he ordained him as a novice. When he spread out and looked at the worn-out cloth the boy had worn, he did not see any part of it that could even be used as a water-strainer, yet he placed it on a tree branch along with the bowl. Having been ordained and having received full ordination, that boy enjoyed the gains and honors that arise for the Buddhas. While wandering about wearing robes of great value, his body became stout. Due to dissatisfaction in the Dispensation, he thought, "What is the use of me wandering about wearing robes given out of faith by the multitude? I will just wear my own rags." He went to that place, took the rags, and admonished himself: "You shameless and impudent person, do you want to discard the place where such clothes are worn and go back to wandering for food with a bowl in hand, wearing these rags?" Thus, taking those rags as the object, he himself admonished himself.
54:
## The Teaching
(143) Is there any man in the world restrained by shame, who avoids reproach as a noble horse avoids the whip?
(144) Like a noble horse touched by the whip, be ardent and filled with spiritual urgency. By faith, virtue, effort, concentration, and discernment of the Dhamma, being endowed with knowledge and conduct and being mindful, you shall leave behind this great suffering.

"Bhadro": noble. "Asso": horse. "Kasā": from the whip that is about to fall on the body. Or, the whip. "Apaharati iva": just as it avoids. "Yo puriso": which man. "Niddaṃ": sleep. "Apabodheti": awakens by abandoning it. "Hirīnisedho": one who restrains evil thoughts with shame. "So puriso": that man. "Lokasmiṃ": in the world. "Koci": someone/rarely. "Vijjati": exists. Or, in another way: "Koci vijjati": is hard to find.

"Bhadro": noble. "Asso": horse. "Kasāniviṭṭho": when struck by the whip. "Ātāpī yathā": just as one who is ardent. "Saṃvegī yathā": just as one who is stirred by spiritual urgency. "Tumhe": you, dear sons. "Ātāpino": possess the effort that burns away the defilements. "Saṃvegino": possess spiritual urgency.

"Bhavatha": become so. "Saddhāya ca": with both mundane and supramundane faith. "Sīlena ca": with the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). "Vīriyena ca": with energy. "Samādhinā ca": with concentration. "Dhammavinicchayena ca": with the wisdom of discernment characterized by knowing what is a cause and what is not. "Sampannā": being endowed with. "Vijjācaraṇā": possessing the three knowledges, the eight knowledges, and the fifteen conducts. "Patissatā": being established in mindfulness. "Anappakaṃ": immeasurable. "Idaṃ dukkhaṃ": this suffering of saṃsāra. "Jahissatha": you shall abandon.

Only while being admonished did his mind become peaceful. That elder, having stored those worn-out rags right there, returned and went back to the monastery. When two or three days had passed again, because of laziness returning, he spoke in the same way and went back again. And again, it was just the same. Thus, seeing the Elder Pilotika going back and forth repeatedly, the monks asked, "Friend, where are you going?" The elder said, "Friends, I am going to my teacher's presence." Speaking in this manner, by taking only his own piece of worn-out rag as the object of meditation and restraining himself, he reached the fruit of Arahatship in just two or three days. The monks said, "Friend, how is it? Why do you not go to your teacher's presence now? Is this not your usual path?" "Friends, when there was association with the teacher, I went. But now, I have cut off that association. Therefore, I cannot go to the teacher's presence." Thus, those monks reported to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the Elder Pilotika is declaring Arahatship." When asked, "Monks, what did he say?", they replied, "Venerable Sir, he said such and such words." Upon hearing those words, the Teacher said, "Yes, monks, when my son had association, he went to the teacher's presence. But now, he has cut off that association; by restraining himself by himself, he has reached the fruit of Arahatship," and he spoke these verses:
55:
(The three knowledges: knowledge of recollecting past lives, knowledge of the divine eye, and knowledge of the destruction of taints. The eight knowledges: insight knowledge, mind-made power, supernormal powers, divine ear, penetration of the minds of others, recollection of past lives, divine eye, and knowledge of the destruction of taints. The fifteen conducts: restraint in virtue, guarding the sense faculties, moderation in eating, wakefulness, faith, shame, fear of wrongdoing, great learning, energy, mindfulness, wisdom, the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna. [According to the fourfold method].)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of the Elder Pilotikatissa ends.

## 11. The Story of Sukha Sāmaṇera
(The Story of Sukha Sāmaṇera)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Udakañhi," concerning Sukha Sāmaṇera.

## The Merchant Gandha Eating a Meal Worth a Hundred Thousand Magnificently
In the past, a great merchant of Bārāṇasī had a son named Gandha Kumāra. When the merchant's father passed away, the King of Bārāṇasī summoned the youth, comforted him, and with great honor, gave him the position of the great merchant. From that day on, the youth became known as the Merchant Gandha. Then, the Merchant Gandha's treasurer opened the doors of the treasury and showed him, saying, "Master, this much is your father's wealth, and this much is your grandfather's wealth." Having looked at the pile of wealth, the Merchant Gandha said, "Why did my father and grandfather not take this wealth with them?" "Master, there is no such thing as taking wealth with one. Beings go taking only the wholesome and unwholesome kamma they have performed." Then the Merchant Gandha thought, "My father and grandfather, because of their foolishness, collected wealth and then abandoned it to go. I, however, will go taking this wealth with me." Thinking thus, he did not think, "I will give alms" or "I will perform worship," but thought, "I will go only after eating all of this." That Merchant Gandha spent a hundred thousand to have a bathing room made of crystal. He gave a hundred thousand to have a seat made. He gave a hundred thousand to have a meal bowl made. He gave exactly a hundred thousand to have a pavilion made at the place of eating. He gave a hundred thousand to have a cover for the meal bowl. With exactly a hundred thousand, he had a lion-supported window well-placed in the house. For his breakfast, he gave a thousand, and for his dinner, he also gave a thousand.
56:
On full moon days, however, he would spend one hundred thousand for the sake of food. On the day he partook of that meal worth a hundred thousand, he would spend another hundred thousand to decorate the city and have the drum beaten, announcing: "Let the people come and behold the manner in which Gandha the Merchant enjoys his meal."

The multitude of people gathered, having constructed tiered platforms. Gandha the Merchant also sat upon a plank worth a hundred thousand in a bathing room worth a hundred thousand, and after bathing with sixteen jars of scented water, he opened the lion-window worth a hundred thousand and sat upon a couch worth a hundred thousand. Then, they placed that meal-bowl worth a hundred thousand into a bowl-stand worth a hundred thousand and served the food worth a hundred thousand. Surrounded by a troupe of dancers, he enjoyed that meal with such magnificent splendor.

## Working as a Servant to Crave the Merchant's Meal

At another time, a certain villager, for the purpose of bringing his own provisions, loaded wood and other supplies into a cart and went to the city, where he stayed at the house of a friend. At that time, it was a full moon day. The drum was beaten in the city, inviting people to behold the elegance of Gandha the Merchant's dining. Then, the city-dwelling friend asked the villager, "Friend, have you ever seen the elegance of Gandha the Merchant's dining?" When he replied, "Friend, I have never seen it," the city friend said, "If that is so, come, let us go. The drum is being beaten in the city; let us behold his great fortune." Thus, the city dweller took his friend, the villager from the countryside, and went. The multitude of people also climbed the tiered platforms to watch. The villager, merely upon smelling the aroma of the rice, said to his city friend, "I have developed a craving for a portion of rice from that bowl."

"Friend, do not desire that; it is impossible to obtain," the friend said. But the villager replied, "Friend, if I do not obtain it, I shall not live." Being unable to restrain him, the city friend stood at the edge of the crowd and shouted loudly three times, "I pay homage to you, Lord!" When asked, "Who is this?", he replied, "It is I, Lord." When asked, "What is the reason for this loud shouting?", he explained, "This villager has developed a craving for a portion of rice from your bowl. Please grant him one handful of rice."

When the merchant replied, "It is impossible to obtain," the friend asked the villager, "Friend, did you hear the merchant's words?" He replied, "I have heard them. Even so, if I obtain it, I shall live; if I do not obtain it, death will surely come to me." Therefore, the city friend shouted again, "Lord Merchant, this man will die if he does not obtain it; please grant him his life."

"My man, a handful of rice is worth a hundred, or even two hundred. If I give to every person who asks, what shall I eat?" the merchant said. The friend replied, "Lord Merchant, this man will surely die if he does not obtain it."
57:
"Please grant him his life," the friend pleaded again. The merchant replied, "It is not possible to obtain it for free. If he truly cannot live without it, let him work as a servant in my house for three years. If he can do this, I will have the bowl of rice given to him." Upon hearing the merchant's words, the villager said to his friend, "Friend, let it be so." Then, leaving his wife and children, he entered the merchant's house, saying, "I will work as a servant for three years for the sake of a bowl of rice." While performing his service, he carried out all duties with great respect. Whether in the house or in the forest, by night or by day, his diligence in all required tasks was clearly evident. He became famous throughout the entire city as "Bhatta-bhātika" (The Meal-Laborer).

## Obtaining the Bowl of Rice After Three Years of Service

Then, when the three years of Bhatta-bhātika's service were completed, the chief cook said, "Lord Merchant, Bhatta-bhātika's three years of work are complete. By working for three years, he has performed a very difficult task. Not a single task has ever been neglected." Thereupon, the merchant gave three thousand—two thousand for his own evening and morning meals and one thousand for Bhatta-bhātika's morning meal—and said, "Today, provide for him the same honors and attendance that are usually provided for me." After saying this, he set aside only one beloved wife named Cintāmaṇi and told the rest of the household, "Today, attend only to Bhatta-bhātika." He then handed over all his wealth and splendor to him.

Bhatta-bhātika bathed with the merchant's scented water in the merchant's own bathing room while sitting on the plank worth a hundred thousand. He wore the merchant's own garments and sat upon the merchant's own couch worth a hundred thousand. The merchant also had the drum beaten in the city, announcing: "Bhatta-bhātika has worked as a servant in the house of Gandha the Merchant for three years and has obtained a bowl of rice. Let the people behold the splendor of his dining." A great multitude of people climbed the tiered platforms to watch. Every place he looked upon seemed to tremble. Dancers stood surrounding him, and the bowl of rice was served and placed before Bhatta-bhātika.

## The Arrival of a Paccekabuddha Before the Meal

As Bhatta-bhātika was washing his hands, a Paccekabuddha on Mount Gandhamādana emerged from meditative attainment on the seventh day. Reflecting, "Where should I go for alms today?", he saw Bhatta-bhātika. Then the Paccekabuddha considered, "This Bhatta-bhātika has obtained a bowl of rice by working for three years. Does he have faith or not?" Knowing that he did have faith, he thought, "Even some who have faith are unable to make an offering. Will he be able to make an offering to me?" Realizing that he would be able to, and that by making an offering to him, the man would attain great fortune...
58:
Even so, some people are unable to provide support and patronage. He reflected again, "Will he be able to provide support to me?" Then, knowing that Bhattabhatika would indeed be able to do so, and that by relying on the cause of supporting him, the man would obtain great wealth and happiness, the Paccekabuddha robed himself, took his alms-bowl, and ascended into the air. Traveling through the sky, he appeared standing directly in front of Bhattabhatika. When Bhattabhatika saw the Paccekabuddha, he thought: "In the past, because I did not give offerings, I have had to work as a servant in another's house for three years just for a single bowl of rice. Now, this rice would sustain me for only one night and one day. If, however, I give it to this Noble One, it will protect me for many thousands of crores of aeons. Therefore, I shall give this bowl of rice to this Noble One alone."

Without putting even a single morsel of the rice—which he had earned by working for three years—into his own mouth, and having dispelled his craving to eat, Bhattabhatika himself lifted the bowl of rice and went to the Paccekabuddha. He handed the bowl to another person, prostrated with the five-point prostration, and then, holding the bowl with his left hand, he poured the alms-food into the Paccekabuddha's bowl with his right hand. When half of the rice remained, the Paccekabuddha covered the bowl with his hand. At that time, Bhattabhatika said to the Paccekabuddha: "Venerable Sir, a single portion meant for one person should not be divided into two. Please do not favor me in this present life; favor me only for the life hereafter. I shall give the entire portion without leaving any remainder."

(Indeed, an offering made without leaving even a little for oneself is called a 'gift without remainder,' and it bears great fruit.)

## Offering, Making Aspirations, and Rejoicing

Having acted in this manner and given everything, Bhattabhatika prostrated again and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, because of a single bowl of rice, I have suffered by working as a servant in another's house for three years. Now, in every place I am reborn, may there be only happiness. May I be a partaker of the Dhamma that you, Venerable Sir, have realized."

The Paccekabuddha said, "May it be as you have aspired," and wishing to give a blessing, he said: "May all your intentions be fulfilled like the Cintāmaṇi jewel that grants all desires, or like the full moon."

"May all that you have wished and aspired for
be fulfilled quickly.
May all your intentions be fulfilled,
like the moon on the fifteenth day.

May all that you have wished and aspired for
be fulfilled quickly.
May all your intentions be fulfilled,
like the wish-fulfilling Mani-jotirasa jewel."

(Detailed word-for-word translation of the verses follows in the source text: Icchitaṃ: what is desired; patthitaṃ: what is aspired; tuyhaṃ: for you; khippameva: very quickly; samijjhatu: may it be fulfilled. Candopannaraso yathā: like the full moon on the fifteenth day. Sabbe: all; saṅkappā: good intentions; pūrentu: may they be fulfilled. Maṇijotiraso yathā: like the Mani-jotirasa jewel which can fulfill all desires.)

After giving this blessing, the Paccekabuddha made a determination: "May this multitude of people remain seeing me until I reach Mount Gandhamādana," and he departed through the air to Mount Gandhamādana. The multitude of people remained there, watching the Paccekabuddha. Upon reaching Mount Gandhamādana, the Paccekabuddha shared and gave that alms-food to five hundred other Paccekabuddhas. All the Paccekabuddhas accepted just enough for their sustenance.
60:
## Becoming Sukha the Youth in the Present Buddha's Era
That Bhattabhatika became friends with Gandha the Treasurer, and they lived together, eating and drinking until the end of their lives. After passing away from that existence, he was reborn in the celestial realm and enjoyed divine bliss for the interval between two Buddhas. When the present Gautama Buddha appeared in the world, he took rebirth in Sāvatthī in the family of a supporter of the Elder Sāriputta. At that time, the mother of the youth who had been Bhattabhatika received pregnancy protection. After a few days, she developed a pregnancy craving, thinking: "Oh, how wonderful it would be if I could offer a meal of a hundred flavors to five hundred monks led by the Elder Sāriputta, wear ochre-dyed garments, take a golden bowl, sit at the end of the seats, and eat the leftovers of those monks." She acted accordingly and satisfied her craving. She also gave similar offerings at the remaining auspicious ceremonies. After giving birth to the son, on the naming day, she said to the Elder: "Venerable Sir, please give the precepts to my son." The Elder asked: "What is his name?" She replied: "Venerable Sir, since my son was conceived, no one in this house has ever experienced suffering (dukkha). Therefore, his name shall be Sukha Kumāra." Hearing this, the Elder took that name, Sukha Kumāra, and gave him the precepts. At that time, the mother thought: "I will not thwart my son's wishes." She also gave offerings in the same manner at his ear-piercing ceremony and other occasions.

## The Ordination of Young Sukha, Formerly Bhattabhatika
When the youth reached the age of seven, he said: "Mother, I wish to ordain as a novice under the Elder Sāriputta." The mother said: "Very well, my dear, I will not thwart your wishes." She invited the Elder Sāriputta, offered him food, and said: "Venerable Sir, my son wishes to ordain as a novice. I will bring this youth to the monastery in the evening." After sending the Elder back, she gathered her relatives and said: "I will perform today the duties that should be done for my son while he is a layman." She adorned her son and, with great splendor and glory, took him to the monastery and handed him over to the Elder Sāriputta. The Elder Sāriputta said to the youth: "My dear, what is called the life of a novice is difficult to practice. Will you be able to find delight in it?" When the youth replied: "Venerable Sir, I will follow your instructions," the Elder gave him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. The parents, wishing to make an offering for his ordination, stayed within the monastery for seven days, offering food of a hundred flavors to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha, and returned to their home in the evening. On the eighth day, when the Elder Sāriputta entered the village with the Saṅgha, he performed his duties at the monastery and, having the novice carry his bowl and robes, entered the village for alms. Along the way, the novice saw irrigation channels and so forth, and asked questions just like Paṇḍita Sāmaṇera. The Elder Sāriputta answered the novice Sukha in the same way he had answered Paṇḍita Sāmaṇera.

## Novice Sukha Attaining the Three Lower Fruits
Upon hearing those explanations, the novice Sukha said: "Venerable Sir, if you would please take your bowl and robes, I wish to return." Therefore, the Elder Sāriputta, not thwarting the novice's wish, said: "Novice, give me my bowl and robes." After taking the bowl and robes, the novice paid homage to the Elder Sāriputta and, as he was returning, said: "Venerable Sir, when you bring food for me, please bring food of a hundred flavors." When the Elder asked: "From where can such food be obtained?", the novice replied: "Venerable Sir, if it cannot be obtained through your merit, it will be obtained through mine."
61:
Then, Venerable Sāriputta gave the key to Sukha Sāmaṇera and entered the village for alms. Sukha Sāmaṇera also went to the monastery, opened the Elder's chamber, entered, closed the door, and sat down, applying wisdom to his own body. Due to the power of Sukha Sāmaṇera's virtues, Sakka's Paṇḍukambala stone throne showed signs of heat. When Sakka looked to see the reason, he saw the novice and thought, "Sukha Sāmaṇera has returned his bowl and robes to his preceptor, intending to practice the Dhamma of a recluse. It is proper for me to go there." He summoned the Four Great Kings and sent them off, saying, "Friends, go and drive away the noisy birds in the forest near Jetavana Monastery." Those four Great Kings did as Sakka commanded and took up guard all around. He commanded the Moon deity and the Sun deity, "Hold back your celestial mansions and stand still." Those Moon and Sun deities also did as Sakka commanded. He himself took up guard at the place where the door-latch string is pulled. The monastery became quiet and silent. The novice developed insight with a concentrated mind and reached the three Paths and Fruits.

## Sukha Sāmaṇera Attaining Arahantship
Venerable Sāriputta thought, "Sukha Sāmaṇera said, 'Please bring food of a hundred flavors.' In whose house might it be possible to get it?" Looking around, he saw a lay supporter who was full of such aspiration. He went to that house, and the devotees, with joyful hearts, saying, "Venerable sir, it is well that you have come here today," took his bowl, invited him to sit, and offered rice porridge and snacks. Because they requested him to preach the Dhamma until the time for the main meal, Venerable Sāriputta preached to those devotees a Dhamma talk worthy of being remembered for a lifetime. Noting the time, he concluded the teaching. Then, they offered him food of a hundred flavors. Seeing the Elder wishing to take that food and depart, they said, "Venerable sir, please eat; we will offer you another portion as well." After serving the Elder his meal, they again filled his bowl. Taking that food, the Elder hurried back to the monastery, thinking, "It is time for my novice to be hungry." On that day, the Buddha had come out early in the morning and, sitting in the Gandhakuṭī, reflected: "Today, Sukha Sāmaṇera returned his bowl and robes to his preceptor, intending to practice the Dhamma of a recluse."
62:
"Will the task of a recluse be completed for this novice?" As He reflected, He saw that the novice had reached the three Paths and Fruits. Investigating further, He saw, "This novice will be able to reach Arahantship today. However, Sāriputta is coming out quickly with food, thinking it is time for the novice to be hungry. If he brings the food before this novice reaches Arahantship, it will be an obstacle for the novice. It is proper for me to go and take up guard at the gatehouse." Thinking thus, He left the Gandhakuṭī and stood at the gatehouse to keep guard.

Venerable Sāriputta also brought the food. Then, the Buddha asked him four questions in the same manner as mentioned below. At the conclusion of the answers to the questions, the novice reached Arahantship.

## Criticism for Eating After Noon
The Buddha called Venerable Sāriputta and said, "Sāriputta, go and give the food to the novice." The Elder went and knocked on the door. The novice came out, performed his duties to his preceptor, and when told, "Perform the task of eating your meal," he realized that Venerable Sāriputta had no need for the food. The seven-year-old boy, having reached Arahantship at that very moment, reflected on the state of Nibbāna, the state of peace, then ate his meal and washed his bowl. At that time, the Four Great Kings released their guard. The Moon and Sun deities also released their celestial mansions. Sakka also released his guard at the door-latch string. The sun appeared only after it had passed the middle of the sky. The monks said, "It seems like evening, yet the novice has just finished his meal. How is it? Today the morning was very long, and the evening is short." The Buddha came and asked, "Monks, what subject are you discussing as you sit here now?" When they informed Him, "Venerable sir, today the morning was very long and the evening is short. The novice has just finished his meal. Indeed, the sun appears only after passing the zenith," He replied: "Monks, it is just so when those with merit practice the Dhamma of a recluse. Today, the Four Great Kings took up guard all around. The Moon and Sun deities stood holding back their mansions. Sakka took up guard at the door-latch string. I myself also took up guard at the gatehouse."
63:
## The Teaching
(145) Irrigators lead the water; fletchers bend the arrow-shaft;
Carpenters shape the wood; those of good conduct discipline themselves.

*Nettikā*, those who lead water, lead the water (*udakaṃ*) to wherever they desire. *Usuukārā*, fletchers, make the arrow (*tejanaṃ*) straight. *Tacchakā*, carpenters, shape the wood (*dāruṃ*) straight or curved as they wish. *Subbatā*, those who are easy to admonish, discipline themselves (*attānaṃ*) to attain the Path and Fruit.

"Today, Sukha Sāmaṇera, having seen those who lead water in channels, fletchers who straighten arrows, and carpenters who make wheels and such, disciplined himself and attained the Fruit of Arahatship." Having said this, the Buddha spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of Sukha Sāmaṇera ends.

Here ends the commentary on the tenth chapter, the Daṇḍavagga.
