## 11. Jarāvagga
## 1. The Story of Visākhā’s Companions
(Visākhāyā Sahāyikānaṃ Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Ko nu hāso kimānando" in reference to the women who were companions of Visākhā.

## The Women who Drank Liquor Secretly
In Sāvatthī, five hundred young men of good family, thinking, "In this way, these women will live without negligence," entrusted their respective wives to the great lay devotee named Visākhā. Whenever those women went to a park or a monastery, they went only with Visākhā. On one occasion, when a seven-day drinking festival was proclaimed, those five hundred women prepared liquor for their husbands. Those men celebrated the drinking festival for seven days, and on the eighth day, when the work-drum was sounded, they left their wives and went to their work.

Then those women thought, "We did not get to drink liquor in the presence of our husbands. There is still leftover liquor. Let us drink this in such a way that those husbands do not know." They went to Visākhā and said, "Lady Visākhā, we wish to see the park." When she said, "Very well, mothers, then depart after performing your necessary duties," they went with her. Secretly bringing the liquor, they drank it in the park and wandered about intoxicated and negligent. 

Visākhā thought, "What these women have done is improper. Now even the heretics will blame me, saying, 'Visākhā, the disciple of the Ascetic Gotama, wanders about drinking liquor.'" Thinking thus, she said to those women, "Mothers, you have done an improper thing. You have caused me to lose my reputation. Your husbands will also be angry with you. What will you do now?" They replied, "Lady Visākhā, we will show the appearance of sick patients (we will pretend to be ill)." She said, "If that is so, you will be revealed by your own actions." 

When those women reached home, they pretended to be ill. Then, when their husbands asked, "Where is such-and-such a woman, and such-and-such a woman?" and heard that they were ill, they realized, "Surely these women must have drunk the leftover liquor." Having noted this, they beat those women and brought them to ruin and disaster.
65:
## The Drunken Women Possessed by a Deity in Front of the Buddha

When those women encountered another drinking festival, they wished to drink again in the same manner. They approached Visākhā and said, "Lady Visākhā, please take us to the park again." Visākhā refused them, saying, "Previously, you caused me to lose my reputation. Go away; I will not take you anymore." After they pacified her, saying, "We will not do such a thing again," they approached her once more and said, "Lady Visākhā, we wish to make an offering to the Buddha. Please take us to the monastery."

When she said, "Mothers, now it is proper. Go and prepare the offerings," those women had perfumes, flowers, and other items placed in baskets. Carrying small pots filled with liquor in their hands, they covered themselves with large cloaks and approached Visākhā. Entering the monastery together with Visākhā, they sat in a suitable place, drank the liquor from the small pots, discarded the pots, and sat before the Blessed One in the Dhamma hall.

Visākhā said, "Venerable Sir, please preach the Dhamma to these women." Due to the force of intoxication, those women, with trembling bodies, gave rise to the thought, "We want to dance; we want to sing." Then, a deity belonging to Māra’s host thought, "I will possess the bodies of these women and display unseemly behavior in front of the ascetic Gotama," and possessed their bodies. Among those women, some began to clap their hands and laugh in front of the Teacher, while others began to dance.

## Admonishing After Inspiring Terror

While the Teacher was reflecting, "What is this?", he came to know the cause and thought, "I will not give an opportunity to those of Māra’s host now. I have not fulfilled the perfections for such a long time for the sake of giving an opportunity to Māra’s host." Therefore, to terrify those women, he emitted dark rays from his eyebrows. Instantly, there was thick darkness. Those women were terrified, struck by the fear of death. Because of that, the liquor in their bellies dried up and disappeared.

The Teacher, vanishing from the throne where he was sitting, stood on the summit of Mount Sineru and emitted white rays from his uṇṇā-loma (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows; a soft, white hair-tuft that curls to the right and points upward in the middle of the forehead between the two eyebrows, being one fathom and a half in length). At that very moment, it was as if a thousand moons had risen. Then, the Teacher addressed those women, "When coming to my presence, it is not proper for you to come heedlessly. It is only because of your heedlessness that the deity of Māra’s host gained an opportunity and made you laugh and so on in a place where laughter is inappropriate. Now, you should strive to extinguish the fires of lust and the rest," and spoke this verse:
66:
## The Teaching

(146) "What laughter, what joy, when the world is constantly burning? Shrouded in darkness, why do you not seek a lamp?"

Constantly: always. When burning: while there is burning by the eleven fires such as lust, or while the multitude of people is burning. Laughter: what is its nature? Joy: what is its nature? (Meaning: is it not something that should not be done?) Shrouded in darkness: while being enveloped by the great darkness of ignorance. You: why do you not seek or create the lamp of wisdom?

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the five hundred women were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

## A Brief Account of the Origin of Liquor

When the Teacher knew that those women were established in unshakable faith (acala-saddhā), he descended from the summit of Mount Sineru and sat on the Buddha-seat. Then Visākhā said to him, "Venerable Sir, this liquor is indeed evil. These women, being of such a nature, were unable to maintain even their basic posture while sitting before a Buddha like you, but stood up, clapped, and began laughing, singing, and dancing."

The Teacher said, "Lay disciple Visākhā, it is true. This liquor is indeed of an evil nature. Depending on this liquor, many beings have come to ruin and destruction." When asked, "Venerable Sir, when did this liquor first originate?", he brought forth a story of the past to explain its origin in detail and preached the Kumbha Jātaka in the Tiṃsanipāta.

The story of Visākhā’s companions ends.

## The Weapon of Victory

Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer the wicked with goodness.
Conquer the stingy with giving; conquer the liar with truth.

With non-anger: by not being angry, one conquers the angry person. With goodness: by having a good nature, one conquers the wicked. With giving: by giving one's own property, one conquers the stingy. With truth: by speaking truthful words, one conquers the liar.

## 2. The Story of Sirimā

(Sirimā-vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Veḷuvana Monastery, preached this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Passa cittakataṃ" concerning Sirimā.

## Who Sirimā Was

That Sirimā was a very beautiful courtesan in the city of Rājagaha. During one rainy season (vassa), she offended a female lay follower named Uttarā, who was the daughter of the treasurer Puṇṇaka and the wife of the son of the great treasurer Sumana. Wishing to please her, she invited the Teacher along with the community of monks for a meal at the house of the lay follower named Uttarā. After the meal was finished, she asked the Teacher for forgiveness and heard the Dhamma teaching of the Buddha's appreciation (anumodanā) on that day. At the end of the verse, she reached the fruit of Stream-entry.
67:
(What has been said so far is the summary of this story. The detailed account will become clear in the commentary on the verse of rejoicing in the Kodhavagga.)

Thus, when Sirimā had attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), she invited the community of monks and, on the following morning, gave a great offering of alms. She then established a permanent offering of Aṭṭhaka-bhatta (alms-food offered to a group of eight monks) to the Saṅgha. From that time onwards, eight monks went to her house regularly. Saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept ghee; please accept milk," and so forth, she would fill the bowls of those monks. The food received by a single monk was sufficient for three or four monks. Every day, alms-food was offered at a cost of sixteen kahāpaṇas. Then one day, a certain monk, after eating the Aṭṭhaka-bhatta intended for the eight monks at Sirimā's house, went to a monastery three yojanas away. Later, in the evening, while he was sitting in the assembly of elders, they asked him, "Friend, where did you come from after having your meal?" When he replied, "I have eaten the Aṭṭhaka-bhatta of Sirimā," they asked again, "Friend, did she offer it in a pleasing manner?" He said, "It is impossible to fully praise Sirimā's food; she offers it in an extremely refined manner. The food received by one monk is enough for three or four. Moreover, her appearance and beauty are even more superior than the offerings she gives. That woman is of such and such a nature," thus he spoke in praise of Sirimā's virtues.

## The Monk Obsessed with Sirimā

At that time, a certain monk, hearing the talk about her virtues, developed affection for her without even having seen her. Thinking, "I must go and see that Sirimā," he stated his seniority (vassa) and inquired about the turn to go. When he was told, "Friend, tomorrow you will be the senior monk of the group and will receive the Aṭṭhaka-bhatta at Sirimā's house," he immediately took his bowl and robes and departed. At dawn the next morning, he entered the place where the food-tickets (salāka) were distributed and, standing as the senior monk of the group, he obtained the Aṭṭhaka-bhatta at Sirimā's house. As for the monk who had eaten there the previous day and departed, at the very moment of his departure, an illness arose in Sirimā's body. Therefore, she took off her ornaments and lay down. Then, Sirimā's maids, seeing the monks who had arrived for the Aṭṭhaka-bhatta, informed her. Sirimā, being unable to take the bowls with her own hands to seat the monks or to serve them, commanded her maids, "Mothers, take the bowls, seat the noble ones, and after serving them gruel and snacks, fill their bowls with rice when it is mealtime and offer it."

They replied, "Very well, mistress," and after ushering the monks in, serving them gruel and snacks, they filled the bowls with rice when it was mealtime and informed her. Sirimā said, "Please support and carry me; I will pay respects to the noble ones." Being carried by the maids to the presence of the monks, she paid respects to them with a trembling body. That monk, looking at Sirimā, thought: "Even while she is ill, the beauty of this woman is of such a nature. How much more would the perfection of Sirimā's beauty be when she is healthy and adorned with all her ornaments?"
68:
Then, the defilements (kilesa) that had been accumulated and stored within him for many crores of years arose. He became devoid of wisdom and, being unable to eat his meal, took his bowl to the monastery, covered it, placed it aside, spread out the edge of his robe, and lay down. Then, although a companion monk pleaded with him, he was unable to eat. He remained without food. 

## The Death of Sirimā

On that very day, in the evening, Sirimā passed away. King Bimbisāra sent a message to the Teacher, saying, "Venerable Sir, Sirimā, the younger sister of Jīvaka, has passed away." Upon hearing this, the Teacher sent a message back to the King, saying, "There is no need for the funeral rites of Sirimā. Have her body placed in the charnel ground (āmaka-susāna) in such a way that crows, dogs, and other animals cannot eat it, and have it guarded." The King did as the Buddha commanded. Three days passed in succession, and on the fourth day, the body became bloated. Maggots flowed out from the nine openings. The entire body broke apart and appeared like a pot of boiling rice.

## The Assembly of Monks and Laypeople Viewing Sirimā's Corpse

King Bimbisāra had a drum sounded throughout the city of Rājagaha, announcing, "Except for those guarding the houses, anyone who does not come to see Sirimā shall be fined eight kahāpaṇas." He also sent word to the presence of the Buddha, saying, "May the community of monks headed by the Buddha come to see Sirimā." The Teacher informed the monks, "We shall go to see Sirimā." That young monk had also remained lying down for four days, refusing to listen to anyone's words and abstaining from food. The food in his bowl had become rotten, and the bowl was covered in grime. Then his companion monk approached him and said, "Friend, the Teacher is going to see Sirimā." Although the young monk was in a state of hunger, he jumped up immediately at the mere mention of the word "Sirimā" and asked, "What did you say?" When told, "The Teacher is going to see Sirimā; will you also go?" he replied, "Yes, I will go." He discarded the rotten food, washed his bowl, put it in its bag, and went along with the community of monks. The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, stood on one side. The community of bhikkhunīs, the royal retinue, the laymen, and the laywomen also stood on their respective sides.

## No One Wants Sirimā Anymore

The Teacher asked the King, "Great King, who is this woman?" "Venerable Sir, she is the sister of Jīvaka, named Sirimā."
69:
## The Teaching

(147) Behold this beautified image, a mass of sores, a heaped-up body, sickly, full of many thoughts, which has no stability or permanence.

*Cittakataṃ*: beautifully adorned with clothes, ornaments, flowers, perfumes, and the like. *Bimbaṃ*: like a doll, beautiful and graceful with limbs and parts that are appropriately long or short. *Samussitaṃ*: erected and supported by three hundred bones. *Āturaṃ*: constantly afflicted and in pain. *Bahusaṅkappaṃ*: that which is imagined and thought of in many ways by the multitude of people. *Arukāyaṃ*: the physical body which is a mass of sores due to the nine openings. *Passa*: behold it. *Yassa*: for this body. *Dhuvam*: permanence. *Ṭhiti*: stability. *Natthi*: there is none indeed.

"It is the woman, Bhante," he reported. When asked, "Is this woman Sirimā?", he replied, "Yes, Bhante, it is Sirimā." The Buddha then said, "If that is so, have a drum beaten throughout the city, announcing: 'Let those who pay a thousand [kahāpaṇas] take Sirimā.'" The King did as the Buddha instructed. However, there was not a single person who said "I will" or "Let her be ours" with pleasure. The King reported to the Blessed One, "Bhante, they do not take her."

"If that is so, Great King, reduce the price," the Buddha said. The King had the drum beaten again, saying, "Let them take her for five hundred kahāpaṇas." Seeing no one willing to take her, he had the drum beaten for two hundred and fifty, two hundred, one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, ten, five, one kahāpaṇa, then for half a kahāpaṇa, a quarter (pāda), a māsaka, and a kākaṇika. Yet, no one desired that Sirimā. Finally, he had the drum beaten, saying, "Let them take her for free, without any price." Still, there was no one who said "I will" or "Let her be ours" with pleasure. The King reported, "Bhante, there is no one who will take her even for free."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, look at this woman who was so beloved by the multitude. In this very city of Rājagaha, they previously had to pay a thousand to get her for just one day. Now, there is no one who wants to take her even for free and without price. Monks, such a form as this reaches decay and destruction. Behold this body (attabhāva) which is constantly afflicted."

Having said this, he spoke this verse:

(The three hundred bones are: 64 hand bones, 64 foot bones, 64 soft bones attached to flesh, 2 heel bones, 4 ankle bones, 4 lower leg bones, 2 knee bones, 2 thigh bones, 2 hip bones, 18 spinal bones, 24 ribs, 14 chest bones, 1 heart bone, 2 collar bones, 2 shoulder blades, 2 upper arm bones, 4 forearm bones, 7 neck bones, 2 jaw bones, 1 nose bone, 2 eye socket bones, 2 ear bones, 1 forehead bone, 1 crown bone, and 9 skull bones—excluding the 32 teeth. Total: 300 bones.)

## The Monk Infatuated with Sirimā Becomes a Sotāpanna

At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Four Noble Truths. That monk also was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala).

The Story of Sirimā ends.
70:
## 3. The Story of Uttarā Therī

(Uttarātherī Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Parijiṇṇamidaṃ," concerning a nun named Uttarā Therī.

## Falling from Exhaustion While Alms-gathering

Uttarā Therī was one hundred and twenty years old from birth. Having wandered for alms and obtained food, she saw a monk on the way and invited him to take the food. When the monk accepted without refusal, she gave him all the food and remained without nourishment. In this way, on the second and third days as well, she gave her food to that same monk at that same place and remained without nourishment. On the fourth day, while going for alms, she saw the Teacher in a narrow place. While stepping back to make way, she trod on the hem of her robe which was hanging down. Unable to steady herself, she lost her balance and fell down headlong. The Blessed One went to Uttarā Therī and said, "Sister, your body is worn out and decayed; it will break up before long," and he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(148) This body is worn out, a nest of diseases, fragile. This putrid mass breaks up, for life ends in death.

*Bhagini*: Sister. *Tava*: your. *Idaṃ rūpaṃ*: this form which is the body. *Parijiṇṇam*: is worn out and decayed by old age. *Roganīḷaṃ*: it is the dwelling place of all diseases. *Pabhaṅguraṃ*: it is fragile and constantly oozing putridity. *Pūti*: being putrid. *Saṃ sandehā*: your body. *Bhijjati*: will soon break up. *Hi*: indeed, that is true. *Jīvitaṃ*: life. *Maraṇantaṃ*: ends in death.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, Uttarā Therī attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the multitude of people.

(This nun was one who practiced the Sāraṇīya Dhamma (Qualities of Communal Harmony):
1. Performing bodily acts with loving-kindness.
2. Speaking verbal acts with loving-kindness.
3. Thinking mental acts with loving-kindness.
4. Sharing obtained gains with fellow practitioners before using them oneself.
5. Maintaining precepts without breaking, piercing, spotting, or mottling them.
6. Being pure in Right View.
If one practices these six things to be remembered for twelve years throughout one's life, the Sāraṇīya Dhamma is fulfilled. The benefit is immense.)

The Story of Uttarā Therī ends.
71:
## 4. The Story of Many Monks Who Overestimated Themselves
(Sambahula-adhimānika-bhikkhu Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching, beginning with the words "Yānimāni," concerning many monks who overestimated themselves, thinking they had attained the fruit of Arahatship.

## The Benefit of the Cemetery
It is said that five hundred monks took meditation subjects from the Teacher and entered the forest. As they strove and exerted themselves with unflagging effort, they attained jhāna. Because their defilements did not manifest, they thought, "Our task as monks is accomplished. Let us go and inform the Teacher of the qualities we have attained." Thus, they returned.

When those monks reached the outer gatehouse, the Teacher said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, there is no need for these monks to enter and see me yet. Let them go to the charnel ground where corpses are discarded, and only after returning from there may they see me."

The Elder went and informed the monks of this matter. The five hundred monks did not say, "What use do we have for a charnel ground?" Instead, thinking, "The Buddha, who is far-sighted, must have seen a reason," they went to the charnel ground. There, upon seeing rotting corpses, they attained the perception of bones (aṭṭhika-saññā) regarding the corpses that had been discarded for one or two days. However, at that moment, they felt lustful attachment (rāga) for the fresh bodies that had just been discarded. In that instant, they realized they still possessed defilements.

While remaining in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), the Teacher sent forth his radiance and, as if speaking in the presence of those monks, said, "Bhikkhus, is it proper or fitting for you to feel lustful delight upon seeing such a collection of bones?" He then spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(149) Yānimāni apatthāni, alābūneva sārade;
Kāpotakāni aṭṭhīni, tāni disvāna kā rati.

(Those bones which are cast away, like gourds in the autumn season, greyish like pigeons—what delight can there be in seeing them?)

[Yānimāni aṭṭhīni: those bones. Apatthāni: which are cast away. Sārade: in the autumn season, struck by wind and sun. Alābūneva: like gourds scattered here and there. Kāpotakāni: having a color like that of a pigeon. Tāni aṭṭhīni disvāna: having seen those bones. Tumhākaṃ rati kā: what delight can there be for you? (The meaning is: it is not at all proper to feel even a slight amount of sensual delight.)]

(In the winter, there are two seasons: Hemanta and Sisira. Similarly, in the summer, there are two: Vasanta and Gimha. In the rainy season, there are two: Vassāna and Sārada. Since there are six minor seasons in total, the period from the first waning day of Tawthalin to the full moon of Tazaungmon is called the Sārada season.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, those monks, while standing right there, attained the fruit of Arahatship. They then came and paid homage to the Blessed One, praising him greatly.

The Story of Many Monks Who Overestimated Themselves ends.
72:
## 5. The Story of Theri Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā
(Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā Therī Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching, beginning with the words "Aṭṭhīnaṃ nagaraṃ kataṃ," concerning the Theri named Rūpanandā, also known as Janapadakalyāṇī (The Beauty of the Country).

## Rūpanandā’s Reflection on Becoming a Bhikkhunī
One day, Princess Rūpanandā, known as Janapadakalyāṇī, reflected thus: "My eldest brother, Prince Siddhattha, renounced the glory of kingship, ordained, and became the Buddha, the supreme person in the world. His son, Prince Rāhula, has also ordained. My beloved husband, Prince Nanda, has ordained. My mother, Queen Gotamī, has also ordained. (At that time, her father, King Suddhodana, had already attained Arahatship under the white parasol in the palace and passed into Parinibbāna, and King Bhaddiya was reigning.) Since so many of my relatives have ordained, what is the use of me staying in the palace? I shall ordain as well."

Thinking thus, she went to the nunnery and ordained.

## Not Ordained Out of Faith
That princess ordained only out of love for her relatives, not out of faith (saddhā). Because of her extreme beauty, she was famously known as Rūpanandā. Having heard that the Teacher says, "Form is impermanent, suffering, and non-self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, and non-self," Rūpanandā thought, "He might speak of the faults in my form, which is so beautiful and pleasing to look at." Thus, she avoided going into the presence of the Teacher.

The citizens of Sāvatthī would give alms early in the morning, and having well-observed the Uposatha precepts, they would wear clean upper robes and, carrying perfumes and flowers, gather at the Jetavana Monastery in the evening to listen to the Dhamma. The community of bhikkhunīs, also having a wholesome desire for the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, would go to the monastery to listen. Those who entered the city after listening to the Dhamma would enter while speaking only of the Buddha's virtues.

(At this point, one should know the four types of standards/measures and their nature:
1. Rūpappamāṇika: Beings who take form as their standard. They gain faith when they see the Buddha's golden body adorned with the major and minor marks. Two-thirds of beings are of this type.
2. Ghosappamāṇika: Beings who take sound as their standard. They gain faith when they hear the fame of the Buddha's virtues based on many hundreds of births, or when they hear the sound of his Dhamma teaching endowed with eight qualities. Three-quarters of beings are of this type.
3. Lūkhappamāṇika: Beings who take austerity as their standard. They gain faith based on the austerity of the Buddha's robes and so on. Nine-tenths of beings are of this type.
4. Dhammappamāṇika: Beings who take Dhamma as their standard. They gain faith thinking, 'Such is the virtue of the Ten-Powered One, such is his concentration, such is his wisdom. The Blessed One is peerless and matchless in virtue, concentration, and wisdom.' Only about one in a hundred thousand is of this type.)

## One Who Wishes to Go to the Buddha's Assembly Without Being Seen
When Rūpanandā heard the talk concerning the Buddha's virtues from the bhikkhunīs and the laywomen, she thought, "They praise my brother's virtues excessively. Even if he were to speak of the faults in my form all day long, how much could he say? It would be good if I were to go with the bhikkhunīs and, without showing myself, see the Buddha, listen to his Dhamma, and then return."

That Rūpanandā then informed the bhikkhunīs, "I, too, will go to listen to the Dhamma today." The bhikkhunīs, with joyful hearts, thought, "It has been a long time since Rūpanandā desired to go and pay respects to the Teacher. Today, the Teacher will give a wonderful teaching with various methods on account of Rūpanandā." They took her with them and departed. From the moment she set out, Rūpanandā thought, "I will not show myself."

Like a crow before a king of swans, her form—
73:
The Blessed One reflected, “Today, Rūpanandā will come to pay her respects to me. What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for her?” As he considered this, he realized, “This Rūpanandā places great importance on physical beauty. She has a strong affection for her own body. Just as one might extract a thorn with a thorn, it is appropriate to use beauty itself to subdue her intoxication with beauty.” Having made this decision, when she entered the monastery, he used his psychic power to create an extremely beautiful young woman, about sixteen years of age, dressed in fine garments, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, and holding a fan while standing near the Blessed One as if fanning him. Only the Buddha and Rūpanandā could see this created woman; others did not see her. Rūpanandā entered the monastery along with the other bhikkhunīs, stood behind them, and after prostrating before the Blessed One with the fivefold touch, she sat among the bhikkhunīs. Looking at the Blessed One from his feet upwards, she saw his body adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks, surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance. While gazing at his face, which possessed the splendor of the full moon, she saw the form of the young woman standing nearby. Looking at that woman and then at herself, she felt as though she were a crow in the presence of a royal golden swan. From the moment she saw that magically created form, her eyes were as if spinning. She thought, “Oh, how beautiful this woman’s hair is! Oh, how beautiful her forehead is!” Her mind was captivated by the splendor of every part of that woman’s body, and she felt a powerful affection for that form.

## From Youth to Old Age, From Old Age to Sickness, From Sickness to Death

The Blessed One, knowing Rūpanandā’s great delight and infatuation with that physical form, even while preaching the Dhamma, [transformed] that form...
74:
“Behold, Nandā, this assembly [of the body], diseased, impure, and putrid; oozing from above and trickling from below, it is much desired by the foolish.

As is this [body], so was that; as was that, so is this. See it as elements, as empty; do not return to the world. Having dispelled desire for existence, one shall live in peace.”

Nandā: Rūpanandā. Āturaṃ: constantly subject to pain. Asuciṃ: impure. Pūtiṃ: putrid. Uggharantan: overflowing and vomiting from the upper orifices. Paggharantan: trickling and leaking from the lower orifices. Bālānaṃ: by the foolish who lack the eye of wisdom. Abhipatthitaṃ: greatly desired and constantly craved. Samussayaṃ: this great body which is a collection of loathsome things. Passa: behold.

Idaṃ: this physical form. Dhātuto: as elements. Suññato: as empty. Passa yathā: just as one should see. Tathā: in the same way. Etaṃ: that physical form. Passa: behold. Etaṃ: that physical form. Dhātuto: as elements. Suññato: as empty. Passa yathā: just as one should see. Tathā: in the same way. Idaṃ: this physical form. Passa: behold. Puna: again. Lokaṃ: to the world. Mā āgami: do not come. Bhave: in the three realms of existence. Chandan: the desire of delight. Virājetvā: having made it fade away. Upasanto: being at peace. Carissati: one shall practice (or, one shall reach the end of Nibbāna).

## The Teaching

(150) A city is built of bones, plastered with flesh and blood, wherein old age and death, conceit and disparagement are deposited.

Aṭṭhīnaṃ: of bones that are set up (bound together by sinews). Maṃsalohitalepanaṃ: plastered with flesh and blood. Nagaraṃ: the house of the body. Kataṃ: is built. Yattha: in which house of the body. Jarā ca: old age. Maccu ca: death. Māno ca: conceit. Makkho ca: disparagement. Ohito: are deposited and dwell for a long time.

[The Buddha] caused the sixteen-year-old appearance to pass away and showed her the form of a twenty-year-old. Rūpanandā, looking at it, thought, “This form is no longer the same as before,” and her mind became somewhat disenchanted. The Blessed One, in gradual succession, showed the woman’s form as that of a woman who had given birth once, then as a middle-aged woman, and then as a decrepit old woman. That bhikkhunī Rūpanandā also gradually felt disenchantment, thinking, “This stage of life has also vanished; that stage of life has also vanished.” When the decrepit old form was shown, she became completely disenchanted upon seeing the appearance of a woman with broken teeth, grey hair, a bent back, crooked like a rafter, leaning on a staff, and trembling. Then, the Blessed One showed that magically created woman being severely oppressed by disease. At that moment, the created woman cast away her staff and palm-leaf fan, uttered a great cry of distress, fell to the ground, and lay there rolling back and forth, immersed in her own excrement and urine.

## Realizing the Nature of Impermanence, Suffering, and Non-self

Bhikkhunī Rūpanandā, seeing that condition, became extremely disenchanted. The Blessed One then showed the death of that created woman. That dead woman immediately reached a state of bloating. From the nine orifices, masses of putrid pus and maggots began to flow out. Crows and other scavengers gathered and began to tear at the body. Bhikkhunī Rūpanandā, observing this, realized the impermanence of the body, thinking, “This young woman has reached old age, sickness, and death in this very place; in this same way, old age, sickness, and death will come to my own body.” Because she saw it as impermanent, she also saw it as suffering and as non-self.

## Rūpanandā’s Establishment in Stream-entry

At that time, the three realms of existence appeared to Bhikkhunī Rūpanandā as if they were ablaze, or like a rotting carcass tied around her neck. Her mind rushed toward the meditation subject. The Blessed One, knowing that Rūpanandā had seen the nature of impermanence, considered, “Will she be able to establish a refuge for herself on her own?” Realizing, “She will not; she needs an external condition,” and wishing to preach a suitable discourse to her, he uttered these verses.

The Blessed One preached this Sutta (these verses) concerning the bhikkhunī named Nandā.
75:
In this way, the bhikkhunī named Nandā followed the teaching and directed her knowledge, thereby attaining the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). After that, for the sake of Rūpanandā’s practice and development of insight (vipassanā) for the three higher paths and fruits, the Buddha, wishing to teach the meditation on emptiness (suññata-kammaṭṭhāna), said: “Nandā, do not perceive that there is any essence in this body; there is not even a slight essence in this body. This body is a city of bones, built by erecting three hundred bones.” Wishing to teach this, he spoke this verse:

## Bhikkhunī Rūpanandā Becomes an Arahant
At the end of the teaching, the Elder Rūpanandā attained the fruit of Arahantship. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude.
The story of Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā Therī ends.

## 6. The Story of Queen Mallikā
(Mallikādevī Vatthu)
The Teacher, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Jīranti ve," concerning Queen Mallikā.

## Queen Mallikā’s Misdeed
One day, Queen Mallikā entered the bathroom, washed her face, and, bending her body down, began to wash her calves. A pet dog, who had entered with her, saw her bending down in that manner and began to attempt unwholesome conduct with her. Queen Mallikā stood there, enjoying the sensation. King Pasenadi of Kosala, looking through a lattice window from the upper palace, saw this. When she came back from the bathroom, he said, "You wicked woman, perish! Why did you do such a thing?" When she asked, "Great King, what have I done?", he replied, "You had relations with a dog." She said, "Great King, such a thing did not happen."
"I saw it myself; I will not believe your words. Perish, you wicked woman!" he said again.
76:
“Great King, if any person enters this bathroom, to the one looking through this lattice window, a single person appears as two,” she spoke untruthfully. “Great King, if you do not believe my words, enter this bathroom; I will look at you through this lattice window,” she said. The King, being of a confused nature, believed Mallikā’s words and entered the bathroom. Queen Mallikā stood at the lattice window, looked, and said, “Extremely foolish King, why are you engaging in such relations with a female goat?” Even though the King said, “Queen Mallikā, I am not doing such a thing,” she replied, “I saw it myself; I will not believe your words.” Hearing this, the King believed, “Indeed, when one enters this bathroom, one person appears as two.” Queen Mallikā thought, “This King, because of his extreme foolishness, has been deceived by me. I have committed a bad deed, and I have falsely accused this King. My deed will be known by the Teacher, by the two Chief Disciples, and by the eighty Great Disciples. Alas, I have committed a very heavy deed.”

## Queen Mallikā Suffers in Hell
This Queen Mallikā had been a companion in giving the Incomparable Almsgiving (Asadisa-dāna) of King Pasenadi of Kosala. In that Incomparable Almsgiving, the wealth sacrificed in a single day was worth fourteen crores. The four items offered to the Tathāgata—the white parasol, the seating throne, the bowl-stand, and the footstool—were of priceless value. At the time of her death, that Queen Mallikā, unable to remember such great sacrifices and only remembering that evil deed, passed away and was reborn in the Avīci hell. King Pasenadi of Kosala, however, loved Queen Mallikā very dearly. Overwhelmed by great grief, after performing the funeral rites for Queen Mallikā, he went to the Teacher to ask, “Where has Queen Mallikā been reborn?” The Teacher acted in such a way that the King would not remember the reason for his coming. The King, after listening to a memorable Dhamma talk in the presence of the Teacher, remembered upon entering the palace and said, “Friends, I went to the Teacher to ask about Mallikā’s place of rebirth, but I forgot. Tomorrow, I will ask again,” and he went again the next day. The Teacher, in succession for seven days, acted in such a way that the King would not remember.

## Release from Hell and Rebirth in Tusita
Queen Mallikā suffered in hell for only seven days, and on the eighth day, passing away from that Avīci hell, she was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
(As for why the Teacher made the King not remember: it was because King Pasenadi loved Queen Mallikā very dearly and she was pleasing to his heart. Therefore, if he heard that Queen Mallikā had been reborn in hell, he might hold a wrong view, thinking, “If such a faithful Mallikā is reborn in Avīci hell, what is the use of giving alms?” and might stop the regular alms-food provided at the palace for five hundred monks, and thus be reborn in hell himself.)
77:
## The Teaching

(151) Truly, the ornate royal chariots wear out; so too does the body reach decay. But the Dhamma of the good does not decay; thus the good reveal it to the good.

*Sucittā*: very beautiful with the seven gems and other ornaments. *Rājarathā*: the royal chariots. *Ve*: indeed. *Jīranti*: they wear out. *Atho*: furthermore. *Sarīrampi*: the body also. *Jaraṃ*: decay. *Upeti*: reaches.

*Sataṃ*: of the good. *Dhammo ca*: the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma). *Jaraṃ na upeti*: does not reach decay. *Evaṃ*: thus. *Santo*: the good. *Sabbhi*: with the good. *Have*: indeed. *Pavedayanti*: they speak and declare.

Therefore, the Buddha caused King Pasenadi of Kosala to be in a state of forgetfulness for seven days. On the eighth day, when the Buddha went out for alms, he went to the palace gate himself. When King Pasenadi heard that the Buddha had arrived, he took the alms bowl and made an effort to ascend the palace. The Buddha showed a sign of wanting to stay in the chariot shed. King Pasenadi let the Buddha stay in that very chariot shed, and with great respect, offered gruel and food. While sitting after paying homage, he said, “Venerable Sir, I came intending to ask about the place of rebirth of Queen Mallikā, but I forgot. O Blessed One, where has that Mallikā been reborn?” The Buddha replied, “Great King, she has been reborn in the Tusita heaven.”

## The King’s Joy and Sorrow

“O Blessed One, if Queen Mallikā were not reborn in the Tusita heaven, who else could be? Venerable Sir, there is no woman like Mallikā. For her, in every posture of sitting or standing, except for the preparation of offerings—thinking, ‘Tomorrow I will give this to the Tathāgata, I will do this merit’—there was no other concern. Venerable Sir, since the time she passed away to the other world, my body can no longer carry or do anything.”

Then the Buddha said to King Pasenadi, “Great King, do not worry so much. This nature of death is a constant law for all beings.” He then asked, “Great King, whose chariot is this?” Hearing this, King Pasenadi placed his hands together on his head and replied, “Venerable Sir, it is the chariot of my grandfather.” “And whose chariot is this?” the Buddha asked again. “Venerable Sir, it is the chariot of my father.” “And whose chariot is this?” “Venerable Sir, this is my chariot.” When he had said this, the Buddha said, “Great King, why did your grandfather’s chariot not reach the state of your father’s chariot? (Meaning it was not as strong and had decayed.) Why did your father’s chariot not reach the state of your chariot?” He continued, “Even a piece of wood of such a nature reaches decay; what then can be said of this physical body? Great King, only the Dhamma of the good does not age or decay. For beings, there is no such thing as not aging or not decaying.” He then spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of Queen Mallikā ends.

## 7. The Story of Elder Lāḷudāyī

(Lāḷudāyitthera Vatthu)

The Buddha, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this teaching beginning with “Appassutāyaṃ,” concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyī.
78:
I had two oxen, O Great King, with which we plowed the field.
One of them is dead, O Lord; please give me a second one, O Ruler.

*Mahārāja*: O Great King. *Me*: to me. *Dve goṇā*: two oxen. *Santi*: there are. *Yehi*: with which two oxen. *Khettaṃ*: the field. *Kasāmase*: we plow. *Deva*: O King. *Tesu*: of those two oxen. *Eko*: one ox. *Mato*: is dead. *Khattiya*: O Ruler of the land. *Dutiyaṃ*: a second companion ox. *Dehi*: please grant out of compassion.

## Preaching Irrelevant Dhamma

When this Elder Lāḷudāyī went to the houses of those performing auspicious ceremonies, he would preach inauspicious discourses such as the Petavatthu beginning with “Tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhanti” (They stand behind the walls). When he went to the houses of those performing inauspicious ceremonies where the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta should be preached, he would preach auspicious words beginning with “Dānañca dhammacariyā ca” (Giving and righteous conduct) or the Ratana Sutta beginning with “Yaṃ kiñci vittaṃ idha vā huraṃ vā” (Whatever wealth there is here or elsewhere). Thus, in various places, while intending to preach one thing, he would preach another, yet he did not realize, “I am preaching irrelevantly.” When the monks heard Lāḷudāyī’s preaching, they reported it to the Buddha: “Venerable Sir, how is it that when Lāḷudāyī goes to auspicious or inauspicious places, he preaches one thing when another should be preached?” The Buddha said, “Bhikkhus, he does not preach like this only now; in the past too, he said one thing when another should have been said,” and he brought forth the past.

## Learning the Verse to Request an Ox

In the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a youth named Somadatta, the son of a Brahmin named Aggidatta, served the King. The King loved and cherished Somadatta. The Brahmin Aggidatta, however, lived by farming. He had two oxen. One of those two oxen died. The Brahmin said to his son, “Dear Somadatta, ask the King for an ox on my behalf and bring it.” Somadatta thought, “If I ask the King, my insignificance will become apparent,” and said, “Father, you yourself should ask the King.” When the father said, “In that case, my son, take me with you,” Somadatta thought, “This Brahmin is of slow wisdom; he does not even know simple words like ‘step forward’ or ‘step back.’ When one thing should be said, he says another by mistake. I will only take him after training him.” Then Somadatta took his father to a cemetery named Vīraṇatthambhaka, tied bundles of grass, and named them, saying, “This bundle is the King, this is the Crown Prince, this is the General.” After showing them to his father in order, he said, “Father, when you reach the King’s palace, you must step forward like this, step back like this, and address the King like this. You must address the Crown Prince like this. When you approach the King, say ‘Jayatu Mahārāja’ (Victory to the Great King).”
79:
I have two oxen, O Great King, with which we plow the field.
Of those, one has died, O Lord; take the second one, O Ruler.

O Great King, noble king. To me, there are two oxen. With those two oxen, we plow the field. O Lord, great king. Of those two oxen, one has died. O Ruler, lord of the land. Take the companion ox.

## The Teaching
(152) This man of little learning grows old like an ox.
His flesh increases, but his wisdom does not increase.

One with little learning, this man, like an ox, grows old. To that man of little learning, only the flesh increases. To that man, wisdom does not increase.

"O Great King—may you be victorious," saying thus, recite this verse and ask for the ox," he taught him, and then made him learn the verse.

## Reciting the Verse for Giving an Ox when Asking for an Ox
That old Brahmin Aggidatta practiced that verse for a year to become proficient. Having told his son of his proficiency, [the son said], "If that is so, father, take a certain gift and come. I will go ahead and stay in the presence of the King." When he said this, [the father] said, "Very well, dear son," and taking the gift, while Somadatta was staying in the presence of the King, he reached the palace with great effort. The King, with a pleased mind, greeted him warmly and said, "Father Brahmin, you have come after a long time. Sit on this seat and speak of what you desire." When he said this, he spoke this verse.

Even when the King said, "Father Brahmin, what are you saying? Speak again," he spoke only that same verse for giving an ox.

## Obtaining the Oxen due to the Son's Excellent Petition
When the King realized that the old Brahmin had spoken in error, he smiled and said, "Dear Somadatta, it seems there are many oxen in your house." When he said this, [Somadatta] replied, "O Great King, if your Majesty grants them, they will indeed be many." Because of this petition, being pleased with the Bodhisatta Somadatta, the King granted the old Brahmin sixteen oxen, ornaments and goods, and a village to reside in as a royal gift (brahmadeyya), and sent the Brahmin away with great honor. The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jataka: "At that time, the King was Ānanda, the Brahmin was Lāḷudāyī, and Somadatta was I myself."
80:
"Monks, not only now, but in the past also, this Lāḷudāyī, because of his little learning, said one thing when another should have been said. A man of little learning is indeed like an ox," he said, and then he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.
The Story of Elder Lāḷudāyī ends.

## The Teaching
(153) Through many births in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Painful is birth again and again.
(154) O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again. All your rafters are broken, the ridge-pole is shattered. My mind has reached the unconditioned; I have attained the destruction of craving.

Again and again, having to undergo rebirth is painful because it is always associated with aging, sickness, and death. Therefore, seeking the house-builder, the carpenter of craving who builds the house of the aggregates, I have searched since making the aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. Through many births in saṃsāra, because I did not obtain the knowledge [of the builder], I have wandered without stability.

O house-builder, the carpenter of craving who builds the house of the aggregates! You have been seen by me, the Buddha, the possessor of Omniscient Knowledge. You are [seen]. You shall not build the house of the aggregates for me again. All your rafters, which are the defilements, have been broken by me. The ridge-pole of the house you built, which is ignorance (avijjā), I have destroyed. My mind has entered into Nibbāna by way of taking it as an object. I have attained Arahattaphala, which is the end of all cravings.

## 8. The Story of the Udāna Verses of Elder Ānanda
(Udānavatthu)
This Dhamma teaching beginning with "Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ" was uttered by the Blessed One as an inspired utterance (udāna) out of joy while sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Later, it was preached when asked by the Elder Ānanda.

## Every Buddha Utters an Inspired Utterance
That Supreme One of the Three Worlds, the Omniscient Buddha, while sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree, even before the sun had set, conquered and destroyed the hosts of Māra. In the first watch of the night, he broke through the mass of darkness of ignorance that covers the sequence of past aggregates. In the middle watch, he purified the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu). In the last watch, out of compassion for beings, he directed his knowledge towards Dependent Origination (paticcasamuppada). Contemplating that noble Dhamma of Dependent Origination by way of forward and reverse order, at the time of dawn, he penetrated and realized Omniscient Knowledge, which has the Path of Arahatship as its basis. Then, uttering the inspired utterance (udāna) that has not been abandoned by hundreds of thousands of Buddhas...
81:
The Buddhas, wishing to utter the joyous utterance (Udāna) which they do not abandon, uttered these verses.

The story of the Udāna verses of Venerable Ānanda ends.

## 9. The Story of Mahādhana the Treasurer's Son
(Mahādhana-seṭṭhiputta-vatthu)

While the Blessed One was residing at the Deer Park in Isipatana, the place where safety is granted to the deer, he gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Acritvā," concerning the son of the treasurer Mahādhana.

## The Treasurer's Son Who Loved Flattery

That treasurer's son was born in Bārāṇasī into a family possessing eighty crores of wealth. At that time, the parents of the treasurer's son thought: "There is a great mass of wealth in our house. We will place this wealth in our son's hands and let him enjoy it as he pleases. There is no need for him to do any other work." Having thought thus, they taught him only dancing, singing, and instrumental music. In that same city of Bārāṇasī, a daughter was also born into another family possessing eighty crores of wealth. Her parents also thought in the same way and taught their daughter only dancing, singing, and instrumental music. When the treasurer's son and the treasurer's daughter reached the proper age, their marriage was celebrated. Later, their parents passed away.
82:
The wealth amounting to twice eighty crores (160 crores) came to be in a single house. The treasurer's son went to serve the King three times a day. At that time, in the city of Bārāṇasī, some rogues thought: "If this treasurer's son becomes a drunkard, it will be comfortable for us. Let us make him a drunkard." Taking liquor, and having tied up snacks, meat, and salt crystals in the corners of their robes, and taking roots and tubers, they sat watching the road where the treasurer's son would return from the royal palace. When they saw him coming, they drank the liquor, put salt crystals in their mouths, chewed the roots, and said: "O Master Treasurer's Son, may you live for a hundred years! Depending on you, may we be able to eat and drink."

## The Treasurer's Son and His Wife Become Homeless

When the treasurer's son heard the words of those rogues, he asked the young attendant following him: "What are these people drinking?" When the attendant said, "Master, they are drinking a certain beverage," he asked, "Is this beverage pleasant?" The attendant replied, "Master, in this world of living beings, there is no drinkable liquid equal to this." Hearing this, the treasurer's son thought, "If that is so, I should also drink," and he had some brought and drank it. Soon after, when the rogues realized that the treasurer's son had become a drinker, they surrounded him. As time went on, his retinue became large. That treasurer's son had liquor brought for a hundred or two hundred coins and drank it. Gradually, he would place heaps of coins at his sitting places and drink, saying: "Bring flowers with these coins, bring perfumes with these; this person is skilled in singing, this one in dancing, this one in music. Give this person a thousand, give that one two thousand." Thus, as he squandered his wealth, before long, he exhausted his own eighty crores of wealth. When he was told, "Master, your wealth is exhausted," he asked, "Is there no wealth belonging to my wife?" When told, "Master, there is," he said, "If so, bring that wealth." He exhausted his wife's wealth in the same manner as his own. Gradually, he sold and spent everything: fields, groves, gardens, carriages, and so on, down to household utensils, rugs, robes, and seats. Later, when the treasurer's son became old, those who had bought and taken the ancestral home of his parents evicted the couple from the house.

## Wandering and Begging, Failing to Attain the Dhamma

Taking his wife, the treasurer's son lived leaning against the walls of others' houses. Carrying a potsherd in his hand, he wandered for alms and had to strive to eat the leftovers of the people.
83:
Then, one day, seeing the son of the treasurer standing at the door of the refectory, receiving leftover food given by young monks and novices, the Buddha manifested a smile. Then, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha the reason for the smile. Desiring to explain the reason for his smile, the Buddha said, "Dear Ānanda, look at this man, the son of the great treasurer Mahādhana, who, having squandered eighty crores of wealth in this very city of Bārāṇasī, now wanders with his wife begging for food. If this treasurer's son had not squandered his wealth in the first stage of life and had applied himself to business, he would have become the foremost treasurer in this very city. If he had left the household life and ordained, he would have attained Arahantship, and his wife would have been established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala). If he had not squandered his wealth in the middle stage of life and had applied himself to business, he would have become the second treasurer. If he had left and ordained, he would have become a Non-returner (Anāgāmī), and his wife would have been established in the fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-phala). If he had not squandered his wealth in the last stage of life and had applied himself to business, he would have become the third treasurer. If he had left and ordained, he would have become a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī), and his wife would have been established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). But now, this treasurer's son has fallen away from worldly wealth and also from the virtues of the Path and Fruit, which is the state of a recluse. Having fallen away, he has become like a heron in a dried-up pond." Having said this, he spoke these verses:

## The Teaching
(155) Not having lived the holy life, not having acquired wealth in youth, they pine away like old herons in a pond without fish.
(156) Not having lived the holy life, not having acquired wealth in youth, they lie like spent arrows from a bow, sighing over the past.

*Brahmacariyaṃ*: the holy life. *Acariitvā*: because of not having practiced. *Yobbane*: in the time of capability. *Dhanaṃ*: wealth. *Aladdhā*: because of not having obtained. Or, those fools who did not obtain it. *Khīṇamaccbeva*: like a pond where fish are exhausted. *Pallale*: in a muddy pond. *Jiṇṇakoñcāva*: like old herons with failing wings. *Jhāyanti*: they brood and pine away.

*Brahmacariyaṃ*: the holy life. *Acariitvā*: because of not having practiced. *Yobbane*: in the time of capability. *Dhanaṃ*: wealth. *Aladdhā*: because of not having obtained. Or, those fools who did not obtain it. *Purāṇāni*: things enjoyed in the past. *Anutthunaṃ anutthunantā*: sighing and grieving. *Cāpā*: from the bowstring. *Atikhīṇā - vinimuttā*: released. *Sarā iva*: like arrows. *Senti*: they shall approach death.
84:
Having passed the three stages of life, they will now approach death because they are unable to uplift themselves. Therefore, it was said: "They lie like spent arrows from a bow." *Purāṇāni anutthunaṃ* means they lie grieving and lamenting over past deeds such as eating, drinking, dancing, singing, and music, saying, "Thus we ate, thus we drank."

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the son of Mahādhana the Treasurer ends.
Here ends the commentary on the Jarāvagga.
The Eleventh Chapter.

## 12. Attavagga
## 1. The Story of Prince Bodhi
(Bodhirājakumāra-vatthu)
"Attānañce..." The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching while staying at the Bhesakaḷā Grove, concerning Prince Bodhi.

## Prince Bodhi's Plot to Kill the Carpenter
That Prince Bodhi had a palace built, unlike any other on earth, appearing as if it were floating in the sky, named Kokanuda. He asked the carpenter, "Have you ever built such a palace elsewhere? Or is this your first such work of craftsmanship?" When the carpenter replied, "Prince, it is indeed my first work of craftsmanship," Prince Bodhi thought, "If this carpenter builds such a palace for someone else, this palace will no longer be a marvel. It is proper for me to kill him, or to cut off his hands and feet, or to pluck out his eyes. If I do so, he will not be able to build a palace for anyone else." He told this matter to his dear friend, a young man named Sañjīvakaputta. That young man thought, "Without doubt, this Prince will destroy the carpenter. Let not a craftsman of such priceless skill perish while I am watching; I shall give him a sign." He approached the carpenter and asked, "Is your work on the palace finished or not?" When the carpenter said, "It is finished," he said, "The Prince wishes to destroy you; protect yourself." The carpenter said, "Master Sañjīvakaputta, you have done a good deed by informing me; I shall know what must be done in this matter." Then, when asked by the Prince, "Friend carpenter, is the work on our palace finished?" he replied, "Prince, it is not yet finished; much remains to be done." When asked, "What kind of work remains?" he said, "Prince, I will tell you later. First, have some wood brought to me." When asked, "What kind of wood should be brought?" he said, "Prince, have dry wood without heartwood brought." Prince Bodhi had it brought and given to him.
86:
## The Carpenter's Escape with a Flying Bird Machine
Then, the carpenter said to Prince Bodhi, "Prince, from this day forth, you should not come to my presence. Why is that? Because when performing delicate work (such as intricate floral carvings), if one speaks with others, the work at hand tends to be distracted. At mealtime, only my wife will bring the food."

The Prince agreed, saying, "Very well." That carpenter, staying inside a chamber, planed the wood and constructed a Garuda-shaped bird machine large enough for his wife and children to stay inside. At mealtime, he instructed his wife, "Sell all the property we have in the house and bring the gold and silver."

The Prince, for the purpose of preventing the carpenter from leaving, had the house surrounded and placed guards. When the bird machine was completed, the carpenter told his wife, "Today, bring all the young sons and daughters and come." After eating his morning meal, he placed his wife and children inside the belly of the bird machine and escaped through the air-vent window.

While the guards were shouting, "Prince, the carpenter is escaping!", the carpenter flew away and descended into the Himālaya. There, he created a city and became the king named Kaṭṭhavāhana.

## The Buddha Does Not Step on the Cloth Spread
Prince Bodhi, thinking, "I shall perform a dedication ceremony for the palace," invited the Blessed One. He had the palace smeared with the four types of fragrances—saffron, cloves, tagara, and incense—and then spread a cloth covering starting from the first threshold. Prince Bodhi was childless; therefore, he spread it thinking, "If I am to have a son or a daughter, the Blessed One will step upon this cloth spread."

When the Blessed One arrived, the Prince prostrated with the five-point prostration, took the bowl, and said, "Venerable Sir, please enter."

The Blessed One did not enter. The Prince requested a second and a third time. Without entering, the Blessed One looked at the Elder Ānanda. Recognizing the sign of the look and knowing that the Buddha did not wish to step on the cloths, the Elder Ānanda said to Prince Bodhi, "Prince, gather up the cloths. The Blessed One will not step on the cloth spread; the Tathāgata has regard for future generations." Thus, he had the cloths removed.

Prince Bodhi, having the cloths removed, invited the Blessed One into the house, served Him respectfully with gruel and hard food, and after the meal, sat in a suitable place, prostrated, and said, "Venerable Sir, I am a supporter who has been of great service to the Blessed Ones. I have gone for refuge three times. It is said that I went for refuge once while still in my mother's womb. A second time during my childhood, and a third time when I reached the age of discretion. Why did You not step on my cloth spread?"

When asked, "Prince, with what thought did you spread the cloths?"
87:
## The Teaching
(157) If one knows oneself to be dear, one should guard oneself well.
During any of the three watches, the wise man should keep vigil.

(If one knows oneself to be dear: If one realizes, "I love and cherish myself." If this is known, one should guard that self so that it is well-protected throughout the three stages of life. If unable to do so for all three, then during one of the three watches—this is a metaphorical meaning not intended here—during one of the three stages of life—this is the intended meaning—the wise man should purify himself.)

"Venerable Sir, I spread them thinking: 'If I am to have a son or a daughter, the Blessed One will step upon my cloth spread.'"

When the Buddha replied, "It was for that very reason that I did not step on them," the Prince asked, "Venerable Sir, how is it? Shall I not obtain a son or a daughter?"

"Prince, you shall not obtain them," the Buddha replied. When asked, "For what reason, Venerable Sir?", the Buddha said, "Because in a previous existence, you and your wife were negligent (pamāda)."

When asked, "Venerable Sir, at what time were we negligent?", the Blessed One brought forth the past and taught him.

## Prince Bodhi's Past
In the past, many hundreds of people set out to sea in a large ship. The ship was wrecked in the middle of the ocean. A husband and wife took hold of a plank and reached an island in the middle of the sea. All the others died right there in the ocean where the ship wrecked. On that island, a great flock of birds lived.

Those two, the husband and wife, seeing no other food and being hungry, roasted bird eggs on charcoal embers and ate them. When the eggs were not enough, they caught and ate the young birds. Thus, they ate them in the first stage of life, the middle stage, and the last stage. In not even one stage of life did they practice non-negligence (appamāda). Not even one of those two practiced non-negligence.

The Blessed One, having shown this past evil deed of Prince Bodhi, said, "Prince, if at that time you or your wife had practiced non-negligence in even one stage of life, a son or a daughter would have been born to you in at least one stage. If even one of you had been non-negligent, because of that person, a son or a daughter would have been born. Prince, one who considers oneself dear should protect oneself with non-negligence during all three stages of life. If one is unable to protect oneself in all three stages, one must protect oneself in at least one stage." Having said this, He spoke this verse:

## Notes on the Teaching
Regarding the phrase "If one knows oneself to be dear, one should guard oneself well," if a layperson, thinking "I will protect myself," enters a well-secured chamber on the upper floor of a palace and lives there with full protection, or if a monk lives in a cave with well-secured and closed doors and windows...
88:
Even living in a cave with doors and windows does not mean one is protecting oneself. One way of protecting oneself is: if a layperson performs meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and virtue (sīla) to the best of their ability; or if a monk performs major and minor duties, scriptural study (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and spiritual exertion, then it is said that they are protecting themselves.

If one is unable to protect oneself in all three stages of life, one should clear and purify oneself in at least one of the stages. If a layperson was unable to perform merit in the first stage of life due to being prone to indulgence and play, they should do so diligently in the middle stage. If they were unable to do so in the middle stage due to the responsibility of supporting a spouse and children, they must certainly do so in the last stage of life. In this way, a layperson should clear and purify themselves. For one who cannot do so, it is not said that they love themselves; they are only acting in a way that leads to the lower realms.

If a monk, due to learning and reciting scriptures in the first stage of life, should neglect his duties and practice, he should diligently strive in the monk's Dhamma in the middle stage. If, in the middle stage, he should be negligent because of inquiring into the meanings, decisions, and reasons of the scriptures learned in the first stage, he must certainly strive in the monk's Dhamma in the last stage of life. In this way, a monk should clear and purify himself. For a monk who cannot do so, it is not said that he loves himself; it is said that he only burns himself with later remorse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, Prince Bodhi was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of Prince Bodhi ends.

## 2. The Story of Elder Upananda the Sakyan

(Upananda Sakyaputta Thera Vatthu)

The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Attānam-eva paṭhamaṃ," while residing at the Jetavana monastery, concerning Upananda the Sakyan.

## One who Preaches Well but is Greedy

That Elder Upananda was very skilled in preaching the Dhamma. Having heard his Dhamma talk related to fewness of wishes and so forth, many monks offered him robes and took up ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). Upananda himself took the requisites discarded by those monks. As the time for the rains retreat approached, he went to the countryside. Then, at a certain monastery, young monks and novices, out of affection and respect for him as a Dhamma preacher, said, "Venerable Sir, please spend the rains retreat here." He asked, "How many rains-residence cloths (vassāvāsika) are received here?" When the young monks and novices replied, "One cloth each, Venerable Sir," he left his sandals there and went to another monastery. Arriving at the second monastery, he asked, "What is received here?" When told, "Two cloths," he left his walking staff there. Arriving at the third monastery, he asked, "What is received here?" When told, "Three cloths," he left his water pot there. Arriving at the fourth monastery, he asked, "What is received here?" When told, "Four cloths," he agreed, saying, "Very well, I will stay here," and after entering the rains retreat there, he preached the Dhamma to both laypeople and monks. Those laypeople and monks honored Upananda with many cloths and robes.
89:
When the rains retreat was over, Upananda sent a message saying, "Since I have left my requisites at the other monasteries, I am entitled to receive the rains-residence cloths. Let them be sent to me." He had all the cloths brought to him, loaded them fully onto a cart, and departed. At that time, in one monastery, two young monks had received two cloths and one blanket. They said together, "Let the two cloths be for you, and let the one blanket be for me," and being unable to divide them, they sat near the road and argued. Seeing Elder Upananda approaching, those two young monks said, "Venerable Sir, please divide these for us." When he said, "You yourselves should divide them," they replied, "Venerable Sir, we cannot; please divide and give them to us." He asked, "In that case, will you abide by my word?" and they agreed, "Yes, we will." Saying, "Very well then," he divided and gave the two cloths to the two monks, and saying, "This blanket is suitable for us who preach and decide on Dhamma matters to wear," he took the very expensive blanket and departed. The young monks, being dissatisfied, went to the Buddha and reported the matter. The Buddha said, "Monks, it is not only now that he has taken your property and caused you dissatisfaction; he has done so before as well," and he brought forth the past.

## The Jackal Judge and the Two Otters

In the past, an otter named Anutīracārī, because he foraged on the shallow riverbank, and an otter named Gambhīracārī, because he foraged in deep water, caught a large Rohita fish. They fell into a dispute, saying, "Let the head part be for me, let the tail part be for you," and being unable to divide it, they saw a jackal and said, "Uncle, please divide this fish for us." The jackal said, "The King has appointed me to the place of judgment. Having sat there for a long time, I have come out for the purpose of exercising my legs. Now, I have no free time." When they pleaded, "Uncle Jackal, please do not do this; please divide it for us," he asked, "Will you abide by my word?" and they agreed, "Uncle, we will." Saying, "Very well then," the jackal cut off the fish's head and placed it in one spot. He placed the fish's tail in another spot. Having done so, he said, "Friends, let the otter who forages on the riverbank take the tail. Let the head be for the otter who forages in deep water. But this middle part shall belong to me, who stands in the law of judgment." Thus, making the two otters understand, he spoke this verse:

Anutīracārī naṅguṭṭhaṃ, sīsaṃ gambhīracārino.
Athāyaṃ majjhimo khaṇḍo, dhammaṭṭhassa bhavissati.

"The tail for the shore-wanderer, the head for the deep-water-wanderer; this middle piece shall belong to the one who stands in justice."

Having recited this verse, he bit the middle part and departed. Those otters, being dissatisfied, remained standing there, looking at the jackal.

The Teacher, having shown this past story, made those monks understand, saying, "Thus, in the past too, he caused you dissatisfaction," and rebuking Upananda...
90:
## The Teaching

(158) One should first establish oneself in what is proper;
Then only should one instruct others.
A wise man should not be defiled.

Attānameva: oneself only. Paṭhamaṃ: first. Paṭirūpe: in a suitable quality. Nivesaye: should establish. Atha: thereafter. Aññaṃ: another. Anusāsati: should instruct. Paṇḍito: a wise person. Na kiliṣṣeyya: should not be defiled.

The Blessed One, revealing the past events, informed those monks, "Thus, this Upananda has caused you dissatisfaction in the past as well." Then, wishing to rebuke Upananda, he said, "Monks, he who instructs others should first establish himself in what is proper and suitable," and spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, those two monks were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude.

The Story of Elder Upananda Sakyaputta ends.

## 3. The Story of Elder Padhānikatissa

(Padhānikatissattheravatthu)

The Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with "Attānañce" while staying at Jetavana Monastery, concerning Elder Padhānikatissa, who was known as the meditator.

## The Teacher who Urges Others without Empathy

That Elder Padhānikatissa took a meditation subject from the Buddha and, taking five hundred monks with him, entered the forest for the rains retreat. He exhorted them, "Friends, you have taken a meditation subject from the living Buddha; practice the recluse's Dhamma without negligence." But he himself went and lay down to sleep. Those monks walked in meditation during the first watch and entered the monastery in the middle watch. When Tissa woke up after sleeping, he went to them and said, "Did you come here with the intention 'We will lie down and sleep'? Go out quickly and practice the recluse's Dhamma." After saying this, he himself went and slept again just as before. The other monks walked in meditation outside the monastery during the middle watch and entered the monastery in the last watch. Elder Tissa woke up again, went to the monks, drove them out of the monastery, and then he himself went back and slept in the same manner. When the Elder acted in this way at all times, the monks were unable to perform their recitations or focus on their meditation.
91:
Their minds became distracted and unsettled. Those monks thought, "Our teacher is extremely energetic; let us investigate him." Upon investigating and seeing the teacher's behavior, they said, "Friends, we are ruined; our teacher makes only empty noise."

Exhausted by extreme sleepiness, not even one monk among those disciples was able to achieve any spiritual distinction.

## The Rooster that Crows at the Wrong Time

When those monks had completed the rains retreat, they went to the Buddha. After the Buddha had exchanged pleasantries with them, he asked, "Monks, how was it? Were you able to practice the recluse's Dhamma without negligence?" The monks then reported the matter to him. The Blessed One said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too, this monk has hindered you." Being requested by the monks, he related the Akālarāvi Kukkuṭa Jātaka in detail:

"Not raised by mother or father, living in a teacherless house, this rooster does not know the right time or the wrong time [to crow]."

Amātāpitu saṃvaḍḍho: one who has not grown up relying on the instruction of parents. Anācariya kule vasaṃ: one who has never lived in a teacher's house. Ayaṃ kukkuṭo: this rooster. Kālaṃ: the time that is right for crowing. Akālaṃ vā: or the time that is not right for crowing. Nābhijānāti: does not know.

The Buddha preached this Akālarāvi Kukkuṭa Jātaka in detail in the Haṃcivagga of the Ekanipāta (Jātaka 119). He then connected the birth story: "At that time, the rooster that used to crow at the wrong time was this Elder Padhānikatissa. These five hundred monks were those youths. I myself was the world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha)." After expanding on this Jātaka, the Buddha said, "Monks, one who wishes to instruct others should make himself well-tamed. Only such a person is said to instruct after being well-tamed," and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(159) If one would act as one instructs others,
Then being well-tamed, one may tame [others].
For the self, indeed, is difficult to tame.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, all five hundred monks attained the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala).

The Story of Elder Padhānikatissa ends.

## 4. The Story of the Elder Nun, Mother of Kumārakassapa
(Kumārakassapamātutherī Vatthu)

"Self is indeed the lord of self..." The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching while residing at Jetavana monastery, concerning the mother of the Elder Kumārakassapa.

## The Pregnant Nun and Devadatta's Ruling

She was the daughter of a merchant in the city of Rājagaha. From the time she reached the age of discretion, she requested permission from her parents to ordain. Although she asked repeatedly, she did not receive permission from her parents. Upon reaching marriageable age, she went to her husband's family, lived as a devoted wife, and managed the household. Soon after, a child was conceived in her womb. Unaware of her pregnancy, she pleased her husband and again requested to ordain. Her husband, not knowing the situation, took her with great honor to the nunnery and had her ordained among the nuns who were followers of Devadatta. Later, when the nuns realized she was pregnant, they asked, "What is this?" She replied, "Sisters, I do not know how this happened. Surely my virtue is stainless."

The nuns took her to Devadatta and asked, "This nun ordained out of faith. We know she is pregnant, but we do not know when it happened. What should we do now?" Devadatta, thinking only, "Let no ill-repute come to the nuns who follow my instruction," decided, "Expel her from the Order."

## The Ruling of Elder Upāli

Hearing this, the young nun said, "Sisters, do not destroy me. I did not ordain for the sake of Devadatta. Come, take me to the Teacher at Jetavana monastery." So, the nuns took her to Jetavana and informed the Teacher. Although the Teacher knew the pregnancy began while she was a layperson, to clear her of others' blame, he summoned King Pasenadi of Kosala, the Great Anāthapiṇဍika, the Lesser Anāthapiṇဍika, the laywoman Visākhā, and other prominent families. He then commanded Elder Upāli, the foremost in Vinaya: "Go, Upāli, and clear the case of this young nun in the midst of the fourfold assembly."

The Elder summoned Visākhā in the presence of the King and entrusted her with the investigation. Visākhā had a curtained enclosure set up. Inside the curtain, she examined the nun's hands, feet, navel, and abdomen. Calculating the months and days, she realized, "She conceived this child while still a layperson," and informed the Elder. Then, in the midst of the assembly, the Elder established her innocence.

## The King Raising the Nun's Son

Later, she gave birth to a son of great power, who had made a resolution at the feet of Padumuttara Buddha. One day, while King Pasenadi was passing near the nunnery, he heard the sound of a child and asked, "What is this?" Being told, "Great King, a son was born to a nun; that is his voice," he took the boy to his palace and gave him to nurses. On the naming day, he was named Kassapa. Because he was raised with the retinue of a prince, he became known as Kumārakassapa. While playing, he struck some boys, and they reviled him, saying, "We were struck by a motherless and fatherless boy." He went to the King and asked, "Great King, they call me motherless and fatherless. Please tell me who my mother is." The King showed him the nurses and said, "These are your mothers." He replied, "It is not possible for me to have so many mothers. I must have only one mother. Please tell me who my real mother is."

## Kumārakassapa Becoming an Arahant

The King thought, "It is impossible to deceive this boy," and said, "Dear boy, your mother is a nun. I brought you from the nunnery." Upon hearing those words, he was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and said, "Great King, please let me ordain." The King said, "Very well, dear boy," and with great honor, had him ordained in the presence of the Teacher. After receiving higher ordination, he became known as Elder Kumārakassapa. He took a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered the forest, and strove, but being unable to attain any distinction, he thought, "I will take the meditation subject again with more detail." He went to the Teacher and stayed in Andhavana (the Blind Men's Grove).

At that time, a monk who had practiced the Dhamma with him during the time of Kassapa Buddha, and who had attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi) and was reborn in the Brahma realm, came from the Brahma realm.
