## The Mother Nun Attaining Arahatship
That nun, having fallen into suffering due to separation from her son, was wandering for alms with a tear-stained face. As soon as she saw the Elder on the road, she cried out, 'My son! My son!' and ran toward him to catch up, but she stumbled and fell. The nun, with milk flowing from her breasts, stood up and, with her robes wet, went and grabbed the Elder. The Elder thought, 'If my mother receives gentle words from me, she will be ruined. I will speak only harsh and stern words to this mother nun.' Then he said to his mother, the Theri, 'What are you doing wandering about? You cannot even cut off a mere affection.' The Theri thought, 'The Elder's words are very harsh and stern.' She asked, 'My son, what did you say?' When he repeated the same words, she thought, 'For twelve years, I have been unable to restrain my tears because of this son. But this son has such a hard and stern heart. What benefit is there for me in this son?' Thinking thus, she cut off her affection for her son and reached the Fruit of Arahatship on that very day.
## Preaching the Nigrodha Jātaka
On another occasion, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: 'Friends, Devadatta ruined Kumāra Kassapa, who was endowed with such supporting conditions (upanissaya), as well as the Theri. But the Teacher became their refuge. Indeed, the Buddhas are constantly compassionate toward the world.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here now?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that I have been a support and refuge for them; in the past also, I was their refuge.' Then he related the Nigrodha Jātaka of the Sီlavagga in the Ekanipāta in detail: 'At that time, the deer named Sākha was Devadatta. His retinue was Devadatta's retinue. The doe whose turn it was to be killed was the Theri. Her son was Kumāra Kassapa. But the king of deer named Nigrodha, who went and sacrificed his life for the pregnant doe, was I myself.' Having thus identified the Jātaka, he showed how the Theri, by cutting off her affection for her son, had made herself her own refuge. He said, 'Monks, because the attainment of heaven or the attainment of the Path, which resides within oneself, cannot be achieved for the sake of another...'

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth.

## 5. The Story of Mahākāla the Lay Follower
(Mahākāla Upāsakavatthu)
While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Attanā hi kataṃ pāpaṃ' concerning a lay follower who was a Stream-enterer named Mahākāla.
## The Uposatha Observer Accused of Being a Thief and Killed
That lay follower Mahākāla, it is said, used to observe the Uposatha on the eighth day of the month and listen to Dhamma talks at the monastery throughout the three watches of the night. At that time, during the night, thieves broke into a house, took a bundle of goods, and fled, dropping the stolen goods because they were pursued by the owners who had been awakened by the sound of brass pots and pans. The owners continued to pursue the thieves. The thieves fled in all four directions. One thief took the path leading to the monastery and, while Mahākāla was washing his face by the pond early in the morning after listening to the Dhamma all night, dropped the bundle of goods in front of him and fled. The people pursuing the thieves saw the bundle and said, 'You broke into our house, stole the goods, and now you are wandering about as if you were listening to the Dhamma!' They seized the lay follower Mahākāla, beat him, clubbed him to death, and left him there. Then, early in the morning, young monks and novices going for water saw the body of the lay follower Mahākāla and said, 'The lay follower who slept after listening to the Dhamma at the monastery has met an unfitting death.' They reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher said, 'Yes, monks, in this existence, the lay follower named Kāla has indeed met an unfitting death. However, regarding his past deeds, he has met a death that is quite fitting.' At the request of the monks, he related the past evil deed of Mahākāla.

## Framing the Husband and Killing Him
In that royal servant's house, there was a certain precious jewel. The servant had the jewel placed inside the cart and, in the early morning, made a sound as if thieves were entering. Then his men reported, "Lord, the precious jewel has been stolen by thieves." The royal servant stationed guards at the village gates and said, "Search those who are leaving the village." The traveler had already yoked his cart early and was departing. Then, those searching the traveler's cart found the precious jewel they had placed there themselves. They threatened and scolded him, saying, "You have stolen the jewel and are fleeing!" They beat him and showed him to the village headman, saying, "Lord, we have caught the thief." The village headman said, "He was given a place to stay and fed in my subordinate's house, yet he has gone off stealing the jewel. Seize that wicked man!" He then had him beaten, killed, and discarded. This was the past evil kamma of Mahākāla the lay devotee. When that royal servant passed away from that life, he was reborn in the Avīci hell. Thus, the Teacher, having shown the past kamma of Mahākāla, said, "Monks, in this way, the evil kamma done by these beings themselves crushes them in the four woeful states," and spoke this verse.

## 6. The Story of Venerable Devadatta
(Devadatta-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yassa accanta-dussīlyaṃ" concerning Devadatta.
## This Craving Like a Māluva Creeper
One day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, Devadatta is immoral and of evil conduct. Because of his craving, which is called the state of being immoral, he has supported Prince Ajātasattu and generated much gain and honor. Having encouraged Prince Ajātasattu to kill his father, he has joined with him and is making efforts to kill the Tathāgata in various ways." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," He said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too, Devadatta made efforts to kill me in various ways." He then told the Kuruṅgamiga-jātaka and other stories, saying, "Monks, the craving that arises due to the extreme immorality of an immoral person, like a māluva creeper entangling a sāla tree and breaking it, casts them into hell and other woeful states," and spoke this verse.
In this context, "accanta-dussīlyaṃ" means the state of being completely immoral. Whether a layperson who, from birth, performs the ten courses of unwholesome action, or a monk who, from the day of his ordination, commits grave offenses (garukāpatti), they are called "extremely immoral." Here, however, this refers to the state of immorality that has come through two or three existences. In the phrase "state of immorality," it refers to the immoral person's... Eka-nipāta,

That obstruction and that evil view of that person are like the fruit of the bamboo. Just as the bamboo plant, when it bears fruit, does so for its own destruction, so too does that person's evil view occur only for his own destruction. Therefore, this verse was spoken.

## 9. The Story of the Lay Follower Cūḷakāla

## The Lay Follower Accused of Being a Thief

One day, in the same manner as described in the story of Mahākāla, thieves who had tunneled into a house were pursued by the owners. When people saw Cūḷakāla, they said, "This man wanders about as if he were listening to the Dhamma, while committing robbery at night. Catch him!" and they beat the lay follower Cūḷakāla.

Some slave girls who were going to the watering place to fetch water saw the beating and said, "Move away, masters! This Cūḷakāla does not do such a thing," and they had Cūḷakāla released. Cūḷakāla went to the monastery and reported to the monks, "Venerable sirs, I was beaten and nearly destroyed by the people. I have obtained my life because of the water-carrying slave girls." The monks reported the matter to the Buddha. Upon hearing the monks' words, the Teacher said, "Monks, the lay follower Cūḷakāla obtained his life because of the water-carrying slave girls and because of his own innocence of the robbery. These beings, having committed evil deeds themselves, are defiled by themselves in hell and other states. But by performing merit, they reach heaven and Nibbāna, and are purified by themselves," and then he spoke this verse.
102:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, Cūḷakāla was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). The teaching of the Dhamma was also beneficial to the assembled audience.
The Story of Cūḷakāla the Lay Follower ends.

## The Teaching
(166) One should not neglect one's own welfare for the sake of another's, however great. Having clearly understood one's own welfare, one should be intent on one's own goal.

Attadatthaṃ: one's own welfare, even if small. Paratthena: by the welfare of another. Bahunāpi: even if it be much. Na hāpaye: one should not neglect. Attadatthaṃ: one's own welfare. Abhiññāya: having known. Sadatthapasuto: being intent on one's own welfare. Siyā: one should be.

## 10. The Story of Elder Attadattha
(Attadattha-thera-vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher (the Buddha) spoke this religious teaching, beginning with "Attadatthaṃ," concerning the Elder Attadattha.

## The Manner of Worship Pleasing to the Buddha
When the Buddha announced his approaching Parinibbāna, saying, "Monks, four months from now, I shall attain Parinibbāna," seven hundred worldling monks, overcome with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), did not leave the Buddha's presence. They wandered about consulting one another, saying, "Friends, what shall we do?"

However, Elder Attadattha thought: "It is said that the Teacher will attain Parinibbāna in four months. I have not yet freed myself from passion. While the Teacher is still alive, I will strive for the sake of the Fruit of Arahantship." Thus, he did not go near the other monks. Then the monks asked him, "Friend, why do you neither come to us nor consult with us?" and they took him to the Teacher, reporting, "Venerable Sir, this monk Attadattha acts in such a manner."

When the Teacher asked him, "Why do you act thus?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, it is said that you will attain Parinibbāna in four months. I am striving to reach Arahantship while you are still alive."
103:
The Teacher gave him his approval and said, "Monks, whoever has affection for me should be like Elder Attadattha. For those who honor me with scents and such do not truly honor me. Only those who practice the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti) truly honor me. Therefore, other monks should also be just like Attadattha." Having said this, he spoke this verse:

(The verse and its word-by-word meaning are as previously stated in the teaching section.)

This was spoken by way of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Therefore, a monk should not neglect the duties of the Saṅgha, such as repairing shrines (cetiya), or duties toward preceptors (upajjhāya), thinking, "I will not neglect my own welfare." Indeed, it is only by fulfilling the duties of proper conduct (ābhisamācārika-vatta) that one realizes the Noble Fruits. Thus, this too is one's own welfare. However, one who has intensely begun insight meditation (vipassanā), seeking realization thinking "today or tomorrow," should indeed fulfill his own task even if it means neglecting duties toward preceptors and the like. Having understood such a form of one's own welfare and recognizing "this is my own goal," one should be devoted and applied to that own goal (sadatthapasuto).

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder was established in Arahantship. The teaching of the Dhamma was also beneficial to the monks who had arrived.
The Story of Elder Attadattha ends.
The twelfth chapter, the Attavagga (Chapter on the Self), is finished.
104:
## 13. Lokavagga (Chapter on the World)
## 1. The Story of a Certain Young Monk
(Dahara-bhikkhu-vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this religious teaching, beginning with "Hīnaṃ dhammaṃ," concerning a certain young monk.

## The Young Monk and Visākhā's Granddaughter
A certain Elder, together with a young monk, went early in the morning to the house of the lay devotee Visākhā. At Visākhā's house, rice gruel was always prepared for five hundred monks.

The Elder, having drunk the gruel there, left the young monk and went to another house. At that time, Visākhā's granddaughter, standing in her grandmother's place, was performing duties for the monks. While she was straining water for the young monk, she saw the reflection of her own face in the water jar and laughed. The young monk also looked at the girl and laughed. Seeing him laugh, the girl said, "The shaven-head (cut-head) is laughing!"

Then the young monk insulted her, saying, "You are the shaven-head! Your mother and father are also shaven-heads!" The girl went crying to her grandmother Visākhā in the kitchen. When asked, "Dear granddaughter, why are you crying?" she told her the reason. Visākhā went to the young monk and said, "Venerable Sir, do not be angry. It is not a grave matter for an Elder like you, who has shorn hair and nails, wears shorn (cut) robes, and wanders for alms carrying a shorn (broken-edged) bowl."

The young monk replied, "Lay devotee, indeed it is so. You know that I have shorn hair and so on. But is it right for this girl to insult me by calling me a shaven-head?" Visākhā was unable to make either the young monk or the girl understand.

## The Buddha's Admonition
At that moment, the Great Elder arrived and asked, "Lay devotee, what is this matter?" Having heard the story, he admonished the young monk, saying, "Go away, friend. This girl did not insult you, who goes for alms with shorn hair, nails, and robes, carrying a shorn bowl. Therefore, be silent."

He replied, "Venerable Sir, that is true. But why do you threaten me instead of threatening your own supporter? Is it right for her to insult me as a shaven-head?"

At that moment, the Teacher arrived and asked, "What is this?" Visākhā reported the matter from the beginning. The Teacher, seeing the young monk's potential (upanissaya) for the Fruit of Stream-entry, thought, "I should follow the inclination of this young monk," and said, "Visākhā, how is it? Is it right for your granddaughter to insult my disciple as a shaven-head merely because he has shorn hair and such?"
105:
## The Teaching

(167) One should not follow a low practice; one should not live with negligence.
One should not follow wrong view; one should not be a world-prolonger.

*Hīnaṃ dhammaṃ*: the low practice of the five cords of sensual pleasure. *Na seveyya*: one should not follow. *Pamādena*: with negligence, characterized by the loss of mindfulness. *Na saṃvase*: one should not live with. *Micchādiṭṭhiṃ*: wrong view. *Na seveyya*: one should not adopt. *Lokavaḍḍhano*: the prolonging of the world. *Na siyā*: should not be.

At that very moment, the young monk stood up, raised his joined palms in salutation, and said, "Venerable Sir, only you, the Exalted One, know this problem well. Our preceptor and the lay devotee Visākhā do not know it well, Bhante." The Teacher, knowing the young monk's suitability to himself, said, "Laughter concerning the cords of sensual pleasure is indeed a low state. It is not proper to follow what is called a low state, nor to live together with negligence," and he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the young monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The teaching of the Dhamma was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of the Unknown Young Monk is finished.

## 2. The Story of King Suddhodana

(Suddhodana Vatthu)

The Teacher spoke this teaching of the Dhamma beginning with "Uttiṭṭhe" while staying at Nigrodhārāma, concerning his father, King Suddhodana.

## The First Alms-round in Kapilavatthu

On one occasion, the Teacher went to Kapilavatthu on his first journey. Having been welcomed by his relatives, he reached Nigrodhārāma. To break the pride of his relatives, he created a jeweled walkway in the sky and preached the Dhamma while walking upon it. The relatives, with hearts of settled faith, paid homage, beginning with King Suddhodana. In that gathering of relatives, he caused the Pokkharavassa rain to fall, which is like rain falling on a lotus pond.
106:
## The Teaching

(168) One should not be negligent in the alms-round; one should practice the Dhamma well.
He who practices the Dhamma lives happily in this world and the next.

(169) One should practice the Dhamma well; one should not practice it poorly.
He who practices the Dhamma lives happily in this world and the next.

*Uttiṭṭhe*: in the alms-food to be received by standing at the doors of others' houses. *Nappamajjeyya*: one should not be negligent. *Sucaritaṃ*: well-practiced. *Dhammaṃ*: the practice of wandering for alms. *Care*: one should practice. *Dhammacārī*: one who habitually fulfills the duty of wandering for alms. *Asmiṃ loke ca*: in this world. *Paramhi ca*: and in the next world. *Sukhaṃ*: happily. *Seti*: lives.

*Sucaritaṃ*: well-practiced. *Dhammaṃ*: the practice of going for alms. *Care*: one should practice. *Duccaritaṃ*: poorly practiced. *Naṃ*: that practice of alms-round. *Na care*: one should not practice. *Dhammacārī*: one who habitually practices the alms-round according to the Dhamma. *Asmiṃ loke ca*: in this world. *Paramhi ca*: and in the next world. *Sukhaṃ*: happily. *Seti*: lives.

When the multitude of people started a conversation concerning that rain, the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past also, I have caused the Pokkharavassa rain to fall at a gathering of my relatives," and he told the Vessantara Jātaka. After hearing the Dhamma teaching, when the relatives departed, not even a single person invited the Teacher. Even the King went away without inviting him, thinking, "Where will my son go if he does not come to my house?" Having gone home, he had gruel and other foods prepared for twenty thousand monks and had seats arranged.

On the following day, the Teacher, entering for alms, reflected, "How was it? When the Buddhas of the past reached their father's city, did they enter the relatives' houses directly, or did they wander for alms in sequence?" He saw that they wandered in sequence. Starting from the first house, he entered and wandered for alms. Princess Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula, saw this from the palace terrace and informed the King. King Suddhodana, unable to even dress himself properly, rushed out, paid homage to the Teacher, and said, "Son, why do you ruin me? You cause me great shame by wandering for alms. Is it not proper for you to wander for alms in this city only after traveling in golden palanquins and such? Why do you make me ashamed?"

"Great King, I do not shame you; I am merely following my own lineage," the Teacher said. "But, son, how can the lineage of living by wandering for alms be my lineage?" the King asked. "Great King, this lineage of wandering for alms is not your lineage; it is my lineage. Many thousands of Buddhas lived only by wandering for alms," the Teacher said, and desiring to preach the Dhamma, he spoke these verses.

(Wandering for alms while being intimate with these six houses: stables, houses of eunuchs, nunneries, houses of old maids, widows, and prostitutes, is called 'bad practice'.)
107:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the royal father, King Suddhodana, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.
The Story of King Suddhodana ends.

## The Teaching
(170) Yathā pubbuḷakaṃ passe, yathā passe marīcikaṃ.
Evaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantaṃ, maccurājā na passati.

*Pubbuḷakaṃ*, a bubble. *Passe yathā*, just as one should observe it as something that arises and then perishes. *Lokaṃ*, the world of the aggregates (khandhas), etc. *Passe*, one should observe it, thinking, "Indeed, it arises and then perishes." *Marīcikaṃ*, a magical illusion or a mirage. *Passe yathā*, just as one should observe it as not being what it appears to be. *Lokaṃ*, the world of the aggregates, etc. *Passe*, one should observe it, thinking, "Indeed, it is not what it appears to be." *Evaṃ*, in this way. *Lokaṃ*, the world of the aggregates, etc. *Avekkhantaṃ*, one who observes. *Maccurājā*, the King of Death. *Na passati*, does not see.

## 3. The Story of the Five Hundred Insight-practicing Monks
(Pañcasatavipassakabhikkhu Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Yathā pubbuḷakaṃ," concerning five hundred monks who were practicing insight meditation (Vipassanā).

## Contemplating the Body Like a Bubble
These five hundred monks, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered the forest and strove diligently. However, as they did not attain any distinction (Arahantship), they thought, "We will take a meditation subject with further distinction," and returned to the Teacher. On their way, they came along while developing the meditation subject of a mirage. At the very moment they entered the monastery, it rained. Standing at the various entrances of the monastery buildings, they saw bubbles and foam rising and breaking due to the force of the downpour. They took this as an object of meditation, thinking, "This body, too, is just like a bubble because of its nature of arising and then breaking." The Teacher, while sitting in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), looked at those monks and, as if speaking with them, sent forth a radiance and uttered this verse:
108:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, those five hundred monks attained Arahantship right where they stood.
The Story of the Five Hundred Insight-practicing Monks ends.

## The Teaching
(171) Etha passathimaṃ lokaṃ, cittaṃ rājarathūpamaṃ.
Yattha bālā visīdanti, natthi saṅgo vijānataṃ.

*Etha*, come. *Rājarathūpamaṃ*, like a king's chariot adorned with the seven kinds of jewels, etc. *Cittaṃ*, variegated with clothes, ornaments, etc. *Imaṃ lokaṃ*, this existence (attabhāva) known as the world of the aggregates, etc. *Passatha*, look at it. *Yattha*, in which existence. *Bālā*, fools who do not know. *Visīdanti*, they sink or flounder. *Vijānataṃ* (vijānantānaṃ), for the wise. *Saṅgo*, attachment such as lust (rāga), etc. *Natthi*, there is none.

## 4. The Story of Prince Abhaya
(Abhayarājakumāra Vatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Etha passathimaṃ lokaṃ," concerning Prince Abhaya.

## The Prince's Grief Over the Dancing Girl
When Prince Abhaya returned after pacifying a rebellion in the border regions, his father, King Bimbisāra, was so pleased that he gave him a dancing girl skilled in dancing and singing, and granted him the kingdom for seven days. For seven days, without leaving the palace, the Prince enjoyed royal splendor. On the eighth day, he went to the riverbank, bathed, and entered the park. Like the minister Santati, he sat watching the dancing and singing of that woman. At that very moment, like the dancing girl of the minister Santati, she passed away due to the force of razor-like winds (sharp internal pains). Because of her death, the Prince was overcome with grief. Thinking, "No one other than the Teacher will be able to quench this grief of mine," he approached the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, please quench my grief." The Teacher consoled him, saying, "Prince Abhaya, in this beginningless Saṃsāra, there is no measure to the tears you have shed while weeping at the death of this woman in this very manner." Knowing that his grief had lessened through that teaching, the Teacher said, "Prince, do not grieve; this is the place where fools flounder," and uttered this verse:
109:
"This body is a place where the ignorant sink," he said, and preached this verse.

## Benefit of the Discourse
At the end of the discourse, Prince Abhaya was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of Prince Abhaya ends.

## 5. The Story of Elder Sammajjana
(Sammajjanattheravatthu)
While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yo ca pubbe," concerning the Elder named Sammajjana, who was so called because he was fond of sweeping.

## Being Fond of Sweeping Without Meditating
That Elder Sammajjana used to go about constantly sweeping, without setting a specific time or limit, whether in the morning or in the evening. One day, taking a broom, he went to Elder Revata, who was sitting in his day-quarters, and thought, "This Elder is very lazy. Having eaten the alms-food offered out of faith by the people, he comes and just sits. Is it not proper for him to take a broom and sweep a certain place?" Elder Revata, thinking, "I will give him an instruction," said, "Come, friend." "What is it, venerable sir?" he asked. "Friend, go and bathe first, then come back," he said. Elder Sammajjana did as Elder Revata said. Then Elder Revata, having him sit in a suitable place, advised him, saying, "Friend, one who is called a bhikkhu should not go about sweeping all the time. Having swept only in the early morning, gone for alms, and returned from the alms-round, one should sit in one's night-quarters or day-quarters and recite the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra), establishing the perception of rise and fall (khayavaya) in one's own body. Only in the evening should one get up and sweep. One should not sweep all the time but should also make an opportunity for one's own meditation."

Abiding by the instruction of Elder Revata, Elder Sammajjana attained Arahantship before long. Consequently, various places became dusty. Then the bhikkhus asked him, "Friend Sammajjana, various places have become dusty. Why do you not sweep?" "Venerable sirs, I did such sweeping during the time I was heedless. Now I am one who is heedful," he replied.
110:
When he said this, the bhikkhus reported to the Buddha, "This Elder is claiming the Fruit of Arahantship." The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, it is true that my son Sammajjana went about sweeping during the time he was heedless. But now, he spends his time in the bliss of the Path and Fruit and does not sweep," and he spoke this verse:

## The Discourse
(172) He who was formerly heedless, but afterwards is not heedless, illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.

Yo: any person. Pubbe: formerly. Pamajjitvā: being heedless by way of performing duties or recitation. Pacchā: afterwards. So: that person. Na pamazzati: is not heedless, spending time with the bliss of the Path and Fruit. So: that person. Abbhā mutto candimā va: like the moon freed from a cloud, which illuminates the world of space. Imaṃ lokaṃ pabhāseti: illuminates this world of the aggregates (khandha), etc.

## Benefit of the Discourse
At the end of the discourse, many bhikkhus attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of Elder Sammajjana ends.

## 6. The Story of Elder Aṅgulimāla
(Aṅgulimālattheravatthu)
While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yassa pāpaṃ," concerning the Elder Aṅgulimāla.

## Elder Aṅgulimāla's Entry into Nibbāna
The story of Elder Aṅgulimāla should be understood by way of the Aṅgulimāla Sutta in the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa. Elder Aṅgulimāla, having been ordained in the presence of the Buddha, attained Arahantship. Then, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, having gone into seclusion and living alone, experienced the bliss of the Fruit of Arahantship. At that time, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):

"He who was formerly heedless, but afterwards is not heedless, illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud."

(The meaning has already been given in the previous story of Elder Sammajjana.)

Having uttered this inspired utterance and so forth, he passed away into the Nibbāna element without any remainder of the aggregates of existence (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). The bhikkhus started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, "Friends, where has Elder Aṅgulimāla been reborn?" The Teacher came and asked, "Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we are gathered for a discussion regarding the place of rebirth of Elder Aṅgulimāla," he said, "Bhikkhus, my son has attained Parinibbāna." "Venerable Sir, has he attained Parinibbāna after killing so many people?" they asked. "Yes, bhikkhus. Formerly, because he did not find a single good friend (kalyāṇamitta), he committed so much evil. But later, because he obtained the support of a good friend, he became heedful."
111:
## The Teaching

(173) Whoever covers the evil deed done with a wholesome deed, that person illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.

"Whose" (Yassa) refers to any person. "Evil deed done" (Kataṃ pāpaṃ) refers to the unwholesome action committed. "With a wholesome deed" (Kusalena) refers to the Path of Arahatship. "Is covered" (Pidhīyati) means it is closed off. "That person" (So) refers to that individual. "Like the moon freed from a cloud" (Abbhā muttovacandimā) means just like the moon emerging from a mass of clouds. "Illuminates this world" (Imaṃ lokaṃ pabhāseti) means they brighten this world of the aggregates and so forth.

Therefore, the Buddha said, "Angulimāla's evil deed has been closed off by wholesome kamma," and he spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many monks and others attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of the Elder Angulimāla ends.

## 7. The Story of the Weaver's Daughter
(Pesakāradhītā-vatthu)

"Blinded is this world" (Andhabhūto)—the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching while staying at the Aggāḷava Shrine, concerning a certain weaver's daughter.

## The Weaver's Daughter who Practiced Dhamma for Three Years

One day, when the Teacher arrived at the city of Āḷavī, the residents of Āḷavī invited him and offered alms. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher, wishing to give a talk of appreciation (anumodanā), said:

1. "Aduvaṃ me jīvitaṃ"—My life is uncertain.
2. "Dhuvaṃ me maraṇaṃ"—My death is certain.
3. "Avassaṃ mayā maritabbameva"—I must surely die.
4. "Maraṇapariyosānaṃ me jīvitaṃ"—My life ends in death.
5. "Jīvitameva aniyataṃ"—Life itself is unstable.
6. "Maraṇaṃ niyataṃ"—Death is stable.

"In this way, develop the meditation on the mindfulness of death (maraṇassati). For those who have not developed mindfulness of death, when their final hour comes, they are like a man without a weapon who sees a venomous snake and is terrified; they pass away in great distress, uttering cries of horror. But for those who have developed mindfulness of death, they are like a man who sees a venomous snake from afar and, catching it with a stick and throwing it away, remains calm; they do not tremble at their final hour. Therefore, mindfulness of death should be developed."

After hearing this teaching, the rest of the people went about their own business. However, one young weaver's daughter, about sixteen years of age, thought, "How wonderful is the speech of the Buddhas! It is proper for me to develop mindfulness of death." She practiced mindfulness of death alone, day and night. The Teacher then left Āḷavī and went to the Jetavana Monastery. That young girl continued to develop mindfulness of death for three full years.
112:
## The Buddha's Journey for the Young Girl

Then one day, as the Teacher surveyed the world at dawn, he saw that young girl within the net of his omniscience. He reflected, "What will happen?" and realized, "This young girl has developed mindfulness of death for three years since the day she heard my teaching. Now, I shall go to Āḷavī and ask her four questions. When she answers them, I will give her praise at each of the four points and speak this verse. At the end of the verse, she will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. Depending on her, the Dhamma teaching will also be beneficial to the great multitude."

Knowing this, he set out from Jetavana surrounded by five hundred monks and in due course arrived at the Aggāḷava Monastery. When the residents of Āḷavī heard that the Teacher had arrived, they went to the monastery and invited him.

At that time, the young girl also heard of the Teacher's arrival. With a joyful heart, she thought, "My father, my lord, my teacher, the Great Gotama Buddha with a face like the full moon, has arrived! Three years ago, I first saw the Teacher of golden hue. Now I shall get to see his golden-hued body and hear his sweet and noble Dhamma."

However, her father, as he was going to the weaving shed, said, "Dear daughter, a garment belonging to someone else is on the loom, and about a span of it is not yet finished. I will finish it today. Therefore, quickly wind the weft-thread (tasara) and bring it to me."

## Listening to Dhamma after Delivering the Shuttle

The young girl thought, "I want to hear the Teacher's Dhamma, but my father has told me this. Should I listen to the Teacher's Dhamma, or should I wind the weft-thread and take it to my father?" Then it occurred to her, "If I do not bring the shuttle, my father might strike or beat me. Therefore, I will wind the shuttle, give it to him, and then listen to the Dhamma." Thinking thus, she sat on a stool and wound the shuttle. The residents of Āḷavī, having served the Teacher with food, took his bowl and stood waiting for the talk of appreciation.

## The Young Girl Arrives Before the Buddha

The Teacher thought, "I have come a journey of thirty yojanas for the sake of this young girl. Even now, she has not yet found the opportunity. When she finds the opportunity, I will preach the Dhamma." Thus, he remained silent. When the Teacher remained silent in this way, no one in the world, including the devas, dared to say anything. 

The young girl, having wound the shuttle and placed it in a basket, was going to her father's place. She stopped at the edge of the assembly and stood looking at the Teacher. The Teacher raised his neck and looked at her. By the manner of his looking, the girl understood, "The Teacher, sitting in the midst of such an assembly, is looking at me and expecting my arrival; he expects me to come into his presence." She set down the basket of shuttles and approached the Teacher.
113:
(Why did the Blessed One look at the young girl? It was because this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "If this young girl goes from this place, she will die as a worldling (puthujjana) and her destination (gati) will be uncertain. But if she comes to me and then departs, she will attain the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and, having a certain destination, will be reborn in the Tusita heaven." Thus he thought and looked at her. For that young girl, there was no such thing as escaping death on that day.)

Recognizing that she was being looked at, the young girl approached the Blessed One, entered within the range of his six-colored rays, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. While she stood there having paid homage to the silent Blessed One in the midst of such an assembly, the Blessed One asked her these questions:

## The Four Questions and Four Answers in Brief
1. "Young girl, where do you come from?" When asked, she replied, "Venerable Sir, I do not know."
2. "Where will you go?" When asked, she replied, "Venerable Sir, I do not know."
3. "Do you not know?" When asked, she replied, "Venerable Sir, I know."
4. "Do you know?" When asked, she replied, "Venerable Sir, I do not know."

## The Assembly's Criticism of the Girl
Thus the Blessed One asked the young girl these four questions. The great multitude of people criticized her, saying, "O friends, look! This weaver's daughter speaks whatever she pleases with the Fully Enlightened One. When asked 'Where do you come from?', should she not have said 'From the weaver's house'? When asked 'Where will you go?', should she not have said 'To the weaving shed'?"

## Detailed Explanation of the Meaning
The Blessed One silenced the great multitude and asked:
1. "Young girl, when asked 'Where do you come from?', why did you say 'I do not know'?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, you know that I have come from the weaver's house. By asking 'Where do you come from?', you were asking from what past life I have come to be born here. But I do not know from what life I have come to be born here. That is why I answered thus."
Then the Blessed One gave her the first approval, saying, "Sādhu, sādhu, young girl! You have answered the very question I intended to ask," and he asked further.
114:
2. "When asked again, 'Where will you go?', why did you say 'I do not know'?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, you know that I am going to the weaving shed carrying this shuttle basket. You were asking where I will be reborn after departing from this life. But I do not know where I will be reborn after passing away from this life. That is why I answered thus."
Then the Blessed One gave her approval for the second time, saying, "You have spoken what I intended to ask," and he asked further.

3. "Then, when asked 'Do you not know?', why did you say 'I know'?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, I know that I must die. That is why I answered thus."
Then the Blessed One gave her approval for the third time, saying, "You have answered the very question I intended to ask," and he asked further.

4. "Then, when asked 'Do you know?', why did you say 'I do not know'?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, I only know that I must die. But I do not know at what time—whether at night, during the day, or in the morning—I shall die. That is why I answered thus."

Then the Blessed One gave her approval for the fourth time. Addressing the assembly, he said, "You did not understand even this much of what this young girl said; you only criticized her. Those who do not have the eye of wisdom are indeed blind. Only those who possess the eye of wisdom are truly endowed with sight," and he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(174) Blind is this world; few here see clearly.
Like a bird escaped from a net, few go to heaven.

"This world" refers to the great multitude of worldly people who are blind due to the absence of the eye of wisdom. "Few here" means that in this world, only a few people—not many—practice insight (vipassanā) by way of impermanence (anicca) and so forth. "Like a bird escaped from a net" means that just as when a clever fowler covers quails with a net and catches them, only a few escape from the net while the rest remain inside, so too, among beings covered by the net of death, many go to the states of deprivation (apāya), and only a few beings go to heaven, or reach a happy destination (sugati) or Nibbāna.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, the young girl was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude.

## The Death of the Girl and the Father's Ordination
The young girl then took her shuttle basket and went to her father. Her father, the weaver, had fallen asleep while sitting. Without noticing this, as she handed him the shuttle basket, it struck the edge of the loom and fell with a sound. The father woke up and, with the sudden impulse of waking, pulled the loom handle (shuttle). The tip of the loom struck the girl in the chest. She died right there and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. When the father looked at his daughter, he saw her fallen and dead, her whole body covered in blood. Great sorrow arose in him. Thinking, "No one else will be able to extinguish my sorrow," he went weeping to the Blessed One, reported the matter, and said, "Venerable Sir, please extinguish my sorrow."
The Blessed One consoled the weaver, saying, "Lay follower, do not grieve. In this Saṃsāra, whose beginning is inconceivable, the tears you have shed at the death of your daughters in this very manner are far more than the water in the four great oceans," and he preached the Anamatagga Sutta.
115:
The weaver, having his grief diminished, requested the Teacher for ordination. Upon receiving the higher ordination, he attained Arahantship in no long time.

The Story of the Weaver's Daughter ends.

## The Teaching
(175) Swans fly on the path of the sun; they fly through the air by psychic power. The wise are led away from the world, having conquered Mara and his host.

Swans fly in the sky, which is the path of the sun. Those who have well-developed the four bases of power (Iddhipādas) fly through the air by psychic power. The wise, having conquered Mara and his army, are led out of this world and reach Nibbāna.

## 8. The Story of Thirty Monks
(Tiṃsabhikkhuvatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this religious teaching beginning with "Haṃsādiccapathe," concerning thirty monks.

## Coming by Land and Returning by Air
One day, about thirty monks living in various regions came to visit the Teacher. The Elder Ānanda, arriving at the time of performing duties for the Teacher, saw those monks and thought, "I will perform my duties after the Buddha has finished his friendly conversation (paṭisanthāra) with these monks," and stood waiting at the gateway. The Teacher, after engaging in friendly conversation with those monks, spoke to them a memorable teaching (sāraṇīyadhamma). Upon hearing the teaching, all those monks attained Arahantship and, rising into the air, departed through the sky. 

When those monks had been gone a long time, the Elder Ānanda approached the Teacher and asked, "Venerable Sir, about thirty monks arrived just now. Where are they?" "They have gone, Ānanda." "By which way did they go, Venerable Sir?" "Through the air, Ānanda." "But Venerable Sir, are they those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava)?" "Yes, Ānanda, they attained Arahantship after hearing the Dhamma in my presence." 

At that moment, swans were flying through the air. The Teacher said, "Ānanda, whoever has well-developed the four bases of power goes through the air like a swan," and spoke this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of the Thirty Monks ends.
116:
## 9. The Story of the Woman Ciñcamāṇavikā
(Ciñcamāṇavikāvatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this religious teaching beginning with "Ekaṃ dhammaṃ," concerning Ciñcamāṇavikā.

## The Plot of the Ascetics
During the first period after Enlightenment, when the disciples of the One of Ten Powers had become numerous, and immeasurable devas and humans had entered the Noble Ground, great gain and honor arose due to the spread of his gathered virtues. 

The ascetics (Titthiyas) became like fireflies at sunrise, their gain and honor destroyed. Standing in the middle of the streets, they said, "Is only the ascetic Gotama the Buddha? We are also Buddhas. Is only a gift given to him of great fruit? A gift given to us is also of great fruit. Therefore, give to us and honor us." Even though they thus informed the people, they did not receive gain and honor. They met in secret and thought, "By what means can we cause dispraise for the ascetic Gotama among the people and destroy his gain and honor?"

## Using Ciñcamāṇā to Destroy the Buddha's Gains
At that time, in the city of Sāvatthī, there was a female wandering ascetic named Ciñcamāṇavikā, who possessed supreme beauty and was perfect in grace, like a celestial nymph. Rays of light seemed to emanate from her body. Then, a harsh-minded ascetic said, "By means of Ciñcamāṇavikā, let us cause dispraise for the ascetic Gotama and destroy his gain and honor." The other ascetics agreed, saying, "This is a way." 

Then, Ciñcamāṇavikā went to the monastery of the ascetics, paid homage, and stood there. The ascetics did not speak to her. She thought, "What is my fault?" and after saying "I pay homage, sirs" three times, she asked, "Sirs, what is my fault? Why do you not speak with me?" They said, "Sister, do you not know that the ascetic Gotama is harming us, wandering about having destroyed our gain and honor?" She replied, "I do not know, sirs. What should I do in this matter?" They said, "Sister, if you wish for our happiness, you must cause dispraise for the ascetic Gotama by means of yourself and destroy his gain and honor."

## How Ciñcamāṇā Accused
She said, "Very well, sirs. This is my responsibility. Do not worry." She departed, and being skilled in feminine wiles, from that day on, when the citizens of Sāvatthī were leaving Jetavana Monastery after hearing the Dhamma, she would wrap herself in a cloak the color of a ladybug and, carrying perfumes and garlands, walk towards Jetavana. 

When asked, "Where are you going at this time?" she would reply, "What is the use of my destination to you?" She would then stay at the monastery of the ascetics near Jetavana. Early in the morning, when the lay devotees were coming out of the city thinking, "We will pay our first respects," she would enter the city as if she had stayed inside Jetavana. When asked, "Where did you stay?" she would say, "What is the use of my dwelling place to you?" After half a month had passed, when asked, she said, "I stay with the ascetic Gotama in the same Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) in Jetavana."
117:
To the worldlings, she caused doubt, thinking, "Is what this Ciñcamāṇavikā says true or not?"; and after three or four months had passed, she showed the appearance of pregnancy by wrapping her belly with coarse cloths; and wrapping a red cloth over it, she made the foolish believe, "I have conceived a child because of the ascetic Gotama"; and after eight or nine months had passed, she tied a round piece of wood to her belly, wrapped a cloth over it, and had the backs of her hands and feet beaten with a cow's jawbone to show swelling; and appearing with weary faculties, in the evening, while the Blessed One was sitting on the adorned Dhamma-throne preaching the Dhamma, she went to the Dhamma hall and, standing before the Blessed One, said: "Great ascetic, you preach the Dhamma to the multitude; your voice is sweet and your lips are well-shaped. As for me, I have conceived a child because of you and am now full-term. You do not know of a lying-in room for me, nor do you know of ghee, oil, and so on. If you cannot do it yourself, you do not even tell one of your attendants—either King Kosala, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, or the laywoman Visākhā—to do what is necessary for this Ciñcamāṇavikā. You only know how to enjoy yourself, but you do not know how to care for the pregnancy." Thus, like one attempting to defile the moon with a lump of dung, she slandered and reviled the Blessed One in the midst of the fourfold assembly.

## The Swallowing of Ciñcamāṇā by the Earth

The Blessed One, pausing his discourse and making a fearless sound like a lion king, said: "Sister, whether what you have said is true or false, only you and I know." She replied: "Yes, great ascetic, it is because it is known only by you and me that this has happened."

At that moment, the Paṇḍukambala stone throne of Sakka, King of Devas, showed signs of heat. Upon reflecting, Sakka realized, "The woman named Ciñcamāṇavikā is falsely reviling the Tathāgata," and thinking, "I will clear up this matter," he went there together with four young deities. The deities took the form of young mice and, in a single stroke, gnawed through the strings that bound the wooden disk. The wind lifted the cloth she was wearing. When the wooden disk fell, it landed on Ciñcamāṇavikā's feet. Both her toes were broken. The people cried out, "Shame on you, wretched woman! You revile the Fully Enlightened One!" They spat on her head and, with clods of earth and sticks in their hands, drove her out of the Jetavana monastery. Then, when she had passed beyond the sight of the Tathāgata, the great earth split open and gave her passage. Flames from Avīci rose up. That Ciñcamāṇavikā, as if wrapping herself in a woolen blanket given by her beloved parents, went and was reborn in Avīci. The gains and honors of the heretics outside the Dispensation declined. For the Blessed One, they increased exceedingly.
118:
Without seeing the fault in another for oneself, whether small or great in every way, a ruler should not inflict punishment without personal investigation.

(Gloss: A ruler, the lord of the land, without seeing the fault of another, and without personally investigating all faults, small and great, should not inflict punishment.)

Again, at dawn in the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a discussion: "Friends, Ciñcamāṇavikā, having falsely slandered and reviled the Fully Enlightened One, who possesses such vast virtues and is worthy of the highest offerings, has met with great destruction."

## Summary of the Mahāpaduma Jataka

The Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," he said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too, this Ciñcamāṇavikā met with destruction because of falsely slandering me." He then related the Mahāpaduma Jataka of the Dwadasa Nipata in detail:

(In the time of King Mahāsammata, there was no punishment exceeding a hundred. There was no cutting of hands or feet or execution beyond banishment. All these came about during the reigns of later kings. The ministers spoke referring to such punishments, as stated in the Commentary on the Dwadasa Nipata Jataka.)

In the Dwadasa Nipata, he preached this Mahāpaduma Jataka in detail. At that time, this Ciñcamāṇavikā was the rival of the mother of the Bodhisatta, Prince Mahāpaduma—that is, she was the Chief Queen of the King. Having invited and enticed the Bodhisatta with unrighteousness and failing to win the prince's heart, she herself disfigured her own body. Showing the appearance of an invalid, she reported to the King, "Your son has brought this ruin upon your sister who was unwilling." The King was enraged and threw the Bodhisatta into the thieves' cliff. Then, a deity guarding the mountain valley received the Bodhisatta and placed him in the hood-chamber of the Naga King. The Naga King took Prince Paduma to the Naga realm and honored him with half of his kingdom.

That Bodhisatta, having lived in the Naga realm for a full year, desired to go forth as an ascetic. He went to the Himavanta region, became an ascetic, and attained the meditative absorptions and higher powers. Then, a forest hunter saw the Bodhisatta ascetic and reported it to the King. The King went to the Bodhisatta ascetic, and after the proper greetings, learned the whole story. He invited the Bodhisatta to take the kingdom, but the Bodhisatta ascetic said, "I have no need for the kingdom. You, O King, should rule righteously, not violating the ten royal virtues and abandoning the four wrong paths." Having been thus advised, the King rose from his seat, weeping and lamenting, and while returning to the city, he asked his ministers on the way: "Because of whom have I been separated from such a virtuous and noble son?"
119:
## The Teaching

(176) For the person who has transgressed one law (of truth), who speaks lies, and who has rejected the world beyond, there is no evil that they cannot do.

*Ekaṃ dhammaṃ*: the one truth. *Atītassa*: who has transgressed. *Musāvādissa*: who is in the habit of speaking falsehoods, not even one word in ten being true. *Vitiṇṇaparalokassa*: who has abandoned the world beyond. *Jantuno*: for the being. *Akāriyaṃ pāpaṃ*: an evil deed that is not to be done. *Natthi*: there is not.

When the ministers reported, "Great King, we were separated because of the Queen," the King had the Queen seized by her head and feet and thrown into the abyss where thieves are hurled. He then entered the city and ruled righteously. At that time, Prince Mahāpaduma was the Bodhisatta, and the Queen, the enemy of the mother (or co-wife), was Ciñcamāṇavikā. Having told this matter, the Blessed One said: "Monks, for those who abandon the one Dhamma called truthful speech, who dwell in falsehood, and who have given up the world beyond, there is no evil deed they cannot commit." He then uttered this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the woman Ciñcamāṇavikā ends.

## 10. The Story of the Incomparable Alms-giving

(Asadisadāna-vatthu)

The Teacher, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Na ve kadariyā" in reference to the Incomparable Alms-giving.

## The Great Alms-giving Competition

On one occasion, the Teacher, having wandered on a journey, entered Jetavana Monastery accompanied by five hundred monks. King Kosala went to Jetavana, invited the Teacher, and having prepared alms for the guests (āgantuka-dāna) the next day, called the citizens, saying, "Come and see my alms-giving." The citizens came and saw the King's alms-giving. The next day, the citizens invited the Teacher, prepared alms, and sent word to the King, saying, "Great King, please come and see our alms-giving as well." When the King saw the citizens' alms-giving, he thought, "These citizens have done even more than my alms-giving. I shall give alms again." Thus, he prepared alms the next day. The citizens, seeing the King's alms, prepared theirs again the next day. In this way, the King could not defeat the citizens, nor could the citizens defeat the King. Then, at the sixth time of giving, the citizens increased their gift a hundredfold and a thousandfold, arranging it in such a way that it could not be said that any particular item was missing from their alms-giving. When the King saw the citizens' alms-giving, he thought, "If I cannot surpass the alms-giving of these citizens, what is the use of my life?" and he lay down, pondering a means to succeed.
120:
## Queen Mallikā's Skillful Arrangement

Then Queen Mallikā approached the King and asked, "Great King, why do you lie down like this? Why do your faculties appear so weary?" The King said to the Queen, "Do you not know now?" "I do not know yet, Sire," she replied. The King then told Queen Mallikā the matter.

Then Queen Mallikā said to the King, "Great King, do not worry. How is it? Have you ever seen or heard of a lord of the earth being defeated by his subjects? I shall arrange the alms-giving for you." Desiring to arrange the Incomparable Alms-giving, she said, "Great King, have a pavilion built with planks of sāla-kalyāṇī wood for five hundred monks to sit within the inner circle; the remaining monks will sit outside the circle. Have five hundred white umbrellas made; five hundred elephants shall stand holding those white umbrellas over the heads of the five hundred monks. Have eight or ten boats made of reddish-gold; they shall be in the middle of the pavilion. Between every two monks, a princess shall sit and grind perfumes. Each princess shall hold a fan and stand fanning two monks. The other princesses shall carry the perfumes as they are ground and put them into the golden boats. Among those princesses, some shall take bunches of blue lotuses and stir the perfumes placed in the golden boats to release the fragrance. The citizens have no princesses, no white umbrellas, and no elephants. By these means, the citizens will be defeated. Great King, do so."

## The Fierce Elephant and Elder Aṅgulimāla

The King said, "Excellent, Queen! Your words are of a beneficial nature," and he had everything done according to the method she described. However, there was one elephant short for one monk. Then the King said to Queen Mallikā, "Dear Queen, there is one elephant missing for one monk; what shall we do?" When she asked, "Sire, are there not five hundred elephants?" he replied, "Queen, there are, but the remaining elephants are fierce and wild. As soon as they see monks, they become as violent as the Veramba winds."

"Sire, I know a place where a fierce young elephant can stand holding an umbrella," she said. When he asked, "Where should we place that fierce elephant?" she replied, "Place him near the noble Elder Aṅgulimāla." The King did exactly as Queen Mallikā said. The young elephant tucked his tail between his thighs, lowered both ears, closed his eyes, and stood still. The multitude of people looked only at the elephant, saying, "Indeed, such a fierce elephant can be made to have no fear or danger!"

## The Great Gift of Fourteen Crores

The King, having served the Sangha headed by the Buddha, prostrated before the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, whatever allowable (kappiya) or unallowable (akappiya) goods are in this alms-hall, I offer them all only to the Exalted One."
121:
The fearless like a bull, the noble, the heroic,
The great seeker, the conqueror,
The craving-free, the cleansed, the awakened—
Him I call a Brahmin.

Usabhaṃ: like a bull because of fearlessness. Pavaraṃ: the most noble. Vīraṃ: possessing firm effort and energy. Mahesiṃ: one who seeks and accumulates the special attributes such as the aggregate of virtue. Vijitāvinaṃ: one who has conquered the three Maras. Anejaṃ: free from craving known as ejā. Nhātakaṃ: one whose defilements have been washed away. Buddhaṃ: one who has clearly and distinctly realized the Four Noble Truths. Taṃ: that person. Brāhmaṇaṃ: as a Brahmin. Ahaṃ: I, the Buddha. Brūmi: do proclaim.

(In that alms-giving, the wealth relinquished in a single day alone amounted to fourteen crores. The four items offered to the Teacher—the white umbrella, the sitting couch, the stand, and the footstool—were of inestimable value. No one else was able to perform such an act of giving to the Buddhas again; therefore, this alms-giving became famous as the 'Asadisa-dāna' [Incomparable Alms-giving]. It is said that this Asadisa-dāna occurs only once for every Buddha, and for all of them, it is a woman who arranges it.)

King Pasenadi had two ministers named Kāla and Juṇha. Among them, Kāla thought: 'Oh, the ruin of the royal family! In a single day, fourteen crores of wealth have gone to waste. These monks, after enjoying this meal, will go and lie down to sleep. Oh, the royal family is ruined!' Juṇha, however, thought: 'Oh, the King's gift is well-given! One who is not established in kingship cannot give such a gift. There is no being to whom the King does not give a share of the merit. I, for one, shall rejoice in this gift.' At the end of the meal, the King took the Teacher's bowl so that the Buddha might deliver the blessing (anumodanā). The Teacher thought: 'The King has given a great gift like a massive flood. Was the multitude able to settle their hearts in faith, or not?' The Teacher, knowing the thoughts of the two ministers, realized: 'If I perform a blessing worthy of the King's gift, Kāla's head will split into seven pieces, while Juṇha will be established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).' Out of compassion for Kāla, the Teacher spoke only a four-line verse to the King who stood there after giving such a gift, and then rising from His seat, He returned to the monastery.

## Elder Angulimāla Who Was Not Afraid of the Fierce Elephant

The monks asked Elder Angulimāla: 'Friend, were you not afraid when you saw the fierce elephant standing there holding the umbrella?' When he replied, 'Friends, I was not afraid,' those monks approached the Teacher and reported: 'Venerable Sir, Angulimāla is claiming the fruit of Arahantship.' The Teacher said: 'Bhikkhus, Angulimāla is not afraid. My sons, who are like chief bulls among the bulls of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), are not afraid.' Having said this, He spoke this verse in the Brāhmaṇa Vagga.

## Giving Only a Four-Line Verse as a Blessing

The King, too, became dejected, thinking: 'Although I stood giving alms to such a congregation, the Teacher did not give a blessing worthy of me, but spoke only a single verse and rose from His seat to depart. Perhaps I did not give a gift worthy of the Teacher, but gave one that was unworthy. Perhaps I did not give appropriate things, but gave inappropriate things. It is possible the Teacher is displeased with me.' He also thought: 'Such an Asadisa-dāna deserves a blessing in accordance with the gift.' Having thought thus, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked: 'Venerable Sir, did I fail to give a gift that should be given? Or did I give inappropriate things instead of appropriate things in accordance with the gift?' When asked, 'Great King, why do you ask this?', he replied: 'Venerable Sir, You did not give a blessing in accordance with the gift.' The Teacher replied: 'Great King, you have indeed given a gift that is suitable and worthy. That is true. This Asadisa-dāna can be given to a Buddha only once. It is difficult to give such a gift again.' When this was said, the King asked: 'Venerable Sir, if that is so, why did You not give a blessing in accordance with the gift?'
122:
## The Teaching

(177) Na ve kadariyā devalokaṃ vajanti,
Bālā have nappasaṃsanti dānaṃ.
Dhīro ca dānaṃ anumodamāno,
Teneva so hoti sukhī parattha.

Kadariyā, the miserly. Ve, indeed. Devalokaṃ, to the world of the gods. Na vajanti, do not reach. Bālā, those who do not know both this world and the next. Havē, indeed. Dānaṃ, giving. Nappasaṃsanti, do not praise. Dhīro ca, only the wise man. Dānaṃ, giving. Anumodamāno, can rejoice. Teneva, for that very reason. So dhīro, that wise man. Parattha, in the hereafter. Sukhī, is happy. Hoti, becomes.

## Impurity of the Assembly

When the Buddha said, "Great King, I did not do so because the assembly was not pure," the King asked again, "Venerable Sir, what is the fault of the assembly?" Then, the Buddha informed King Kosala of the thoughts of the two ministers and explained that he had not performed the appreciation (anumodanā) out of compassion for the minister Kāla.

## Banishing Minister Kāla and Granting Sovereignty to Minister Juṇha

The King asked, "Friend Kāla, is it true that you thought in this way?" When Kāla replied, "It is true," the King said, "When I am giving my own property along with my wife and children without taking anything of yours, what harm does it do to you? Go, fellow! Let whatever wealth I have given you remain yours, but leave my country!" After banishing Kāla from the country, he summoned the minister Juṇha and asked, "Is it true that you thought in this way?" When Juṇha replied, "It is true," the King said, "Uncle, it is well! I am pleased. You, Juṇha, take my retinue and give alms for seven days in the same manner as I have given." After handing over the sovereignty of the kingdom for seven days, he said to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, look at the behavior of the fool! He struck a blow against the alms-giving I have performed in this way."

The Buddha said, "Great King, it is true. Those who are fools do not rejoice in the giving of others and are destined for a miserable state (duggati). The wise, however, rejoice even in the giving of others and are destined for the celestial realm (sagga)." Having said this, he spoke this verse:
123:
## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the minister Juṇha was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled crowd. Juṇha, having become a Stream-enterer, gave alms for seven days in the same manner as the King had given.

The Story of the Incomparable Alms-giving (Asadisa-dāna-vatthu) ends.

## 11. The Story of Kāla, the Son of Anāthapiṇḍika

(Anāthapiṇḍikaputta-kāla-vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Pathabyā ekarajjena," concerning the youth named Kāla, the son of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.

## Keeping a Sham Uposatha for the Sake of Money

Although he was the son of such a merchant endowed with faith, that youth Kāla did not wish to go to the presence of the Buddha, nor did he wish to see him when he came to the house. He did not wish to hear the Dhamma, nor did he wish to perform services for the Saṅgha. Even when his father, the merchant, said, "Dear son, do not do this," he did not listen to his father's words. Then his father, Anāthapiṇḍika, thought, "If this person wanders about holding such views, he will be destined for the Avīci hell. It is not proper that my son should go to hell while I am watching. In this world, there is no being who cannot be broken by the gift of wealth; I will break him with wealth."

Then he said to Kāla, "Dear son, observe the Uposatha, go to the monastery, listen to the Dhamma, and then return; I will give you a hundred kahāpaṇas." When Kāla asked, "Father, will you really give them?", he replied, "Dear son, I will give them." That youth Kāla, having taken the pledge three times, observed the Uposatha and went to the monastery. As for listening to the Dhamma, he had no such intention. Having slept in a comfortable place, he returned home early in the morning. Then the merchant father said, "My son has observed the Uposatha; quickly bring gruel and other food for my son," and ordered them to be given. Kāla said, "I will not eat yet because I have not received the kahāpaṇas," and he rejected the gruel and other food as they were brought.

Then the merchant father, unable to bear the distress, had the bag of kahāpaṇas given to him. Only after taking that bag of kahāpaṇas with his hand did the youth Kāla eat the gruel and other food. Then, on the following day, the merchant sent him again, saying, "Dear son, I will give you a thousand kahāpaṇas; stand before the Buddha, learn one verse of the Dhamma, and then return." Kāla went to the monastery and, standing before the Buddha, intended to learn just one verse and run back. Then the Buddha made him unable to memorize it easily. That youth Kāla, being unable to memorize that verse, thought, "I will learn the next verse," and continued to listen.
124:
## The Discourse

(178) Better than sole sovereignty over the earth, or going to heaven; better than lordship over all the worlds, is the fruit of Stream-entry.

Better than the luxury of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti); better than attaining the bliss of the heavenly realms and the Brahma realms; better than lordship over the entire world—the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) is more excellent.

## From a False Observant to a True One

At that time, the youth [Kāla] listened, thinking, "I will learn it." The Teacher also made it so that he could not easily memorize the words. The youth, standing and listening with the intent "I will learn the next verse," was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.

On the following day, he entered Sāvatthī together with the community of monks headed by the Buddha. The Great Treasurer [Anāthapiṇḍika], seeing him, thought, "Today, my son's appearance is indeed pleasing." The youth also thought, "Oh, if only my father would not give me the coins in the presence of the Teacher today; if only he would conceal my status as an Uposatha observer for the sake of money." However, the Teacher already knew that he had observed the Uposatha yesterday for the sake of money.

The Great Treasurer offered rice gruel to the community of monks headed by the Buddha and also gave some to his son. The youth sat in silence, drank the gruel, ate the hard food, and ate the meal. At the conclusion of the Teacher's meal, the Great Treasurer placed a bundle of a thousand coins before his son and said, "Dear son, I sent you to the monastery to observe the Uposatha, saying I would give you a thousand. This thousand is for you." When the youth saw the coins being given in front of the Teacher, he felt very ashamed and said, "I have no need for the coins." Even when told, "Take it, dear son," he did not take it.

Then his father, the Great Treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika, paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, today my son's appearance is very pleasing." When asked, "Great Treasurer, in what way?", he replied, "Previously, I sent this youth to the monastery saying I would give him a thousand coins."
125:
On the following day, he did not want to eat because he had not yet received the coins. But today, even when given, he does not want the coins, Venerable Sir." The Buddha said, "Great Treasurer, it is true. Today, in your son's heart, the fruit of Stream-entry is indeed more excellent than the prosperity of a Universal Monarch, or the prosperity of the heavenly realms and the Brahma realms," and he spoke this verse [Verse 178].

## The Benefit of the Discourse

At the end of the discourse, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the youth Kāla, son of the Treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika, ends.

Here ends the Chapter on the World (Lokavagga).

The thirteenth chapter.
126:
## 14. Buddhavagga

## 1. The Story of the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya
(The Story of Māra's Daughters)

The Teacher, while staying at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, spoke this Dhamma discourse beginning with "Yassa jitaṃ," concerning the three daughters of Māra: Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā. However, the discourse was set in Sāvatthī and spoken again to the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya in the Kuru country.

## Choosing the Buddha as a Groom

In the Kuru country, there was a daughter of a Brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya, who was also named Māgaṇḍiyā. She was a maiden of supreme beauty. Many wealthy Brahmin families and wealthy Khattiya families, desiring her, sent messages to the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, saying, "Give us your daughter." But the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya rejected them all, saying, "You are not suitable or worthy of my daughter."

Then one day, at dawn, as the Buddha surveyed the world, he saw the Brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya entering the net of his knowledge. Considering "What will happen?", he saw that the Brahmin and his wife possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the three paths and fruits. The Brahmin was constantly tending the fire outside the village. In the morning, the Teacher took his bowl and robes and went to that place. The Brahmin, looking at the beauty and splendor of the Teacher, thought, "In this world, there is no man like this. He is suitable and worthy of my daughter. I will give my daughter to him." He said to the Buddha, "Ascetic, I have a daughter. Not seeing a man suitable for her, I have not given her to anyone. You are suitable and worthy of her. I wish to give her to you as a wife (pādaparicārikā). Wait here until I bring her."

The Teacher, hearing the Brahmin's words, neither delighted in them nor forbade them. The Brahmin went home and said to his wife, "Lady, today I have seen a man suitable for our daughter. We shall give her to him." He had the daughter adorned and, taking her along with his wife, went to that place. A great crowd of people, filled with curiosity, also came out.

## The Buddha's Footprint

The Buddha did not stay in the place indicated by the Brahmin, but having left a footprint (pada-cetiya) there, he stood in another place.

(The footprints of the Buddhas appear only in the place where they resolve, "Let such and such a person see this footprint." No one else can see that footprint in any other place.)
127:
For one who is lustful, the footprint is arched;
For one who is hateful, it is heavily pressed at the heel.
For one who is deluded, the footprint is dragged along;
For one who has drawn back the veil, such is this footprint.

O Brahmin! The footprint of one prone to lust is arched, being hollow in the middle. The footprint of one prone to anger is pressed down forcefully with a deep heel. The footprint of one prone to delusion is dragged along as if by sloth. This footprint, which is perfectly level and complete with the hundred and eight marks like a golden footstool, belongs to the Great Being who has torn open the roof of craving and escaped from the three realms.

When the Brahmin’s wife, who was traveling with him, asked, “Where is that man?”, the Brahmin looked around and, seeing the footprint, said, “I told him to wait in this place,” and pointed, saying, “This is his footprint.” Because she was highly skilled in the Vedas regarding the knowledge of marks, she said, “Brahmin, this is not the footprint of one who enjoys sensual pleasures.” The Brahmin replied, “O lady, you see a crocodile in a water-cup! I have seen that ascetic and told him, ‘I will give you my daughter,’ and he has accepted my word.” She responded, “Brahmin, although you say so, this footprint belongs only to one whose defilements are exhausted,” and she recited this verse found in the Suttanipāta Commentary and other texts.

## Māra’s Unease

Then the Brahmin said to his wife, “O lady, do not make such a harsh noise; come quietly,” and as they went, he saw the Teacher and pointed him out to her, saying, “This is the man.” He then approached the Teacher and said, “Ascetic, I will give you my daughter.” The Teacher did not say, “I have no need for your daughter,” but instead said, “Brahmin, I shall tell you a certain true matter; will you listen?” When the Brahmin replied, “Speak, O ascetic, I will listen,” the Teacher related the events of the past, starting from his Great Renunciation.

## A Brief Account of the Buddha’s Life

The Bodhisatta, having renounced the glory of the kingdom, mounted the horse Kanthaka and, with the minister Channa as his companion, was departing for the forest. When he reached the city gate, Māra stood there and said, “Siddhattha, turn back! On the seventh day from now, the Wheel Treasure will appear to you.” The Bodhisatta replied, “Māra, I know this, but I have no need for that Wheel Treasure.” When asked, “For what purpose then do you renounce?”, he replied, “For the sake of Omniscience.” Māra then said, “If that is so, from this day forward, if you think even a single thought of sensual desire or the like,”

Whose victory no one in the world follows.
That Buddha, whose range is infinite, the trackless,
By what track will you lead him?

(180) In whom there is no entangling, embroiling
Craving to lead him anywhere.
That Buddha, whose range is infinite, the trackless,
By what track will you lead him?

Zālinī: Having a net that entangles and binds above and below; or, one that creates a net; or, like a net (meaning craving). Visattikā: Clinging to objects such as forms; or, the cause of a clinging mind; or, bringing poison; or, bearing poisonous flowers and fruits; or, consuming poison (it is craving itself).
