"I shall know what you have done to me," he said. From that time on, Māra followed the Bodhisatta for seven years, watching for a lapse. The Blessed One, having practiced the difficult austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for six years, relying on the extraordinary power of effort and energy of a Great Man, realized Omniscience at the foot of the Bodhi tree. While enjoying the bliss of the Fruit of Arahatship, he stayed at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree during the fifth week. Then Māra thought, "Though I have followed him for this long, watching for a lapse, I have not seen any fault in this Prince Siddhattha. Now this Prince Siddhattha has transcended my realm." Feeling dejected, he sat on the main road.

## The Temptation by the Three Daughters of Māra

Then the three daughters of Māra named Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, thinking, "Our father the King of Devas is not seen; where could he be now?" looked and saw Māra sitting in such a state. They approached him and asked, "Father, why are you so dejected?" Māra told his daughters the reason. Then the daughters said to Māra, "Father, do not worry; we will bring that Prince Siddhattha under our control and fetch him." "Dear daughters, this Prince Siddhattha, the Great Buddha, cannot be brought under control by anyone." "Father, we are women; we will bind that Buddha Siddhattha with the snares of passion and bring him right now. Do not worry." Having said this, they approached the Blessed One and said, "Ascetic, we wish to serve at your feet."

The Blessed One did not take notice of the words of those three goddesses in his mind. He did not even open his eyes to look. Again, the daughters of Māra thought, "The desires of men are indeed various, high and low. Some men have affection for young maidens. Some have affection for women in their first youth. Some have affection for women in their middle age. Some have affection for women in their later years. We will tempt that Buddha Siddhattha in various ways." Each of them, by the power of youth and beauty, created a hundred forms of themselves, becoming young maidens, women who had never given birth, women who had given birth once, women who had given birth twice, middle-aged women, and elderly women. They approached the Blessed One seven times and said, "O Ascetic, we wish to serve at your feet."
129:
The Blessed One did not take notice of those words in his mind. How did he remain? He remained focused only on the Supreme Destruction of Acquisitions (anuttara upadhisaṅkhaya), which is Nibbāna—the end of the four types of acquisitions (upadhi): the acquisition of sensual pleasures (kāmūpadhi), the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi) which is the root of suffering, the acquisition of defilements (kilesūpadhi) which is the ground for suffering in the lower realms, and the acquisition of volitional formations (saṅkhārūpadhi) consisting of the twenty-nine wholesome and unwholesome volitions which are the ground for the suffering of birth and existence. Then the Blessed One said to the three daughters of Māra, who still did not depart, "Go away! What object do you see that you strive so? Such various forms of temptation should not be performed before the Buddhas and Arahats who are free from passion. The Tathāgata has abandoned passion and the rest. By what means will you bring that Buddha under your control?" and he spoke these verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many deities attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. The three daughters of Māra vanished right there.

## The Teaching for Māgaṇḍiya's Attainment of Anāgāmī

The Blessed One, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said, "O Brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya, in the past I saw these three daughters of Māra. They were endowed with bodies that were not entangled with phlegm and such, bodies like blocks of gold. Even then, I had no desire for sexual intercourse. Your daughter's body, however, is full of the thirty-two types of impurities. It is like a pot of filth that has been beautifully decorated on the outside. Let me say one last thing: even if my foot were smeared with filth, and this maiden Māgaṇḍiya were standing at the threshold, even so, I would not want to touch the body of that maiden Māgaṇḍiya with my foot," and he spoke this verse.
130:
“Having seen Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, there was no desire even for sexual intercourse. What is this body, full of urine and excrement? I would not wish to touch it even with my feet.”

Taṇhā: the goddess named Taṇhā; Arati: the goddess named Arati; Ragā: the goddess named Ragā. Having seen [them], there was no desire, not even a slight wish for the act of mutual pleasure (sexual intercourse). Having seen this maiden Māgaṇḍī, who is full of urine and excrement, how could such a desire arise? I do not wish to touch her even with my feet.

At the end of the teaching, both the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his wife were established in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala).

The Story of the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya ends.

## 2. The Story of the Descent from the Deva Realm
(Devorohaṇavatthu)

The Teacher (the Buddha) spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Ye jhānappasutā dhīrā” at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa, concerning many devas and humans. However, the teaching originated in Rājagaha.

## The Hanging of the Sandalwood Bowl by the Merchant of Rājagaha
At one time, the merchant of Rājagaha, in order to be free from danger and to protect ornaments and other items that might slip off due to negligence, had a protective enclosure made of netting and went to play in the waters of the Ganges. At that time, a red sandalwood tree (rattacandana) that grew on the upper bank of the Ganges, having its roots washed away by the river water, fell and was broken into pieces as it struck against various rocks. Subsequently, a block of sandalwood the size of a large water pot, having been smoothed by rubbing against stones and being buffeted by the waves, floated down in due course, covered in moss, and got caught in the merchant’s net. The merchant asked, “What is this?” and upon hearing it was a block of wood, he had it brought to him. To investigate what kind of wood it was, he had it planed with the tip of an adze. At that moment, the red sandalwood, with a color like lac-dye, became apparent. Now, the great merchant was neither a right-believer nor a wrong-believer; he was of a neutral disposition. He thought, “There is much red sandalwood in my house; what shall I do with this piece?” Then this thought occurred to him: “In this world, there are many who say, ‘We are Arahants, we are Arahants,’ but I do not see even a single Arahant. I will have a bowl turned on a lathe in my house, place it in a carrier, and hang it sixty cubits high in the air by a series of bamboo poles, saying, ‘If there is an Arahant, let him come through the air and take it.’ Whoever can take it, I will go to him for refuge along with my wife and children.” Following his plan, he had the bowl turned, raised it on a series of bamboo poles, and said, “Whoever is an Arahant in this world, let him come through the air and take this bowl.”
131:
## The Sectarians’ Pretense to Obtain the Sandalwood Bowl
The six sectarian teachers said, “This is suitable only for us; give that sandalwood bowl to us.” The merchant replied, “Come through the air and take it.” Then, on the sixth day, the naked ascetic Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta sent his disciples, saying, “Go and tell the great merchant: ‘This is suitable for our teacher; do not make him come through the air for the sake of a trifling object. Please give me this bowl.’” Those disciples went and spoke to the merchant as their teacher had instructed. The merchant replied, “Only the person who is able to come through the air and take it shall have it.”

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, wishing to go himself, gave a signal to his disciples: “I will act as if I wish to fly up by lifting one hand and one foot. You must grab me by my hands and feet, pull me down to the ground, and say, ‘Teacher, what are you doing? Do not reveal the hidden qualities of an Arahant to the multitude for the sake of a wooden bowl!’” He then went to the place where the sandalwood bowl was and said to the merchant, “Great merchant, this bowl is suitable for me, not for others. Do not wish for me to fly into the air for the sake of a trifling object; give the bowl to me.” The merchant replied, “Venerable sir, take it only by flying through the air.”

Then Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said, “In that case, move aside, move aside!” and after making his disciples move away, he lifted one hand and one foot as if to fly into the air. At that moment, his disciples grabbed him by his hands and feet, pulled him down to the ground, and said, “Teacher, why are you performing this act of flying? What is the use of showing the hidden qualities of an Arahant to the multitude for the sake of a miserable, low, wooden bowl?” Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta then said to the merchant, “Great merchant, these disciples will not let me fly up; give the bowl to me.” The merchant replied, “Venerable sir, take it by flying through the air.” Thus, although the sectarians strove for six days, they did not obtain the sandalwood bowl.

## The Psychic Power of Venerable Piṇḍola
On the seventh day, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, saying, “We shall go for alms in Rājagaha,” went and stood on a flat rock. While they were putting on their robes, some scoundrels started a conversation: “Friends, formerly six teachers roamed the world saying, ‘We are Arahants.’ Today is the seventh day since the merchant of Rājagaha raised the bowl, saying, ‘If there is an Arahant, let him come through the air and take it.’ Yet there is not a single person who can fly into the air saying, ‘I am an Arahant.’ Today, the non-existence of Arahants in the world is known to us.” Having heard this talk—
132:
(One who seeks alms is called Piṇḍola. Piṇḍa means alms-food; ulati means to seek. Therefore, he is known as Piṇḍola. His original name was Bhāradvāja. This monk ate a great deal of food, and his alms-bowl was also large. Because the Buddha did not allow him a bowl-bag, he frequently placed the bowl face down on the ground under his couch and took it out again; due to this frequent handling, the rim wore down and the bowl became small. It was only then that the Buddha allowed a bowl-bag, as stated in the Saṃyutta Commentary.)

Upon hearing the words of those drunkards, Venerable Moggallāna said to Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, “Friend Bhāradvāja, do you hear the words of these drunkards? They speak as if they wish to test the Buddha’s Dispensation. You possess great psychic power and great majesty. Go, travel through the air and take that bowl.”

“Friend Moggallāna, you are the foremost among those with psychic powers. You take this bowl. Only if you do not wish to take it will I take it.” When Moggallāna replied, “Friend, you take it,” Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for supernormal knowledge. Rising from it, he lifted a stone slab three gāvutas in size with his big toe, and holding it with the tip of his foot, he made it hover in the sky like a tuft of cotton. He then circled the city of Rājagaha seven times.

That stone slab appeared as if it were a lid covering the city of Rājagaha, which was three gāvutas in extent. The citizens of Rājagaha, terrified that the stone slab would fall and crush them, placed winnowing trays and baskets on their heads and hid themselves here and there. On the seventh circuit, the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja broke the stone slab and revealed himself. Seeing the Elder, the great multitude cried out, “Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, please hold your stone slab firmly! Do not destroy us all!” The Elder then kicked the stone slab away with the tip of his foot. It flew back and settled exactly in its original place.

## Offering the Sandalwood Bowl to the Elder

The Elder stood upon the roof of the merchant's house. Seeing him, the merchant prostrated himself and said, “Venerable sir, please descend.” He invited the Elder, who had descended from the sky, to sit, had the sandalwood bowl brought down, filled it with the four sweet delicacies (catumadhura), and offered it to the Elder. The Elder took the bowl and headed toward the monastery. At that time, those who had gone to the forest or to secluded places had not seen that miracle. They gathered and followed the Elder, saying, “Venerable sir, please show the miracle to us as well.” The Elder showed the miracle to them and then proceeded to the monastery.

(Catu + madhura means four delicious tastes: ghee, oil, honey, and molasses. Some say ghee is 19 kyats and sesame oil is 8 kyats, totaling 27. Honey is 17 kyats and molasses is 10 kyats, totaling 27. After boiling the ghee and oil and letting them cool, honey and molasses are added and stirred continuously until well-blended. When boiled over a fire, it becomes a mixture of 54 parts. If one-fourth of a tical of five types of cumin is added and a spoonful is eaten regularly every night and morning, it is said to be a life-extending tonic.)
133:
## Enacting the Training Rule

When the Blessed One heard the tumultuous noise of the great crowd of people following Venerable Piṇḍola, he asked, "Ānanda, what is this noise?" When he was told, "Venerable Sir, Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja flew through the air and took the sandalwood bowl. This noise is coming from the vicinity of Venerable Piṇḍola," the Buddha had Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja summoned and asked, "Is it true, Bharadvāja, that you did this?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Buddha rebuked him, saying, "Bharadvāja, why did you do such a thing?" He then had the bowl broken into small pieces and given to the monks to be ground into eye-ointment. Subsequently, he enacted the training rule: "Miracles must not be displayed."

## The Heretics' Attempt to Compete in Miracles

When the heretics heard, "It is said that the Ascetic Gotama had that bowl broken and enacted a training rule for his disciples to prevent the display of miracles," they thought, "The disciples of the Ascetic Gotama will not transgress the enacted training rule even for the sake of their lives, and the Ascetic Gotama himself will surely observe it. Now we have found our opportunity." Thinking thus, they went about the city streets announcing, "Out of concern for our own virtues, we did not display our qualities to the public for the sake of a wooden bowl in the past. However, the disciples of the Ascetic Gotama displayed their qualities to the public for the sake of a mere bowl. The Ascetic Gotama, in his cleverness, had the bowl broken and enacted a training rule. Now, we shall perform miracles together with him."

## King Bimbisāra's Inquiry

When King Bimbisāra heard this, he went to the Blessed One and asked, "Venerable Sir, is it true that you have enacted a training rule for your disciples to prevent the display of miracles?" "It is true, Great King," the Buddha replied. "Now the heretics are saying they will perform miracles together with you. What will you do now, Venerable Sir?" the King asked. "If they perform them, Great King, I shall perform them too," the Buddha said. "But has not a training rule been enacted by you, Venerable Sir?" the King asked again. "Great King, I did not enact the training rule for myself; it was enacted only for my disciples," the Buddha replied. When the King asked, "Venerable Sir, can there be a training rule that excludes you and applies only to others?", the Buddha said, "In that case, Great King, I shall ask you a question in return. Great King, is there a royal garden in your domain?" "There is, Venerable Sir," the King replied. "Great King, if the public were to eat mangoes and other fruits in your garden, what should be done to them?" "They should be punished, Venerable Sir," the King replied. "But are you, Great King, allowed to eat them?" "Yes, Venerable Sir, there is no punishment for me. I am allowed to eat what belongs to me," the King replied. "Great King, just as your authority prevails over a kingdom of three hundred yojanas, and there is no punishment for you when you eat mangoes in your own garden while there is for others, so too does my authority prevail over a hundred thousand million universes. There is no such thing as a transgression of the enacted training rule for me, though there is for others. I shall perform the miracle."

## The Heretics' Dilemma

When the heretics heard the Buddha's words, they consulted one another, saying, "Now we are ruined. It is said that the Ascetic Gotama enacted the training rule only for his disciples, not for himself. He himself wishes to perform a miracle. What shall we do?" The King then asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, when will you perform the miracle?" "Four months from now, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, Great King," the Buddha replied. "Where will you perform it, Venerable Sir?" the King asked. "I shall perform it near the city of Sāvatthī, Great King," the Buddha replied.

(The reason the Blessed One pointed to such a distant place was that Sāvatthī is the place where all Buddhas perform the Great Twin Miracle. Furthermore, he pointed to a distant place so that a great multitude of people could assemble.)
134:
## The Heretics' Boastful Words
When the heretics heard those words, they consulted among themselves: “In four months from now, the ascetic Gotama will perform a miracle in Sāvatthī. For now, let us follow him without letting him go. When the multitude sees us and asks, ‘Why is this being done?’, we will tell them, ‘We have declared that we will perform a miracle together with the ascetic Gotama.’ He is fleeing, and we are following him to prevent his escape.”

## The Heretics' Pavilion for the Miracle
The Blessed One, having wandered for alms in Rājagaha, departed. The heretics also departed right behind the Blessed One and stayed at the places where he took his meals. At those places, they had their morning meal the next day. When asked by people, “What is the reason for following the Buddha like this?”, they replied in the same manner as they had planned. The multitude also followed, thinking, “We shall see the miracle.” In due course, the Blessed One reached Sāvatthī. The heretics also went along with him, and having urged their supporters, they obtained a hundred thousand [pieces of money]. They had a pavilion built with acacia posts, covered it with blue lotuses, and sat there, saying, “We will perform the miracle here.”

## Clearing Mango Trees within One Yojāna
King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One and said, “Venerable Sir, the heretics have built a pavilion. I, too, will build a pavilion for the Blessed One.” The Buddha replied, “Enough, Great King, I have a builder for my pavilion.” “Venerable Sir, excluding me, who else would be able to build it?” “Sakka, the King of Devas, will be able to do so.” “Venerable Sir, where will you perform the miracle?” “At the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, Great King.” When the heretics heard that he would perform the miracle at the foot of a mango tree, they informed their supporters and had every mango tree within a distance of one yojāna—even saplings that had sprouted that very day—uprooted and thrown into the forest.

## The Gardener Offers a Mango to the Buddha
On the full moon day of Āsāḷha, the Blessed One entered the city of Sāvatthī. A gardener of the King named Kaṇḍa saw a large ripe mango inside a leaf-nest made by red ants. Desiring its scent and taste, he chased away the crows that were flocking to it. While he was taking it to the King for his consumption, he saw the Blessed One on the way and thought: “If the King eats this mango, he might give me eight or sixteen kahāpaṇas. That reward from the King would not be enough for my livelihood even for a single lifetime. However, if I offer this to the Blessed One, it will surely bring me welfare and benefit for a long time throughout many existences.” Thinking thus, the gardener named Kaṇḍa offered the ripe mango to the Blessed One. The Blessed One looked at the Elder Ānanda. Then, the Elder Ānanda took the bowl offered by the Four Great Kings out of its bag and placed it in the hand of the Blessed One.
135:
(The bowl offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma at the time of the Great Renunciation disappeared when Sujātā offered the milk-rice. The golden bowl offered by Sujātā was floated away in the Nerañjarā River on that very day. On the day forty-nine days after the Enlightenment, when receiving the cakes offered by Tapussa and Bhallika, the four bowls offered individually by the Four Great Kings were pressed together into one bowl with four rims. It is this bowl that is referred to.)

## The Kaṇḍamba Mango Tree
The Blessed One gestured toward the bowl to receive the mango fruit, and then showed his intention to stay at that very spot. The Venerable Ānanda spread out a robe and offered it. When the Buddha sat upon the prepared seat, the Venerable Ānanda strained water, crushed the ripe mango to make a juice, and offered it to the Blessed One. After the Blessed One had consumed the mango juice, he said to the gardener named Kaṇḍa, "Plant this mango seed right here, having scratched up the earth." The gardener did as he was told. The Buddha then washed his hands over the mango seed. As soon as he washed his hands, a mango tree with a trunk as thick as a plow-head and fifty cubits in height sprang up. In the four directions, there were four great branches, and one at the top, making five great branches, each fifty cubits long. At that very moment, the mango tree became covered with flowers and fruits, and in every part, there were clusters of ripe mangoes. The monks who followed behind came along eating the ripe mangoes. When King Kosala heard the news that such a mango tree had grown, he stationed guards, saying, "No one must break or cut down this mango tree." Because it was planted by the gardener named Kaṇḍa, it became known as the Kaṇḍamba tree.

## The Destruction of the Heretics' Pavilion
The drunkards, having also eaten the ripe mangoes, mocked them, saying, "Hey, you wretched heretics! You said, 'The ascetic Gotama will perform a miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree,' and so you had the young mango trees that were planted that very day within a league uprooted. But this tree is indeed the Kaṇḍamba tree!" Saying this, the drunkards pelted them with the leftover mango seeds. Sakka, the King of Devas, commanded the deity Vātavalāhaka, "Uproot the pavilion of the heretics with winds and cast it into a filthy place." The deity did as Sakka commanded. He also commanded the deity Suriya, "Lower the solar disk and scorch them." The deity did as commanded. Again, he commanded the deity Vātavalāhaka, "Go and raise a whirlwind." The deity did so, and the heretics' bodies, dripping with sweat, were covered with dust. They looked like lumps of red clay. He then commanded the deity Vassavalāhaka, "Let fall great drops of rain." The deity did as commanded. Then, the bodies of the heretics looked like spotted cows.

## The Flight of the Heretics
Those heretical ascetics, being overcome with shame, fled in every direction. As they were fleeing, a farmer who was a follower of the heretic named Pūraṇa Kassapa thought, "Now is the time for my noble masters to perform a miracle; I shall go and witness it." He released his oxen and took the pot of gruel and the rope he had brought early in the morning.
136:
As he was coming, he saw Pūraṇa Kassapa fleeing in that manner and asked, "Venerable sir, I have come today thinking, 'I shall witness the miracle of my masters.' Where are you going?" Pūraṇa replied, "What use have you for a miracle? Give me this pot and the rope." Taking the pot and rope given by the farmer, he went to the riverbank. He tied the pot to his neck with the rope and, out of great shame, without saying a single word, he jumped into a deep pool of water. Causing bubbles to rise, he died and was reborn in the Avīci hell.

## Gharaṇī Upāsikā Requests to Perform a Miracle
The Blessed One created a jeweled walkway in the sky. One end of it was at the eastern edge of the world system, and the other end was at the western edge. In the afternoon, as the shadows lengthened, in the midst of the assembly that had gathered, spanning thirty-six leagues, the Blessed One thought, "Now is the time to perform the miracle." He emerged from the Gandhakuṭi and stood at the front of the monastery. At that time, a female lay follower named Gharaṇī, an Anāgāmī possessed of great psychic power, approached the Buddha and said, "Venerable Blessed One, while a daughter like me exists, there should be no need for the Blessed One to trouble himself. I shall perform the miracle, Lord."

"Dear daughter Gharaṇī, what kind of miracle will you perform?" the Buddha asked. "Venerable sir, I shall turn the great earth into water in this world system, and diving like a water-fowl, I shall show myself at the eastern edge of the world system. Likewise, I shall appear at the western, northern, and southern edges, as well as in the center. When the great multitude sees me and asks, 'Who is this?', they will be told, 'This is the lay follower named Gharaṇī. This is merely the power of a single woman named Gharaṇī; what then must the power of the Buddha be like?' In this way, the heretics will flee without even seeing the Blessed One," she replied.
137:
## The Buddha Refuses
Then the Blessed One said to Gharaṇī, "Dear daughter Gharaṇī, I know that you are capable of performing such a miracle. However, this assembly was not organized for your sake," and thus he refused her. Gharaṇī thought, "The Blessed One does not permit me; surely there must be someone else who is more capable of performing a miracle than I am," and she remained in a suitable place.

## Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika
The Blessed One, thinking, "In this way, their virtues shall become manifest," and intending to utter a fearless and brave lion's roar in the midst of the assembly that extended thirty-six yojanas, asked the others, "How would you perform a miracle?" They fearlessly uttered a lion's roar in the presence of the Buddha, saying, "Venerable Sir, we shall do it in this way." Among them, the householder Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika thought, "While there is a noble lay disciple like me, an Anāgāmī (Non-returner), the Blessed One should not have to undergo such hardship." When asked, "How will you do it?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, I shall manifest a form as large as a Great Brahmā, twelve yojanas in height, and in the midst of this assembly, I shall clap my hands with a sound like a great thunderclap. 

When the people ask, 'What is this sound?' they will be told, 'It is the sound of the householder Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika clapping his hands like a Brahmā.' The heretics (titthiyas) will then say, 'If even a householder has such power, what must the power of the Buddha be like?' and they will flee even before seeing the Blessed One."

## The Buddha Does Not Permit
The Blessed One said to the householder Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika, just as he had said to Gharaṇī, "I know your power," and did not permit him to perform the miracle.

## The Novice Nun named Cīrā
Then, a seven-year-old novice nun named Cīrā, who had attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, I shall perform a miracle." When asked, "Dear Cīrā, how will you do it?" she replied, "Venerable Sir, I shall bring Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and the Himavanta mountains, and arrange them in a row in this place. I shall then fly through them without obstruction, like a female swan. When the people see me and ask, 'Who is this?' they will be told, 'It is the novice nun named Cīrā.' The heretics will then say, 'If even a seven-year-old novice nun has such great power, what must the power of the Buddha be like?' and they will flee even before seeing the Blessed One."

(From this point onwards, similar statements should be understood as having been spoken in succession.)

The Blessed One also said to the novice nun Cīrā, "I know your power," and did not permit her to perform the miracle.

## Cunda Sāmaṇera
Then, a novice monk named Cunda, who was seven years old from birth and had attained the four analytical insights and destroyed the taints (arahant), approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, I shall perform a miracle." When asked, "How will you do it?" Cunda Sāmaṇera replied, "Venerable Sir, I shall take the great Jambu tree, which is the banner of Jambudīpa, upon my shoulder, shake it, and bring the great Jambu fruits to feed this entire assembly. I shall also bring Pāricchattaka flowers and come to pay homage to the Blessed One." The Buddha refused Cunda Sāmaṇera's offer to perform a miracle, saying, "I know your power."

## The Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā
Then, the Elder Nun named Uppalavaṇṇā paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, I shall perform a miracle." When asked, "How will you do it?" she replied, "Venerable Sir, I shall manifest an assembly of twelve yojanas all around, and surrounded by a retinue thirty-six yojanas in circumference, I shall come in the form of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) and pay homage to the Blessed One." The Buddha refused the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā's offer to perform a miracle, saying, "I know your power."

Wherever the load is heavy, wherever the path is deep (with mud),
There they yoke the black bull, and he carries that burden.

From wherever (yato), from which place; the path is difficult to travel due to much mud (gambhīravattanī), it becomes so. At that time (tadā), in that place; they yoke (yuñjanti) the bull named Kaṇha. That bull named Kaṇha (so) carries (vahate) that very heavy burden (taṃ dhuraṃ).

Manaññameva bhāseyya, nāmanuññaṃ kudācanaṃ.
Manaññaṃ bhāsamānassa, garuṃ bhāraṃ udaddhari.
Dhanañca naṃ alābhesi, tena cattamano ahu.

One should speak only pleasant words (manuññameva). One should never (kudācanaṃ) speak unpleasant words (amanuññaṃ). For the Brahmin who spoke pleasant words (manuññaṃ bhāsamānassa), the bull pulled (udaddhari) the heavy (garuṃ) load (bhāraṃ) of a hundred carts. He caused that Brahmin (naṃ) to obtain wealth (dhanañca). Because of obtaining that wealth (tena), the Brahmin was joyful (attamano/cattamano).

## Venerable Moggallāna

Then the Venerable Moggallāna, having paid homage to the Blessed One, said, “Venerable Sir, I shall perform a miracle.” When asked, “How will you do it?”, he replied, “Venerable Sir, I shall place Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, between my teeth and chew it like a kidney bean or a mustard seed.” When asked, “What else will you do?”, he replied, “I shall make this great earth like a mat and roll it up, placing it between my fingers.” When asked, “What else will you do?”, he replied, “I shall spin this great earth like a potter's wheel and let the people eat the essence of the earth.” When asked, “What else will you do?”, he replied, “I shall place this earth on my left hand and, with my right hand, place these beings on another continent.” When asked, “What else will you do?”, he replied, “I shall make Mount Sineru the handle of an umbrella, lift up the great earth as the canopy, and holding it with one hand like a monk carrying an umbrella, I shall walk in the air.” The Blessed One said, “I know your power,” but did not grant him permission to perform the miracle. Venerable Moggallāna thought, “The Teacher surely knows someone capable of performing a miracle far superior to mine,” and stood at a respectful distance.

## No One Else Can Carry the Buddha's Burden

Then the Blessed One said to Venerable Moggallāna, “Dear Moggallāna, this bundle of flowers was not tied for your sake. I carry an incomparable burden; there is no one else capable of carrying my burden. Why should there be someone capable of carrying my burden now? That would be truly marvelous. Even when I was born in the animal realm (ahetuka-tiracchāna), there was no one else capable of carrying my burden.” Being asked by the Elder, “When was that, Venerable Sir?”, the Blessed One brought forth the past—

Expanding upon this Kaṇha Usabha Jātaka from the Ekanipāta, Kuruṅgavagga, and wishing to explain that same matter specifically, he spoke this verse:

He preached this Nandivisāla Jātaka from the Ekanipāta, Kuruṅgavagga in detail. After preaching, the Blessed One ascended the jeweled walkway. The assembly in front of him extended for twelve leagues, and likewise for twelve leagues to the back, the north, and the south. In the midst of the assembly, which measured twenty-four leagues across, the Blessed One performed the Twin Miracle of fire and water.

## Performing the Twin Miracle of Fire and Water

In this world, the Blessed One performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared with his disciples. From the upper part of the Blessed One's body, a mass of fire proceeds; from the lower part of his body, a stream of water proceeds. From the lower part of his body, a mass of fire proceeds.
139:
From the upper part of his body, a stream of water issued; from the front part of his body, fire. From the back part of his body, water. From the back part of his body, fire. From the front part of his body, water. From the right eye, fire. From the left eye, water. From the left eye, fire. From the right eye, water. From the right ear, fire. From the left ear, water. From the left ear, fire. From the right ear, water. From the right nostril, fire. From the left nostril, water. From the left nostril, fire. From the right nostril, water. From the right shoulder, fire. From the left shoulder, water. From the left shoulder, fire. From the right shoulder, water. From the right arm, fire. From the left arm, water. From the left arm, fire. From the right arm, water. From the right side, fire. From the left side, water. From the left side, fire. From the right side, water. From the right foot, fire. From the left foot, water. From the left foot, fire. From the right foot, water. From the fingers and toes, fire; from the fingers and toes, water. From the gaps between the fingers and toes, fire. From the gaps between the fingers and toes, water.

From each and every pore, a mass of fire issued. From each and every pore, a stream of water issued. With the six-colored rays—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant—the Blessed One, in his natural form, performed the walking meditation. A created Buddha (nimmitabuddha) stood, sat, or lay down. While the Blessed One walked, stood, or sat, the created one lay down. This is the knowledge of the Tathāgata concerning the Twin Miracle.

The Blessed One performed this miracle while walking on that jeweled path. By the power of the meditative attainment on the fire-kasiṇa (tejokasiṇa), a mass of fire issued from the upper part of his body. By the power of the meditative attainment on the water-kasiṇa (āpokasiṇa), a stream of water issued from the lower part of his body. To show that fire issues from where water issued, and water issues from where fire issued, it is said "from the lower part, from the upper part," and so on. This method applies to all parts. In this performance of the Twin Miracle of water and fire, the mass of fire did not mix with the stream of water, nor did the stream of water mix with the mass of fire. Both ascended as far as the Brahma-world and fell at the rim of the universe (cakkavāḷa). The six-colored rays of the Blessed One were like molten gold poured from jars, or like a stream of liquid gold flowing from a mechanical tube; they ascended from one universe, reached the Brahma-world, and returned to encircle the rim of the universe. The entire universe became like a single illuminated Bodhi-shrine with curved rafters.

## Realization of the Dhamma and the Created Buddha

On that day, while performing the Twin Miracle and walking, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the great multitude at intervals. Even while preaching, he did not cease his efforts but provided comfort to the multitude. At that moment, the great multitude raised shouts of "Sādhu" in appreciation.
140:
At the time when that multitude of people was shouting "Sādhu" in appreciation, the Blessed One, looking into the minds of such a vast assembly, understood the mental processes of each individual through the sixteen modes. 

(In this way, the minds of the Buddhas are of swift occurrence.) 

Whichever person had faith in a particular Dhamma or a particular miracle, he preached the Dhamma and performed the miracle according to that person's inclination. While the Dhamma was thus being preached and the miracles performed, the great multitude attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. However, the Teacher, not seeing anyone else in that assembly capable of asking questions by grasping his own mind, created a created Buddha (nimmitabuddha). The Teacher answered the questions asked by the created Buddha, and the created Buddha answered the questions asked by the Teacher. When the Blessed One was walking in meditation, the created Buddha assumed one of the other postures, such as standing. To illustrate this point, it is said: "The created one also walks in meditation," and so forth. By seeing the miracles performed by the Teacher in this way and by hearing the Dhamma discourse, twenty crores of beings in that assembly attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths.

## Ascending to the Tāvatiṃsa Heaven

While still performing the miracles, the Teacher reflected, "Where did the Buddhas of the past spend the rains retreat after performing these miracles?" Seeing that they spent the rains retreat in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and preached the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to their mothers, he lifted his right foot and placed it on the summit of Mount Yugandhara, then lifted his left foot and placed it on the summit of Mount Sineru. Thus, in a distance of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas, there were three foot-steps and two strides. 

(It should not be understood that the Blessed One stretched out his feet to step. Indeed, only when the Blessed One was about to place his foot did the mountains come to the sole of his foot to receive it. When the Blessed One had stepped, those mountains rose and stood in their own places.)

## Sakka's Reflection

When Sakka saw the Teacher, he thought, "The Teacher will surely spend this three-month rains retreat on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat. It will be of great benefit to many deities. When the Teacher has entered upon the rains retreat on this Paṇḍukambala stone seat, other deities will not be able to place even a hand on it. This Paṇḍukambala stone seat is sixty yojanas in length..."
141:
Has he gone to Cittakūṭa, or Kelāsa, or Yugandhara?
We do not see the Sambuddha, the Chief of the World, the Bull among Men.

O friends! Has the Blessed One gone to Mount Cittakūṭa? Or has he gone to Mount Kelāsa? Or has he gone to Mount Yugandhara? We do not see that Buddha, who is the most noble among gods and men, the Chief of the three worlds.

The Wise One, delighting in seclusion, will not come back to this world.
We do not see the Sambuddha, the Chief of the World, the Bull among Men.

The Buddha, possessed of firm concentration, is one who delights in seclusion. He will not come back to this world again. We do not see the Sambuddha, who is the most noble among gods and men, the Chief of the world.

"It is fifty yojanas in width and fifteen yojanas in thickness; even when the Buddha sits, it will be as if it were empty," Sakka thought. The Buddha, knowing the intention of the King of Devas, cast his double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) to cover the Paṇḍukambala stone seat. The King of Devas thought again, "He first cast the robe to cover it, but he himself will sit in a small space." The Buddha, knowing his intention, sat down, making the Paṇḍukambala stone seat fit within the folds of his inner robe, just as a great monk who wears robes from the dust-heap might sit on a low stool.

## The Lamentation of the Multitude

At that very moment, the great multitude looked for the Buddha but did not see him. It was as if the moon had set, or the sun had set. The multitude, lamenting in this way, spoke this verse.

Reciting this verse, they lamented. Others said, "The Buddhas delight in seclusion. Our Teacher might have gone to another country or province out of modesty, thinking, 'I have performed such a miracle before such a crowd.' We shall not see him now." Lamenting thus, they spoke this verse.

They asked Venerable Moggallāna, "Venerable Sir, where is the Teacher?" Although he knew, he said, "Ask Venerable Anuruddha," with the noble intention that the virtues of other monks should also become known. The people asked Venerable Anuruddha as Moggallāna had suggested, "Venerable Sir, where is the Teacher?" He replied, "He has gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to spend the rains retreat on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat and to preach the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to his mother." When they asked, "Venerable Sir, when will he return?", he said, "After preaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka for three months, he will return on the day of the Mahāpavāraṇā."

Then the people, thinking, "We will not leave until we see the Blessed One," built an encampment right there at the site of the miracle in Sāvatthī. It is said that the sky was their only roof.

Lest the physical impurities of that vast crowd become apparent, the great earth provided an opening; everywhere, the ground remained perfectly clean. The Teacher had already told Venerable Moggallāna, "Moggallāna, you should preach the Dhamma to this assembly; Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika will provide the food."
142:
When the Buddha was in Tāvatiṃsa, on the Paṇḍukambala stone,
At the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, the Supreme Man dwelt.

Deities from the ten thousand world-systems, having assembled,
Pay homage to the Sambuddha, who dwells on the summit of the mountain.

No deity shines with splendor in the presence of the Sambuddha;
Surpassing all deities, the Sambuddha alone shines.

When the Buddha, the Supreme Man, dwelt in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven on the stone seat named Paṇḍukambala at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree; then, the deities dwelling in the ten thousand world-systems, having assembled, paid homage to the Sambuddha dwelling on the summit of Mount Meru. No deity or Brahma can shine with splendor in the presence of the Sambuddha. Or, they cannot shine because of the Buddha's own radiance. Surpassing all deities and Brahmas, the Sambuddha alone shines in his glory.

"Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika will provide food and sustenance," the Buddha had said. Therefore, throughout those three months of the rains retreat, Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika alone provided the assembly with morning gruel, rice, hard food, betel, oil, perfumes, flowers, and ornaments. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna preached the Dhamma. He also answered the questions of those who came from time to time to see the miracle.

## The Assembly of Deities

While the Buddha was spending the rains retreat on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat to preach the Abhidhamma to his mother, deities and Brahmas from the ten thousand world-systems surrounded him. Therefore, these verses were spoken.

Thus, the Buddha sat, overwhelming all deities and Brahmas with his own physical radiance. His mother came from the Tusita heaven and sat on his right side. The young deva Indaka also came and sat on the right side. The young deva Aṅkura sat on the left side. As more powerful deities assembled, Aṅkura had to move away and found a place twelve yojanas distant. Indaka, however, remained right there on the right side.

## The Young Deva Aṅkura

The Buddha, looking at both young devas and wishing to make known the great fruit of offerings given to those worthy of offerings in his Dispensation, spoke this verse: "Aṅkura, for a long period of ten thousand years, you gave great gifts, arranging a row of hearths twelve yojanas long. Now, having come to my assembly, you have a place twelve yojanas away. What is the reason for this?"

The Sambuddha, looking at Aṅkura and Indaka,
Praising the worthy recipient, spoke these words:

"Aṅkura, you gave a great gift over a long period.
Having come to my presence, do you sit so far away?"

The Sammāsambuddha, looking at the young deva Aṅkura and the young deva Indaka, wishing to manifest the greatness of the fruit of giving to a worthy recipient, spoke these words: "Aṅkura, you have given a great gift for a long period of ten thousand years. When you come near me, do you have to sit in a very distant place?"

## Indaka the Deva
When Aṅkura the deva spoke thus, the Blessed One said to Indaka the deva, “Indaka, you sit by my right side; why do you remain there without moving away?” “Venerable Sir, like a farmer sowing a few seeds in a good field, I obtained the perfection of a worthy recipient,” he said, and wishing to reveal the greatness of giving to a worthy recipient, he spoke these verses.

## Indaka’s Past Deed
What was the past merit performed by this Indaka? It is said that when the Elder Anuruddha entered the village for alms, the person who was to become Indaka offered a single spoonful of alms-food that he had brought for himself. The merit of Indaka performed at that time became more fruitful than the gift given by Aṅkura, who had prepared a row of hearths twelve yojanas long and gave gifts for ten thousand years. Therefore, he spoke in this way.

## Giving with Discrimination
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said, “Aṅkura, a gift should be given after due discrimination; when given with discrimination, it yields great fruit like seeds sown in a good field. You, however, did not do so; therefore, your gift did not become one of great fruit.” Wishing to clarify this meaning, he said—

Therefore, what is given to those free from hatred yields great fruit.
Fields are marred by weeds; this generation is marred by delusion.
Therefore, what is given to those free from delusion yields great fruit.
Giving should be done with discrimination; where it is given, it yields great fruit.

What is given to them yields great fruit,

Therefore (tasmā): for that reason. With discrimination (viceyya): having selected and investigated. In that person (tattha): in that person. Or: to that person. Giving (dānaṃ): the gift. Should be given (dātabbaṃ): should be offered. With discrimination (viceyya): having selected and investigated. Giving (dānaṃ): the act of giving. Is praised by the Sugata (sugatappasatthaṃ): is praised by the Buddhas. In this world of living beings (idha jīvaloke): in this world of beings. Those worthy of offerings (ye dakkhiṇeyyā): those noble recipients of offerings. Exist (santi): there are. To those noble recipients of offerings (etesu): in them or to them. What is given (dinnāni): the gifts that are offered. Like seeds (bīzāni yathā): like seeds. Sown (vuttāni): that are planted. In a fertile field (sukhette): in a good field of land. Yield great fruit (mahapphalāni): they have great benefits.

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the Supreme Buddha, the Pinnacle of the Three Worlds, wishing to teach the Dhamma even further, spoke these verses:
