At the end of the teaching, both the deity Ankura and the deity Indaka were established in the fruit of Stream-entry. The Dhamma teaching given in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven was also a beneficial teaching for a great multitude of people.

## The Teaching of Abhidhamma

Thereafter, the Buddha, while seated in the midst of the celestial assembly, began the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—'Wholesome states, unwholesome states, indeterminate states' (kusalā dhammā, akusalā dhammā, abyākatā dhammā)—for the sake of the deity Santussita, who had been his mother. He taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka continuously for three months. While teaching, when it was time for the alms round, he would create a replica Buddha and say, 'Let him teach this much of the Dhamma until I return.' He would then go to the Himālaya, chew the Nagalatā tooth-stick (a sweet creeper found in the Naga realm), wash his face at Lake Anotatta, bring alms-food from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), and take his meal while sitting in the Great Sāla-tree grove. The Elder Sāriputta would go there and perform duties for the Blessed One. After the meal, the Buddha would say, 'Sāriputta, today I have taught this much of the Dhamma; you should teach it to the monks who are your disciples.'

(It is said that five hundred young men of good family, having gained faith during the Twin Miracle, had gone forth in the presence of the Elder. It was with reference to those five hundred monks that he spoke to the Elder Sāriputta.)

After speaking thus, he would return to the celestial realm and resume teaching from where the replica Buddha had left off. The Elder Sāriputta also went and taught the Abhidhamma to those five hundred monks. While the Buddha was still staying in the celestial realm, those five hundred monks became masters of the seven books of the Abhidhamma.
145:
(Those five hundred monks, in the time of Kassapa Buddha, were five hundred small bats. While hanging inside a cave, they heard two elders reciting the Abhidhamma as they practiced walking meditation. They took the sound as an object of their attention.)

## Masters of the Abhidhamma
Those five hundred bats did not know, "These are the aggregates; these are the elements," and so on. Merely by taking the sound as an object, when they passed away from that state as bats, they were reborn in the celestial realm. Those deities, after enjoying celestial bliss for the interval between two Buddhas, passed away from that celestial realm and were reborn into noble families in Sāvatthī. Having gained faith during the performance of the Twin Miracle, they ordained in the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta and were the very first to become masters of the seven books of the Abhidhamma. The Teacher also taught the Abhidhamma in that manner throughout the three months of the rains retreat. At the conclusion of this Abhidhamma teaching, eighty billion deities attained penetration of the Four Noble Truths. The deity Santussita, who had been the mother, Queen Mahāmāyā, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.

(In this story, it appears as though the mother, Mahāmāyā, was reborn in the celestial realm as a goddess. However, some Sanskrit texts mention that during the practice of austerities, the goddess Mahāmāyā came and wept. In the Commentary on the Therīgāthā, it says "reborn in a male form" (*purisabhāvena jātaṃ*); in the Maṇidīpa, "reborn in the Tusita realm in a male form" (*purisabhāveneiva nibbattī*); in the Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭီကā, "headed by the deity who was the mother" (*mātudevaputta-pamukhānaṃ*); in the Jātaka-ṭီကā, "of the deity who was the mother" (*mātudevaputtassa*); and in one commentary, "the deity Santussita" (*Santussita-devaputto*).)

## Venerable Moggallāna Ascends to the Buddha
That assembly, thirty-six leagues in circumference, thinking, "Now, on the seventh day, it will be the day of the Great Pavāraṇā at the end of the rains," approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and said, "Venerable Sir, it is proper to know the day of the Teacher's descent. We will not depart without seeing the Teacher." Hearing these words, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said, "Very well, lay followers," and right there, diving into the earth, he resolved, "Let the assembly see me, Moggallāna, as I ascend to the foot of Mount Sineru." He appeared like a pale woolen thread strung with rubies as he ascended through the core of Mount Sineru. People watched him, saying, "He has ascended one league; he has ascended two leagues." The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna ascended as if lifting the Teacher's feet with his head, paid homage, and said, "Exalted Buddha, the assembly wishes to depart only after seeing the Lord. At what time will you descend?"

## From Tāvatiṃsa to Saṅkassa
"Dear Moggallāna, where did your elder brother Sāriputta spend the rains retreat?" the Buddha asked. When Moggallāna replied, "Exalted Buddha, he spent the rains in the city of Saṅkassa," the Buddha said, "Dear Moggallāna, seven days from today, on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā, I shall descend at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa. Let those who wish to see me come to that city of Saṅkassa. From Sāvatthī to the gate of Saṅkassa is thirty leagues. On a journey of this distance, no one needs to worry about provisions. Let them come as if they were going to a nearby monastery to listen to the Dhamma, having observed the Uposatha precepts." To that assembly...
146:
...tell them this." The Venerable Moggallāna replied, "Very well, Exalted Buddha," and went to inform them as the Buddha had instructed.

## The Descent via the Triple Stairway
When the All-Knowing Buddha had completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā, he said to Sakka, the King of Devas, "Great King, I shall go to the path of the human world." Sakka created three stairways: one of gold, one of jewels, and one of silver. The bases of these three stairways rested at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa, and their tops rested on the summit of Mount Sineru. Among these three stairways, the golden stairway on the right side was for the deities. The silver stairway on the left side was for the Mahābrahmās. The jewel stairway in the middle was for the Buddha. The Teacher of gods and men, standing on the summit of Mount Sineru at the time of his descent from the celestial realm, performed the Twin Miracle and looked upward. At that moment, the world was open and clear all the way to the Brahma realms. Then he looked downward, and it was open and clear all the way to Avīci. Then he looked toward the cardinal and intermediate directions, and many hundreds of thousands of world-systems became one open space. Deities saw humans, and humans saw deities; everyone saw each other face to face. The Buddha emitted the six-colored rays. On that day, because they beheld the Buddha's glory, there was not a single person in the thirty-six-league assembly who did not aspire for Buddhahood. The deities descended by the golden stairway, the Mahābrahmās by the silver stairway, and the Fully Enlightened Buddha descended by the jewel stairway.

## Various Offerings by the Deities
The celestial musician Pañcasikha, taking the Beluva lute which had the color of a ripe wood-apple, stood on the right side and descended while making an offering to the Buddha with the sweet sound of his celestial lute. Mātali, the companion and assistant of Sakka, stood on the left side, holding celestial perfumes and flowers, and descended while paying homage and making offerings. Mahābrahmā held the white parasol, and the deity Suyāma fanned with the yak-tail fan. The Teacher, accompanied by this retinue, descended and stood at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa. The Venerable Sāriputta also came and paid homage to the Buddha. Because the Venerable Sāriputta had never before seen the Buddha descending with such magnificent glory, he said:

Na me diṭṭho ito pubbe, na suto uda kassaci.
Evaṃ vagguvado satthā, tussitā gaṇimā gato.

*Tussitā*: from the presence of the mother; or, from the celestial realm. *Gaṇiṃ*: to the city of Saṅkassa where all people have gathered. *Āgato*: having descended and arrived. *Evaṃ vagguvado*: endowed with such radiant and beautiful glory. *Satthā*: our Teacher, the Buddha. *Ito pubbe*: before this day. *Me*: by me. *Na diṭṭho*: has never been seen. *Uda*: furthermore. *Kassaci*: from anyone. *Na suto*: has never been heard.
147:
Having expressed his joy with these and other words, he said, "Venerable Sir, today all devas and humans cherish and long for the Exalted One."

Then the Teacher said to the Venerable Sāriputta, "Sāriputta, Buddhas who are endowed with such qualities are indeed dear to devas and humans," and wishing to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(181) Those wise ones devoted to meditation,
Delighting in the peace of renunciation,
Even the devas long for them,
The Fully Enlightened ones, the mindful.

*Ye dhīrā*: those wise ones. *Jhānappassutā*: those who are practiced in the two types of jhāna through the five masteries such as adverting, etc. *Nekkhammūpasame*: in the renunciation that is the peace of Nibbāna (renunciation as going forth should not be taken here). *Ratā*: they delight. *Satīmataṃ*: those who possess mindfulness. *Sambuddhānaṃ*: those who have realized the Four Noble Truths. *Tesaṃ dhīrānaṃ*: for those wise ones. *Devāpi*: even the devas (and humans as well). *Pihayanti*: they cherish and long for them.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, thirty crores of beings attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. Five hundred monks, who were the co-residents (saddhivihārika) of the Elder Sāriputta, were established in Arahantship.

## Questioning at the Acala Cetiya in Saṅkassa
(It is said that all Buddhas do not abandon the practice of performing the Twin Miracle and then spending the rainy season in the deva world before descending at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa. The place where the right foot first touches the ground at the gate of Saṅkassa is known as the site of the Acala Cetiya.)

While standing at the site of the Acala Cetiya at the gate of Saṅkassa, the Teacher asked questions within the scope of worldlings and others.

When the worldlings had answered the questions within their own scope, they were unable to answer questions within the scope of a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). Likewise, Stream-enterers were unable to answer questions within the scope of Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī) and so on. The other Great Disciples were unable to answer questions within the scope of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was unable to answer within the scope of the Venerable Sāriputta. Even the Venerable Sāriputta was unable to answer questions within the scope of a Buddha. The Exalted One looked toward all directions, starting from the East; everywhere appeared as a single open space. In the eight directions, devas and humans, and above as far as the Brahma world, and below the earth-dwelling devas, Yakkhas, Nāgas, and Garuḍas, raised their joined palms and said, "Venerable Sir, there is no one in this place who can answer this question. Please investigate right there where the Buddha resides."

The Teacher thought, "Sāriputta is weary. Although he—"
148:
"Those who have comprehended the Dhamma, and the many learners (sekhas) here;
Tell me, O Sage, when asked, their way of life, O Noble One."

"O Noble One (Mārisa), my eldest son Sāriputta. *Idha*: in this world. *Saṅkhatā*: those many things called the conditioned. *Ye ca dhammā*: and those states. (*Se* has no separate meaning). *Sekhā*: those many things called learners. *Ye ca dhammā*: and those states. *Santi*: they exist. *Tesaṃ*: of those states. *Nipako*: what is the maturity? *Iriyaṃ*: what is the conduct? *Puṭṭho*: being asked, my eldest son Sāriputta. *Me*: to me. *Brūhi*: please answer."

"The sands of the Ganges may be exhausted,
The water in the great ocean may be exhausted,
The dust of the earth may be exhausted,
But my wisdom shall not be exhausted."

"*Gaṅgāya*: in the river Ganges. *Vālukā*: the sand. *Khīye*: even if it were exhausted. *Mahaṇṇave*: in the great ocean. *Udakaṃ*: the water. *Khīye*: even if it were exhausted. *Mahiyā*: in the earth. *Mattikā*: the dust. *Khīye*: even if it were exhausted. *Mama*: of me, your disciple Sāriputta. *Vissajjane*: in answering. *Yā buddhi*: whatever wisdom. *Atthi*: there is. *Sā buddhi*: that wisdom. *Na khīye*: cannot be exhausted."

Although he had no doubt, he was uncertain regarding the Buddha's intent, thinking, "By making which state among the aggregates (khandha) and others the starting point should I answer this practice? I might not be able to grasp the Exalted One's intention."

The Teacher, thinking, "If I do not give him a lead, he will not be able to answer; I shall give a lead to Sāriputta," and wishing to show the way, said, "Sāriputta, do you see this reality (bhūta)?"

(It is said the Buddha thought: "When Sāriputta answers by grasping my intention, he will answer by way of the aggregates.")

As soon as the lead was given to the Venerable Sāriputta, the question became clear to him in a hundred ways, a thousand ways, and a hundred thousand ways. The Venerable Sāriputta, standing upon the lead given by the Exalted One, answered the question.

(It is said that setting aside the Fully Enlightened One, there is no other person capable of reaching the level of the Venerable Sāriputta's wisdom.)

## The Lion's Roar of Venerable Sāriputta
For that very reason, the Venerable Sāriputta, standing before the Exalted One, uttered a brave shout like a lion's roar: "Venerable Sir, even if it rained for an entire aeon (kappa), I am capable of counting and recording that 'this many raindrops fell into the great ocean, this many raindrops fell on the earth, and this many raindrops fell on the mountains'." The Exalted One also said to him, "Sāriputta, I know your capability to count them."

There is no comparison for the wisdom of that Venerable One. Therefore, it was said:

## Excerpt from the Parosahassa Jātaka
Even though he was a monk of such great wisdom, because he did not see the end or the limit of the question asked within the Buddha's scope, he had to answer the question only by standing upon the lead given by the Exalted One. When they heard this, the monks started a discussion: "When a question was asked that the entire multitude of people could not answer, the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, alone was able to answer it."
149:
When the Blessed One heard these words, he said, "Not only now, Sāriputta, has he solved a problem that many people were unable to solve; in the past also, this Sāriputta solved it," and to bring forth the past, he spoke these verses:

Parosahassaṃ pi samāgatānaṃ,
Kandeyyuṃ te vassasataṃ apaññā.
Ekova seyyo puriso sapañño,
Yo bhāsitassa vijānāti atthaṃ.

Even if more than a thousand fools gather and lament for a hundred years, they cannot understand the meaning of what is spoken. Better is a single wise man who understands the meaning of what is spoken.

He preached this Parosahassa Jātaka from the Ekanipāta, Littavagga, in detail.

The Story of the Descent from the Deva Realm is finished.

## 3. The Story of Erakapatta the Naga King
(Erakapatta-nāgarāja-vatthu)

The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Kiccho manussapaṭilābho" (Difficult is the attainment of human birth), while residing at the foot of the seven Sirīsa trees near the city of Bārāṇasī, concerning the Naga King named Erakapatta.

## The Song Seeking the Arising of a Buddha
In the past, during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha, this Naga King was a young monk. While traveling by boat on the Ganges River, he grabbed a leaf from an eraka grass bush. Even though the boat was moving with speed, he did not let go, and the leaf was torn off. Thinking, "This is only a minor offense," he did not confess it. Although he practiced the Dhamma of a recluse in the forest for twenty thousand years, at the time of death, it felt as if the eraka leaf was clinging to his neck. Wishing to confess the offense but seeing no other monk, he felt remorse, thinking, "My virtue is not pure." After passing away from that life, he was reborn as a Naga King the size of a dugout canoe made from a single tree. His name was Erakapatta (Erakapatta = leaf of the eraka grass). As soon as he was reborn and looked at his physical form, he felt remorse, thinking, "After practicing the Dhamma of a recluse for such a long time, I have been reborn in a rootless (ahetuka) womb, in a place where frogs are the food." Later, he had a daughter. He spread his great hood on the surface of the water in the middle of the Ganges, placed his daughter on it, and made her dance and sing.

(The Naga King's thought was: "By this means, if a Buddha arises in this world, I will surely hear the news of his arising.")
150:
Kiṃsu adhippatī rājā, kiṃsu rājā rajjissaro.
Kathaṃsu virajo hoti, kathaṃ bāloti vuccatīti.

Who is the king who rules? How is a king a ruler of dust? How does one become free from dust? Who is called a fool? She sang this song.

Chadvārādhippatī rājā, rajjamano rajjissaro.
Arajjaṃ virajo hoti, rajjaṃ bāloti vuccatīti.

The king who rules the six doors is the king. One who is lustful is a ruler of dust. One who is not lustful is free from dust. One who is lustful is called a fool.

"To whoever can provide the counter-song to my song, I will give my daughter along with great Naga wealth." Thus, on the Uposatha day once every half-month, he placed his daughter on his hood. Standing there, she danced and sang.

People living throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, thinking "We will take the Naga maiden," went and sang counter-songs according to the power of their own wisdom. The Naga maiden rejected those counter-songs. While she was singing like this, standing on the hood once every half-month, one Buddha-interval (Buddha-antara) passed.

## Receiving the Good News of the Buddha's Arising
Then, our Teacher arose in the world. One day, at dawn, while surveying the world, he saw the youth named Uttara, along with Erakapatta the Naga, entering the net of his knowledge. Reflecting on "What will happen?", he saw: "Today is the day Erakapatta the Naga King places his daughter on his hood to dance. This youth Uttara, while learning the counter-songs given by me, will become a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). Taking those songs, he will go to the Naga King. When Erakapatta hears those counter-songs, he will know that a Buddha has arisen and will come to me. When he arrives, I will preach a verse in that great assembly. At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings will attain the realization of the Dhamma (the Four Noble Truths)."

The Blessed One went to that place. Near the city of Bārāṇasī, there were seven Sirīsa trees. He sat at the foot of one of those trees. People living in Jambudīpa gathered, wishing to take the counter-song. The Teacher, seeing the youth Uttara passing by not far away, said, "Come, Uttara." "What is it, Bhante?" he asked. "Come here first," the Teacher said. When he came, paid homage, and sat down, the Teacher asked, "Where are you going?" "To the place where Erakapatta the Naga King's daughter sings." "Do you know the counter-songs?" "I know them, Bhante." "Recite them first." When he recited the counter-songs according to his own understanding, the Teacher said, "Uttara, these are not the counter-songs. I will give you the counter-songs; will you take them and go?" "Yes, Bhante."

## The Song Answers Taught by the Buddha
The Teacher said, "Dear Uttara, when the Naga maiden has finished singing, you should sing these counter-songs:"

(The meaning of the song sung by the Naga maiden is: 1. Kiṃsu adhippatī rājā - Who is the king who rules?...)
151:
By what is the fool carried away? How does the wise man dispel it?
How does one become secure from bondage? Being asked, tell me that.

*Bālo*: the fool. *Kena*: by what [dhamma]. *Vuyhati*: is carried away. *Paṇḍito*: the wise man. *Kathaṃ*: in what way. *Nudati*: dispels or removes the thing that carries one away. *Yogakkhemī*: one who has reached security from the four bonds. *Kathaṃ hoti*: how does he become so? *Taṃ*: that problem. *Pucchito*: you who are asked. *Me akkhāhi*: tell me.

2. *Kiṃsu rājā rajjissaro* means: In what way is a king one who is a master of dust? Or, one who is mastered by dust?

3. *Kathaṃsu virajo hoti* means: For what reason does that king become free from dust?

4. *Kathaṃ bālo ti vuccati* means: For what reason, or whom, is called a fool? This is the meaning.

The meaning of the counter-song which is the answer is:

1. *Chadvārādhipati rājā* means: He who is the master of the six doors. Even at a single door, he is not overcome by sense objects such as forms; such a person is called a king.

2. *Rajjāmāno rajjissaro* means: He who is prone to delight in various sense objects; such a person who delights is called a master of the impurity of dust. Or, one who is mastered by dust.

3. *Arajjaṃ* means: One who is without delight is called free from dust.

4. *Rajjaṃ* means: Because of delighting, or one who has delight, is called a fool.

This is the meaning.

Having taught the counter-songs to the youth Uttara in this way, the Blessed One said: "Dear Uttara, when you sing this counter-song, the young Nāga maiden will sing another verse in response to this counter-song. When she sings thus, you should sing this counter-song to that Nāga king."

The fool is carried away by the flood; the wise man dispels it through effort.
One detached from all bonds is called secure from bondage.

*Bālo*: the fool. *Oghana*: by the four floods. *Vuyhati*: is carried away. *Paṇḍito*: the wise man. *Yogā*—*yogena*: through the effort known as Right Exertion (*sammappadhāna*). *Nudati*: dispels the four floods. *Sabbayogavisaṃyutto*: the person who is detached from all four bonds. *Yogakkhemīti*: as one secure from the four bonds. *Vuccati*: is called.

(The meaning of that counter-song verse is: The fool is carried away by the fourfold flood, such as the flood of sensual desire. The wise man dispels that flood through the effort called Right Exertion. He who is not joined with any bonds like the bond of sensual desire is called one who has reached security from the four bonds. This is the meaning.)

## The Nāga King Rejoices and People Drown

While learning this counter-song, the youth Uttara established himself in the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Having become a Stream-enterer, he took that verse and went, saying, "O friends, I have brought the counter-song to the song; give me way!" He went by stepping on the knees of the great crowd that stood without any gap. The young Nāga maiden, standing on the hood of her father the Nāga king, sang the song "Who is the king who is the master?" while dancing. The youth Uttara sang the counter-song "The king who is the master of the six doors." Again, the young Nāga maiden sang the song "By what is one carried away?" to the youth Uttara. Then, singing the counter-song to the young Nāga maiden, the youth Uttara spoke this verse: "One is carried away by the flood." As soon as the Nāga king heard that counter-song, he knew that a Buddha had arisen and thought, "I have never heard such a word during the entire interval between two Buddhas. Indeed, friends, a Buddha has arisen in the world!"
152:
## The Teaching

(182) Hard is the winning of the human state; hard is the life of mortals.
Hard is the hearing of the True Dhamma; hard is the appearance of Buddhas.

*Manussapaṭilābho*: obtaining the state of a human being. *Kiccho*: is difficult. *Maccānaṃ*: of mortals. *Jīvitaṃ*: life or longevity. *Kicchaṃ*: is difficult or rare. *Saddhammassavanaṃ*: hearing the True Dhamma. *Kicchaṃ*: is difficult or rare. *Buddhānaṃ*: of the Buddhas. *Uppādo*: the appearance or arising. *Kiccho*: is difficult or extremely rare.

Having never heard such a sound before, he thought, "O friends, truly a Buddha has arisen in the world!" and with a joyful heart, he struck the water with his tail. Great waves arose. Both banks broke. In a place about one *usabha* wide on both sides, people sank into the water. The Nāga king placed this many people on his hood, lifted them up, and set them on dry land.

## The Nāga King's Sorrow before the Buddha

The Nāga king approached the youth Uttara and asked, "Sir, where is the Teacher?" When told, "Great King, he is dwelling at the foot of a certain tree," the Nāga king said, "Sir, come, let us go," and went together with the youth Uttara. The great crowd also followed along with the Nāga king. The Nāga king went, entered within the six-colored rays, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood weeping and lamenting. Then the Blessed One said to the Nāga king, "Great King, what is this grief?" "Venerable Sir, I was a disciple of a Buddha like you, Kassapa the Blessed One, and practiced the recluse-dharma (*samaṇadhamma*) for twenty thousand years. Yet that practiced recluse-dharma was unable to deliver me from the state of a rootless animal. Depending on the mere act of snapping a small *eraka* grass leaf, I took a rootless rebirth and was born in a place where one moves by crawling on the breast. During the entire interval between two Buddhas, I did not obtain human status, nor did I hear the True Dhamma, nor did I see a Buddha like you, Venerable Sir." Hearing the words of the Nāga king's petition, the Blessed One said:

"Great King, the state of a human being is indeed rare; likewise, hearing the True Dhamma is rare; likewise, the appearance of a Buddha is rare. This human state and so forth are obtained with difficulty and hardship." Desiring to preach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. The Nāga king also should have attained the fruit of Stream-entry on that day. However, although he should have attained it, he did not because he was an animal. That Erakapatta Nāga king, in the five circumstances known as taking rebirth, sloughing the old skin, falling into a deep sleep, engaging in sexual intercourse with a Nāga of the same species, and passing away, Nāgas must assume only their Nāga form, and thus they suffer.
153:
Having reached the state of not being weary in those five places, he was able to wander about in the form of a young man.

The Story of Erakapatta, the King of Dragons, ends.

## The Exhortation of the Buddhas

(183) Not doing any evil, the attainment of the wholesome, the purification of one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

(184) Patience is the highest austerity, forbearance; the Buddhas say Nibbāna is supreme. He is not a renunciant who strikes another; he is not an ascetic who harms another.

(185) Not reviling, not harming, restraint in the Pātimokkha, moderation in eating, dwelling in a secluded place, and devotion to higher mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Sabbapāpassa: not doing any evil. Kusalassa upasampadā: the fulfillment of the wholesome. Sacittapariyodapanaṃ: the purification of one's own mind. These all are the teaching of the Buddhas.

Khantī: patience, which is called forbearance (titikkhā), is the highest practice of austerity in this teaching. The Buddhas—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Savakabuddhas—say that Nibbāna, the cessation of defilements, is supreme. One who is prone to killing and harming others is not called a renunciant (pabbajita). One who harms others is not called an ascetic (samaṇa).

Anūpavādo: not accusing or reviling. Anūpaghāto: not harming or killing. Pātimokkhe saṃvaro: restraint and closing off [of the senses] in the Pātimokkha virtue, which is the foremost. Mattaññutā: knowing the measure in food. Pantañca sayanāsanaṃ: dwelling in a secluded monastery. Adhicitte āyogo: making an effort in the training of higher mind, which is the mastery of the mind called the eight attainments. These all are the teaching of the Buddhas.

## 4. The Story of the Question of Venerable Ānanda regarding the Uposatha
(Ānandattherapañhavatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with "Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ" in reference to a question asked by Venerable Ānanda.

## The Uposatha of the Seven Buddhas

While staying in a place for daytime rest, Venerable Ānanda thought: "The Teacher has spoken of the mothers and fathers, the life span, the Bodhi tree of enlightenment, the assembly of disciples, the assembly of chief disciples, and the chief attendant of the seven Buddhas. However, he has not yet spoken of the Uposatha. How is it? Was the Uposatha of those Buddhas the same as this Uposatha, or was it different?" He approached the Teacher and asked about that matter. Since there was only a difference in time for those Buddhas, and no difference in the discourse, [the Teacher explained]. To elaborate, the Buddha Vipassī performed the Uposatha once every seven years. The exhortation given on a single day was sufficient for seven years. The Buddha Sikhī and the Buddha Vessabhū performed the Uposatha every six years. The Buddha Kakusandha and the Buddha Koṇāgamana performed the Uposatha every year. The Buddha Kassapa performed the Uposatha once every six months.
154:
The exhortation given on a single day by the Buddha Kassapa was sufficient for six months. Therefore, our Teacher, having declared this difference in time of those former Buddhas, said, "Their verse of exhortation is this very one," and wishing to make manifest the identical Uposatha of all Buddhas, he spoke these verses.

(By 'anūpavāda', verbal virtue is taught. By 'anūpaghāta', bodily virtue is taught. By 'pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro', the virtue of restraint in the Pātimokkha and the virtue of restraint of the senses are taught. By 'mattaññutā', the virtue of purity of livelihood and the virtue concerning requisites are taught. By 'pantañca sayanāsanaṃ', suitable lodging and dwelling are taught. By 'adhicitte', the eight attainments are taught. Thus, by this verse, the three trainings are also taught.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many reached the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of the Question of Venerable Ānanda regarding the Uposatha ends.
155:
## 5. The Story of the Discontented Monk (Anabhirata Bhikkhu Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Na kahāpaṇavassena," concerning a certain monk who was discontented with the Dispensation.

## The Monk Who Wished to Disrobe

This monk, having been ordained in the Dispensation and attained higher ordination, was sent by his preceptor to a certain place to study the Pali texts. While he was there, his father fell ill. The father, wishing to see his monk son but unable to find anyone capable of summoning him, passed away while lamenting in his grief for his son. Before he died, he handed over a hundred kahāpaṇas to his younger son, saying, "Use this for the cost of my son's bowl and robes," and then passed away. When the young monk returned, his younger brother fell at his feet, weeping and rolling on the ground, and said, "Venerable sir, your father passed away while lamenting for you. He left a hundred kahāpaṇas in my hands. What shall I do with this money?"

The young monk initially refused, saying, "I have no need for money." Later, however, he thought, "What is the use of living by wandering for alms at others' houses? It is possible to live depending on those hundred kahāpaṇas. I will disrobe." Oppressed by discontent, he neglected his recitations and meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), becoming pale like one suffering from jaundice. When young novices and monks asked him why he looked so haggard, he replied, "I am bored (with the monkhood)." They informed his teachers and preceptors, who then took him to the Teacher. The Teacher asked, "Is it true that you are discontented?" When he replied, "Yes, Bhante," the Teacher asked, "Why have you done this? Do you have any means of livelihood?" He replied, "Yes, Bhante." "What do you have?" "A hundred kahāpaṇas, Bhante." "In that case, bring some pebbles from somewhere; we shall count them to see if it is possible to live on that amount or not." He brought the pebbles.
156:
As far as the sun and moon revolve, shining and illuminating the quarters, all beings dwelling on this earth are but the servants of Mandhātā.

## The Teaching

(186) Not by a rain of coins is satisfaction found in sensual pleasures. Sensual pleasures are of little sweetness and much suffering; knowing this, the wise man,

(187) Even in celestial pleasures, finds no delight. The disciple of the Fully Enlightened One delights in the destruction of craving.

"Not by a rain of coins" means that even if it rained the seven kinds of jewels, there is no satisfaction in either the objects of desire or the defilement of desire. Thus, craving is difficult to satisfy. "Little sweetness" means they provide small happiness, like a dream. "Much suffering" means they involve much pain, as mentioned in the categories of suffering. "Knowing this" means understanding these sensual pleasures in this way. "Even in celestial pleasures" means even if offered the pleasures of the devas, he would not find delight in them, just like the Venerable Samiddhi. "Delights in the destruction of craving" means he is devoted to Arahatship and Nibbāna, dwelling with a longing for them. "Disciple of the Fully Enlightened One" refers to a practitioner monk born from hearing the Dhamma taught by the Fully Enlightened One.

(The Buddha continued:) "Count and see if it is possible to live on that amount or not."

## The Allocation and the Mandhātu Jātaka

The young monk brought the pebbles. Then the Teacher said to him, "First, set aside fifty kahāpaṇas for your personal use, twenty-four for two oxen, and this much for seeds, for the yoke and plow, and for the hoe, sickle, and axe." When counted in this way, the hundred kahāpaṇas were insufficient. Then the Teacher said, "Monk, your kahāpaṇas are few. How can you fulfill your craving by depending on them? In the past, there were kings who, having ruled as Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti), were able to cause a rain of jewels to fall knee-deep over an area of twelve yojanas just by snapping their fingers. Even after ruling the celestial realm for as long as the lifetimes of thirty-six Sakkas, they passed away without having satisfied their craving." At the monk's request, the Teacher related the past and detailed the Mandhātu Jātaka from the Tika Nipāta.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, that discontented monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled multitude.

The Story of the Discontented Monk ends.

## 6. The Story of the Brahmin Aggidatta (Aggidatta Brāhmaṇa Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Bahuṃ ve saraṇaṃ yanti," concerning Aggidatta, the chaplain of King Kosala, who was sitting on a mound of sand.
157:
## The King of Kosala's Respect

That Aggidatta the Brahmin had been the chaplain (purohita) of King Mahākosala. When King Mahākosala passed away, King Pasenadi Kosala, thinking, "He is my father's chaplain," treated him with great respect, kept him in that same position, and would go out to meet him whenever Aggidatta came to attend on him. Saying, "Teacher, please sit here," he would offer him a seat equal to his own. Aggidatta thought, "This king shows me excessive respect. However, it is not possible to always capture the hearts of kings. The so-called happiness of royal splendor is only truly enjoyable with those of equal age. I am now old; it is proper for me to ordain."

## Aggidatta the Brahmin Renounces the World

That chaplain, having obtained permission from King Pasenadi Kosala to ordain, had a drum beaten throughout the city, and within seven days, gave away all his wealth in charity and became an ascetic outside the [Buddha's] dispensation. Following his example, ten thousand men also ordained.

## Aggidatta's Instruction

Aggidatta, living together with those ten thousand ascetics between the countries of Aṅga, Magadha, and Kuru, gave this instruction: "Dear ones, if thoughts of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka) or such things arise in anyone, let that person take a handful of sand from the river and pour it in this place."

Those ten thousand ascetics agreed, saying, "Very well," and whenever sensual thoughts and so on arose, they acted according to that instruction. In time, a great mound of sand was formed. A Naga king named Ahichatta took possession of that sand mound. The inhabitants of Aṅga, Magadha, and the Kuru country brought great offerings and gave alms to those ten thousand ascetics month after month. To those people of Aṅga, Magadha, and Kuru, Aggidatta gave this instruction: "Go to the mountains for refuge, go to the forests for refuge, go to the groves for refuge, go to the trees for refuge. By seeking refuge in this way, you will be released from all the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha)." He also instructed his own resident disciples with this same teaching.

## One Who Guides Wrongly

Our Bodhisatta, having made the Great Renunciation and attained Supreme Enlightenment, was at that time staying at the Jetavana Monastery near Sāvatthī. While surveying the world at dawn, he saw the Brahmin named Aggidatta together with his resident disciples entering within the net of his Supreme Knowledge. Knowing that "All of these people are possessed of the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for Arahatship," in the evening, he said to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna: "Friend Moggallāna, do you see the Brahmin Aggidatta leading a great multitude of people into a place that is not a true landing-place (atittha)? Go and give them instruction."

"Venerable Sir, they are many; it is not a task I can handle alone. If the Exalted One also comes, it will be manageable," he replied. The Buddha said, "Friend Moggallāna, I too shall come. You go on ahead."
158:
## Venerable Moggallāna and Aggidatta

The Elder Mahāmoggallāna, going on ahead, thought: "These people are powerful and numerous. If I say something when they are all gathered together in one place, they might all rise up in groups." Thinking thus, by his psychic power, he caused a rain with large drops to fall. When the large raindrops fell, they got up one by one and entered their respective leaf huts. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna stood at the door of Aggidatta the Brahmin's leaf hut and said, "Aggidatta."

When Aggidatta heard the Elder's voice, he thought, "In this world, there is no one capable of calling me by name. Who could it be that calls me by name?" Due to his stiff pride, he said, "Who is this calling me?"

"Brahmin, it is I," he replied. "What are you saying?" "For just this one night, please tell me of a place to stay here." "There is no place to stay here; there is only one leaf hut for one person."

"Aggidatta, humans go to humans, cattle go to cattle, and ascetics go to the presence of ascetics. Do not act like this; give me a place to stay." "What, are you an ascetic?" he asked. "Yes, I am an ascetic."

"If you are an ascetic, where is your carrying pole and water strainer? What are your ascetic requisites?" "I have my requisites, but it is troublesome to carry them separately while traveling. Therefore, Brahmin, I carry them within [my body] as I travel." Aggidatta, saying "Will you be able to travel carrying them?" became angry with the Elder.

## The Psychic Contest Between Moggallāna and the Naga King

Then the Elder Moggallāna said to Aggidatta, "Aggidatta, do not be angry with us. Tell me of a place to stay." When he said, "There is no place to stay here," the Elder asked, "Who lives on this sand mound?" "A Naga king lives there," he replied. "Give me this place," the Elder said. "It is not possible to give it; the Naga king's business there is heavy (dangerous)." "Let it be so heavy; just give it to me." "If that is the case, you yourself shall know," Aggidatta said.

Then the Elder Moggallāna went towards the sand mound. The Naga king, seeing the Elder coming, thought, "This monk is coming here. He probably does not know of my presence. I will kill him by emitting smoke," and he emitted smoke. The Elder thought, "This Naga king probably thinks, 'Only I can emit smoke; others cannot,'" and he himself emitted smoke. The smoke rising from both their bodies reached as far as the Brahma world. Both clouds of smoke did not harm the Elder but harmed only the Naga king. The Naga king, unable to endure the force of the smoke, burst into flames. The Elder also entered the fire element (tejo-dhātu) and burst into flames along with him. The flames rose as far as the Brahma world. Both sets of flames did not harm the Elder but harmed only the Naga king. Then his whole body became like it was ablaze with torches. The group of hermits, looking on, thought, "The Naga king is burning the monk. Alas, the good monk has perished because he did not listen to our words."
159:
## The Discourse
(188) Driven by fear, men go to many a refuge, to mountains and forests, to parks and tree-shrines.
(189) That, indeed, is no secure refuge; that is not the supreme refuge. Having come to that refuge, one is not released from all suffering.
(190) But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, sees with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths:
(191) Suffering, the origin of suffering, the transcending of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering.

The smoke rising from the bodies of both reached as far as the Brahma realm. Both clouds of smoke did not harm or oppress the Elder Moggallāna, but they did harm and oppress the Naga king. The Naga king, unable to endure the intensity of the smoke, emitted flames. The Elder Moggallāna also entered the meditative attainment of the fire element (tejo-kasiṇa) and emitted flames together with the Naga king. The flames rose as far as the Brahma realm. Both sets of flames did not harm or oppress the Elder Moggallāna, but they did harm and oppress the Naga king. At that time, the Naga king's entire body appeared as if it were being burned all over by torches. The group of ascetics, watching, thought: "The Naga king is burning the monk. The monk is indeed a good monk; because he did not listen to our words, he is meeting his ruin." After taming the Naga king and making him free from the poison of pride, Moggallāna sat on the sand heap. The Naga king, having created a hood the size of a gabled house, held it over the Elder's head, encircling the sand heap with his coils.

## The Arrival of the Blessed One
The group of ascetics went to the Elder early in the morning, thinking, "We shall find out whether the monk is dead or alive." When they saw the Elder sitting upon the sand heap, they raised their joined palms in praise and said, "O monk, were you not harmed by the Naga king?" The Elder replied, "Do you not see the Naga king standing with his hood over me?" The ascetics said, "Friends, the monk's deed is truly wonderful; such a Naga king has been tamed!" and they stood surrounding the Elder Moggallāna. At that moment, the Blessed One arrived. Upon seeing the Blessed One, the Elder Moggallāna rose from his seat and paid homage. Then the ascetics asked the Elder, "Is this great monk greater than you?" He replied, "This Blessed One is my Teacher; I am his disciple." The Buddha sat upon the sand heap. The group of ascetics, thinking, "First, this is the power of the disciple; what then will the power of the Teacher be like?" raised their joined palms and praised the Blessed One greatly.

## Taking Refuge in the Triple Gem to Escape Suffering
The Blessed One called the Brahmin Aggidatta and said, "Aggidatta, when you give advice to your disciples and supporters, what do you say to them?"
160:
(192) This refuge is truly secure; this refuge is supreme. Having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.

*Manussā*: people. *Bhayatajjitā*: being terrified by fear. *Bahuṃ*: many. *Pabbattāni ca*: mountains. *Vanāni ca*: forests. *Ārāmarukkha-cetiyāni ca*: parks, gardens, and shrines consisting of prominent trees. *Ve*: indeed. *Saraṇaṃ*: as a refuge. *Yanti*: they go to.

*Etaṃ saraṇaṃ*: all these refuges such as forests and mountains. *Kho*: indeed. *Khemaṃ*: a secure refuge. *Na*: is not. *Etaṃ saraṇaṃ*: all these refuges such as forests and mountains. *Uttamaṃ*: a supreme refuge. *Na*: is not. *Etaṃ saraṇaṃ*: these refuges such as forests and mountains. *Āgamma*: relying upon. *Ekopi*: even a single person. *Sabbadukkhā*: from all the sufferings of the round of rebirth, such as birth and so on. *Na pamuccati*: cannot be released.

*Yo ca*: but he who. *Buddhañca*: the Buddha. *Dhammañca*: the Dhamma. *Saṅghañca*: the Saṅgha. *Saraṇaṃ*: as a refuge. *Gato*: has gone to. *Cattāri*: the four. *Ariyasaccāni*: Noble Truths. *Sammā*: well. *Paññāya*: with wisdom. *Passati*: sees.

*Dukkhañca*: Suffering. *Dukkhasamuppādañca*: the Origin of Suffering which causes suffering. *Dukkhassa atikkamañca*: the Cessation of Suffering which is the transcending of suffering. *Dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ*: leading to the peace of Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering. *Ariyaṃ*: the Noble. *Aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ*: consisting of eight factors. *Maggaṃ*: the Path. *Passati*: he sees.

*Tassa*: for that person (or for the one who has known the Four Truths). *Etaṃ saraṇaṃ*: this refuge in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. *Kho*: indeed. *Khemaṃ*: is secure. *Etaṃ saraṇaṃ*: this refuge in these three. *Uttamaṃ*: is supreme. *So ca puggalo*: and that person. *Etaṃ saraṇaṃ*: this refuge in these three. *Āgamma*: relying upon. *Sabbadukkhā*: from all the sufferings of the round of rebirth. *Pamuccati*: can be released.

When asked, "What do you say when giving advice?" Aggidatta replied, "I say: 'Go for refuge to this mountain; go for refuge to this forest, this park, this tree. One who has reached the state of taking refuge in this mountain and so on can be released from all suffering.' This is how I advise my disciples and lay followers." The Blessed One then said, "Aggidatta, one who takes refuge in these mountains and so on cannot be released from suffering. Those who have reached the state of taking refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—can be released from all the sufferings of the round of rebirth," and He spoke these verses.

## All Ascetics Become Arahants
At the end of the discourse, all those ascetics attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Paying homage to the Blessed One, they requested ordination. The Blessed One, stretching out his right hand from the chamber of his robes, said: "Etha bhikkhavo, sammā caratha brahmacariyaṃ" — "Come, monks, lead the holy life well." At that very moment, they became like senior elders of sixty years' standing, bearing the eight requisites.

## Elder Aggidatta Displays Psychic Power
That day was also the day when people living in the kingdoms of Aṅga, Magadha, and Kuru came bringing offerings. When they arrived with their offerings and saw all those former ascetics and the disciples of the Buddha, they wondered: "Is our Brahmin Aggidatta the Great, or is the Recluse Gotama the Great?" They thought: "Because the Recluse Gotama has come here, Aggidatta must be the Great one." The Blessed One, perceiving the inclination of those country-folk, said: "Aggidatta, clear the doubts of the assembly."
161:
Aggidatta, thinking, "I shall aspire only to this much of the cutting off of doubt," ascended into the air seven times by the power of his psychic potency. After descending repeatedly and bowing to the Teacher, he declared his discipleship, saying, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am a disciple."

The Story of Aggidatta the Brahmin ends.

## The Teaching
(193) Rare is the noble person (purisājañño); he is not born everywhere. Wherever that wise one (dhīro) is born, that family prospers in happiness.

Purisājañño: the noble person. Dullabho: is hard to find; or, is rare. So: that noble person. Sabbattha: in every place, in every family. Na jāyati: is not born. Dhīro: the wise one who is unshakable. So: that noble person. Yattha: in whichever family. Jāyati: is born. Taṃ kulaṃ: that family. Sukhaṃ: having happiness. Edhati: prospers.

## 7. The Story of the Question of Venerable Ānanda
(Ānandattherapañhavatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with "Dullabho," in reference to a question asked by Venerable Ānanda.

## The Place where the Noble Person is Born
One day, while Venerable Ānanda was sitting in a secluded place during the day, he reflected: "The Teacher has spoken about the birthplaces of noble elephants and others, saying, 'A noble elephant is born in the Chaddanta family or the Uposatha family; a noble horse is born in the Sindhava family or the Valāhaka king of horses family; a noble bull is born in the Dakkhinapatha region.' The Teacher has thus described the birthplaces of noble elephants and so on. But where is a noble person born?" He approached the Teacher, bowed, and after sitting in a suitable place, asked about this matter. The Teacher said, "Ānanda, a noble person is not born everywhere. Specifically, he is born in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), which is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. Even when born there, he is not born in just any family, but only in one of the families of Khattiya-mahāsāla (noble warriors of great wealth) or Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla (brahmins of great wealth)." He then spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth.

The Story of the Question of Venerable Ānanda ends.
162:
## The Teaching
(194) Happy is the birth of the Buddhas; happy is the teaching of the True Dhamma. Happy is the harmony of the Sangha; happy is the practice of those in harmony.

Buddhānaṃ: of the Buddhas. Uppādo: the birth/arising. Sukho: is happy. Saddhammadesanā: the teaching of the True Dhamma. Sukhā: is happy. Saṅghassa: of the Sangha. Sāmaggī: harmony/unity of mind. Sukhā: is happy. Samaggānaṃ: of those who are in harmony. Tapo: the ascetic practice. Sukho: is happy.

## 8. The Story of Many Monks
(Sambahulabhikkhuvatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with "Sukho buddhānaṃ," in reference to the conversation of many monks.

## Choosing Happiness
One day, five hundred monks were sitting in the assembly hall and initiated this conversation: "Friends, what is happiness in this world?" In that discussion, some monks said, "There is no happiness like the happiness of royalty." Some said, "There is no happiness like the happiness derived from the five cords of sensual pleasure." Some said, "There is no happiness like the pleasure of eating fine rice with meat and so on." The Teacher went to where those monks were and asked, "Monks, for what conversation are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a conversation," the Teacher said, "Monks, what are you saying? All this happiness is included within the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha). In this world, the birth of a Buddha, the hearing of the True Dhamma, the harmony of the Sangha, and the state of being joyful—this alone is happiness." He then spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, those five hundred monks were established in Arahatship. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude of people.

The Story of Many Monks ends.
163:
## 9. The Story of the Golden Stupa of Kassapa Buddha
(Kassapa-dasabalassa Suvaṇṇa-cetiya-vatthu)
The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Pūjārahe' while traveling on a journey, concerning the golden stupa of Kassapa, the One of Ten Powers.

## The Traditional Site of the Stupa
Our Blessed One, born of the Gotama lineage, who like previous Buddhas has come well (Sugata), departed from Sāvatthī and, while traveling in due course toward the city of Bārāṇasī, arrived at a certain deity-shrine near the Brahmin village of Todeyya, accompanied by a large community of monks. While staying there, the Blessed One sent the Treasurer of the Dhamma, Venerable Ānanda, to call a Brahmin who was plowing a field nearby. When that Brahmin arrived, he did not pay homage to the Blessed One but instead stood after paying homage only to that deity-shrine. The Blessed One, who speaks kindly, asked, 'Brahmin, what do you consider this place to be?' The Brahmin replied, 'O Gotama, I worship this place as the site of a stupa handed down through our tradition.' The Blessed One encouraged him, saying, 'Brahmin, you have done well in worshipping this place.'

## Four Persons Worthy of a Stupa, Three Types of Shrines
Hearing this, the monks became doubtful, wondering, 'For what reason did the Blessed One encourage him so?' Then, to dispel the monks' doubt, the Blessed One preached the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta from the Majjhima Nikāya. By his psychic power, he manifested in the sky the golden stupa of Kassapa Buddha, which was one league (yojana) in height, as well as another golden stupa, and showed them to the great multitude. He said, 'Brahmin, it is most fitting to worship such stupas worthy of honor.' Following the method shown in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, he proclaimed the four persons worthy of a stupa: a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, an Arahant disciple, and a Cakkavatti king. He specifically explained the three types of shrines: the 'Sarīra-cetiya' (shrine of bodily relics), the 'Uddissa-cetiya' (shrine of representation/images), and the 'Paribhoga-cetiya' (shrine of use, such as the Bodhi tree and requisites like robes). He then spoke these verses:

## The Teaching
(195) To one who honors those worthy of honor—whether the Buddhas or their disciples—who have transcended conceptual proliferation (papañca) and have crossed over grief and lamentation;

(196) To one who honors such as these, who are quenched (nibbute) and free from fear from any quarter—no one is able to calculate the merit [of such an act] as being 'this much.'

Pūjārahe: those worthy of honor. Papañca-samatikkante: those who have transcended the three types of conceptual proliferation, namely craving, views, and conceit. Tiṇṇa-soka-pariddave: those who have crossed over grief and lamentation. Buddhe vā: the Fully Enlightened Buddhas. Yadivā: or else. Sāvake vā: the disciples of the Buddha. Pūjayato ca: of one who honors. Tādise: such as these described. Nibbute: those who have attained Nibbāna, the extinguishing of the fires of defilements. Akutobhaye: those who have no fear from any object of existence. Te: those Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples who have attained Nibbāna. Pūjayato ca: of one who honors. Puññaṃ: the merit. Ettaṃ: is this much. Iti: thus. Kenaci api: by anyone, whether Brahma, deva, or human. Alternatively: Kenaci api: by any means of estimation, weighing, or measuring. Saṅkhātuṃ: to calculate in terms of its beneficial results. Na sakkā: is not possible.
164:
(Because the merit of one who honors the living Buddha and others, or the Buddha and others who have attained Parinibbāna, is incalculable, it is stated in the Vimānavatthu Pali:)

Whether the Buddha is alive or has attained Nibbāna, if the mind is equal, the fruit is equal. For because of the clarity of mind, beings go to a happy destination.

Tiṭṭhante ca: in the living Buddha and others. Nibbute cāpi: and in the Buddha and others who have attained Nibbāna. Citte: if the mind. Same: is equal. Phalaṃ: the fruit. Samaṃ: is equal. Cetopaṇidhi-hetu hi: because of the clarity of mind. Sattā: beings. Sugatiṃ: to a happy destination. Gacchanti: go.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, that plowing Brahmin became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). The great golden stupa, one league in height, remained in the sky for seven days. A great assembly took place. For seven days, the people worshipped the great stupa in various ways. At that time, those with wrong views experienced the destruction of their false beliefs. By the power of the Buddha, the stupa returned to its original place. At that very moment, a great stone stupa appeared at that site.

The Story of the Golden Stupa of Kassapa Buddha ends.

## Comparison Regarding the Golden Stupa
In the city of Rājagaha, an obscure Brahmin heard that it was impossible to take the measure of the Great Ascetic Gotama. When the Blessed One entered for alms, the Brahmin took a bamboo pole sixty cubits long and stood outside the city gate. When the Buddha arrived, he stood nearby holding the pole. The pole reached only to the Blessed One's knees. Again, the next morning, he joined two bamboo poles together and stood nearby. The Blessed One made his waist appear clearly above the two poles and asked, 'Brahmin, what are you doing?' He replied, 'I am taking the measure of Your Reverence.' The Buddha said, 'Brahmin, even if you were to join all the bamboos that fill the entire universe, you would not be able to take my measure. That is true. I did not fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) in such a way that another could take my measure. Brahmin, the Buddha, who has come well like previous Buddhas, is incomparable and matchless.' He then spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

To one who honors such as these, who are quenched and free from fear from any quarter—no one is able to calculate the merit as being 'this much.'

At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings drank the nectar of the Dhamma (attained Nibbāna).

This is from the commentary on the Sīlakkhandhavagga, specifically the passage found in the fourth sutta, the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta.

## 15. Sukhavagga
## 1. Ñātikalahavūpasamana-vatthu
(The Story of the Settling of the Quarrel among Relatives)

While the Buddha was staying among the Sakyans, he taught this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Susukhaṃ vata' for the purpose of settling a quarrel that had arisen among his relatives.

## The Battle between the Kapilavatthu and the Koliyas
Between the city of Kapilavatthu and the city of Koliya, there was a river named Rohiṇī. The Sakyan princes had a single dam built across the river to cultivate their crops. Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops began to wither, the laborers and workers from both cities gathered. Among them, the residents of Koliya said, 'If this water is shared by both cities, it will not be enough for you, nor will it be enough for us. Our crops, however, will reach maturity with just one more watering. Please give this water to us.' The residents of Kapilavatthu replied, 'If you fill your granaries while we are left with nothing, we will not be able to go from door to door of your houses carrying baskets, bags, and purses, even if we take with us Jāmbūnada gold, blue sapphires, or pure and black coins. Our crops will also reach maturity with just one more watering. Therefore, give this water to us.'

When they said, 'We cannot give it,' and the others replied, 'We also cannot give it,' the argument escalated. One man stood up and struck another, who then struck him back. Thus, they continued to strike one another, insulting each other's royal lineages and intensifying the quarrel. The laborers of Koliya said, 'Go away with your children who live in Kapilavatthu! Those Sakyans who, like dogs and jackals, cohabited with their own sisters—what can their elephants, horses, shields, and weapons do to us?' The laborers of Kapilavatthu replied, 'Go away now with your children afflicted by leprosy! Those Koliyans who, being helpless and homeless like animals, lived in Kola trees—what can their elephants, horses, shields, and weapons do to us?' Those laborers went and reported the matter to the ministers in charge, and the ministers reported it to the royal families.
166:
## The Teaching
(197) Happy indeed we live, free from hatred among the hateful.
Among hateful men, we dwell free from hatred.
(198) Happy indeed we live, free from affliction among the afflicted.
Among afflicted men, we dwell free from affliction.
(199) Happy indeed we live, free from striving among the striving.
Among striving men, we dwell free from striving.

'Those of us who, in the midst of men who possess the five types of hatred, can live without hatred; we, being free from the five types of hatred among those who possess them, live indeed very happily.'
'Those of us who, in the midst of men who are afflicted by defilements, can live without being afflicted by defilements; we, being free from affliction among those who are afflicted, live indeed very happily.'
'Those of us who, in the midst of men who strive and worry over the pursuit of sensual pleasures, can live without such striving; we, being free from striving among those who are intensely striving in matters of desire, live indeed very happily.'

After that, the Sakyan royalty set out in battle array, saying, 'We shall show the strength and power of those who cohabited with their sisters.' The Koliya princes also set out in battle array, saying, 'We shall show the strength and power of those who lived in Kola trees.'

## The Buddha’s Journey to Admonish Them
At dawn, as the Buddha surveyed the world, he saw his relatives and thought, 'If I do not go, these people will be destroyed. It is proper that I go.' Thus, he traveled alone through the air and sat cross-legged in the sky over the middle of the Rohiṇī River. When the relatives saw the Buddha, they cast aside their weapons and paid homage to him.

## Which is More Valuable: Water or Royalty?
Then the Buddha addressed the princes, 'Great Kings, what is the cause of this quarrel?' When they replied, 'Venerable Sir, we do not know,' he asked again, 'Who would know now?' They replied, 'The Viceroy will know; the Commander-in-Chief will know.' In this manner, they questioned down to the laborers, who finally reported, 'Venerable Sir, the quarrel is over water.' The Buddha asked, 'Great Kings, how much is water worth?' They replied, 'Venerable Sir, water is of little value.' He asked again, 'Great Kings, how much is royalty worth?' They replied, 'Venerable Sir, royalty is of inestimable value.' The Buddha then said, 'It is not proper for you to destroy inestimable kings for the sake of water which is of little value.' They remained silent. Then the Buddha addressed them, saying, 'Great Kings, why do you act in such a manner? If I were not here today, a river of blood would flow. What you have done is improper. You live with hatred, possessed of the five types of enmity; I live without hatred. You live afflicted by defilements; I live unafflicted. You live striving in the pursuit of sensual pleasures; I live without striving.' Having said this, he taught these verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the discourse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other stages.
The Story of the Settling of the Quarrel among Relatives ends.
167:
## The Teaching

(200) Happy indeed we live, we who have nothing.
We shall be feeders on joy, like the Ābhassara gods.

Evil Māra, for us, there is no impediment such as lust and so forth. We live indeed very happily. Like the Brahmas born in the Ābhassara realm who have joy as their food, we too shall have joy as our food.

## 2. The Story of Māra
(Māravatthu)

While the Buddha was staying at the brahmin village of Pañcasālā, he spoke this Dhamma teaching, "Happy indeed we live," regarding Māra.

## Māra Preventing the Buddha from Receiving Alms

One day, the Buddha, seeing the potential (upanissaya) for five hundred maidens to attain the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), stayed near that village. On a festival day, those maidens went to the river, bathed, and after adorning themselves, headed towards the village. The Buddha also entered that village for alms. At that time, Māra possessed the bodies of all the villagers so that the Buddha would not receive even a single ladle of food. When the Buddha was leaving the village with his bowl as clean as it was washed, Māra stood at the village gate and asked, "O Monk, did you receive alms?" The Buddha replied, "O Evil One, did you not act in such a way that I would not receive alms?"

Māra then said, "In that case, Venerable Sir, please enter again."

At that moment, the five hundred maidens arrived at the village gate, saw the Buddha, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. Māra also said to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, not having received alms, are you oppressed by the suffering of hunger?" The Buddha said, "O Evil Māra, even if we receive nothing today, we shall spend the time with the bliss of joy, just like the Great Brahmas in the Ābhassara realm," and spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, all five hundred maidens were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The Story of Māra ends.
168:
## The Teaching

(201) Victory breeds hatred; the defeated live in pain.
The peaceful live happily, giving up both victory and defeat.

Victory - One who conquers others increases enmity. The defeated person lives in suffering. The peaceful one, an Arahant whose defilements are extinguished, lives happily, having abandoned both victory and defeat.

## 3. The Story of King Kosala's Defeat
(Kosalarañño Parājayavatthu)

While the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana monastery, he spoke this Dhamma teaching, "Victory breeds hatred," regarding the defeat of King Kosala.

## King Kosala Intending to Die After Defeat

It is said that King Kosala, wishing to reclaim the village named Kāsi which was given by his father, King Mahākosala, when King Bimbisāra of Rājagaha and Queen Videhī were married, fought with his nephew Ajātasattu and was defeated three times. Upon being defeated for the third time, he thought, "I am unable to defeat even a child who still smells of milk. What is the use of my life?" Thinking thus, King Kosala fasted and lay on his couch. Then, the news of the King spread throughout the city. The monks informed the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, it is said that King Kosala was defeated three times over the village of Kāsi. Having been defeated and returned, he thought, 'I cannot defeat even a child who still smells of milk. What is the use of my life?' and is now fasting and lying on his couch." Hearing the words of those monks, the Buddha said, "Monks, the winner breeds hatred. The loser sleeps in suffering with an unhappy mind," and spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people reached the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of King Kosala's Defeat ends.

## 4. The Story of a Certain Clan Maiden
(Aññatarakuladārikāvatthu)

While the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana monastery, he spoke this Dhamma teaching, "There is no fire like lust," regarding a certain young maiden.

## The Teaching

(202) There is no fire like lust; there is no crime like hatred.
There is no suffering like the aggregates; there is no bliss higher than peace.

*Rāgasamo*: like lust. *Aggi*: fire. *Natthi*: there is not. *Dosasamo*: like hatred. *Kali*: crime or fault. *Natthi*: there is not. *Khandhasamā*: like the aggregates that must be constantly borne. *Dukkhā*: sufferings. *Natthi nasanti*: there are not. *Santiparaṃ*: higher than Nibbāna. *Sukhaṃ*: bliss. *Natthi*: there is not.

## Serving the Saṅgha on the Wedding Day

The parents of that young woman, having arranged her marriage, invited the Buddha on the wedding day. The Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks, went to that house and sat down. That young bride, too, was moving to and fro, performing tasks such as filtering drinking water for the community of monks. Her husband stood there watching her. While he was watching her under the influence of lustful desire, defilements arose repeatedly within him. Because he was overwhelmed by the darkness of delusion known as ignorance, that young man could not serve the Buddha, nor could he serve the eighty Great Elders. Stretching out his hand, he formed the intention, "I will grab that young bride."

The Buddha, perceiving his intention, acted in such a way that he could not see the woman. When the young man could no longer see her, he stood looking at the Buddha. When the young man stood looking at Him, the Buddha said to him regarding the young woman, "There is no fire like the fire of lust; there is no fault like the fault of anger; there is no suffering like the suffering of bearing the burden of the aggregates; there is no bliss like the bliss of Nibbāna," and He spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, both the young woman and the young man were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). After they were established as Stream-enterers, the Buddha made them visible to each other again.

The Story of a Certain Family's Daughter ends.

## 5. The Story of the Lay Disciple whose Ox was Lost

(Ekaupāsakavatthu)

While residing in the city of Āḷavī, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Jighacchā" (Hunger), concerning a certain lay supporter whose ox was lost.
170:
## The Buddha's Compassion for a Poor Man

One day, while the Buddha was residing in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) of the Jetavana Monastery, He surveyed the world in the early morning and saw a poor man in the city of Āḷavī. Knowing that the man possessed the potential (upanissaya) for spiritual attainment, He traveled to Āḷavī accompanied by five hundred monks. The residents of Āḷavī invited the Buddha. That poor man also heard that the Buddha had arrived and made up his mind, "I will listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha." On that very day, one of his oxen ran away. When he thought, "What should I do? Shall I search for the ox, or shall I listen to the Dhamma?", he decided, "I will search for the ox first and listen to the Dhamma later," and left his house early in the morning.

The residents of Āḷavī, having seated the community of monks headed by the Buddha and served them food, took the alms-bowls to receive the words of appreciation (anumodanā). The Buddha thought, "I have come on a journey of thirty leagues for the sake of this poor man. That poor man is still in the forest searching for his ox. I will preach the Dhamma only when he arrives," and He remained silent. When that poor man found the ox at midday, he drove it into the herd and thought, "Even if there is nothing else I can do, I will at least pay homage to the Buddha." Although he was oppressed by hunger, he did not intend to go home but came quickly to the Buddha's presence, paid homage to Him, and sat in a suitable place.

## The Buddha Ordering Food to be Served

When the poor man arrived and stood there, the Buddha said to the person managing the offerings, "Is there any leftover food from the Saṅgha?" When the person replied, "Venerable Sir, everything is still available," the Buddha said, "Then feed this man first." That attendant, following the Buddha's instructions, had the man sit down and respectfully served him with rice-gruel and various kinds of food. After the poor man had eaten, he washed his mouth.

(It is said that in the entire Three Baskets of the Piṭaka, apart from this instance, there is no other place where the Buddha arranged for someone to be fed.)

With his physical distress calmed, the poor man's mind became concentrated. Then the Buddha preached the graduated discourse to him and revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the end of the teaching, the poor man was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Buddha, having given the words of appreciation, rose from His seat and departed. A great crowd of people followed the Buddha and then returned. While the monks were walking together with the Buddha, they began to complain, "Friends, look at the Buddha's action! On other days, there is nothing like this, but today, upon seeing a single man, He inquired about and arranged for rice-gruel and other food to be given." The Buddha turned back, stood still, and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" After hearing the matter, He said, "Yes, monks, I came on a journey of thirty leagues through the wilderness because I saw the potential of that lay disciple. He was extremely hungry. From early morning, [searching for] the ox..."
171:
## The Teaching

(203) Hunger is the greatest illness; conditioned things are the greatest suffering. Having known this as it really is, Nibbāna is the highest bliss.

Hunger (jighacchā) is the supreme illness. Conditioned things (saṅkhārā), namely the five aggregates, are the supreme suffering. Having known this nature as it really is, the wise person realizes Nibbāna. Nibbāna is the highest bliss, superior to all other forms of happiness.

"On other days, it was not like this, but today, as soon as he saw that man, he had gruel and other things prepared and given to him," they criticized. The Teacher, having turned back and stood still, asked, "Monks, what are you talking about?" When he heard the reason, he said, "Monks, it is true. I, having come a difficult journey of thirty yojanas, came because I saw the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of that lay devotee. That poor man was extremely hungry. From early morning, he had to wander in the forest searching for his ox. I thought that if the Dhamma were preached while he was suffering from the pain of hunger, he would not be able to penetrate it. Therefore, I acted in this way. There is no illness like the illness of hunger," and he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the discourse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. 

The Story of the Lay Devotee Whose Ox was Lost ends.

## 6. The Story of King Pasenadi of Kosala
(Pasenadikosalavatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, preached this Dhamma discourse beginning with "Health is the greatest gain," concerning King Pasenadi of Kosala.

## Overeating is the Cause of Suffering

On one occasion, King Pasenadi of Kosala ate a bucketful (one dona) of cooked rice with suitable curries and side dishes. One day, after having eaten his morning meal, before the drowsiness caused by the food had worn off, he went to the Teacher. Being in a state of exhaustion, he rolled from side to side. Although oppressed by sleepiness, he was unable to lie down straight, so he sat in a suitable place. Then the Teacher said to King Kosala, "Great King, how is it? Have you come before your exhaustion has subsided?" "Venerable Sir, it is true. Since the time I finished my meal, I have been in great distress," he replied. Then the Teacher said to King Kosala, "Great King, eating too much causes such suffering," and he spoke this verse.

For the man who is always mindful, knowing moderation in the food he has received, his ailments become thin; he digests slowly, preserving his life.

Sadā: always. Satīmato: for one who is mindful. Laddhabhojane: in the food received. Mattaṃ jānato: for one who knows moderation. Assa manujassa: for that man. Vedanā: feelings (ailments). Tanukā: thin (diminished). Bhavanti: they become. Āyupālayaṃ: protecting life. Saṇikaṃ: slowly. Jīrati: it digests.

When one is sluggish and a glutton, a sleeper who rolls around as he lies, like a great hog fed on grain, that dullard enters the womb again and again.

Mahāvarāhova: like a great hog. Niddāyitā: prone to sleepiness. Samparivattasāyī: prone to rolling around while sleeping. Hoti: becomes. Tadā: at that time. Lakkhaṇāni: the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Manasikātuṃ: to reflect upon. Na sakkoti: he is unable. Amanasikaronto: being unable to reflect. ## Eating in Moderation is the Cause of Happiness

After admonishing with this verse, saying, "Great King, it is proper to eat food in moderation; for one who eats in moderation, there is happiness," and wishing to admonish further, the Buddha spoke this verse:

King Pasenadi of Kosala was unable to learn the verse. He said to a young man named Sudassana, his nephew who was standing nearby, "Dear son, learn this verse." After learning the verse, the young man asked the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, what should I do?" Then the Teacher told him, "When the King is eating, at the time of his final mouthful, recite this verse. When the King, having understood the meaning, discards that mouthful, you should remove as many grains of rice from the King's cooking portion as there were in that discarded mouthful."

Saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir," the young man recited that verse every evening and morning when the King was eating his final mouthful, and reduced the rice grains according to the number in the discarded mouthful. Upon hearing the verse, the King also gave a thousand coins each time. Later, the King became established in the moderation of eating only one measure (nāḷika) of rice, attained happiness, and his body became lean.

Then one day, he went to the Teacher, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, I have now found happiness; I am now capable of chasing and catching even deer and horses. Previously, there was only war with my nephew (Ajātasattu). Now, I have given my daughter named Vajirā to my nephew, and that village (Kāsika) has been given to her as 'bath powder money' (dowry); the conflict with my nephew has been settled. For this reason too, I have found happiness. The royal ruby, an ancestral heirloom, which was lost in my palace the other day, has also come back into my hands now."

(204) Health is the highest gain, contentment is the highest wealth.
Trust is the highest kinsman, Nibbāna is the highest bliss.

Ārogyaṃ: the state of being free from disease. Paramā: is the supreme. Lābhā: gain. Santuṭṭhi: contentment and delight with the possessions one has obtained. Paramā: is the supreme. Dhanaṃ: wealth. “For this reason also, happiness has arisen for me, Venerable Sir. Desiring intimacy with the disciples of the Blessed One, a Sakyan princess has also come to my palace. For this reason also, happiness has arisen for me, Venerable Sir,” the King addressed. The Buddha said, “Great King, health is indeed the highest gain. There is no wealth like the state of being contented with whatever is obtained. Trust is the highest kinsman. There is no bliss like Nibbāna,” and then He spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of King Pasenadi Kosala ends.

## 7. The Story of Elder Tissa
(Tissa-thera Vatthu)
While residing in the city of Vesālī, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Pavivekarasaṃ' concerning a certain monk.

When the Buddha said, “Monks, I shall pass into Parinibbāna four months from now,” seven hundred monks in the presence of the Buddha were struck with anxiety.
