## 8. The Story of Sakka's Service
(Sakkavatthu)

While staying at the village of Veḷuva, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Sāhu dassanam" concerning Sakka, the king of devas.

## Sakka Carrying the Buddha's Waste

When the Blessed One had released the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) and it became known that an illness of dysentery had arisen, Sakka, the king of devas, thought, "It is proper for me to go to the Teacher and perform the duty of nursing the sick." He then discarded his form which was three gāvutas in height, approached the Teacher, and remained there massaging the Teacher's feet with his hands. Then the Teacher asked him, "Who is this?" "Venerable Sir, I am Sakka," he replied. "Why have you come?" the Teacher asked again. "Venerable Sir, I have come to serve the Blessed One who is unwell," he replied. "Sakka, to the devas, the scent of humans is like a rotting corpse tied to the neck from a hundred yojanas away. You should go, Sakka; I have monks who are my attendants," the Teacher said.

"Venerable Sir, I have come because I caught the scent of the Blessed One's virtue while standing at the summit of Mount Sineru, eighty-four thousand yojanas high. I alone will serve you, Venerable Sir." Having said this, Sakka did not allow anyone else to even touch the vessel used for the Teacher's bodily waste with their hands; he carried it out on his own head without even a hint of facial contraction (disgust), as if he were carrying a vessel of perfumes. Having thus cared for the Teacher, he departed only when the Teacher was comfortable.

The monks started a conversation: "Oh, how great is Sakka's affection for the Teacher! Having abandoned such celestial luxury, he performed service by carrying the vessel of the Teacher's bodily waste on his head, without even a hint of facial contraction, as if he were carrying a vessel of perfumes."

(Note: Āyu + saṅkhāra = the fruition attainment that sustains life. In some places, life itself is called āyu-saṅkhāra; here, it does not mean life, but the fruition attainment that sustains life. During the last rains retreat at the village of Veḷuva, the Buddha became unwell from the beginning of the retreat. He sustained himself through the āyu-saṅkhāra of fruition attainment. When the month of Tabodwe arrived, he decided not to enter that attainment for more than three months and thus released the āyu-saṅkhāra of fruition attainment.)

(206) Good is the sight of the Noble Ones; living with them is always happy. By not seeing fools, one may be constantly happy.

(207) He who consorts with fools grieves for a long time. Living with fools is always painful, like living with an enemy. But living with the wise is happy, like a meeting of kinsmen.

(208) Therefore, follow the steadfast, the wise, the learned, the dutiful, the virtuous, and the noble. One should follow such a good and intelligent person, as the moon follows the path of the stars.

*Ariyānaṃ*: the Noble Ones who are virtuous. *Dassanaṃ*: seeing them. *Sāhu*: is good. *Thannivāso*: living together with the virtuous and having the opportunity to perform great and small duties for them. *Sadā*: at all times. *Sukho*: is happy. *Bālānaṃ*: fools. *Adassanena*: because of not seeing them. *Niccameva*: only ever. *Sukhī*: being happy. *Siyā*: would be.

*Hi*: indeed, that word is true. *Bālasaṅgatacārī*: one who wanders in the company of the ignorant and foolish. *Dīghaṃ addhānaṃ*: for a long time. *Socati*: grieves. *Amittena*: with an armed enemy or a dangerous enemy like a poisonous snake. *Saṃvāso*: living together. *Sabbadā*: at all times. *Dukkho iva*: just as it is painful. *Evaṃ*: in this same way. *Bālehi*: with the ignorant and foolish. *Saṃvāso*: living together. *Sabbadā*: at all times. *Dukkho*: is painful.

*Ñātīnaṃ*: with parents and other kinsmen. *Samāgamo*: being together. *Sukhasaṃvāso*: just as it is a happy living together. *Dhīro va*: only the wise person. *Sukhasaṃvāso*: is a happy living together. *Hoti*: it is.

*Tasmā hi*: therefore indeed. *Dhīrañca*: one who is steadfast and possesses concentration (*samādhi*). *Paññañca*: one who possesses both mundane and supramundane wisdom. *Bahussutañca*: one who is learned and has wide knowledge. *Dhorayha*: one who has the habit of bearing the burden that leads to the fruit of Arahantship. *Sīlavatavantaṃ*: one who possesses the practice of virtue (*sīla*) and the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). *Ariyaṃ*: one who is far from defilements. *Taṃ tādisaṃ*: such a person. *Sumedhaṃ*: one who has excellent and beautiful wisdom. *Sappurisaṃ*: the virtuous person. *Nakkhattapathaṃ*: the path of the stars in the sky. *Candimā*: the moon. *Bhajati iva*: just as it follows. *Bhajetha*: one should follow.

"It is not surprising that Sakka, the King of Gods, shows such love and devotion to me. This Sakka, depending on me, gave up his old state of Sakka and, becoming a Sotāpanna, reached the state of a young Sakka. When he came, trembling with the fear of death and preceded by the Gandhabba deity named Pañcasikha, I said to that Sakka, who was seated in the midst of the celestial assembly in the Indasāla Cave:

'Ask me, Vāsava, whatever question you desire in your mind. I will bring an end to each and every question for you.'

After saying this, the Buddha dispelled Sakka's doubts and preached the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, fourteen crores of beings attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. Sakka, while remaining in his seat, attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpattiphala*), and passing away, was reborn through instantaneous rebirth as a young Sakka. In this way, I have been of great benefit to this Sakka. It is not surprising that Sakka shows love and devotion to me. O Bhikkhus, seeing the Noble Ones is happy; living together with those Noble Ones in one place is also happy. But being together with the ignorant and foolish, all of this is suffering," the Buddha said, and then preached these verses.
177:
The meaning is: one should follow and associate with such a virtuous person who is wise, endowed with mundane and supramundane wisdom, learned, possessing the habit of bearing the burden known as the practice leading to Arahatship, endowed with the practices of virtue and dhutaṅga, and noble due to being far from defilements—just as the moon follows the sky, the path of the stars, which is stainless.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of Sakka's Service ends.
The Commentary on the Chapter on Happiness (Sukhavagga) is finished.
The Fifteenth Chapter.
178:
## 16. Piyavagga
## 1. Tayojanapabbajitavatthu
(The Story of Three People Who Went Forth)

While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Ayoge," concerning three people who had gone forth.

## Three People Who Could Not Part

In Sāvatthī, there was an only son in a certain family who was dear and pleasing to his parents. One day, after hearing a Dhamma talk given by monks who had been invited to the house for an offering of thanks (anumodanā), he desired to go forth and asked his parents for permission. His parents did not grant it. The youth thought, "I will go and ordain only when my parents are not looking."

Subsequently, whenever the youth's father went out, he would entrust the son to the mother, saying, "Watch over this son." When the mother went out, she would entrust him to the father. One day, when the father was away, the mother, thinking "I will watch the son," sat on the ground spinning thread, leaning against one doorpost and blocking the other with her feet. The youth, planning to deceive her and leave, said, "Mother, please move aside a bit; let me go and relieve myself." When the mother drew back her feet, he left quickly for the monastery. Approaching the monks, he requested, "Venerable sirs, please ordain me," and he was ordained in their presence.

Then the youth's father returned and asked the mother, "Where is my son?" When she replied, "Lord, he was just here," the father looked around and, not seeing him, thought, "He must have gone to the monastery." Upon going to the monastery and seeing his son ordained, he wept and lamented, saying, "Dear son, why do you destroy me?" Thinking, "Now that my son has ordained, what will I do staying at home? What benefit is there?" he himself requested the monks and ordained.

Then the youth's mother thought, "Why are my son and my husband taking so long?" Wondering, "Could it be that they have gone to the monastery and ordained?" she went to the monastery to look for them. Seeing that both had ordained, she thought, "Now that these have ordained, what use is the house to me?" and she herself went to the nunnery and ordained. Even after they had ordained, they were unable to live apart. They spent their days sitting together and talking, both in the monks' monastery and in the nuns' quarters. Because of this, they harassed and troubled both the monks and the nuns.
179:
Then one day, the monks reported their behavior to the Teacher. The Teacher summoned the three and asked, "Is it true that you act in this way?" When they replied, "It is true," he said, "Why do you do this? This is not the practice (yoga) for those who have gone forth." They replied, "Venerable Sir, we cannot live apart." The Teacher said, "From the time of going forth, such behavior is improper. Not seeing the loved and seeing the unloved is indeed suffering. Therefore, one should not make anything dear or undear among beings and formations (saṅkhāra)." He then spoke these verses:

## The Teaching

(209) Applying oneself to what is not to be applied to,
And not applying oneself to what is to be applied to,
Giving up the goal, grasping the dear,
One envies those who apply themselves.

(210) Do not ever associate with the loved,
Nor with the unloved at any time.
Not seeing the loved is suffering,
And seeing the unloved is suffering.

(211) Therefore, do not make anything dear,
For separation from the dear is evil.
There are no bonds for those
For whom there is neither dear nor unloved.

*Ayoge*: in improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra); or, in frequenting the six improper resorts such as the resort of prostitutes. *Attānaṃ*: oneself. *Yuñja (yuñjanto)*: one who is habitually exerting. *Yogasmiṃ*: in proper attention. *Ayojayaṃ (ayojayanto)*: one who is not habitually exerting. *Atthaṃ*: the benefit of the threefold training such as higher virtue (adhisīla). *Hitvā*: having abandoned. *Piyaggāhī*: one who is excessively attached to the five strings of sensual pleasure. *Attānuyoginaṃ*: to those who habitually exert themselves. *Piheti*: envies.

*Piyehi*: with dear beings or formations. *Kudācanaṃ*: even for a moment. *Mā samāgañchi*: do not associate. *Appiyehi*: with unloved beings or formations. *Kudācanaṃ*: even for a moment. *Mā samāgañchi*: do not associate. *Piyānaṃ*: of dear beings or formations. *Adassanaṃ*: not seeing due to separation. *Dukkhaṃ*: is suffering. *Appiyānaṃ*: of unloved beings or formations. *Dassanaṃ*: seeing due to proximity. *Dukkhaṃ*: is suffering.

*Tasmā*: therefore. *Kiñci*: any being or formation. *Piyaṃ*: dear. *Na kayirātha*: one should not make. *Hi*: indeed. *Piyāpāyo*: separation from the dear. *Pāpako*: is evil. *Yesaṃ*: for those. *Piyāppiyaṃ*: dear and unloved...
180:
There is none. For those persons, the bodily bonds (kāyagantha) such as covetousness (abhijjhā) and so forth do not exist.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. As for those three persons, they said, "We cannot live apart from each other," and they returned to lay life and went back to their homes.

The Story of the Three Ordained Persons ends.

## 2. The Story of a Certain Householder
(Aññatarakuṭumbikavatthu)
The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Piyato jāyatī," while residing at Jetavana Monastery, concerning a certain householder.

## Admonishing the Lay Devotee whose Son Died
When his son passed away, that householder was so overcome by grief for his son that he went to the cemetery and wept. He was unable to restrain his sorrow. In the early morning, as the Teacher surveyed the world, he saw the householder's potential (upanissaya) for the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). Returning from his alms round, he took a companion monk and went to the householder's door. Hearing of the Teacher's arrival, the householder, thinking "He must wish to converse with me," invited the Teacher in and prepared a seat in the middle of the house. After the Teacher sat down, he came and sat in a suitable place. Then the Teacher asked him, "Lay devotee, why are you in distress?" When the householder informed him of the suffering caused by separation from his son, the Teacher said, "Lay devotee, do not worry. This thing called death does not occur in only one place, nor to only one person. As far as there is the arising of existence, it occurs to all beings. Not even a single conditioned thing (saṅkhāra) is permanent. Therefore, one should reflect wisely: 'Whatever is of the nature to die, dies; whatever is of the nature to break, breaks.' One should not sorrow. Even the wise of old, when their sons died, did not sorrow, reflecting 'Whatever is of the nature to die, dies; whatever is of the nature to break, breaks,' and they practiced only the meditation on the mindfulness of death (maraṇānussati)." When asked, "Venerable Sir, who did this, and when? Please tell me," the Teacher brought forth a story of the past to clarify the matter.
181:
## Excerpt from the Uraga Jātaka
Just as a snake sheds its old skin and goes on with its body,
So when the body is useless and the deceased has passed away,
While being burned, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives.
Therefore, I do not grieve for him; he has gone to his own destination.

Lord, my son, like a snake that leaves its old skin and goes away, so he has left his own body and gone. When the lifeless body is thus of no use, and when he has passed away to another world, what benefit is there in pity and weeping?

Just as this body, being pierced and burned, does not know pleasure or pain, so it does not know the weeping of relatives. Therefore, I cannot grieve for this deceased son's body. Whatever destination (gati) there is for that son, he has gone to that destination.

## The Teaching
(212) From affection arises sorrow, from affection arises fear.
For one who is free from affection, there is no sorrow; whence could there be fear?

From affection, sorrow arises. From affection, fear arises. For one who is liberated from affection, there is no sorrow; how could there be fear?

"At what time did they do this? Please tell me, Venerable Sir," he requested. To clarify this matter, the Teacher brought forth the past.

After expanding on the Uraga Jātaka in the Pañcaka Nipāta in this way, the Teacher said, "Thus in the past, when their beloved sons died, the wise did not act as you do now, lay devotee—abandoning your work, being without food, and wandering about weeping. Instead, through the power of the meditation on mindfulness of death, they did not sorrow, they partook of food, and they attended to their work. Therefore, do not think, 'My beloved son has died.' When sorrow or fear arises, it arises only depending on affection." Having said this, he spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the householder was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of a Certain Householder ends.

## 3. The Story of Visākhā
(Visākhāvatthu)
The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Pemato jāyatī," while residing at Jetavana Monastery, concerning the lay devotee Visākhā.

## Admonishing Visākhā whose Granddaughter Died
It is said that Visākhā placed her granddaughter, a young girl named Sudattā, in her own position to manage the major and minor affairs for the Saṅgha of monks in her house. Later, that granddaughter Sudattā passed away. After having the body of the deceased Sudattā discarded and buried, Visākhā was unable to restrain her grief. Being in great distress and unhappiness, she went to the presence of the Buddha, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place.
182:
## The Teaching
(213) From affection arises sorrow, from affection arises fear.
For one who is free from affection, there is no sorrow; whence fear?

From affection (pema), sorrow arises. From affection, fear arises. For one who is completely free from affection, there is no sorrow; how could there be fear?

At that time, the Blessed One said to Visākhā, "Visākhā, why are you sitting here distressed, unhappy, with a tearful face, weeping?" Visākhā reported the matter and said, "Venerable Sir, my beloved granddaughter was one who was perfect in her duties; now I no longer see such a person."

"Visākhā, how many people are there in the city of Sāvatthī?" the Buddha asked. "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One himself has told me there are seventy million," she replied. "If all these people were like your granddaughter, would you desire them?" "Yes, Venerable Sir, I would."

"How many people die daily in Sāvatthī?" "Venerable Sir, many people die."

"If that is the case, would it not be that you would never have a time free from sorrow? You would spend your days and nights only weeping and lamenting," the Buddha said. "Venerable Sir, let it be; I understand now," she replied. Then the Blessed One said to Visākhā, "If you understand thus, do not grieve; both sorrow and fear arise only from the affection of craving (pema)," and he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people reached the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of Visākhā ends.

## 4. The Story of the Licchavī Princes
(Licchavī Vatthu)
While residing at the Gabled House Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) near the city of Vesālī, the Buddha spoke this teaching beginning with "Ratiyā jāyatī" concerning the Licchavī princes.

## A Fight Because of a Woman
On a certain festival day, those Licchavī princes, adorned with various incomparable ornaments, left the city to go to the park. When the Blessed One entered for alms and saw the Licchavī princes, he informed the monks thus: "Monks, do you see the Licchavī princes? Let those who have never seen the Tāvatiṃsa gods look upon these Licchavī princes." Having said this, he entered the city. The Licchavī princes, while going to the park, took a certain courtesan with them. Because of that woman, they were overcome by jealousy and struck one another, so that their blood flowed like a river's current.
183:
## The Teaching
(214) From delight arises sorrow, from delight arises fear.
For one who is free from delight, there is no sorrow; whence fear?

From delight (rati), sorrow arises. From delight, fear arises. For one who is completely free from delight, there is no sorrow; how could there be fear?

Then, they came carrying the Licchavī princes on litters. The Blessed One, having finished his meal, was departing from the city. When the monks saw the Licchavī princes being carried in that manner, they said to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, early this morning the Licchavī kings left the city adorned like gods, but now, because of a single woman, they have come to such ruin."

The Buddha said, "Monks, when sorrow or fear arises, it arises only by depending on delight (rati)," and he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people reached the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of the Licchavī princes ends.

## 5. The Story of the Young Man Anitthigandha
(Anitthigandha Kumāra Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Buddha spoke this teaching beginning with "Kāmato" concerning the young man named Anitthigandha.

## Seeking a Woman as Beautiful as a Golden Statue
That young man Anitthigandha was a being who had passed away from the Brahma realm and was born into a very wealthy family in the city of Sāvatthī. From the day he was born, he did not wish to go near women; if a woman picked him up, he would cry. They had to breastfeed him by holding him with a cloth ring. When Anitthigandha reached the age of maturity, his parents said, "Dear son, we shall arrange a marriage for you." He refused, saying, "I have no need for a woman."

Being repeatedly entreated, he summoned five hundred goldsmiths, gave them a thousand nikkhas of red gold, and had them cast a solid gold statue of a woman that was exceedingly beautiful and pleasing. Once again, his parents said, "Dear son, if you do not marry, the family lineage will not endure. We shall bring a maiden for you." He replied, "If that is the case, if you can bring a maiden of such a nature for me..." [showing them the golden statue].
185:
## The Teaching

(215) From lust arises grief, from lust arises fear.
For one who is free from lust, there is no grief; whence could there be fear?

From lust (kāma), meaning from sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) and sensual passions (kilesa-kāma), grief arises. From lust, fear arises. For one who is completely free from lust, there is no grief. How could there be fear?

When the youth heard the news, hearing that there was a maiden even more beautiful than the golden statue, he developed affection just by hearing of her and said, "Let her be brought quickly." While the young maiden was being brought in a carriage, due to her extreme delicacy, she developed an illness caused by the jolting of the carriage and passed away on the way. The youth kept asking, "Has she arrived? Has she arrived?" To the youth who was asking with great affection, they did not tell him immediately but waited for two or three days before telling him the news of her death. The youth, thinking, "I did not get to live together with such a woman," became dejected, and the suffering of grief overwhelmed him as if a great mountain were crushing him.

## The Youth Finds Relief

The Teacher, seeing the youth's supporting conditions (upanissaya), went to the door of that house while wandering for alms. Then the youth's parents invited the Teacher inside and respectfully served him food. At the end of the meal, the Teacher asked, "Where is the youth Anitthigandha?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, the youth has stopped eating and is staying inside his room," the Teacher said, "Call him." The youth came, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place. The Teacher asked, "Youth, has great grief arisen in you?" He replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir. Because I heard that such a woman died on the way, great grief has arisen in me. Therefore, even food does not please me, Venerable Sir." Then the Teacher asked, "Youth, do you know what your grief is based on?" He replied, "I do not know, Venerable Sir." The Teacher said, "Youth, great grief arises based on lust. Both grief and fear arise based on sensual objects and sensual passions," and he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the youth Anitthigandha was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The Story of the Youth Anitthigandha ends.

## 6. The Story of a Certain Brahmin (Aññatarabrāhmaṇa Vatthu)

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Taṇhāya jāyatī" concerning a certain Brahmin.

## The Teacher's Daily Visit to the Plowing Field

That Brahmin was a person of wrong view. One day, he went to the riverbank to clear his field. The Teacher, seeing the perfection of that Brahmin's supporting conditions (upanissaya), went to him. Even though the Brahmin saw the Teacher, he remained silent without performing any act of respect. Then the Teacher spoke to the Brahmin first, saying, "Brahmin, what are you doing?" He replied, "O Gautama, I am clearing the field." The Teacher said only that much and left. On the following day, when the Brahmin came to plow the field, the Teacher went to him and asked, "Brahmin, what are you doing?" Hearing the reply, "O Gautama, I am plowing the field," the Teacher left. On subsequent days, the Teacher went and asked in the same way, and hearing the replies, "O Gautama, I am sowing the field, I am weeding, I am guarding," the Teacher left.
186:
## The Teaching

(216) From craving arises sorrow, from craving arises fear. For one who is completely free from craving, there is no sorrow; whence would there be fear?

Taṇhāya: because of craving that arises at the six sense-doors. Soko: sorrow. Jāyati: arises. Taṇhāya: because of craving that arises at the six sense-doors. Bhayaṃ: fear or danger. Jāyati: arises. Taṇhāya: from craving. Vippamuttassa: for one who is liberated. Soko: sorrow. Natthi: does not exist. Bhayaṃ: fear or danger. Kuto atthi: from where would it exist?

Then one day, a Brahmin said to the Blessed One, "O Venerable Gotama, you have been coming here since the day I cleared my field. If my crops reach successful completion, I shall share them with you. I will not eat them myself without first giving to you. From this day forward, you are my friend."

## Assisting the Grieving Brahmin

At another time later on, the Brahmin's crops reached successful completion. That elderly Brahmin thought, "My crops have reached completion; I shall have them harvested tomorrow." Having made the necessary preparations for the harvest, a great rainstorm fell during the night and carried away all the crops, leaving the field as if it had been scraped bare. The Blessed One, however, had known from the very first day that those crops would not reach completion. Early in the morning, the Brahmin went thinking, "I shall go look at the field," and upon seeing the empty field, he was overcome with intense sorrow. He thought, "The ascetic Gotama has been coming since the day I cleared my field. I also told that ascetic Gotama, 'When these crops reach completion, I shall share them with you; I will not eat them myself without first giving to you; from this day forward, you are my friend.' This wish of mine has not reached fulfillment." Thus, he stopped eating and lay down on his couch.

Then the Teacher went to the door of his house. When the Brahmin heard of the Teacher's arrival, he said, "Bring my friend here and let him sit." The attendants did as the Brahmin said. After the Teacher was seated, he asked, "Where is the Brahmin?" When told, "He is lying in his room," the Teacher had him summoned. When the Brahmin came and sat in a suitable place, the Teacher asked, "Brahmin, what has happened?"

"O Venerable Gotama, you have been coming since the day I cleared my field. I also said that when the crops reached completion, I would share them with you. That wish of mine has failed to be fulfilled. Therefore, sorrow has arisen in me. Even food is no longer pleasing to me," he replied. Then the Teacher asked him, "Brahmin, do you know what your sorrow has arisen in dependence upon?"

When the Brahmin replied, "O Venerable Gotama, I do not know. Do you know, Venerable Sir?", the Teacher said, "Yes, Brahmin, I know. When sorrow or fear arises, it arises in dependence upon craving that occurs at the six sense-doors," and he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the Brahmin was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala).

The Story of a Certain Brahmin is finished.
187:
## The Teaching

(217) One who is endowed with virtue and insight, established in the Dhamma, a knower of truth, and who fulfills his own duties—him the people hold dear.

Sīladassanasampannaṃ: endowed with the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), and the knowledge of the Path and Fruit. Dhammaṭṭhaṃ: established in the nine supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma). Saccavedinaṃ: accustomed to speaking the truth through the knowledge of the Truths. Attano kammakubbānaṃ: one who performs and fulfills his own duties of the three trainings (sikkhā). Taṃ puggalaṃ: that person. Jano: the multitude of people. Piyaṃ: affection, reliance, and endearment. Kurute - karoti: they make/do.

## 7. The Story of the Five Hundred Boys
(Pañcasatadārakavatthu)

While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this religious teaching beginning with "Sīladassanasampannaṃ" concerning five hundred boys on the road.

## The Great Merit of Venerable Mahākassapa

One day, while the Teacher was entering the city of Rājagaha for alms, accompanied by eighty Great Elders and surrounded by five hundred monks, he saw five hundred boys carrying baskets of cakes, leaving the city to go to a park on a festival day. Those boys also paid homage to the Teacher and then went their way. Those boys did not say even to a single monk, "Please accept some cakes, Venerable Sir."

After the boys had gone, the Teacher said to the monks, "Monks, will you eat some cakes?" "Venerable Sir, where are the cakes?" they asked. "Did you not see those boys passing by carrying baskets of cakes?" he said. "Venerable Sir, boys of such nature do not give cakes to anyone," they replied. "Monks, although those boys did not invite me or you with cakes, the owner of the cakes is coming behind. It is proper to go only after eating the cakes," he said.

When the boys saw the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera coming behind, they were filled with affection and their bodies were suffused with a surge of joy. They set down the baskets of cakes, paid homage to the Venerable Mahākassapa with the five-point prostration, and lifting up the cakes together with the baskets, they said to the Elder, "Venerable Sir, please accept them."

Then the Elder said to the boys, "This Teacher of ours, the Great Buddha, is sitting at the foot of a tree having called the assembly of monks. Take your offerings and go, and share them with the assembly of monks; give them as offerings." They replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and turning back, they went together with the Venerable Mahākassapa. After offering the cakes, they stood in a suitable place watching, and at the end of the meal, they offered water.
188:
The monks criticized, saying, "These boys offer alms out of personal acquaintance; they do not invite the Buddha or the senior elders with cakes, but upon seeing Venerable Mahākassapa, they come with the baskets of cakes themselves." The Buddha, hearing the monks' words, said, "Monks, a monk like my son Mahākassapa is beloved by gods and humans. They only perform offerings of the four requisites to such a monk," and he spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, all those five hundred boys were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The Story of the Five Hundred Boys ends.

## 8. Story of a Certain Anāgāmī Elder
(Eka-anāgāmitthera-vatthu)
While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this teaching beginning with "Chanda-jāto" concerning a certain noble Anāgāmī Elder.

## The Anāgāmī Person and the Suddhāvāsa Realm
One day, the resident pupils (saddhivihārika) who took the Elder as their preceptor (upajjhāya) asked, "Venerable Sir, is there any special attainment (visesa-adhigama) that you have achieved?" The Elder thought, "Even laypeople can reach the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmī-phala). I will only speak to these monks when I reach the Fruit of Arahatship." Out of modesty, he did not say anything and, upon passing away, was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma realm. Then, the resident pupils of the Anāgāmī Elder, weeping and lamenting, went to the Buddha, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place while still crying. The Buddha asked those monks, "Monks, why are you crying?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, our preceptor has passed away." The Buddha said, "Monks, let it be so; do not worry. This death is a constant nature (dhuvadhamma)."

"Venerable Sir, that is true; we know this. However, we asked our preceptor about his special attainment. That preceptor passed away without saying anything, and for that reason, we are distressed."
189:
When they said this, the Buddha said, "Monks, do not worry. Your preceptor reached the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmī-phala). Thinking, 'Even laypeople reach this Fruit of Non-returning. I will only speak to the monks after reaching the Fruit of Arahatship,' your teacher, out of modesty, did not say anything to you and, after passing away, was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma realm. Therefore, monks, be comforted. Your preceptor has attained a mind unattached to the eleven sensual realms (kāma-bhūmi)," and he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(218) One who has desire for the Undeclared (Nibbāna), whose mind is permeated with it, and whose heart is not bound to sensual pleasures, is called "One who flows upwards" (Uddhaṃsota).

Whichever monk has a desire to act, or has reached exertion, in the Undeclared Nibbāna; if his mind is fully permeated with it; and if he has a mind not bound or attached to the eleven sensual realms; that monk is called "One who flows upwards" (Uddhaṃsota).

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, those monks were established in the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahatta-phala). The teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude of people.

The Story of a Certain Anāgāmī Elder ends.

## 9. Story of Nandiya
(Nandiya-vatthu)
While residing at Isipatana, the Buddha spoke this teaching beginning with "Cirappavāsiṃ" concerning a young man named Nandiya.

## Becoming a Spouse through Compatibility
In the city of Bārāṇasī, it is said there was a son named Nandiya born to a family endowed with faith. That young man Nandiya was a suitable son for his parents. He was endowed with faith and devotion to the Triple Gem. He was also one who served and attended to the Saṅgha. When Nandiya reached the proper age, his parents wished to bring Revatī, the daughter of his maternal uncle from the house across the street, to be his wife. However, Revatī had no faith or devotion to the Triple Gem and had no habit of giving or charity. Young Nandiya did not want Revatī. Then Nandiya's mother said to Revatī, "Dear daughter Revatī, in this house of ours, smear the sitting area for the Saṅgha with perfumes and so on, and spread the seats. Place the bowl-stands. When the monks arrive, take their bowls and have them sit; filter the drinking water with a water-filter (dhammakaraṇa), and after they have eaten, wash the bowls. If you perform these major and minor duties, you will be one who pleases my son." Revatī did exactly as Nandiya's mother said.

Then, when she told her son, "Revatī is now capable of being disciplined, my son," he consented, saying, "If that is so, it is well." They fixed a date and performed the marriage ceremony. Then, Nandiya said to Revatī, "If you can serve the Saṅgha and my parents..."
190:
“If you are able to attend to the Saṅgha of monks and my parents, you shall be allowed to live in this house; be heedful.” Revatī consented, saying, “Very well.” For a few days, she acted as if she possessed faith, and while serving and attending to her husband, she gave birth to two sons. Eventually, the young Nandiya’s parents passed away. All the wealth and authority in the house then fell to Revatī alone.

## The Appearance of the Celestial Mansion Before the Donor's Death

From the time of his parents' passing, the young Nandiya became a great lord of alms (mahādānapati) and established regular offerings to the Saṅgha of monks. He also established a regular supply of cooked food at the door of his house for the poor, travelers, and others. Later, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher and recognizing the benefits of offering a dwelling, he had a four-sided hall (catusālā) adorned with four chambers built at the Isipatana Mahāvihāra. He had couches, stools, and other furniture laid out, and upon completing the dwelling, he offered it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, pouring the ceremonial water of dedication to the Tathāgata. 

Simultaneously with the falling of the water of dedication into the Teacher’s hand, a divine mansion (vimāna) made of the seven gems appeared in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. It was twelve leagues in extent in all directions and a hundred leagues in height, and it was filled with a host of celestial nymphs. 

One day, while the Elder Mahā Moggallāna was wandering through the celestial realms, he stood near that mansion. When the sons of the gods came into his presence, he asked them, “Sons of the gods, for whom has this divine mansion, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, arisen?” Then, the sons of the gods, wishing to inform him of the owner of the mansion, said, “Venerable sir, this mansion has arisen for the householder’s son named Nandiya, who built and offered a monastery to the Teacher at Isipatana.”

## The Message from the Nymphs to the Donor

When the host of celestial nymphs saw the Elder Moggallāna, they descended from the mansion and said, “Venerable sir, we have been reborn here with the thought, ‘We shall be the attendants of the young Nandiya.’ However, not seeing the owner of the mansion, Nandiya, we have become very weary and bored.
191:
Leaving behind human prosperity to take up divine prosperity is like breaking a clay pot to take up a golden one. Venerable sir, please tell the young Nandiya to come here for the sake of reaching this heaven.” 

The Elder Mahā Moggallāna returned from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, approached the Teacher, and asked, “Venerable sir, does divine prosperity arise even for those who are still living in the human world and have performed meritorious deeds?” 

“Moggallāna, did you not see for yourself the divine prosperity that has arisen for the householder Nandiya in the celestial realm? Why do you ask me?” 

“It is so, venerable sir, it does arise,” he replied. 

Then the Teacher said to him, “Moggallāna, why do you speak thus? Just as when a son or a brother who has been away for a long time returns from his travels, someone standing at the village gate sees him and runs quickly to the house to announce, ‘So-and-so has arrived!’ Then his relatives, greatly delighted, run out quickly and welcome the long-absent one, saying, ‘Dear one, have you returned? Dear one, are you healthy and well?’ In the very same way, when a woman or a man who has performed meritorious deeds in this human world leaves this world and goes to the next, the deities welcome them, taking up the ten kinds of divine gifts, and greeting them with the words, ‘I will be first! I will be first!’” Having said this, he spoke these verses:

## The Teaching

(219) When a man who has been long absent returns safely from afar, 
His kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers rejoice at his arrival.

(220) In the same way, when one who has performed merit goes from this world to the next, 
His merits receive him, as kinsmen receive a dear one who has returned.

*Cirappavāsiṃ*: one who has been away for a long time. *Sotthiṃ*: having attained prosperity and arriving safely. *Dūrato*: from a distant place. *Puriṃsa*: a man. *Ñāti*: those of the mother’s or father’s lineage. *Mittā*: friends. *Suhajjā*: those with intimate hearts. *Āgataṃ*: having arrived. *Abhinandanti*: they greatly rejoice and delight.

*Tatheva*: for that very reason. *Katapuññampi*: a person who has performed merit. *Asmā lokā*: from this world. *Paraṃ lokaṃ*: to the next life. *Gataṃ*: when they have gone. *Puññāni*: merits. *Piyañātī*: like dear kinsmen. *Piyañātiṃ*: a beloved kinsman. *Paṭiggaṇhanti*: they welcome with joy by bestowing prosperity such as long life and beauty.

(The ten divine gifts are: divine life, beauty, happiness, retinue, and power; and the five divine sense objects: sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of Nandiya ends.
The Chapter on Affection (Piyavagga) is finished.

## 17. Kodhavagga
## 1. The Story of Princess Rohinī
(Rohinīkhattiyakaññāvatthu)
While residing at the Nigrodhārāma monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Kodhaṃ jahe," concerning the princess named Rohinī.

## Rohinī’s Skin Disease and the Donation of a Refectory
On one occasion, the Venerable Anuruddha went to the city of Kapilavatthu together with five hundred monks. When the relatives of the Venerable Anuruddha heard that the Elder had arrived, they went to the monastery to see him, except for the Elder's sister, the princess named Rohinī. The Venerable Anuruddha asked his relatives, "Where is Rohinī?" "Venerable sir, she is at home," they replied. "Why has she not come to this monastery?" he asked. "Venerable sir, a skin disease called chaviroga has broken out on her body, and she is too ashamed to come," they answered. Upon hearing this, the Venerable Anuruddha sent for her, saying, "Go and call Rohinī."

When Rohinī arrived, wearing a cloth wrap, the Elder asked, "Rohinī, why did you not come?" "Venerable sir, a skin disease has broken out on my body; therefore, I was too ashamed to come," she replied. "Is it not proper for you to perform merit?" he asked. "Venerable sir, what merit should I perform?" she inquired. "Have a refectory (āsanasāla) built," he instructed. "With what funds shall I build it, venerable sir?" she asked. "Do you not have any jewelry?" he asked. "I do, venerable sir," she replied. "How much is it worth?" "It would be worth ten thousand [pieces of money], venerable sir." "In that case, sell that jewelry and have a refectory built," he advised. "Venerable sir, who will build it for me?" she asked. The Venerable Anuruddha looked at the relatives standing nearby and said, "Let it be your responsibility." "But venerable sir, what will you do?" they asked. "I will also remain right here," he said, and then added, "In that case, bring the timber for the construction of that refectory."
193:
## The Teaching
(221) One should abandon anger; one should give up pride;
One should transcend all fetters.
Suffering does not befall one who does not cling to mind and body (nāmarūpa),
And who is without possessions.

*Kodhaṃ*: anger; *jahe*: one should abandon. *Mānaṃ*: pride; *vippajaheyya*: one should give up. *Sabbasaṃyojanaṃ*: all fetters; *atikkameyya*: one should transcend. *Nāmarūpasmiṃ*: in mind and body; *asajjamānaṃ*: not clinging. *Akiñcanaṃ*: one who is without defilements such as lust. *Taṃ puggalaṃ*: that person; *dukkhā*: sufferings; *nānupatanti*: do not follow/befall.

## Relief from Ailment through Meritorious Deeds
The relatives agreed, saying, "Very well, venerable sir," and brought the materials. While supervising the construction of the refectory, the Venerable Anuruddha told Rohinī: "Have a two-story refectory built. From the time the planks are laid on the upper floor, constantly sweep the lower floor and arrange the seats. Constantly set out jars of drinking water."

Rohinī agreed, saying, "Very well, venerable sir." She sold her jewelry and had the two-story refectory built. From the time the upper floor was planked, she performed tasks such as sweeping the lower floor. Monks resided there regularly. Then, while Rohinī was sweeping the refectory, her skin disease began to fade away. When the refectory was completed, she invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Having filled the refectory, she offered exquisite food and snacks to the community of monks headed by the Buddha.

When the Buddha had finished his meal, he asked, "Whose donation is this?" "Exalted Buddha, it is the donation of my sister, Princess Rohinī," [Anuruddha] replied. "But where is she?" the Buddha asked. "Exalted Buddha, she is at home," they replied. "Call her," the Buddha said. Rohinī did not wish to come. However, the Buddha had her called even though she was unwilling. When she arrived and sat down after paying homage, the Buddha asked, "Rohinī, why did you not come?" "Exalted Buddha, there is a skin disease on my body; therefore, I was too ashamed to come," she replied. "Do you know because of what this disease arose in you?" he asked. "I do not know, Exalted Buddha," she answered. "It arose because of your anger," the Buddha said. "Exalted Buddha, what evil did I do?" she asked. "In that case, listen," the Buddha said. Then the Buddha related this story of the past to Rohinī.

## Rohinī’s Past Evil Deed
In the past, the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī conceived a grudge against one of the king's dancing girls. Thinking, "I will cause her suffering," she had many cowhage fruits (kapikacchu) brought. She summoned the dancing girl to her presence and, in such a way that the girl would not know, placed cowhage powder in her bed and between her robes and carpets. As if playing a prank, she also scattered it on the girl's body. At that very moment, the girl's body became covered in itchy boils like burns. The girl, itching intensely, went and lay on her bed. There too, she suffered excruciating pain as if being bitten by the cowhage powder. At that time, Rohinī was that Chief Queen. The Buddha, having related this story of the past, said, "Rohinī, at that time, you committed that evil deed. Indeed, it is not proper to harbor even a small amount of anger or envy," and he spoke this verse:
194:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. Rohinī also was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry, and at that very moment, her body became golden in hue.

## The Dispute of the Four Devas over Rohinī and Sakka's Decision
When Rohinī passed away from that existence, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven at the boundary of the territories of four devas, possessing a beautiful and delightful appearance. Upon seeing the goddess Rohinī, the four devas were filled with affection and, each claiming, "She was born within my boundary," they went to Sakka, the King of Devas, and said, "Lord, a dispute has arisen among us concerning this goddess. Please judge this matter."

Sakka, too, felt affection for her as soon as he looked at her and asked, "From the time you first saw this goddess, how have your minds been affected?"

Then one deva said, "Great King, the mind that has arisen in me cannot remain still, like a great war drum on a battlefield."
The second deva said, "My mind flows swiftly like a mountain river."
The third deva said, "From the time I saw this goddess, my eyes have popped out like the eyes of a crab."
The fourth deva said, "My mind cannot remain steady, like a banner hoisted on a stupa."

Then Sakka said to the devas, "Dear friends, your minds are still of a nature that can be restrained. As for me, if I get this goddess, I shall live; if I do not, I shall die."

The devas replied, "Great King, we have no need for your death," and they departed, yielding the goddess Rohinī to Sakka. She became Sakka's beloved and dear consort. Whenever she said, "We wish to go to such-and-such a festival," Sakka was unable to refuse her words.

The Story of Princess Rohinī ends.

## 2. The Story of an Unknown Monk
(Aññatarabhikkhu Vatthu)
While residing at the Aggāḷava Shrine, the Teacher spoke this legal discourse beginning with "Yo ve uppatitaṃ," concerning an unknown monk.
195:
## The Teaching
(222) Whoever restrains rising anger like a rolling chariot,
Him I call a charioteer; others are merely rein-holders.

(Yo: whoever. Ve: indeed. Uppatitaṃ: arisen. Kodhaṃ: anger. Bhantaṃ rathaṃ vāraye iva: as if restraining a swiftly rolling chariot. Vāraye: should restrain. Taṃ: that person. Sārathiṃ: as a skilled charioteer. Ahaṃ: I, the Buddha. Brūmi: call. Itaro jano: other people, such as the charioteers of kings or sub-kings. Rasmi-ggāho: are merely rein-holders. [Meaning they are not true charioteers].)

## How the Tree Deity Restrained Her Mind
When the Teacher had permitted dwellings for the Saṅgha, and when the treasurer of Rājagaha and others were building dwellings, a monk from Āḷavī, wishing to build a dwelling for himself, saw a beautiful tree and began to cut it down. A young deity who was born in that tree, standing with her young son in her arms, pleaded, "Venerable sir, do not cut down my mansion; I will not be able to wander about homeless with my son."

That monk, thinking, "I will not find such a tree elsewhere," did not heed her words. The deity thought, "If he sees this child first, he might stop," and placed her son on a branch. The monk, unable to stop the axe he had already raised, accidentally cut off the child's arm. The deity, filled with intense anger, raised both hands, thinking, "I will strike and kill him!" but then she reflected: "This monk is virtuous. If I kill him, I will go to hell. Other deities, seeing monks cutting their trees, will follow my example and kill monks, saying, 'Such-and-such a deity killed a monk in this way.' Furthermore, this monk has a master; I will report this only to his master, the Buddha."

Having so reflected, she lowered her raised hands and, weeping, went to the Teacher, paid homage, and stood at a respectful distance. Then the Teacher asked her, "Deity, what is the matter?"

She reported the whole matter in detail, saying, "Lord, your disciple did such a thing to me. I wanted to kill him, but after reflecting on such-and-such reasons, I did not kill him and have come here instead."

Upon hearing her report, the Teacher said, "Excellent, excellent, deity! You have done well in restraining your rising anger, just as one restrains a rolling chariot," and spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the deity was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled multitude.

## The Buddha Points Out a Tree to the Deity
Even after becoming a Stream-winner (Sotāpanna), the deity remained weeping and lamenting. Then the Teacher asked her, "Deity, what is the reason?" She replied, "Lord, my mansion has been destroyed."
196:
When she asked, “What should I do now, Bhante?”, the Buddha said, “Enough, Devatā, do not worry; do not be anxious. I shall give you a mansion.” Pointing to a tree near the Gandhakuṭi in Jetavana Monastery, where a deity had passed away the previous day, he said, “The tree in that particular place is vacant; go and dwell there.” The deity went there. From that time on, even powerful deities who came were unable to displace her, saying, “This mansion was given to her by the Buddha.” With this incident as the cause, the Blessed One prescribed the Bhūtagāma training rule for the monks.

The Story of a Certain Monk is finished.

## 3. The Story of the Laywoman Uttarā
(Uttarāupāsikā Vatthu)

While staying at Veluvana Monastery, the Buddha, after finishing his meal at the house of Uttarā, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Akkodhena jine kodhaṃ,” in reference to the laywoman named Uttarā.

## The Poor Man Punna Goes to Plow

The following is the sequence of events for this verse: In the city of Rājagaha, a poor man named Punna lived by working for the merchant Sumana. His household consisted of only two people: his wife and his daughter named Uttarā. One day, a proclamation was made in Rājagaha that a seven-day festival was to be celebrated. Hearing this, the merchant Sumana called Punna, who had arrived early in the morning, and said, “Friend, our attendants wish to celebrate the festival. What about you, friend? Will you celebrate the festival or will you work for hire?” Punna replied, “Master, festivals are for those who have wealth. In my house, there is not even enough rice for tomorrow’s gruel. What use have I for a festival? If I can get the oxen, I will go to plow.” Sumana said, “If that is so, take the oxen.” Punna took the strong oxen and the plow, and said to his wife, “Dear, the city folk are celebrating the festival. Because of my poverty, I shall go to work for hire. Today, cook double the amount of rations for me and bring the food.” Having said this, he went to the field.
197:
“I shall go to work for hire because of my poverty. Cook double the rations for me today and bring the food,” he said, instructing his wife, and then went to the field.

## Offering Water and Tooth-wood to Venerable Sāriputta

Venerable Sāriputta had been in the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) for seven days. Having emerged on that day, he looked to see, “Whom should I favor today?” Seeing Punna appearing within the net of his knowledge, he considered, “Does this man have faith? Will he be able to favor me?” Knowing that Punna had faith and the ability to favor him, and that because of that favor he would obtain great wealth, the Elder took his bowl and robes and went to Punna’s plowing place. He stood looking at a bush by the edge of a well. As soon as Punna saw the Elder Sāriputta, he stopped plowing and paid homage to the Elder with the five-point prostration. Thinking, “He must have need of tooth-wood,” he prepared a suitable piece of tooth-wood and offered it. Then the Elder took out his bowl and water filter and gave them to him. Punna, thinking, “He must have need of drinking water,” took them, filtered the water, and offered it.

Venerable Sāriputta thought, “This man lives at the back of others' houses. If I go to his house door, his wife will not be able to see me. I will stay right here until she comes onto the road carrying his food.”

## Punna’s Wife Offers Alms

The Elder spent a short time there, and knowing that the poor woman had set out on the road, he headed toward the city. The poor woman, seeing the Elder in the middle of the road, thought: “Sometimes I have a gift to give but I do not see the Noble One; sometimes I see the Noble One but I have no gift. Today, I see the Noble One and I also have this gift. Will he favor me?” Having thought this, she set down the food container, paid homage to the Elder with the five-point prostration, and said, “Bhante, without considering whether this food is coarse or fine, please favor your poor servant.” The Elder held out his bowl. While the woman was offering the food from the container with one hand, the Elder covered the bowl with his hand when half the food had been given, saying, “Enough.” The woman said, “Bhante, this is one portion for one person; it cannot be divided into two. Please do not favor your servant for this present world, but favor me for the world beyond. I wish to give it all without remainder.” After saying this, she poured all the food into the Elder Sāriputta’s bowl and made a wish, saying, “May I be a sharer of the Dhamma that you have seen.” Venerable Sāriputta said, “May it be so,” and while still standing, he gave the blessing (anumodanā). Then he sat down in a comfortable place where water was available and finished his meal. The woman returned home, searched for more rice, and cooked again. Punna, having plowed about half a karīsa of land and being unable to endure his hunger, released the oxen, went under the shade of a tree, and sat watching the road.
198:
## How Maung Punna’s Wife Explained to Increase Merit

The poor woman returned home, searched for rice, and cooked the meal again. Punna, having plowed an area of about eight karīsas, was unable to endure his hunger. He released the oxen, went into the shade of a tree, and sat looking out toward the road. At that time, Punna’s wife, carrying the meal, saw Punna and thought: “This man is sitting there looking at the road, oppressed by hunger. If he rebukes me, saying ‘You are very late,’ and strikes me with the goad-stick, the merit I have performed will be in vain. I will tell him beforehand.” Thinking thus, she said: “Lord, please gladden your heart for this one day. Do not make the merit I have performed fruitless. While I was bringing your meal early this morning, I saw the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, on the way. I gave your meal to him, went back, cooked another meal, and have now come. Lord, please gladden your heart.”

The poor man, Punna, asked, “Sister, what did you say?” and after hearing the matter again, he rejoiced in her words with a faithful heart, saying: “Sister, it is very good that you gave my meal to the Noble One. I, too, gave him a tooth-stick and water for washing his face early this morning.” Since he had received his meal late, his body was exhausted, so he placed his head in his wife’s lap and fell asleep.

## From Mud to Gold

Then, the entire area that Maung Punna had plowed that morning, starting from the very dust, turned into red gold and stood shining like a heap of kaṇikāra flowers. When Maung Punna woke up and looked, he said to his wife: “Sister, that whole plowed area appears to me as gold. Is it because I received my meal so late that my eyes are spinning?” The wife replied, “Lord, it appears the same to me as well.” Then Punna stood up, went to the plowed area, took a lump, and struck it against the end of the plowshare. Realizing it was indeed gold, he thought: “Oh, how wonderful! The offering given to the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, has shown its fruit this very day. It is not possible to hide and use such a vast amount of wealth.” He filled the bowl his wife had brought with gold and went to the royal palace. Having received permission from the King, he entered and paid homage. When the King asked, “Friends, what is the matter?” he reported: “Your Majesty, today the entire area I plowed has turned into gold. It is proper to have this gold brought in.”

When asked, “Who are you?” he replied, “I am the one named Punna, Your Majesty.” When asked again, “What merit did you perform today?” he replied, “Your Majesty, early this morning I offered a tooth-stick and water for washing the face to the Venerable Sāriputta. My wife also offered the meal she was bringing for me to the Venerable Sāriputta.” Upon hearing this, the King said, “Friends, it is said that the gift given to the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, has shown its fruit this very day.” He then asked, “Friend Punna, what shall I do?” Punna replied, “Please send many thousands of carts...”
199:
"Please send for and bring the gold, Your Majesty," he requested. Thus, the King dispatched the carts.

## Maung Punna Receiving the Title of Treasurer

When the King's men took the gold, saying, "This is the King's property," every bit of gold they took turned into mere lumps of earth. The men returned and reported this to the King. When asked, "What did you say when you took it?" they replied, "We said it was Your Majesty's property." The King said, "Friends, where would I get such wealth?" and then commanded, "Go and take it, saying, 'This is Maung Punna's property.'" The men did as the King commanded. Every bit of property they took remained as gold. Having collected all the gold, they made a heap in the palace courtyard. The heap was eighty cubits high. The King summoned the citizens and asked, "Is there anyone in this royal city who possesses this much gold?" When they replied, "No, Your Majesty," he asked again, "What rank should be bestowed upon this man to honor him?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it is fitting to honor him with the Treasurer's parasol." Based on his great wealth, the King conferred upon Punna the title of "Bahudhana Setthi" (Treasurer of Great Wealth), along with vast possessions and the Treasurer's parasol, thus elevating him to the rank of Treasurer.

## Attaining the Stage of Stream-Entry

Then, Treasurer Maung Punna said to the King, "Your Majesty, we have lived in another's house for so long. Please grant us a place to reside." The King pointed out the site of a former treasurer's house, saying, "If that is so, look there; that thicket is visible. Clear that thicket and build your house." Within just two or three days of clearing the site, Punna found many pots of gold striking against one another. He reported this to the King, saying, "Your Majesty, please take possession of these pots of gold." The King replied, "You alone should take the pots of gold obtained through your own merit." Having acquired great wealth, he built a house. He celebrated the house-warming ceremony and the ceremony of receiving the parasol simultaneously, and for seven days, he offered alms to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Then, the Blessed One gave a discourse of appreciation to Treasurer Punna, preaching the Dhamma in progressive order. At the conclusion of the discourse, three people—Treasurer Punna, his wife, and his daughter Uttara—attained the stage of Stream-entry (Sotāpanna).

## Daughter Uttara's Distress in a House of Wrong View

Later, the Great Treasurer of Rājagaha desired to have Punna's daughter, Uttara, for his son and made a formal request. Punna replied, "I cannot give her." The Rajagaha Treasurer said, "Do not do this. It was only by depending on us for so long that you obtained this wealth and prosperity. I want you to give your daughter Uttara to my son." Punna replied, "That Treasurer's son holds wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi). My daughter cannot live without the Triple Gem."
200:
"Therefore, I cannot give my daughter Uttarā to the son of that treasurer," he said. Then, many noblemen, including various treasurers, pleaded with the treasurer Punna, saying, "Do not break your friendship with the great treasurer of Rājagaha. Please give your daughter Uttarā to that treasurer's son."

Punna the treasurer, having accepted the words of the noblemen and treasurers, gave his daughter away on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha. From the time Uttarā arrived at her husband's house, she was unable to attend to monks or nuns, to give alms, or to listen to the Dhamma. When two and a half months had passed in this way, she asked an attendant nearby, "How many days are left of the Vassa?" When the attendant replied, "My lady, there are fifteen days left," Uttarā sent a message to her father: "Why have you placed me, your daughter, in such a prison? It would be better for me to be branded with hot iron and called someone else's slave. It is not right to give me to such a family of wrong-view (micchādiṭṭhi). Since I arrived here, I have not been able to perform even a single meritorious deed, such as seeing the monks."

## Uttarā Asks Permission to Perform Meritorious Deeds

Then, Uttarā's father, Punna the treasurer, feeling distressed and saying, "Alas, my daughter is in misery," sent fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas. He sent them with the instruction: "In this city of Rājagaha, there is a courtesan named Sirimā who charges a thousand coins a day. Use these coins to hire Sirimā to attend to your husband, and then you yourself perform meritorious deeds." Uttarā summoned Sirimā and said, "Friend, take these coins and attend to your friend with great care for these fifteen days." Sirimā agreed, saying, "Very well." Uttarā took Sirimā to her husband. When the husband saw Sirimā, he asked, "What is this about?" Uttarā requested, "My lord, let my friend Sirimā attend to you for fifteen days. During these fifteen days, I wish to give alms and listen to the Dhamma." Seeing the exceptionally beautiful Sirimā, the treasurer's son felt lustful affection and agreed, saying, "Very well."

Uttarā then invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, saying, "Venerable Sir, for these fifteen days, please do not go elsewhere but accept alms-food only at this house." Having obtained the Buddha's consent, she thought with a joyful heart, "From today until the Great Pavāraṇā day on the full moon of Assayuja, I shall have the opportunity to attend to the All-Enlightened One and listen to the Dhamma." She went about the kitchen managing all the tasks, saying, "Boil the gruel like this; fry the cakes like this." Then, Uttarā's husband, thinking, "Tomorrow will be the Pavāraṇā day of the full moon," stood at the window facing the kitchen. Looking out, he wondered, "What is that foolish woman Uttarā doing as she goes about?" He saw Uttarā, the daughter of Punna the treasurer, covered in sweat, smeared with ashes, and stained with charcoal and soot, busily managing the work. He thought, "Oh, how very foolish she is!"
201:
“In such a place as this, I do not enjoy this wealth and luxury; I shall serve the shaven-headed monks,” she said, and with a joyful heart, she went about her duties. He [the husband] laughed and walked away.

## Sirimā’s Anger and Uttarā’s Loving-kindness

When Uttarā’s husband walked away, Sirimā, who was staying with him, looked through that very window, wondering, “Why is this treasurer’s son laughing?” Seeing Uttarā, she thought, “He is laughing while looking at Uttarā; surely he must be intimate with her.”

Harboring a grudge against Uttarā, Sirimā thought, “I will cause her suffering.” She descended from the palace, entered the kitchen, and taking a ladle of boiling ghee from where cakes were being fried, she headed straight toward Uttarā. Seeing Sirimā approaching, Uttarā thought, “My friend has been of great service to me. The universe (Cakkavāḷa) is too narrow, the Brahma world (Brahma-loka) is too low; the virtue of my friend is indeed great. Because of her, I have gained the opportunity to give alms and to hear the Dhamma. If there is any anger in me toward this Sirimā, let this ghee burn me. If there is none, let it not burn me.” Thus, she suffused Sirimā with loving-kindness (mettā). The boiling ghee poured onto Uttarā’s head became like cold water.

## The Beating of Sirimā

Then, thinking, “This ghee must have cooled down,” Sirimā filled the ladle again and approached. Seeing this, Uttarā’s maidservants cried out, “You ill-bred, wicked woman! Get away! It is not fit for you to pour boiling ghee on our mistress!” They rose from here and there, struck her with hands and feet, and threw her to the ground. Although Uttarā tried to stop them, she could not. Then Uttarā stood over Sirimā, restrained all the maids, and admonished Sirimā, saying, “Why did you commit such a grave deed?” She bathed her with warm water and massaged her with oil cooked a hundred times (satapāka-tela). At that moment, Sirimā realized her status as an outsider and thought, “I have committed a grave deed by pouring boiling ghee on this Uttarā just because the treasurer’s son smiled. Uttarā did not command her maids to ‘Seize her!’ Even when I was being mistreated, she restrained all the maids and did only what was helpful to me. If I do not ask for her forgiveness, my head might split into seven pieces.” She prostrated at Uttarā’s feet and said, “Lady, please forgive me.”

## The Requirement to Ask Forgiveness from the Buddha

“I am a daughter who has a father. If my father forgives, I shall also forgive,” Uttarā replied. Sirimā said, “Lady, let it be so. I will also ask for forgiveness from your father, the Treasurer Puṇṇa.” Uttarā said, “Treasurer Puṇṇa is my father who caused my birth in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). If my father who causes the end of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) forgives, then I shall forgive.” Sirimā asked, “Who is your father who causes the end of the cycle?”

## The Teaching

(223) Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer the wicked with goodness.
Conquer the stingy with giving; conquer the liar with truth.

*Kodhaṃ*: an angry person; *akkodhena*: with non-anger; *jine*: one can conquer. *Asādhuṃ*: a bad person; *sādhunā*: with goodness; *jine*: one can conquer. *Kadariyaṃ*: a person who is very stingy and does not wish to give; *dānena*: with giving; *jine*: one can conquer. *Alikavādinaṃ*: a person who speaks falsehoods; *saccena*: by speaking the truth; *jine*: one should conquer.

“He is the All-Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) who knows the Four Noble Truths,” Uttarā replied. Sirimā said, “I am not acquainted with that Buddha.” Uttarā said, “I will arrange it. Tomorrow, the Blessed One will come to this house with the community of monks (Bhikkhu-saṅgha). You should bring whatever offerings you can obtain, come to this house, and ask for the Buddha's forgiveness.”

Sirimā agreed, saying, “Very well, lady.” She rose, went to her home, and commanded her five hundred attendant women to prepare various kinds of hard food and curries. The next morning, she took those offerings to Uttarā’s house but did not dare to place them in the bowls of the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Uttarā herself took all the offerings and made the arrangements. After the meal was finished, Sirimā, along with her attendants, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha.

## Uttarā’s Loving-kindness

Then the Buddha asked Sirimā, “What is your situation?” She replied, “Venerable Sir, yesterday I committed such an act. Then my friend Uttarā restrained her maids who were beating and harassing me, and she only did me favors. Knowing her virtue, I asked for her forgiveness. Then she told me she would forgive me only if the Exalted One forgives.” The Buddha asked, “Is it so, Uttarā?” “Yes, Venerable Sir, my friend Sirimā poured boiling ghee on my head.” “What did you think then?” “Venerable Sir, I thought: ‘The universe is too narrow, the Brahma world is too low; the virtue of my friend Sirimā is indeed great. Because of her, I have gained the opportunity to give alms and to hear the Dhamma.’

‘If there is any anger in me toward this Sirimā, let this ghee burn me. If there is none, let it not burn me.’ Having thought thus, I suffused Sirimā with loving-kindness, Venerable Sir.” The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent, Uttarā! It is proper to conquer anger in this way. One should conquer an angry person with non-anger. One should conquer a person who reviles and abuses with non-reviling and non-abusing. One should conquer a stingy person with one's own gifts. One should conquer a liar with truthful speech that is real and unerring.” Then he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, Sirimā, along with her five hundred women, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The Story of the Laywoman Uttarā ends.

## 4. Mahāmoggallānattherapañha Vatthu
(The Story of the Questions of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna)

While the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery, he spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with the words "Saccaṃ bhaṇe," regarding a question asked by the Elder Moggallāna.

## Reaching the Deva World by Merely Speaking the Truth

One day, Elder Mahāmoggallāna traveled to the deva world. Standing at the door of a mansion belonging to a powerful deity, he spoke to the deity who had approached, paid homage, and stood there: "Deity, your celestial splendor and prosperity are great. What good deed did you perform to attain this celestial bliss?" The deity replied, "Venerable Sir, please do not ask me," and requested to be excused. It is said that the deity spoke thus because they were ashamed of their own small deed.

When Elder Mahāmoggallāna insisted, "You must tell me," the deity said, "Venerable Sir, I have never given alms, I have never made offerings, and I have never heard the Dhamma. I only strictly guarded the truth (spoke only the truth)."

## A Wise Wife of a Wicked Husband Reaching the Deva World

Elder Mahāmoggallāna then went to the doors of other mansions and questioned other goddesses. Those goddesses also tried to hide their deeds in the same manner, but being unable to resist the Elder, one goddess first explained: "Venerable Sir, among the meritorious deeds such as giving alms, there is no merit that I have performed. However, during the time of the appearance of Kassapa Buddha, I was a servant of others. My husband was extremely cruel and harsh. He would hit my head and break it with whatever piece of wood or stick he happened to grab. When anger arose in me, I admonished and restrained myself, saying, 'This man is your master; he has the power to brand you with a hot iron or to cut off your nose and other parts. Do not be angry.' Thus, I never gave way to anger. Because of that lack of anger, I have attained this celestial prosperity."

## Reaching the Deva World through Small Acts of Merit

Another goddess explained: "Venerable Sir, while I was guarding a sugarcane field, I gave a stick of sugarcane to a monk." Another goddess said, "I once gave a single wood-apple (timbaru)." Another said, "I once gave a single cucumber (eḷāluka)." Another said, "I once gave a single phārusa fruit." Another said, "I gave a handful of roots." Another said, "I gave a handful of neem leaves." In this manner, they reported the small gifts they had given and said, "For this reason, we have attained this celestial prosperity."

Elder Mahāmoggallāna, having heard the meritorious deeds performed by those goddesses, approached the Buddha and asked: "Exalted Buddha, is it possible to attain celestial prosperity merely by speaking the truth, or
204:
## The Teaching

(224) Speak the truth; do not yield to anger;
Give, even if it is but a little, when asked.
By these three means,
One may go to the presence of the gods.

*Saccaṃ*: the truth. *Bhaṇe*: one should speak. *Na kujjheyya*: one should not get angry at others. *Yācito*: when asked. *Appampi*: even a little. *Dajjā (dadeyya)*: one should give. *Etehi tīhi ṭhānehi*: by these three causes. *Devānaṃ*: of the gods. *Santike*: to the presence. *Gacche*: one should go.

"...merely by quenching anger, or merely by giving very small things such as a wood-apple?" Thus he asked the Buddha. "Dear son Moggallāna, why do you ask me? Have the deities not already told you this matter?" When the Buddha spoke thus, Moggallāna replied, "Exalted Buddha, that is true. I believe that celestial prosperity should indeed be attained by such a small amount of merit."

Then the Buddha said to Elder Moggallāna, "Dear son Moggallāna, indeed, by merely speaking the truth, by merely abandoning anger, and by giving even a small gift, one can reach the deva world," and he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and other fruits.

The Story of the Questions of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna ends.

## 5. Buddhapitubrāhmaṇa Vatthu
(The Story of the Brahmin who was the Buddha's Father)

While the Buddha was staying in the Añjana Grove near the city of Sāketa, he spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with the words "Ahiṃsakā ye," regarding a question asked by the monks.

## The Buddha Meeting His Former Mother and Father

When the Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks, entered the city of Sāketa for alms, an elderly Brahmin living in Sāketa was leaving the city. Seeing the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) inside the city gate, he fell at the Buddha's feet, firmly grasped his ankles, and said, "Son, is it not true that parents should be looked after by their children in their old age? Why have you not shown yourself to us, your father and mother, for so long? I have seen you now; come so that your mother may see you too." He then took the Buddha to his house.

There, the Buddha sat on the prepared seat together with the community of monks. The Brahmin's wife also came, fell at the Buddha's feet, and said, "Son, where have you been for so long? Should not parents be attended to in their old age?" She then told the children, "Come, pay homage to your elder brother," and made them pay homage.

Both of them, with joyful hearts, served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with alms-food and said, "Venerable Son, please take alms regularly at this house." When the Buddha replied, "Buddhas do not take alms regularly at only one place," they said, "In that case, Bhante, please send those who come to invite you to us."

Even in a person not seen before, one may certainly place trust.
Through previous association, or by present benefit;
Thus is that love born, like a lotus in the water.

*Pubbe*, in a past life. *Sannivāsena vā*, through having lived together. *Paccuppannahitena vā*, or through performing great benefits in the present. *Evaṃ*, for these two reasons. *Taṃ pemaṃ*, that love. *Jāyate*, is born. *Kimiva*, like what? *Udake*, in water. *Uppalaṃ vā*, a blue lotus. *Padumaṃ vā*, or a red lotus. *Jāyate yathā*, just as it is born due to the two causes of water and mud.

“If that is so, O Blessed One—please send those who come to invite the Buddha for a meal to us.” From that day on, the Buddha sent those who came to invite him, saying, “Go and tell the old Brahmin.”

They went and said, “We invite the Buddha for a meritorious deed tomorrow.” The next morning, the Brahmin took bowls of rice and curry from his house and went to where the Buddha was staying. If there was no invitation elsewhere, the Buddha performed the meal-rite only at the Brahmin’s house. Both of them, constantly offering their gifts to the Buddha and listening to the Dhamma, attained the fruit of Anāgāmi.

## Relating the Past Story

The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, the Brahmin knows that King Suddhodana is the Buddha’s father and Queen Mahāmāyā is his mother. Knowing this, he and the Brahmin lady still call the Buddha ‘our son.’ The Buddha also consents to what they say. What is the reason?” Hearing their talk, the Buddha said, “Bhikkhus, both of them are calling their own son ‘son,’” and he brought forth the past story.

“Bhikkhus, in the past, this Brahmin was my father for five hundred consecutive births, my junior uncle for five hundred births, and my senior uncle for five hundred births. That Brahmin lady was also my mother for five hundred consecutive births, my junior aunt for five hundred births, and my senior aunt for five hundred births. Thus, I grew up in the hands of the Brahmin for fifteen hundred births, and in the hands of the Brahmin lady for fifteen hundred births. Thus, showing that he was their son for three thousand births, he spoke these verses:

## Preaching the Jarā Sutta at the Funeral of the Former Mother and Father

The Buddha lived depending on that family for three months. Both of them realized the fruit of Arahatship and attained Parinibbāna. Then, after performing great honors for those who had attained Parinibbāna, they were both placed in a single gabled palanquin and carried away. The Buddha, surrounded by five hundred monks, went to the cemetery together with those who were carrying them. A great crowd came out to follow, saying, “They are the mother and father of the Buddhas.”
