(225) The sages who are harmless, and always restrained in body;
They go to the deathless state, where having gone, they do not sorrow.

*Ahiṃsakāye*, those who have a non-harming body. *Ye munayo*, those Asekha-munis. *Niccaṃ*, always. *Kāyena*, through the door of the body. *Saṃvutā*, they guard themselves securely. *Te*, those Asekha-munis. *Yattha ṭhāne*, to which place of Nibbāna. *Gantvā*, having gone. *Na socare*, they do not sorrow or suffer. *Accutaṃ*, without shifting. *Taṃ ṭhānaṃ*, to that place of Nibbāna. *Yanti*, they reach.

The Buddha entered a rest house near the cemetery and stayed there. People paid homage to the Buddha, stood in a suitable place, and made polite conversation with him, saying, “Venerable Sir, do not think or worry that ‘My mother and father have passed away.’” The Buddha did not reject them by saying, “Do not speak like this,” but observing the inclination (*āsaya*) of the assembly, he wished to preach the Dhamma suitable for that moment:

Short indeed is this life; one dies within a hundred years.
Even if one lives beyond that, one still dies of old age.

*Idaṃ jีvitaṃ*, this life. *Appaṃ vata*, is indeed short. *Vassasatāpi*, even from a hundred years. *Oraṃ*, within. *Mīyati*, one dies. *Yo*, whoever. *Aticca*, having surpassed. *Cepi jīvati*, if they should live. *Atha*, even then. *So*, that person. *Jarasāpi*, by the ripening and withering of old age. *Mīyati*, one dies.

He preached this Jarā Sutta from the Aṭṭhakavagga of the Sutta Nipāta. At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. The monks, not knowing that the Brahmin and his wife had attained Parinibbāna, asked, “Venerable Sir, what is their future destination?”

The Buddha said, “Bhikkhus, for such Asekha-munis, there is no such thing as a future destination. Such persons reach only the great Nibbāna, which is without shifting and without death,” and he spoke this verse:

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Sotāpatti and so forth.

## 6. The Story of the Slave Girl named Puṇṇā of the Treasurer of Rājagaha
(Puṇṇadāsī-vatthu)

The Buddha preached this Dhamma teaching starting with “Sadā jāgaramānānaṃ” while staying at Gijjhakūṭa Hill, concerning a slave girl named Puṇṇā of the Great Treasurer of Rājagaha.

## The Slave Girl Puṇṇā Offering Broken-Rice Cakes

One day, that slave girl named Puṇṇā was given a large amount of paddy to pound. That slave girl, even at night, lighting a lamp...
207:
Because she had to pound rice, she stood in the breeze outside with her body soaked in sweat to relieve her fatigue. At that time, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, the Mallian, was the assigner of lodgings for the monks. Having listened to the Dhamma, he went ahead of the monks who were returning to their respective dwellings, making his fingers glow like torches to show the way, thus creating light for the monks. When the servant girl named Puṇṇā saw all those monks wandering about by that light, she thought, "I am oppressed by my own suffering and cannot sleep even at this hour; but for what reason are the venerable ones not sleeping?" Then, thinking, "Surely some monk must be unwell, or perhaps there is danger from snakes," she made a mental note. Early in the morning, she took some rice bran, moistened it with water, shaped it into a cake in her palm, and baked it over glowing coals. Placing it in the fold of her garment, she set out toward the landing place with her water pot, intending to eat it on the way to the river.

The Blessed One also set out on that same path to enter the village for alms. When Puṇṇā saw the Blessed One, she thought, "On other days when I saw the Blessed One, I had no gift to offer; when I had a gift, I did not see the Blessed One. Now, I have a gift and the Blessed One is present before me. If he would accept it without considering whether it is coarse or fine, I would like to offer this cake." Having thought thus, she set her water pot aside, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept this coarse gift and show me favor."

The Blessed One looked at the Venerable Ānanda, who then brought forward the bowl offered by the Four Great Kings, and the Buddha accepted the cake. Puṇṇā, having placed the cake in the Blessed One's bowl, paid homage with the five-point prostration and said, "Venerable Sir, may the Dhamma that you have realized be fulfilled in me as well." The Blessed One, remaining standing, gave the blessing, "May it be so as you have wished."

## The Buddha Partaking of the Meal in the Presence of the Donor

The servant girl named Puṇṇā then thought, "Although the Blessed One has shown me favor by accepting the cake, he will surely not eat it. He will likely give it to a crow or a dog further along, and then go to the house of a king or a prince to partake of fine food." The Blessed One, reflecting on what Puṇṇā was thinking and knowing the movement of her mind, looked at the Venerable Ānanda and signaled his intention to sit down. The Venerable Ānanda spread out a robe. The Blessed One sat down right there outside the city and partook of the meal. Deities from throughout the entire world-system squeezed out divine essence suitable for gods and humans, like honey from a honeycomb, and infused it into that rice-bran cake.

(Atula-upāsaka-vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Porāṇametaṃ" concerning the lay disciple named Atula.

## Blaming because of not hearing the Dhamma as desired
This lay disciple was a resident of Sāvatthī and had a following of five hundred lay disciples. One day, taking those lay disciples with him, he went to the monastery to hear the Dhamma. Desiring to hear the Dhamma from the Venerable Revata, he paid homage to him and sat down. However, that Venerable Revata delighted in seclusion and lived alone like a lion; therefore, he did not say anything to the disciple Atula. The lay disciple Atula, becoming angry thinking, "This elder says nothing at all," stood up and went to the Venerable Sāriputta and stood at one side. When the Venerable Sāriputta asked, "For what reason have you come?", he replied, "Venerable Sir, I approached the Venerable Revata with these lay disciples to hear the Dhamma. That elder said nothing to me. Therefore, I became angry with him and have come here. Please preach the Dhamma to us."

Then the elder said, "In that case, lay disciples, sit down," and he preached the Abhidhamma in great detail. The lay disciple Atula thought, "The Dhamma is indeed very subtle. The elder has preached only the Abhidhamma in great detail. What use is this Abhidhamma to us?" Becoming angry, he took his followers and went to the Venerable Ānanda.

When the Venerable Ānanda asked, "What is the matter, lay disciples?", they replied, "Venerable Sir, we approached the Venerable Revata to hear the Dhamma. Not receiving even a single word of conversation from him, we became angry and went to the Venerable Sāriputta. He also preached to us only the very subtle and extensive Abhidhamma. Thinking, 'What use is this great Abhidhamma to us?', we became angry with him too and have come here. Venerable Sir, please preach the Dhamma to us."

(227) This is an ancient thing, O Atula; it is not only of today. They blame him who sits silent, they blame him who speaks much, they also blame him who speaks in moderation. There is no one in the world who is not blamed.
(228) There never was, nor will there be, nor is there now, a person who is wholly blamed or wholly praised.
(229) But he whom the wise praise, after observing him day after day, as being of flawless conduct, sagacious, and endowed with wisdom and virtue—
(230) Who is worthy to blame him, who is like a coin of refined gold? Even the gods praise him; by Brahmā, too, is he praised.
Atula, the lay follower named Atula. Etam, this blame and praise. Porāṇam, has existed since ancient times. Etam, this blame and praise. Ajjatanāmiva, is not as if it just happened today. Na hoti, it is not so. Tuṇhīmāsīnampi, even one who usually remains silent. Nindanti, they blame. Bahubhāṇinampi, even one who usually speaks much. Nindanti, they blame. Mitabhāṇimpi, even one who speaks in moderation. Nindanti, they blame. Loke, in the world. Anindito, one who is not blamed, or one who is free from blame. Natthi, does not exist.
Ekantaṃ, exclusively. Nindito, blamed. Posovā, a man. Ekantaṃ, exclusively. Pasaṃsito, praised. Posovā, a man. Na ca ahu, has never existed in the past. Na ca bhavissati, nor will exist in the future. Etarahi ca, and even now in the present. Na vijjati, does not exist.
Acchiddavuttiṃ, one whose conduct and training are unbroken, or one whose livelihood is flawless. Medhāviṃ, one who is wise with sharp, essence-grasping wisdom. Paññāsīlasamāhitaṃ, one who is endowed with mundane and supramundane wisdom and the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). Yaṃ bhikkhuṃ, which monk. Viññū, the wise. Suve suve, day after day. Anuvicca, knowing who should be praised and who should be blamed. Pasaṃsanti, they praise.
Taṃ bhikkhuṃ, that monk. Jambonadassa, of Jambu-river gold. Nikkhaṃ iva, like a nikkha coin. Ko, who. Nindituṃ, to blame. Arahati, is worthy? Naṃ bhikkhuṃ, that monk. Devāpi, even the devas. Pasaṃsanti, they praise. So bhikkhu, that monk. Brahmunāpi, even by the multitude of Great Brahmas of the ten thousand world systems. Pasaṃsito, is praised.
"We have come to this place out of anger, Bhante; please preach the Dhamma to us," they said. "If so, sit and listen," the Teacher said, and then the Elder Ānanda preached a brief Dhamma discourse, making it very easy for those lay followers to understand.
## There is No One Wholly Blamed or Wholly Praised
Those lay followers became angry with the Elder Ānanda as well, and went to the presence of the Buddha. Having paid homage, they sat in a suitable place. Then the Buddha asked those lay followers, "Lay followers, for what reason have you come?" "Bhante, we have come to listen to the Dhamma," they replied. When they said this, the Buddha asked again, "But have you heard the Dhamma?" "Bhante, first we approached the Elder Revata; that Elder Revata did not say a single word to us. Being angry with that Elder Revata, we approached the Elder Sāriputta; that Elder Sāriputta preached a great deal of Abhidhamma to us. Because we could not keep that Abhidhamma in mind, we became angry and approached the Elder Ānanda."
"The Elder Ānanda preached only a very small amount of Dhamma to us, Bhante. Being angry with that Elder Ānanda as well, we have come to this place," they said. When the Buddha heard the words of the lay follower Atula, He said, "Lay follower Atula, this blame has been a common practice since ancient times. It is natural to blame those who remain silent, those who speak much, and those who speak little. There is no one who is only blamed, nor...
211:
...is there anyone who is only praised. Even great kings are blamed by some and praised by others. Even the great earth, the moon, and the sun are blamed by some and praised by others. Even the Fully Enlightened One, who preaches the Dhamma while sitting in the midst of the fourfold assembly, is blamed by some and praised by others. The blame or praise of the foolish is of no account. Only the blame of a wise person who can understand quickly is truly blame, and their praise is truly praise," and He spoke these verses.
(A nikkha is defined as: 4 grains = 1 chin-yway; 2 chin-yway = 1 māsaka; 5 māsaka = 2 akkha (10 yway); 8 akkha = 1 dhāraṇa (40 yway); 5 dhāraṇa = 1 suvaṇṇa (200 yway); 5 suvaṇṇa = 1 nikkha (1000 yway).)
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the five hundred lay followers were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry.
The Story of Atula the Lay Follower ends.
## 8. The Story of the Group of Six Monks
(Chabbaggiya Vatthu)
The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching starting with "Kāyappakopaṃ..." while residing at Veḷuvana Monastery, concerning the Group of Six monks.
212:
## The Teaching

(231) One should guard against bodily agitation; one should be restrained in body. Forsaking bodily misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the body.

(232) One should guard against verbal agitation; one should be restrained in speech. Forsaking verbal misconduct, one should practice good conduct with speech.

(233) One should guard against mental agitation; one should be restrained in mind. Forsaking mental misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the mind.

(234) The wise are restrained in body, and also restrained in speech. The wise are restrained in mind; they are indeed perfectly restrained.

Kāyappakopaṃ: bodily misconduct. Rakkheyya: one should guard against. Kāyena: through the bodily door. Saṃvuto: restrained. Siyā: should be. Kāyaduccaritaṃ: bodily misconduct. Hitvā: having abandoned. Kāyena: through the bodily door. Sucaritaṃ: good conduct. Care: one should practice.

Vacīpakopaṃ: verbal misconduct. Rakkheyya: one should guard against. Vācāya: through the verbal door. Saṃvuto: restrained. Siyā: should be. Vacīduccaritaṃ: verbal misconduct. Hitvā: having abandoned. Vācāya: through the verbal door. Sucaritaṃ: good conduct. Care: one should practice.

Manopakopaṃ: mental misconduct. Rakkheyya: one should guard against. Manasā: through the mental door. Saṃvuto: restrained. Siyā: should be. Manoduccaritaṃ: mental misconduct. Hitvā: having abandoned. Manasā: through the mental door. Sucaritaṃ: good conduct. Care: one should practice.

Dhīrā: the wise. Kāyena: through the bodily door. Saṃvuta: are securely restrained. Atho: furthermore. Vācāya: through the verbal door. Saṃvuta: are securely restrained. Manasā: through the mental door. Saṃvuta: are securely restrained. Te dhīrā: those wise ones. Ve - ekantena: indeed/certainly. Suparisaṃvutā: are those who are well and thoroughly restrained.

## The Monks Wearing Wooden Sandals

One day, while the Blessed One was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, He heard the sound "khaṭa-khaṭa" made by the Chabbaggiya monks who were walking to and fro on a stone slab wearing wooden sandals and holding staffs with both hands. The Buddha asked, "Dear Ānanda, what is that sound?" Ānanda replied, "Lord, it is the 'khaṭa-khaṭa' sound made by the Chabbaggiya monks walking to and fro wearing sandals." Based on this, the Buddha promulgated a training rule (sikkhāpada) and said, "A monk should guard his body and so forth." Desiring to preach the Dhamma, He spoke these verses.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of the Chabbaggiya monks ends.
The explanation of the Chapter on Anger (Kodha Vagga) is finished.
The seventeenth chapter.
213:
## 18. Mala Vagga

## 1. The Story of the Butcher's Son
(Goghātakaputta Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Paṇḍupalāsova dāni'si," concerning the son of a certain butcher.

## Saying He Cannot Eat Without Meat

In Sāvatthī, it is said there was a butcher who killed cows, took the choice meat, had it cooked, and ate it while sitting with his wife and children. He also made a living by selling meat for a price. For fifty-five years, while performing this work of a butcher, he never once offered even a single ladle of rice gruel (yāgu) or food to the Teacher who resided at the nearby Jetavana Monastery. That butcher was not in the habit of eating rice without meat. One day, after selling beef during the day, he gave a piece of meat to his wife to cook for himself and went to bathe. At that time, a friend of the butcher came to the house and said to the butcher's wife, "Please give me a little of the beef intended for sale; a guest has arrived at my house." When she replied, "There is no beef for sale; your friend sold all the meat and has now gone to bathe," he said, "Do not do this; if there is still a piece of meat, please give it."

When she said, "There is no other meat except the piece set aside for your friend," the man who wanted the meat thought, "There is no meat other than that set aside for my friend, and my friend cannot eat rice without meat. This butcher's wife will not dare to give it," and he himself took that meat and departed.

When the butcher returned after bathing, his wife brought the rice, serving it along with the cooked greens she had prepared. He asked, "Where is the meat?" When she replied, "Lord, there is none," he said, "Did I not personally give you the meat to cook before I left?" She replied, "Your friend came and said, 'A guest has arrived at my house, give me some meat for sale.' Although I told him, 'There is no meat other than that set aside for your friend, and your friend cannot eat without meat,' he took that meat himself by force and left." The butcher said, "I cannot eat rice without meat; go and bring that meat back."
214:
## How the Butcher Cut Off the Tongue and Ate It, Receiving Immediate Retribution

When the butcher said, "I cannot eat," and had the rice set aside, he took a knife and went to where a cow was standing at the back of the house. He reached into the cow's mouth, pulled out its tongue, and cut it off at the root with the knife. He then roasted it over hot coals, placed it on top of his rice, and sat down to eat. After eating a morsel of rice, he put a piece of the meat into his mouth. At that very moment, the butcher's own tongue was severed and fell into his bowl of rice. At that instant, he received retribution exactly corresponding to his karma. Like the cow, with a stream of blood flowing from his mouth, he entered the house and crawled around on his knees, moaning and wailing. At that time, the butcher's son was standing nearby, watching his father. Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, look at your father, the butcher, who is crawling around on his knees in the middle of the house, moaning like a cow. This suffering will fall upon your head. Without looking back or worrying about me, flee and seek your own safety."

Terrified of death, the son paid homage to his mother and fled. Having fled, he reached the city of Takkasilā. The butcher, moaning and crawling in the middle of the house like a cow, passed away and was reborn in the Avīci hell. The cow also died.

## The Son Reaching Takkasilā and Prospering

The butcher's son went to Takkasilā and learned the craft of a goldsmith. Later, when his teacher was going to a village, he said, "You must make an ornament of such a kind," and departed. The young man made the ornament exactly as instructed. When the teacher returned and saw the ornament, he thought, "This young man is capable of making a living anywhere," and gave him his daughter, who had reached marriageable age, in marriage. The butcher's son then prospered with sons and daughters.

## Returning to Sāvatthī and Meeting the Buddha

Later, when his sons reached adulthood and mastered their crafts, they went to Sāvatthī. While living there and establishing their households, they became endowed with faith and devotion. Their father, however, reached old age without having performed any meritorious deeds in Takkasilā. Then his sons, thinking, "Our father is old," had him summoned to their presence. Thinking, "We shall give an offering for our father's benefit," they invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha. The next day, they seated the community of monks headed by the Buddha inside their house and served them respectfully. At the conclusion of the meal, they said to the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, we have given this jīvabhatta (life-meal) for our father. Please give a talk of appreciation for our father's sake."

The Teacher addressed him, saying, "Lay follower, you are now advanced in years; your body is ripe; you are like a withered leaf. You have no provisions of merit for your journey to the next world. Make a refuge for yourself. Be wise; do not be foolish." While giving the appreciation, he spoke these two verses:
215:
## The First Day's Teaching

(235) You are now like a withered leaf;
The messengers of Yama have approached you.
You stand at the threshold of departure,
And you have no provisions for the journey.

(236) Make an island for yourself;
Strive quickly; be wise.
With impurities blown away and free from stain,
You shall reach the divine realm of the Noble Ones.

"O lay follower! You have now become like a withered leaf that has been severed and fallen to the ground. The messengers of Yama—the minions of death—have come near you. You stand at the very mouth of decline and non-growth. For you, there are no provisions of merit, like the rice and other supplies for a traveler going to the next world.

Therefore, make for yourself a refuge of merit, like an island for one whose ship has wrecked at sea. In doing so, strive quickly; exert effort with great speed. By establishing a refuge of meritorious deeds for yourself, be wise. One who performs merit while still capable, before reaching the mouth of death, is called wise. Be such a person; do not be an ignorant fool. By exerting effort in this way, having removed the impurities of lust and so forth, and being free from the stains of defilements, you shall reach the five Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), which are the divine realms where the Noble Ones are born."

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, that lay follower, the son of the butcher, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled crowd.

## Hearing the Dhamma the Next Day After Becoming a Stream-enterer

The children of that lay follower again invited the Teacher for the sake of merit on the following day. After giving the offering and when the Teacher had finished his meal, they said at the time of the appreciation, "Venerable Sir, this meal is also a meal dedicated to our father while he is still alive. Please give a talk of appreciation for this father of ours alone." The Buddha, wishing to give the appreciation to him, spoke these two verses:
216:
## The Second Day's Discourse

(237) Your life is now drawn to a close; you have set out for the presence of Yama. There is no resting place for you along the way, and you have no provisions for the journey.

(238) So make an island for yourself; strive quickly and be wise. With impurities blown away and free from blemish, you shall not again enter birth and decay.

O lay devotee! You are now of advanced age. You stand prepared to go to the presence of Yama, the King of Death. There will be no staying in between for you. You do not yet have the provisions of merit.

Therefore, you should make for yourself a refuge of merit, which is like a great island. Strive quickly. Be wise. Having removed the impurities such as lust and being free from defilements, you shall not again come to birth and old age.

## The Son of the Cattle-Butcher Attaining the Fruit of Non-Returning

(By the lower two verses, the Path of Non-Returning was taught. In these upper two verses, the Path of Arahatship was taught. Even though it was taught thus—just as a King might prepare a mouthful of food according to the size of his own mouth and give it to his son, but the young prince can only take as much as fits his own mouth—similarly, although the Blessed One taught the Dhamma by way of the higher paths, the lay devotee, by the power of his own supporting conditions (upanissaya), reached the lower Fruit of Stream-entry, and at the end of this appreciative discourse (anumodanā), he reached the Fruit of Non-Returning. For the rest of the assembly, the Dhamma teaching was also beneficial.)

The story of the son of the cattle-butcher ends.
217:
## 2. The Story of a Certain Brahmin
(Aññatarabrāhmaṇa Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching starting with "Anupubbena," concerning a certain Brahmin.

## From Clearing Grass to Becoming a Hall-Donor

One day, that Brahmin went out early in the morning and stood watching the monks as they were putting on their robes in the place where they dress. That place was overgrown with grass. Then, while one monk was putting on his robe, the edge of the robe touched the grass and became wet with dewdrops. The Brahmin thought, "It is proper to make this place free of grass." On the following morning, he took a hoe, went there, and cleared the ground, making it like a threshing floor. On another morning, he went to that place again and saw that while the monks were dressing, the edge of a monk's robe fell on the ground and was soiled by dust. He thought, "It is proper to spread sand here," and he brought sand and spread it. Then one day, before the noon meal, the sun was very hot.

At that time also, seeing the sweat pouring from the bodies of the monks as they dressed, he thought, "It is proper for me to build a pavilion here," and he built a pavilion. On another morning, early in the day, it rained; there was a continuous drizzle. Then too, the Brahmin stood watching the monks and saw them with robes soaked by rain. He thought, "It is proper for me to build a hall here." He had a hall built and then thought, "Now I will perform the hall-dedication ceremony." He invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha.

Having seated the monks both inside and outside and offered alms, at the end of the meal, he took the Blessed One's bowl for the sake of the appreciative discourse (anumodanā) and said, "Venerable Sir, while I was standing and watching the monks at the time they were dressing, I saw this and that, and I thought I would do this and that." He related the whole matter from the beginning. When the Blessed One heard the Brahmin's words, He said, "Brahmin, those who are wise, moment by moment, little by little, performing merit, gradually remove their own impurities of unwholesomeness," and He spoke this verse:

## The Discourse

(239) Gradually, moment by moment, little by little, the wise person should blow away his own impurities, just as a smith removes the dross of silver.

Just as a smith removes the impurities of silver, so the wise person of sharp wisdom, gradually, whenever the opportunity arises, performing merit little by little, should remove his own impurities such as lust.
218:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, the Brahmin was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude of people.
The Story of the Unknown Brahmin ends.

## 3. The Story of Elder Tissa
(Tissatthera-vatthu)
The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Ayasāva malaṃ," while residing at Jetavana Monastery, concerning a monk named Elder Tissa.

**Becoming a Louse Due to Attachment to a Robe**
This Elder Tissa was a clansman living in Sāvatthī. Having ordained and attained full ordination, he became known as Elder Tissa. Later, while spending the rains retreat at a country monastery, he received a thick robe-cloth eight cubits long. After the retreat, he took that cloth and went to his sister, placing it in her hands. The sister thought, "This cloth is not suitable for my brother," so she cut the cloth with a sharp knife, shredded it, pounded it in a mortar, carded it, beat it, rolled it, spun it into fine thread, and had it woven into a cloth. Elder Tissa, having prepared thread and needles, gathered young monks and novices who were skilled in robe-making, went to his sister, and said, "Give me my cloth; I will have a robe made." The sister brought out a nine-cubit cloth and placed it in the hands of her younger brother, Elder Tissa. Tissa took the cloth, spread it out, looked at it, and said, "My cloth was thick and eight cubits long. This cloth is fine and nine cubits long. This is not my cloth; it is yours. I have no need for this cloth of yours. Give me only that cloth of mine." When she said, "Venerable sir, this is indeed your cloth; please take it," he still did not want it.
Then, after she informed him of everything she had done, saying, "Venerable sir, this is indeed your cloth," she gave it to him. He took the cloth and went to the monastery to begin the work of making the robe.
219:
## The Teaching
(240) Ayasāva malaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ, tatuṭṭhāya tam-eva khādati.
Evaṃ atidhonacārinaṃ, sāni kammāni nayanti duggatiṃ.
Malaṃ: rust or impurity. Ayasāva: from iron itself. Samuṭṭhitaṃ: arises. Tato: from that iron. Uṭṭhāya: having arisen. Tam-eva: that very iron. Khādati iva: as if eating it. Evaṃ tathā: in the same way. Atidhonacārinaṃ: a monk who uses the four requisites without reflection. Sāni kammāni: those unwholesome kamma which are one's own and arise within oneself. Duggatiṃ: to a state of woe. Nayanti: they lead.

"Venerable sir, this is indeed your cloth; please take it," she offered. Elder Tissa took the cloth, went to the monastery, and began the work of making the robe. At that time, Elder Tissa's sister provided rice-gruel, meals, and so on for the robe-makers. On the day the robe was finished, she made an extra-special offering. Elder Tissa, looking at the robe, felt a strong attachment to it and thought, "I will wear this tomorrow." He folded it and placed it on the robe-rack. That night, being unable to digest the food he had eaten in the morning, he passed away and was reborn as a louse in that very robe.

## Rebirth in Tusita Heaven from the State of a Louse
When Elder Tissa's sister heard of his passing, she fell at the feet of the monks and wept. The monks performed the funeral rites for Elder Tissa's body. Since there was no one to attend to the sick, the robe fell to the Saṅgha. They brought it out, saying, "Let us distribute this robe." That louse cried out, "These monks are plundering my property!" and ran back and forth. The Teacher, while sitting in the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), heard that sound with his divine ear-element and said, "Dear Ānanda, tell them to set aside Tissa's robe for seven days." Elder Ānanda did as the Buddha commanded.

That louse passed away on the seventh day and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. On the eighth day, the Teacher commanded, "Distribute Tissa's robe and take it." The monks did as commanded. The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Why did the Teacher have Tissa's robe set aside for seven days and only allow it to be taken on the eighth day?" The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," he said, "Monks, Tissa was reborn as a louse in his own robe. When you were about to distribute it, he cried out, 'These monks are plundering my property!' and ran back and forth."

"If you had taken the robe while he was a louse, he would have felt ill-will toward you and been reborn in hell. Therefore, I had the robe set aside. Now, this Tissa has been reborn in the Tusita heaven. Therefore, I allow you to take the robe." When he said this, the monks remarked, "Venerable sir, this thing called craving (taṇhā) is indeed heavy." The Teacher replied, "Monks, it is true that craving is heavy for these beings."
220:
For example, just as rust, which is the impurity arising from iron, eats away and destroys that very iron, making it unfit for use, so too does this craving arise within the internal continuity of these beings and cause them to be reborn in hell and other such states, leading them to ruin. Having said this, the Buddha preached this verse.

(The four requisites are called 'dhona'. One must use them with the mindful reflection: 'I use this requisite for this purpose.' A monk who practices by overstepping that mindfulness is called an 'atidhonacārī'. This means a monk who uses the four requisites without reflection.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of Elder Tissa ends.

## 4. The Story of Elder Lāḷudāyī

(Lāḷudāyittheravatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher (the Buddha) gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Asajjhāyamalā' concerning Elder Lāḷudāyī.

## Boasting without the Ability to Preach

In the city of Sāvatthī, it is said that there lived about five crores of noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka). There were also about two crores of worldlings (puthujjana). Among them, the noble disciples who had attained the paths and fruits would give alms in the morning, and in the afternoon, they would take ghee, oil, honey, molasses, robes, and other offerings to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. After listening to the Dhamma and upon their return, they would speak words of praise concerning the virtues of Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna. When Elder Udāyī heard their words, he said, 'You speak thus after hearing their Dhamma. If you were to hear my Dhamma teaching, how could you remain silent?' When the people heard Elder Udāyī's words, they thought, 'This must be another Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika). It is proper for us to listen to the Dhamma from this elder as well.' So one day, they requested the Elder, saying, 'Venerable Sir, today is our day for listening to the Dhamma. Therefore, Venerable Sir, after we have given alms to the Saṅgha, please preach the Dhamma to us during the day.' Elder Udāyī consented to their request.

## Falling into a Latrine due to Excessive Boasting

When the time for listening to the Dhamma arrived and the people came and said, 'Venerable Sir, please preach the Dhamma to us,' Elder Udāyī sat on the preaching seat, held an ornate fan, and began to tremble. Because he could not see even a single verse or a single passage of Dhamma to preach, he said, 'I will recite the Sarabhañña (intoning of Pali) to make the Pali text clear with my voice. Let another Dhamma preacher preach the Dhamma first,' and he descended from the seat. The people had another Dhamma preacher preach the Dhamma and then once again had Elder Udāyī ascend the seat for the purpose of intoning (sarabhāṇa). Again, Udāyī could not see anything to say and said, 'I will preach at night. Let another intone the Sarabhañña,' and he descended from the seat. The people had another intone the Sarabhañña and then again invited the Elder at night. Even at night, Udāyī could not see anything to preach and said, 'I will preach at dawn. Let another preach during the night,' and he descended again. 

The lay followers had another preach during the night and once again invited Elder Udāyī at dawn. Once again, he could not see anything to preach. (A Sarabhāṇaka is one who recites the Pali text with a melodious voice.)
221:
He said, 'Let another person recite the Pali text with a melodious voice,' and he descended from the preaching seat again. The people had another Sarabhāṇaka recite the Pali and then invited Elder Udāyī again during the night. Even at night, Elder Udāyī could not see any Dhamma to preach and said, 'I will preach in the early morning at dawn. Let another Dhamma preacher preach during the night,' and he descended again.

Those lay followers had another Dhamma preacher preach during the night and once again invited Elder Udāyī in the early morning at dawn. Once again, Elder Udāyī could not see any Dhamma to preach. The great crowd, holding clods of earth, sticks, and so on, threatened him, saying, 'You blind fool! When the virtues of Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna were being spoken of, you said this and that. Why do you not preach now?' and they pursued the fleeing Elder Udāyī. While fleeing, Elder Udāyī fell into a latrine.

The great crowd started a conversation: 'Today, when the conversation about the virtues of Venerable Sāriputta was taking place, Elder Udāyī was very envious and proclaimed himself a Dhamma preacher. When the people offered him honor and said they would listen to the Dhamma, he sat on the preaching seat four times but could not see any Dhamma related to what should be preached. Because he tried to compete and challenge our master, Venerable Sāriputta, the people took up clods, sticks, and so on, and while he was fleeing from their threats, he fell into a latrine.'

## The Pig who Challenged the Lion

The Teacher (the Buddha) arrived and asked, 'Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit gathered here now?' When they replied, 'With such and such a subject, Lord,' the Buddha said, 'Monks, it is not only now; in the past also, this Lāḷudāyī was submerged in a cesspool.' He then brought forth the past:

'I have four legs, friend; you too, friend, have four legs.
Come, friend, turn back! Why do you run away in fear?'

'You are impure, with foul-smelling hair, O pig; you are stinking.
If you wish to fight, I give you the victory, friend.'

'Friend, O King of Lions. I have four legs. Friend, O King of Lions, you too have four legs. Friend, O King of Lions, come! Please turn back. Are you fleeing because you are afraid of me?'

'O wretched pig, you are impure. You have hair that smells strongly of rot. You have a disgusting odor that spreads around. If you truly wish to fight, O foolish pig, I give the victory to you.'

Expanding on this Jātaka found in the Daḷhavagga of the Dukanipāta, the Buddha explained that at that time, the lion was Sāriputta and the pig was Lāḷudāyī. Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, 'Monks, Lāḷudāyī has learned only a small amount of Dhamma, but he does not practice recitation.'
222:
## The Teaching
(241) Non-recitation is the stain of mantras; non-exertion is the stain of houses; sloth is the stain of beauty; heedlessness is the stain of a guard.

Mantras, including the learned Pariyatti and various arts, have non-recitation as their stain. Houses have the lack of exertion and effort as their stain. Sloth is the stain of physical appearance. Heedlessness is the stain of one who guards.

[The Buddha] declared that the pig had become Lāḷudāyī. Having brought forth this religious teaching, the Blessed One said, "Bhikkhus, the monk named Lāḷudāyī has learned only a small portion of the Dhamma. Yet he does not recite it. To learn the entire Pariyatti without distinction and then fail to recite it is merely a stain upon that learned Pariyatti," and then he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of Elder Lāḷudāyī ends.

## 5. The Story of a Certain Young Man
(Aññatarakulaputta Vatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Blessed One spoke this religious teaching, "Malitthiyā duccaritaṃ," and so forth, concerning a certain young man.

## The Stain of Women
For that young man, they brought a young maiden of equal status. From the day she was brought, she was unfaithful to her husband.
223:
## The Teaching
(242) Misconduct is the stain of a woman; stinginess is the stain of a giver. Evil states are indeed stains, both in this world and the next.

(243) A stain worse than these stains is ignorance, the ultimate stain. Having abandoned this stain, be stainless, O monks!

Misconduct, the act of transgressing against one's husband, is the stain of a woman. Stinginess is the stain of a person who gives. Evil, unwholesome states are indeed stains in this world and in the world beyond.

I shall speak of a stain more excessive than those aforementioned stains. Ignorance, the state of not knowing, is the ultimate stain. O my beloved sons, monks! You should abandon and discard this stain of ignorance and become ones who are free from stains.

Because that young man was ashamed of that maiden's excessive misconduct, he was unable to appear before anyone. Consequently, he ceased his services to the Buddha and other duties. After a few days had passed, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. When the Buddha asked, "Lay disciple, why have you not been seen?", he reported the matter. Then the Blessed One said to him, "Lay disciple, in the past too, I have said that women are like rivers and such. A wise man should not be angry with those women. However, you do not remember because it is veiled by [past] lives." Being requested by that lay disciple, the Buddha spoke:

"Just as a river, a path, a tavern, a hall, or a water-stand [are common to all], so are women in this world; there is no limit to them."

Thus, having expanded upon the Anabhirati Jātaka from the Itthivagga of the Ekanipāta, the Buddha said, "Lay disciple, for a woman, misconduct by transgressing against her husband is a stain. For a person who gives alms, stinginess is a stain. For beings in this present world and the world beyond, unwholesome kamma is a stain because of its nature to destroy. Ignorance, however, is a stain more excessive than all other stains," and then he spoke these verses.
224:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The story of an unknown clansman is finished.

## The Teaching
(244) Life is easy for the shameless, who is as bold as a crow, a backbiter, one who intrudes, is impudent, and leads a corrupt life.
(245) But life is difficult for the modest one, who always seeks purity, who is detached, humble, lives a pure life, and is discerning.

Monks, for a monk who is shameless, life is easy to live. By being bold as a crow, by destroying the virtues of others, by pretending to do what others have done, by being impudent in body, speech, and mind—life is easily maintained. Thus, by being corrupt, one leads a miserable life.

For a monk who is modest, life is difficult to live. By always seeking purity in bodily actions and so forth, by not being attached to livelihood, by not being impudent—life is lived with difficulty. Thus, a monk of pure livelihood, seeing [the Dhamma] as supreme, lives with difficulty.

## 6. The Story of the Monk named Cūḷasāri
(Cūḷasārivatthu)
While the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, he told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Su-jīvaṃ," concerning a co-resident of Venerable Sāriputta named Cūḷasāri.

## The Monk Relying on Medical Practice
One day, that monk named Cūḷasāri, having practiced medicine and obtained excellent food, was leaving with it when he saw Venerable Sāriputta on the way. He said, "Venerable sir, I obtained this excellent food by practicing medicine. You will not receive such food elsewhere. Please partake of this. I will continue to practice medicine and bring such food for you regularly." Hearing the words of Cūḷasāri, Venerable Sāriputta remained silent and departed. The monks went to the monastery and reported the matter to the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Monks, one who is shameless is impudent and like a crow. By standing in the twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood (anesanā), such a person lives happily. But one endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) lives with difficulty." He then uttered these verses.

## Notes on the Teaching
A monk whose sense of shame and fear is severed can live easily by standing in the twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood, saying things like "She is my mother" to one who is not his mother, or "He is my father" to one who is not his father. The nature of being "bold as a crow" is like a daring crow that, wanting to take gruel and so forth from houses, perches on walls and, knowing it is being watched, pretends not to look, as if preoccupied or drowsy. While people are driving it away saying "Shu! Shu!", it watches for a lapse, flies down, takes a beakful from the dish, and flies away.
225:
Similarly, a shameless person enters the village with other monks and marks the places where gruel and rice are available.

In that village, the other monks, having gone for alms and taken just enough to sustain themselves, go to the refectory, reflect [on the purpose of food], drink their gruel, practice meditation, recite the texts, and sweep the refectory. But this monk, without doing anything, heads straight for the village. Even when the other monks look at him saying, "Look at this one," he pretends not to see, acts as if preoccupied, as if drowsy, as if unfastening his robe-button, or as if adjusting his robe. Saying, "I have such and such a task," he rises from his seat and enters the village. He approaches one of the houses he marked in the morning. Even if the householders have slightly closed the door and are staying inside talking, he pushes the door open with one hand and enters to sit down. Then, seeing him, even if they are unwilling, they make him sit and offer whatever gruel or food they have. Having eaten as much as he desires, he takes the remainder in his bowl and leaves. This monk is called "bold as a crow." It is meant that for such a shameless person, life is easy.

"Destroying the virtues of others" (dhamsinā) means he destroys the reputation of great elders by saying things like, "Such and such an elder is of few wishes," and then adding, "But are we not also of few wishes?" Hearing the words of such a monk who speaks of the virtues of the great, people think, "This monk is also endowed with virtues such as having few wishes," and they think he should be given offerings.

However, from the time he receives those gains, being unable to maintain the quality of having few wishes to satisfy the minds of wise men who judge with wisdom, he falls away even from those regular gains. Thus, a person who destroys virtues ruins both his own gains and the gains of others. "One who intrudes" (pakkhandinā) refers to one who acts by jumping in. He shows the work of others as if it were his own. In the early morning, while other monks perform duties at the cetiya courtyard and so forth, sit for a while in meditation, and then rise to enter the village, he washes his face, robes himself in a pale yellow robe, applies eye-salve, anoints his head, and thus adorns himself. Then, as if sweeping, he gives two or three strokes with the broom and stands facing the gateway. When lay devotees come early in the morning to worship the cetiya or offer flowers, seeing him, they think, "This great monastery is kept clean because of this young monk."
226:
Saying, "Do not neglect this monk," they think he should be given to. Thus, a monk who mimics what others do also lives easily. He also lives easily through harshness of body, speech, and mind. A monk who lives long by such a livelihood is said to live a defiled life. That livelihood is indeed wicked.

A monk endowed with shame and fear (hiri-ottappa) lives with difficulty. He does not call those who are not his mother "my mother" and so on; he loathes unrighteously obtained requisites like excrement. Seeking according to the Dhamma, he makes his living by wandering for alms from house to house, and thus lives a life of hardship. By seeking pure bodily actions and so on, and by not being attached to or concerned with his livelihood, he lives a life of hardship and is called one of pure livelihood. Because he is a monk of pure livelihood, seeing such a livelihood alone as noble, he lives with difficulty through a life of poverty.

## Fruit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many reached the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so on.

The story of the monk named Cūḷasāri ends.

## The Teaching
(246) Whoever destroys life, and speaks what is not true,
Takes in the world what is not given, and goes to another's wife.

(247) And the man who indulges in drinking intoxicants and fermented spirits,
Even here in this world, he digs up his own root.

(248) Know this, O man: evil states are unrestrained.
Let not greed and unrighteousness oppress you for long-term suffering.

"Whoever" (yo naro): That person. "Destroys life" (pāṇaṃ atipāteti): Quickly takes the life of another. "And speaks what is not true" (musāvādañca bhāsati): Speaks so as to destroy the welfare of others. "In the world" (loke): In the world of beings.

"What is not given" (adinnaṃ): Another's property not given by the owner through body or speech. "Takes" (ādiyati): Steals. "And goes to another's wife" (paradārañca gacchati): Commits adultery.

"Whoever" (yo naro): That person. "And the drinking of intoxicants and fermented spirits" (surāmerayapānañca): The drinking of the five kinds of surā and five kinds of meraya. "Indulges in" (anuyuñjati): Practices. "This man" (eso naro): This person. "Even here in this world" (idheva lokasmiṃ): Even in this present world. "His own" (attano): His own. "Root" (mūlaṃ): The root of his wealth, such as fields and property. "Digs up" (khaṇati): Digs up and destroys.

## 7. The Story of the Five Hundred Lay Followers
(Pañca-upāsaka-vatthu)

The Teacher, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching, "Yo pāṇaṃ..." starting with the five hundred lay followers.
(In the Aṭṭhakathā Pali, it is mentioned only as Pañca-upāsaka-vatthu.)

## The Cause of the Dispute over Virtue
Among those five hundred lay followers, some kept only the precept (sikkhāpada) which is the volition (cetanā) to abstain from quickly taking the life of others. Others kept the other precepts. One day, they fell into a dispute, saying, "I do a difficult thing. I keep a difficult practice." They went to the Teacher, paid homage, and reported the matter. When the Teacher heard their words, he said, "Without making even a single virtue inferior, all virtues are indeed difficult to keep," and spoke these verses.

The five kinds of surā (liquor):
1. Piṭṭhasurā: liquor made from flour.
2. Pūvasurā: liquor made from cakes.
3. Odanasurā: liquor made from cooked rice.
4. Kiṇṇapakkhittā: liquor made with yeast.
227:
5. Sambhārasamyuttā: liquor mixed with ingredients such as gallnuts.
(Piṭṭha, pūva, odana, kiṇṇa, sambhārā.)

The five kinds of meraya (fermented spirits):
1. Pupphāsava: spirit made from flowers.
2. Phalāsava: spirit made from fruits.
3. Madhvāsava: spirit made from honey.
4. Guḷāsava: spirit made from molasses or sugar cane.
5. Sambhārasamyuttā: spirit mixed with ingredients such as triphala.
(Puppha, phalā, madhvā, guḷa, sambhāra, the five merayas.)

"O man" (bho purisa): O man who is not firm in the five precepts. "Thus" (evaṃ): In this way. "You" (tvaṃ): You. "Know" (jānāhi): Know. "Evil states" (pāpadhammā): Wicked states. "Are unrestrained" (asaññatā): Are devoid of self-restraint of the body and so on. "And greed" (lobho ca): Greed. "And unrighteousness" (adhammo ca): Anger (dosa). "These" (ime): These unwholesome states. "For a long time" (ciraṃ): For a long duration. "For suffering" (dukkhāya): For the sake of the suffering of hell and so on. "You" (taṃ): You. "Let them not oppress" (mā randhayuṃ): Let them not entangle or torment you.

## Fruit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the five hundred lay followers were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to those who had arrived.

The story of the five hundred lay followers ends.

## 8. The Story of the Young Monk Tissa
(Tissa-dahara-vatthu)

The Teacher, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching, "Dadāti ve..." starting with a young monk named Tissa.
228:
He might boast much, having gone to another district. Should he follow and spoil it, enjoy the riches, O Kaṭāhaka.

So, that person. Aññaṃ, to another. Janapadaṃ, district. Gato, when he has gone. Bahumpi, much indeed. Vikattheyya, he might disparage or boast. Kaṭāhaka, O one named Kaṭāhaka. Anvāgantvāna, when [someone] has followed later. Dūseyya, he might spoil it. Bhogē, the riches. Bhuñja, enjoy.

## The Monk who Disparaged Donors
That young monk Tissa went about disparaging the alms-giving of the noble disciples such as the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and the female lay devotee Visākhā, who had given to the extent of five hundred millions. He even disparaged the Peerless Alms-giving (Asadisadāna) of the great King Kosala. When he received cold food at the various places of alms-giving, he disparaged it as "too cold." When he received hot food, he disparaged it as "too hot." When a small amount was given, he disparaged it, saying, "Why do these people give so little?" When much was given, he disparaged it, saying, "It seems there is no place to store things in their house; shouldn't they give just enough for the monks' sustenance? They waste so much gruel and rice in vain." However, regarding his own relatives, he would praise them, saying, "Oh, our relatives' house is like a well for the monks coming from the four directions," and so on.

## Investigating the Lineage of the Disparaging Young Monk
(That young monk was the son of a gatekeeper who, while wandering with carpenters in the countryside, reached Sāvatthī and went forth as a monk.)

Then the monks, seeing that young monk disparaging the people's alms-giving and so on, thought, "Let us investigate him." They asked, "Friend, where do your relatives live?" Hearing that they lived in a village of such-and-such a name, they sent a few young monks there. Those young monks went there, and when they were seated in the refectory by the villagers and received hospitality, they asked, "There is a young monk named Tissa who left this village and went forth. Who are his relatives?" The people thought, "There is no youth from a noble family in this village who has left to go forth. Who are these venerable ones talking about?" Then they said, "Venerable sirs, there is one person named Tissa, the son of a gatekeeper, who wandered with carpenters and went forth. You must be referring to him." When the young monks learned that Tissa had no wealthy or powerful relatives in that village, they returned to Sāvatthī and said, "Venerable sirs, Tissa goes about boasting for no reason at all."
229:
They reported that matter to the monks. The monks also reported it to the Blessed One.

## A Glimpse of the Kaṭāhaka Jātaka
The Blessed One said, "Monks, he does not go about speaking disparaging words only now; in the past too, he was one who spoke disparagingly." Being requested by the monks, he brought forth the past story and explained this Kaṭāhaka Jātaka in detail. "Monks, if a person becomes disgruntled when others give a little or much, coarse or fine food, or when they give to others but not to him, then for that person, neither absorption (jhāna), nor insight (vipassanā), nor the paths and fruits (magga-phala) and so forth can arise." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

## The Teaching
(249) People give according to their faith, according to their devotion. Therein, he who is disgruntled regarding the food and drink of others does not attain concentration by day or by night.

(250) But he in whom this [disgruntlement] is fully cut off, uprooted, and destroyed, he indeed attains concentration by day or by night.

Yathāpāsādanaṃ, according to one's devotion. Yathāsaddhaṃ, according to one's faith. Ve, indeed. Jano, people. Dadāti, they give. Paresaṃ, of others. Tattha pānabhojane, regarding that drink and food. Yo ca, and whoever. Maṅku, becomes disgruntled, thinking it is too little or too coarse. Bhavati, he becomes. So, that person. Divā vā, by day. Rattiṃ vā, or by night. Samādhiṃ, concentration. Na adhigacchati, does not attain.

Yassa ca, but for whom. Etaṃ, this unwholesome state of disgruntlement. Samucchinnaṃ, is well cut off. Mūlaghaccaṃ katvā, having uprooted it. Samūhataṃ, is removed without remainder. So, that person. Ve, indeed. Divā vā, by day. Rattiṃ vā, or by night. Samādhiṃ, concentration. Adhigacchati, attains.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of the young monk Tissa ends.

## 9. The Story of the Five Lay Followers
(Pañca-upāsaka-vatthu)
The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, "There is no fire like lust," while residing at Jetavana, concerning five lay followers.

## The Reason for Falling Asleep while Listening to Dhamma, etc.
Those five donors, desiring to hear the Dhamma, went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place. To the Buddhas, the thought does not arise: "This one is a kshatriya, this one is a brahmin, this one is wealthy, this one is poor; I will teach the Dhamma excellently to this one, but not to that one."
230:
His mind does not arise in such a way [of partiality]; when he preaches the Dhamma, he does not do so by singling out any particular person. Making respect for the Dhamma his foremost guide, he preaches as if the celestial Ganges were descending from the sky. While the Tathāgata was preaching in this manner, among those sitting in his presence, one sat sleeping. One sat scratching the ground with his finger. One sat shaking a tree. One sat looking up at the sky. One, however, listened to the Dhamma respectfully.

Venerable Ānanda, while fanning the Teacher and observing the behavior of those five lay devotees, said to the Teacher: “Venerable Sir, you preach the Dhamma to these five people like the roar of a great thundercloud. Yet, even while you are preaching the Dhamma, these people sit doing this and that.”

## The Past of the Five Listeners

“Dear Ānanda, do you not know these five lay devotees?” the Teacher asked. “Indeed, I do not know, Venerable Sir,” he replied. “Among these five, the one who sits sleeping has been reborn in the serpent realm for five hundred births, and was accustomed to sleeping with his head placed upon his coils. Even now, he has a habit of sleeping and is currently asleep; therefore, the sound of my Dhamma does not enter his ears.”

When the Buddha said this, Ānanda asked, “Venerable Sir, did he undergo these births in succession, or were they intermittent?” “Dear Ānanda, the births of one who arises intermittently—sometimes as a human, sometimes as a deity, sometimes as a nāga—cannot be delimited even by Omniscient Knowledge. However, in a continuous succession, this man was reborn in the nāga realm for five hundred births, and even while sleeping, he remains unsatisfied with sleep. The man who sits scratching the ground with his fingers was reborn as an earthworm for five hundred births and spent them digging the earth; even now, he is just digging the earth and cannot hear the sound of my Dhamma. The man who sits shaking the tree was reborn as a monkey for five hundred births in succession; even now, by the power of his past habit, he is just shaking the tree, and the sound of my Dhamma does not enter his ears. The man who sits gazing at the sky was reborn as an astrologer for five hundred births; even now, by the power of his past habit, he is still gazing at the sky today, and the sound of my Dhamma does not enter his ears. This man who sits listening to the Dhamma respectfully, however, was reborn for five hundred births in succession as a brahmin who mastered the three Vedas and recited the mantras; even now, he listens respectfully as if he were comparing and reciting the mantras.”
231:
## The Teaching

(251) There is no fire like lust; there is no seizer like hatred.
There is no net like delusion; there is no river like craving.

'Rāgasamo': there is no fire like lust. 'Gaho': there is no seizer like hatred. 'Jālaṃ': there is no net like delusion. 'Nadī': there is no river like craving.

## Is Listening to the Dhamma Easy or Difficult?

“Venerable Sir, your Dhamma teaching cuts through the skin and so on, reaching and remaining in the bone marrow. Why is it that these lay devotees cannot listen respectfully even while you are preaching?” Ānanda asked. “Dear Ānanda, you likely think that my Dhamma is something easily heard and very pleasant to listen to,” the Teacher replied. “Is it then, Venerable Sir, something difficult to hear and not very pleasant to listen to?” “Yes, Ānanda, it is so.” “For what reason, Venerable Sir?”

“Dear Ānanda, these beings have not heard the words ‘Buddha,’ ‘Dhamma,’ or ‘Saṅgha’ even in many hundreds of thousands of kotis of aeons. Therefore, they are unable to listen to this Dhamma. In this saṃsāra, whose beginning is unknown, these beings have come along hearing only various kinds of 'animal talk' (tiracchānakathā) which are contrary to the Path and Fruition. Therefore, they can go about singing and dancing in drinking circles, places of amusement, and courtyards. They are unable to listen to the Dhamma.”

When the Buddha said this, Ānanda asked again, “Venerable Sir, depending on what thing are they unable to do so?” Then the Teacher said to Ānanda, “Dear Ānanda, they are unable because of lust, because of hatred, because of delusion, and because of craving. There is no fire like the fire of lust; that fire of lust burns beings leaving no ashes behind. Even the world-destroying fire that arises due to the appearance of seven suns burns the world leaving nothing behind, yet that fire burns only occasionally. There is no time when the fire of lust does not burn. Therefore, there is no fire equal to lust, no seizer equal to hatred, no net equal to delusion, and no river equal to craving.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, the lay devotee who was listening to the Dhamma respectfully was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to those who had assembled.

The Story of the Five Lay Devotees ends.
232:
## 10. The Story of Meṇḍaka the Great Treasurer
(Meṇḍaka-seṭṭhi-vatthu)
While the Buddha was staying in the Jātiya Grove near the city of Bhaddiya, he spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Sudassaṃ vajjaṃ" concerning Meṇḍaka the Great Treasurer.
(Meṇḍaka + Seṭṭhi = Ram + Treasurer; meaning a treasurer who possessed many golden ram statues capable of providing everything desired.)

## How Meṇḍaka the Great Treasurer Got His Name
While the Buddha was wandering through the regions of Aṅga and Uttara, he saw the potential (upanissaya) for Meṇḍaka the Great Treasurer, his wife named Candapadumā, his son Dhanañjaya the Treasurer, his daughter-in-law Sumanadevī, his granddaughter Visākhā, and his servant Puṇṇa to be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Thus, he traveled to the city of Bhaddiya and stayed in the Jātiya Grove. Meṇḍaka the Great Treasurer heard of the Buddha's arrival. 

Why was this treasurer named Meṇḍaka? In the backyard of his house, in an area of about eight karīsas, golden ram statues the size of elephants, horses, and bulls emerged from the earth, bumping their backs against one another. In the mouths of these golden rams were placed balls of thread of five colors. Whenever there was a need for ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so on, or for clothing, gold, silver, and so on, if one were to pull the balls of thread from the mouths of those golden rams, even from the mouth of a single golden ram, enough ghee, oil, honey, molasses, clothing, gold, and silver would come out to suffice for all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa. From that time on, he became famous as Meṇḍaka the Great Treasurer.

## The Past of Meṇḍaka the Great Treasurer
What was the past meritorious deed of this Meṇḍaka the Great Treasurer? In the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was the nephew of a householder named Avaroja, and he himself was named Avaroja, the same as his uncle. At that time, his uncle strove to build a Gandhakuṭi (fragrant chamber) for the Buddha. The nephew, Avaroja, went to his uncle and said, "Uncle, let us both build it together." When the uncle refused, saying, "I will build it alone, without associating with others," the nephew thought, "If a Gandhakuṭi is built in this place, it is fitting to have a rest house named Kuñjara in this other place." He then had timber brought from the forest. He decorated one pillar with gold, one with silver, one with rubies, and one with the seven kinds of jewels. He had all the beams, door frames, doors, shutters, windows, rafters, and roof tiles made and decorated with gold and other precious materials. In front of the Gandhakuṭi, he built the Kuñjara rest house for the Buddha using the seven kinds of jewels.
233:
On top of that rest house were blankets made of solid red gold and pinnacles made of coral. In the middle of the Kuñjara rest house, he built a jewel pavilion. He had a Dhamma seat (pulpit) established. The legs of that Dhamma seat were made of solid red gold. Likewise, the four frames were made of solid red gold. He had four golden ram statues made and placed under the four legs of the seat. He had two golden ram statues made and placed under the footstool. He had six more golden ram statues made and placed surrounding the pavilion. The Dhamma seat was first woven with cotton threads, then with gold threads in the middle, and with pearl threads on top. The backrest of the Dhamma seat was made of sandalwood.

Thus, after completing the Kuñjara rest house, while celebrating the great dedication ceremony, he invited Vipassī Buddha along with 6,800,000 monks and gave great alms for four months. On the final day, he offered sets of three robes (ticīvara). Among those monks, even the most junior member of the Saṅgha received a robe worth a hundred thousand.

## Encountering a Great Famine
Having performed such meritorious deeds in the time of Vipassī Buddha, after passing away from that life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In this Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), he was born into a wealthy family in the city of Bārāṇasī and became known as the Bārāṇasī Treasurer. One day, while going to serve the king, he saw the court chaplain (purohita) and asked, "Teacher Brahmin, have you observed and considered the constellations for a moment?" When the chaplain replied, "Yes, I have considered them; what other business do we have?" the treasurer asked, "If so, what will be the situation in the country?" The chaplain replied, "A danger will arise." "What kind of danger?" he asked. "Great Treasurer, it is the danger of famine (chātaka-bhaya)," the chaplain replied. "When will it happen?" he asked. "It will happen three years from today," the chaplain said. Upon hearing these words, the Bārāṇasī Treasurer had extensive plowing done, bought only grain with the wealth he had in his house, built two hundred and fifty granaries, and filled all the granaries with rice.
234:
When the granaries could not hold the grain, they filled large jars and other vessels, and buried the remaining grain in pits in the ground. After burying and storing it, they mixed the leftover grain with earth and plastered it onto the walls. Once, when a famine occurred, the great merchant consumed the grain that had been stored. When the grain in the granaries and large jars was exhausted, he called his servants and attendants and said, "Friends, go! Go to the foot of the mountains and sustain yourselves. Those who wish to return to me in times of plenty, come back; those who do not wish to return, sustain yourselves there at the foot of the mountains."

Those servants and attendants, weeping and with tear-filled faces, paid homage to the great merchant and pleaded with him. He allowed them to stay for seven days, after which they did as the merchant had said. Only one servant named Puṇṇa, who performed all tasks great and small, remained with the great merchant. Along with this servant Puṇṇa, there were only five people: the merchant's wife, the merchant's son, and the merchant's daughter-in-law [and the merchant himself]. When the grain stored in the pits in the ground was also exhausted, these five people scraped the earth plastered on the walls, moistened it with water, and sustained themselves with the grain obtained from the walls.

## The Arrival of a Paccekabuddha Before the Meal

At that time, while the famine prevailed, the wife of the great merchant of Bārāṇasī, the mistress of the house, found that even the earth containing grain on the walls was exhausted. She scraped the remaining earth from the base of the walls, moistened it with water, and obtained about half an aḍḍhāḷhaka of paddy. After pounding it, she obtained one nāḷi of rice. Thinking, "In times of famine, thieves are numerous," and fearing the danger of thieves, she placed it in a pot, sealed it, and buried it in the ground. Then the great merchant, returning from serving the king, said to his wife, "Dear, I am very hungry. Is there anything to eat or drink?" The merchant's wife did not say there was nothing when there was. She said, "There is one nāḷi of rice." When asked, "Where is that rice?", she replied, "Fearing the danger of thieves, I have buried it."

"If that is so, take out that rice and cook something," he said. She asked, "My lord, if I prepare gruel (yāgu), it will serve for two times. If I cook rice (bhatta), it will serve only once. What shall I cook?" He said, "We have no other means of support. Let us eat rice and die. Just cook the rice." The merchant's wife then cooked the rice, divided it into five portions, served the merchant's portion, and placed it before him. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha on Mount Gandhamādana emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) after seven days.

Therefore, that Paccekabuddha, looking with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), saw: "A famine has arisen throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. In the merchant's house, rice from one nāḷi has been cooked for five people. Will these people have faith? Will they be able to support me?" Seeing their state of faith and their ability to provide support...
235:
Seeing that he was capable of providing support and assistance, the Paccekabuddha took his bowl and robes and stood right at the doorway in front of the great merchant, revealing himself.

## The Aspiration of the Future Wealthy Merchant Meṇḍaka
Upon seeing the Paccekabuddha, the great merchant felt a clear and joyful mind. He reflected, "In the past, because I did not give alms, I now encounter such a famine. Indeed, this rice can sustain me for only a single day. But an offering made to a Paccekabuddha will bring me welfare and happiness for many millions of aeons." With this thought, he set aside his bowl of rice, approached the Paccekabuddha, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and invited him into the house. After the Paccekabuddha was seated, the merchant washed his feet, placed them on a golden footstool, took the bowl of rice, and poured the food into the Paccekabuddha's bowl. When half of the food remained, the Paccekabuddha covered the bowl with his hand. Then, the merchant said to him, "Venerable Sir, this rice is but a single portion cooked from one nāḷi of rice for five people. It is not possible to divide this one-fifth portion into two. Please do not show me favor in this present life; I wish to give it all without remainder." Having said this, he offered all the rice. After giving, he made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, in whatever place I am reborn, may I never again see such a danger of famine. From now on, may I be able to give seed-grain to all the inhabitants of the whole of Jambudīpa. May I not have to make a living by working with my own hands. Having had twelve hundred and fifty granaries cleaned, and having bathed my head, as soon as I sit at the doors of those granaries and look upward, may showers of red sāli rice fall and fill all the granaries. In every life I am reborn, may this very woman be my wife, this very person be my son, this very woman be my daughter-in-law, and this very person be my servant."

## The Aspirations of the Merchant's Wife and Others
The merchant's wife also thought, "While my husband is oppressed by hunger, it is not proper for me to eat." She gave her portion to the Paccekabuddha and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, now and in every future life in the cycle of rebirths, may I never encounter such a danger of famine. Even when I place a pot of rice before me and distribute food to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, as long as I do not rise from my seat, may the place from which I take the food remain as full as it was. May this very man be my husband, this very person be my son, this very woman be my daughter-in-law, and this very person be my servant."

The merchant's son also gave his portion of rice to the Paccekabuddha and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, from this day forward, may I never see such a danger of famine. Even when I carry a bag containing a thousand coins and give coins to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, may this bag of a thousand coins remain as full as it was. May these very people be my mother and father, and may this woman be my wife and this person be my servant."

The merchant's daughter-in-law also gave her portion of rice to the Paccekabuddha and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, from this life forward, may I never see such a danger of famine. Even when I place a basket of grain before me and give seed-grain to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, may it never be known to be exhausted."
236:
"In every existence I am born, may these very people be my father-in-law and mother-in-law; may this very man be my husband, and this very person be my servant," she made this aspiration.

The servant of the merchant, named Puṇṇa, also offered his portion of rice to the Paccekabuddha and made an aspiration: "From this existence onwards, may I never encounter or see such a danger of famine. May all these people be my masters. When I plow the field, let there be seven furrows, each as wide as a wooden trough—three on the right, three on the left, and one in the middle."

## The Paccekabuddha Giving Blessings and Departing

At the end of everyone's aspirations, the Paccekabuddha said, "May it be as you have wished," and recited:

May what you have wished and longed for
Be fulfilled quickly.
May all your intentions be fulfilled,
Like the moon on the fifteenth day.

May what you have wished and longed for
Be fulfilled quickly.
May all your intentions be fulfilled,
Like a wish-fulfilling gem.

After the Paccekabuddha had joyfully given the blessing (anumodanā), he thought, "It is proper for me to inspire faith in these people." He then made a determination: "May these people be able to see me until I reach Mount Gandhamādana," and he departed. They remained there, watching him. Having arrived, he shared that food with five hundred other Paccekabuddhas. Through the power of the Paccekabuddha, that food was sufficient for all five hundred Paccekabuddhas. The donors remained there, watching.

## The Washed Pot Filling with Rice

After midday had passed, the merchant's wife washed the rice pot, covered it with a lid, and set it aside. The merchant, overcome by hunger, lay down and fell asleep. Waking up in the evening, he said to his wife, "My dear, I am very hungry. Are there not some burnt rice crusts left at the bottom of the pot?" Although the merchant's wife knew she had washed the pot, she did not say "There is none." Instead, thinking, "I will tell him after opening the pot," she rose, went to the pot, and opened it. Immediately, the pot was full of rice with the color of jasmine buds. The lid of the pot was pushed up. Upon seeing the rice, the merchant's wife was filled with joy throughout her body and said to the merchant, "Rise, my lord! I washed the pot and closed it, but now it is full of rice the color of jasmine buds. Meritorious deeds are indeed to be performed; giving is indeed worthy of being done. Rise, my lord, and eat!"

The merchant's wife served the father and son. When the two had finished eating and risen, she sat with her daughter-in-law and gave rice to the servant Puṇṇa. No matter how much was taken out, the rice did not decrease; only the mark where the ladle had scooped once remained visible. On that very day, the granaries and other storage places became full again, just as they had been before. The merchant had it proclaimed in the city, "Rice has appeared in the merchant's house! Let those who need rice come and take it!"
237:
People took seed-rice from that great treasurer's house. All the inhabitants of Jambudīpa lived depending on that great treasurer of Bārāṇasī.

## The Merit of the Great Treasurer Meṇḍaka
When that great treasurer of Bārāṇasī passed away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. Wandering through the celestial and human realms, he was reborn into a treasurer's family in the city of Bhaddiya during the time our Buddha appeared. The treasurer's wife was also reborn into a family of great wealth, and upon reaching maturity, she went to the house of that very treasurer. Depending on the treasurer's past meritorious deeds, rams of the aforementioned kind appeared at the back of the house.

The son was indeed their son, the daughter-in-law was the daughter-in-law, and the servant was the servant. Then one day, the great treasurer Meṇḍaka, wishing to test his merit, had twelve hundred and fifty granaries cleaned. After bathing his head, he sat at the door and looked up. All the granaries were filled with the aforementioned red hill-paddy. The treasurer, wishing to test the merit of the others as well, said to his wife, son, and others, "You all should also test your merit."

## The Merit of the Great Treasurer's Wife Candapadumā
Then the treasurer's wife, adorned with all ornaments, took a single measure (salay) of rice while a great crowd watched. She had that rice cooked into a meal and sat on a seat prepared at the gateway. Holding a golden ladle, she had it proclaimed, "Let those who desire food come!" She filled the vessels brought by each person who came and gave it to them. Even though she gave all day long, only the spot where she took the rice with the ladle was visible. Because she had previously offered alms-food to past Buddhas and the community of monks (Saṅgha) by holding the rice pot with her left hand and the ladle with her right hand, filling their bowls in this very manner, a lotus (paduma) mark appeared filling her left palm, and a moon-disc (canda) mark appeared filling her right palm. Furthermore, because she used to wander about filtering water for the community of monks with a water-filter (dhammakaraka) held in her left hand, a moon-disc mark appeared filling her right sole, and a lotus mark appeared filling her left sole.

Because of these marks, they named that treasurer's wife Candapadumā.

## The Merit of the Son, Daughter-in-law, and Servant
The treasurer's son also bathed his head, took a bag containing a thousand coins (kahāpaṇas), and said, "Let those who desire coins come!" He filled the vessels brought by each person who came and gave them. The thousand coins in the bag remained as they were.

The treasurer's daughter-in-law also adorned herself with all ornaments, took a basket of grain, and sat in the open courtyard. Saying, "Let those who desire seed-rice come!", she filled the vessels brought by each person who came and gave it to them. The basket remained as full as it was.
238:
The treasurer’s servant named Puṇṇa, also adorned with all kinds of ornaments, yoked the oxen to golden yokes with golden ropes. Holding a golden goad, he marked the two oxen with the five-finger marks of sandalwood, placed golden casings on their horns, and went to the field to drive them. Seven furrows were broken: three on the right, three on the left, and one in the middle. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa took whatever they desired—rice, seeds, silver, gold, and so on—only from the house of Meṇḍaka the treasurer.

## Attaining the Path and Fruit in the Presence of the Buddha
These five individuals possessed great merit. When the treasurer, who possessed such great power, heard that the Teacher had arrived, he set out to welcome the Teacher. On the way, he saw the heretics (Titthiyas).
