The heretics tried to stop him, saying, 'Treasurer, why do you, who believe in the efficacy of action (kiriyavāda), go to the ascetic Gotama, who teaches the non-efficacy of action (akiriyavāda)?' However, he disregarded their words, went to the Teacher, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. Then the Teacher gave him a graduated discourse. At the end of the teaching, Meṇḍaka the treasurer attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and informed the Teacher how the heretics had spoken ill of him and tried to prevent him from coming. Then the Teacher said to him, 'Treasurer, it is the nature of these beings that they do not see their own faults, however great they may be. But they make the non-existent faults of others appear as if they exist and broadcast them everywhere like winnowing chaff.' He then spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(252) The faults of others are easily seen, but one's own are hard to see.
For one winnows the faults of others like chaff,
But hides one's own, like a cunning gambler hides a losing throw.

'Of others' (aññesaṃ): the faults (vajjaṃ) of another, even if as small as an atom, are 'easily seen' (sudassaṃ), meaning they can be seen with ease. But one's own (attano) faults, even if very great, are 'hard to see' (duddasaṃ). 'For' (hi): for that reason, that person places the faults of others in a prominent place, such as in the midst of the Saṅgha, and 'winnows' (opunāti) them as if winnowing chaff (bhusaṃ). 'Like a cunning gambler hides a losing throw' (kaliṃva kitavā saṭho): here, one's own self, because of its state of being faulty, is called 'kali'. The act of concealing with branches and the like is called 'kitavā'. The bird-hunter is called 'cunning' (saṭho). Just as a bird-hunter, wishing to catch and kill birds, conceals himself like a gambler, so too one hides one's own faults.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of Meṇḍaka the Treasurer ends.
239:
## The Teaching
(253) For one who constantly sees the faults of others and is always irritable, their taints increase; they are far from the destruction of taints.

Paravajjānupassissa: for one who repeatedly looks for the faults of others. Niccaṃ: always. Ujjhānasaññino: having the perception of wanting to criticize or disparage. Tassa: for that monk. Āsavā: the taints. Vaḍḍhanti: increase. So: that monk. Āsavakkhayā: from the path of Arahantship, which is the end of the four taints. Ārā: is very far.

## 11. The Story of the Elder Ujjhānasaññī
(Ujjhānasaññittheravatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Paravajjānupassissa," concerning an elder named Ujjhānasaññī.

## Seeking Faults to Criticize
That Elder Ujjhānasaññī used to wander around seeking only the faults and lapses of the monks, saying, "This person dresses like this; this person wears his robe like that." The monks reported to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, a certain elder named so-and-so acts in this way." The Buddha said, "Monks, if one stands on the head of the rules and gives such advice, it is not fault-finding. However, if one constantly wanders about seeking the lapses of others with the perception of wanting to criticize, not even one spiritual distinction such as jhāna will arise for that person; only the taints will increase." He then spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the Elder Ujjhānasaññī ends.

## 12. The Story of Subhadda the Wanderer
(Subhaddaparibbājakavatthu)
While lying on the couch of his Parinibbāna in the Sal grove of the Malla kings at the bend of Kusinārā, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Ākāse," concerning Subhadda the Wanderer.
240:
## The Teaching
(254) There is no footprint in the sky. There is no recluse outside [the Dhamma]. Mankind delights in conceptual proliferation; the Tathāgatas are free from conceptual proliferation.

(255) There is no footprint in the sky. There is no recluse outside. There are no eternal conditioned things. There is no agitation for the Buddhas.

Ākāse: in the sky. Padaṃ: a footprint. Natthi eva: there is simply none. Bāhire: outside of my Dispensation. Samaṇo: a monk who has attained the paths and fruits. Natthi eva: there is simply none. Pajā: the multitude of beings. Pappañcābhiratā: they greatly delight in conceptual proliferations that expand the cycle of rebirth. Tathāgatā: the Buddhas. Nippappañcā: are free from conceptual proliferations that expand the cycle of rebirth.

Ākāse: in the sky. Padaṃ: a footprint. Natthi: there is none. Bāhire: outside of this Dispensation. Samaṇo: a monk who has attained the paths and fruits. Natthi: there is none. Sassatā: eternal. Saṅkhārā: the conditioned things of the five aggregates. Natthi: there are none. Buddhānaṃ: for the Buddhas. Iñjitaṃ: agitation through craving, conceit, and views. Natthi: there is none.

## Meeting the Buddha at the Last Moment
In the past, when two brothers were giving the first-fruits of their harvest as alms nine times during a single crop, this Subhadda the Wanderer, being unwilling to give, hesitated and stayed behind, giving only at the very end. Therefore, he did not get to see the Buddha during the early period of Enlightenment or the middle period. However, in the final period, when it was time for the Buddha's Parinibbāna, he thought, "I have asked elderly wanderers about my doubts regarding three questions, but I did not ask the recluse Gotama, thinking he was young. Now it is the time for the recluse Gotama to attain Parinibbāna. Later, I might feel remorse because I did not ask the recluse Gotama." Thus, he approached the Buddha. Although he was forbidden by the Elder Ānanda, the Buddha granted him permission, saying, "Dear Ānanda, do not forbid Subhadda; let him ask me his questions." He was then brought inside the curtain and, sitting near the couch, he asked these questions: "O Venerable Gotama, how is it? Is there such a thing as a footprint in the sky? Is there a recluse outside of this Dispensation? Are there such things as eternal conditioned things?" Then, the Buddha, wishing to explain the non-existence of those footprints and so forth to Subhadda the Wanderer, taught the Dhamma with these verses:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, Subhadda the Wanderer was established in the fruit of a Non-returner. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled company.

The story of Subhadda the Wanderer ends.

The Explanation of the Chapter on Impurities (Mala Vagga) is finished.

The Eighteenth Chapter.
241:
(257) One who leads others non-arbitrarily, by Dhamma and impartiality, that wise guardian of the Dhamma is called "established in Dhamma."

Yena: by whatever reason. Atthaṃ: the matter that has come for judgment. Sāhasā: by speaking erroneously or arbitrarily. Naye: one should decide. Tena: by such a reason. Dhammaṭṭho: one established in Dhamma. Na hoti: he is not.

## 19. Dhammaṭṭha Vagga
## 1. The Story of the High Officials who Judge
(Vinicchayamahāmattavatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Na tena hoti," concerning the high officials who judge.

## Unfair Judgment through Bribes
One day, after wandering for alms in a village near the north gate of Sāvatthī and returning from the alms-round, the monks were coming back to the monastery through the center of the city. At that moment, a storm arose and it rained. They entered the nearby hall of justice and saw the judges taking bribes and deciding that the rightful owners were not the owners. Seeing this, they thought, "Oh, these officials are very unrighteous! We had thought that these people judged according to the Dhamma." When the rain stopped, they went to the monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, and sitting in a suitable place, reported the matter. The Buddha said, "Monks, those who follow the dictates of favoritism and so forth and decide a matter arbitrarily are not called 'established in Dhamma.' Only those who investigate the offense with wisdom and decide non-arbitrarily according to the offense are called 'established in Dhamma'." He then spoke these verses:

## The Teaching
(256) One is not established in Dhamma because one decides a case arbitrarily. The wise one should investigate both what is right and what is wrong.
242:
(Being established in favoritism, one speaks false words and makes one who is not the owner of property the owner. Being established in anger, one speaks false words to one's enemies and makes the actual owner of property not the owner. Being established in delusion, when making a decision after taking a bribe, one looks here and there as if thinking of something else and, speaking false words, removes the other person saying, 'This person wins, this person loses.' Being established in fear, even if a certain powerful person loses, one makes them reach victory. This judge is said to decide a case by speaking false words. Even though he is established in the law of adjudication, he is not called one who stands in Dhamma.)

Yo ca paṇḍito: And that wise person. Atthañca: the true cause. Anatthañca: and the false cause. Ubho: both of these. Niccheyya: having decided. Vadati: speaks.

Asāhasena: by speaking without falsehood. Dhammena: by the law of adjudication. Samena: according to the fault, he leads others to victory or defeat. Dhammassa: of the Dhamma. Gutto: one who guards. Medhāvī: the wise one endowed with sharp wisdom of the essence of Dhamma. So paṇḍito: that wise person. Dhammaṭṭhoti: as one who stands in Dhamma. Pavuccati: is called.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people reached the fruit of Sotāpatti and so forth.
The story of the Great Ministers of Justice is finished.

## The Teaching
(258) Na tena paṇḍito hoti, yāvatā bahu bhāsati.
Khemi averī abhayo, paṇḍito ti pavuccati.

Yo: Whoever. Yāvatā: by as much as. Bahuṃ: much speech. Bhāsati: speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha and so forth. Tena: by that much talkativeness. So: that person. Paṇḍito nāma: called wise. Na hoti: is not. Yo ca: But whoever. Khemī: is safe. Averī: is free from the five enemies. Abhayo: does not act to cause fear to others. So: that person. Paṇḍito ti: as wise. Pavuccati: is called.

## 2. The Story of the Group of Six Monks
(Chabbaggiyavatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching, "Na tena paṇḍito hoti," etc., concerning the Group of Six monks (Chabbaggiya).

## Disturbance in the Refectory
Those Group of Six monks were wandering about, causing disturbance and confusion in the refectory both in the monastery and in the village. Then one day, when the monks had finished their meal in the village and returned, they asked the junior monks and novices, "Friends, how was the refectory?" "Venerable sirs, do not ask. The Group of Six monks said, 'Only we are clever and sharp; only we are wise. We will beat these monks, pour rubbish and dust on their heads, and drag them out.' Saying so, they grabbed us by our backs, poured rubbish and dust on us, and caused disturbance and confusion in the refectory." When they said this, the monks went to the presence of the Blessed One and reported that matter.
243:
The Blessed One said, "Monks, I do not call one who speaks much and oppresses others 'wise.' Only one who is safe, free from enmity, and acts to be free from danger do I call 'wise'," and he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people reached the fruit of Sotāpatti and so forth.
The story of the Group of Six monks is finished.

Adhicetaso appamajjato, munino monapathesu sikkhato.
Sokā na bhavanti tādino, upasantassa sadā satīmato.

Adhicetaso: To one who has the most noble mind of the fruit of Arahatship. Appamajjato: to one who is diligent in practicing faultless Dhamma. Monapathesu: in the three trainings which are the cause of the knowledge of the path of Arahatship. Sikkhato: to one who has practiced. Tādino: to one endowed with the quality of Tādi (steadfastness). Upasantassa: to one who is calmed by the calming of passion and so forth. Sadā: at all times. Satīmato: to one endowed with mindfulness. Munino: to the Arahat. (Or) within the Arahat. Sokā: sorrows caused by separation from pleasant objects and so forth. Na bhavanti: do not occur.

## 3. The Story of the Arahat Elder Ekudāna
(Ekudānakhīṇāsavattheravatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching, "Na tāvatā," etc., concerning the Arahat named Elder Ekudāna.

## The Verse for which the Devas Shouted Sādhu
That Arahat lived alone in a forest grove. That Arahat studied only one Udāna verse. That studied Udāna verse was:

That Elder Ekudāna, on Uposatha days, would himself announce the hearing of Dhamma and recite this verse. There would be the sound of the devas' applause and shouting of "Sādhu," like the sound of the earth splitting. Later, on one Uposatha day, two monks who were bearers of the Tipiṭaka, each with a following of five hundred, arrived at the dwelling place of that Elder Ekudāna. As soon as Elder Ekudāna saw those monks, with a joyful heart, he said, "Venerable sirs, you have done a good thing by coming here. Today we shall hear the Dhamma of the venerable ones." When asked, "Friend, are there those who wish to hear Dhamma here?", he replied, "Venerable sirs, there are those who wish to hear Dhamma. This forest grove, on the day of hearing Dhamma, is filled with the echoing sound of the devas' applause."

## Devas Do Not Shout Sādhu for Every Sermon
Among those two Elders, one Tipiṭaka-bearing Elder initiated the discourse and preached until the end. The other Tipiṭaka-bearing Elder explained the meaning in detail. Not even a single deva gave a shout of applause.
244:
## The Teaching

(259) One is not a Dhamma-bearer just because he speaks much.
But he who, having heard even a little, sees the Dhamma with his mental body,
And who is not negligent regarding the Dhamma—he is indeed a Dhamma-bearer.

**Yāvatā**: by as much as the reason of learning, upholding, and reciting, etc. **Bahu bhāsati**: speaks much. **Tāvatā**: by that much reason of merely being able to speak. **Dhamma-dharo**: a bearer of the Dhamma. **Na hoti**: is not. **Yo ca**: but whoever. **Appam pi**: even a little Dhamma. **Sutvāna**: having heard. **Dhammaṃ**: the Four Noble Truths. **Kāyena**: with the mental body (nāmakāya). **Passati**: sees and knows. **Yo ca**: and whoever. **Dhammaṃ**: the Dhamma. **Nappamajjati**: is not negligent. **Sa**: he (those two types of persons). **Ve**: indeed. **Dhamma-dharo**: is called a Dhamma-bearer. **Hoti**: is.

Those monks said, "Friend, you said that on the day you heard the Dhamma, the deities in this forest grove gave loud applause. What kind of sound was this applause?" When he replied, "Venerable sirs, on other days, the sound of applause would echo all at once. But as for today, I do not know the reason why it happened like this," they said, "Friend, if that is so, you please preach the Dhamma first."

That Elder Ekudāna, holding a fan and sitting in the preaching seat, preached only that same verse. The deities gave the sound of applause with a great noise. At that time, the monks who were the retinue of those two [Tripitaka-bearing] Elders complained, "The deities living in this forest grove give applause by looking at faces. Even when monks who bear the Tripitaka preach this much Dhamma, they do not say even a word of praise; yet when this old Elder preaches a single verse, they give applause with a great sound."

On another day, when Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya had gone to attend to the Blessed One and had just departed, about thirty forest-dwelling monks arrived, saw Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, sat down. ## 5. The Story of Many Monks
(Sambahulabhikkhu Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Na vāk-karaṇamattena," in reference to many monks.

## Monks Desiring Gain and Honor
On one occasion, some elder monks saw young monks and novices performing various duties, such as dyeing robes, only for their own teachers. They thought: "We too are skilled in the science of grammar, yet we have no such service. What if we approach the Teacher and say, 'Venerable Sir, we are skilled in grammar. Please command the young monks and novices not to recite or study the Dhamma with others without first purifying it with us.' If we do this, our gains and honors will increase."

They approached the Teacher and spoke as they had planned. Having heard their words, the Teacher understood: "In this Dispensation, such a thing should be said only with the intent of preserving the lineage. These monks, however, are motivated by gain and honor." He then said, "I do not say that you are 'good-natured' merely because you can speak well. Only he who has completely uprooted those unwholesome states like envy through the Path of Arahatship is truly good-natured." He then spoke these verses.

## 6. The Story of the Monk Hatthaka
(Hatthaka Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Na muṇḍakena samaṇo," in reference to a monk named Hatthaka.

## Not a Recluse by a Shaven Head Alone
That monk named Hatthaka used to send word to those of other sects with the intention of engaging in debate. He would make appointments, saying, "Come to such-and-such a place at such-and-such a time; let us engage in a debate of doctrines." He would go to that place beforehand and say, "Look, the heretics dare not come because they fear me. This very failure to appear is their defeat." He went about issuing challenges in this manner. He would cover one statement with another (evading the truth). When the Teacher heard that the monk Hatthaka was acting in this way, He had Hatthaka summoned and asked, "Is it true, Hatthaka, that you are doing this?" When Hatthaka replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Buddha rebuked him, saying, "Why do you act thus? One who speaks such false words does not become a recluse (samaṇa) merely by shaving the head. Only the monk who remains having stilled all evils, small or large, is truly a recluse." He then spoke these verses:

## 7. The Story of a Certain Brahmin

While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this religious teaching beginning with "Na tena bhikkhu so hoti," concerning a certain unnamed Brahmin.

## Not a Bhikkhu Merely by Begging
That Brahmin, having gone forth in a sect outside the Dispensation, while wandering for alms, thought: "The ascetic Gotama calls his disciples who wander for alms 'bhikkhus'; it is fitting that he should call me a 'bhikkhu' as well." He approached the Teacher and said, "O Teacher Gotama, I also live by wandering for alms; please call me a 'bhikkhu' as well."

Then the Teacher said to him, "Brahmin, I do not call one a bhikkhu merely because he begs for alms. One who undertakes and practices discordant or foul-smelling conduct is not called a bhikkhu. But he who reflects upon all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) with wisdom and wanders—he is indeed called a bhikkhu," and he spoke these verses.

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

## 8. The Story of the Non-Buddhist Ascetics
(Titthiya Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this religious teaching beginning with "Na monena," concerning the non-Buddhist ascetics (titthiyas).

Those ascetics, at the places where they ate, would depart after uttering auspicious words to the people, such as: "May you be free from danger, may you be happy, may your life be long; there is mud in such a place, there are thorns in such a place, one should not go to such a place."

However, during the early period of Enlightenment (Pathama-bodhi) when the preaching of Dhamma and the giving of thanks (anumodanā) had not yet been permitted, the monks would depart from the dining hall without giving thanks to the people. The people complained, saying, "We hear auspicious words from the non-Buddhist ascetics, but the venerable ones depart in silence."

The monks reported this matter to the Teacher. The Teacher permitted them, saying, "Monks, from this day forward, give thanks as you please in dining halls and other places; speak words of Dhamma to those who approach and sit near you; preach the Dhamma."

The monks did as the Buddha permitted. Because the people heard the teachings such as the giving of thanks, they became enthusiastic, invited the monks, and went about performing offerings and honors.

## One Cannot Be Called a Sage Merely by Silence
The non-Buddhist ascetics then complained, saying, "We practice the conduct of a sage (muni) by remaining silent. But the disciples of the ascetic Gotama go about speaking many words in dining halls and other places."

When the Buddha heard of this, he said, "Monks, I do not say that one is a sage merely by remaining silent. Some do not speak because they do not know; some do not dare to speak because they lack confidence; some do not speak out of stinginess, wishing that others may not know this matter of profound meaning through their silence. Therefore, one is not a sage merely by silence; only by the calming of evil is one truly a sage," and he spoke these verses.
250:
(One is truly a sage only through the path-knowledge known as the practice of sageliness, by remaining silent in the sense of avoiding evil; one is not a sage merely by remaining silent while lacking such practice. Such a person is merely one of an empty nature, lacking wisdom and understanding.)

Yo ca paṇḍito, and that wise person; tulaṃ paggayha ṭhito viya hutvā, being like one who stands holding a scale; varaṃ, taking the noble Dhamma; pāpāni parivajjeti, avoids evil unwholesome deeds. Tena, for that reason; so paṇḍito, that wise person; munī, is called a sage.

(The analogy is this: a person holding a scale removes what is in excess and adds what is lacking. Similarly, just as one removes the excess, a person removes and avoids evil. Just as one adds what is lacking, a person fulfills and practices merit to completion. By doing so, taking only the noble Dhamma known as virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they are able to avoid evil unwholesome actions. For that stated reason, that person is called a sage.)

Yo muni, that monk who; ubho loke, knows both worlds, known as the internal aggregates and external aggregates; munāti, knows them. Tena, for that reason; so muni, that monk; muni, a sage; pavuccati, is so called.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of the Titthiyas ends.

## 9. The Story of the Fisherman named Ariya
(Bālisika Vatthu)

While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, "Na tena ariyo hoti," and so forth, concerning a fisherman named Ariya.

## One Who Takes Life is Not Noble
One day, the Teacher, perceiving the supportive condition (upanissaya) for the Path of Stream-entry in the fisherman named Ariya, went for alms in a village near the north gate of Sāvatthī. Returning from that village surrounded by the community of monks, the Teacher saw the fisherman catching fish with a hook and line. At that moment, the fisherman, seeing the community of monks led by the Buddha, cast aside his fishing rod and stood still.
251:
The Teacher stopped and stood at a place not far from him and asked the names of Elder Sāriputta and others: "What is your name?" The elders also replied with their respective names, saying, "I am Sāriputta, Lord," "I am Moggallāna, Lord." The fisherman thought, "The Teacher is asking everyone's name. I suppose he might ask my name too." The Teacher, knowing his wish, asked, "Lay follower, what is your name?" When he replied, "Venerable Sir, my name is Ariya," the Teacher said, "Lay follower, those who take life like that are not called 'Ariya' (Noble). Those who are Noble are established in the state of non-harming towards the multitude of beings," and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(270) One is not noble because one harms living beings.
By not harming all living beings, one is called "Noble."

Yena, by that reason which; pāṇāni hiṃsati, one harms and oppresses living beings; tena, by that reason of harming; ariyo na hoti, one is not called Noble. Sabbapāṇāni ahaṃsā, because of not harming or oppressing any living beings; ariyoti pavuccati, one is called Noble.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the fisherman named Ariya was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

## 10. The Story of Many Monks Endowed with Virtue, etc.
(Sambahula-sīlādi-sampanna-bhikkhu Vatthu)

While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, "Na sīlabbatamattena," and so forth, concerning many monks who were endowed with virtue and other qualities.

## Not at Peace Until the Taints are Destroyed
Among those monks, some had this thought: "We possess perfected virtue, we are observers of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), we are very learned, we dwell in secluded lodgings, we are attainers of jhāna. For us, Arahantship will not be difficult to attain; we shall reach Arahantship on whatever day we wish." Among them, those who were Non-returners (Anāgāmī) also thought: "For us now, Arahantship will not be difficult to obtain." One day, all those monks approached the Teacher...
252:
## The Teaching

(271) Not by mere moral conduct and vows, nor by much learning, nor by the attainment of concentration, nor by dwelling in solitude.

(272) Do I experience the bliss of renunciation (Anāgāmi-phala) not attained by worldlings. O bhikkhu, do not be confident [of having ended suffering] as long as you have not reached the destruction of the taints (Arahantship).

O Bhikkhu, dear monk. (The Buddha used the singular form to address any one of those many monks). By mere moral conduct and vows (sīlabbatamattena): by the fourfold purity of virtue and the thirteen ascetic practices. By much learning (bāhusaccena): by being able to learn the Three Piṭakas. By the attainment of concentration (samādhilābhena): by attaining the eight meditative attainments. By dwelling in solitude (vivittasayanena): by living in a secluded forest monastery. (The words 'pana' and 'athavā' are omitted in this explanation.)

Not attained by worldlings (aputhujjanasevitaṃ): that which is not resorted to by worldlings; or, that which is resorted to only by the Noble Ones (Ariyas). The bliss of renunciation (nekkhammasukhaṃ): the bliss of the Fruit of Non-Returning (Anāgāmi-phala). I experience (phusāmi): I reach/attain.

By mere attainment of this much (iti ettakamattena vā): by merely attaining the bliss of the Fruit of Non-Returning. O Bhikkhu, dear monk. As long as you have not reached (appatto): if you have not yet reached. The destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayaṃ): the bliss of the Fruit of Arahantship. Do not be confident (vissāsaṃ na āpādi): do not reach the state of being complacent in existence.

While they were staying there after approaching and paying homage, the Buddha asked, "O monks, has your task as monks truly reached its end?" When thus asked, the monks replied, "Venerable Sir, we are monks of such and such nature; therefore, we remain thinking, 'We are capable of reaching Arahantship at any moment we desire.'"

Hearing their words, the Buddha said, "Monks, a monk should not say 'Our suffering in the round of rebirth is little' merely by having pure fourfold virtue and so on, or merely by reaching the bliss of the Fruit of Non-Returning. Until the destruction of taints is reached, one should not let the thought 'I have attained happiness' arise." Having said this, he spoke these verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, those many monks were established in Arahantship. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of Many Monks Endowed with Virtue, etc., ends.

## 1. The Story of the Five Hundred Monks
(Pañcasatabhikkhu Vatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko," while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, concerning five hundred monks.

## Bringing Dhamma into Conversation

It is said that after those five hundred monks had wandered through the countryside with the Teacher and returned to Sāvatthī, they sat in the service hall and discussed the paths they had traveled, saying, "The road from such-and-such a village to such-and-such a village is smooth; the road to such-and-such a village is rough, it has gravel, it has no gravel," and so on. In this manner, they discussed matters related to paths based on the roads they had traveled.

The Teacher, seeing that those five hundred monks possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for attaining Arahantship, went to the service hall, sat on the prepared seat, and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such-and-such a discussion," he said, "Monks, this is an external path. A monk should perform the work to be done on the Noble Path traveled by the Noble Ones." He then added, "By doing so, a monk can be liberated from all the suffering of the round of rebirth," and spoke these verses.

(Whether it be footpaths (jaṅghamagga), cart tracks (sakaṭamagga), and so on, or the paths associated with the sixty-two views—among all paths, that path which, by means of the eight factors such as Right View, abandons the eight factors such as wrong view, taking Nibbāna as the object and accomplishing the tasks of fully understanding the Truth of Suffering, abandoning the Truth of the Origin, realizing the Truth of Cessation, and developing the Truth of the Path—that Eightfold Path is especially excellent.)

Of truths (saccānaṃ), the four words (caturo padā) [the Four Noble Truths] are the best (seṭṭhā).
254:
(Whether it be the truth of speech as in 'Speak the truth, do not yield to anger'; or conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) such as 'the Brahmin named Sacca' or 'the King named Sacca'; or the truth of views (diṭṭhi-sacca) such as 'This alone is truth, all else is false'; or the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca) such as 'The Noble Truth of Suffering'—among all these truths, the four factors starting with 'The Noble Truth of Suffering' are supreme, because they are to be fully understood, realized, abandoned, developed, and because of their nature of singular and truthful penetration.)

Among all states (dhammā), detachment (virāga), which is Nibbāna, is the best.

(The Buddha taught: 'Monks, as far as there are conditioned or unconditioned states, detachment is said to be the foremost among them.' Therefore, among all states, Nibbāna is supreme.)

Among bipeds, the Tathāgata, the Seeing One who possesses the five eyes, is the best.

(The word 'ca' in the phrase 'dvipadānañca' has a collective sense, including mental states (arūpa-dhammā). Therefore, the Buddha is supreme even over mental states.)

For the purification of vision (the path and its fruit), this Eightfold Path is the only path; there is no other path besides this Eightfold Path. You should follow this Eightfold Path. Following this path is the bewildering of Māra.

Indeed, if you follow this Eightfold Path, you will make an end of all suffering in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Having known the path that can extract the thorns such as lust...

(Having known it through personal realization, without relying on hearsay from others.)

I have taught you this Eightfold Path.

You must make the effort (ātappa) that burns away the defilements.

(The effort made to prevent unarisen unwholesome states and to abandon arisen unwholesome states is called 'ātappa' because it burns away the defilements. One must exert this effort to attain the path.)

The Tathāgatas are only teachers. Those who follow the path as taught and meditate with the two types of jhāna will be released from the bonds of Māra.

(The Buddhas only teach the way. Therefore, those who practice according to the teaching and meditate using both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) jhānas will be released from the bonds of Māra, known as the suffering of the round of rebirth in the three planes.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, those monks were established in Arahatship. The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of the Five Hundred Monks is finished.

(277) 'All conditioned things are impermanent.' When one sees this with wisdom,
Then one becomes weary of suffering. This is the path to purification.

Monks, all conditioned things are impermanent. When one sees this with insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), then one becomes weary of the suffering of saṃsāra. This weariness is the path to the benefit of Nibbāna, which is purification.

## 2. The Story of the Characteristic of Impermanence (Aniccalakkhaṇa Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, gave this teaching starting with 'Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā' concerning five hundred monks.

## The Benefit of Past Practice on Impermanence

Those monks, having taken a subject of meditation from the Teacher, went to the forest and strove diligently. However, failing to reach Arahatship, they returned, thinking, 'We shall learn the meditation subject more specifically.' The Teacher, reflecting on what would be suitable for them, realized: 'In the time of Kassapa Buddha, these monks practiced the characteristic of impermanence for twenty thousand years. Therefore, it is appropriate to teach them a single verse regarding the characteristic of impermanence.' He said, 'Monks, all conditioned things in the realms of existence such as the sensual realm are indeed impermanent, in the sense of non-existence after having come to be,' and spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, those five hundred monks were established in Arahatship. The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of the Characteristic of Impermanence is finished.

## 3. The Story of the Characteristic of Suffering (Dukkhalakkhaṇa Vatthu)

The story for the second verse is similar in nature to the first one already mentioned.

## The Benefit of Past Practice on Suffering

At that time, the Buddha, knowing that those monks had previously applied their minds and made efforts regarding the characteristic of suffering, said: 'Monks, all five aggregates are indeed suffering, in the sense of being constantly oppressed,' and spoke this verse.

## Verse
(278) "All conditioned things are suffering"—when one sees this with wisdom, then one grows weary of suffering. This is the path to purity.

*Sabbe*: all. *Saṅkhārā*: conditioned things. *Dukkhā*: are suffering. *Iti*: thus. *Yadā*: when. *Paññāya*: with the wisdom of insight. *Passati*: one sees. *Atha*: then (upon seeing thus). *Dukkhe*: of the suffering of the round of rebirths. *Nibbindati*: one grows weary. *Esa*: this (weariness). *Visuddhiyā*: for the sake of the purity of Nibbāna. *Maggo*: is the path. *Hoti*: it is.

The Story of the Characteristic of Suffering is finished.

## Verse
(279) "All phenomena are non-self"—when one sees this with wisdom, then one grows weary of suffering. This is the path to purity.

*Sabbe*: all. *Dhammā*: phenomena (the five aggregates). *Anattā*: are not-self (do not follow one's will). *Iti*: thus. *Yadā*: when. *Paññāya*: with the wisdom of insight. *Passati*: one sees. *Atha*: then (upon seeing thus). *Dukkhe*: of the suffering of the round of rebirths. *Nibbindati*: one grows weary. *Esa*: this (weariness). *Visuddhiyā*: for the sake of the purity of Nibbāna. *Maggo*: is the path. *Hoti*: it is.

## 4. Anattalakkhaṇāvatthu
(The Story of the Characteristic of Non-self)
In this third verse, the story is the same as the previous ones.

## The Benefit of Previous Practice on Non-self
However, in this third story and verse, the Blessed One, knowing that those monks had repeatedly practiced the contemplation of the characteristic of non-self in the past, said, "Monks, all aggregates are indeed non-self because they do not follow one's will," and then spoke this verse.

The rest is the same as the previous story.

The Story of the Characteristic of Non-self is finished.

## 5. Padhānakammikatissattheravatthu
(The Story of Elder Tissa, the Striver)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Uṭṭhānakālamhi," concerning the Elder named Padhānakammika Tissa.

## The Lazy Monk's Later Regret
It is said that five hundred young men of good family living in Sāvatthī ordained in the presence of the Teacher, took meditation subjects, and went to the forest. Among those five hundred monks, one monk remained behind at that very Jetavana Monastery. The remaining monks practiced the Dhamma in the forest and, having attained Arahatship, returned to Sāvatthī, thinking, "We shall inform the Teacher of the virtues we have attained." When they were wandering for alms in a certain village about one league from Sāvatthī...
257:
He who desires to do later the tasks that should have been done earlier, like the lazy youth who broke the green Varuna wood thinking it was dry wood, suffers later.

*Yo*: he who. *Pubbe*: in the time before (at the outset). *Karaṇီyāni*: the tasks that should be done. *Pacchā*: later. *So*: (this is a grammatical marker for the ablative case). *Kātun*: to do. *Icchati*: desires. *Sa*: he. *Varuṇakaṭṭhabhañjova*: like the lazy youth who broke the green Varuna wood thinking it was dry wood. *Pacchā*: in the later time. *Anutappati*: suffers repeatedly.

## Verse
(280) One who does not strive when it is time to strive, though young and strong, is full of indolence; with a mind of sunken thoughts and lazy, such a person does not find the path of wisdom.

*Uṭṭhānakālamhi*: at the time when one should make an effort. *Anuṭṭhahāno*: not making an effort. *Yuvā*: being in the first stage of life. *Balī*: being endowed with strength. *Ālasiyaṃ upeto*: reaches the state of a lazy person (meaning, he eats and sleeps). *Saṃsannasaṅkappamano*: one whose mind is not filled with good thoughts. *Kusīto alaso*: a very lazy person. *Paññāya*: with wisdom. *Daṭṭhabbaṃ*: which should be seen. *Maggaṃ*: the Noble Path. *Na vindati*: does not attain.

Seeing them wandering for alms in a certain small village, a lay devotee offered them gruel, rice, and other food. After listening to the talk of appreciation (anumodanā), he invited them again for the next morning's merit. Those monks reached Sāvatthī on that very day, put away their bowls and robes, and in the evening, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Teacher, expressing great joy, engaged in friendly conversation with those monks. Then, their companion monk who had stayed behind at the Jetavana Monastery thought, "The Teacher's mouth seems insufficient to hold all the friendly words He is speaking with these monks. But because there is no Path or Fruit in my continuum, He does not speak with me. This very day, I will strive to attain Arahatship and approach the Teacher to make Him speak with me."

## The Lazy Monk Breaks His Leg Due to Effort
Those monks also informed the Teacher, saying, "Venerable Sir, on the way here, a lay devotee invited us for tomorrow's merit. We wish to go there early in the morning." Then, the monk who was their companion, while walking on the meditation path (caṅkama) throughout the three watches of the night, fell down on a stone slab at the end of the path due to sleepiness, and his thigh bone broke. He cried out with a loud voice. His companion monks, recognizing his voice, ran here and there. While they were lighting lamps and performing the necessary duties for the monk with the broken thigh, dawn broke. They did not get the opportunity to go to the village they were invited to. Then the Teacher asked the monks, "Monks, did you not go to the village for alms?" They replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir," and reported the incident.

## Reference to the Varuna Jātaka
The Teacher said, "Monks, this monk has not only now caused an obstacle to your gains. He did so in the past as well." Being requested by the monks, He brought forth the past and detailed the Varuna Jātaka from the Ekanipāta, Varuṇavagga. At that time, those monks were the five hundred students, this monk was the lazy student, and the Teacher was the world-honored teacher.
258:
"The lazy young man was once this monk with the broken thigh bone; and I myself was the teacher," the Blessed One brought this Dhamma teaching and said, "O monks, he who does not exert effort when it is time to exert effort, who is full of unfulfilled thoughts, who is lazy—such a person cannot attain the special Dhamma such as Jhāna," and then he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of Elder Padhānakammika Tissa ends.

## 6. The Story of the Pig-faced Ghost
(Sūkarapetavatthu)
The Teacher, while staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Vācānurakkhī' concerning a pig-faced ghost.

## The Pig with a Tail Growing in Its Mouth
One day, while the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was descending from Gijjhakūṭa Hill with the Elder Lakkhaṇa, he smiled at a certain place. When asked by the Elder Lakkhaṇa, "Friend, what is the cause for your smile?", he replied, "Friend, it is not the time for this question; ask me in the presence of the Teacher." After wandering for alms in Rājagaha with the Elder Lakkhaṇa and returning from the alms-round, they went to the Veḷuvana Monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down. Then the Elder Lakkhaṇa asked him about that matter. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna said, "Friend, I saw a ghost. His body was three gāvutas in size, and it was like a human body. But his head was like that of a pig, and a tail had grown in his mouth, from which maggots were oozing out. I had never seen such a being before; seeing that being, I smiled."

The Teacher said, "Monks, my disciples live as those who have vision," and continued, "I too saw that being at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Even though I saw him, I did not speak of it out of compassion for others, thinking, 'Those who do not believe me would suffer harm.' Now, having Moggallāna as a witness, I speak. Monks, what Moggallāna says is true."

## Two Very Harmonious Elders
Hearing those words, the monks asked the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, what was the past evil deed of that pig-faced ghost?" The Buddha said, "Monks, if so, listen," and brought forth the past story...
259:
...and preached the past evil deed of that pig-faced ghost.

In the time of the Buddha Kassapa, two elders lived in harmony in a small village. Among those two elders, one had sixty years of seniority (vassa), and the other had fifty-nine years. The younger elder of fifty-nine years used to carry the bowl and robes of the elder of sixty years. He performed all the major and minor duties like a novice (sāmaṇera). While those two elders were living in harmony like brothers born from the same womb, a certain Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika) arrived at their dwelling place.

At that time, it was also a day for listening to the Dhamma. The elders said to that Dhamma preacher, "O virtuous one, please preach a Dhamma discourse to us out of favor." The Dhamma preacher preached the Dhamma. The elders, with joyful hearts thinking, "We have found a Dhamma preacher," took him the next morning to the nearby village for alms. After finishing their meal in that village, they had him preach to the people, saying, "Friend, please preach the Dhamma a little further from where you preached yesterday." When the people heard the Dhamma discourse, they invited him again for the next day. In this way, they took the Dhamma preacher for alms in the surrounding villages for two days each.

## How the Dhamma Preacher Slandered
But the Dhamma preacher thought, "These two great elders are very soft and gentle. It would be proper for me to make both of them flee and live in this monastery myself." In the evening, he went to attend to the senior elder. When the other monks had left, he returned and approached the senior elder, saying, "Venerable Sir, there is something I wish to say." When given permission, "Friend, speak," he thought for a moment (pretending to deliberate) and said, "Venerable Sir, this kind of talk is very blameworthy," and left without saying anything. He went to the second elder and did the same. On the second day, he did the same. On the third day, when the two elders became very anxious, he approached the senior elder and said, "Venerable Sir, there is something I wish to say, but I do not dare to speak in your presence." When pressed by the elder, "Let it be, friend, just speak," he asked, "Venerable Sir, is the second elder a person of shared enjoyment (sambhogā) with you?" "Virtuous one, why do you say such a thing? We are like brothers born from the same womb. Whatever is obtained by one of us is also obtained by the other. I have never seen any fault in this younger elder for all this time." When he said this, the preacher asked again, "Venerable Sir, is this really true?" When told, "Friend, it is true," he said, "Venerable Sir, the second elder told me: 'Virtuous one, you are a son of a good family. This senior elder is a shameful (lajjī) and virtuous (pesala) person; if you have shared enjoyment with him, do so with careful investigation.' He has been telling me this since the day I arrived." As soon as the senior elder heard the words of the Dhamma preacher, his mind became filled with fierce anger, and he broke like a clay pot made by a potter hit by a staff.
260:
The Dhamma preacher also rose and went to the second elder, and spoke to him in the same manner. The second elder was also broken in the same way.

## The Separation of the Two Senior Elders

Among those two elders, for such a long time, not even one had ever entered for alms separately. Even though they had never done so, on the following morning, they entered for alms separately. The second elder arrived first and waited in the refectory. The senior elder arrived later. Upon seeing the senior elder, the junior elder thought, "How is it? Should I take the bowl and robes of this senior elder, or should I not?" Although he thought, "I will not take them now," he then softened his heart, thinking, "Be that as it may, I have never done such a thing before. It is not proper for me to neglect my duty." He approached the senior elder and said, "Venerable sir, please give me your bowl and robes."

The senior elder snapped his fingers and said, "Go away, ill-disciplined monk! You are not fit to take my bowl and robes." The junior elder replied, "Very well, venerable sir. I too had already thought that I would not take your bowl and robes." Then the senior elder said, "Friend, junior monk, what do you think? Do you think I have any attachment to this monastery?" The junior elder replied, "Venerable sir, what about you? Do you think that I have any attachment to this monastery?" The senior elder said, "This monastery is yours," and taking his bowl and robes, he departed. The junior elder also departed. Those two, the senior elder and the junior elder, did not even travel by the same path; one took the path through the west gate, and the other through the east gate. The Dhamma preacher pleaded, "Venerable sirs, do not do this! Do not do this!" But when they said, "Stay, friend Dhamma preacher," he stopped.

## Being Unable to Restrain Tears Upon Meeting

On the following morning, when that Dhamma preacher entered the nearby village for alms, the people asked, "Venerable sir, where are the two noble elders?" He replied, "Lay followers, do not ask. Your two teachers had a quarrel yesterday and left. Even though I pleaded with them, I could not make them return." Among those people, the foolish ones remained silent. However, those endowed with wisdom and discernment thought, "For such a long time, we have never seen any fault in these two noble elders. If trouble has arisen for them, it must have arisen because of this Dhamma preacher." Thus, they became distressed.

Those two senior elders did not find any peace of mind wherever they went. The senior elder thought, "Oh, the deed done by the junior monk is very grave indeed! He told the visiting monk, whom he had seen for only a moment, 'Do not associate with the senior elder.'"

The junior elder also thought, "Oh, the deed done by the senior elder is very grave indeed! He told the visiting monk, whom he had seen for only a moment, 'Do not associate with this junior monk.'" For those two senior elders, activities such as recitation and the practice of meditation could not be accomplished. After a hundred years had passed, those two senior elders arrived at a monastery in the western region.
261:
## The Teaching

(281) Guarded in speech, well-restrained in mind, and let one do no unwholesome deed with the body. One should purify these three paths of action, and one may attain the path proclaimed by the seers.

*Vācānurakkhī*: one is constantly guarded in speech by avoiding the four types of verbal misconduct. *Mamasā*: with the mind, by not allowing covetousness and so on to arise. *Susāṃvuto*: one is well-restrained. *Kāyena ca*: and by the body. *Akusalaṃ*: unwholesome deeds. *Na kkayirā*: one should not do. *Tayo ete kammapathe*: these three paths of action. *Visodhaye*: one should purify. *Evaṃ*: when purified in this way.

*Isippaveditaṃ*: proclaimed in various ways by the virtuous ones such as the Buddha. *Maggaṃ*: the Eightfold Path. *Ārādhaye*: one may achieve or attain.

For both of those senior elders, only a single dwelling place was available. When the senior elder entered and lay down on the couch, the junior elder also entered. As soon as the senior elder saw the junior elder, he recognized him and could not hold back his tears. The junior elder also recognized the senior elder and, with eyes full of tears, thought, "Should I speak or should I not?" Thinking, "That matter was not something worthy of belief," he paid homage to the senior elder and said, "Venerable Sir, for all this time I have been traveling while carrying your bowl and robes; have you ever seen anything inappropriate in my physical actions or other behaviors?" When he asked this, the elder replied, "Friend, I have never seen such a thing."

## The Dhamma-preacher Becoming a Pig-Ghost

"Venerable Sir, if you have never seen such a thing, why did you tell the Dhamma-preacher not to associate with this junior monk?" When asked this, the elder replied, "Friend, I did not say such a thing; it was you who reportedly said such things about me." When the junior monk replied, "Venerable Sir, I did not say that either," the two senior elders realized at that moment, "That Dhamma-preacher must have said this because he wished to divide us," and they confessed their faults to each other. Those two senior elders, who had not found peace of mind for a hundred years, became reconciled on that day and consulted together, saying, "Come, let us go; we shall expel that Dhamma-preacher from that monastery." They departed and in due course arrived at that monastery. When the Dhamma-preacher saw the two elders, he approached to receive their bowls and robes. The two elders snapped their fingers and said, "You are not a person fit to reside in this monastery." That Dhamma-preacher, unable to remain steady, fled immediately. At that time, the monastic practice he had performed for twenty thousand years was unable to support or save him. When he passed away from that life, he was reborn in the Avīci hell. After being cooked there for the interval between two Buddhas, he is now experiencing suffering on Gijjhakūṭa Mountain with the physical form previously described. Thus, the Buddha preached the past evil kamma of that pig-ghost. Having brought forth the past evil kamma of that pig-ghost, the Buddha said, "Monks, one who is called a monk should be peaceful in body and so on," and he spoke this verse:
262:
## The Benefits of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so on.

The Story of the Pig-Ghost ends.

## 7. The Story of Elder Poṭṭhila

(Poṭṭhilattheravatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher (the Buddha) spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yogā ve," concerning an elder named Poṭṭhila.

## Being Called "Empty" Despite Being Learned

That Elder Poṭṭhila was a master of the Three Pitakas (Tepiṭaka) during the dispensations of seven Buddhas (Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and Gotama) and taught the scriptures to five hundred monks. Our Buddha thought, "This monk Poṭṭhila does not have even the slightest thought of 'I will work for my own escape from the suffering of Saṃsāra.' I shall cause this monk Poṭṭhila to feel spiritual urgency (saṃvega)." From that time on, whenever Elder Poṭṭhila came to pay respects to Him, the Buddha would say, "Come, Empty (Tuccha) Poṭṭhila; pay homage, Empty Poṭṭhila; sit down, Empty Poṭṭhila; go, Empty Poṭṭhila," and so on. Even when he rose and left, the Buddha would say, "Empty Poṭṭhila has gone."

Elder Poṭṭhila reflected, "I master the Three Pitakas along with the Commentaries; I teach the scriptures to eighteen large groups of five hundred monks. Yet, the Teacher constantly calls me 'Empty Poṭṭhila.' Surely, the Teacher calls me this because of my lack of meditative absorption (jhāna) and such attainments." Having developed spiritual urgency, that monk Poṭṭhila thought, "Now I shall enter the forest and perform the duties of a recluse." Having thought thus, he prepared his own bowl and robes and, in the early dawn, departed along with a monk who was leaving after finishing his studies behind all the other monks. The monks who were residing and reciting in the precinct did not recognize him as their teacher. When Elder Poṭṭhila had traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty leagues, he arrived at a forest dwelling where thirty monks resided. Approaching those thirty monks, he said to the Chief Elder of the Sangha, "Venerable Sir, please be my refuge and support."

"Friend, you are a Dhamma-preacher. You have mastered the Three Pitakas by heart. We ourselves should learn something from you. Why do you speak like this?" When asked, he replied again, "Venerable Sirs, please do not do this; please be my refuge and support."

(All of those thirty monks were indeed Arahants.)
263:
## The Teaching

(282) From application, wisdom indeed arises; from non-application, the loss of wisdom. Knowing this two-fold path of gain and loss, let one so establish oneself that wisdom may grow.

From application (yoga), through wise reflection on the thirty-eight objects of meditation, vast wisdom (bhūri) that is like the earth truly arises. From non-application, the destruction and exhaustion of wisdom arises. Having known this two-fold path—the path of the increase of wisdom and the path of the non-increase of wisdom—let one establish oneself in meditation in such a way that wisdom increases.

## Subduing the Pride of the Learned One

When he had spoken thus, the senior Elder, thinking, "This monk Poṭṭhila may have pride because of his mastery of the Piṭaka," sent him to the second Elder. That second Elder also spoke to Poṭṭhila in the same manner as the senior Elder. In this way, all the senior Elders sent him from one to another until they sent him to a seven-year-old novice (sāmaṇera) who was sitting in his daytime quarters performing needlework. By sending him thus, they removed the pride of the monk Poṭṭhila.

With his pride subdued, Poṭṭhila approached the novice, raised his hands in salutation, and said, "O virtuous novice, please be my refuge."

"O teacher, how wonderful! Why do you say such a thing? You are elderly, of great age and seniority, and possess great learning. It is I who should learn something from you," the novice replied.

"O virtuous novice, do not do this. Please, just be my refuge," Poṭṭhila said.

"Venerable sir, if you are one who can endure admonishment, I shall be your refuge," the novice said.

"O virtuous novice, I am one who can endure admonishment. If you tell me to enter a fire, I shall enter the fire indeed," he replied.

Thereupon, the novice pointed to a pond nearby and said, "Venerable sir, enter this pond just as you are, dressed and robed."

(The novice's instruction was very appropriate. Even though he knew that Elder Poṭṭhila was wearing very expensive double-layered robes, he said this to test whether the Elder was truly capable of enduring admonishment.)

Elder Poṭṭhila, at that single word, descended into the water. When the edges of his robes became wet, the novice said, "Venerable sir, please come back." When the Elder returned and stood there at that single word, the novice taught him thus:

## The Dhamma Taught by the Seven-Year-Old Novice

"Venerable sir, in a certain anthill, there are six holes. A lizard has entered into the interior through one of those six holes. A person wishing to catch that lizard closes the other five holes, breaks open the sixth hole, and catches it through the entrance. In the same way, venerable sir, among the objects occurring at the six doors, you should close the five doors such as the eye door, etc., which are other than the mind-door (manodvāra),
264:
and establish your work at the mind-door."

To the monk Poṭṭhila, who was of great learning, this much teaching alone was like the lighting of a lamp. Saying, "O virtuous novice, let it be just this much," he applied his insight to the physical body (karajakāya) and began to practice the Dhamma of a recluse.

The Teacher (the Buddha), while sitting at a distance of one hundred and twenty leagues, looked at the monk Poṭṭhila and reflected, "Just as this monk is now possessed of vast wisdom, so too is it proper for him to establish himself." Then, diffusing his radiance as if speaking face-to-face with Poṭṭhila, he spoke this verse:

(Among the forty meditation objects, this refers to the thirty-eight meditation objects, excluding the two—the light kasina and the space kasina—which are not mentioned in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pali.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, Elder Poṭṭhila was established in Arahatship.

The story of Elder Poṭṭhila ends.

## 8. The Story of the Five Elderly Elders
(Pañcamahallakattheravatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Cut down the forest" (Vanaṃ chindatha) concerning many elderly monks.

## The Elderly Monks Weeping Over the Death of the Good Cook

It is said that while they were laypeople in the city of Sāvatthī, they were wealthy householders and friends who performed meritorious deeds together. Having heard the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, they thought, "We are now old; what is the use of living the household life?" They requested ordination from the Teacher and became monks. However, because of their old age, they were unable to master the Pali scriptures. They had a leaf-roofed hut built at the edge of the monastery and lived there together. Even when they went for alms, they mostly went to the houses of their former wives and children to eat. Among those elderly monks, the former wife of one of them was named Madhurapācikā. This female lay devotee was very helpful to all those elderly monks.

Therefore, all the elderly monks would take the food they had received and sit and eat at the house of that lay devotee, Madhurapācikā. Madhurapācikā would also offer them various well-prepared curries and dishes. One day, Madhurapācikā was afflicted by a certain illness and passed away. When she died, those elderly monks gathered at their friend's leaf-roofed hut, and embracing each other by the neck, they wept and lamented, saying, "The lay devotee Madhurapācikā, who knew how to cook such delicious food, has died!"

When other monks ran to them from all around and asked, "Friends, what is the reason for this weeping?" they replied, "Venerable sirs, the former wife of our friend the Elder has passed away. That lay devotee was a person who was very helpful to us. We are weeping because we wonder where we shall find such a lay devotee now."
265:
Are our jaws tired? Our mouths are parched.
We are giving up, we cannot reach the end; the great ocean remains just as full.

O crows! We are drawing out the ocean water with our beaks to dry it up. We cannot reach the end. Indeed, our jaws are weary. Our mouths are dry. The great ocean is as full as ever.

## The Teaching
(283) Cut down the forest [of defilements], not the [literal] tree; from the forest [of defilements] fear arises. Having cut down both the forest and the brushwood [of defilements], be without a forest, O monks.

(284) For as long as the brushwood [of desire] of a man for women is not cut down, even to the slightest degree, so long is his mind attached, like a suckling calf to its mother.

Monks, cut down the forest. Do not cut down the [literal] tree. From the forest, danger such as lions and so forth arises. Having cut down the forest (the large trees that grew first) and the brushwood (the small trees that grew later), be those who are free from defilements.

## Summary of the Samudda-kāka Jātaka
The monks were discussing a topic in the Dhamma hall. The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what subject are you gathered here discussing now?" When they informed him of the topic, he said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too, these elderly monks were born in the crow lineage. While wandering along the shore of the ocean, a female crow was swept into the sea by a wave and died. Lamenting and crying, they thought, 'We will rescue that female crow,' and they became exhausted by trying to bale out the ocean water with their beaks."

Relating this story of the past, he elaborated on this Samudda-kāka Jātaka from the Ekaka Nipāta:

[The verse mentioned above was repeated.]

After finishing the Jātaka, he addressed those monks, saying, "Monks, because you have relied on the forest of lust, hatred, and delusion, you have encountered this suffering. It is proper to cut down that forest. By cutting it down in this way, you will be free from suffering." He then spoke these verses.

(This is the unintended meaning given by those who do not understand the hidden meaning:)

Monks, cut down the forest of defilements. Do not cut down literal trees.

(When the Buddha said, "Cut down the forest," those newly ordained monks thought, "The Teacher is telling us to take axes and cut down the forest," and the desire to cut down trees arose in them. At that time, wishing to prevent them by saying, "I said this referring to the forest of defilements such as lust, not literal trees," he said, "not the tree.")

From the forest of defilements, dangers such as birth (jāti) and so forth arise.

(Just as dangers like lions arise from a literal forest, so too do dangers like birth arise from the forest of defilements.)

Having cut down the great defilements that cause rebirth (vana) and the lesser defilements that produce results during the course of existence (vanatha) with the knowledge of the fourth path (Arahatta-magga).

(Large trees are called "vana." Small trees are called "vanatha" because they stand in that forest. Alternatively, trees that grew first are "vana," and those that grew subsequently are "vanatha.")
266:
Similarly, the very great defilements that pull one toward rebirth in existence are called "vana." The defilements that produce results during the course of existence (pavatti) are called "vanatha." Alternatively, the defilements that arose first are "vana," and those that arise subsequently are "vanatha." Both types of defilements must be cut down with the knowledge of the fourth path.

Be without a forest, meaning be free from defilements.

(This is the intended meaning given by those who understand the hidden meaning.)

Indeed, for as long as the brushwood of defilements, even as small as an atom, is not cut down in a man toward women, for that long, that man's mind is attached, just as a suckling calf is attached to its mother.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, those five elderly theras were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of the Five Elderly Theras ends.

## 9. The Story of the Goldsmith's Son
(Suvaṇṇakāratthera Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Ucchinda," concerning a co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika) of Venerable Sāriputta Thera.

## Sending to the Buddha because Meditation did not Appear
It is said that a very handsome son of a goldsmith was ordained in the presence of Venerable Sāriputta Thera. The Thera, thinking, "Lust is often prevalent in the young," gave him the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) to suppress lust. However, that meditation was unsuitable for him. Therefore, although he entered the forest and strove for the entire three months of the rainy season, he did not gain even a single-pointedness of mind. Returning to the Thera, when asked, "Friend, has the meditation subject appeared to you?" he reported the situation. Then the Thera, thinking, "It is not proper to give up just because the meditation is not yet successful," explained that same meditation subject well and gave it to him again. Even the second time, being unable to produce any distinction in the Dhamma, he returned and reported to the Thera. Then the Thera explained that same meditation subject again with reasons and similes. He returned yet again and reported the failure of the meditation. The Thera thought, "A monk who is a practitioner knows when sensual desire and so forth are present in himself, and knows when they are not. This monk is a practitioner, not a non-practitioner; he is one who practices, not one who does not. However, I do not know his inclination (ajjhāsaya). He must be one who is to be guided by a Buddha (Buddha-veneyya)." Thinking thus, he took the young monk and approached the Teacher in the evening, reporting the whole matter: "Venerable Sir, this is my co-resident pupil. I gave him this meditation subject for this reason."

## Attaining Jhana through the Meditation on Red
When he had reported this, the Teacher said, "This knowledge of underlying tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) is the domain only of the Buddhas, who have fulfilled the perfections, made the ten-thousandfold world system echo, and attained omniscience."
267:
"How is it? From what family did this monk go forth to become a recluse?" Upon reflecting thus, the Buddha knew, "He went forth from a family of goldsmiths." Looking back at his past lives, He saw five hundred consecutive births of this young monk in the family of goldsmiths. He thought, "This young monk, having worked as a goldsmith for a long time, has repeatedly worked with red gold, thinking 'I will make Karnikāra flowers, Padumma lotuses, and so on.' Therefore, the meditation on the loathsomeness of the foul (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) is not suitable for him; only a pleasant meditation object is appropriate."

He then addressed the Elder Sāriputta, "Dear Sāriputta, you have exhausted this monk for four months by giving him a meditation subject. Today, in the evening after the meal, you shall see him attain the Fruit of Arahantship. You may go." Having dismissed the Elder Sāriputta, the Buddha used His psychic power to create a golden Padumma lotus as large as a cartwheel, making it appear as if water drops were dripping from its leaves and stalk. He gave it to the monk, saying, "Bhikkhu, take this Padumma lotus, place it on a heap of sand at the edge of the monastery, sit before it in a cross-legged posture, and perform the preliminary work (parikamma) by repeating 'Lohitakaṃ, Lohitakaṃ—How red it is! How red it is!'"

Even as he received the created Padumma lotus from the Teacher's hand, the monk's mind became clear and joyful. He went to the edge of the monastery, piled up sand, inserted the lotus stalk into the heap, and sat before it in a cross-legged posture, beginning the preliminary work of "Lohitakaṃ, Lohitakaṃ." At that very moment, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) were removed from the young monk. Access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) arose. Immediately after that access concentration, he attained the first jhāna. Having mastered it in five ways, while still seated, he attained the second jhāna and the others. Having gained mastery, he sat playing with the jhānas through the fourth jhāna.

## Bringing about Insight
When the Teacher knew that the young monk had attained the jhānas, He reflected, "Will this monk be able to produce the higher distinction of the Path and Fruit by his own nature?" Knowing that he would not be able to, He resolved, "Let that Padumma lotus wither." The lotus, as if crushed by hands, became withered and turned dark in color. The monk, emerging from jhāna, looked at the lotus and thought, "How is this? This Padumma lotus is clearly oppressed by decay (jarā), which is old age and withering. If even this non-sentient (anupādinnaka) matter produced by the seasons is thus oppressed by decay, what need is there to say of this sentient (upādinnaka) body produced by kamma? This body, too, will be overwhelmed, oppressed, and destroyed by old age and death." Thus, he perceived the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa).

(When the mark of impermanence is seen, the mark of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) and the mark of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) are also seen.)

To that young monk, the three realms of existence appeared as if they were ablaze, or like a rotting corpse tied around one's neck.
268:
At that moment, not far from the young monk, some boys went down into a pond, plucked water lilies (kumuda), and made a heap on the dry land. The monk looked at the water lilies in the water and on the land. Then, the water lilies in the water appeared very beautiful to him, as if dripping with water. But those on the land were withered at their tips. He thought, "Decay thus strikes the non-sentient (anupādinnaka) matter produced by the seasons; why would it not strike the sentient (upādinnaka) matter produced by kamma?" He saw the marks of impermanence, suffering, and non-self very clearly. The Teacher, knowing "Now the meditation subject has become clear to this monk," while remaining in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), sent forth a radiance. That radiance struck the monk's face. Then, while he was looking, wondering "What is this light?", the Teacher appeared as if standing right before him. He stood up and raised his hands in salutation. Then the Teacher, noting what was suitable for him, spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(285) Cut off your affection, as one plucks an autumn lotus with the hand.
Cherish only the path to peace, the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.

*Sāradikaṃ*: occurring in the autumn season, the month of Tazaungmon. *Kumudaṃ*: a water lily. *Pāṇinā*: with the hand. *Chindati iva*: as if plucking. *Attano*: one's own. *Sinehaṃ*: the affection of craving (taṇhā). *Ucchinda*: cut off with the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. *Nibbānaṃ*: Nibbāna. *Sugatena*: by the Buddha. *Desitaṃ*: has been taught. *Santimaggameva*: only the Eightfold Path that leads to Nibbāna. *Brūhaya*: develop.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, that young monk, the co-resident (saddhivihārika) pupil of the Elder Sāriputta, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The Story of the Goldsmith's Son Elder ends.

## 10. The Story of the Great Merchant Mahādhana
(Mahādhana-vāṇija-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Idha vassaṃ," concerning a merchant named Mahādhana.

## Thinking "I Cannot Die Yet"
That merchant, it is said, came from Bārāṇasī to Sāvatthī for trade, filling five hundred carts with cloth dyed with safflower. Having reached the riverbank, he thought, "I will cross the river tomorrow," and stayed there, unyoking the carts. During the night, a great storm arose and it rained. The river remained full of water for seven days. The townspeople also celebrated a festival for seven days. The need for the safflower-dyed cloth was over. The merchant thought, "I have come from afar. If I return again, there will be delay. I will stay right here through the four months of the rainy season, the four months of winter, and the four months of summer, doing my business and selling these clothes." The Teacher, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, knew the merchant's thought and smiled. When the Elder Ānanda asked the reason for the smile, He said, "Dear Ānanda, do you see the great merchant Mahādhana?"
269:
## The Teaching

(286) Idha vassaṃ vasissāmi, idha hemantagimhisu.
Iti bālo vicinteti, antarāyaṃ na bujjhati.

"Idha" means in this place, in this very spot. "Idañcidañca" means while performing such and such tasks. "Vassaṃ" means for the four months of the rainy season. "Vasissāmi" means I shall stay. "Idha" means in this place. "Idañcidañca" means while performing such and such tasks. "Hemantagimhisu" means in the four months of winter and the four months of summer. "Vasissāmi" means I shall stay. "Iti" means in this way. "Bālo" means the fool who does not know the benefits of this world or the next. "Vicinteti" means he thinks. "Antarāyaṃ" means the danger to his own life, thinking 'I shall die at this time, in this place, or in this year.' "Na bujjhati" means he does not know.

When [the Venerable Ānanda] replied, "I see him, Bhante," the Buddha said, "That great merchant, not knowing the danger to his life, has made the plan to stay right here on this riverbank for this whole year to sell his goods and cloth."

When asked, "Bhante, will there be danger for him?", the Buddha replied, "Yes, Ānanda, it is true that there will be danger; living for only seven more days, that merchant will fall into the mouth of Death." Then He spoke these verses from the Bhaddekaratta Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pāḷi:

Ajjeva kiccamātappaṃ, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve.
Na hi no saṅgaraṃ tena, mahāsenena maccunā.
Evaṃ vihāriṃ ātāpiṃ, ahorattamatanditaṃ.
Taṃ ve bhaddekarattoti, santo ācikkhate muni.

"Ajjeva" means today itself. "Ātappaṃ" means the effort that burns up defilements. "Kiccaṃ/Kātabbaṃ" means it should be done. "Suve" means tomorrow. "Maraṇaṃ" means death. "Ko" means who. "Jaññā" means can know. "Hi" is used for emphasis. "Mahāsenena" means with a great army. "Tena maccunā" means with that King of Death. "Saṅgaraṃ" means an agreement, or bargaining, or giving bribes, or gathering an army. "No" means for us. "Na hi atthi" means there is certainly none.

"Ahorattaṃ" means throughout the day and night. "Evaṃ vihāriṃ" means one who dwells in this manner. "Ātāpiṃ" means one who has the effort that burns up defilements. "Yo puggalo" means such a person. "Atthi" exists. "Atanditaṃ" means having effort that discards laziness. "Taṃ puggalaṃ" means that person. "Ve" means indeed. "Bhaddekarattoti" means a noble person who has a single auspicious night. "Santo" means the one who has stilled passion and other defilements. "Muni" means the Buddha. "Ācikkhate" means He declares.

## The Merchant's Trepidation and Meritorious Deeds

When [the Venerable Ānanda] said, "Exalted Buddha, let me go to that merchant; I wish to tell him," the Buddha replied, "Go freely and courageously, Ānanda." The Elder Ānanda went to the place where the caravan was camped and walked for alms. The merchant welcomed the Elder with food and offerings. Then the Elder asked him, "For how long will you stay in this place?" The merchant replied, "Venerable Sir, I have come from a far distance. If I were to return now, it would take a long time. Therefore, I will stay here for this whole year, sell my goods and cloth, and then depart."

The Elder said, "Lay disciple, it is difficult to know the danger to one's life; it is proper to be diligent." When the merchant asked, "Venerable Sir, will there be danger to my life?", the Elder replied, "Yes, lay disciple, it is true; your life will last for only seven more days."

The merchant, filled with trepidation, invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and gave a great offering of alms for seven days. At the end, he took the Buddha's bowl for the purpose of hearing the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā). Then the Buddha, giving the appreciation to the merchant, said, "Lay disciple, come here; one who is wise should not think 'I shall stay in this place only, I shall stay at this time, I shall perform such and such tasks.' Rather, one should only contemplate the danger to one's own life." Then He spoke this verse:
270:
## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the discourse, the merchant was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled crowd.

## The Merchant's Death and Rebirth in Tusita

The merchant followed the Buddha to see Him off, and upon returning, he lay down on his bed saying, "A pain like a headache has arisen in me." While lying there, he passed away and was reborn in the Tusita celestial mansion.

The Story of the Merchant Mahādhana ends.

## The Teaching

(287) Taṃ puttaphasusammattaṃ, byāsattamānasaṃ naraṃ.
Suttaṃ gāmaṃ mahoghowa, maccu ādāya gacchati.

## 11. The Story of Kisāgotamī

(Kisāgotamī Vatthu)

The Buddha spoke this teaching beginning with "Taṃ puttaphasusammattaṃ" while dwelling at the Jetavana monastery, concerning Kisāgotamī. (The story has been told in detail in the commentary on the verse in the Sahassavagga: "Better than a hundred years lived without seeing the Deathless State is a single day lived by one who sees the Deathless State.")

## Dying Before Desires are Fulfilled

At that time, the Buddha asked, "Dear daughter Kisāgotamī, have you obtained even a pinch of mustard seeds?" She replied, "Exalted Buddha, I did not," and added, "In the entire village, those who have died are far more numerous than those who are living." Then the Buddha said to Kisāgotamī, "You think that only your son has died; this nature of death is a constant law for all sentient beings. King Death, like a great flood, drags away all beings before their desires are fulfilled and flings them into the ocean of the four woeful states (apāya)." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, He spoke this verse:

"Puttaphasusammattaṃ" means one who is greatly intoxicated with sons, daughters, bulls, cows, and so forth. (This refers to a person who, upon obtaining children endowed with beauty and strength, or animals such as cattle, thinks: 'My children are very beautiful, strong, wise, and capable of all tasks; my bulls are very handsome, healthy, and able to carry great loads; my cows give much milk.' Thus, they are greatly intoxicated and negligent because of their children and cattle.)

"Byāsattamānasaṃ" means having a mind that craves more than what is obtained, or having a mind deeply attached to what has been obtained.
