(This refers to a person who, upon obtaining gold, silver, or requisites like a bowl or robes, craves far more than that and has a mind of great attachment; or one who is deeply attached to whichever of the six sense objects, such as visible forms, or whichever of the various requisites they have obtained.)

"Taṃ naraṃ" means that man. "Suttaṃ" means who has fallen asleep. "Gāmaṃ" means the collective villagers. "Mahogho" means a great flood. "Ādāya gacchati iva" means as if taking away and going. "Maccu" means Death. "Ādāya gacchati" means takes away and goes.
271:
(Just as a great flood of deep and wide rivers carries away everything, even down to a dog, from a village that has fallen into sleep, so does Death carry away a person of such a nature as described.)

(It has been stated in the 13th story of the 8th Sahassavagga how she became a nun after being established as a Stream-enterer, and attained Arahantship by developing insight while watching a lamp flame.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, Kisāgotamī was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled multitude.

The Story of Kisāgotamī ends.

## The Teaching
(288) Sons are no protection, nor father, nor kinsmen;
For one overcome by the Ender (Death), there is no protection among relatives.

(289) Realizing this fact, the wise man, restrained by virtue,
Should quickly clear the path leading to Nibbāna.

'Tāṇāya' means for the sake of support and refuge. 'Putta' means sons and daughters. 'Pita' means parents. 'Bandhavā' means relatives and friends other than parents and children. 'Antakena adhipannassa' means for one overcome by death. Among relatives, there is no state of being a protector.

## 12. The Story of Paṭācārā
(Paṭācārā-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Na santi puttā' concerning Paṭācārā.

(The story has been told in detail in the commentary on the verse: 'Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ udayabbayaṃ; ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato udayabbayaṃ' in the Sahassavagga.)

## Children and Others are Not a Refuge
At that time, the Teacher, knowing that Paṭācārā's grief had become thin, said: "Dear daughter Paṭācārā, those called sons and others are unable to be a protection, a refuge, or a shelter for one going to the next world. Therefore, even though they exist, those sons and others are as if they do not exist. A wise person should purify their virtue and should only clear the path that leads to Nibbāna." Having said this, he spoke these verses:

(In the continuous course of life, sons and others may be a source of reliance by providing food and drink or by managing affairs; however, at the time of death, they are said to be non-existent as shelters because they are unable to prevent death by any means.)

'Etaṃ atthavasaṃ' means knowing this reason. 'Paṇḍito' means the wise person. 'Sīlasaṃvuto' means being restrained by the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla). 'Nibbānagamanaṃ maggaṃ' means the path of the eightfold constituents leading to Nibbāna. 'Khippameva visodhaye' means one should quickly clear it.
272:
(It has been stated in the 12th story of the Sahassavagga how she became a nun after being established as a Stream-enterer, and attained Arahantship by developing insight while pouring water.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, Paṭācārā was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. Many others also reached the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of Paṭācārā ends.

The Commentary on the Maggavagga is finished.

The Twentieth Chapter.
273:
## 21. Pakiṇṇakavagga

## 1. The Story of the Buddha's Past Deeds
(Attanopubbakamma-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Mattāsukhapariccāgā' concerning his own past deeds.

## The Three Calamities of Vesālī
At one time, the city of Vesālī was prosperous, flourishing, and densely populated. In that city of Vesālī, there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings who ruled by turns. (There were 7,707 kings.) For the residence of those 7,707 kings, there were as many palaces, as many gabled houses, and for their recreation in the gardens, there were as many parks and lotus ponds. At a later time, that city of Vesālī became famine-stricken and had poor, failed crops. In that city, due to the fear of starvation, poor people died first. Because of the stench of the corpses discarded here and there, non-human beings (demons) entered the city. Due to the affliction by non-humans, many more people died. Because of the loathsomeness of the stench of those corpses, the 'fly-disease' (plague) broke out among living beings. Thus, three calamities arose: the fear of famine, the fear of non-humans, and the fear of disease.

## Deliberating to Escape the Calamities
The citizens gathered and said to the king: "Great King, three calamities have arisen in this city. From now back to seven generations of kings, such calamities have never occurred before. Such calamities only arise during the time of unrighteous kings." The king caused a general assembly to be held in the council hall and said: "If there is any unrighteousness in me, investigate it." The inhabitants of Vesālī, investigating the entire lineage, found no fault in the king and said: "Great King, there is no such fault in you." Then they deliberated: "By what means can this fear of death be appeased for us?" During that deliberation, some said: "It may be appeased by making offerings (bali), by prayer, and by performing auspicious rites." However, even after performing all those rituals, they were unable to prevent the calamities. Then others said: "There are the six great teachers of great power; if they come here, the fear might be appeased." Others said: "The Fully Enlightened One has appeared in the world. That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the benefit of all beings; he is of great psychic power and great majesty. If he comes here..."
274:
(Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambala, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta) possess great majesty. If these six teachers arrive in this city, the danger will be appeased.” Others said, “The Buddha has appeared in the world. That Blessed One is of great glory and teaches the Dhamma for the benefit of all beings. He has great psychic power and majesty. If that Blessed One comes, these dangers will vanish.”

## Inviting the Buddha

Everyone was exceedingly pleased with these words and asked, “Where is that Blessed One residing now?” At that time, as the time for the rains retreat approached, the Teacher was residing at Veluvana Monastery, having given His word to King Bimbisāra. At that time, a Licchavī named Mahāli, who had attained the fruit of Stream-entry along with King Bimbisāra, was present in that assembly. The residents of Vesālī prepared many gifts, informed King Bimbisāra, and sent Mahāli the Licchavī and the son of the court chaplain, saying, “Please invite the Teacher to this city of Vesālī.” They went, presented the gifts to King Bimbisāra, explained the situation in Vesālī, and requested, “Great King, please send the Teacher to our country.” King Bimbisāra replied, “You yourselves should see to it,” and gave his consent. Those who came to invite Him approached the Buddha, paid homage, and requested, “Venerable Sir, three calamities have arisen in Vesālī. When the Blessed One arrives, they will be appeased. Please, Venerable Sir, let us go.” Hearing their words, the Teacher reflected: “When the Ratana Sutta is preached in Vesālī, its protection will spread throughout a hundred billion world systems. At the conclusion of the Sutta, eighty-four thousand beings will realize the Four Noble Truths, and those three calamities will be appeased.” Knowing this, He accepted their invitation.

## King Bimbisāra Escorting the Buddha

Hearing that “The Teacher has accepted the journey to Vesālī,” King Bimbisāra had a proclamation made in the city, approached the Buddha, and asked, “Venerable Sir, have You accepted the journey to Vesālī?” When told, “Yes, Great King,” he said, “In that case, Venerable Sir, please wait for a while; I will first prepare the road.” He then had the five-yojana stretch of land between Rājagaha and the Ganges River leveled, established a monastery at every yojana, and informed the Teacher of the time for departure. The Teacher set out on the journey with five hundred monks. Within each yojana, King Bimbisāra had five-colored flowers scattered knee-deep, raised banners, flags, and plantain trees, and provided tiered umbrellas. He held two white umbrellas over the Blessed One and one white umbrella over each monk. Accompanied by his retinue, he made offerings of flowers, scents, and so on, hosted the Teacher at each monastery, gave great alms, and reached the banks of the Ganges in five days. He then decorated a boat on the Ganges and sent a message to the people of Vesālī, saying, “Prepare the road and come to welcome the Buddha.”
275:
Those people of Vesālī, thinking, "We shall perform a double offering," had the ground between Vesālī and the Gaṅgā, spanning three yojanas, leveled. They prepared a double honor for the Blessed One with four white umbrellas and for each monk with two white umbrellas. Arranging tiers of umbrellas and making offerings, they came and stood on the bank of the Gaṅgā. King Bimbisāra joined two boats together, erected a pavilion, decorated it with flower garlands and other ornaments, and prepared a seat made of all kinds of jewels for the Buddha. The Blessed One sat upon that seat. The monks also boarded the boat and sat surrounding the Blessed One. King Bimbisāra, wishing to see them off, waded into the water up to his neck and said, "Venerable Sir, I shall remain here on the bank of the Gaṅgā until the Blessed One returns." Having said this, he sent the boat off and turned back.

## The Falling of the Pokkharavassa Rain in Vesālī

When the Blessed One had traveled a distance of one yojana along the Gaṅgā, He reached the boundary of the people of Vesālī. The Licchavī kings, wishing to welcome the Blessed One, waded into the water up to their necks, brought the boat to the shore, and invited the Blessed One to descend from the boat. As soon as the Blessed One stepped onto the shore, a great cloud arose and a Pokkharavassa rain (a lotus-leaf rain) fell. In all places, water flowed knee-deep, thigh-deep, waist-deep, and so on, washing all the corpses into the Gaṅgā. The ground became completely pure. The Licchavī kings invited the Blessed One to stay at every yojana, making great offerings and performing double honors, and in three days, they brought Him to Vesālī.

## Venerable Ānanda Reciting the Ratana Sutta Paritta

Sakka, the King of Devas, arrived surrounded by a host of devas. Due to the assembly of powerful devas, the non-human beings (amanussa) mostly fled. In the evening, the Buddha stood at the city gate and addressed Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, learn this Ratana Sutta and, walking with the Licchavī princes between the three walls of Vesālī, perform the protection (paritta)."

Venerable Ānanda learned the Ratana Sutta given by the Buddha, took water in the Buddha's stone bowl, and standing at the city gate, he reflected on the Buddha's virtues: starting from the time He made the aspiration for Buddhahood, the ten perfections (pāramīs), the ten minor perfections (upapāramīs), and the ten ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramīs), thus the thirty perfections in total; the five great sacrifices; the three modes of conduct, namely, conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā), conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), and conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariyā); and in His final birth, His descent into the womb, His birth, His great renunciation, His practice of austerities (dukkaracariyā), His victory over Māra at the Bodhi-pallanka, His attainment of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), His preaching of the Dhammacakka, and the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). Reflecting on all these virtues of the Buddha, he entered the city of Vesālī and, throughout the three watches of the night, he walked between the three walls, reciting the Ratana Sutta as a protection.
276:
Perfections (pāramī) refer to the ten wholesome qualities that lead to the other shore of Nibbāna: generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), renunciation (nekkhamma), wisdom (paññā), energy (viriya), patience (khanti), truthfulness (sacca), determination (adhiṭṭhāna), loving-kindness (mettā), and equanimity (upekkhā). Secondary perfections (upapāramī) refer to these ten wholesome qualities practiced while disregarding one's limbs and organs to reach the shore of Nibbāna. Ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramī) refer to these ten wholesome qualities practiced while disregarding one's life to reach the shore of Nibbāna.

The Five Great Sacrifices (pañcamahāpariccāga) are described in various ways: sacrificing noble wealth, children, wife, kingdom, and limbs—this is according to the Abhidhāna. Limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, children and wife—according to the Sīlakkhandhavagga, the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, and the Aṅguttara Commentary. Limbs, children and wife, kingdom, one's own body, and eyes—according to the Mūlapaṇṇāsa and the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta Commentary. Limbs, eyes, one's own body, kingdom, children and wife—according to the Sutta Mahāvagga-ṭīkā. Limbs, one's own body, wealth, children and wife, kingdom—according to the Itivuttaka and Suttanipāta Commentaries. Limbs, life, wealth, kingdom, children and wife—according to the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary. Wealth, limbs, children, wife, and life—according to the Vessantara Jātaka Commentary. Wealth, children, wife, limbs, and life—according to the Jinālaṅkāra. Thus, they are described in various ways (some only differing in order).

## The Benefits of Reciting the Ratana Sutta
As soon as the Venerable Ānanda recited the word 'Yaṃkiñci', the water sprinkled upwards fell upon the non-human beings (amanussa). From the moment he began reciting the verse 'Yānīdha bhūtāni', the water droplets, like silver crest-jewels, traveled through the air and fell upon the bodies of the sick people. At that very moment, their illnesses were calmed and cured, and the people rose up and surrounded the Venerable Ānanda. From the word 'Yaṃkiñci' onwards, all the non-human beings who were touched by the water droplets did not stay but fled through various gates, even those who had been dwelling in heaps of rubbish or against the walls. Those gates became so crowded that there was no room; when they could not find a way out through the gates, they even broke through the walls to flee. The great multitude of people smeared the assembly hall in the center of the city with all kinds of perfumes, hung a canopy decorated with golden stars and other ornaments above, prepared a seat for the Buddha, and then invited the Teacher. The Teacher sat upon the prepared seat. The community of monks and the assembly of Licchavī princes also sat surrounding the Teacher. Sakka, the king of devas, surrounded by a host of devas, stood in a suitable place. The Venerable Ānanda, having circled the entire city, arrived together with the great multitude of people whose illnesses had been cured, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down. The Teacher, looking at the Elder and the assembly, preached that very same Ratana Sutta. At the conclusion of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma.

## The Honor Shown upon the Return from Vesālī
In this way, the Buddha preached it again the following morning, and continued to preach the Ratana Sutta for seven days. Knowing that all dangers had been calmed, he informed the Licchavī princes and departed from the city of Vesālī. The Licchavī kings, performing double the honors, escorted the Teacher to the banks of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River over the course of three days.

The Naga kings born and living in the Ganges thought, 'Humans are paying honor to the Tathāgata; why should we not do the same?' They created boats made of gold, silver, and jewels, and arranged thrones made of gold, silver, and jewels. They covered the waters of the Ganges with five-colored lotuses and requested the Teacher, 'Venerable Sir, please show us favor as well,' inviting the Teacher to board their respective boats.

## Honor from Devas, Brahmas, and Nagas
'Both humans and...
277:
The Nagas also paid homage to the Buddha. Thinking, 'Why should we not do the same?', all the devas and Brahmas, starting from the earth-dwelling deities up to the Akanittha Brahma realm, performed acts of worship. Among those worshippers, the Nagas held up tiers of umbrellas, each one league in size. Below them, the Nagas, and on the ground, the earth-dwelling deities (bhummā) inhabiting great trees, small trees, mountains, and so forth, and in the sky, the sky-dwelling deities (ākāsaṭṭha)—thus, starting from the Naga realm and extending to the limits of the universe up to the Brahma realm, they raised and held tiers of umbrellas. Between the umbrellas were banners, and between the banners were flags. In the spaces between these umbrellas, banners, and flags, there were offerings of flower garlands, perfumes, powders, incense, and so on. The young devas, adorned with all kinds of ornaments and assuming festive attire, moved through the sky while shouting.

(It is said that only these three assemblies were truly great: the assembly at the Twin Miracle, the assembly at the descent from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to the city of Saṅkassa, and this assembly at the crossing of the Ganges.)

## The Creation of Created Buddhas and the Journey to the Naga Realm
On the other bank, King Bimbisāra, having prepared honors twice as great as those performed by the Licchavī princes, stood waiting for the arrival of the Blessed One. The Teacher, observing the great generosity of the kings on both banks of the Ganges and knowing the aspiration of the Nagas and others, created a Buddha-image (nimmitabuddha) on each and every boat, each surrounded by five hundred monks. Each created Buddha sat beneath a white umbrella, a wish-fulfilling tree (kapparuakkha), and various flower garlands, surrounded by a host of Nagas. Among the earth-dwelling deities and others, he also created a Buddha-image with an entourage in each and every place. Thus, when the entire universe became a single decoration, a single assembly, and a single festival, the Teacher, wishing to favor the Nagas, boarded a boat made of jewels. Each of the monks also boarded a boat. The Naga kings led the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to the Naga realm. After listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher throughout the three watches of the night, on the second day, they served the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with divine hard and soft food.

After the Teacher had given the words of appreciation (anumodanā), he departed from the Naga realm. Honored by the deities of the entire universe, he crossed the Ganges River with five hundred boats. King Bimbisāra went to welcome him, helped the Teacher down from the boat, and having performed honors twice as great as those performed by the Licchavī princes, he led the Teacher toward the city of Rājagaha in five days, just as before.
278:
## Discussion in the Assembly of Monks
On the second day, after the monks had returned from their alms round in the village, they gathered in the Dhamma hall in the evening and spoke: "How marvelous is the power of the Buddhas! How marvelous is the devotion of gods and humans toward the Buddha! Even on the great Ganges river, on the eight-yojana road from both sides, the kings, out of devotion to the Buddha, have leveled the ground, strewn sand, and spread flowers of various colors knee-deep. By the power of the Nagas, the water of the Ganges is covered with five-colored lotuses. Tiered umbrellas have been raised as far as the Akanittha heaven. The entire universe appears as if it were a single decoration, a single grand festival." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your discussion as you sit here now?" When they replied, "It is this subject, Bhante," he said, "Monks, this honor and hospitality did not arise through my power as a Buddha, nor through the power of Nagas, Devas, or Brahmas. Rather, it arose through the power of a small sacrifice made in the past." Being requested by the monks, he brought forth the story of the past.
## The Past Story of Susīma Paccekabuddha
In the past, there was a Brahmin named Saṅkha in the city of Takkasilā. His son, a youth named Susīma, was about sixteen years old. One day, he approached his father and said, "Father, I wish to go to the city of Bārāṇasī to study the Vedas." Then his father said to him, "In that case, dear son, a certain Brahmin there is my friend. Go to him and study." Having agreed, saying "Very well," he gradually made his way to Bārāṇasī, approached that Brahmin, and informed him that he had been sent by his father. Then, accepting him as "the son of my friend," the Brahmin, after Susīma had rested from his fatigue, began to teach him the Vedas on an auspicious day. That youth Susīma, learning much and learning quickly, retained everything he learned from his teacher without loss, like lion's oil poured into a golden vessel. Before long, having learned all the arts to be learned from his teacher's presence, while reciting them, he saw only the beginning and the middle of the arts he had learned, but not the end. He approached his teacher and said, "I see only the beginning and the middle of this art, but not the end." When the teacher said, "Dear son, I too do not see it," he asked, "Then, teacher, who knows the end?" The teacher replied, "Dear son, these sages dwell in Isipatana; they would know. Approach them and ask."
## The Youth Susīma Becoming a Paccekabuddha and Attaining Parinibbāna
Being told thus by his teacher, the youth Susīma approached a Paccekabuddha and said, "I have heard that you, venerable sirs, know the end."
279:
"Is it true, Venerable Sirs?" he asked. "It is true," they replied. "If so, please teach me, Venerable Sirs," he requested. "We do not teach those who are not monks. If you desire this knowledge, you must ordain," they said. The young man Susīma agreed, saying, "Very well, Venerable Sirs," and ordained in the presence of those Paccekabuddhas. Then, the Paccekabuddhas told the monk Susīma, "Learn this first," and taught him the abhisamācārika (conduct of proper behavior), such as "This is how you should dress; this is how you should robe yourself." While practicing that abhisamācārika conduct, because he was endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), he soon realized Paccekasambodhi (individual enlightenment). He became as famous throughout the city of Bārāṇasī as the full moon in the sky, reaching the pinnacle of gain and fame. However, because he had performed a deed leading to a short life in the past, he attained Parinibbāna not long after. When he passed away, the Paccekabuddhas and the great multitude performed the funeral rites, took the relics, and built a stupa at the city gate.

## The Brahmin Father Saṅkha Honoring the Stupa
The Brahmin named Saṅkha thought, "It has been a long time since my son left; I will find out news of him." Desiring to see his son, he departed from Takkasilā and eventually reached Bārāṇasī. Seeing a large gathering of people, he thought, "Surely one of these people will know news of my son." He approached them and asked, "A young man named Susīma came to this city of Bārāṇasī. Do you know anything about him?" "Yes, Brahmin, we know. He studied the three Vedas under a certain Brahmin, then ordained, realized Paccekasambodhi, and attained Parinibbāna. This stupa that has been erected is the stupa of that Paccekabuddha Susīma," they replied. Upon hearing this, the Brahmin Saṅkha struck the ground with his hands, weeping and wailing. He went to the courtyard of the stupa, pulled up the grass, brought sand in his upper garment and spread it in the courtyard, sprinkled water from a water-pot, made an offering of wild flowers, raised a banner made from his cloth, fastened his own umbrella above the stupa, and then departed.

## Connecting Merit and Its Results
The Teacher, bringing forth this past story, said, "Monks, at that time, I was the Brahmin Saṅkha. I pulled up the grass in the courtyard of the stupa of the Paccekabuddha Susīma. As a result of that deed, they have cleared the eight-league road of stumps and thorns, making it clean and level. I spread sand at the stupa of that Paccekabuddha Susīma. As a result of that merit, they have spread sand along the eight-league road. I made an offering of wild flowers there. As a result of that merit, flowers of various colors have been strewn along the eight-league road, and for the distance of one league, the water of the Ganges is covered with five-colored lotuses. I sprinkled water from a water-pot at that stupa. As a result of that merit, a 'lotus-shower' (Pokkhara-vassa) like the rain in a lotus pond fell in the city of Vesālī. I raised banners and offered an umbrella at that stupa. As a result of that merit, as far as the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm, the entire universe has become like a single festival, filled with banners, streamers, and tiered umbrellas."
280:
...it became like a single festival. "Thus, monks, this honor and hospitality has arisen for me neither through the power of a Buddha, nor through the power of Nagas, Devas, or Brahmas. Rather, it has arisen through the power of a small sacrifice made in the past." Having said this, desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(290) If by renouncing a small pleasure,
One sees a great pleasure,
The wise man should give up the small pleasure,
Looking to the great pleasure.

Matta-sukha-pariccāgā: by renouncing a small pleasure of limited measure. Vipulaṃ sukhaṃ: if one sees the great, extensive happiness of Nibbāna. Atha: then, seeing thus. Vipulaṃ sukhaṃ sampassaṃ: the wise man (dhīra) who clearly sees the great happiness of Nibbāna should give up the small pleasure.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of the Teacher's Own Past Deed is finished.

## 2. The Story of the Woman who Ate Hen's Eggs
(Kukkuṭa-aṇḍa-khādikā Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Pura-dukkhūpadhānena' concerning a woman who ate hen's eggs.

## Becoming an Ogress by Following the Tongue's Desire
Not far from the city of Sāvatthī, there was a village named Paṇḍura. A fisherman lived in that village. While he was coming to Sāvatthī, he saw turtle eggs in the Aciravatī River. He took those turtle eggs, went to Sāvatthī, had them cooked in a house, and while eating, gave one turtle egg to a young girl in that house. After eating that turtle egg, from that day on, the girl did not desire any other kind of food. When she no longer wanted other food, her mother took a hen's egg from the nesting place where the hen laid eggs and gave it to her. After eating the hen's egg, she became bound by the craving for taste (rasa-taṇhā). From that day on, she herself would take and eat the hen's eggs.
281:
## The Teaching

(291) He who seeks his own happiness by inflicting pain on others, being entangled in the bond of hatred, is not released from hatred.

Seeing the young woman take and eat her eggs every time she laid them, the hen became distressed and agitated because of her. Harboring a grudge, she made a wish: "When I pass away from this life, may I be reborn as an ogress and be able to eat the children you give birth to." After she died, she was reborn as a cat in that very same house. When the other woman died, she was reborn as a hen in that same house. The hen laid eggs; the cat came and ate them, doing so a second and third time. The hen then made a wish: "Three times you have eaten my eggs, and now you wish to eat me. When I pass away from this life, may I be able to eat you along with your offspring." After she died, she was reborn as a leopardess. The other died and was reborn as a doe. When the doe gave birth, the leopardess came and ate the doe along with her fawns. Thus, eating each other, they caused suffering to one another through five hundred existences. Finally, one was reborn as an ogress and the other as a noblewoman in Sāvatthī.

(From this point onwards, the story should be understood in the same manner as stated in the verse "Na hi verena verāni" in the Story of Kāḷī the Ogress.)

In this context, the Teacher said, "Hatred is appeased by non-hatred; it is never appeased by hatred," and wishing to teach the Dhamma to both of them, he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the ogress established herself in the Refuges, undertook the five precepts, and was freed from hatred. The noblewoman was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled crowd.

The Story of the Woman who Ate Hen's Eggs ends.
282:
## 3. The Story of the Bhaddiya Monks
(Bhaddiya-bhikkhu-vatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with "Yaṃ hi kiccaṃ" while staying at Jātiyāvana near the city of Bhaddiya, concerning the monks who were residents of Bhaddiya.

## Rebuking the Monks for Wearing Various Decorated Sandals

Those monks residing in Bhaddiya were individuals devoted to decorating their sandals. As it is stated in the texts: At that time, the monks of Bhaddiya lived devoted to various ways of decorating sandals. They made or had others make sandals of grass, sandals of muñja-grass, sandals of reeds, sandals of palm leaves, sandals of wool, and sandals of blankets. They neglected the recitation of the texts, the questioning of the meanings, the higher virtue (adhisīla), the higher mind (adhicitta), and the higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Other monks, knowing of their behavior, complained and informed the Teacher. The Teacher rebuked those monks, saying, "Monks, you came for one purpose (the goal of Arahantship), yet you are devoted to another purpose (sandals)," and wishing to teach the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

## The Teaching

(292) What should be done is cast aside, but what should not be done is performed. For the arrogant and heedless, the taints (āsavas) increase.

(293) For those whose mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) is always well-established, who do not follow what should not be done but are constant in what should be done, for those mindful and clearly comprehending ones, the taints come to an end.

Whatever is the duty of a monk, that duty is cast aside. (The duty of a monk includes guarding the boundless aggregate of virtue, living in the forest, practicing ascetic duties (dhutanga), and delighting in meditation from the time of ordination. It means these monks of Bhaddiya cast aside their own duty.)

However, they perform what is not the duty of a monk. (Decorating umbrellas, decorating shoes, decorating sandals, bowls, cups, water-strainers, waistbands, and shoulder straps are not the duties of a monk. It means they perform these non-duties.)

For those who possess haughty pride and are heedless due to a lack of mindfulness, the four taints increase.

For those who have well-established mindfulness of the body, which is the meditation of repeatedly contemplating the thirty-two parts of the body at all times, they do not perform non-duties such as decorating. They are constantly and respectfully devoted to the duties to be performed by monks, such as the aggregate of virtue. For those who are mindful and possess the four types of clear comprehension, the four taints reach their end and cessation.
283:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, those monks residing in the city of Bhaddiya were established in the fruit of Arahatship. The teaching was also beneficial to those who had arrived.
The Story of the Bhaddiya Monks ends.

## The First Teaching
(294) Having killed mother and father, and two warrior kings,
Having destroyed a kingdom together with its subjects, the Brahmin goes untroubled.

Mother: mother. Father: father. Having killed: having killed. Two warrior kings: two kings of the noble warrior caste. Having killed: having killed. Together with its subjects: together with the spy or together with the tax-collecting minister. Kingdom: the great kingdom. Having destroyed: having destroyed. The Brahmin: the Brahmin (Arahat). Untroubled: being free from suffering. Goes: goes.

## 4. The Story of Elder Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya
(Lakuṇṭakabhaddiyattheravatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher (the Buddha) spoke this legal discourse beginning with "Mātaraṃ," concerning the Elder Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya.

## Happiness from Killing Parents Called Craving and Conceit
One day, many visiting monks approached the Teacher, who was sitting in his day-quarters, paid homage to him, and sat in a suitable place. At that moment, Elder Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya passed by not far from the Blessed One. The Teacher, knowing the thoughts of those visiting monks, looked at them and said, "Monks, look! This monk, having killed his mother and father, goes about free from suffering."

When he said this, those visiting monks looked at each other's faces, wondering, "What is the Teacher saying?" and fell into doubt. They asked, "Venerable Sir, why do you say this?" Desiring to preach the Dhamma to those monks, the Teacher spoke this verse:

(This is the literal meaning which is not the intended spiritual meaning.)

Mother: having killed the mother called Craving (taṇhā). Father: having killed the father called Conceit (māna).

(Because it is taught, "Craving gives birth to man," craving is called the mother because it causes beings to be born in the three realms of existence. Conceit is called the father because pride arises by relying on the father, thinking, "I am the son of such-and-such a king or such-and-such a great minister." This means abandoning that craving and conceit.)

Two kings: having killed the two sovereign kings called the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) and the view of nihilism (uccheda-diṭṭhi).

(Just as the masses must attend upon and rely on a sovereign king, all wrong views must attend upon and rely on the two great views of eternalism and nihilism. Therefore, the two great views of eternalism and nihilism are called the two sovereign kings. This means abandoning those two great views.)

Together with its subjects: together with the tax-collecting minister called delight and lust (nandīrāga). Kingdom: having destroyed the great kingdom of the twelve bases (āyatana).

(The twelve bases are like a great kingdom because they expand and proliferate. The craving of delight and lust, which relies on those bases and is fond of them, is called the tax-collecting minister. This means abandoning the twelve bases together with that delight and lust.)

Brahmin: the Arahat who has put away evil. Untroubled: being free from suffering. Goes: exists, or goes to Nibbāna.
284:
(Because he has destroyed craving, conceit, wrong views, the bases, and delight and lust with the sword of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship, the noble Arahat, whose taints are exhausted, goes about free from the suffering of the round of rebirths.)

(This is the intended spiritual meaning.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, those visiting monks were established in the fruit of Arahatship.

## > (In the second verse, it is also the same as before.)
At that time, the Teacher spoke concerning only Elder Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya. Desiring to preach the Dhamma to the visiting monks, the Teacher spoke this verse:

## The Second Teaching
(295) Having killed mother and father, and two learned kings,
Having destroyed the tigerish fifth, the Brahmin goes untroubled.

Mother: mother. Father: father. Having killed: having killed. Kings: who are kings. Two learned: two Brahmins. Having killed: having killed. The tigerish fifth: the path which has the tiger-infested path as the fifth. Having destroyed: having destroyed. The Brahmin: the Brahmin (Arahat). Goes: goes.

(This is the literal meaning which is not the intended spiritual meaning.)

Mother: having killed the mother called Craving. Father: having killed the father called Conceit. Kings: who are kings. Two learned: the two Brahmins called the view of eternalism and the view of nihilism. Having killed: having killed.

(In this verse, because the Teacher is the Lord of Dhamma (Dhammissara) and is skilled in the method of teaching, he spoke by making the great views of eternalism and nihilism into two Brahmin kings.)

The tigerish fifth: having completely destroyed the group of five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), of which Doubt (vicikicchā) is the fifth, which is like a tiger-infested path.

(A path that is difficult to travel because it is haunted by fierce tigers and is full of danger is called "tigerish" (veyaggha). The hindrance of doubt is also called "tigerish" because it is similar to that. The group of five hindrances, of which doubt is the fifth, is called "the tigerish fifth." It refers to the five hindrances. This means completely destroying that group of five hindrances called the tigerish fifth with the sword of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship.)

Brahmin: the Arahat who has put away evil. Untroubled: being free from suffering. Goes: exists, or goes to Nibbāna.

(The rest is exactly the same as before.)

(This is the intended spiritual meaning.)

The Story of Elder Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya ends.

## 5. The Story of the Wood-cart Driver's Son
(Dārusākaṭikaputtavatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this legal discourse beginning with "Suppabuddhaṃ," concerning the son of a wood-cart driver.

## "Namo Buddhassa" and the Boy of Wrong View
In the city of Rājagaha, two boys—one the son of a man with right view and the other the son of a man with wrong view—frequently played a game of marbles together. Among them, whenever the son of the man with right view threw the marble, he would reflect on the Buddha's qualities (Buddhānussati) and say, "Namo Buddhassa" (Homage to the Buddha) before throwing. The son of the man with wrong view, dedicating his throw to the qualities of the heretics (titthiyas), would say, "Namo Arahantānaṃ" (Homage to the Arahants—referring to heretics) before throwing.
285:
Among those two boys, the son of the one with Right View won and was victorious. The son of the one with Wrong View, however, lost. When the son of the one with Wrong View saw the actions of the son of the one with Right View, he thought, "This person, by recollecting thus and speaking thus while throwing the dice, defeats me. I too will do the same," and he practiced the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati). Then one day, the boy's father, having yoked the cart and going for the sake of firewood, took the boy along. Having filled the cart with wood in the forest and returning, he unyoked the oxen at a pleasant place with water near a cemetery outside the city and ate his meal. Then, in the evening, his oxen entered the city along with a herd of cattle entering the city. The cart driver, following the oxen, entered the city, and having seen and caught the oxen in the evening, he could not reach the city gate in time as he was coming out. The gate was closed before he arrived. Thus, when the gate was closed, the young son of that cart driver fell asleep alone under the cart during the night.
## Reciting upon being Pulled by an Ogre
The city of Rājagaha was naturally full of ogres (yakkhas). This boy also fell asleep near the cemetery. Two ogres saw the boy there. One ogre held wrong views and was like a thorn to the Dispensation; the other ogre held right views. Among those two ogres, the one with wrong views said, "This boy is our food; let us eat him." The one with right views forbade him, saying, "Enough, do not let it please you." Although forbidden by the ogre with right views, that ogre did not heed his words and, seizing the boy by the feet, pulled him. Because the boy had practiced the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha, at the moment he was pulled, he recited, "Namo Buddhassa" (Homage to the Buddha). The ogre, terrified by a great fear, retreated and stood still.
## Being Arrested as a Thief of the Golden Tray from the Palace
Then, the ogre with right views said to the ogre with wrong views, "We have done something that should not have been done together. Let us perform a penalty for the sake of this boy," and he stood guarding the boy. The ogre with wrong views entered the city, filled King Bimbisāra's royal food tray, and brought the food. Then, both of them, becoming like the boy's mother and father, placed the food near him and made him eat. Thinking, "May only the King see these letters, and no one else," and clearly revealing the matter, they wrote letters on the royal tray by their ogre power. They placed the tray in the wood-cart, guarded it all night, and then departed.
286: ## The Teaching. (296) The disciples of Gotama always awake happily, those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Buddha day and night. (297) The disciples of Gotama always awake happily, those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Dhamma day and night. (298) The disciples of Gotama always awake happily, those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Saṅgha day and night. (299) The disciples of Gotama always awake happily, those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the body day and night. (300) The disciples of Gotama always awake happily, those whose minds day and night delight in non-violence. (301) The disciples of Gotama always awake happily, those whose minds day and night delight in meditation. "Of whom" (yesaṃ): for those. "By day" (divā ca) and "by night" (ratto ca). "Constantly" (niccaṃ): without interruption. "Directed toward the Buddha" (buddhagatā): mindfulness that arises by taking the qualities of the Buddha as the object. "Exists" (atthi). (The royal food tray was placed on the wood-cart, and they departed after guarding it for the three watches of the night. These words are not found in some commentaries.) Again, the next day at dawn, people made an uproar saying, "Thieves have stolen the royal food tray from the King's palace." Having closed the gates and searched, they did not see it in the city. Leaving the city and searching here and there, they saw the golden tray among the wood. Saying, "This boy is the thief," they arrested the boy and showed him to the King. When King Bimbisāra saw the letters, he asked, "Dear son, how did this happen?" The boy replied, "Great King, I do not know. My mother and father came at night, fed me, and stood guarding me. I thought, 'My mother and father are guarding me,' and being without fear or trembling, I fell asleep. This much only I know, O King." At that time, the boy's mother and father also arrived at that place. The King, having known the matter, took those three people to the presence of the Blessed One, reported everything, and asked, "Venerable Sir, is it only the Recollection of the Buddha that is a protection, or are the Recollection of the Dhamma and others also protections?" Then the Blessed One said to the King, "Great King, it is not only the Recollection of the Buddha that is a protection. For those whose minds are well-developed in six ways, there is no need for other protection, shielding, or mantras and medicines." Desiring to show the six points, the Blessed One spoke these verses. (If mindfulness directed toward the qualities of the Buddha, such as 'Iti pi so bhagavā arahaṃ,' is constantly present, those people awake well at all times. If they cannot do so constantly, those who recollect the Buddhānussati in their minds three times a day, or twice, or even once, are said to awake well.) "Disciples of Gotama" (gotamasāvakā): the disciples who have heard the Dhamma of the Buddha born of the Gotama lineage. "They" (te). "Always" (sadā). "Awake well" (suppabuddhaṃ pabujjhanti). "Of whom" (yesaṃ): for those. "By day" (divā ca) and "by night" (ratto ca). "Constantly" (niccaṃ). "Directed toward the Dhamma" (dhammagatā): mindfulness that arises by taking the qualities of the Dhamma as the object. "Exists" (atthi). "Disciples of Gotama" (gotamasāvakā). "They" (te). "Directed toward the body" (kāyagatā): mindfulness that exists by way of the thirty-two parts of the body and so on. "Exists" (atthi).
287:
(Mindfulness directed to the body [kāyagatāsati] means mindfulness arising by way of the thirty-two parts [hair, body hair, etc.], or by way of the nine cemetery contemplations, or by way of the determination of the four elements, or by way of the fine-material jhānas such as the internal blue kasiṇa.)

(The nine cemetery contemplations are explained in the Satipaṭṭhāna Suttas. They refer to a corpse cast away in a cemetery: 1. Swollen and blue-black. 2. Red where flesh is abundant, white where pus collects, and generally dark and decaying. 3. Festering with trickling pus. 4. Being bitten and torn by crows, dogs, vultures, etc. 5. A skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews. 6. A skeleton without flesh, smeared with blood, held together by sinews. 7. A skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by sinews. 8. A skeleton no longer held together by sinews, with bones scattered in various directions—hand-bones here, foot-bones there, etc. 9. Bones bleached white like a conch shell, bones more than a year old, or bones crumbled into dust. These are the nine cemetery contemplations taught by way of insight [vipassanā].)

Gotama-sāvakā, the disciples of the Buddha Gotama. Te, they. Sadā, at all times. Suppabuddhaṃ, a good awakening. Pabujjhanti, they awaken.

Yesaṃ, for those. Divā ca, by day. Ratto ca, and by night. Niccaṃ, constantly. Ahiṃsāya, in the meditation on compassion [karuṇā-bhāvanā] which is non-violence. Rato, delighting. Mano, the mind. Atthi, there is. Gotama-sāvakā, the disciples of the Buddha Gotama. Te, they. Sadā, at all times. Suppabuddhaṃ, a good awakening. Pabujjhanti, they awaken.

Yesaṃ, for those. Divā ca, by day. Ratto ca, and by night. Niccaṃ, constantly. Bhāvanāya, in the meditation on loving-kindness [mettā-bhāvanā]. Rato, delighting. Mano, the mind. Atthi, there is. Gotama-sāvakā, the disciples of the Buddha Gotama. Te, they. Sadā, at all times. Suppabuddhaṃ, a good awakening. Pabujjhanti, they awaken.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the boy, together with his parents, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry [sotāpatti-phala]. Later, they went forth as monastics, and all three attained the fruit of Arahantship. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to those who had gathered.

The Story of the Wood-cart Driver’s Son ends.

## 6. The Story of the Vajjian Monk
(Vajjiputtaka-bhikkhu-vatthu)
While residing at the Mahāvana near the city of Vesālī, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Duppabbajjaṃ" concerning a certain monk of the Vajjian clan.

## How a Deity Admonished the Weary Monk
The following words are spoken in reference to that monk. A certain monk of the Vajjian clan was living in a certain forest grove near Vesālī. At that time, a festival was being held throughout the night in Vesālī. Hearing the sounds of drums, music, and shouting from Vesālī, the monk lamented and recited this verse at that time:

(The five types of musical instruments [tūriya] are: 1. Ātata: drums covered with leather on one side, such as the pot-drum. 2. Vitata: drums covered with leather on both sides. 3. Ātatavitata: drums entirely covered with leather. 4. Susira: hollow wind instruments like the flute or trumpet. 5. Ghana: solid percussion instruments like gongs, bells, or cymbals. These five are called the five kinds of musical instruments.)

Ekakā mayaṃ araññe viharāma, apaviddhaṃva vanasmiṃ dārukaṃ.
Etādisikāya rattiyā, kosu nāmamhehi pāpiyo.

Vanasmiṃ, in the forest. Apaviddhaṃ, cast away. Dārukaṃ iva, like a log of wood. Ekako va, alone indeed. Mayaṃ, we. Araññe, in the forest. Viharāma, live. Dāni, now. Etādisikāya, on such a. Rattiyā, night. Amhehi, than us. Pāpiyo nāma, one who is more wretched. Ko su, who indeed could it be?
288:
Ekako va tvaṃ araññe viharasi, apaviddhaṃva vanasmiṃ dārukaṃ.
Tassa te bahukā pihayanti, nerayikā viya saggagāminaṃ.

Bho bhikkhu, O monk! Vanasmiṃ, in the forest. Apaviddhaṃ, cast away. Dārukaṃ va, like a log of wood. Ekako, alone. Tvaṃ, you, monk. Araññe, in the forest. Viharasi, reside. Nerayikā, those in hell. Saggagāminaṃ, for those going to heaven. Pihayanti viya, just as they envy and long for. Bahukā, many people. Tassa te, for you, noble monk. Pihayanti, envy and long for you, venerable sir.

## The Teaching
(302) Duppabbajjaṃ durabhiramaṃ, durāvāsā gharā dukhā.
Dukkho samānasaṃvāso, dukkhānupatitaddhagū.
Tasmā na caddhagū siyā, na ca dukkhānupatito siyā.

Duppabbajjaṃ, it is difficult to go forth in the Dispensation. Durabhiramaṃ, it is difficult to delight in practicing the monk's Dhamma. Durāvāsā, being difficult to live in with suffering.
Gharā - gharāvāsā, the household life. Dukhā, is very painful and wearying. Asamānasaṃvāso, living together with those who are not like-minded. Dukkho, is very painful. Addhagū, the traveler who must journey through the long road of Saṃsāra. Dukkhānupatito, repeatedly falls into suffering.

Tasmā, therefore. Addhagū, a traveler on the long road called the suffering of Saṃsāra. Na ca siyā, one should not be. Dukkhānupatito ca, and one who repeatedly falls into suffering. Na siyā, one should not be.

That monk was a prince in the Vajjian state who had renounced the kingship he received by turn to go forth as a monk. In the city of Vesālī, on the full moon day of the month of Kattika (Kaumudī), when the water-lilies bloom, a festival was held throughout the three watches of the night, decorated with banners and flags throughout the city, as if joined with the Cātumahārājika heaven. He heard the continuous sounds of drums and other musical instruments being played, and the sounds of harps and lutes. In Vesālī, there were seven thousand kings, seven hundred kings, and seven kings; and there were just as many viceroys, generals, and so on. When these kings and others, fully adorned, descended to the streets for the festival, the monk, while walking on a sixty-cubit long cloister-walk [caṅkama], saw the full moon standing in the middle of the sky. Standing and leaning against a plank at the end of the cloister-walk, he looked at himself, lacking the turban and ornaments, like a log of wood cast away in the forest. He thought, "Is there anyone more wretched than us?" Although he was naturally endowed with virtues such as forest-dwelling [āraññaka], at that moment he was overcome by discontent [anabhirati] and spoke thus. A deity residing in that forest grove, thinking, "I will stir this monk with spiritual urgency [saṃvega]," spoke thus:
289:
Upon hearing this verse being recited, that monk approached the Buddha the next morning, paid homage, and stayed. The Buddha, being aware of the situation and wishing to show the suffering of a householder living in the world, combined the five types of suffering and taught this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, when that monk saw the five causes of suffering, he became weary of suffering. He broke through the five lower fetters and the five higher fetters and attained the Fruit of Arahatship.

The story of the Vajjiputtaka monk ends.

## The Teaching
(303) Faithful, endowed with virtue, possessed of fame and wealth,
Whatever region he frequents, there he is honored.

Saddho: endowed with both mundane and supramundane faith. Sīlena: with virtue. Sampanno: one who is endowed. Yaso: having a retinue. Bhogasamappito: being endowed with wealth and possessions. Yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ: to whatever region. Bhajati: he approaches or frequents. Tattha tattheva: in that very place. Pūjito: he is honored. Hoti: he is.

## 7. The Story of Citta the Householder
(Citta Gahapati Vatthu)
The Teacher taught this Dhamma teaching starting with "Saddho" while staying at the Jetavana monastery, concerning Citta the Householder.

## Being Honored Wherever a Faithful Person Goes
(This was expanded in the commentary on the verse "Asantaṃ bhāvanamiccheyya" in the Bāla Vagga of the Citta Gahapati story. The verse was also taught there in that Bāla Vagga. Indeed, it is said in that story:)

"Venerable Sir, does this gain and honor arise for Citta the Householder only when he comes to your presence? Or does it also arise when he goes elsewhere?" he asked.
290:
"Dear Ānanda, whether he comes to my presence or goes elsewhere, it happens for Citta the Householder. This lay follower is faithful. He has confidence in the Triple Gem. He is endowed with virtue. Such a person, to whatever region he approaches, in that very place, gain and honor arise for him." Having said this, he taught this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of Citta the Householder ends.

## 8. The Story of Cūḷasubhaddā
(Cūḷasubhaddā Vatthu)
The Teacher taught this Dhamma teaching starting with "Dūre santo" while staying at the Jetavana monastery, concerning the daughter of Anāthapiṇḍika named Cūḷasubhaddā.

## Cūḷasubhaddā and the Son of the Merchant with Wrong View
Since childhood, the son of a merchant named Ugga, who lived in the city of Ugga, was a friend of Anāthapiṇḍika. While studying under the same teacher, they made a pact: "When we reach adulthood and have children, if one asks for a daughter for his son, the other must give his daughter." Both reached adulthood and became great merchants in their respective cities. Later, Ugga the merchant, engaging in trade, went to Sāvatthī with five hundred carts. Anāthapiṇḍika called his daughter Cūḷasubhaddā and said, "Dear daughter, your father's friend, the merchant Ugga, has arrived. All duties to be performed for him are your responsibility." Cūḷasubhaddā agreed, and from the day he arrived, she personally prepared the side dishes, arranged flowers, perfumes, and ointments. At mealtime, she prepared bathing water and performed all duties well from the time of his bath. When Ugga the merchant saw Cūḷasubhaddā's perfect conduct, he was pleased. One day, while conversing pleasantly with Anāthapiṇḍika, he reminded him of their childhood pact and asked for Cūḷasubhaddā for his son.

## Cūḷasubhaddā Having to Follow to Ugga City
However, that merchant Ugga naturally held wrong views. Therefore, when the matter of the merchant Ugga was reported to the Buddha...
291:
What are your ascetics like? You praise them so much.
What is their virtue? What is their conduct? Tell me this, as I am asking you.

“Tuyhaṃ” means of you, the daughter-in-law Cūḷasubhaddā. “Samaṇā” means the monks. “Kīdisā” means what is their nature? “Ne” means those monks. “Bāḷhaṃ kho” means very much indeed. “Pasaṃsasi” means you praise. “Kiṃ sīlā” means what are their habits? “Kiṃ samācarā” means what is their conduct? “Taṃ” means that matter. “Pucchitā” means you, dear daughter, who are being asked. “Me” means to me. “Akkhāhi” means please explain.

The Buddha, seeing the potential (upanissaya) of Ugga the Treasurer, gave his permission. Anāthapiṇḍika, after consulting with his wife, accepted the Treasurer's proposal and fixed a date. Just as the Great Treasurer Dhanañjaya gave away Visākhā, Anāthapiṇḍika gave his daughter Cūḷasubhaddā in marriage with great honor. He called her and gave her the ten admonitions, such as “Dear daughter, a daughter-in-law living in her father-in-law's house must not take the inner fire outside.” He also appointed eight householders as guarantors, saying, “If any fault should be alleged against my daughter in the place she goes, you must clear her name.” On the day of her departure, he gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha, making the splendor of the fruits of his daughter's past good deeds manifest to all. With such great honor, he sent his daughter away. When she eventually reached the city of Ugga, a great multitude, including her father-in-law's family, came out to welcome her. 

To make her splendor manifest, like Visākhā, she showed herself to the entire city while standing in her carriage. Upon entering the city, she accepted the gifts sent by the citizens and redistributed them appropriately, thus binding the whole city to her through her virtues.

## Cūḷasubhaddā Does Not Pay Homage to the Heretics

On a festive day, her father-in-law, while honoring the naked ascetics (Acelakas), sent a message: “Dear daughter, come and pay homage to our ascetics.” Out of shame, she was unable to look at the naked ascetics and did not wish to go. Although the father-in-law sent for her repeatedly, she refused. He became angry and said, “Drive her out!” Cūḷasubhaddā thought, “It is not right to blame me without cause,” and summoned the eight householders to explain the matter. When the eight householders realized her innocence, they informed the Treasurer Ugga. The Treasurer told his wife, “This Cūḷasubhaddā does not pay homage to my ascetics, saying they are shameless.” The mother-in-law, wondering, “What are her ascetics like, whom she praises so much?” summoned Cūḷasubhaddā and spoke this verse:
292:
## Proclaiming the Virtues of the Monks

When asked in such a way, Cūḷasubhaddā, wishing to specifically reveal the virtues of the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha to her father-in-law, said:

(a) Santindriyā santamānasā, santaṃ tesaṃ gataṃ ṭhitaṃ.
Okkhibttacakkhū mitabhāṇī, tādisā samaṇā mama.

(a) Those monks who possess such qualities have calmed faculties, such as the eye. They have calmed minds. Their walking is calm. Their standing is calm. They have downcast eyes. They are moderate in speech. Such monks are mine.

(b) Kāyakammaṃ suci nesaṃ, vācākammaṃ anāvilaṃ.
Manokammaṃ suvisuddhaṃ, tādisā samaṇā mama.

(b) The bodily action of those monks is pure. Their verbal action is clear. Their mental action is very pure. Such monks are mine.

(c) Vimalā saṅkhamuttābhā, suddhā antarabāhirā.
Puṇṇā suddhehi dhammehi, tādisā samaṇā mama.

(c) Those monks who possess such qualities are stainless. They are like a newly polished conch. Their internal and external natures are pure. They are full of pure qualities. Such monks are mine.

(d) Lābhena unnato loko, alābhena ca onato.
Lābhālābhena ekaṭṭhā, tādisā samaṇā mama.

(d) The world of people rises with gain and falls with loss. Those monks who possess such qualities remain steadfast in the same state through both gain and loss. Such monks are mine.

(e) Yasena unnato loko, ayasena ca onato.
Yasāyasena ekaṭṭhā, tādisā samaṇā mama.

(e) The world of people rises with fame and falls with obscurity. Those monks who possess such qualities remain steadfast in the same state through both fame and obscurity. Such monks are mine.

(f) Pasaṃsāyunnato loko, nindāyāpi ca onato.
Samā nindāpasaṃsāsu, tādisā samaṇā mama.

(f) The world of people rises with praise and falls with blame. Those monks who possess such qualities have an equal mind in both blame and praise. Such monks are mine.

(g) Sukhena unnato loko, dukkhenāpi ca onato.
Akampā sukhadukkhesu, tādisā samaṇā mama.

(g) The world of people rises with happiness and falls with suffering. Those monks who possess such qualities are unshakable in both happiness and suffering. Such monks are mine.

(With these words and others, she pleased her father-in-law.)

## Inviting the Sangha Headed by the Buddha

Then, when Cūḷasubhaddā was asked, "Can you show your monks to us as well?" and she replied, "I can,"

They said, "If so, do whatever is necessary so that we may see them." Cūḷasubhaddā agreed, saying, "Very well." She prepared a great offering for the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Standing on the upper level of the palace, facing the Jetavana monastery, she respectfully prostrated with the fivefold touch (pañcapatiṭṭhita). Reflecting on the virtues of the Buddha, she made offerings of flowers, scents, and incense. She made a resolution: "Venerable Sir, I invite the community of monks headed by the Buddha for tomorrow's meritorious deed. By this sign of mine, may the Teacher know that he has been invited." She then threw eight handfuls of jasmine flowers into the sky. The flowers traveled and formed a floral canopy over the Teacher as he was preaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly.

At that moment, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, having heard the Dhamma discourse, also invited the Teacher for the next day's meritorious deed. The Teacher said, "Householder, I have already accepted the meal for tomorrow." When asked, "Venerable Sir, no one arrived before me. Whose invitation have you accepted?" the Teacher replied, "Cūḷasubhaddā's, householder."
293:
## The Teaching

(304) The virtuous shine from afar, like the Himalayan mountains.
The wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night.

Like the king of mountains, the Himālaya, shines clearly; so too, the virtuous who dwell in distant places shine clearly.

When it was asked, "Venerable Sir, to whom have you given your consent?", the Buddha replied, "Householder, I have been invited by Cūḷasubhaddā." When it was further submitted, "Exalted Buddha, Cūḷasubhaddā lives in the city of Ugga, which is more than one hundred and twenty leagues away from this city of Sāvatthī," the Buddha said, "Householder, it is true. Even though they dwell in a distant place, the virtuous manifest themselves as if they were standing right before one's eyes," and he spoke this verse:

(Because of the calming of passions such as lust, only the Buddhas and others are truly called 'Santo' or the virtuous. However, in this context, 'Santo' refers to those beings who have performed meritorious deeds and made aspirations in the presence of previous Buddhas, who possess abundant roots of merit, and who have developed meditation. Even though such virtuous ones dwell afar, they become manifest as they enter the path of the Buddhas' knowledge. Just as the king of mountains, the Himālaya—which is three thousand leagues in length and breadth, five hundred leagues in height, and adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks—appears clearly to those staying far away as if it were standing right in front of them, so too do they shine clearly.)

Just as arrows shot in the night do not appear; so too, the wicked who dwell even here, near me, do not appear.

(The 'Asanto' or the wicked refer to foolish persons who give weight only to the benefits of the present life, who cannot transcend the world beyond, who have eyes that see only material gains, and who have entered the monkhood for the sake of a livelihood. Such persons, even if they sit near the right knee of the Buddhas, do not appear and are not known. Like arrows shot in the night—an darkness endowed with four factors [the new moon, a dense forest, a cloudy sky, and midnight]—they cannot be known because of the absence of past causes that serve as a supporting condition.)

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

## The Buddha's Journey to the City of Ugga

Sakka, the King of Devas, knowing that "The Teacher has accepted the invitation of Cūḷasubhaddā," commanded the celestial architect Vissakamma, "Create five hundred pinnacled buildings and tomorrow, convey the community of monks headed by the Buddha to the city of Ugga." On the following day, at dawn, Vissakamma created five hundred pinnacled buildings and stood at the gate of the Jetavana monastery. The Buddha, having specially selected five hundred Arahants who were pure and free from taints, sat in the pinnacled buildings with his retinue and traveled to the city of Ugga. Ugga the merchant, along with his retinue, following the method given by Cūḷasubhaddā, was watching the path by which the Tathāgata would come. Upon seeing the Buddha arriving with great glory and splendor, his mind was filled with faith. Performing great honor with flowers and such, he and his retinue welcomed and paid homage to the Buddha. After offering a great donation, he invited the Buddha repeatedly and offered great alms for seven days.
294:
The Buddha, having noted what was suitable for Ugga the merchant, preached the Dhamma. Starting with the merchant, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma (Dhammābhisamaya). To support Cūḷasubhaddā, the Buddha instructed the Elder Anuruddha, "You shall remain here in this city of Ugga," and then returned to Sāvatthī. From that time on, the people of that city became endowed with faith.

## The Story of Cūḷasubhaddā Ends.

## The Teaching

(305) Sitting alone, sleeping alone, wandering alone, diligent,
Taming oneself alone, one should delight in the forest's edge.

One should resort to sitting alone in solitude and sleeping alone in solitude.

## 9. The Story of the Elder Ekavihārī

While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with "Ekāsanaṃ," concerning the Elder named Ekavihārī, who was accustomed to dwelling alone.

## Dwelling Alone

That Elder, it is said, slept alone, sat alone, walked in meditation alone, and stood alone. Thus, he became well-known among the four assemblies. Then, other monks reported to the Tathāgata, "Venerable Sir, this Elder is of such a nature." The Buddha, saying "Excellent! Excellent!" gave him his approval and spoke on the benefits of seclusion, saying, "A monk should indeed be one who dwells in seclusion," and he spoke this verse:
295:
(Even while sitting in the midst of a thousand monks, if one does not abandon one's basic meditation subject and sits with that mental application, it is called 'sitting alone'.)

Being diligent, wandering alone while practicing and striving, taming oneself alone, one should be one who delights in the secluded forest.

(While thus taming oneself, one should delight only in the forest's edge, which is secluded from the sounds of women, men, and so forth. For it is not possible for one who dwells in a crowd to tame oneself in this way.)

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. From that time on, the great multitude of people aspired only to dwelling alone.

The Story of the Elder Ekavihārī Ends.

The Commentary on the Miscellaneous Chapter (Pakiṇṇaka Vagga) is Finished.

The Twenty-first Chapter.
296:
## 22. Nirayavagga
## 1. The Story of the Female Wanderer Sundarī
(Sundarīparibbājikāvatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Abhūtavādī' in reference to the female wanderer named Sundarī.

## The Accusation by the Female Wanderer Sundarī
(At that time, the Blessed One was revered, honored, esteemed, and worshipped. This story appears in detail in the Udāna Pali; however, in this Dhammapada Commentary, the following sequence of words is merely a summary.)

## The Deliberation of the Heretics
When great gains and offerings, like the mighty flood of the five great rivers, arose for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, the other sectarians, whose gains and offerings had ceased, became lusterless like fireflies at sunrise. They gathered together and deliberated: 'Since the ascetic Gotama appeared, our gains and offerings have been cut off. No one even knows of our existence. With whom could we unite to bring disrepute to the ascetic Gotama, and by causing him to be blamed and discredited, make his gains and offerings disappear?'

## Using the Female Wanderer Sundarī
While they were deliberating, this thought occurred to them: 'By uniting with the female wanderer Sundarī, we shall be able to succeed.' Having said this, one day, when Sundarī entered the monastery of the sectarians and stood there after paying respects, they remained silent and did not speak to her. Although she spoke to them repeatedly, she received no reply and asked, 'Noble sirs, has someone perhaps oppressed you?' They replied, 'Sister, do you not see the ascetic Gotama wandering about, oppressing us and causing our gains and offerings to be cut off?' She asked, 'What should I do in this matter?' They said, 'Sister, you are very beautiful and have attained the height of loveliness. Bring disrepute upon the ascetic Gotama, make the great multitude believe your words, and thus cause his gains and offerings to be cut off.'

## How Sundarī Accused the Buddha
Hearing the words of the sectarians, she consented, saying, 'Very well,' and departed. From then on, taking flowers, perfumes, ointments, camphor, and pungent fruits, she would go towards the Jetavana Monastery in the evening when the great multitude, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Teacher, were entering the city. When asked, 'Where are you going?' she would say, 'I am going to the presence of the ascetic Gotama; I, indeed, with the ascetic Gotama—'
297:
After a few days, the sectarians gave money to some rogues and said, "Go, kill Sundarī and discard her body in the heap of flower refuse near the ascetic Gotama's Fragrant Chamber, then return." Those rogues did exactly as the sectarians had said.

## Killing Sundarī and Discarding Her Near the Fragrant Chamber
After the murder, the sectarians raised a hue and cry, saying, "We do not see Sundarī," and informed King Pasenadi of Kosala. When asked, "Where do you have suspicion?" they replied, "These days she stays at Jetavana; we do not know what has happened to her there." The King gave permission, saying, "In that case, go and search for her."

## Spreading Rumors
Taking their own attendants, they went to Jetavana and searched. Upon finding her in the heap of flower refuse, they placed her on a litter, entered the city, and informed the King: "The disciples of the ascetic Gotama, thinking 'We shall hide the evil deed done by our teacher,' have killed Sundarī and discarded her in the heap of flower refuse."

King Pasenadi of Kosala said, "In that case, go and wander through the city." The sectarians went through the city streets, saying, "Look at the deed of the Sakyan ascetics!" and then returned to the palace gate.

## Placing Sundarī's Corpse in the Cemetery
The King had Sundarī's corpse placed on a platform in the charnel ground and ordered it to be guarded. Except for the noble disciples (ariyasāvakas), the people of Sāvatthī mostly wandered about inside and outside the city and in the woods, reviling the monks and saying, "Look at the deed of the Sakyan ascetics!"

The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, "In that case, you disciples should address the people in this way," and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(306) The speaker of untruth goes to hell,
And also he who, having done a deed, says "I did not do it."
Both of them, being men of base actions,
Become equal in the hereafter.

**Abhūtavādī**: One who habitually speaks untruths and makes false accusations against others without seeing any fault. **Katvā**: One who, having committed an evil deed, says "I did not do it." **Pecca samā bhavanti**: Both these persons, having gone to the next world, become equal in their destination by entering hell. Their destination is the same, though their lifespan there may not be; those who have done much evil suffer long in hell, while those who have done little suffer for a shorter time.
298:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

## Investigating the Killer of Sundarī
King Pasenadi of Kosala sent his royal men, saying, "Go and investigate to find out the truth about Sundarī being killed by others."

## Truth Revealed Through Drunkenness
Then, those drunkards, drinking liquor with the coins given by the heretics, began to quarrel with one another. One man said to another, "You killed the female wanderer Sundarī with a single blow and hid her in the heap of flower refuse, and now you are drinking liquor with the coins received for that killing. Let it be, let it be!" The royal officers arrested those drunkards and presented them to the King. Then the King questioned those drunkards, "Did you kill her?" When they replied, "Yes, Your Majesty," he questioned them again, "Who told you to kill her?" They replied, "Your Majesty, the heretics outside the Dispensation told us to kill her." The King summoned the heretics and questioned them. The heretics confessed just as the drunkards had. "If that is so, go," the King ordered, "and wander through the city saying this: 'Desiring to cast blame and reproach upon the Ascetic Gotama, we killed this Sundarī. There is no fault in the Ascetic Gotama or his disciples; the fault is ours alone.'" The heretics did as the King commanded. Only then did the foolish masses believe. Both the heretics and the drunkards received the punishment for murder. From that time on, great offerings and honor accrued to the Buddhas.

The story of Sundarī the female wanderer ends.

## 3. The Story of the Monks Living on the Banks of the Vaggumudā River
(Vaggumudātīriya Bhikkhu Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing in the Mahāvana forest near the city of Vesālī, told this religious teaching beginning with "Seyyo ayoguḷo," concerning the monks living on the banks of the Vaggumudā River.

(The story appears in the Uttari-manussa-dhamma Pārājika.)

## Boasting of Dhamma for the Sake of Livelihood
At that time, the Blessed One asked the monks residing on the banks of the Vaggumudā River: "Monks, is it true that for the sake of your bellies, you spoke to laypeople, boasting of your own attainments in the qualities of the Noble Ones—such as Jhana, Path, and Fruit—which are superior to the ten wholesome courses of action?" When the monks replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Buddha rebuked them in many ways and spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other higher stages.
The story of the monks residing on the banks of the Vaggumudā River ends.

## The Teaching
(309) Four states befall the heedless man who consorts with another's wife: the acquisition of demerit, lack of comfortable sleep, blame as the third, and hell as the fourth.

(310) There is the acquisition of demerit and an evil destination; the pleasure of the frightened man and the frightened woman is brief; and the king imposes a heavy punishment. Therefore, a man should not consort with another's wife.

*Evaṃ*: in this way, *tassa*: to that person, *apuññalābho ca*: there is the acquisition of demerit. *Tena*: because of that demerit, *pāpikā*: an evil, *gatī ca*: destination such as the four lower realms, *hoti*: occurs. *Bhītassa*: of the frightened man, *bhītāya*: with the frightened woman, *ratī ca*: the pleasure, *thokikā*: is very brief. *Rājā ca*: the king also, *garukaṃ*: a heavy, *daṇḍaṃ*: punishment such as the cutting off of hands and feet, *paṇeti*: inflicts. *Tasmā*: because there are so many faults, *naro*: a man, *paradāraṃ*: another's wife, *na seve*: should not consort with.

## 4. The Story of Khemaka the Merchant's Son, Nephew of Anāthapiṇḍika
(Khemakaseṭṭhiputtavatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching starting with "Cattāri ṭhānāni" concerning the merchant's son named Khemaka, who was the nephew of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.

## The Merchant's Son Who Was Frequently Arrested
That merchant's son named Khemaka was said to be extremely handsome. Generally, when women saw him, they were overcome by passion and were unable to maintain their composure. Khemaka himself was also afflicted by the evil kamma of desiring the wives of others. At that time, the king's men caught him at night and presented him to the King. King Pasenadi of Kosala, thinking "I am ashamed before the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika," released him without saying a single word.
301:
However, that merchant's son Khemaka did not refrain from his actions. Subsequently, the king's men caught him a second and a third time and presented him to the King; the King simply released him. The great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, hearing of this matter, took Khemaka to the Teacher, reported the situation, and said, "Venerable Sir, please preach the Dhamma to this Khemaka." The Buddha, having spoken words to cause spiritual urgency (saṃvega) to Khemaka and showing the faults of consorting with another's wife, spoke these verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, the merchant's son named Khemaka was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. From that day forward, the multitude of people spent their time in happiness.

## Khemaka the Merchant's Son's Past Aspiration
What was the past wholesome deed of that merchant's son named Khemaka? It is said that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was an excellent wrestler. Having offered two golden banners at the golden stupa of the Buddha, he made an aspiration: "Except for my female relatives, may all other women fall in love with me upon seeing me." This was the past merit of Khemaka. Therefore, in whatever place he was born, other men's wives could not maintain their composure upon seeing him.
The story of Khemaka the merchant's son, nephew of Anāthapiṇḍika, ends.

## 5. The Story of the Monk Who Was Difficult to Admonish
(Dubbacabhikkhuvatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching starting with "Kuso yathā" concerning a certain monk who was difficult to admonish.

## Cutting Grass Despite Knowing the Vinaya
It is said that a certain monk, without intention, cut a blade of grass. When remorse (kukkucca) arose in him, he approached another monk and asked, "Friend, what happens to a monk who cuts grass?" reporting his own action. When he asked thus, the other monk said to him, "You consider that there is some fault because of the act of cutting grass;"
302:
## The Teaching

(311) Just as kusa grass, if wrongly grasped, cuts the very hand; so the ascetic life, if wrongly handled, drags one to hell.

(312) Any slack deed, any corrupt practice, a suspect holy life—none of these bears great fruit.

(313) If there is something to be done, let one do it; let one strive for it firmly. For a slack ascetic only scatters more dust.

*Duggahito*: wrongly grasped. *Kuso*: kusa grass.
*Hatthameva*: the hand itself. *Anukantati yathā*: just as it cuts. *Evaṃ*: in the same way. *Dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ*: wrongly handled. *Sāmaññaṃ*: the ascetic life. *Dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ*: an ascetic who handles it wrongly. *Nirayāya*: to hell. *Upakaḍḍhati*: drags.

"You think that because of cutting grass, nothing happens; there is no fault here, but one is released after confessing," he said, and then he himself pulled up grass with both hands. The monks reported this matter to the Teacher. The Teacher rebuked that monk in many ways and, wishing to teach the Dhamma, spoke these verses.

(Though it is called kusa grass, any grass with sharp edges, even a palm leaf at the least, will cut the hand of one who grasps it wrongly. Similarly, the ascetic life, known as the practice of a recluse, if handled wrongly through broken or spotted precepts, will cause one to be reborn in hell.)
