*Sithilaṃ*: done slackly. *Yaṃkiñci*: any whatsoever. *Kammañca*: deed. *Saṅkiliṭṭhaṃ*: corrupt. *Yaṃ vatañca*: that practice.

(It is corrupt by wandering in places where alms should not be sought.)

*Saṅkassaraṃ*: that which is remembered with suspicion or dread. *Yaṃ brahmacariyañca*: that holy life.

(When seeing the Saṅgha assembled for a task such as the Uposatha, he thinks with suspicion, "Surely these monks have assembled because they know my conduct and wish to expel me.")

*Atthi*: there is. *Taṃ*: that practice. *Tassa*: for that person. *Mahapphalaṃ*: of great fruit. *Na hoti*: is not.

(Because it is not of great fruit for that monk, it is also not of great fruit for the donors who offer him alms.)

*Yaṃ kammaṃ*: whatever deed. *Ce kayirā*: if one should do. *Naṃ kammaṃ*: that deed. *Kayirātha*: one should indeed do. *Enaṃ*: that deed. *Daḷhaṃ*: firmly. *Parakkame*: one should strive.

(One should practice by doing it firmly, not just as a mere formality or a slack undertaking.)

*Hi*: indeed. *Sithilo*: slackly performed. *Paribbājo*: the ascetic life. *Bhiyo*: more. *Rajaṃ*: the dust of lust and so on. *Ākirate*: scatters/pours.

(An ascetic life that has become broken or spotted due to slackness cannot remove the internal dust of lust and so on; instead, it pours more new dust of lust over the old.)
303:
## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people reached the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so on. That difficult-to-admonish monk also established himself in restraint, later developed insight, and reached the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala).

The Story of the Difficult-to-Admonish Monk ends.

## The Teaching

(314) Better is a bad deed left undone; a bad deed brings remorse later. Better is a good deed done, which, having done, one does not regret.

*Yaṃ dukkaṭaṃ*: whatever evil deed. *Katvā*: because of doing. *Pacchā*: later. *Tappati*: one suffers remorse. *Taṃ dukkaṭaṃ*: that evil deed. *Akataṃ*: not doing. *Seyyo*: is better.

## 6. The Story of the Woman Overcome by Envy
(Issāpakatitthi-vatthu)

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with "Akataṃ," concerning a certain woman overcome by envy.

## Cutting the Ears and Nose of the Housemaid

It is said that the husband of that woman had an affair with a housemaid. Overcome by envy, the woman bound the maid's hands and feet, cut off her ears and nose, and threw her into a very secure secret room. She closed the door and, to hide her deed, said, "Master, come, let us go to the monastery to hear the Dhamma." She took her husband to the monastery and sat listening to the Dhamma.

At that time, some visiting relatives of the woman arrived at the house, opened the door, and seeing the maid in that miserable state, released her. The housemaid followed them to the monastery and, standing in the midst of the fourfold assembly, reported the matter to the Buddha. When the Buddha heard the words of the housemaid, he said, "Regarding what is called misconduct, one should not do even the slightest evil, thinking 'Others do not know this of me.' Even if others do not know, one should only do good. For misconduct, even if done in secret, causes remorse later. Good conduct only generates joy." He then spoke this verse:

(It is better not to do an evil deed that is blameworthy and leads to the lower realms. For that evil deed brings remorse every time it is remembered.)

*Yaṃ sukataṃ*: whatever blameless deed. *Katvā*: because of doing. *Pacchā*: later. *Nānutappati*: one does not regret. *Taṃ sukataṃ*: that blameless deed. *Katañca*: the doing of it. *Seyyā*: is better.

(It is good to do only blameless deeds that increase happiness and lead to a good destination. After doing such a good deed, one does not suffer remorse when remembering it later; only joy arises. That good deed is excellent.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, both the lay disciple (the husband) and the woman were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. They also freed the housemaid on the spot and made her a practitioner of the Dhamma.

The Story of the Woman Overcome by Envy ends.
304:
## The Teaching

(315) Just as a border city is guarded,
Both within and without,
So should you guard yourself.
Let not the moment pass you by.
For those who let the moment pass,
Suffer when consigned to hell.

Paccantaṃ: the border. Nagaraṃ: the city. Santarabāhiraṃ: together with the interior and exterior. Gutthaṃ yathā: just as it is made secure. Evaṃ: in the same way. Attānaṃ: yourself. Gopeṭha: guard securely.

## 7. The Story of Many Monks
(Sambahulabhikkhu Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, starting with "Nagaraṃ yathā," concerning many visiting monks.

## One Should Guard Oneself Securely

Those monks, having entered the rains retreat (Vassa) in a certain border region, lived comfortably during the first month. In the middle month, robbers came, attacked the village where they went for alms, and took the people as captives. From then on, as the people were fortifying that border city to ward off the robbers, they did not get the opportunity to serve and attend to the monks respectfully. Having lived through a difficult and uncomfortable Vassa, the monks went to Sāvatthī to see the Teacher after the retreat. They paid homage to the Teacher and sat in a suitable place. (Those who are captured alive during war or robbery are called captives.) After the Teacher had exchanged pleasantries with those visiting monks, he asked, "Monks, did you live comfortably?"

"Venerable Sir, we lived comfortably during the first month. In the middle month, robbers attacked the village. From then on, as the people had to fortify the city, they did not get the opportunity to serve us respectfully. Therefore, we did not live comfortably during the Vassa, Venerable Sir."

When they said this, the Teacher said, "Monks, do not worry. What is called living comfortably is always difficult to find. For a monk, just as those people guarded their city securely, it is proper to guard one's own self (attabhāva) securely." He then spoke this verse:

(Monks, just as those people made that border city secure with strong gates and walls, thus securing the interior, and with watchtowers and moats, thus securing the exterior; in this way, making it well-guarded both within and without—so too should you establish mindfulness, closing the six internal doors (senses) and not letting go of the gatekeeper, mindfulness. Just as the six external sense objects, when grasped, lead to the harm of the internal ones, you should make them firm by not grasping, and wander without abandoning the gatekeeper, mindfulness, to prevent their entry, thus guarding yourself.)

Vo: you. Khaṇā: the moment, which is the time of a Buddha's appearance. Mā upaccagā: do not let it pass.
305:
(For the person who does not guard himself in this way, this moment of a Buddha's appearance, the moment of being born in the Middle Country, the moment of attaining Right View, and the moment of having the six sense bases intact—all these moments pass away. Let not that moment pass you by.)

Hi: indeed. Khaṇātītā: those who have let the moment of a Buddha's appearance pass. Nirayamhi: in hell. Samappitā: being consigned. Socanti: they grieve.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, those visiting monks, having attained spiritual urgency (saṃvega), were established in the Fruit of Arahatship.

The Story of Many Monks ends.

## The Teaching

(316) They are ashamed of what is not shameful,
And not ashamed of what is shameful.
Embracing wrong views,
Beings go to a woeful state.

(317) They see fear in what is not fearful,
And see no fear in what is fearful.
Embracing wrong views,
Beings go to a woeful state.

Ye sattā: those beings. Alajjitāye: by the alms bowl, which is not shameful. Lajjanti: they are ashamed.

## 8. The Story of the Nigantha Ascetics
(Nigantha Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, starting with "Alajjitāye," concerning the Niganthas (Jain ascetics).

## Those Ashamed of What is Not Shameful

One day, when the monks saw the Niganthas, they started a conversation: "Friends, these Nigantha ascetics are better than those who are completely uncovered (naked ascetics). These Niganthas at least cover one side in front. They seem to have a sense of shame."

Hearing this, the Niganthas said, "We do not cover ourselves because of shame. Rather, particles of dust and the like are also living beings, connected to the life faculty (jīvitindriya). We cover ourselves for this reason: so that those particles do not fall into our alms bowls." They spoke many words back and forth in debate with the monks. When the monks approached the Teacher and sat down, they reported the matter. The Teacher said, "Monks, those who are ashamed of the alms bowl, which is not shameful, and are not ashamed of the limbs, which are shameful, have a woeful state as their destination." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

(Because they wander covering the alms bowl, which is not shameful, they are said to be ashamed of what is not shameful.)

Lajjitāye: by the limbs, which are shameful. Na lajjare: they are not ashamed.

(Because they wander without covering the shameful limbs, they are said to be not ashamed of what is shameful.)

Micchādiṭṭhisamādānā: those who embrace wrong views. Te sattā: those beings. Duggatiṃ: to a woeful state. Gaccanti: they go.

(Being ashamed of what should not be ashamed of, and not being ashamed of what should be ashamed of, is a wrong view, whether by taking it as empty or in another way. Those beings with wrong views who wander embracing such views reach woeful states like hell.)

Ye sattā: those beings. Abhaye: in the alms bowl, which is not fearful. Bhayadassino: they are accustomed to seeing fear.
306:
(Because of the alms bowl, dangers such as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, and defiled misconduct do not arise; therefore, the alms bowl is called 'fearless' [without danger]. One who covers that alms bowl out of fear is called one who sees fear in what should not be feared.)

And in the [shameful] parts where there is fear, they see no fear.

(Because lust and other defilements tend to arise based on the shameful parts of the body, those parts are called 'fearful' [dangerous]. By not covering those parts, one is called one who sees no fear in what is fearful.)

Beings who undertake wrong views go to a state of woe (duggati).

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many Niganthas, their hearts filled with spiritual urgency, went forth as monks. The teaching was also beneficial to those who had arrived.

The Story of the Niganthas ends.

## 9. The Story of the Disciples of the Titthiyas

(Titthiyasāvakavatthu)

The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching starting with 'Avajje' while residing at Jetavana Monastery, concerning the disciples of the Titthiyas.

## How Those with Wrong Views Came to Revere the Buddha

On one occasion, lay followers of other sects (Titthiyas) saw their children playing with the children of lay followers who had right view. When the children returned home, the parents made them swear an oath: "You must not pay homage to the monks who are sons of the Sakyans, nor should you enter their monastery."

One day, while playing near the outer gate of Jetavana Monastery, they became thirsty. They sent one son of a Buddhist lay follower, saying, "Go there, drink water, and bring some for us too."

The boy went to the monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, drank water, and informed Him of the matter. The Buddha said, "You drink the water yourself, then go back and send the other boys here to drink water as well."

The boys came and drank water. The Buddha had them summoned and gave them a suitable Dhamma talk, establishing them in unshakable faith and in the Refuges and Precepts.
307:
...and in the precepts. When the boys reached their homes, they told their parents about it. Then, the parents became distressed and lamented, thinking, "Our sons have become those with ruined views!"

Then, many wise neighbors came and spoke words of Dhamma to calm their distress. Hearing the neighbors' words, the parents said, "We shall hand these children over to the Ascetic Gotama himself," and they went to the monastery with a large group of relatives. The Buddha, perceiving their inclinations and wishing to teach the Dhamma, spoke these verses:

## The Teaching

(318) Those who perceive fault in the faultless,
And see no fault in the faulty,
Beings who undertake wrong views,
Go to a state of woe.

(319) Knowing fault as fault,
And the faultless as faultless,
Beings who undertake right views,
Go to a happy destination.

Those beings who have the view that there is fault in the faultless, true Dhamma; and who are accustomed to seeing no fault in the faulty, false Dhamma; because they have undertaken wrong views, those beings go to a state of woe (duggati).

Those beings who, knowing the faulty, false Dhamma as faulty; and knowing the faultless, true Dhamma as faultless; because they have undertaken right views, those beings go to a happy destination (suggati).

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, all of them were established in the Three Refuges. As they continued to listen to the Dhamma, they were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The Story of the Disciples of the Titthiyas ends.

The Chapter on Hell (Niraya Vagga) ends.
308:
## The Teaching

(320) As an elephant in battle endures an arrow shot from a bow, so shall I endure abuse; for many people are indeed unvirtuous.

## 23. Nāgavagga

## 1. The Story of the Self-Tamed
(Attadantavatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching, "As an elephant...", concerning himself.

(The story is detailed in the commentary to the opening verse of the Appamādavagga. Indeed, in that commentary, the following was said:)

## An Issue Should Be Settled Where It Arises

Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, being unable to do anything to the five hundred palace ladies led by Sāmāvatī, thought, "I will do what should be done to the ascetic Gotama." She gave bribes to the townspeople and ordered them, "When the ascetic Gotama enters the city and wanders about, abuse and revile him along with slaves and laborers and drive him away."

The heretics, who had no faith in the Triple Gem, followed the Teacher as he entered the city and abused and reviled him with the ten forms of abuse: "You are a thief, a fool, a deluded one, a thief (again), a camel, an ox, a donkey, a denizen of hell, an animal; there is no happy destination for you, only a miserable destination is to be expected for you."

Hearing those words of abuse, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, these townspeople of Kosambī are abusing and reviling us. Let us go elsewhere from here."

"Where shall we go, Ānanda?" the Teacher asked.

"To another city, Venerable Sir," he replied.

"If people there abuse and revile us, where shall we go then, Ānanda?" the Teacher asked again.

"From there, we shall go to another city, Venerable Sir," he replied.
309:
(321) They lead the tamed to an assembly; the king mounts the tamed. Among humans, the tamed is best, he who endures abuse.

(322) Excellent are tamed mules, and noble horses from Sindh, and great tusker elephants; but more excellent than those is the self-tamed.

*Nāga*: like a battle elephant. *Sangāme*: in the battlefield. *Cāpato*: from a bow. *Patitaṃ*: released and fallen. *Saraṃ*: various large and small arrows. *Titikkhati iva*: just as it endures. *Evaṃ*: in the same way. *Ahaṃ*: I, the Buddha. *Ativākyaṃ*: transgressive speech and abuse. *Titikkhissaṃ*: will endure.

When asked, "If people there abuse and revile us, where shall we go then, Ānanda?", he replied, "From there, we shall go to another city, Venerable Sir." The Buddha then said, "Ānanda, it is not proper to do so. Where an issue arises, it is only proper to go elsewhere once that issue has been settled there." He then asked, "Ānanda, who are they that are abusing and reviling?" Ānanda replied, "Venerable Sir, everyone from the slaves and laborers downwards is abusing and reviling us."

"Ānanda, I am like a great tusker elephant that has entered the battlefield. Just as it is the responsibility of a great tusker elephant entered into battle to endure arrows coming from the four directions, so too is it my responsibility to endure the words spoken by many unvirtuous persons," the Buddha said. Desiring to teach the Dhamma concerning himself, he spoke these verses:

(Just as a well-tamed battle elephant entering a fight endures spear-thrusts and the like, and endures arrows released from a bow that fall upon its body without being distressed, so too will I endure such transgressive speech—this is the meaning.)

*Hi saccaṃ*: it is true that one should endure. *Jano*: the people of the worldly realm. *Bahu dussīlo*: many are unvirtuous.

(The multitude of people in this worldly realm are mostly unvirtuous; they wander about uttering words according to their own preferences, causing friction and offense. In such cases, endurance and equanimity are my responsibility—this is the meaning.)

*Samitiṃ*: into the midst of a multitude. *Gacchantā*: those who go. *Dantaṃ*: a tamed ox or a tamed horse. *Nayanti*: they lead them yoked to a vehicle.

(When people go into the midst of a crowd at garden festivals and such, they lead tamed oxen or horses yoked to their vehicles—this is the meaning.)

*Rājā*: a sovereign king. *Dantaṃ*: a tamed elephant or horse vehicle. *Abhirūhati*: he mounts.

(A sovereign king traveling with such vehicles also mounts only a tamed elephant or horse—this is the meaning.)

*Manussesu*: among humans. *Yo*: whoever. *Ativākyaṃ*: transgressive, offensive, and reckless speech. *Titikkhati*: is able to endure. *So*: such a person. *Danto*: is tamed. *Seṭṭho*: and is especially noble or especially praised.

(Among humans, too, a noble person tamed through the four paths can endure such transgressive speech even when spoken repeatedly. He is not agitated and not distressed; such a person is tamed and noble—this is the meaning.)

*Assatarā*: mules born from a donkey and a mare. *Ājānīyā*: noble horses capable of quickly knowing what is required. *Sindhavā ca*: and horses born in the Sindh region. *Kuñjarā*: those called tuskers. *Mahānāgā ca*: and great elephants. *Dantā*: only when tamed through training. *Varā*: are they excellent.

## > (They are not excellent without being trained and tamed—this is the meaning.)

*Attadanto*: a person who is tamed through training by the four noble paths. *Tato*: is more excellent than those aforementioned. *Varaṃ - varataraṃ*: is exceedingly noble.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, the entire multitude of people who had taken bribes and stood at the streets and crossroads abusing and reviling attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of the Self-Tamed is finished.
310:
## The Teaching
(323) Not by these vehicles could one go to the untrodden region,
as a tamed person goes by means of a self that is well-tamed.

"By these vehicles" means by these vehicles such as elephant-carriages. "To the untrodden region" means to the region of Nibbāna, which is called "untrodden" (agata) because it has never been reached before. "Could not go" means one is unable to reach it.

## 2. The Story of the Monk who was formerly an Elephant Trainer
(Hatthācariya-pubbaka-bhikkhu-vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, told this religious teaching beginning with "Na hi etehi" in reference to a certain monk who was formerly an elephant trainer.

## One should strive to reach the unreached region
One day, on the bank of the Aciravatī River, that monk saw an elephant trainer who was unable to train an elephant to perform a desired action. He called out to the monks standing nearby and said, "Venerable sirs, if this elephant trainer were to pierce this elephant in such-and-such a place, he would be able to train it to perform this action very quickly."

The elephant trainer, hearing the monk's words, did as the monk said and was able to tame the elephant well. Those monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One had the monk summoned and asked, "Is it true that you said this?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Buddha rebuked him, saying, "Vain man, what benefit is there to you in an elephant-vehicle or any other tamed vehicle? There is no one who is able to go to the untrodden region by these vehicles. It is only possible to go to the untrodden region by means of a self that is well-tamed. Therefore, tame only yourself; what benefit is there to you in taming those elephants?" Having said this, he uttered this verse:

(323) Not by these vehicles could one go to the untrodden region,
as a tamed person goes by means of a self that is well-tamed.

(The meaning is that no person can reach the region of Nibbāna, called "untrodden" because it has never been reached even in a dream, by means of these elephant-vehicles and so on.)

"As" (yathā) refers to the means of reaching. "By a well-tamed self" (sutantena attanā) and "by the taming of the path of meditation" (dantena), the "tamed person" (danto) reaches the destination.

(The meaning is that a wise person who is well-tamed—first by taming the sense faculties such as the eye, and later by developing the Noble Path—reaches that untrodden region. Therefore, taming oneself is nobler than taming that elephant.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of the Monk who was formerly an Elephant Trainer ends.
311:
## 3. The Story of the Sons of the Old Brahmin
(Parijiṇṇa-brāhmaṇa-putta-vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing in Sāvatthī, told this religious teaching beginning with "Dhanapālo" in reference to the sons of a certain worn-out old Brahmin.

## The Suffering of the Brahmin who gave away his entire Inheritance
In Sāvatthī, there was a Brahmin who possessed a wealth of eight hundred thousand. When his four sons reached of age, he arranged their marriages and gave them four hundred thousand.

Later, when the Brahmin's wife died, the sons consulted each other, saying, "If our father brings another wife, the family wealth will be divided among the children born from her womb. Let us now take good care of him." They attended to him with excellent food and clothing, and performed services such as massaging his hands and feet.

One day, while they were massaging his hands and feet after he woke from a daytime nap, they each spoke of the faults of household life and pleaded, "Father, we will look after you in this manner for the rest of your life. Please grant us the remaining four hundred thousand as well." The father Brahmin gave one hundred thousand to each son, keeping only enough for his own clothing, and handed over all his possessions and enjoyments in four portions.

The eldest son looked after the father for two or three days. Then one day, seeing the old Brahmin returning from his bath, the daughter-in-law stood at the gateway and said, "Father, did you give anything extra, like a hundred or a thousand, to the eldest son? Did you not give two hundred thousand to each of all the sons? Do you not know the way to the houses of the other sons?"

## Approaching the Buddha
The old Brahmin, angered, said, "Perish, you low-born woman!" and went to the house of another son. After two or three days, he was driven away from that house in the same manner and went to the house of another. Thus, unable to enter even a single house, he was ordained as a white-robed ascetic (paṇḍaranga-pabbajja). As he wandered for alms, over time he became worn out by old age. His body became withered due to poor food and poor sleeping conditions. Returning from his alms round, he lay down on his back and fell asleep. Upon waking and sitting up, he looked at himself and saw no refuge or support in his sons. He thought, "It is said that the Ascetic Gotama does not frown, has a cheerful countenance, speaks pleasantly, and is skilled in welcoming others. If I approach the Ascetic Gotama, I might receive a kind welcome."

The old Brahmin adjusted his robes, took his alms bowl and staff, and went to the presence of the Blessed One. This has also been said (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).
312:
## Verses Taught by the Buddha to the Elderly Brahmin

At whose birth I rejoiced, and whose growth I desired,
They, consulting with their wives, drive me away like dogs driving a pig.
Wicked and vile, they call me 'Father, Father,'
But like demons in the form of sons, they abandon me in my old age.
Like an old horse of no use is deprived of fodder,
So the father of these fools, now elderly, begs at others' houses.
My staff is indeed better for me than disobedient sons;
It keeps away a fierce ox and also a fierce dog.
In the darkness, it goes before me; in deep water, it finds a footing.
By the power of the staff, though I stumble, I stand firm.

With whose birth (yehi jātehi), I (ahaṃ) once rejoiced (nandissaṃ). And whose (yesañca) prosperity and growth (bhavaṃ) I once desired (icchihaṃ). Those (te) sons, consulting (sampuccha) with their wives (dārehi), drive me away (vārenti) just as dogs (sā) drive away a pig (sūkaraṃ).

Those who are not virtuous (asantā), the vile and foolish sons (jammā), like demons (rakkhasā) in the form of sons (puttarūpena), they say (bhāsare kira) to me (maṃ), 'Father, Father' (tāta tātāti). Those four foolish sons (te) abandon (jahanti) me who has reached old age (vayogataṃ).

Like an old (jiṇṇo) horse (asso) that is no longer fit for use (nibbhogo) is deprived (apanīyati iva) of fodder (khādanā), so am I cast out (apanīyāmi). Because of being thus cast out, the elderly (thero) father (pitā) of these fools (bālakānaṃ) must beg (bhikkhati) at the houses of others (paragāရေsu).

My (me) staff (daṇḍo) alone is indeed better (seyyā kira). Disobedient sons (anassavā puttā) who provide no refuge—or those who do not listen to their parents—are not noble. My (me) staff (daṇḍo) can ward off (vāreti) even a fierce (caṇḍaṃ) ox (goṇampi). Moreover (atho), it can ward off (vāreti) even a fierce dog (caṇḍakukkurampi).

In the darkness (andhakāre), it is a guide that goes before me (pure hoti). In deep water (gambhီre), it finds a footing (gādhaṃ edhati). By the power (ānubhāvena) of the staff (daṇḍassa), even if I slip and stumble (khalitvā), I can stand firm (patitiṭṭhati).

(This is true. The following words are spoken in the Pāḷi Canon. At that time, a certain wealthy Brahmin, whose body was emaciated and whose clothes were soiled, approached the place where the Blessed One was staying and sat in a suitable place. This is the account given in the Pāḷi Canon.)

The Blessed One, after exchanging friendly greetings with the elderly Brahmin who was sitting in a suitable place, said this: "Brahmin, why is your body so emaciated? Why are your clothes so soiled?"

"O Venerable Gotama, I have four sons in this world. Those four sons, after consulting with their wives, have driven me out of the house."

When he said this, the Buddha replied: "If that is so, Brahmin, learn these verses and recite them when a large crowd of people is gathered in the assembly hall, and when your sons are also present."

## Restoration of Happiness through the Power of the Verses

Thus, that Brahmin, having learned those verses from the Blessed One, entered the assembly on a day when the Brahmins were gathered together. When his sons, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, were sitting in the midst of the Brahmins on seats worthy of the noble, he thought, "Now is the time for me to enter." He went into the middle of the assembly, raised his hand, and said, "Sirs, I wish to recite some verses to you. Please listen." When they replied, "Brahmin, speak, we are listening," he stood and recited them.
313:
(At that time, there was a custom among people: "A child who consumes the parents' wealth but does not support them shall be put to death.")

Therefore, those four sons of the Brahmin prostrated at their father's feet and begged, "Father, please grant us our lives." The Brahmin, due to his soft heart, said, "Friends, do not destroy my sons; they will support me." Then the people said to the sons, "Friends, from this day forward, if you do not support your father well, you shall be put to death."

Fearing for their lives, the four sons seated their father on a chair and carried him themselves to the house. They anointed his body with oil, massaged him, and bathed him with scented powder and other things. They then called the Brahmin women and said, "From this day forward, support our father well. If you are negligent, we shall punish you." They then fed him choice food. Due to the good food and comfortable sleep, after a few days, the Brahmin regained his strength and his faculties became radiant. Looking at his own body, he thought, "I have obtained this prosperity because of the Samana Gotama." To offer a gift, he took a pair of cloths and went to the Blessed One. After exchanging friendly greetings, he sat in a suitable place, placed the pair of cloths at the Blessed One's feet, and said, "O Venerable Gotama, we Brahmins seek wealth for our teachers. The Venerable Gotama is my teacher. May the Venerable Gotama accept this teacher's fee."

## The Brahmin Establishes Regular Alms for the Buddha

Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One accepted the pair of cloths and taught the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, the Brahmin was established in the Three Refuges and said, "O Venerable Gotama, my sons give me four regular portions of food. From those four, I offer two portions to the Blessed One." Then the Teacher said to the Brahmin, "Brahmin, it is a good intention. However, we shall go only to places that please us," and dismissed him. The Brahmin went home and told his sons, "Dear sons, the Samana Gotama is my friend. I have offered him two regular portions of food. When the Samana Gotama arrives, do not be negligent." The sons agreed, saying, "Very well."

The next morning, while wandering for alms, the Teacher went to the door of the eldest son's house. Seeing the Teacher, the eldest son took the bowl, invited him inside, seated him on a throne worthy of noble ones, and offered choice food. The next day, the Teacher went to the house of another son, and so on, visiting all the sons' houses in order. All of them performed the same acts of honor and hospitality.

## The Sons Also Gain Faith in the Buddha

One day, when the eldest son was preparing a festive ceremony, he asked his father, "Father, to whom shall we give the festive offering?" When the father replied, "I know no others; the Samana Gotama is my friend," the son said, "If that is so, Father, please invite him for tomorrow's merit-making along with five hundred monks." The Brahmin did as his son said. The next morning, the Teacher, accompanied by his retinue, went to the eldest son's house. In the house, which was smeared with fresh cow-dung and decorated with all kinds of ornaments, the son seated the community of monks headed by the Buddha and served them with pure, delicious milk-rice and choice hard food. During the meal, the four sons of the Brahmin...
314:
...served them with honey-rice-porridge with little water and choice hard food. During the meal, the four sons of the Brahmin sat near the Teacher and said, "O Venerable Gotama, we support our father and are not negligent. Look at our father's physical condition."

The Teacher said, "You have done a good deed. Supporting one's parents is indeed the practice of the wise of old." Desiring to tell in detail the Mātuposaka Nāgarāja Jātaka found in the Ekādasa Nipāta, beginning with "Tassa nāgassa vippavāsena, virūḷhā sallakī ca kuṭajā ca," he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(324) The tusker named Dhanapāla,
With pungent temple-secretion, difficult to restrain,
Being bound, does not eat a morsel;
The tusker remembers the elephant-forest.

Dhanapāla: This was the name of the tusker caught in the delightful elephant-forest by the elephant trainer sent by the King of Kāsī.

Kaṭukabhedano: Having sharp must. (When elephants are in must, their temples burst. Even normally, elephants at that time are so fierce they ignore the goad, spear, or trident. The elephant Dhanapāla was extremely fierce and difficult to restrain.)

Baddho: Being bound, he does not eat food. (Even though he was not literally tied, he was taken to the elephant stable, surrounded by ornate curtains, and placed on ground with a beautiful ceiling above. Although the King served him various excellent flavors of food worthy of a king, he did not wish to eat anything. Referring to the fact that he was confined in the stable, it is said "being bound, he does not eat a morsel.")

Kuñjaro: The tusker longs for the elephant-forest where his mother lives. (The great tusker did not remember the elephant-forest as a place of pleasure; rather, his blind old mother was suffering due to separation from her son. That tusker thought, "My duty of supporting my parents is not fulfilled. What use is this food to me?" He yearned only for the righteous duty of supporting his parents. Since that duty could only be fulfilled by living in that elephant-forest, it is said "the tusker remembers the elephant-forest.")
315:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
While the Blessed One was relating this past practice of his, all those Brahmins, with tears flowing and hearts softened, listened attentively. Then, the Blessed One, knowing they were ready, revealed the Four Noble Truths and preached the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, the old Brahmin, together with his four sons and four daughters-in-law, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).
The Story of the Sons of the Old Brahmin ends.

## 4. The Story of King Pasenadi of Kosala
(Pasenadikosala Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Middhī yadā hoti," concerning King Pasenadi of Kosala.

## The Fault of Overeating
On one occasion, King Pasenadi of Kosala used to eat a meal cooked from a doṇa (a bucket) of rice, along with suitable curries and side dishes. One day, after having eaten his breakfast, without dispelling the drowsiness caused by the meal, he went to the presence of the Blessed One. Being exhausted, he tossed and turned here and there, and although heavily oppressed by sleepiness, he was unable to lie down straight and sat to one side. Then the Blessed One said to King Pasenadi, "Great King, have you come without resting?" "Yes, Bhante, since the time I finished my meal, I have been in great discomfort," he replied. Then the Blessed One said to him, "Great King, such suffering occurs to one who overeats," and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(325) When one is drowsy and a glutton,
Sleepy and rolling as he lies,
Like a great hog nourished on fodder,
The dull-witted one enters the womb again and again.

Yadā, when. Puriso, a man. Middhī ca, is oppressed by sloth and torpor.
Hoti, it so happens. Mahagghaso ca, and is a glutton, eating much like one of the five types of gluttons. Hoti, it so happens. Nivāpapuṭṭho, like one nourished on fodder. Mahāvarāho va, like a great domestic hog. Niddāyī, he is prone to sleep. Sampariwattasāyī, he sleeps tossing and turning.

(The five types of gluttons are:
1. Āhārahathaka: One who eats so much that he says, "Please take my hand," because he cannot get up.
2. Alaṃsāṭaka: One who eats so much that his clothes fall off and he does not even want to put them back on.
3. Tatthapaṭṭaka: One who eats so much that he has to roll around right in that spot.
4. Kākamāsaka: One who eats so much that a crow could peck at the food in his mouth.
5. Bhuttavamitaka: One who eats so much that he vomits everything he ate. These are the five types of gluttons.)

Tadā, then. Amanasikārā, because of the lack of reflection. Mando, the dull-witted person. Punappunaṃ, again and again. Gabbhaṃ, into the mother's womb. Upeti, he approaches (is reborn).
316:
For the man who is always mindful,
Knowing the measure in the food he has received,
His ailments become thin (diminished),
He ages slowly, preserving his life.

Sadā, at all times. Satīmato, for one who is mindful. Laddhabhojane, in the food received. Mattaṃ, the measure. Jānato, for one who knows. Assa manujassa, for that person. Vedanā, the ailments (pains). Tanukā, become thin (diminished). Bhavanti, they are.
Saṇikaṃ, slowly. Jīrati, he ages. Āyupālayaṃ, the preservation of life. Atthi, there is.

(At that time, that man is unable to reflect on impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Because he cannot reflect on impermanence, suffering, and non-self, he is not yet free from dwelling in the mother's womb.)

## The Benefit of Knowing the Measure in Eating
At the end of the teaching, the Blessed One, for the benefit of King Pasenadi of Kosala, spoke this verse:
[The verse mentioned above]
Then he had the youth Uttara learn it and instructed him, "Recite this verse clearly when the King is being served his meal; by this means, you should reduce his food." The youth Uttara did as the Blessed One had instructed. On another occasion, King Pasenadi of Kosala, being established in the measure of a single nāḷika (a small measure) of rice, and having a light body and attaining happiness, developed confidence in the Teacher and performed the Incomparable Alms-giving (Asadisa Dāna) for seven days. During the appreciation of the alms-giving, many people attained the high distinctions of Jhāna, Path, and Fruit.
The Story of King Pasenadi of Kosala ends.

## 5. The Story of Sānu Sāmaṇera
(Sānusāmaṇera Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Idaṃ pure," concerning the novice named Sānu.

## How Sānu Sāmaṇera Preached and Shared Merit
That Sānu Sāmaṇera was the only son of a certain female lay devotee. At that time, she had him ordained as a novice while he was still young. From the time of his ordination, that novice was virtuous and possessed of good conduct. He performed the duties for his teachers, preceptors, and visiting monks. On the eighth day of the month, he would rise early in the morning, place water in the water-stand, sweep the place for preaching Dhamma, prepare the seats, light the lamps, and announce the listening of Dhamma with a sweet voice. The monks, knowing the strength and ability of that novice, encouraged him, saying, "Novice, recite the Pali text in a clear and resonant voice."
317:
The novice did not make any excuses such as "My heart aches" or "My body is unwell." Instead, he ascended the Dhamma-seat and recited the Pali verses with a melodic intonation (sarabhañña) as if the celestial river Ganges were descending from the sky. Upon descending, he said, "I share the merit gained from this recitation with my parents."

## The Ogress Mother from a Past Life
The novice's [human] parents did not know that the merit had been shared. However, his mother from the immediately preceding life had been reborn as a yakkhiṇī (ogress). She came along with other deities, listened to the Dhamma, and said, "Dear son, I rejoice in the merit you have shared (Sādhu)." Indeed, a monk endowed with virtue is beloved by the world, including the devas. Therefore, the deities felt a sense of shame and reverence toward the novice, regarding him like the Great Brahmā or a great mass of fire. Out of respect for the novice, they also looked upon the yakkhiṇī with great honor and spoke words of praise. In the assemblies of yakkhas for listening to the Dhamma and other gatherings, they would offer the yakkhiṇī the seat of honor, the first water, and the first portion of food, calling her "Sānu's mother." Even yakkhas of great power, upon seeing her, would step aside from the path or rise from their seats.

## Novice Sānu Returns Home to Ask for Lay Clothes
Later, as Novice Sānu grew older and his faculties matured, he was oppressed by dissatisfaction (anabhirati). Unable to dispel this discontent, with long hair and nails and wearing soiled inner and outer robes, he took his bowl and robes and went alone to his mother's house without informing anyone. When the laywoman, his mother, saw her son, she paid homage and asked, "Dear son, why is it that in the past you came here with your teachers and preceptors or with young novices, but today you have come alone?" The novice then informed her of his dissatisfaction with the Dispensation. Although the laywoman advised her son by pointing out the faults of household life in various ways, she was unable to convince him. Thinking, "Perhaps he might realize it by his own nature," she did not let him go yet and said, "Dear son, please wait a while until I prepare congee for you. After you have drunk the congee and finished your meal, I will take out and give you the pleasant clothes that will delight your heart." Having said this, she prepared a seat for him. The novice sat down. In just a moment, the laywoman prepared and offered him congee and snacks. After that, saying "I will prepare the meal," she sat not far away and began washing the rice.

## Novice Sānu Possessed by the Ogress
At that time, the yakkhiṇī wondered, "Where is the novice?" and reflected on whether he had received any alms-food. When she saw him sitting there with the desire to disrobe, she thought, "The novice will cause me to feel shame in the midst of the powerful deities. I shall go and create an obstacle to his disrobing."
318:
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight,
And during the special period of observance, endowed with the eight factors,
Those who observe the Uposatha and lead the holy life—
With them, the Yakkhas do not play; so have I heard from the Arahants.
But today I see the Yakkhas playing with Sānu.

Those who observe the Uposatha on the fourteenth day of the waxing and waning fortnights; on the fifteenth day of the waxing and waning fortnights; and on whichever eighth day of the waxing and waning fortnights there may be; and on the special days of observance (the days before and after), well-kept and endowed with the eight factors; and who lead the holy life—with them, the Yakkhas do not play. Thus have I heard the words of the Arahants. Now, today, I see the Yakkhinīs playing with the novice Sānu.

On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight,
And during the special period of observance, endowed with the eight factors,
Those who observe the Uposatha and lead the holy life—
With them, the Yakkhas do not play; it is good that you have heard this from the Arahants.

Those who observe the Uposatha on the fourteenth day of the waxing and waning fortnights; on the fifteenth day of the waxing and waning fortnights; and on whichever eighth day of the waxing and waning fortnights there may be; and on the special days of observance, well-kept and endowed with the eight factors; and who lead the holy life—with them, the Yakkhas do not play. Thus, it is good that you have heard the words of the Arahants.

Thinking, "I shall create an obstacle to the novice's desire to disrobe," the Yakkhinī approached the novice, possessed his body, twisted his neck backward, and he fell to the ground with saliva flowing. When the laywoman saw her son's distorted state, she rushed to him, embraced him, and laid him on her lap. All the villagers came and performed rituals such as making offerings. The laywoman, wailing, recited these verses:

## Words spoken while possessed by the Yakkha

Upon hearing the words of the laywoman, the mother of the novice named Sānu, the Yakkhinī uttered these words and then recited these verses:

Tell Sānu when he awakens, these are the words of the Yakkhas:
Do not perform an evil deed, whether in the open or in secret.
If you will do or are doing an evil deed,
There is no escape from suffering for you, even if you fly away to escape.

Tell the novice Sānu, who has awakened and regained consciousness, these words of the Yakkhas: "Do not perform an evil deed, such as the desire to disrobe, whether in the open or in secret. If you will do or are doing such an evil deed, there is no escape from suffering for you, even if you fly away to escape."

After saying, "Even if you fly away like a bird after committing the evil deed of wanting to disrobe, there is no escape for you," the Yakkhinī released the novice.

## Conversation with the mother after the Yakkha left

The novice opened his eyes and saw his mother with disheveled hair, breathing heavily and weeping loudly, and all the villagers gathered there. Not knowing he had been possessed by a Yakkha, he thought, "Previously I was sitting on a bench, and my mother was sitting nearby washing rice. But now I am lying on the ground. What is this?" While still lying there, he spoke to his mother:
319:
“Mother, people weep for the dead, or for one who is no longer seen alive. But Mother, seeing me alive, why do you weep for me?”

“Mother, the great lay devotee. ‘For the dead’—they weep for those who have died. ‘Or for one who is no longer seen alive’—they also weep for such a person. Mother, the great lay devotee. ‘Seeing the novice alive’—though you see me alive. Mother, the great lay devotee. ‘Why do you weep for me?’—for what reason do you weep for me?”

“Son, people weep for the dead, or for one who is no longer seen alive. And he who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, returns here again—for him too, son, they weep; for though alive, he is as one dead again.”

“Dear son, the novice. ‘For the dead’—they weep for those who have died. ‘Or for one who is no longer seen alive’—they also weep for such a person. Son, dear son. ‘And he who’—that person who. ‘Having abandoned sensual pleasures’—having given up the strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Again’—once more. ‘Returns here’—returns to this world of laypeople. Son, dear son. ‘For him too’—they weep for that person as well. ‘Indeed’—that is true. ‘He’—that person. ‘Though alive’—while still living. ‘Is as one dead’—is called one who has died again.”

“You have been pulled out from the hot ashes, dear son, yet you wish to fall back into the hot ashes. You have been pulled out from hell, dear son, yet you wish to fall back into hell.”

“Dear son, the novice. You, dear son, ‘having been pulled out from the hot ashes’—having been rescued from the heat of the embers. ‘Into the hot ashes’—into the embers. ‘To fall’—to fall back. ‘You wish’—you desire again. Dear son, the novice. You, dear son, ‘having been pulled out from hell’—having been rescued from the realm of hell. ‘Into hell’—into the realm of hell. ‘To fall’—to fall back. ‘You wish’—you desire again.”

“Run forward, venerable sirs! To whom shall we complain? You wish to be burnt again, like a bundle of goods pulled out from a fire.”

“‘Run forward’—please just run forward. ‘To you’—dear son. ‘Goodness’—may it be. ‘To whom’—to whom. ‘Shall we complain’—shall we make this known? ‘From the fire’—from the place where a literal fire is burning brightly. ‘Pulled out’—having been rescued. ‘A bundle of goods’—being like a bundle of wealth. ‘Again’—once more. ‘To be burnt’—to be consumed by fire. ‘You wish’—you desire.”

At that time, the mother of Sānu Sāmaṇera, wishing to show the fault in returning to the lay life for one who has gone forth after abandoning the sensual pleasures of objects and defilements, spoke this verse.

Thus, making the life of a householder appear like hot ashes and like a great hell, and wishing to show the fault in living as a householder, she spoke this verse again.

Thereafter, she recited this verse to show Sānu Sāmaṇera: “Dear son—may goodness be with you. As for us, we rescued you, our young son, like rescuing goods from a burning house, and you have been living as a monk in the Buddha’s Dispensation. Yet you wish to be burnt again by the fire of the household life. Run forward! Be a protection and a guard for us. To whom shall we report this matter to make it known? To whom shall we complain so that they may look upon us constantly?”

## Sānu Sāmaṇera’s Vow Not to Disrobe

While his mother, the lay devotee, was speaking, Sānu Sāmaṇera took those words to heart and said, “I no longer have any desire for the state of a layman.” Then, Sānu Sāmaṇera’s mother, with a joyful heart, said, “Dear son, it is well,” and after feeding him with excellent food, she asked, “Dear son, how old are you?” Learning that he had completed twenty years of age, she had the triple robes prepared. Sānu Sāmaṇera, being fully equipped with bowl and robes, received higher ordination. Thereafter, the Teacher, wishing to inspire the newly ordained Bhikkhu Sānu to strive in restraining the mind, said: “For one who does not restrain this mind, which wanders for a long time among various objects, there is no such thing as well-being. Therefore, one should apply effort in restraining the mind, just as a mahout restrains an elephant in rut with a hook,” and he spoke this verse:
320:
## The Teaching

(326) Formerly this mind wandered as it liked, where it wished, and as it pleased. Today I shall thoroughly restrain it, as a mahout with a hook restrains an elephant in rut.

“This mind”—this very mind. “Formerly”—in the past. “As it liked”—by whatever cause it desired. “Where it wished”—on whatever object it desired. “As it pleased”—according to its pleasure. “Wandered”—it has wandered and roamed before.

“Today”—on this day. “As a mahout”—as a skilled elephant trainer holding a hook. “An elephant in rut”—an elephant intoxicated with pride. “With a hook”—by means of the hook. “Restrains”—just as he restrains. “I”—I. “That mind”—that very mind. “Thoroughly”—through wise reflection. “Shall restrain”—I shall now restrain. Thus, “effort”—should be made.

“Therefore, one should exert effort in restraining the mind, just as one restrains a noble elephant in rut with a hook,” the Buddha said, and preached this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, many deities who had approached to listen to the Dhamma along with Bhikkhu Sānu attained the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

That Venerable Sānu, having learned the word of the Buddha known as the Tipiṭaka, became a great Dhamma preacher. He lived for one hundred and twenty years, and after causing a stir throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, he attained Parinibbāna.

The story of Sānu Sāmaṇera ends.

## 6. The Story of the Elephant Pāveyyaka

While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Appamādarata,” concerning an elephant named Pāveyyaka belonging to King Kosala.

## The Elephant Pāveyyaka Stuck in the Mud

It is said that when that elephant named Pāveyyaka was young, he possessed great strength. At a later time, being oppressed by the force of the wind of old age, he descended into a large lake, became stuck in the mud, and was unable to get out. When the multitude of people saw that noble elephant, they started saying, “Even an elephant of such nature has now reached this state of weakness.” When King Pasenadi of Kosala heard of this matter, he ordered the elephant trainer, “Teacher, go and pull that elephant out of the mud.” The elephant trainer went to that place, displayed the signs of a battlefield, and had the battle drums beaten. Then, the elephant Pāveyyaka, who was proud by nature, rose up with speed and stood upon the dry ground. The monks saw this event and reported it to the Teacher.

The Teacher said, “Bhikkhus, that noble elephant has just now pulled himself out from the literal mud where he was submerged.”
321:
## The Teaching
(327) Be delighted in heedfulness; guard your own mind. Extricate yourself from the difficult path, like an elephant sunk in the mud.

"Be delighted in heedfulness" means being greatly devoted to the non-absence of mindfulness. "Guard your own mind" means protecting one's mind so that it does not transgress toward sense objects such as forms.

"You, however, are plunged and sunk in the mire of defilements. Therefore, exerting right effort, you too should extricate yourselves from that mire of defilements," the Buddha said, and then spoke this verse.

(This means one must guard one's mind so as not to transgress toward sense objects like forms, etc.)

"Like an elephant sunk in the mud" means just as an elephant stuck in the mire exerts effort with its trunk and feet to pull itself out and stand on dry land, so too should you pull yourselves out of the mire of defilements and establish yourselves on the dry land of Nibbāna.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, those monks were established in the fruit of Arahatship.

The story of the Pāveyyaka elephant ends.

## 7. The Story of Many Monks
(Sambahulabhikkhu Vatthu)
The Teacher, while staying in the Rakkhita forest grove supported by the Pālileyyaka elephant, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Sace labhetha" concerning many monks.

## Venerable Ānanda's Journey to the Pālileyyaka Forest
(This story appears in the commentary on the verse "Pare ca na vijānanti" in the Yamaka Vagga. All those words have already been spoken.)

The fact that the Tathāgata was staying there, being served by the noble elephant Pālileyyaka, became famous throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. From the city of Sāvatthī, great families such as the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and the great female lay devotee Visākhā sent messages to Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Venerable sir, please show us the Teacher."

Also, five hundred monks living in various regions, having completed the rains retreat, approached Venerable Ānanda and requested, "Friend Ānanda, it has been a long time since we heard a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One's presence. Friend Ānanda, we beg of you, we wish to receive the opportunity to hear a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One's presence."
322:
## The Teaching
(328) If one should find a wise companion, a fellow traveler who lives well and is firm in wisdom, one should wander with him, joyful and mindful, overcoming all dangers.
(329) If one should not find a wise companion, a fellow traveler who lives well and is firm in wisdom, then like a king leaving behind a conquered kingdom, one should wander alone like a Mātaṅga elephant in the forest.
(330) Living alone is better; there is no companionship with a fool. One should wander alone and do no evil, being free from care like a Mātaṅga elephant in the forest.

Nipakaṃ: having mature wisdom. Saddhiṃ caraṃ: being a fellow practitioner. Sādhuvihārī: having a good way of living. Dhīraṃ: having firm wisdom. Sahāyaṃ: a good friend. Sace labhetha: if one should find. Evaṃ labhanto: if one finds such. Sabbāni: all. Parissayāni: manifest and unmanifest dangers. Abhibhuyya: having overcome and destroyed.

Elder Ānanda, leading those five hundred monks, went to the Pālileyyaka forest. Thinking, "It is not proper to approach the Blessed One, who has been living in solitude for the three months of the rains, with so many monks," he approached the Teacher alone.

## The Elephant King Pālileyyaka and Elder Ānanda
When the elephant king Pālileyyaka saw Elder Ānanda, he took up a stick and ran toward him. The Blessed One looked and said, "Move away, Pālileyyaka, do not hinder him; this monk is my attendant." The elephant king threw down the stick right there and asked to take the bowl and robes. Elder Ānanda did not give them. The elephant king thought, "If this monk is well-trained in duties, he will not place his requisites upon the stone slab where my teacher sits." Elder Ānanda placed the bowl and robes on the ground.
(That is correct. Those who are accomplished and skilled in duties do not place their own requisites on the seat or bed of teachers who are to be respected.)

## Staying Alone if a Good Companion is Not Found
Elder Ānanda paid homage to the Blessed One and sat in a suitable place. When the Blessed One asked, "Have you come alone?" and heard that he had come with five hundred monks, He asked, "Where are they?" When told, "I left them outside because I did not know your intention," the Buddha said, "Call them." Elder Ānanda did as the Blessed One commanded. The Blessed One exchanged friendly greetings with those five hundred monks. The monks said, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is delicate as a Buddha and delicate as a Khattiya. You have performed a difficult task by staying alone, standing and sitting for the three months of the rains. We suppose there was no one to perform duties or provide water for washing the face."
323:
When it was reported, "There is indeed no one to offer water for washing the face and so on," the Teacher said, "Monks, the elephant named Pārileyyaka performs all duties for me. If one finds such a good companion, it is proper to live together; if not, living alone is better." He then spoke these verses in the Nāgavagga:

(Lions, tigers, and so on are called manifest perils. Lust, hatred, delusion, and so on are called hidden perils.)

*Tena*: with that good friend. *Saddhiṃ*: together. *Attamano*: with a joyful mind. *Satimā*: being mindful. *Careyya*: should wander or live.

*Nipakaṃ*: possessing mature wisdom. *Saddhiṃcaraṃ*: a companion. *Sādhuvihāriṃ*: living well. *Dhīraṃ*: possessing firm wisdom. *Sahāyaṃ*: a good friend. *No ce labhetha*: if one does not find. *Evaṃ alabhamāno*: not finding such. *Eko*: alone. *Care*: should wander.

Like whom? *Rājā*: a king. *Vijitaṃ*: conquered. *Raṭṭhaṃ*: kingdom. *Pahāya*: having abandoned. *Ekakovacarati*: wanders alone. *Mātaṅgo*: named Mātanga. *Nāgo*: this noble elephant. *Araññe*: in this forest. *Ekakovacarati*: wanders alone. *Evaṃ*: in this way. *Eko*: alone. *Care*: should wander.

(A king who has conquered territory thinks, 'This kingship is a cause for great negligence. What use is this kingdom to me?' and having abandoned the conquered realm, enters the great forest, ordains as an ascetic, and wanders alone in the four postures. Similarly, one should wander alone. Another example: this noble elephant, Pārileyyaka, reflecting that living crowded by other elephants is difficult, and because he moves swiftly, he is called Mātanga; having left the herd, he lives alone in every posture in this great forest. Thus, one should live alone.)

*Ekassa*: of one who is alone, i.e., a monk. *Caritaṃ*: wandering or living. *Seyyo*: is better.

(For a monk who has delighted in solitude since the time of ordination, living alone is indeed better.)

*Bāle*: in a fool. *Sahāyatā*: the state of companionship, i.e., the Dhamma of the virtuous. *Natthi*: does not exist.

(The Minor Morality, Middle Morality, and Major Morality; the ten subjects of discourse (1. talk on wanting little, 2. talk on contentment, 3. talk on seclusion, 4. talk on non-association, 5. talk on arousing energy, 6. talk on virtue, 7. talk on concentration, 8. talk on wisdom, 9. talk on liberation, 10. talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation); the thirteen ascetic practices; insight knowledge; the four paths; the four fruits; the three knowledges; the six supernormal powers; and the Great Deathless Nibbāna—this collection of Dhamma is...)
324:
(...called 'companionship,' the Dhamma of the virtuous. It is impossible to attain this Dhamma by relying on a fool. Therefore, 'there is no companionship in a fool.' For this reason, one should wander alone in all postures and should not commit even small evils.)

*Araññe*: in the forest. *Appossukko*: without care. *Mātaṅgo*: named Mātanga. *Nāgo*: the noble elephant. *Carati*: wanders. *Evaṃ*: in this way. *Eko*: alone. *Hutvā*: being. *Care*: should wander. *Pāpāni ca*: and evil deeds. *Na kayirā*: should not do, even small ones.

(Just as the noble elephant named Mātanga wanders happily wherever he wishes in this forest, without care, without attachment, and without fear, so should one wander alone and not commit even the slightest evil.)

Therefore, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching to those monks, wishing to show that if you do not find a suitable companion, you must wander alone.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the five hundred monks were established in the fruit of Arahantship.

The Story of Many Monks is finished.

## 8. The Story of Māra (Māravatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with 'Atthamhi' while staying in a small forest hut in the Himalayan region, concerning Māra.

## Māra’s Request for the Buddha to Rule

At that time, kings ruled by oppressing the people. The Blessed One, seeing the people oppressed by punishments due to the rule of unrighteous kings, thought out of compassion: "Is it possible to rule righteously, without killing or causing to kill, without conquering or causing to conquer, without grieving or causing to grieve?"

The evil Māra, knowing the Blessed One's thought, reflected: "The ascetic Gotama is thinking whether it is possible to rule. Now he might wish to rule. Kingship is a cause for negligence. If he rules, I might get an opportunity. I will go and encourage him." He approached the Teacher and said: "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One rule! Let the Sugata rule righteously, without killing or causing to kill, without conquering or causing to conquer, without grieving or causing to grieve!"

## Māra’s Dhamma and the Buddha’s Dhamma are Different

Then the Teacher said to Māra: "Evil One, for what reason do you speak thus to me? What do you see in me that makes you say this?" Māra replied: "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One has truly well-developed the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda). If the Blessed One so desired, he could resolve that the Himalaya, the king of mountains, be gold, and it would become gold. I will also perform whatever tasks are to be done with that gold and wealth. Therefore, may the Blessed One rule righteously." Thus, these two verses were spoken.
325:
## The Teaching
(331) Friends are a blessing when a need arises; contentment is a blessing with whatever there is. Merit is a blessing at the end of life; the abandoning of all suffering is a blessing.
(332) In this world, filial piety towards one's mother is a blessing; filial piety towards one's father is a blessing. In this world, respect for recluses is a blessing; respect for noble ones is a blessing.
(333) Virtue is a blessing even until old age; faith firmly established is a blessing. The attainment of wisdom is a blessing; the non-doing of evil is a blessing.

'Atthasmiṃ', when one's task or business. 'Jātasmiṃ', has arisen. 'Sahāyā', good friends. 'Sukhā', are a cause of happiness.

'A mountain of gold, even if doubled, is not enough for a single person; knowing this, the wise should live righteously.'

'He who has seen the cause from which suffering arises, how could that person incline towards sensual pleasures? Knowing that attachment is a bond in the world, a person should train for the removal of that very attachment.'

'Suvaṇṇassa', made of gold. 'Pabbatassa', a mountain. 'Kevalo' or 'Kevalassa', pure or entire. 'Jātarūpassa', gold. 'Dvittāva', even twice that much. 'Ekassa', for one person. 'Nālaṃ', is not enough. 'Iti', thus. 'Vidvā', the wise who knows. 'Samaṃ', rightly. 'Care', should live/practice.

'Yatonidānaṃ', because of which cause. 'Yo jantu', which being. 'Dukkhaṃ', the suffering of the round of rebirths in the three planes. 'Adakkhi', has seen. 'Tatonidānaṃ', because of that cause. 'So jantu', that being. 'Kāmesu', in the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Kathaṃ', how. 'Nameyya', could incline? 'Loke', in the world. 'Jantu', a being. 'Upadhiṃ', the substrate of existence such as sensuality. 'Saṅgoti', as an attachment. 'Viditvā', having known. 'Tasseva', for that very attachment. 'Vinayāya', for the removal. 'Sikkhe', should train.

Having caused trepidation with these verses, the Buddha said, "O Evil Māra, your advice is one thing; my advice is another. There is no such thing as consultation with you according to the Dhamma. I, the Buddha, advise in this way," and then spoke these verses:

(When a task arises, such as sewing robes or settling a legal issue for a monk, or farming or being oppressed by those with powerful factions for a layperson, a good friend who is able to accomplish or settle that task is a cause of happiness.)

'Itarītarena', with whatever property is obtained other than what is not yet obtained. 'Yā tuṭṭhī', which contentment. 'Atthi', there is. 'Sā tuṭṭhī', that contentment. 'Sukhā', is a blessing.

(Laypeople who are not content with their own property strive to commit crimes like breaking through walls to steal. Monks also strive in various improper ways of seeking requisites. Such laypeople and monks cannot find happiness. Therefore, being content with whatever little or much of one's own property one has obtained is a blessing.)

'Jīvitasaṅkhayamhi', at the time of death when one is about to pass away. 'Puññaṃ', merit performed as desired. 'Sukhā', is a blessing. 'Sabbassa', of all. 'Dukkhassa', suffering of the round of rebirths. 'Pahānaṃ', the abandoning. 'Sukhaṃ', is a great blessing.
326:
(The Path and Fruition of Arahantship, which is the abandoning of all suffering of the round of rebirths, is called happiness in this world.)

'Loke', in the world. 'Mātteyyatā', proper conduct towards one's mother. 'Sukhā', is a blessing. 'Atho', furthermore. 'Petteyyatā', proper conduct towards one's father. 'Sukhā', is a blessing.

(By these two phrases, only the service to parents is taught. When parents know that their children do not wish to serve them, they might bury their wealth in the ground or give it away to others. For those children who do not serve their parents, blame increases. Upon death, they are likely to be reborn in the Gūtha Hell. Children who respectfully serve their parents can obtain their inheritance and receive praise. Upon death, they are reborn in the celestial realm. Therefore, proper conduct and service towards parents is taught as a blessing.)

'Loke', in the world. 'Sāmaññatā', proper conduct towards recluses. 'Sukhā', is a blessing. 'Atho', furthermore. 'Brahmaññatā', proper conduct towards the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahant disciples who have warded off evil. 'Sukhā', is a blessing.

(By these two, the proper service to those recluses and Arahants with the four requisites is taught. Such service is also taught as happiness in the world.)

'Yāva jarā', until old age. 'Sīlaṃ', virtue. 'Sukhaṃ', is a blessing.

(Ornaments such as ruby earrings and crimson clothes only look beautiful on those at certain ages. The ornaments of the young do not look beautiful in old age, and the ornaments of the old do not look beautiful in youth; they only cause anger by inviting ridicule such as "Is this person mad?". Virtue, such as the five or ten precepts, is beautiful for both the young and the old at all ages. It only brings joy by inviting praise such as "Oh, this person is very virtuous!")

'Saddhāpatiṭṭhitā', the unwavering establishment of both mundane and supramundane faith. 'Sukhā', is a blessing. 'Paññāyapaṭilābho', the attainment of both mundane and supramundane wisdom. 'Sukho', is a blessing. 'Pāpānaṃ', of evil deeds. 'Akaraṇaṃ', the non-doing. 'Sukhaṃ', is a blessing.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many deities attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths.

The story of Māra ends.
The explanation of the Nāga Vagga is finished.
The twenty-third chapter.
327:
The Chapter on the Elephant is finished.

## 24. Taṇhāvagga
## 1. The Story of the Fish Kapila
(Kapilamacchavatthu)

"For the man..." — The Teacher, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning a fish named Kapila.

## The Monk Kapila

In the past, after the Blessed One Kassapa had attained Parinibbāna, two brothers of good family left the household life and ordained in the presence of the disciples. Among those two monks, the elder brother was named Sāgata, and the younger brother was named Kapila. Their mother was named Sādhinī, and their younger sister was named Tāpanā. They also ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Thus, after the four members of the family had ordained, the two brothers performed their major and minor duties toward their teachers and preceptors. One day, they asked, "Venerable Sir, how many duties (dhura) are there in this Dispensation?" and upon hearing that "There are two duties: the duty of study (ganthadhura) and the duty of insight (vipassanādhura)," the elder brother, thinking, "I will fulfill the duty of insight," stayed with his teachers and preceptors for five years. Having taken a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) leading up to Arahantship, he entered the forest, and through his efforts, he attained Arahantship.

But the younger monk thought, "I am still young. I will fulfill the duty of insight when I am old." He set aside the duty of insight and began the duty of study, learning the Three Pitakas. Based on his scriptural learning (pariyatti), he gained a large following, and because of that following, great gain (lābha) arose. He became intoxicated with the pride of great learning and was overwhelmed by craving for gain. Thinking himself very wise, he declared what was allowable (kappiya) as "unallowable," and what was unallowable as "allowable." He also declared what was blameworthy (sāvajja) as "blameless," and what was blameless as "blameworthy." Although he was advised by virtuous monks who loved their precepts, saying, "Friend Kapila, do not speak thus," and who showed him the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya, he went about insulting and disparaging them, saying, "What do you know? You are like empty fists!"

## The Elder Brother, Mother, and Sister of Monk Kapila

Then, the monks informed his elder brother, the Elder Sāgata, of this matter.
328:
The Elder Sāgata approached the monk Kapila and advised him, "Friend Kapila, the right practice (samma-paṭipatti) of those like you is the life of the Dispensation. Therefore, do not abandon practice and speak against what is allowable. Do not speak thus." Even though he was so advised, Kapila did not heed the words of his elder brother. Despite this, the Elder advised him two or three times. When Kapila still would not accept the advice, the Elder, knowing "This monk Kapila does not heed my words," said, "Friend, you will be known by your own deeds," and departed.

From that day on, the virtuous monks shunned the monk Kapila. Being of bad conduct and surrounded by those of bad conduct, one day in the Uposatha hall, he took a fan and sat on the Dhamma seat, intending to recite the Pātimokkha. He asked the monks assembled in the Uposatha hall, "Is the Pātimokkha being recited, friends?" Seeing the monks remain silent, thinking, "What is the use of giving an answer to this monk?", he said, "Friends, there is no Dhamma or Vinaya. What is the use of hearing or not hearing the Pātimokkha?" and rose from his seat. Thus, he caused the decline of the Blessed One Kassapa's teaching of the scriptures (pariyatti-sāsana). The Elder Sāgata attained Parinibbāna on that very day. At the end of his life, the monk Kapila was reborn in the Great Avīci Hell. His mother and sister, having followed his views and having insulted and reviled the virtuous monks, were also reborn in that same Avīci Hell.

## The Benefit of Virtue of the Five Hundred Robbers

At that time, five hundred men lived as robbers, plundering villages and the like. Pursued by the country folk, they fled into the forest. Seeing no other refuge in that forest, they saw a certain forest-dwelling monk. They paid homage to him and said, "Venerable Sir, be our refuge."

The Elder said, "For you, there is no refuge like virtue (sīla). All of you, undertake the Five Precepts." They accepted, saying, "Very well, Bhante," and undertook the precepts. Then the Elder advised them, "Now you are virtuous. Even for the sake of your lives, you must not transgress the precepts, nor should you harbor ill-will in your hearts." They accepted, saying, "Very well, Bhante."

Afterward, when the country folk reached that place and searched here and there, they saw the robbers and took the lives of all of them. Upon their death, they were reborn in the deva world. The leader of the robbers became a chief deva. Having wandered between the deva and human worlds for the interval between two Buddhas, they were reborn in this Buddha's era in a large fishing village of five hundred families near the gates of the city of Sāvatthī. The chief deva took conception in the house of the head fisherman, and the others in other houses. Thus, the conception and the birth from their mothers' wombs of all those five hundred devas occurred on the same day.
329:
The chief fisherman had a search conducted to see if there were other boys born in the village on that same day. Upon learning of their birth, he thought, "These boys shall be the companions of my son," and provided provisions for the sustenance of all those children.

All those boys became playmates together in the dust and, in due course, reached the age of maturity. Among those youths, the son of the chief fisherman became a noble man, endowed with fame and power. As for the monk Kapila, after being cooked in hell for the interval between two Buddhas, he was reborn as a large fish in the Aciravatī River due to his remaining karma, possessing a golden complexion but a foul-smelling mouth.

## Kapila the Fish Arrives at Jetavana Monastery

Then one day, those fisherman friends took nets and other gear, saying, "Let us catch fish," and cast them into the river. At that time, the fish named Kapila entered into their net. Upon catching that fish, all the inhabitants of the fishing village raised a loud shout, crying out, "When the sons of the fishermen first went to catch fish, they caught a golden-colored fish! Now the King will give us much wealth!"

Those friends placed the fish in a boat, and carrying the boat, they went to the presence of the King. When King Pasenadi of Kosala saw them carrying the boat and asked, "What is this?", they replied, "O King, it is a fish." Seeing the golden-colored fish, the King thought, "The Teacher will know the reason for this fish's golden color," and had the fish taken to the presence of the Blessed One. As soon as the fish opened its mouth, the entire Jetavana monastery became filled with an exceedingly foul odor.

The King asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, why does this fish have a complexion like gold? And why, Venerable Sir, does a foul odor waft from its mouth?"

"Great King, in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, this fish was a monk named Kapila. He was very learned and had a large following, but he was overcome by greed for gain. He would revile and abuse those who did not accept his words, and he caused the decline of the Blessed One Kassapa's Sasana. Because of that evil kamma, he was reborn in the Avīci hell, and now, due to the remaining results, he has been reborn as a fish. Because he taught the words of the Buddha for a long time and spoke of the Buddha's virtues, he obtained this golden complexion as a result of that merit. However, because he reviled and abused the monks, a foul odor wafts from his mouth."
330:
## The Teaching

(334) For a person who leads a negligent life, craving grows like a māluvā creeper. He leaps from life to life like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest.

(335) Whomsoever this vile craving, which is sticky in the world, overcomes, his sorrows increase like bīraṇa grass well-watered by rain.

(336) But he who overcomes this vile craving, which is difficult to conquer in the world, sorrows fall away from him like drops of water from a lotus leaf.

(337) Therefore, I say unto you: Good luck to all of you who have gathered here! Dig up the root of craving, as one seeking the fragrant root digs up the bīraṇa grass. Let not Māra break you again and again, like the stream breaks the reeds.

For a person who leads a negligent life (pamattacārino), characterized by the lapse of mindfulness, meditation, insight, and the paths and fruits do not grow. Just as the māluvā creeper grows, entwining and surrounding a tree for its destruction, so too does craving grow for such a person, arising again and again dependent on the six sense doors.

## Kapila the Fish Speaks Human Language

When the Buddha said, "Great King, I shall have that fish speak," the King entreated, "Venerable Sir, please have him speak." Then the Teacher asked the fish, "Are you Kapila?" When the fish replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, I am Kapila," the Buddha asked, "Where have you come from?" "From the great Avīci hell, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Where has your elder brother, the elder named Sāgata, gone?" "He has attained Parinibbāna, Venerable Sir." "Where is your mother, named Sādhinī?" "She is in the great hell, Venerable Sir." "And where is your younger sister, Tāpanā?" "She is in the great hell, Venerable Sir." "Where will you go now?" the Buddha asked again. "To the great Avīci hell itself, Venerable Sir," he said. Overcome by remorse, he struck the boat with his head and, dying at that moment, was reborn in hell. The great multitude was struck with dismay, and their hair stood on end.

Then the Blessed One, observing the state of mind of the assembly gathered at that moment, preached the Kapila Sutta from the Sutta Nipāta, which begins, "The practice of Dhamma and the practice of the holy life; this they say is the highest wealth," to suit the occasion, and spoke these verses:

(For a person who practices negligently with the characteristic of lack of mindfulness, jhāna, vipassanā, and the paths cannot grow. Just as the māluvā creeper grows to destroy the tree it entwines, so too craving only increases for that person as it arises repeatedly through the six doors.)

Like a monkey (vānarova) seeking fruit (phalam icchaṃ) runs from tree to tree in the forest (vanasmiṃ), so that being leaps (plavati) from one existence to another (hurāhuraṃ).

(The person who follows the will of craving must run to various existences. The example is a monkey seeking fruit in the forest; it reaches for a branch of a tree, lets go of it to grab another, and if it does not get a branch, it cannot be said to be sitting still. Similarly, a person following craving, running through various lives, cannot be said to have reached a state where craving does not occur even when an object is not obtained.)

In the world (loke), this vile (jammī) craving of the six doors, called visattikā (clinging), whomsoever (yaṃ) it overcomes (sahate)...
331:
(It means that it arises and increases within that person.)

For that person, sorrows increase like the bīraṇa grass that grows because of rain. 

(Just as the bīraṇa grass, which grows due to the repeated rains in the rainy season, becomes strong and flourishes, so too does craving, which has its root in the cycle of existence, increase greatly within that person.)

And whoever in this world can overcome this base craving, which is extremely difficult to abandon, sorrows fall away from that person like water drops from a lotus leaf.

Monks, for that reason, I shall speak to you. May there be goodness for all of you as many as have gathered here in unity. 

(It means: Do not meet destruction like the monk Kapila, who became a fish and fell into hell.)

Just as one who desires the usīra root digs up the bīraṇa grass, dig up the root of the craving of the six doors.
