(It means: Just as one digs up the bīraṇa grass with a large hoe, one must dig up the very root of craving with the knowledge of the path of Arahatship.)

Just as the river current, coming with great force, destroys the reed, let not Māra destroy you again and again.

(It means: Just as the river current coming with great speed destroys the reed growing in the river, you must act so that the Māra of defilements, the Māra of death, and the Māra of the devas cannot destroy you, dear sons, again and again.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the five hundred sons of the fishermen, having reached a state of spiritual urgency and desiring to make an end of suffering, became monks in the presence of the Teacher. Before long, they realized Nibbāna, the end of suffering, and together with the Teacher, they came to share the same attainment of the imperturbable dwelling (āneñjavihāra-samāpatti).

The story of Kapila the fish ends.

## 2. The Story of the Young Sow
(Sūkarapotikā-vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yathāpi mūle," concerning a young dung-eating sow.
332:
## Even a Brahma Must Become a Pig
On one occasion, while the Teacher was entering the city of Rājagaha for alms, he saw a young sow and manifested a smile. Seeing the circle of radiance from his teeth as he smiled, the Elder Ānanda asked the reason for the smile: "Exalted Buddha, what is the cause, what is the reason for manifesting a smile?"

Then the Teacher said to Ānanda, "Ānanda, do you see that young sow?" "Yes, Bhante, I see her," he replied. "That young sow was once a hen near a refectory during the dispensation of the Buddha Kakusandha. That hen, having heard the sound of the Dhamma while a certain monk practicing meditation was reciting the Vipassanā meditation subjects, passed away from that state as a hen and was reborn in a royal family, becoming a princess named Ubbari.

Later, while entering the place of cleansing, she saw a heap of maggots. There, she developed the perception of maggots (puḷuvaka-saññā) and attained the first jhāna. That Princess Ubbari, after remaining in that royal life for the full span of her life, passed away from that existence and was reborn in the Brahma world. Having passed away from that Brahma world, she was tossed about by the power of the destination of rebirth (gati) and has now been reborn in the species of pigs. Seeing this reason, I have manifested a smile."

Upon hearing these words, the monks, headed by the Elder Ānanda, were struck with great spiritual urgency (saṃvega). The Teacher, having caused spiritual urgency in those monks and revealing the danger of craving for existence, spoke these verses while standing in the middle of the street:

(338) Just as a tree, though cut down, grows again if its root is unharmed and firm, so also, when the latent tendency of craving is not destroyed, this suffering arises again and again.

(339) For whom the thirty-six streams of craving, which flow towards pleasant objects, are strong, those thoughts based on passion carry away that person of wrong view.

(340) The streams flow everywhere; the creeper (of craving) arises and stands. Seeing that creeper has arisen, cut its root with wisdom.

(341) To a being, there arise pleasures that are bedewed and attached. Those who are bound to such pleasures and seek happiness are indeed the men who undergo birth and aging.

(342) People pursued by craving crawl around like a snared hare. Bound by the fetters of attachment, they undergo suffering again and again for a long time.

(343) People pursued by craving crawl around like a snared hare. Therefore, one should dispel craving, desiring one's own dispassion.

If the root is unharmed and firm, even if cut above, that tree grows again. Similarly, if the latent tendency of craving in the six doors is not yet cut by the knowledge of the path of Arahatship, this mass of suffering, such as rebirth, arises again and again.
333:
(Just as a tree, though cut down, grows again if its five types of roots—those spreading in the four directions and the one going downwards—remain uninjured and firm despite dangers such as cutting, splitting, burning, or piercing, even so, if the latent tendency of defilement residing in the six sense doors is not yet destroyed or uprooted by the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship, this suffering, consisting of birth and so forth, arises again and again in various existences.)

For that person in whom the thirty-six streams of craving that flow towards pleasant objects are strong, great thoughts based on passion carry away that person of misguided vision.

(There are thirty-six types of craving: eighteen based on the six internal bases through sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence; and eighteen based on the six external bases through the same three types.)

Those people of misguided vision, who have corrupted wisdom, are carried away by great thoughts based on passion—which are the three types of wrong thoughts—because these thoughts arise repeatedly and take hold of them.

(This means that without relying on meditative absorption or insight, they are carried away by evil thoughts that rely only on passion, which act as a 'grasping' force that becomes great through repeated occurrence.)

The streams of craving flow everywhere towards all sense objects.

Craving is like a creeper because of its nature to entangle and bind. It arises through the six doors and stays fixed on the six sense objects. Having seen that creeper of craving, one should cut its root with the wisdom of the Path of Arahatship.

(This means that seeing where craving arises, one should cut the root with the wisdom of the Path, just as one would cut a creeper growing in the forest with a knife.)
334:
(The streams flow from all states of existence.)

Craving is like a creeper because of its nature to entangle. It arises from the six doors and remains fixed on the six sense objects. Having seen that creeper of craving that has arisen, one should cut its root with the wisdom of the Path of Arahatship.

(This means that seeing where craving arises, one should cut the root with the wisdom of the Path, just as one would cut a creeper growing in the forest with a knife.)

Pleasures that are constantly flowing and smeared with the moisture of craving occur to the person who follows the will of craving. Those people, relying on pleasure and seeking worldly happiness, certainly undergo birth, aging, sickness, and death.

Beings, surrounded by craving which causes terror, are terrified like a hare caught in a snare by a hunter in the forest. Bound by the ten fetters and the seven types of attachments such as passion, they undergo suffering such as birth and so forth again and again for a long time.

Beings, surrounded by craving which causes terror, are terrified like a hare caught in a snare. Therefore, a monk who desires Nibbāna—the fading of passion—should dispel craving; he should pull it out and cast it away through the Path of Arahatship.

## The Benefit of the Discourse
At the end of the discourse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

## The Piglet Becoming a Minister’s Wife
When that young piglet passed away from that existence, she was reborn in a royal family in the region of Suvaṇṇabhūmi. Passing away from that life, she was reborn in Bārāṇasī. Passing away from Bārāṇasī, she was reborn in the house of a horse trader in the port of Suppāraka. Passing away from that life, she was reborn in the house of a ship's captain in the port of Kāvira. Passing away from that life, she was reborn in a wealthy and powerful family in the city of Anurādhapura. Passing away from that life, she was reborn in Bhokkanta village to the south of Anurādhapura as the daughter of a householder named Sumana, and she herself was named Sumanā. Later, when her father had to abandon that village, he went to the district of Dīghavāpī and lived in a village called Mahāmuni. While there, a minister of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī named Lakuṇဍက Atimbara, who had gone there on some business, saw the householder’s daughter Sumanā. He performed a grand wedding ceremony and took her to Mahāpuဏ္ဏ village.

## Ordaining and Becoming an Arahant
At that time, the Great Elder Mahā Anuruddha, who resided at the great monastery of Koṭipabbata, was wandering for alms in Mahāpuဏ္ဏ village. Seeing Sumanā, the minister’s wife, standing at her door, he said to the monks: "Friends, this piglet has become the wife of the Great Minister Lakuဏ္ဍက Atimbara. How truly wonderful!"
335:
Upon hearing the words of the Elder, Sumana, the daughter of the treasurer and wife of the minister, connected her past lives and attained the knowledge of recollecting past births (jātissara-ñāṇa). At that very moment, filled with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she requested permission from her husband, the minister, and with great honor, she ordained in the presence of the Theri named Pañcabala. After listening to the discourse on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta at the Tissa Mahāvihāra, she was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Later, during the suppression of the Damiḷa, she went to Bhokkanta village, the residence of her relatives. While living there, she heard the Āsīvisopama Sutta at the Kalla Mahāvihāra and attained Arahantship.

## Entering Nibbāna after Recounting Thirteen Lives

On the day of her Parinibbāna, being questioned by the monks and nuns, the Arahant Theri Sumana related her entire history without interruption to the community of nuns. In the midst of the assembled community of monks, she consulted with the Elder Mahātissa, a reciter of the Dhammapada residing at Maṇḍalārāma, saying: "In the past, I was born in the human realm. After passing away from that life, I was born as a hen. In that life as a hen, my head was cut off by a hawk, and I was reborn in the city of Rājagaha. Having ordained among the female wanderers (paribbājikā), I was reborn in the realm of the first Jhana. After passing away from that Jhana realm, I was reborn in a treasurer's family. Passing away not long after, I entered the womb of a pig. After passing away from that life, I was reborn in Suvaṇṇabhūmi; from there, in the city of Vārāṇasī; from there, at the port of Suppāraka;

From there, in the port of Kāvīra; from there, in the city of Anurādhapura; and from there, in the village of Bhokkanta."

"Having thus passed through thirteen existences, both favorable and unfavorable, I have now become weary of them, ordained, and attained the fruit of Arahantship. May all of you, venerable ones, achieve fulfillment through diligence (appamāda)." After speaking thus and inspiring spiritual urgency in the fourfold assembly, she attained Parinibbāna.

The Story of the Young Sow is finished.

## 3. The Story of the Disrobed Monk
(Vibbhantabhikkhu-vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yo nibbanatho," concerning a certain monk who had disrobed.

## The Benefit of a Good Friend and the Attainment of Jhana by a Thief

That disrobed monk had been a co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika) of the Elder Mahākassapa. Although he had attained the four Jhanas, he saw an unsuitable object (visabhāga-ārammaṇa) at the house of his uncle, a goldsmith. With his mind attached to that object, he disrobed. Later, people drove him out of the house because he was lazy and unwilling to work.

Due to association with evil friends, he made a living through theft and wandered about.
336:
One day, he was caught, his hands were bound tightly behind his back, and he was beaten with whips at every crossroads as he was led to the execution ground. As the Elder Mahākassapa was entering for alms, he saw the thief being led out through the south gate. He had the bonds loosened and said, "Reflect again on the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) you practiced before." Through the Elder's advice, the thief regained mindfulness and once again attained the fourth Jhana. Then, they took him to the execution ground to kill him and prepared to impale him on a stake. He was neither afraid nor terrified. At that time, although the people standing in various directions raised weapons such as swords, spears, and forks, they saw him remaining fearless. They exclaimed, "Look, friends, at this man! In the midst of hundreds of men with weapons in their hands, he is neither terrified nor trembling. How wonderful! How marvelous!" Filled with wonder and amazement, they raised a great shout. Having seen this, the people reported the matter to King Bimbisāra. Upon hearing this, the King said, "Release the thief." They also went to the Teacher and reported the matter. The Teacher, emitting a radiance and wishing to preach the Dhamma to him, spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(344) He who, being free from the forest (of craving), is yet inclined to the forest (of household life), and who, though free from the forest, runs back to the forest—look at that person! Though free, he runs back into bondage.

Yo, whichever person. Nibbanatho, is without the small tree that stands in the forest. Vanādhimutto, is inclined toward the forest. Vanamutto, being free from the forest. Vanameva, only to the forest. Dhāvati, runs. Etha, come. Taṃ puggalaṃ, that person. Passatha, look. Eso, this person. Mutto, being free. Bandhanameva, only to bondage. Dhāvati, runs.

(This is the metaphorical meaning, not the primary sense.)

Yo puggalo, whichever person. Nibbanatho, is without the attachment known as the small tree. (Meaning: having abandoned the small tree or brushwood called attachment to the state of a layman and having ordained.)

Vanādhimutto, is able to incline the mind toward the forest of practice. (Meaning: inclines the mind toward the forest of practice called Jhana-attainments and divine abidings.)

Vanamutto, being one who is free from the forest of craving. Vanameva, only to the forest of craving. Dhāvati, runs back. (Meaning: although he has escaped from the forest of craving called the bondage of household life, he runs back only to that forest of craving called the bondage of household life.)

Etha, come. Taṃ puggalaṃ, that person. Passatha, look. Eso, this person. Mutto, being free from the bondage of household life. Bandhanameva, only to the bondage of household life. Dhāvati, runs back.

(This is the direct and primary meaning.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

Upon hearing this teaching, while still sitting on the tip of the stake in the midst of the king's men, the man developed the meditation on the rise and fall (udayabbaya-kammaṭṭhāna). Having applied the three marks of existence (tilakkhaṇa) and contemplating conditioned things (saṅkhāra), he attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Experiencing the bliss of meditative attainment (samāpatti-sukha), he flew into the air and went to the Teacher through the sky. After paying homage to the Teacher and ordaining, he attained Arahantship in the midst of the assembly, including the King.

The Story of the Disrobed Monk is finished.
337:
## 4. The Story of the Prison-house
(Bandhanāgāravatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Na taṃ daḷhaṃ," concerning a prison-house.

## The Prison and the Bond of Defilements
At one time, many thieves—those who break through walls and thickets, highwaymen, and murderers—were captured and presented to King Kosala. The King had those thieves bound with wooden shackles, ropes, and iron chains. About thirty monks living in the countryside, wishing to see the Teacher, arrived and paid their respects. On the following day, while walking for alms in the city of Sāvatthī, they went past the prison and saw those thieves. After returning from their alms round, in the evening, they approached the Tathāgata and asked: "Venerable Sir, today while walking for alms, we saw many thieves in the prison bound by shackles and so on, suffering greatly. They are unable to break those bonds and escape. Venerable Sir, is there any other bond stronger than these?"

The Teacher replied: "Monks, what are these called bonds? That which is the bond of defilements, known as craving for wealth, grain, children, wives, and so on—this is a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times stronger than those. Even though it is so great and difficult to cut, wise men of old cut this bond, entered the Himālaya, and ordained." Having said this, he brought forth the past:

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor householder's family. When he reached the age of maturity, his father passed away. He worked for hire to support his mother. Then his mother, even though he was unwilling, brought a young woman of good family into the house as his wife, and later the mother passed away. A child was conceived in his wife's womb. Not knowing that she was pregnant, he said, "Dear, you live by working for hire; I shall go and ordain." She said, "Lord, am I not pregnant? Wait until I have given birth and seen the child, then you may ordain." He agreed, saying, "Very well." When she had given birth, he asked again, "Dear, you have given birth safely; now I shall ordain." Then she said, "Wait until the child is weaned from the breast," and she became pregnant again. He thought, "It is impossible to go if I get her consent. I shall flee and ordain without telling her."
338:
Without telling her, he rose in the night and fled. Then the city guards seized him. He said, "Sirs, I am a supporter of my mother; please release me." Having secured his release, he stayed in a certain place, ordained as a hermit, attained the supernormal knowledges and meditative attainments, and lived enjoying the bliss of jhāna. While living there, he uttered this exclamation: "This bond of wife and children, this bond of defilements, so difficult to cut, has indeed been cut by me."

The Teacher, having brought this past story and revealing the exclamation uttered by him, spoke these verses:

## The Teaching
(345) That is not a strong bond, say the wise,
Which is made of iron, wood, or hemp.
But that attachment to jeweled earrings,
And the longing for sons and wives—

(346) That bond is strong, say the wise,
Which pulls down, is loose, yet hard to escape.
Having cut even this, they wander forth,
Without longing, renouncing sensual pleasures.

*Ayasaṃ*: made of iron; such as iron chains. *Dārujaṃ*: made of wood; such as wooden shackles. *Pabbajaṃ*: made of babbaja grass; such as ropes. All these, the wise—such as the Buddhas—do not call strong bonds.

In jeweled earrings (*maṇikuṇ္ဍalesu*), those who are intensely lustful (*sārattarattā*) have that passion (*rāga*). In sons and wives, there is that craving or longing (*apekkhā*). This bond made of defilements, the wise call a strong bond.

*Ohārinaṃ*: pulling down, because it drags one down to the four woeful states. *Sithilaṃ*: loose, because it does not cut the skin, hide, or flesh at the point of binding, nor does it draw blood; it allows one to perform work on land or water without even realizing one is bound. *Duppamuñcaṃ*: hard to release, because once the bond of defilements has arisen through greed, it is difficult to release from the place where it has bitten.

The Teacher said: "Monks, how can these be called bonds? In truth, there is that bond of defilements called craving for wealth, grain, sons, wives, and so on. This bond of defilements is a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand times stronger and firmer than those shackles and so on. Even though it is so great and firm, wise men of old cut that bond which is difficult to cut, entered the Himālaya, and ordained." Thus he brought forth the past.

## The Past Story of Cutting the Bond
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor family. When he reached maturity, his father passed away. The Bodhisatta worked for hire to support his mother. Then his mother, even though he was unwilling, brought a young woman into the house, and later the mother passed away. A child was conceived in his wife's womb. Not knowing she was pregnant, he said, "Dear, you live by working for hire; I shall ordain." She said, "Lord, am I not pregnant? Wait until I have given birth and seen the child, then you may ordain." He agreed, and after she gave birth, he asked again. She said, "Wait until the child is weaned," and she became pregnant again. He thought, "It is impossible to go with her consent; I shall flee without telling her." He rose in the night and fled. The city guards caught him, but he said, "Sirs, I am a supporter of my mother; please release me." After being released, he stayed in a certain place, ordained as a hermit, and having attained the supernormal knowledges and meditative attainments, lived enjoying the bliss of jhāna.
339:
That hermit, while staying in that very place, uttered this joyful inspired utterance (udāna): "I have indeed cut the bond of defilements, known as the bond of wife and children, which is so difficult to sever." The Blessed One, bringing forth this past account and wishing to make manifest the inspired utterance joyfully uttered by the Bodhisatta, preached these verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.
The Story of the Prison-house (Bandhanāgāra-vatthu) ends.

## 5. The Story of Khema Theri
(The Story of Khema Theri)
The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Ye rāgarattā" concerning Khema, the chief queen of King Bimbisāra.

## Queen Khema, Intoxicated by Her Beauty
That Queen Khema, having made an aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara, was exceedingly beautiful and pleasing to behold. However, having heard that the Teacher spoke of the faults of physical beauty, she did not wish to go to the Teacher's presence. King Bimbisāra, knowing her intoxication with her own beauty, had songs composed about the splendor and virtues of the Veḷuvana garden and gave them to performers and others. Upon hearing the voices of those performers singing those songs, it was as if Queen Khema had never seen the Veḷuvana garden before. She asked, "About which garden are you singing?" When they replied, "O Queen, we are singing about your own Veḷuvana garden," she desired to go to the garden.

The Teacher, knowing her arrival, sat in the midst of the assembly and, while preaching the Dhamma, created a very beautiful woman standing beside him, holding a palm-leaf fan and fanning him. As soon as Queen Khema entered, she saw that woman and thought: "People say the Fully Enlightened One speaks of the faults of beauty, yet this woman stands fanning the Teacher. I do not even reach a sixteenth part of this woman's beauty. I have never seen such a woman's beauty before. I think they must be accusing the Teacher falsely." Thinking thus, she did not even pay attention to the sound of the Tathāgata's discourse but stood there gazing only at that woman.

## Queen Khema Attaining Stream-entry
The Teacher, knowing her great admiration for that beauty, showed that form through the stages of life, such as youth, and in the same manner as mentioned in the stories of Janapadakalyāṇī and Rūpanandā Theri, finally showed it reduced to mere bones. When Khema saw that transformation, she thought: "Even such a form as this has reached destruction and decay in just a moment. Indeed, there is no essence in this beauty!"
340:
The Teacher, observing the movement of her mind, said: "Khema, you thought there was essence in this beauty. Now look at the essence-less nature of this woman's form," and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(347) Ye rāgarattānupatanti sotaṃ,
sayaṃ kataṃ makkaṭakovā jālaṃ.
Etampi chetvāna vajanti dhīrā,
anapekkhino sabbadukkhaṃ pahāya.

Ye: Those beings who. Rāgarattā: are infatuated with passion. Te: those beings. Makkaṭako: like a spider. Sayaṃ kataṃ: which it has made itself. Jālaṃ: into the web. Anupatati iva: just as it falls back into. Sayaṃ kataṃ: which they have made themselves. Sotaṃ: into the stream of craving. Anupatanti: they fall repeatedly.

## Behold, Khema, this body—afflicted, impure, and putrid; oozing and trickling, yet yearned for by the foolish.
Kheme: Queen Khema. Āturaṃ: always afflicted with pain. Asuciṃ: impure. Pūtiṃ: putrid. Uggharantaṃ: oozing and overflowing upwards. Paggharantaṃ: trickling from the nine openings. Bālānaṃ: by the foolish. Abhipatthitaṃ: greatly yearned for and delighted in. Samussayaṃ: behold this collection of the five aggregates of mind and matter.

At the conclusion of the verse, Queen Khema was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

Then the Teacher, saying: "Khema, these beings are infatuated with passion, corrupted by hatred, and blinded by delusion; they are unable to cross over the stream of their own craving and remain stuck right there," and wishing to preach the Dhamma, spoke this verse:

(Just as a spider, having made a web of threads, stays in the center at the hub, and when a grasshopper or a fly falls at the edge, it goes quickly, pierces it, drinks its essence, and then returns to stay in that same spot; in the same way, those beings who are infatuated with passion, corrupted by hatred, and blinded by delusion, fall repeatedly into the stream of craving they have made themselves. They are unable to depart; thus it is difficult to cross.)

Dhīrā: The wise. Etampi: even this bond of craving. Chetvāna: having cut. Anapekkhino: being without longing or attachment. Sabbadukkhaṃ: all the suffering of the round of rebirths. Pahāya: having abandoned through the Path-knowledge. Vajanti: they go.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, Queen Khema was established in Arahatship. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude.

The Teacher said to King Bimbisāra: "Great King, it is proper for Queen Khema either to ordain or to attain Parinibbāna." The King replied: "Venerable Sir, please let her ordain; Parinibbāna is not suitable." Therefore, Queen Khema ordained and became a foremost female disciple.

(If one becomes an Arahat while in lay clothes, one must either ordain or pass away on that very day. This is because the state of Arahatship is not compatible with the inferior status of a layperson.)
The Story of Khema Theri ends.

## 6. The Story of the Treasurer's Son Uggasena
(The Story of Uggasena)
The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Muñca pure" concerning the treasurer's son Uggasena.
341:
## The Merchant's Son and the Dancer

It is said that five hundred dancers, every year or every six months, would go to the city of Rājagaha and perform a festival for seven days in the presence of King Bimbisāra. They would receive much gold and silver, and the gifts given in between were beyond measure. A great multitude of people stood on tiered platforms and the like to watch the festival. At that time, a certain dancer, the daughter of a tumbler who was capable of leaping, climbed a bamboo pole and, revolving on top of that pole, danced and sang while walking in the air at the end of the pole.

At that time, a merchant's son named Uggasena, standing on the tiered platforms with a friend, looked at that dancer. He fell in love with her, captivated by the movements of her hands and feet. Having returned home, he thought, "If I get that dancer, I shall live; if I do not get her, let death come to me right here." Thus, he refused food and lay down on his bed. When his mother and father asked, "Dear son, what pain afflicts you?", he replied, "If I get that dancer's daughter, I will have life. If I do not get her, I will surely die in this very place." Although they said, "Dear son, do not do this; we will bring you another maiden suitable for our family and wealth," he lay there saying the same thing as before.

Then, the great merchant, the father of the youth Uggasena, though he pleaded much, was unable to convince his son. Therefore, he summoned Uggasena's friend, gave him a thousand coins, and sent him saying, "Take these coins and tell him to give his daughter to my son." The dancer's father replied, "I will not give her for coins. However, if that youth Uggasena cannot live without getting this daughter, then let him wander together with us; I will then give him my daughter." When this was reported, the mother and father told their son about the matter. The youth Uggasena said, "I will wander together with them." Despite their pleas, he disregarded his parents' words, left the house, and went to the dancer. The dancer's father gave his daughter to the merchant's son Uggasena and wandered about with him, demonstrating their skills in villages, market towns, and royal capitals.

## The Husband Learning Skills due to the Wife's Pride

That dancer, having lived with the merchant's son Uggasena, soon gave birth to a son. While playing with the child, she would say:

"Son of a cart-guard, son of a porter, son of one who knows nothing!"
342:
(The merchant's son Uggasena also had to perform the unyoking of their carts and wander to the grazing grounds at their stopping places. When they demonstrated their skills, he had to carry the bundles of wealth they received. It was with reference to that very situation that the dancer, while playing with her young son, spoke in that manner.)

When the merchant's son Uggasena realized that the dancer was singing those words with reference to him, he asked her, "Are you speaking with reference to me?" When she replied, "It is true, I speak with reference to you," he said, "If that is the case, I shall run away." The dancer said, "What benefit is it to me whether you run away or stay?" and repeatedly sang that same song. (It is said that the dancer, relying on her own beauty and the wealth she earned, did not think anything of the merchant's son Uggasena.)

Uggasena, wondering, "On what account does this dancer have such pride?", realized, "She is proud because of her skill." He then thought, "Let it be so; I will learn the skill." He approached his father-in-law, learned the skills known by him, and after demonstrating those skills in villages and market towns, eventually arrived at the city of Rājagaha. He had it announced, "On the seventh day from now, the merchant's son Uggasena will demonstrate his skill to the city dwellers."

## The Buddha's Arrival during the Performance

The city dwellers had tiered platforms and the like constructed and gathered on the seventh day. Uggasena also climbed a sixty-cubit bamboo pole and stood on its tip. On that day, the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw Uggasena entering the net of His knowledge. Reflecting on "What will happen?", He knew, "Tomorrow the merchant's son will stand on the tip of a bamboo pole to show his skill. A great multitude will gather to watch him. There, I will preach a verse of four lines. Upon hearing it, eighty-four thousand beings will attain the realization of the Dhamma, and Uggasena will be established in Arahantship."

The Teacher, noting the time on the following day, entered Rājagaha for alms, surrounded by the community of monks. Just as the Teacher was entering the city, Uggasena gave a finger-signal to the great multitude to raise a shout of applause. Standing on the tip of the bamboo pole, he somersaulted seven times in the air and landed back on the tip of the pole. At that moment, as the Teacher entered the city, He acted in such a way that the assembly did not look at Uggasena, but looked only at the Teacher Himself. Uggasena, looking at the assembly, thought, "The assembly is not looking at me!" and became dejected. He thought, "I have practiced this skill for a whole year. Now that the Teacher has entered the city, the assembly does not look at me but looks only at the Teacher. My demonstration of skill has indeed become in vain."

## Venerable Moggallāna and Uggasena

The Teacher, knowing Uggasena's thought, addressed the Venerable Moggallāna, saying, "Go, Moggallāna, tell the merchant's son to demonstrate his skill." The Elder went and, standing beneath the bamboo pole, addressed the merchant's son and spoke this verse:
343:
“Come, look, son of a dancer, Uggasena of great strength! Perform in the arena for the assembly; make the great crowd laugh.”

Uggasena of great strength. Uggasena by name. Son of a dancer. “Come,” I urge you. “Look!” In the assembly. The performance. Perform. The great crowd. Make them joyful.

“Come, look, O one of great wisdom, Moggallāna of great psychic power! I shall perform in the arena for the assembly; I shall make the great crowd laugh.”

O one of great psychic power. O one of great wisdom. Venerable Moggallāna. “Come,” I urge you. Please look. In the assembly. The performance. I shall perform. The great crowd. I shall make them joyful.

## The Teaching
(348) Let go of the past, let go of the future, let go of the middle, crossing to the further shore of existence. With a mind liberated in every way, you shall not again undergo birth and old age.

In the past aggregates. Attachment. Let go.

When Uggasena heard the words of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, he became delighted in heart. Thinking, “The Teacher, I suppose, wishes to see my skill,” he spoke this verse while standing on the very tip of the bamboo pole.

Having spoken thus, he leaped from the tip of the bamboo pole into the air, somersaulted fourteen times in the sky, and descending, stood again on the tip of the bamboo pole. Then the Teacher, saying to Uggasena, “Uggasena, one who is wise should abandon attachment to the aggregates of the past, future, and present, and be freed from birth and so forth,” spoke this verse:

(It means one should let go of attachment (ālaya) that clings to past aggregates, the desire (nikanti) that delights in them, the obsession (ajjhosāna) that enters into them, the longing (patthanā) that craves them, the uprising (pariyuṭṭhāna) that pierces, the grasping (gāha) that seizes, the misapprehension (parāmāsa) that wrongly touches, and the craving (taṇhā) that lusts after them.)

In the future aggregates. Let go. In the middle, the present aggregates. Let go. Of the three realms of existence. One who has reached the further shore. Having become.

(It means if one can let go in this way, one reaches the further shore by means of the power of a ‘further-shore-goer’—which consists of fully knowing, abandoning, developing, and realizing all three realms of existence.)

In all conditioned things (saṅkhata). With a mind that is liberated. Again. Birth and old age. You shall not approach.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. The treasurer’s son Uggasena, while still standing on the tip of the bamboo pole, attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Descending from the pole, he approached the Teacher, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and requested ordination.

## Uggasena’s Ordination
Then the Teacher, stretching out his right hand, said, “Come, monk (Ehi Bhikkhu),” and so forth. At that very moment, he became like an Elder of sixty years’ standing, equipped with the eight requisites. Then the monks asked him, “Friend Uggasena, were you not afraid when descending from the tip of the sixty-cubit bamboo pole?” When he replied, “Friends, I have no fear,” they informed the Teacher, “Venerable Sir, Uggasena says he does not fear.”
344:
“Having cut every fetter, he who truly does not tremble, who has transcended attachments and is disjoined, him I call a Brahmin.”

Whoever. All ten fetters (saṃyojana). Having cut. Truly. Does not tremble or fear because of craving. One who has transcended the attachments of lust and so forth. One who is disjoined from the four yokes (yoga). That person. I. One who has put away evil. Call.

“Venerable Sir, the monk Uggasena says he does not fear; he speaks what is not true and claims the fruit of Arahantship,” they reported. The Teacher said, “Monks, monks like my son Uggasena, who have cut the fetters, do not fear; they do not tremble,” and spoke this verse in the Brāhmaṇa Vaggā.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

## Uggasena’s Past
One day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a discussion: “Friends, what was the reason that a monk so endowed with the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for Arahantship had to wander with dancers because of a dancer’s daughter? And what was the cause for his supporting conditions for Arahantship?” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When told, “We are gathered for such and such a discussion,” he said, “Monks, both of these were done by this Uggasena himself,” and to clarify the matter, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when the golden shrine of the Buddha Kassapa was being built, some young men of good family living in Bārāṇasī loaded many kinds of food onto carts and went to the site of the shrine to perform manual labor. On the way, they saw an Elder entering for alms. Then a young woman of good family, seeing the Elder, said to her husband, “My lord, the noble one is entering for alms. We have much food in our cart. Bring his bowl; let us give alms.” The husband brought the bowl, filled it with food, and placed it in the Elder’s hand. Both husband and wife made a wish: “Venerable Sir, may we be partakers of the very Nibbāna seen by you.”

## Becoming a Dancer due to Verbal Misconduct against an Arahant
That Elder was an Arahant whose taints were exhausted. Therefore, looking at them and knowing that their wish would be fulfilled, he smiled. Seeing that smile, the woman said to her husband, “My lord, our noble one is smiling; he must be a dancer.” The husband also said to her, “It will be so, my dear,” and went on. This was the past karma of the couple. Having stayed there for the duration of their lives, they were reborn in the deva world. Passing away from there, the woman was reborn in a dancer’s house, and the man in a treasurer’s house. Because the man had given that reply to his wife, “It will be so, my dear,” he had to wander together with the dancers.
345:
Depending on the alms-food offered to the Arahant Elder, he attained the fruit of Arahantship. That acrobat's daughter also thought, "The path my husband takes is the path I shall take," and having ordained, she too was established in the fruit of Arahantship.

The story of Uggasena, the treasurer's son, is finished.

## 7. The Story of Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise
(Cūḷadhanuggaha Paṇḍita Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Vitakkamanthitassa," concerning the wise man named Cūḷadhanuggaha.

## From a Drink of Water to Dissatisfaction

A certain young monk took his bowl-ticket at the place where tickets are distributed, took the ticket-gruel, and went to the dining hall to drink it. Not finding water in that dining hall, he went to a house for water. As soon as a young girl in that house saw the young monk, she fell in love with him and said, "Venerable Sir, if you have need of drinking water again, please come only to this house."

From then on, whenever the monk did not find water, he went only to that house. The girl would take the monk's bowl and offer him drinking water. As time passed, she also offered him gruel, and one day, she invited him to sit in that very house and offered him alms-food. Sitting near the monk, she initiated a conversation, saying, "Venerable Sir, there is nothing that is not available in this house; we simply lack a man to manage the household."

After hearing the young girl's words for only two or three days, the monk became dissatisfied (with the holy life). One day, visiting monks saw him and asked, "Friend, why are you so thin? Why is your complexion as pale as a withered leaf?" When he replied, "Friends, I am dissatisfied," they took him to his teachers and preceptors. The teachers and preceptors then brought the monk to the Teacher and reported the matter.

The Teacher asked, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Why, having ordained in the Dispensation of a Buddha like me, who is possessed of supreme effort, do you allow yourself to be called 'dissatisfied' instead of 'Stream-enterer' or 'Once-returner'? Heavy indeed is the deed you have done." He then asked, "For what reason are you dissatisfied?"

When the monk replied, "Bhante, a woman spoke to me in this way," the Teacher said, "Monk, it is not surprising that she acted thus. In the past, she abandoned the foremost wise man in all of Jambudīpa, and having conceived an affection for a man she had just seen for a moment, she brought that foremost wise man to his death." At the request of the monks to clarify this matter, he told the story of the past.

## The Past Story of the Woman Who Handed the Sword Hilt to a Robber

In the past, when he was the wise man Cūḷadhanuggaha, he studied under a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha) in Takkasilā. The teacher, being pleased, gave him his daughter. While traveling to Vārāṇasī with her, at the entrance of a forest, he killed fifty robbers with fifty arrows. When the arrows were exhausted, he caught the robber chief, threw him to the ground, and said, "Dear sister, bring me the sword." At that moment, she conceived an affection for the robber she had just seen and placed the hilt of the sword in the robber's hand. Thus, the robber killed the wise man. As the robber chief was leaving with the woman, he thought, "If this woman sees another man, she will have me killed just as she did her own husband.
346:
## Verses from the Jātaka
Sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ samādāya, pāraṃ tiṇṇosi brāhmaṇa.
Paccāgaccha lahuṃ khippaṃ, mampi tārehi dānito.
Asanthutaṃ maṃ cirasanthutena, nimīni bhotī adhuvaṃ dhuvena.
Mayāpi bhotī nimineyya aññaṃ, ito ahaṃ dūrataraṃ gamissaṃ.
Kāyaṃ eḷagalagumbe, karoti ahuhāsiyaṃ.
Nayīdha naccaṃ vā gītaṃ vā, tāḷaṃ vā susamāhitaṃ.
Anamhīkāle susoṇi, kinu jagghasi sobhaṇe.
Siṅgāla bāla dummedha, appapaññosi jambuka.
Jīno macchañca pesiñca, kapaṇo viya jhāyasi.
Sudassaṃ vajjamaññesaṃ, attano pana duddasaṃ.
Jīnā patiñca jārañca, maññe tvaññeva jhāyasi.
Evametaṃ migarāja, yathā bhāsasi jambuka.
Sānnūnāhaṃ ito gantvā, bhattu hessāṃ vasānugā.
Yo hare mattakaṃ thālaṃ, kaṃsathālampi so hare.
Katañceva tayā pāpaṃ, punapevaṃ karissasi.

Thinking, "What use is this woman to me?" he saw a river and left the woman on this bank. Taking her bundle of belongings, he said, "Stay on this bank for as long as I am transporting the bundle to the other side." Having said this, he abandoned her on that bank and departed. To make this clear, the Teacher spoke these verses:

## The Woman's Plea while Standing on This Bank
"Brahmin (or Master), you have taken all the goods and crossed to the other side. Come back quickly; help me cross from here as well."

## The Thief's Reply while Standing on the Other Bank
"O lady, you have exchanged your permanent husband of long acquaintance for me, a stranger and an impermanent one. You might exchange me for another as well; I shall go far away from here."

(When the thief fled with the goods, the woman entered a thicket and wept. At that time, the King of Devas, taking the form of a jackal and carrying a piece of meat in its mouth, went to the water's edge. When he reached the woman, the deva Mātali took the form of a fish and jumped out of the water in front of the jackal. The jackal dropped the meat to catch the fish. Then, the deva Pañcasikha took the form of a hawk, swooped down, and flew away with the meat. The fish also jumped back into the water. Having lost both the meat and the fish, the jackal stared at the grass in dejection. Seeing this, the woman in the thicket laughed loudly, and the jackal spoke:)

"Who is this woman laughing so loudly in the thicket of eḷagala grass? Here, there is no dancing, no singing, nor the well-timed clapping of hands. O fair-waisted one, O beautiful one, why do you laugh at a time when you should be weeping?"
347:
## The Teaching
(349) For the person who is disturbed by thoughts, who is of strong passion, who looks for the beautiful, craving grows more and more. He indeed makes the bond strong.
(350) But he who delights in the stilling of thoughts, who always meditates on the foul, being mindful—he will make an end (of craving), he will cut the bond of Mara.

'Vitakkamathitassa' means being constantly crushed and oppressed by thoughts such as sensual thoughts. 'Tibbarāgassa' means having intense passion, or thick and abundant passion. 'Subhānupassino' means one who habitually views things as beautiful, due to letting the mind go by grasping the sign of beauty in pleasant objects.

## The Woman's Words to the Jackal
'O foolish, witless jackal named Jambuka! You are of little wisdom. Having lost both the fish and the piece of meat, you grieve like a wretched person who has lost a thousand pieces of wealth and is left alone.'

## The Jackal's Reply
'The faults of others are easily seen, but one's own faults are hard to see. You yourself, having lost both the husband given by your parents and the paramour met on the road, must be grieving a hundred times more than I, I think.'

## The Woman's Confession in Regret
'O Jambuka, king of beasts! It is just as you say. I have become exactly as you described. Having gone from here and found a husband again, I will certainly live according to my husband's will.'

## Sakka's Final Shaming Words
'He who steals a clay bowl would also steal a bowl made of bronze, gold, or silver. You have already committed an evil deed, and you will surely do such evil again.'

Having thus detailed the Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka in the Pañcaka Nipāta, the Teacher said: 'At that time, you, O monk, were the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha. That woman is now this young girl. And Sakka, the king of gods, who came in the form of a jackal to rebuke her, was I myself.' Then he advised: 'Thus, that woman, out of affection for a thief she had just met, deprived the greatest wise man in all of Jambudīpa of his life. O monk, live having cut off the craving for existence that has arisen because of that woman.' Desiring to preach the Dhamma further, he spoke these verses:
348:
(Meaning: having a mind released by grasping the sign of beauty in pleasant objects, etc.)
'Jantuno': for the being. 'Taṇhā': craving for the six doors. 'Bhiyyo pavaḍḍhati': increases greatly. 'Esa eso jantu': such a person. 'Bandhanaṃ': the bond of craving. 'Daḷhaṃ karoti': makes firm.

'Yo': the person who. 'Vitakkūpasame va rato': delighting only in the meditation on the foul (asubha-jhāna) which stills wrong thoughts and so forth. 'Sadā sato': being always mindful. 'Asubhaṃ bhāvayate': develops the ten kinds of foulness. 'Esa eso puggalo': this person. 'Kho': indeed. 'Byanti kāhiti': will make an end of, or cause the disappearance of, craving for existence. 'Esa eso puggalo': this person. 'Mārabandhanaṃ': the bond of Mara, known as the round of rebirth in the three planes. 'Checchati': will cut.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, that young monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled people.
The Story of the Wise Cūḷadhanuggaha ends.

## The Teaching
(351) He who has reached the goal, who is fearless, without craving, without blemish, has cut the thorns of existence; this is his final body.
(352) Without craving, without attachment, skilled in the interpretation of words, knowing the arrangement of letters and their sequence—he is indeed called one of final body, one of great wisdom, a great man.

## 8. The Story of Mara
(Māra Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Niṭṭhaṅgato' concerning Mara.

## Frightening Rāhula in the Form of a Great Elephant
One day, at an unseasonable time in the evening, many elders entered Jetavana Monastery and, going to the place where Venerable Rāhula resided, made him leave his place. Venerable Rāhula, not finding another place to stay, lay down at the entrance of the Buddha's Gandhakuti. At that time, Venerable Rāhula had attained Arahatship and was only eight years old. Mara, staying in the Vasavatti heaven, saw Venerable Rāhula lying at the entrance of the Gandhakuti and thought: 'The painful finger (Rāhula) of the recluse Gotama is sleeping outside the Gandhakuti, while the Lord himself is sleeping inside. If the finger is oppressed, the Lord himself will be oppressed.' Mara created the form of a great elephant king and, coming there, wrapped his trunk around Venerable Rāhula's head and made a loud trumpeting sound like a heron. The Teacher, while sitting inside the Gandhakuti, knew it was Mara and said: 'O Mara, even a thousand like you cannot cause fear to my son. My son is without fear, free from craving, of great energy, and of great wisdom.' He then spoke these verses:

'Yo': the person who. 'Niṭṭhaṅgato': has reached the end, which is the fruit of Arahatship. (In this Dispensation, the fruit of Arahatship of monks is called 'Niṭṭha'; meaning he has reached that goal.) 'Asantāsī': has no nature of fear because of the absence of passion, etc. 'Vītatṇho': has craving that has departed. 'Anaṅgaṇo': is without defilements. 'Bhavasallāni': the thorns that lead to the three planes of existence. 'Acchindi': has cut. 'Etassa ayaṃ samussayo': this body of his. 'Antimo': is associated with the final birth.

'Yo': the person who. 'Vītatṇho': has craving that has departed. 'Anādāno': has no grasping or attachment to the aggregates, etc. 'Niruttipadakovido': is skilled in grammar and in words. (Meaning: is skilled and proficient in the four analytical insights.) 'Akkharānaṃ': of the letters. 'Sannipātañca': the collection or combination. 'Pubbāparāni ca': the preceding letters by the following ones, and the following letters by the preceding ones. 'Jaññā': knows.
349:
(Knowing the subsequent letter by the preceding letter means: when the beginning is clear but the middle and end are not, knowing 'this is the middle and this is the end of these letters.' Knowing the preceding letter by the subsequent letter means: when the end is clear but the beginning and middle are not, knowing 'this is the middle and this is the beginning of these letters.' Even when only the middle is clear, knowing 'this is the beginning and this is the end of these letters.')

*Antimasārīro*: one who possesses a body that is in its final state. *Mahāpañño*: one of great wisdom.

(This means being endowed with wisdom capable of grasping the meanings (*attha*), the teachings (*dhamma*), the language (*nirutti*), and the ready wit (*paṭibhāna*), as well as the aggregate of virtue (*sīla*), etc.)

*Mahāpuriso*: a Great Man, so called because of having a mind liberated from the defilements. Thus it is said.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-phala*) and so forth. The Evil Mara, realizing 'The Ascetic Gotama knows me,' vanished right then and there.

The Story of Mara ends.

## 9. The Story of the Ajivaka named Upaka

(Upakājīvaka Vatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Sabbābhibhū' while on the journey, concerning the Ajivaka named Upaka.
350:
## The Teaching

(353) I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all, unsullied in all things.
Having renounced all, liberated in the destruction of craving, having realized this by myself, whom should I point to as my teacher?

Upaka, Upaka. I am the conqueror of all (*Sabbābhibhū*), having overcome and destroyed all things of the three planes of existence (*tebhūmaka*). I am the knower of all (*Sabbavidū*), knowing the things in the four planes that should be known. In all things, I am unsullied by craving and wrong view regarding the things of the three planes. I am the renouncer of all, having abandoned all things of the three planes. In the destruction of craving (*taṇhākkhaye*), I have a mind liberated in the Fruit of Arahatship, which is the destruction of craving. Having realized by myself, having personally known the Four Noble Truths, whom should I point to, saying 'This is my preceptor or teacher'?

## The First Meeting with Upaka

On one occasion, the Teacher, having attained Omniscience and having spent the seven weeks at the site of the Bodhi tree, took his bowl and robes and set out for the city of Vārāṇasī, intending to turn the Wheel of Dhamma. While traveling the journey of eighteen yojanas, he saw the Ajivaka named Upaka on the way. That Ajivaka, upon seeing the Teacher, asked: 'Friend, your faculties, such as the eyes, are very serene; your complexion is pure and bright, and you have a radiant glow. Friend, on whose account have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve of?' Then, the Teacher said to Upaka, 'I have no preceptor or teacher,' and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching and Upaka's Attitude

At the conclusion of the teaching, the Ajivaka named Upaka neither delighted in nor rejected the words of the Tathāgata. Instead, he shook his head, wagged his tongue, and taking a side path, went to a certain place where hunters lived.

The Story of the Ajivaka named Upaka ends.

## 10. The Story of Sakka’s Questions

(Sakkapañha Vatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Sabbadānaṃ' while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, concerning Sakka, the King of Devas.
351:
## Going to the Great Kings for the Devas' Questions

On one occasion, the devas of Tāvatiṃsa gathered together and raised four questions: "Among gifts, which is the greatest? Among tastes, which is the greatest? Among delights, which is the greatest? Why is the destruction of craving alone said to be the greatest and most noble?"

Not even a single deva was able to decide these four questions. One deva asked another deva, and that one asked another, and in this manner, questioning one another, they wandered through the ten thousand world systems for twelve years. Having failed to see the meaning of the questions even after such a long time, the devas residing in the ten thousand world systems gathered and went to the Four Great Kings. When asked, "Dear ones, why has such a great assembly of devas gathered?", they replied, "We have raised four questions and, being unable to decide them, we have come to your presence, O Great Kings."

When asked, "Dear ones, what are these questions?", they replied, "Among gifts, tastes, and delights, which gift, taste, and delight is the most excellent? And why is the destruction of craving the most excellent? We have come because we are unable to decide these questions."

## Going to the Buddha with Sakka

The Four Great Kings said, "Dear ones, we also do not know the meaning of these questions. However, our lord Sakka can think of matters conceived by a thousand eyes and know them in an instant. He excels us in wisdom and merit. Come, let us go to the presence of Sakka."

Saying this, they took the host of devas and went to Sakka, the King of Devas. When Sakka asked, "Dear ones, why has such a great assembly of devas gathered?", they explained the matter to him.

Sakka said, "Dear ones, no other person is able to know the meaning of these questions; these questions are the domain of the Buddhas. Where is the Teacher residing now?" Hearing that he was at Jetavana, he said, "Come, let us go to his presence." Accompanied by the host of devas, at night, illuminating the entire Jetavana monastery with their radiance, they approached the Teacher. After paying homage and standing at a respectful distance, the Buddha asked, "Great King, why have you come with such a large host of devas?" Sakka replied, "Venerable Sir, the host of devas has raised these specific questions. There is no one else capable of knowing their meaning. Please reveal the meaning of these questions to us."

352:
## The Teaching

(354) The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts; the taste of Dhamma excels all tastes.
The delight in Dhamma excels all delights; the destruction of craving overcomes all suffering.

Sabbadānaṃ: all gifts. Dhammadānaṃ: the gift of preaching the Dhamma. Jināti: excels/conquers. Sabbarasaṃ: all tastes. Dhammaraso: the taste of Dhamma. Jināti: excels. Sabbaratiṃ: all delights. Dhammarati: delight in the Dhamma. Jināti: excels.

Taṇhakkhayo: the destruction of craving, or the Fruit of Arahantship which is the end of craving. Sabbadukkhaṃ: all suffering. Jināti: excels/overcomes.

"There is no one else capable of knowing the meaning of these questions. Venerable Sir, please clearly show the meaning of these questions to us." When Sakka requested thus, the Buddha said, "Great King, well said. I have fulfilled the perfections and made the great sacrifices only for the sake of cutting away the doubts of those like you, having penetrated the Omniscient Wisdom. The answer to the questions you asked is: among all gifts, the gift of Dhamma is supreme; among all tastes, the taste of Dhamma is supreme; among all delights, delight in Dhamma is supreme; and the destruction of craving is supreme because it leads to the Fruit of Arahantship." Having said this, he preached this verse.

## Notes on the Teaching

If one were to offer robes as soft as the core of a banana tree to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants sitting continuously throughout the world system up to the Brahma realm, the appreciation of the Dhamma given through a four-line verse at that gathering would be superior. That gift of robes is not worth even a sixteenth part of that verse. Thus, the preaching, teaching, and listening to the Dhamma are noble. The merit for the person who causes many people to hear the Dhamma is immense.

The gift of Dhamma, even in the form of an appreciation through a four-line verse, is superior to: the gift of choice alms-food filling the bowls of such a congregation; the gift of medicine like ghee and oil filling their bowls; the building and offering of countless hundreds of thousands of monasteries like Mahāvihāra or palaces like Lohapāsāda; or the sacrifices made by Anāthapiṇḍika and others for the sake of monasteries. Why is this? Because those who perform such meritorious deeds can only do so after hearing the Dhamma; they cannot do so without hearing it. If these beings did not hear the Dhamma, they would not give even a ladleful of gruel or a spoonful of rice. For this reason, the gift of Dhamma is supreme above all gifts.

Furthermore, setting aside the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, even those like Venerable Sāriputta, who possess wisdom capable of counting the raindrops in a rain falling for a whole aeon, could not attain the Fruit of Stream-entry by their own nature. Only after hearing the Dhamma preached by Venerable Assaji and others did they realize the Fruit of Stream-entry. Through the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, they realized the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection. Great King, for this reason too, the gift of Dhamma is the most excellent. Therefore, it was said: "Sabbadānaṃ dhammadānaṃ jināti."

All tastes, such as scents and flavors, and even the most excellent taste of divine ambrosia, are only causes for falling into the round of rebirth and experiencing suffering. Only the taste of Dhamma, consisting of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the nine supramundane states, is the best and most excellent among all tastes. Therefore, it was said: "Sabbarasaṃ dhammaraso jināti."
353:
Delight in sons, delight in daughters, delight in wealth, delight in women, and various delights such as dancing, singing, and music—all these many kinds of delight exist in the world. All such delights lead only to falling into the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) and experiencing suffering. However, that delight which arises within one who is preaching the Dhamma, listening to the Dhamma, or teaching the Dhamma, produces a state of rapture, causes tears to flow, and makes the hair stand on end. This delight brings an end to the round of rebirths and culminates in Arahantship. Therefore, among all delights, such delight in the Dhamma is the most excellent. Thus, it was said: 'The delight in Dhamma excels all delights' (Sabba-ratiṃ dhammarati jināti).

The destruction of craving, which is Arahantship arising at the end of the exhaustion of craving, is the most excellent of all because it overcomes the entirety of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha). Thus, it was said: 'The destruction of craving excels all suffering' (Taṇhakkhayo sabbadukkhaṃ jināti).

## The Benefit of the Teaching
While the Teacher was explaining the meaning of this verse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the penetration of the Dhamma (the Four Noble Truths).

## Sakka's Request to Share Merit
Sakka, King of Devas, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, paid homage to the Teacher and said: 'Venerable Sir, when such a supreme and noble gift of Dhamma is given, for what reason do you not have the merit shared with us? From this day forward, Venerable Sir, please have the merit shared with us after preaching to the community of monks.' Hearing his words, the Teacher assembled the community of monks and said: 'Monks, from today onwards, whether it be a great Dhamma assembly, an ordinary Dhamma talk, or a discussion with those seated nearby, or even at the very least, after giving a talk of appreciation (anumodanā), you should share the merit with all beings.'

The Story of Sakka's Questions ends.

## 11. The Story of the Childless Treasurer
(Aputtaka-seṭṭhi Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Hananti bhogā,' concerning the treasurer named Aputtaka, who had no children.

## The Death of Aputtaka the Treasurer
Having heard of the death of that great treasurer, King Pasenadi of Kosala inquired, 'To whom does the wealth of one without an heir belong?' Upon hearing 'To the King,' he had the wealth transported from the treasurer's house to the royal palace for seven days. Then, he approached the Teacher. When asked, 'Well, Great King, from where do you come at this time of day?', he replied, 'Venerable Sir, a treasurer and householder has died here in Sāvatthī. I have just come after transporting his heirless wealth to the royal palace.'

(The full details should be understood as they appear in the Sutta of the Sagāthā-vagga Saṃyutta, Kosala Saṃyutta, Second Chapter, the tenth Sutta.)
354:
When that great treasurer was served various choice foods of excellent flavor in a golden dish, he would say, 'Do humans really eat such food? Are you trying to mock me in this house?' and he would strike those who brought the food with clods of earth, sticks, or rods, driving them away. Saying, 'This is the food for humans,' he would eat broken rice with sour gruel as his second dish. Even when pleasing clothes, vehicles, and umbrellas were presented, he would strike those people with clods and rods, driving them away, and would wear coarse hempen garments. He traveled in a dilapidated chariot with a leaf awning held over him. When the King reported this, the Teacher recounted the treasurer's past deeds.

## The Past Karma of Aputtaka the Treasurer
'Great King, in the past, that treasurer was a householder and once offered alms-food to a Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī. Having said, "Give alms-food to the recluse," he rose from his seat and left. While that faithless and foolish treasurer left after saying this, his wife, who was endowed with faith and devotion, thought: "It has been a long time since I heard the word 'Give' from this treasurer's mouth. Today, I shall fulfill my heart's desire and offer alms-food." She took the Paccekabuddha's bowl, filled it with choice food, and offered it. As the treasurer was returning, he saw the Paccekabuddha and asked, "Recluse, did you receive anything?" Taking the bowl and seeing the choice alms-food, he felt regret and thought: "It would have been better if my slaves or laborers had eaten this choice alms-food. For if they ate it, they would work for me. But this recluse will go, eat, and then sleep. My alms-food is wasted!"'

'Furthermore, that treasurer once took the life of his brother's only son for the sake of the inheritance. It is said that while the boy was walking along holding the treasurer's finger, he said things like, "This little cart belongs to my father; this ox belongs to him." Then the treasurer thought, "Even now he speaks like this. When this boy reaches maturity, who will be able to guard the wealth in this house?" He took the boy to the forest, seized him by the neck near a bush, and killed him by snapping his neck like a root or a tuber, then discarded him right there. This was his past deed.'

(Therefore, the passage beginning with 'Yaṃ kho so' was taught in the Saṃyutta Nikāya.)

## Falling into the Mahāroruva Hell
'Great King, because that treasurer and householder offered alms-food to the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī, by the result of that wholesome deed, he was reborn seven times in the heavenly world, a happy destination. By the remaining result of that same wholesome deed, he served as a treasurer seven times in this very city of Sāvatthī. Great King, because that treasurer and householder felt regret after giving, thinking, "It would have been better if my slaves or laborers had eaten this choice alms-food," as a result of that regret, his mind did not incline toward enjoying grand and choice food...'
355:
## The Teaching
(355) Riches ruin the foolish, but not those who seek the beyond. Through craving for riches, the foolish person ruins himself as if he were ruining others.

Wealth ruins the foolish. Wealth cannot ruin those who seek Nibbāna. Through craving that depends on wealth, the foolish person ruins himself, just as he might ruin others.

That treasurer's mind did not incline toward using excellent clothes or vehicles; his mind did not incline toward enjoying the various excellent five cords of sensual pleasure. "O Great King, because that treasurer killed his brother's only son for the sake of wealth, as a result of that unwholesome kamma, he suffered in hell for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years. As a remaining result of that same unwholesome kamma, for the seventh time, this childless wealth must be entered into the royal treasury. O Great King, the old merit of that childless treasurer is exhausted, and he has not accumulated new merit. Now, O Great King, that treasurer is suffering in the Mahāroruva hell," the Buddha said.

After hearing the Buddha's words, the King said, "Venerable Sir, it is indeed a heavy kamma! Having such great wealth, he neither enjoyed it himself nor performed meritorious deeds while a Buddha like you was residing in a nearby monastery."

The Buddha replied, "So it is, Great King. Foolish people, even when they obtain wealth, do not seek Nibbāna. Craving that arises depending on wealth kills these foolish people for a long night," and then He spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of the Childless Treasurer (Aputtakaseṭṭhi) ends.

## 12. The Story of the Celestial Being Aṅkura
(Aṅkuravatthu)
The Teacher, while residing on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, spoke this teaching beginning with 'Tiṇadosāni' concerning the celestial being Aṅkura.

## Giving with Discrimination
(The story has been detailed in the verse 'Ye jhānappasutā dhīrā' in the Buddha Vagga. That is true; that story has been told. In that story, the teaching was given concerning the celestial being Indaka.)
356:
Giving should be done with discrimination, where the gift yields great fruit. Giving with discrimination is praised by the Sugata. Whatever worthy recipients (dakkhiṇeyya) there are here in this world of beings, gifts given to them have great fruit, like seeds sown in a fertile field.

Where, or to whom, a gift is given that yields great fruit, therefore, one should give with discrimination to that person. Giving with discrimination is praised by the Buddhas. Whatever worthy recipients there are in this world of beings, gifts given to those worthy recipients have great fruit, like seeds sown in a fertile field.

## The Teaching
(356) Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has passion as its blemish. Therefore, a gift given to those free from passion yields great fruit.
(357) Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has hatred as its blemish. Therefore, a gift given to those free from hatred yields great fruit.
(358) Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has delusion as its blemish. Therefore, a gift given to those free from delusion yields great fruit.
(359) Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has desire as its blemish. Therefore, a gift given to those free from desire yields great fruit.

Fields are blemished because of the growth of weeds. This generation of beings is blemished because of passion. Therefore, a gift given to the Arahants who are free from passion yields great fruit.

When the Elder Anuruddha entered the village for alms, that celestial being Indaka once offered a single spoonful of alms-food that he had brought for himself. That merit of Indaka became much more fruitful than the alms given by Aṅkura, who had provided a row of ovens twelve yojanas long for ten thousand years. Therefore, it was said so. When this was said, the Teacher, wishing to clarify this matter, said, "Aṅkura, giving should be done with discrimination. Such a gift given with discrimination is indeed of great fruit, like seeds sown in fertile soil. You, however, did not do so; therefore, your gift did not yield great fruit."

Having spoken thus, and wishing to teach the Dhamma further, He spoke these verses:

(Weeds such as Sāmāka grow and destroy the crops in the fields; therefore, they cannot yield much fruit. Similarly, passion arising within beings destroys them; therefore, a gift given to those persons is not of great fruit, but a gift given to Arahants is of great fruit.)

Fields are blemished because of the growth of weeds. This generation of beings is blemished because of hatred. Therefore, a gift given to the Arahants who are free from hatred yields great fruit.

Fields are blemished because of the growth of weeds. This generation of beings is blemished because of delusion. Therefore, a gift given to the Arahants who are free from delusion yields great fruit.

Fields are blemished because of the growth of weeds. This generation of beings is blemished because of evil desire. Therefore, a gift given to the Arahants who are free from desire yields great fruit.
357:
"Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has passion as its blemish. Therefore, a gift given to those free from passion yields great fruit."

The same method applies to the remaining verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, both the celestial being Aṅkura and the celestial being Indaka were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of the Celestial Being Aṅkura ends.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Craving (Taṇhā Vagga) is finished.

The Twenty-fourth Chapter.
358:
Through firm persistence in the advice of the wise,
And through undauntedness and fear of danger,
We did not come under the power of the ogresses;
That safety of mine arose from great fear.

Kusalūpadese, in the advice of the wise Paccekabuddhas. Daḷhāya, firmly. Dhitiyā ca, also through the exercise of persistence. Bhayabhīrutāya, through the fear of the mind and the trembling of the body. Anivattitattā ca, also because of being undaunted. Rakkhasīnaṃ, of the ogresses. Vasaṃ, under the power. Na āgamimhase, we did not go. Me, for me. Mahatā, from great. Bhayena, danger. Sa so-sotthibhāvo, that state of safety. Jāto, has arisen.

## 25. Bhikkhuvagga
## 1. Pañcabhikkhu Vatthu
(The Story of the Five Monks)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Cakkhunā saṃvaro," concerning five monks.

## The Five Doors Should Be Guarded
Among those five monks, each one guarded only one of the five doors, such as the eye-door. Then one day, they gathered and argued, saying, "I guard a door that is difficult to guard. I guard a door that is difficult to guard." Thinking, "We will know this matter after asking the Teacher," they approached the Teacher and asked, "Venerable Sir, while we guard the eye-door and so on, each of us considers the door he guards to be the one most difficult to guard. Among us, who indeed guards the door that is difficult to guard?"

The Teacher, without favoring or disparaging even a single monk, said, "Monks, all these doors are indeed difficult to guard. However, it is not only now that you are unrestrained in these five places; in the past too, you were unrestrained. Because of being unrestrained and not following the advice of the wise, you reached the end of your lives." When requested by the monks, "When was that, Venerable Sir?", the Teacher related the story of the past, the Takkasila Jātaka.
359:
## The Teaching
(360) Restraint in the eye is good, good is restraint in the ear.
Restraint in the nose is good, good is restraint in the tongue.
(361) Restraint in the body is good, good is restraint in speech.
Restraint in the mind is good, good is restraint in everything.
The monk restrained in everything is freed from all suffering.

Cakkhunā, through the eye-door. Saṃvaro, guarding or preventing the arising of lust, hatred, and delusion. Sādhu, is good. Sotena, through the ear-door. Saṃvaro, restraint. Sādhu, is good. Ghānena, through the nose-door. Saṃvaro, restraint. Sādhu, is good. Jivhāya, through the tongue-door. Saṃvaro, restraint. Sādhu, is good.

Kāye, through the body-door. Saṃvaro, restraint. Sādhu, is good. Vācāya, through speech. Saṃvaro, restraint. Sādhu, is good. Manasā, through the mind. Saṃvaro, restraint. Sādhu, is good. Sabbattha, in all the six doors. Saṃvaro, restraint. Sādhu, is good. Sabbattha, in all the six doors. Saṃvuto, he who is restrained. Bhikkhu, the monk. Sabbadukkhā, from all the suffering of the round of rebirths. Pamuccati, is freed.

## The Past of the Monks
Expanding on the story of the Takkasila Jātaka from the past: when the royal line reached its end through the power of the ogresses, the Bodhisatta, who had attained the consecration, sat on the royal throne under the white parasol. Looking at the perfection of his own glory, he uttered this verse as an exclamation (udāna): "This thing called effort should indeed be made by beings."

Having shown this verse, the Teacher said, "At that time, you five men, carrying weapons and surrounding the Bodhisatta who set out to take the kingdom of Takkasila, were traveling along the way. You were unrestrained in the sense objects like forms brought by the ogresses through the eye-door and so on. Not following the advice of the wise, you hesitated and stayed behind, and were thus devoured by the ogresses and reached the end of your lives. But I, being well-restrained regarding those objects, did not heed the ogress who followed behind in the form of a goddess, and reached Takkasila safely.

I was the king who obtained the kingdom of the country."
360:
After concluding the Jataka in this way, the Buddha said, "Monks, a monk should guard all his sense-doors; only those who guard those doors are released from all the suffering of the round of rebirths." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, those five monks were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of the Five Monks ends.

## 2. The Story of the Monk who Killed a Swan
(Haṃsaghātaka-bhikkhu Vatthu)
The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Hatthasaṃyato", while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, concerning a monk who killed a swan.

## The Monk with Unguarded Hands
It is said that two friends living in Sāvatthī ordained among the monks. Having attained higher ordination, they mostly traveled together. One day, they went to the Aciravatī River, and after bathing, they stood in the sun to dry themselves, engaging in pleasant conversation. At that moment, two swans were flying through the sky. Then, a young monk picked up a pebble and said, "I will hit the eye of one of those young swans."

The elder monk said, "You will not be able to."

"Let the eye on this side be; I will hit the eye on the other side," he said again.

"You will not be able to do that either," the elder replied.

"In that case, just watch," the young monk said. He picked up a sharp pebble and threw it at the back of the swan. Hearing the sound of the pebble, the swan turned its head to look. At that moment, the monk picked up a round pebble and threw it, hitting the eye on the far side so that it came out through the eye on this side.

The swan, crying out and spinning around, fell right at the feet of those monks. Monks standing here and there saw this and said, "Friends, having ordained in the Buddha's dispensation, you have done something unbecoming by taking the life of a living being." They took those monks and presented them to the Tathāgata.

The Teacher asked, "Monk, is it true that you have taken the life of a living being?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Buddha said, "Monk, why did you do such a thing after ordaining in this dispensation that leads to liberation? Even before a Buddha had arisen, ancient wise men, while living in the midst of the household life, felt remorse even over small matters. But you, having ordained in such a Buddha's dispensation, did not feel even a bit of remorse." Having said this, at the request of those monks, the Teacher brought forth the past.
361:
## Eleven People Practicing the Garudhamma
In the past, when King Dhanañjaya was reigning in the city of Indapatta in the Kuru kingdom, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of that king's chief queen. In due course, when he reached the age of wisdom, he learned the arts in the city of Takkasilā and was appointed to the position of Viceroy by his father. Later, upon his father's passing, he attained the kingship. Without violating the Ten Royal Virtues, he practiced the Kuru-dhamma.

(The Kuru-dhamma refers to the Five Precepts.)

The Bodhisatta kept those Five Precepts of the Kuru-dhamma pure and clean. Just as the Bodhisatta observed them, so did his mother, his chief queen, his younger brother the Viceroy, the Brahmin Chaplain, the land-measuring minister, the charioteer, the treasurer, the grain-measuring minister (also called the 'establisher'), the doorkeeper, and the courtesan. Thus, while these eleven people were observing the Five Precepts of the Kuru-dhamma, it did not rain in the Kaliṅga kingdom while King Kaliṅga was reigning in the city of Dantapura. At that time, the Bodhisatta's auspicious state elephant named Añjanasannibha possessed great merit. The citizens, believing that if that elephant were brought it would rain, made a request to the king.

## Making it Rain
