King Kaliṅga sent brahmins for the purpose of bringing that elephant. Those brahmins went and requested the elephant from the Bodhisatta. To show the reason for their request, the Teacher spoke this verse:

"Tava saddhañca sīlañca, viditvāna janādhipa.
Vaṇṇam añjanavaṇṇena, kaliṅgasmiṃ nimimhase."

(O King, ruler of men, having known your faith and virtue, we wish to take away wealth such as gold and silver to King Kaliṅga, because we desire the auspicious elephant which has the color of dark eye-ointment.)

(In this way, the Teacher told this Kurudhamma Jataka in the Tika Nipāta.)

Even though the auspicious elephant was brought, it still did not rain. Therefore, believing that "That king observes the Kuru-dhamma, and that is why it rains in his country; let us write down the Kuru-dhamma he observes on a golden plate and bring it," King Kaliṅga again sent brahmins and ministers. When those ministers and brahmins went and made their request, all those people, starting with the King, felt some remorse regarding their own virtue and initially refused, saying, "Our virtue is not pure." However, being repeatedly entreated by the brahmins and ministers who said, "The virtue is not broken by this much," they each spoke of their own virtue. As soon as King Kaliṅga saw the Kuru-dhamma brought and written on the golden plate, he undertook and practiced it well. Then it rained in his kingdom. The country became free from danger, prosperous, and peaceful.
362:
The courtesan was Uppalavaṇṇā; the doorkeeper then was Puṇṇa.
The rope-holder was Kaccāna; the grain-measurer was Kolita.
Sāriputta was then the merchant; Anuruddha was the charioteer.
The brahmin was Kassapa Thera; the viceroy was Ānanda the Wise.
The chief queen was the mother of Rāhula; Māyādevī was the mother.
The King of Kuru was the Bodhisatta; thus you should remember the Jātaka.

At that time, the courtesan was Uppalavaṇṇā. The doorkeeper was Puṇṇa Thera. The rope-holding minister was Kaccāna Thera. The grain-measuring minister was Kolita (Maha Moggallāna).

At that time, the merchant was Sāriputta. The charioteer was Anuruddha. The brahmin was Kassapa Thera. The viceroy was Ānanda the Wise.

The chief queen was the mother of Rāhula, Yasodharā. The mother was the chief queen named Māyā. The King who ruled the Kuru kingdom was I, the Bodhisatta. Thus, you should remember and bear this Jātaka in mind.

## The Teaching
(362) Restrained in hand, restrained in foot,
Restrained in speech, the best of the restrained;
Delighting in the internal, composed,
Alone and contented—him they call a bhikkhu.

One who restrains the hand by not playing or striking others, etc. One who restrains the foot. One who restrains the speech by not telling lies, etc. One who has a restrained body. One who delights in the meditation subject known as the internal sphere (gocarajjhatta). One who has a composed mind. Being one who dwells alone, one has a mind greatly delighted with the Dhamma one has attained. Him, they call a bhikkhu.

## Identification of the Eleven Characters
The Blessed One, having brought forth this past account, identified the Jātaka:

"Bhikkhu, in this way, even in the past, the wise felt remorse regarding the breach of their virtue even when a slight doubt arose. But you, having gone forth in the Dispensation of a Buddha like me, have committed an extremely grave unwholesome deed by taking the life of another. One called a bhikkhu should be restrained in hands, feet, and speech," and thus He spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many reached the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth.

The Story of the Bhikkhu who killed a Swan is finished.
363:
## 3. The Story of Kokālika
(Kokālikavatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "He who is restrained in mouth" in reference to Kokālika.

## Lack of Restraint in Speech
(The story appears in the Pali texts as "Then the bhikkhu Kokālika approached where the Blessed One was." The meaning of that Pali text should be understood in the manner already stated in the Commentary.)

When the bhikkhu Kokālika was reborn in the Paduma hell, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma hall: "Alas, the bhikkhu Kokālika has reached destruction because of his own mouth. Indeed, for that Kokālika who only reviled the two Chief Disciples, the earth opened up and gave him passage."

The Teacher, having arrived and asked, "Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" and being told, "We are gathered for such a discussion," said, "Bhikkhus, not only now, but in the past also, the bhikkhu Kokālika was destroyed because of his own mouth." Being requested by the monks who wished to hear that account, He brought forth the past to make the matter clear.

## The Past Story of the Talkative Tortoise
In the past, a tortoise lived in a certain lake in the Himālaya region. Two young swans, while wandering for food, made friends with that tortoise and became firm friends. One day, they asked the tortoise, "Friend tortoise, our dwelling place in the golden cave at the foot of Mount Cittakūṭa in the Himālayas is a delightful place. Would you like to go with us?"

When he replied, "Sons of the swan king, how can I go?", they said, "If you are able to guard your mouth, we will carry you." When he said, "I will guard my mouth; please take me and go," those young swans agreed, saying "Very well." They had the tortoise bite a stick, and they themselves bit the two ends of the stick and flew up into the sky.

When the village children saw the tortoise being carried by the swans in that manner, they said, "Two swans are carrying a tortoise with a stick!" The tortoise, wanting to say, "You wicked children, if my friends are carrying me, what is that to you?", let go of the stick from the place he was biting because of the swift speed of the swans. At the moment they reached above the palace of the King of Vārāṇasī, he fell into the open sky and split into two pieces. The Teacher, having brought forth this past account, said:

Indeed, the tortoise killed himself while uttering a word.
Though the stick was well-held, he killed himself by his own speech.

The tortoise, while speaking a word, alas, killed himself. While the stick was well-held, he killed himself with his own speech.
364:
“Seeing this, O best of men in effort, one should let loose speech that is skillful and not excessive. Behold the tortoise, gone to ruin through much talking.”

O best of men in effort, O great King who is noble among men due to your exertion. Having seen even this matter. One should speak speech that is skillful and faultless, which does not exceed the boundary of what the wise should say. Behold the tortoise, who has come to ruin because of speaking too much.

Having thus expanded this Bahubhāṇika Jātaka in the Dukanipāta, the Teacher said, “Monks, a monk should be restrained in speech, of good conduct, not agitated, and of a peaceful mind,” and then spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(363) The monk who is restrained in speech, who speaks with wisdom and is not agitated, who explains the meaning and the Dhamma—his speech is sweet.

Whosoever monk is restrained in speech (meaning he does not even address servants or outcasts as ‘you low-born’ or ‘you immoral one’). He speaks after reflecting with wisdom. He is not agitated and thus has a peaceful mind. He explains both the meaning and the Pali text. The speech of such a monk is sweet in flavor.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of Kokālika ends.

## 4. The Story of Elder Dhammārāma
(Dhammārāmattheravatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with “Dhammārāmo,” concerning the Elder named Dhammārāma.
365:
## The Teaching
(364) The monk who dwells in the Dhamma, delights in the Dhamma, reflects on the Dhamma, and recollects the Dhamma, does not fall away from the True Dhamma.

One for whom the Dhamma of Samatha and Vipassanā is a dwelling place. Delighting in the Dhamma of Samatha and Vipassanā. Repeatedly thinking, reflecting, and attending to the Dhamma of Samatha and Vipassanā. Recollecting the Dhamma repeatedly. Such a monk does not fall away from the True Dhamma, which consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the nine supramundane states.

## The Monk Who Worships According to the Buddha’s Wish
When the Buddha announced, “From this day, after four months have passed, my Parinibbāna will take place,” many thousands of monks went about surrounding the Buddha. Among them, the worldling monks were unable to restrain their tears. Spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in the Arahants. All the monks went about in groups, saying, “What shall we do?”

However, a monk named Dhammārāma did not approach the other monks. When asked by the monks, “Friend, why do you stay without approaching us?” he did not even give a reply, but thought, “The Teacher will attain Parinibbāna after four months. I am not yet free from passion. I will strive to reach the Fruit of Arahatship while the Teacher is still alive.” Thus, dwelling alone, he reflected on, thought about, and recollected the Dhamma taught by the Teacher.

The monks reported to the Buddha, “Venerable Sir, the monk named Dhammārāma does not have even a bit of affection for you. He does not even consult with us, saying, ‘The Teacher will attain Parinibbāna; what shall we do?’” The Teacher had that monk Dhammārāma summoned and asked, “Is it true that you do this?” “It is true, Venerable Sir,” he replied. When asked, “For what reason?” he answered, “Venerable Sir, you will attain Parinibbāna after four months. I still have passion. I am reflecting on, thinking about, and recollecting the Dhamma you have taught and exhorted, with the intention of reaching the Fruit of Arahatship while you are still alive.”

Upon hearing this, the Buddha gave him praise, saying, “Sādhu, Sādhu!” and said, “Monks, any other monk who has affection for me should be just like Dhammārāma. Those who worship me with flowers, incense, and so forth do not truly worship me. Only those who practice the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (the nine supramundane states) truly worship me.” He then spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, that monk Dhammārāma was established in the Fruit of Arahatship. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.
The Story of Elder Dhammārāma ends.
366:
## The Teaching

(365) One should not despise one's own gain, nor live envying others. A monk who envies others does not attain concentration.

(366) Even if a monk receives little, if he does not despise his own gain, the gods surely praise him, who is of pure livelihood and not slothful.

'A monk' means a person who has been ordained. 'One's own gain' refers to the gains that arise for oneself. 'Should not despise' means one should not look down upon or disregard it.

## 5. The Story of the Monk who Associated with the Opposing Side
(Vipakkasevakabhikkhu Vatthu)

While residing at the Veluvana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with 'Salābhaṃ', concerning an obscure monk who used to associate with various factions.

## A Monk of Weak Mind who Easily Follows Others

A certain monk who belonged to Devadatta's faction was said to be a friend of that monk who associated with various groups. That friend, a follower of Devadatta, saw his companion returning after wandering for alms with other monks and having finished his meal, and asked, "Where did you go?"

When the monk replied, "I went to such and such a place to wander for alms," the friend asked again, "Did you receive alms-food?"

When he replied, "Yes, I did," the friend said, "In this place, we have great gains and offerings. Stay here for two or three days."

Following the words of the monk from Devadatta's faction, that monk who was prone to joining any group stayed at Devadatta's place for two or three days before returning to his own monastery. Then, the other monks reported to the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, this monk enjoys the gains and offerings that arise for Devadatta; he is a partisan of Devadatta."

The Teacher had the monk summoned and asked, "Is it true that you did this?"

"Venerable Sir, it is true. I stayed there for two or three days depending on a young monk at Devadatta's place, but I do not favor Devadatta's views," he replied.

## A Brief Mention of the Mahilāmukha Jātaka

Then the Blessed One said to him, "Even if you do not favor his views, you wander about as if you favor the views of whoever you see. You have not done this only now; in the past, you were of the same nature."

When the monks requested, "Venerable Sir, we have seen it ourselves now, but please tell us how he wandered about in the past as if favoring the views of various people," the Blessed One brought forth the past story:

"Listening to the words of former thieves,
Mahilāmukha wandered about striking and killing;
But listening to the words of the well-restrained,
That noble elephant stood firm in all virtues."

After explaining this Mahilāmukha Jātaka in detail, the Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, a monk should be content with his own gains. It is not proper to covet the gains of others. For a monk who covets the gains of others, not even one state among the jhānas, insight, the paths, or the fruits can arise. Only for one who is content with his own gains do jhānas and other states arise." Wishing to teach the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

(365) One should not despise one's own gain, nor live envying others. A monk who envies others does not attain concentration.
367:
(366) Even if a monk receives little, if he does not despise his own gain, the gods surely praise him, who is of pure livelihood and not slothful.

(A monk who abandons the practice of wandering for alms from house to house and makes a living through improper means is said to despise his own gain. It means he loathes and detests it.)

'Others' gain' means the gains of other people. 'Envying' means coveting. 'Should not live' means one should not practice in that way. 'A monk who envies others' gain' means a monk who becomes anxious about the robes and other requisites of others. Such a monk 'does not attain concentration', meaning he does not achieve either access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or fixed concentration (appanā-samādhi).

'If he does not despise his own gain' means even if he receives little, a monk who wanders for alms from house to house in order, regardless of whether the families are high or low, is said to not despise his own gain.

'The gods surely praise him' means the gods truly praise and extol such a monk who is 'of pure livelihood' because his life is meaningful, and who is 'not slothful' because he makes his living by relying on the strength of his legs and is not lazy.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other fruits.

The Story of the Monk who Associated with the Opposing Side ends.

## 6. The Story of the Brahmin Pañcaggadāyaka
(Pañcaggadāyaka Brāhmaṇa Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with 'Sabbaso', concerning a Brahmin named Pañcaggadāyaka (The Giver of Five First-fruits).

## The Brahmin Woman who Lacked Faith in the Buddha

That Brahmin used to give the 'first-fruit of the field' at the time of clearing and harvesting the crop. He gave the 'first-fruit of the threshing floor' at the time of threshing. He gave the 'first-fruit of the granary' at the time of storing the grain. He gave the 'first-fruit of the pot' at the time of cooking in the rice pot. He gave the 'first-fruit of the plate' at the time of serving the rice into the dish. Thus, he was accustomed to giving these five kinds of first-fruits. He never ate without giving to anyone who arrived. Therefore, he became known as 'Pañcaggadāyaka'.

The Teacher, seeing the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the three fruits in both the Brahmin and his wife, went to their house at the Brahmin's mealtime and stood at the door.
368:
Whether from the top, the middle, or the remainder,
He who lives on the gifts of others receives an alms-portion.
He is not given to praise, nor is he a disparager;
Him the wise call a sage.

Regarding the alms-food: whether it be the first portion, the middle portion (the half-remainder), or the final scraps, one should receive it. A person who subsists on the gifts of others should consume that alms-food. There is no benefit in praising it.

One who has the habit of speaking with humility, such a person the wise, such as the Buddhas, make known as a sage. Or, they declare him so.

The Brahmin was eating at the entrance of the house, facing inward. He did not see the Blessed One standing at the door. The Brahmin woman, however, while serving the Brahmin, saw the Blessed One and thought: “This Brahmin eats only after giving the first portion in five places. Now the ascetic Gotama has arrived and is standing at the door. If the Brahmin sees this ascetic Gotama and takes his own food to give to him, I will not be able to cook again.” Thinking “In this way, he will not see the ascetic Gotama,” she stood with her back to the Teacher, concealing him from the Brahmin, stooping down as if covering the full moon with her palm. While standing thus, she glanced at the Teacher with half an eye, wondering, “Has he gone or is he still there?” The Teacher remained standing right there. Fearing the Brahmin might hear, she did not say “Pass on,” but after stepping back, she whispered softly, “Pass on, sir.”

## The Faithful Brahmin

The Buddha shook his head, indicating “I will not go.” When the Teacher, the world-honored Master who is revered by the whole world, shook his head saying “I will not go,” she was unable to contain herself and laughed loudly. At that moment, the Teacher emitted a radiance toward the interior of the house. The Brahmin, even while sitting with his back turned, heard the sound of the woman's laughter and, seeing the brilliance of the six-colored rays, beheld the Teacher.

(Indeed, Buddhas do not depart from a village or a forest without showing themselves to those possessed of the necessary supporting conditions.)
369:
## The Teaching

(367) He who has no sense of 'mine' in name and form in every way,
And who does not grieve over what is non-existent,
He is truly called a bhikkhu.

For whomsoever there is no attachment or clinging in the sense of 'I' or 'mine' regarding all name and form—the five aggregates consisting of the four mental aggregates like feeling and the aggregate of form—he does not grieve even when that name and form reaches destruction and decay. He does not suffer, thinking 'My form is destroyed... my consciousness is destroyed,' but sees it as 'That which is subject to destruction and decay has been destroyed.' Such a person, who is free from the sense of 'mine' even while name and form exist, and who does not grieve when they are gone, is called a bhikkhu.

Upon seeing the Blessed One, the Brahmin said, “Lady, you have ruined me! You have committed a grave deed by not telling me that the Blessed One, the son of King Suddhodana, had arrived and was standing at the door.” Taking the half-eaten bowl of food, he went to the Teacher and said, “O Venerable Gotama, I eat only after giving the first portion in five places. From this food, I have divided it in the middle and eaten only one portion; one portion still remains. Would you please accept this alms-food of mine?”

### Teaching on Being Like a Peta and Accepting Leftovers

The Blessed One did not say, “I have no need for your leftover food,” but instead said, “Brahmin, the first portion is suitable for me; the middle portion, half-eaten and divided, is also suitable for me; and even the last scrap of food is suitable for me. Indeed, Brahmin, we are like the departed (petas) who live on what is given by others.” Having said this, he recited this verse from the Uraga Vagga of the Sutta Nipāta.

As soon as the Brahmin heard those words, his heart was filled with faith. Thinking, “Oh, how wonderful! Although he is a prince, the lord of the island, he did not say 'I have no need for your leftover food,' but spoke in this way,” he asked the Teacher a question while still standing at the door: “Venerable Gotama, you call your disciples 'bhikkhus.' To what extent is one called a bhikkhu?” The Teacher, considering “What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for him?” reflected, “Both these people, in the time of Kassapa Buddha, heard the words of monks speaking about 'name and form' (nāmarūpa). It is appropriate to teach them Dhamma without abandoning the topic of name and form.” He then said, “Brahmin, one who does not lust after or cling to name and form, and who does not grieve, is called a bhikkhu,” and recited this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, both husband and wife were established in the Fruit of Non-Returning (Anāgāmi-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled multitude.

The Story of the Brahmin who gives the Five First Portions ends.

## 7. The Story of Many Monks
(Sambahulabhikkhu Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching, “Mettāvihārī,” concerning many monks.

## The Monk Soṇa Preaching to the Buddha

On one occasion, while the Venerable Mahā Kaccāyana was residing on Mount Pavatta near the city of Kuraraghara in the Avanti country, a lay follower named Soṇa, who was accustomed to wearing ornaments worth ten million, having gained faith in the Elder's Dhamma talk, desired to ordain in the Elder's presence. The Venerable Mahā Kaccāyana said, “Lay follower Soṇa, it is difficult to eat only one meal a day for life...”
370:
Desiring to go forth, he was refused twice by the Elder, who said, “Soṇa, the holy life of eating one meal a day and sleeping alone for a lifetime is difficult.” However, having great zeal for the monkhood, he requested the Elder for the third time and was ordained as a novice. Due to the scarcity of monks in the Southern Region (Dakkhiṇāpatha), he received higher ordination only after three years had passed. Desiring to see the Teacher in person, he asked permission from his preceptor and, taking the message given by him, gradually reached Jetavana. Having paid homage to the Teacher and exchanged greetings, he was granted lodging by the Teacher in the same Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). Having spent much of the night in the open air, he entered the Gandhakuṭi in the later part of the night and spent that portion on the lodging provided for him. At dawn, being invited by the Teacher, he recited all sixteen of the Aṭṭhakavagga suttas in the sarabhañña style. Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, the Blessed One, expressing great appreciation, gave him a “Sādhu” call, saying, “Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!” Hearing the “Sādhu” given by the Teacher, the earth-dwelling deities, nāgas, and supaṇṇas likewise gave “Sādhu” calls up to the Brahma world.

## The Mother of Venerable Soṇa and the House-Guardian Deity
At that moment, in the city of Kuraraghara, a hundred and twenty leagues away from Jetavana, the house-guardian deity in the home of the great laywoman disciple, the mother of the Elder, also gave a “Sādhu” call with a loud voice. Then the laywoman asked the deity, “Who is this giving a Sādhu call?” “Sister, it is I,” the deity replied. “Who are you?” she asked. “I am the deity residing in your house,” it replied. “Previously, you never gave me a Sādhu call; why do you give one today?” she asked. “I am not giving the Sādhu call to you,” the deity replied. “If not, then to whom are you giving it?” she asked. “To your son, the Elder Soṇa Koṭikaṇṇa,” it replied. “What has my son done?” she asked. “Today, your son stayed with the Teacher in the same Gandhakuṭi and preached the Dhamma. Having heard your son’s Dhamma, the Teacher was pleased and gave a Sādhu call. Because of the Blessed One’s Sādhu call, a single Sādhu call has resonated from the earth-dwelling deities up to the Brahma world. Therefore, I too give a Sādhu call to the Elder Soṇa.” When this was said, she asked, “Lord deity, how is it? Did my son preach to the Teacher, or did the Teacher preach to my son?” “Your son preached to the Teacher,” the deity replied. While the deity was speaking thus, fivefold joy (pīti) arose in the laywoman and suffused her entire body. Then the thought occurred to her: “If my son is able to stay with the Teacher in the same Gandhakuṭi and preach the Dhamma to the Teacher, he will surely be able to preach to me as well. When my son arrives, I will organize a Dhamma hearing and listen to his Dhamma talk.”
371:
## Venerable Soṇa’s Request for the Five Allowances
When the Teacher gave the “Sādhu” call, Venerable Soṇa thought, “Now is the time to convey the message given by my preceptor.” He then requested five allowances from the Blessed One, starting with the higher ordination in the border regions by a group of monks with a Vinaya expert as the fifth member. After staying in the presence of the Teacher for a few days, he asked permission, saying, “I will go to see my preceptor,” and leaving Jetavana, he gradually reached the presence of his preceptor.

(He received all five requested allowances. These five are:
1. Because monks are scarce in the border regions, the ability to perform higher ordination with a group of five monks, including a Vinaya expert (whereas ten are required in the Middle Country).
2. Because the ground is rough in the border regions, the ability to wear multi-layered sandals (whereas only single-layered ones are allowed in the Middle Country).
3. Because people in the border regions value bathing, the ability to bathe constantly (whereas in the Middle Country, one may bathe only once every fifteen days).
4. Because people in the border regions use skins as mats, the ability to use sheepskins and deerskins as mats (whereas in the Middle Country, no skins are allowed).
5. For a monk traveling to another place, the ability to perform the Vinaya procedure for a robe within ten days of receiving it. These are the five.)

## Venerable Soṇa’s Mother Organizes a Dhamma Talk
The preceptor, Venerable Mahākaccāyana, on the following morning, took Venerable Soṇa and went for alms, arriving at the door of his mother’s house. Upon seeing her son, the laywoman, with a joyful heart, paid homage and respectfully served him food. She then asked, “Dear son, is it true that you stayed with the Teacher in the same Gandhakuṭi and preached the Dhamma to the Teacher?” When he asked, “Laywoman, who told you this?” she replied, “Son, the house-guardian deity in this house gave a Sādhu call with a loud voice. When I asked who it was, it said ‘It is I,’ and told me such and such. Hearing those words, the thought occurred to me: ‘If my son, Venerable Soṇa, could preach the Dhamma to the Teacher, he will surely be able to preach to his mother as well.’” Then she said to Venerable Soṇa, “Son, since you were able to preach the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, you will surely be able to preach to your mother as well. Son, on such-and-such a day, I will organize a Dhamma hearing and listen to your Dhamma.” The Elder consented. The mother, having given offerings to the Saṅgha, left only one maidservant to guard the house and took her entire retinue to a pavilion built in the city for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. She went to listen to the Dhamma talk of her son, the Elder, who had ascended the decorated Dhamma seat to preach.

At that time, nine hundred thieves were wandering about, looking for an opportunity to break into the laywoman’s house. Her house was surrounded by seven walls and had seven gatehouses. In various places, fierce dogs were tied up. Inside the house, at the place where water falls from the roof, a moat had been dug and filled with lead. During the day, it remained molten and boiling due to the heat of the sun, but at night, it became hard and solid. Next to it, large iron bars were fixed continuously into the ground. Because of this security and because the laywoman remained inside the house, the thieves had found no opportunity. However, knowing that she had gone out that day, they broke through a tunnel...
372:
## Thieves Entering the House During the Dhamma Talk
At that time, nine hundred thieves were wandering around, looking for an opportunity at the house of that great laywoman. Her house was surrounded by seven layers of walls and had seven gates. At each gate and various locations, fierce dogs were tied up. Inside the house, at the place where the eaves dripped, a moat was dug and filled with molten lead. During the day, this lead would melt in the sun's heat and remain as if boiling. At night, it would become hard and rough. Beyond that lead moat, many iron spikes and stakes were planted in the ground without any gaps. Because of such protection and the fact that it was located within the laywoman's compound, the thieves could not find an opportunity. On that day, learning that the laywoman had gone to listen to the Dhamma, they tunneled through and entered the house by going beneath the lead moat and the iron spikes. The chief thief sent a man to the mother of Elder Soṇa, saying, "If that laywoman hears that we have entered this house and turns back toward the house, kill her by striking her with a sword." That chief thief went and stood near the laywoman. Meanwhile, the thieves lit lamps inside the house and opened the door to the coin treasury.

## Scolding the One Who Reported the Thieves
When the maidservant guarding the house saw the thieves, she went to the laywoman and reported, "Mistress, many thieves have entered the house and opened the door to the coin treasury." Then the laywoman called the maid and sent her back, saying, "Let the thieves take whatever coins they see. I shall continue to listen to my son's Dhamma talk. Do not create an obstacle to my hearing the Dhamma. Go back to the house." The thieves emptied the coin treasury and then opened the silver treasury. The maid came again and reported the matter. The laywoman called her and sent her back again, saying, "Let the thieves take whatever they desire. Do not disturb me." The thieves emptied the silver treasury and then opened the gold treasury. The maid went again and reported the matter to the laywoman. Then the laywoman addressed her, "Hey, maid! You have come to me many times. Even though I said, 'Let the thieves take whatever they please, I shall continue to listen to my son's Dhamma talk, do not disturb me,' you do not heed my words and keep coming back repeatedly. If you come back again now, I shall know what to do with you. Just go back to the house."

## The Thieves Apologizing
When the chief thief heard the laywoman's words, he thought, "Thunderbolts should strike and split the heads of those who steal the property of such a woman." He went to the thieves and said, "Quickly return the laywoman's property to its original state." Those thieves refilled the coin treasury with coins, and the silver and gold treasuries with silver and gold. This is indeed the nature of things: the Dhamma protects the one who practices the Dhamma. As it is said:

"The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by the Dhamma;
The Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.
This is the benefit of the Dhamma well-practiced:
The one who lives by the Dhamma does not go to a state of woe."
373:
The thieves also went and stood at the place where the Dhamma was being preached. Elder Soṇa, having preached the Dhamma, descended from the preaching throne as dawn broke. At that moment, the chief thief prostrated at the laywoman's feet and said, "Mistress, please forgive me." When she asked, "Dear son, what is the reason for this apology?" he replied, "I stood there with a grudge against you, wishing to kill you." She replied, "If that is so, son, I forgive you." When the remaining thieves also spoke and apologized in the same manner as the chief thief, and she said, "Sons, I forgive you," the thieves said, "Mistress, if you forgive us, please have your son grant us ordination." She paid respects to her son and said, "Son, these thieves, being inspired by my virtues and your Dhamma talk, are asking for ordination. Please ordain them." The Elder said, "Very well," and had the fringes of their clothes cut off, dyed them with red clay, ordained them, and established them in the precepts. At the time of their higher ordination, he gave each of them a separate meditation subject. Those nine hundred monks took their nine hundred individual meditation subjects, climbed a mountain, and practiced the duties of a recluse while sitting under the shade of various trees.

The Teacher, while sitting in the Jetavana Great Monastery a hundred and twenty leagues away, looked at those monks. Determining a Dhamma teaching suitable for their conduct, he radiated light and, as if sitting right in front of them, spoke these verses:

## The Teaching
(368) The monk who dwells in loving-kindness and has faith in the Buddha's Dispensation will attain the state of peace, the bliss of the stilling of formations.
(369) Empty this boat, O monk! When emptied, it will go lightly for you. Having cut off lust and hatred, you will then go to Nibbāna.
(370) Cut off the five, abandon the five, and further cultivate the five. A monk who has gone beyond the five attachments is called "one who has crossed the flood."
(371) Meditate, O monk! Do not be negligent. Do not let your mind delight in the strands of sensual pleasure. Do not, through negligence, swallow the iron ball and then cry out while burning, "This is suffering!"
(372) There is no meditation for one without wisdom; there is no wisdom for one who does not meditate. In whom there are both meditation and wisdom, he is indeed in the presence of Nibbāna.
(373) For a monk who has entered an empty house, who has a peaceful mind, and who clearly perceives the Dhamma, there is a superhuman delight.
(374) Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates, one attains joy and happiness. That is the Deathless for those who know it.
(375) Here, this is the beginning for a wise monk: guarding the senses, contentment, and restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
(376) Associate with noble friends who are of pure livelihood and are not slothful. One should be friendly in conduct and skilled in behavior. Then, full of joy, one will make an end of suffering.

[Word-by-word gloss of the verses follows:]
Whichever monk dwells in the meditation of loving-kindness and has faith in the Dispensation of the Buddha, that monk will attain Nibbāna, the state of peace which is the stilling of formations and supreme bliss.

O monk, empty this boat of the self by casting out the water of wrong thoughts. Your boat of the self, once the water of wrong thoughts is cast out, will reach Nibbāna quickly. Cut off the fetter of lust and the fetter of hatred. After cutting them and reaching the fruit of Arahantship, you will reach Nibbāna without residue.

For this reason, He spoke this verse:
"The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by the Dhamma;
The Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.
This is the benefit of the Dhamma well-practiced:
The one who lives by the Dhamma does not go to a state of woe."

The thieves went and stood at the place of hearing the Dhamma. Elder Soṇa, having preached the Dhamma, descended from the throne at dawn. At that moment, the chief thief prostrated at the laywoman's feet and said, "Mistress, please forgive me." When she asked, "Dear son, what is the reason for this apology?" he replied, "I stood there with a grudge against you, wishing to kill you." She replied, "If that is so, son, I forgive you." When the remaining thieves also spoke and apologized, she said, "Sons, I forgive you." Then the thieves said, "Mistress—"
374:
"If you would forgive us, we wish to be granted monkhood under your ladyship's son," they said.

## The Ordination of the Nine Hundred Thieves

The mother of the Elder, paying homage to her son, said, "Dear son, these thieves have gained faith in my virtues and in your Dhamma discourse, and they request to become monks. Please ordain them." The Elder replied, "Very well," and had the fringes of their garments cut off and dyed with red earth. He then ordained them as novices (sāmaṇeras) and established them in the precepts. After they became fully ordained monks, he gave each of the nine hundred monks a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) individually. Those nine hundred monks, taking their respective meditation subjects, climbed a mountain and practiced the Dhamma while staying under the shade of various trees. The Buddha, residing at the great Jetavana Monastery one hundred and twenty leagues away, looked upon those monks. Having discerned the appropriate teaching according to their temperaments, He radiated His aura as if He were sitting right before them and preached these verses:

(Just as a boat filled with water in the great ocean, when its leaks are plugged and the water is bailed out, becomes light and can reach the desired port quickly without sinking;)
375:
(...similarly, this body-boat is filled with the water of wrong thoughts. When the leaks such as the eye-door are plugged with restraint and the water of wrong thoughts is bailed out, it becomes light and will quickly reach the haven of Nibbāna without sinking in the round of rebirth.)

Cut the five—the five lower fetters that lead to the lower realms—with the first three paths (magga). Abandon the five—the five higher fetters that lead to the Brahma realms—with the path of Arahantship.

Further, one should develop the five—the five faculties (indriya) such as faith (saddhā). A monk who has transcended the five attachments—greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, and wrong view—is called "one who has crossed the flood," meaning he has crossed the four floods (ogha).

Meditate, O monk! Do not be negligent, being heedless in bodily actions and so forth. Do not let your mind delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. Being negligent, do not swallow the red-hot iron ball. While burning in hell, do not cry out, "This is suffering!"

There is no meditation for one who lacks the wisdom associated with effort that produces meditation. There is no wisdom for one who does not meditate.

In whom there are both meditation and wisdom, that person is indeed in the presence of Nibbāna.

For one who has entered a secluded place and sits without abandoning the meditation subject, with a peaceful mind, and who contemplates the Dhamma with right reason, there arises a superhuman delight—the delight of insight and attainment (samāpatti)—which is not common to householders.

Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the five aggregates, in whatever manner or at whatever preferred time, one gains joy and gladness. For those who know, that joy and gladness is the Deathless Nibbāna itself.

For a wise monk in this Dispensation, these are the beginning: guarding the senses such as the eye, and contentment with the four requisites.
376:
(By this statement, the two virtues of purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla) and virtue concerning the requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla) are taught.)

And there is restraint in the Pātimokkha, the great virtue. This purity of the fourfold virtue is the very beginning, the first step toward attaining Nibbāna or gaining joy and gladness.

Associate with noble friends who are of pure livelihood and are not idle.

One should be friendly in conduct, being endowed with both material hospitality and hospitality of the Dhamma. One should be skilled in conduct, being proficient in both virtue and duties.

Consequently, being full of joy that arises from friendliness and skill in conduct, one shall make an end of all the suffering of the round of rebirth.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

Thus, at the conclusion of each verse among these verses taught by the Blessed One, a hundred monks at a time attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) while remaining in their respective places. All those monks then flew into the air, crossed the difficult journey of one hundred and twenty leagues through the sky, and praised the golden-hued body of the Tathāgata, paying homage at His feet.

The Story of the Many Monks ends.
377:
## The Teaching

(377) Just as the jasmine plant sheds its withered flowers, so, O monks, should you shed passion and hatred.

Vassikā: the jasmine plant. Maddavāni: the withered ones. Pupphāni: old flowers. Pamuñcati viya: just as it sheds from the stalk. Evaṃ: in the same way. Bhikkhavo: O monks. Tumhe: you. Rāgañca: passion as well. Dosañca: and hatred. Vippamuñcetha: should shed.

## 8. The Story of the Five Hundred Monks
(Pañcasatabhikkhu Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Vassikā viya pupphāni," concerning five hundred monks.

## Striving for the Dhamma in Comparison with Flowers

Those five hundred monks, having taken a meditation subject from the Buddha, were practicing the Dhamma of a recluse in the forest. When they saw the jasmine flowers that had bloomed in the early morning falling from their stalks in the evening, they strove with diligence, thinking, "We shall be liberated from passion and other defilements even before you fall from your stalks."

The Buddha, observing those monks, said, "Monks, a monk indeed should strive to be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths, just like a flower that is liberated by falling from its stalk." While remaining in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), he sent forth an aura of light and uttered this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, all those monks were established in Arahantship.

The Story of the Five Hundred Monks ends.

## 9. The Story of Elder Santakāya
(Santakāyatthera Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Santakāyo," concerning the Elder named Santakāya.

## The Monk who was Reborn from a Lion's Existence

That Elder Santakāya was said to have no fidgeting of hands or feet. He possessed a calm physical presence, free from any bodily agitation.

(That Elder was an Elder who came from a lion's existence.)
378:
## The Teaching

(378) Calm in body, calm in speech, calm and well-composed, a monk who has vomited the world's bait is called "one who is at peace."

Santakāyo: one who has a calm body due to the absence of killing and so forth. Santavāco: one who has calm speech due to the absence of lying and so forth. Santavā: one who has a calm mind due to the absence of covetousness and so forth. Susamāhito: one whose body, speech, and mind are well-composed. Vantalokāmiso: one who has vomited the world's bait by means of the four paths. Bhikkhu: a monk. Upasanto: is called a person whose passion and other defilements have been extinguished within.

Lions, having taken their prey for a day, enter one of the silver, gold, or coral caves. They lie down on the surface of red arsenic or yellow orpiment powder for seven days. On the seventh day, they rise and look at the place where they lay. If they see the red arsenic or yellow orpiment powder scattered because of the movement of their tail, ears, or limbs, they think, "This movement is not suitable for you by birth or lineage," and they lie down again for another seven days without food. If the powder is not scattered, they think, "This state of being free from movement is suitable for your lineage." They then emerge from the cave, stand majestically, look towards the cardinal and intermediate directions in order, roar the lion's roar three times, and depart to seek food. This monk was a monk who came from such a lion's existence. Seeing the calm conduct of that monk, the other monks reported to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, we have never before seen a monk like Elder Santakāya. In the place where this Elder Santakāya sits, there is no movement of hands, no movement of feet, and no bodily agitation."

Upon hearing the words of those monks, the Buddha said, "Monks, a monk indeed should be one who is calm in body and so forth, just like Elder Santakāya," and he uttered this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, that Elder Santakāya was established in Arahantship. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of Elder Santakāya ends.

## 10. The Story of Elder Naṅgala
(Naṅgalakulatthera Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Attanā codayattānaṃ," concerning Elder Naṅgala.

## The Rags that Tormented the Future Arahant

A poor man used to earn his living by working for others. A monk, seeing that poor man walking along carrying a plow and wearing a piece of tattered cloth, said, "Is it not better for you to ordain as a monk than to live such a life?"
379:
## The Teaching
(379) Exhort yourself by yourself; examine yourself by yourself. Thus self-guarded and mindful, O bhikkhu, you shall live in happiness.
(380) For self is the lord of self; for self is the refuge of self. Therefore, restrain yourself, as a merchant restrains a noble horse.

Attanā: by oneself. Attānaṃ: oneself. Codaya: exhort and reproach. Attanā: by oneself. Attānaṃ: oneself. Paṭimaṃsetha: should examine. Bhikkhu: O monk. Evaṃ: when this is done. So tvaṃ: you. Attagutto: being guarded by yourself. Satimā: being possessed of established mindfulness. Sukhaṃ: happily. Vihāhisi: shall live.

Attā hi: for self alone. Attano: of self. Nātho: is the support, the foundation, the refuge. Hoti: it is so. Ko hi: who indeed. Paro: another person. Attano: of self. Nātho: refuge. Siyā: could possibly be? Attā hi: for self alone. Attano: of self. Gati: is the destination, the foundation, the refuge. Tasmā: therefore. Vāṇijo: as a horse-trader. Bhadraṃ: a good. Assaṃ: noble horse. Saṃyamati iva: just as he carefully tends and restrains it. Evaṃ: in the same way. Attānaṃ: oneself. Saṃyama: carefully guard and restrain, giving no opportunity for unwholesome states to arise.

When he pleaded, "Venerable Sir, who would want to ordain me, who lives in such poverty and hardship?", the Elder replied, "If you wish to be ordained, I will ordain you." He then said, "Very well, Venerable Sir, if you will ordain me, I shall become a monk." Thereupon, the Elder took the poor man to Jetavana Monastery, bathed him with his own hands, placed him in the pavilion (māḷaka) or enclosure, and ordained him. He then had the plow and the worn-out cloth the man had been wearing hung on a tree branch right there at the boundary of the pavilion. Even after his higher ordination, he was known simply as Nangala Thera (the Plow Elder). While living on the gains and offerings made to the Buddha, Nangala Thera became weary and dissatisfied. Unable to dispel his discontent, he thought, "I will no longer go about wearing these robes given out of faith; I shall return to lay life." He went to the foot of that tree and scolded himself: "You shameless one, you impudent fellow! Do you want to wear this worn-out cloth again, return to lay life, and live by manual labor?" While he was thus scolding himself, his mind became refined. He returned, but after two or three days, he became dissatisfied again and scolded himself just as before. Again, his mind settled. In this manner, whenever dissatisfaction arose, he would go to the tree where the worn-out cloth and plow were kept and scold himself.

## Nangala Thera Becomes an Arahant
Seeing him going to that place frequently, the monks asked, "Friend Nangala Thera, why do you go there?" Nangala Thera replied, "Venerable sirs, I am going to my teacher." Within just a few days, he attained Arahantship.
380:
The monks teased Nangala Thera, saying, "Friend Nangala Thera, the path you used to travel seems neglected now. We suppose you no longer go to your teacher?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, it is true that I do not go. I used to go when there was an attachment. Now, that attachment is severed for me; therefore, I go no more." Hearing this, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, saying, "This monk Nangala is speaking what is not true and is claiming the fruit of Arahantship." The Buddha said, "Monks, it is true. My son Nangala has reached the end of the monk's task by reproaching himself." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the discourse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other fruits.
The story of Nangala Thera ends.

## 11. The Story of Vakkali Thera
(Vakkaliတ္ထေရဝတ္ထု)
The Buddha, while staying at Veḷuvana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Pāmojjabahulo," concerning the Elder Vakkali.

## Vakkali Thera, Excessive in Faith
That Venerable Vakkali was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī. When he came of age, he saw the Buddha entering the city for alms. Having gazed upon the perfection and beauty of the Buddha's physical body, he could not get enough of it. He thought, "In this way, I shall always be able to see the Buddha," and so he ordained in the presence of the Buddha. He spent his time following the Buddha to gaze at him, staying wherever he could see the Possessor of Ten Powers, and neglecting his duties of recitation, meditation, and reflection. The Buddha, waiting for Vakkali's knowledge to mature, said nothing at first. When he knew that Vakkali's knowledge had reached maturity, he said, "Vakkali, what is the use of your gazing at this foul body? Vakkali, he who truly sees the Dhamma sees me."
381:
## The Teaching

(381) Pāmojjabahulo bhikkhu, pasanno buddhasāsane.
Adhigacche padaṃ santaṃ, saṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukhaṃ.

Pāmojjabahulo: having much joy and gladness. Buddhasāsane: in the Dispensation of the Buddha. Pasanno: one who has faith and delight. Bhikkhu: a monk. Saṅkhārūpasamaṃ: which is the stilling of formations. Sukhaṃ: the pinnacle of bliss. Santaṃ: peaceful. Padaṃ: Nibbāna. Adhigacche: should attain.

"He truly sees me. He who does not see the Dhamma does not see me," he said while giving advice. Even though he was thus advised, the monk Vakkali was unable to give up seeing the Buddha and go elsewhere.

## Dismissing Elder Vakkali

Then, the Buddha, thinking, "This monk will not attain liberation without experiencing spiritual urgency," as the time for the rains retreat approached, went to Rājagaha. On the day of entering the retreat, he dismissed him, saying, "Go away, Vakkali; go away, Vakkali." That monk Vakkali thought, "The Buddha does not even speak to me; therefore, I cannot stay in the Buddha's presence for these three months. What is the use of my life? I will throw myself off the mountain." He then climbed Gijjhakūṭa Mountain. The Buddha, knowing the Elder Vakkali's mental distress, thought, "If this monk does not find relief in my presence, he might destroy his supporting conditions for the Paths and Fruits." Thus, he emitted a radiance to show himself. At that moment, from the time he saw the Buddha, Vakkali's great sorrow was dispelled. Just as one fills a dried-up pond with a stream of water, the Buddha, in order to arouse strong joy and gladness in Elder Vakkali, spoke this verse:

Elder Vakkali Becoming an Arahant

After speaking this verse, the Buddha stretched out his hand to Elder Vakkali and spoke these verses:

Ehi Vakkali mā bhāyi, olokehi tathāgataṃ.
Ahaṃ taṃ uddharissāmi, paṅke sannaṃva kuñjaraṃ.

Ehi Vakkali mā bhāyi, olokehi tathāgataṃ.
Ahaṃ taṃ mocayissāmi, rāhuggahaṃva sūriyaṃ.

Ehi Vakkali mā bhāyi, olokehi tathāgataṃ.
Ahaṃ taṃ mocayissāmi, rāhuggahaṃva candimaṃ.

Vakkali, dear Vakkali. Ehi: come. Mā bhāyi: do not fear. Tathāgataṃ: the Buddha, who has come like the previous Buddhas. Olokehi: look upon me. Ahaṃ: I. Taṃ: you. Paṅke: in the mud. Sannaṃ: sunk. Kuñjaraṃ iva: like a great elephant. Uddharissāmi: shall lift you up from the mud of defilements.

Vakkali, dear Vakkali. Ehi: come. Mā bhāyi: do not fear. Tathāgataṃ: the Buddha, who has come like the previous Buddhas. Olokehi: look upon me. Ahaṃ: I. Taṃ: you. Rāhuggahaṃ: seized by Rahu. Sūriyaṃ iva: like the sun. Mocayissāmi: shall set you free from the grasp of defilements.

Vakkali, dear Vakkali. Ehi: come. Mā bhāyi: do not fear. Tathāgataṃ: the Buddha, who has come like the previous Buddhas. Olokehi: look upon me. Ahaṃ: I. Taṃ: you. Rāhuggahaṃ: seized by Rahu. Candimaṃ iva: like the moon. Mocayissāmi: shall set you free from the grasp of defilements.

He spoke these verses. Elder Vakkali, thinking, "I have seen the One of Ten Powers, and I have even received the call 'Come!'" aroused great joy. Not seeing a path to walk, he leaped into the air towards the presence of the One of Ten Powers. While his first foot was still poised on the mountain peak, he reflected on the verse taught by the Buddha. While still in the air, he suppressed his joy and reached Arahantship together with the four analytical insights. He then descended while paying homage to the Buddha and stood in the Buddha's presence.
382:
Afterward, the Buddha placed Elder Vakkali in the foremost position among those resolved through faith (Saddhādhimutta).

(The Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya states that while others must be encouraged to increase their faith, this Elder's faith could not be diminished; thus, he received the title of foremost in faith.)

The Story of Elder Vakkali ends.

## 12. The Story of Sumana Sāmaṇera

(Sumana Sāmaṇera Vatthu)

The Buddha, while residing at the Pubbārāma monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yo have," concerning Sumana Sāmaṇera.

## The Aspiration and Meritorious Deed of the Future Elder Anuruddha

(In this story, the following is the chronological account.)

In the time of Padumuttara Buddha, a certain clansman saw the Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost position among those possessing the Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu) in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Desiring that attainment, he invited the Buddha and for seven days gave a great offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. He made an aspiration, saying, "Venerable Sir, may I also become the foremost among those possessing the Divine Eye in the Dispensation of a future Buddha." Padumuttara Buddha, looking 100,000 aeons into the future and seeing that the clansman's aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied: "One hundred thousand aeons from now, in the Dispensation of Gotama Buddha, you will become the Elder named Anuruddha, foremost among those possessing the Divine Eye." Hearing this prophecy, the clansman felt as if he would reach that attainment the very next day. After the Buddha's Parinibbāna, he asked the monks about the preliminary practices for the Divine Eye. He surrounded a golden stupa seven leagues high with thousands of lamp-stands and performed an offering of lights.

## The Offering of the Poor Man Annabhāra

After performing the offering of lights, when he passed away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. After wandering through the celestial and human realms for 100,000 aeons, in this Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), he was born into a poor family in Bārāṇasī. Depending on the merchant Sumana, he earned his living as a grass-cutter. His name was Annabhāra. The merchant Sumana also constantly gave great offerings in that city of Bārāṇasī. One day, a Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha emerged from the attainment of cessation (Nirodha-samāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana. Thinking, "Whom shall I bless today?" he realized, "Today, it is proper for me to bless the poor man Annabhāra. Right now, he will be returning home from the forest carrying grass." Taking his bowl and robes, he traveled by psychic power and stood directly in front of Annabhāra.
383:
When Annabhāra saw the Paccekabuddha standing with an empty bowl, he asked, "Venerable sir, did you receive alms?" When the Paccekabuddha replied, "O man of great merit, we shall receive," Annabhāra said, "In that case, venerable sir, please wait a moment." He then dropped his bundle of grass and ran quickly to his house. He asked his wife, "Dear, is there the portion of rice kept for me, or is there not?" When she replied, "My lord, it is there," he returned quickly, took the Paccekabuddha's bowl, and thought to himself: "When I had the desire to give, I had no gift to offer; when I had a gift to offer, I could not find a recipient. Today, however, I have found a recipient and I also have a gift. What a great gain it is for me!"

## The Aspiration: "May I Never Hear the Word 'There is None'"

Thinking thus, he went to his house, had the rice placed in the bowl, brought it back, and placed it in the hands of the Paccekabuddha, making this aspiration:

Iminā pana dānena, mā me dāliddiyaṃ ahu.
Natthīti vacanaṃ nāma, mā ahosi bhavābhave.

"Venerable sir, by the power of this volition of offering alms: In whatever existence I am born, may I never be born into a poor family. May the word 'there is none' (natthi) never exist for me."

He continued his prayer: "Venerable sir, may I be liberated from such a difficult and painful livelihood. May I be one who never even hears the word 'there is none'."

## The Deity's Approval of the Poor Man's Gift

The Paccekabuddha said, "O man of great merit, may it be as you have aspired," and after performing the rejoicing (anumodanā), he departed. At that time, the deity residing in the parasol of Sumana the Treasurer, exclaimed:

Aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ, upariṭṭhesu supaṭiṭṭhitaṃ.

"Oh, what a gift! A supreme gift! It is well-established in the Great Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha!"

Saying this, the deity gave a shout of approval (sādhu) three times. Then the Treasurer asked the deity, "Why have you not seen me giving alms for such a long time?" The deity replied, "I did not give the shout of approval regarding your gift. However, because I was so pleased with the alms-food given by the poor man Annabhāra to the Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha, I uttered this shout of approval." Upon hearing this, Sumana the Treasurer thought, "How wonderful! Although I have been giving alms for so long, I could not make the deity give a shout of approval. Yet Annabhāra, who lives depending on me, has made the deity give a shout of approval with just a single offering of alms-food. I shall make that alms-food mine by doing what is appropriate for his gift." He then summoned Annabhāra and asked, "Did you give anything to anyone today?" Annabhāra replied, "Yes, my lord. I gave my portion of rice for today to the Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha." The Treasurer said, "Come, friend, take these kahāpaṇas and give that alms-food to me." Annabhāra replied, "I cannot give it, my lord." The Treasurer increased the offer up to a thousand kahāpaṇas, but Annabhāra would not give it even for a thousand. Then the Treasurer said, "Friend, let it be so. If you cannot give the alms-food, then take the thousand kahāpaṇas and give me the share of the merit (patti) of that gift." Annabhāra replied, "I will consult with the venerable one and let you know." He then ran quickly and caught up with the Paccekabuddha, asking, "Venerable sir, Sumana the Treasurer offers a thousand kahāpaṇas and asks for the share of merit from the alms-food given to you. What should I do, sir?"
384:
The Paccekabuddha then gave a simile to Annabhāra: "Wise man, suppose in a village of a hundred families, a lamp is lit in one house. If the rest of the people come with their own oil and wicks, light them from that lamp, and take them away, would the light of the first lamp be said to still exist or not?" Annabhāra replied, "Venerable sir, the light would become even brighter." The Paccekabuddha said, "In the same way, wise man, whether it be a single ladle of gruel or a single spoonful of rice, when one gives a share of the merit of one's own alms-food to others, the merit increases by as many people as one gives it to. You gave only one portion of alms-food, but by giving a share to the Treasurer, there are now two portions of alms-food—one for you and one for him."

## The Treasurer Gives a Thousand and Shouts Sādhu

Annabhāra said, "Very well, venerable sir," and after paying homage to the Paccekabuddha, he went to the Treasurer and said, "My lord, please take the share of the merit." The Treasurer said, "In that case, take these kahāpaṇas." Annabhāra replied, "I am not selling the alms-food; I give the share of merit to you, my lord, out of faith." The Treasurer said, "You give out of faith, and I, too, honor your virtues. Take this, dear man. From this day forward, do not work with your own hands. Build a house on the main street and live there. Whatever you need, take it all from me."

Alms-food given to a Paccekabuddha who has just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) yields its fruit on that very day. Therefore, when the King heard of this event, he summoned Annabhāra, took a share of the merit, gave him great wealth and possessions, and appointed him to the position of a Treasurer.

## Rebirth as Prince Anuruddha

That Treasurer Annabhāra became a friend of Sumana the Treasurer and performed meritorious deeds throughout his life. After passing away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. After wandering through the realms of gods and humans, during the time of our Buddha's appearance, he took conception in the house of Amitodana the Sakyan in the city of Kapilavatthu. After ten months, his mother gave birth to him. They named the boy Anuruddha. Prince Anuruddha was the younger brother of Prince Mahānāma and the son of the Buddha's paternal uncle. He was extremely delicate and possessed great merit. One day, while the six princes were playing with marbles and wagering cakes, Anuruddha lost and sent a message to his mother for cakes. His mother filled a large golden tray with cakes and sent them. After eating the cakes, he played again, lost again, and sent for more in the same way. Thus, cakes were brought three times. On the fourth occasion, his mother sent word, "Now, there are no cakes (natthi pūva)." Having never heard the word "natthi" (there is none) before, he perceived it as a name and thought, "There must be cakes called 'Natthi-pūva' now." He then sent a message saying, "Go and bring the 'Natthi-pūva' cakes."
385:
## Not Understanding the Word "None"
Upon hearing his mother's words, because he had never heard the word "none" before, he formed the perception that "none-cakes will now appear," and sent a message saying, "Go, bring the none-cakes."

Then, when Prince Anuruddha's mother was told, "Lady, please give the none-cakes," she thought, "My son has never heard the word 'none' before. How can I make him understand the state of 'none'?" Having thought this, she washed a golden bowl, covered it with another golden bowl, and sent it, saying, "Dear, now give this golden bowl to my son."

At that moment, the deities guarding the city thought, "Our master, when he was the poor man Annabhāra, gave his own portion of food to the Paccekabuddha named Uparittha and made a wish: 'May I never hear the word "none".' If we, knowing this, were to remain indifferent, our heads would split into seven pieces." Thinking thus, they filled the golden bowl with divine cakes.

That servant took the golden bowl, placed it near the prince, and opened it. The fragrance of those cakes permeated the entire city. As soon as a piece of cake was placed in his mouth, the flavor pervaded the seven thousand nerves of taste and remained there.

## Always Consuming "None-Cakes"
Prince Anuruddha thought, "It seems my mother did not love me before today. At other times, she never prepared such 'none-cakes' for me." Having thought this, Prince Anuruddha went to his mother and said, "Mother, do you not love your son?"

When she replied, "Dear, what are you saying? You are dearer to me than my own eyes and the flesh of my heart," he said, "Mother, if you truly love your son, why did you not give me such 'none-cakes' before?"

The mother asked the servant, "Dear, was there anything in the bowl?" He replied, "Yes, Lady, the bowl was full of cakes. I have never seen such cakes before."

Prince Anuruddha's mother reflected, "My son is one who has performed meritorious prayers; the deities must have sent divine cakes to my son Anuruddha." Prince Anuruddha also said to his mother, "Mother, I have never eaten such cakes before. From this day forward, please send only 'none-cakes' for me."

From that day on, whenever Prince Anuruddha said he wished to eat cakes, his mother would wash a golden bowl, cover it with another, and send it. The deities would fill that bowl. In this way, while living in the midst of the household life, Prince Anuruddha did not know the meaning of the word "none" and consumed only divine cakes.

## Three Princes, Three Perspectives
When the Sakyan princes were ordaining in succession to form an entourage for the Blessed One, the Sakyan king named Mahānāma said:
386:
The three of them—Anuruddha, Bhaddiya, and Kimbila—discussed, "Where does food originate?" Among them, Kimbila said, "It originates in the granaries." This was because one day he had seen grain being poured into a granary; therefore, with the perception that "food arises in the granary," he spoke thus.

Then Bhaddiya said to him, "You do not know," and added, "Food originates in the cooking pot." This was because one day he had seen food being served from a cooking pot, and he formed the perception that "it arises right there"; therefore, he spoke thus.

Anuruddha said to both of them, "Both of you do not know," and said, "Food originates in a large golden bowl placed inside a pedestal tray about a cubit high." This was because he had never seen rice being threshed nor food being cooked; he only saw the food already served in a golden bowl and placed before him. Therefore, he formed the perception that "it arises only in the bowl"; thus, he spoke in that way.

## The Ordination of Prince Anuruddha
How could this son of a noble family, possessing such great merit that he did not even know the origin of food, know about various types of work? Therefore, Prince Mahānāma said, "Brother Anuruddha, come, I shall instruct you on how to live the household life. First, the field must be ploughed."

[The text continues with Mahānāma explaining the endless cycle of farm work.] Having heard about the endless nature of the work described by his brother, Anuruddha said, "I have no need for the household life." He asked his mother for permission and, together with five other Sakyan princes led by Bhaddiya, went forth. He approached the Teacher at the Anupiya Mango Grove and ordained.

After ordaining, he practiced the right path and, in due course, realized the Threefold Knowledge (tevijjā). While sitting in a single seat, he became capable of surveying the thousandfold world system with his Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu) as if looking at myrobalan fruits placed in the palm of his hand. He then uttered this inspired utterance:

"I know my former lives, the divine eye is purified,
I am a possessor of the threefold knowledge, attained in psychic power; I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching."

Reflecting on what deed led to this attainment, he realized, "I made the aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara." Further reflecting, he knew, "While wandering in saṃsāra, at a certain time in Bārāṇasī, I lived depending on the treasurer Sumana and was known as Annabhāra."

"In the past, I was Annabhāra, a poor grass-cutter;
I gave an alms-offering to the such-like Uparittha."
387:
When he heard from his elder brother in this manner about the never-ending nature of household duties and tasks, he reflected, “I have no need for living in the household life.” Having asked permission from his mother, he departed together with the five Sakyan princes, led by Bhaddiya. Approaching the Blessed One at the mango grove named Anupiya, he was ordained. After ordaining, by practicing the good conduct, he gradually realized the three knowledges (tevijjā). Being able to see a thousand world systems with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) while sitting in a single place, as if looking at myrobalan fruits placed in the palm of his hand, he uttered this verse.

Having joyfully uttered this inspired solemn utterance (udāna), he reflected, “Due to what merit performed in the past have I attained such fulfillment?” He then knew, “I have made an aspiration at the feet of Padumuttara Buddha.” Furthermore, he knew that while wandering through the cycle of rebirths (saṃsāra), at a time of such a name, he had been a grass-cutter named Annabhāra in the city of Bārāṇasī, who lived depending on the great merchant Sumana. He then recited this verse.

## Journeying to Favor Sumana

At that time, this thought occurred to the Venerable Anuruddha: “There was my friend, the great merchant Sumana, who gave kahāpaṇas and took a share of the merit from the alms-food I gave to the Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha. Where might that Sumana Seṭṭhī be reborn now?” Then he saw him: “In the Vindhya forest (Vañjhāṭavi), at the foot of a mountain, there is a market town named Muṇḍa. There, a lay devotee named Mahāmuṇḍa has two sons, Mahāsumana and Cūḷasumana. Among them, he has been reborn as Cūḷasumana.” Having seen this, he considered, “If I go there, will it be beneficial or not?” As the Venerable Anuruddha investigated, he saw this: “If I go there, Cūḷasumana will depart from the household life and ordain as a novice at only seven years of age; and at the very end of the shaving of his hair (khuragge), he will reach Arahantship.” Having seen this, as the time for the Rains Retreat (Vassa) drew near, he traveled through the air and descended at the village gate. The lay devotee named Mahāmuṇḍa was an old acquaintance of the Elder. Seeing the Elder putting on his robe at the time for alms-round, he said to his son Mahāsumana, “Dear son, my master, the Venerable Anuruddha, has arrived. Go and take the Elder’s bowl before anyone else does. I will prepare the seat.” Mahāsumana did as he was told.

## Cūḷasumana’s Ordination and Attainment of Arahantship

The lay devotee named Muṇḍa, having respectfully served the Venerable Anuruddha with alms-food inside the house, received a promise from him to stay for the three months of the Rains Retreat. The Elder accepted. Then, having looked after the Elder for the three months as if he were looking after him for a single day, on the day of the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā) at the end of the retreat, he brought three robes, as well as molasses, oil, rice, and so on, and placing them at the feet of the Elder, said, “Venerable Sir, please accept these.” “Enough, lay devotee, I have no need for this rice and such,” the Elder replied. “In that case, Venerable Sir, this is what is called the gain of the Rains-residence; please accept it,” he requested again. “I will not accept it, lay devotee.” “Venerable Sir, why do you not accept it?” “I have neither a lay-steward (kappiyakāraka) nor a novice (sāmaṇera) with me.” “In that case, Venerable Sir, my son named Mahāsumana will become a novice.” “Lay devotee, I have no need for Mahāsumana.” “In that case, Venerable Sir, please ordain the young boy named Cūḷasumana.” The Elder consented, saying “Very well,” and ordained Cūḷasumana. At the very end of the shaving of his hair with the razor, Cūḷasumana reached Arahantship.

## Taking Sumana Sāmaṇera to the Himalayas

The Venerable Anuruddha stayed there in that market town of Muṇḍa with the novice Sumana for about half a month. Then, saying “I will go to see the Teacher,” he asked permission from the novice’s relatives and, traveling only through the air, descended at a forest hut in the Himalayan region. The Venerable Anuruddha was by nature one who had aroused energy. While he was walking to and fro (caṅkamana) in that forest hut during the first and last watches of the night, a stomach ailment (wind in the stomach) arose. Seeing him looking exhausted, the novice asked, “Venerable Sir, what is hurting you?” “Novice, I have wind in the stomach...”
388:
"Listen to me, O Naga King, of great power and mighty prowess. Give me a jar of drinking water; I have come for the sake of medicine."

O Naga King, of great power and mighty prowess, listen to my words. I have come for the sake of medicine. Please give me a jar of drinking water.

"In the eastern direction, the great river named Ganges flows into the great ocean; from there you should take water."

In the eastern direction, the great river named Ganges flows into the great ocean. From that Ganges river, you should take water.

"From here alone shall I take the water; it is this very water I need. If you have strength and power, O Naga King, then prevent me."

From this very Anotatta Lake alone shall I take the water. It is only this Anotatta water that I desire. O Naga King, if you have strength and power, then try to stop me.

"Novice, if you have the prowess of a great man, I welcome your words; take my water."

O novice, if you have the prowess performed by great men, I welcome your words. Take my water.

The wind ailment in the stomach of the venerable Anuruddha, who was accustomed to walking in meditation throughout the last watch of the night, arose. Then, seeing the venerable Anuruddha in a state of exhaustion, Sumana Sāmaṇera asked, "Venerable sir, what kind of pain do you have?" When he replied, "The wind in my stomach has arisen," the novice asked, "Venerable sir, has it ever arisen before?" "Yes, novice," he replied. "Venerable sir, by what medicine will there be relief?" he asked. "Novice, if I obtain drinking water from Lake Anotatta, there will be relief," he said. "Venerable sir, if relief comes from that Anotatta water, I shall fetch it," he said. "Novice, will you be able to fetch it?" he asked. "Venerable sir, I can," he replied.

## Venerable Anuruddha's Wind Ailment and the Request for Water from Lake Anotatta

"If that is so, the Naga King named Pannaga in Lake Anotatta knows me. Inform that Naga King and fetch a jar of drinking water for the sake of medicine," he said. Sumana Sāmaṇera, saying "Very well, venerable sir," paid homage to his preceptor, rose into the air, and traveled to the place five hundred yojanas away. On that day, the Naga King, surrounded by a multitude of Naga dancers, desired to play in the water. As soon as he saw the novice coming, he became angry. "This shaveling ascetic wanders about scattering the dust from his feet upon my head. He must be coming for drinking water from Lake Anotatta. I will not give him water now," he thought. He then lay down, covering the fifty-yojana great Lake Anotatta with his hood, like covering a rice pot with a large lid. The novice, observing the Naga King's behavior and knowing "This Naga King is angry," spoke this verse:

## The Naga King Who Did Not Wish to Give Water

Hearing those words, the Naga King spoke this verse:

Hearing those words, the novice thought, "This Naga King will not give it of his own will. I shall take the water only after overpowering this Naga King by force and making my power known." He said, "Great Naga King, my preceptor, Venerable Anuruddha, has sent me to fetch water only from Lake Anotatta. Therefore, I shall take it only from this Lake Anotatta. Move aside; do not hinder me," and the novice spoke this verse:

Then the Naga King said this to Sumana Sāmaṇera:
389:
"Listen to me, O Naga King, of great power and mighty prowess. Give me a jar of drinking water; I have come for the sake of medicine."

O Naga King, of great power and mighty prowess, listen to my words. I have come for the sake of medicine. Please give me a jar of drinking water.

## The Gathering of Devas and Brahmas to Witness the Battle

Then the novice said to the Naga King, "Great Naga King, very well, I shall take it." When the Naga said, "If you are able, then take it," the novice replied, "In that case, know it well," and after taking the Naga's promise three times, he thought, "I should fetch the water while demonstrating the power and majesty of the Buddha's Dispensation." He then went to the presence of the deities dwelling in the sky. The sky-dwelling deities came, paid homage, and stood there asking, "Venerable sir, what is the matter?" He said, "A battle will take place between me and the Naga King named Pannaga on the surface of Lake Anotatta. Go there and witness the victory and defeat." In this manner, Sumana Sāmaṇera approached the Four Great Kings, and then Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Nimmānarati, and Paranimmitavasavatti, and informed them of the matter. After that, he went successively as far as the Brahma world. There, the Brahma kings came, paid homage, and stood there asking, "Venerable sir, what is the matter?" and he informed them. Thus, Sumana Sāmaṇera traveled and informed everyone in an instant, excluding only the Asaññasatta and Arūpa Brahmas. Hearing the words of Sumana Sāmaṇera, all the deities gathered, filling the sky without any gap, like sesame powder packed in a tube, over the surface of Lake Anotatta.

## The Battle Between the Novice and the Naga King

When the host of Devas and Brahmas had gathered, the novice, standing in the air, said to the Naga King:

Then the Naga King said this to Sumana Sāmaṇera:

"Novice, if you have the prowess of a great man, I welcome your words; take my water."

O novice, if you have the prowess performed by great men, I welcome your words. Take my water.

Sumana Sāmaṇera, having taken the Naga King's promise three times, while still standing in the air, created a Brahma-body twelve yojanas in size. Descending from the sky, he stepped on the Naga King's hood and pressed it down so that it faced downwards. At that very moment, just by being stepped upon, the Naga King's hood flattened out like wet leather stepped on by a strong man, and the hood-bulges became only the size of ladles.

## The Naga King, Ashamed, Pursues to Kill

From the places released by the Naga King's hoods, jets of water as large as palm trunks gushed up. Sumana Sāmaṇera filled his water jar while still in the air. The host of Devas and Brahmas gave a cry of applause. Then the Naga King, being greatly ashamed and becoming angry at the novice, his eyes turned red like the color of hibiscus flowers...
390:
The Naga king named Pannaka was ashamed and became angry at the novice, and his eyes became the color of Jayakusuma flowers. He thought, “This novice has shamed me by gathering the assembly of devas and taking the water. I will seize him, thrust my hand into his mouth, and crush his heart; or I will seize him by his feet and hurl him to the other side of the Gaṅgā.” He pursued him with great speed. Even though he pursued him, he was unable to catch the novice. The novice went and placed the water in the hand of his preceptor and said, “Please drink, Bhante.” The Naga king also arrived from behind and said, “Venerable Anuruddha, the novice has brought this water without it being given by me; do not drink it.” He asked, “Novice, is it true as this Naga says?” The novice replied, “Please drink, Bhante; I have brought the water given to me by this Naga king.”

## The Naga and the Novice Become Friends
Venerable Anuruddha, knowing that for an Arahant novice there is no such thing as telling a lie, drank the water. At that very moment, his illness was appeased.
