Again, the Naga king said to the Elder, “Bhante, the novice has shamed me by gathering the entire assembly of devas. I wish to either split his heart or seize him by his feet and hurl him to the other side of the Gaṅgā.” The Elder said, “Great Naga king, the novice possesses great power. You will not be able to wage war against the novice. Go and ask for his forgiveness.”

(The Naga king himself also knew the power of the novice, but he had pursued him only because he was so ashamed.)

Then, at the word of Venerable Anuruddha, he asked the novice for forgiveness and established a friendship with him, saying, “From this day forward, if there is a need for water from Lake Anotatta, there is no need for you to come yourself. Please send word to me; I myself will bring it and offer it.” Having said this, he departed.

## Teasing Sumana Sāmaṇera
Venerable Anuruddha then took the novice and set out. The Teacher, knowing the Elder's coming, sat looking out for the Elder's arrival at the mansion of Visākhā, Migāra’s mother. When the monks saw Venerable Anuruddha arriving, they went out to meet him and received his bowl and robes. At that time, some young monks and novices took the novice by the head, ears, and arms, shaking him and teasingly saying, “Little brother novice, are you not bored or weary?” When the Blessed One saw the behavior of those young monks and novices, He thought, “The action of these monks is indeed grave. They are seizing the novice as if they were seizing a swift poisonous snake by the neck. They do not know his power. Today, it is proper for me to make the virtues of Sumana Sāmaṇera manifest.” Venerable Anuruddha arrived, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down. After the Blessed One had exchanged pleasantries with Venerable Anuruddha, He informed Venerable Ānanda.

He informed him thus: “Ānanda, I wish to wash my feet with water from Lake Anotatta. Give the jars to the novices and have them fetch the water.”

## The Five Hundred Novices Unable to Fetch Water
Venerable Ānanda gathered the five hundred novices who were at the Pubbārāma monastery.
391:
(Among those five hundred novices, Sumana Sāmaṇera was the youngest of all.)

Venerable Ānanda said to the eldest of all the novices, “Novice, the Blessed One wishes to wash His feet with water from Lake Anotatta. Take a jar, go, and fetch the water.” The eldest novice replied, “Bhante, I am unable,” and did not wish to go. Venerable Ānanda asked the remaining novices in order. They too refused in the same manner.

(If one asks, “Were there no Arahant novices among these five hundred?” the answer is: there were. However, those Arahant novices did not wish to go, knowing, “This bundle of flowers (task) was not tied for our sake, but was tied only for the sake of Sumana Sāmaṇera.” The worldling novices did not wish to go simply because of their own inability.)

Finally, when it reached Sumana Sāmaṇera’s turn, the Elder said, “Novice, the Blessed One wishes to wash His feet with water from Lake Anotatta. It is said you must take a jar and fetch the water.”

## Sumana Sāmaṇera Goes to Fetch Water
Sumana Sāmaṇera replied, “If the Blessed One has me fetch it, I shall fetch it, Bhante.” He paid homage to the Blessed One and asked, “Blessed One, is it true that I am to fetch water from Lake Anotatta?” “Yes, Sumana,” He replied. Then Sumana Sāmaṇera took one of the large jars—made of solid gold and donated by the lay devotee Visākhā—which was used in the monastery and could hold the water of sixty ordinary jars. Thinking, “I have no need to lift this large jar and place it on my shoulder,” he held it by the rim, letting it hang down, and then rose into the air and flew towards the Himalayas. When the Naga king saw Sumana Sāmaṇera coming from afar, he went to meet him, took the jar on his shoulder, and said, “Bhante, while a servant like me exists, why have you come yourself? If there was a need for water, why did you not even send a message?” Having filled the jar with water and lifting it himself, he said, “Bhante, please go ahead; I myself will carry and deliver it.” Sumana Sāmaṇera replied, “Great Naga king, please stay. The Blessed One commanded only me.” Having turned the Naga king back, he held the jar by the rim with his hand and returned through the air. Then the Teacher, seeing Sumana Sāmaṇera coming, addressed the monks: “Look, monks, at the grace of the novice; he shines in the sky like a king of swans.”

He then placed the water jar down, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood there. Then the Teacher asked him, “How many years old are you, Sumana?” “I am seven years old, Bhante.” “If that is so, Sumana, from today onwards, be a monk (bhikkhu),” and saying this, He granted him the inheritance ordination (upasampadā).
392:
## The Teaching

(382) Indeed, the young monk who strives in the Buddha's teaching illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.

Even if young; that monk who indeed strives with diligence in my Buddha's teaching. That monk can illuminate this world of the aggregates (khandhas) and so forth, like the moon freed from a cloud.

## Inheriting the Status of a Monk at the Age of Seven

That Sumana Sāmaṇera, having set down the water pot, remained paying homage to the Blessed One. Then, the Blessed One said to Sumana Sāmaṇera, "Dear Sumana, how old are you?" When he replied, "Venerable Sir, I am seven years old," the Buddha granted him the inheritance of higher ordination (upasampadā), saying, "Dear Sumana Sāmaṇera, if that is so, from this day forth, be a monk."

(Only these two novices, Sumana Sāmaṇera and Sopāka Sāmaṇera, received higher ordination at the age of seven. Regarding the inheritance of monkhood:
1. Becoming a monk through the words "Ehi bhikkhu" (Come, monk).
2. Becoming a monk by taking the three refuges (Saraṇagamana).
3. Becoming a monk by accepting admonition (as in the case of Venerable Mahā Kassapa).
4. Becoming a monk by answering questions (as in the case of Sopāka Sāmaṇera).
5. Becoming a monk by accepting the heavy rules (Garudhamma) (as in the case of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī).
6. Becoming a monk by being allowed to send a messenger (as in the case of the nun Aḍḍhakāsī).
7. Becoming a monk through two steps: once by the motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha kamma) in the community of nuns, and once by the motion and three proclamations in the community of monks (for women).
8. Becoming a monk by the motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha kamma) (for current monks).
Among these eight ways of becoming a monk, Sumana Sāmaṇera's ordination is similar to the fourth type. In the Vinaya, it is referred to as Pañhābyākaraṇa Upasampadā (Ordination by Answering Questions); in this Commentary, it is referred to as Dāyajja Upasampadā (Inheritance Ordination). Both mean the same giving of inheritance.)

When Sumana Sāmaṇera thus became a monk, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, how wonderful it is! Such is the power and majesty of such a young novice; we have never seen such power and majesty before this day." The Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "We are gathered for such a discussion," He said, "Monks, in my teaching, even one who is young, if he practices rightly, can indeed attain such fulfillment," and wishing to teach the Dhamma, He spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people reached the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of Sumana Sāmaṇera ends.
The Chapter on the Monk (Bhikkhu Vagga) ends.
The twenty-fifth chapter.
393:
## 26. Brāhmaṇa Vagga

## 1. The Story of the Brahmin with Great Faith
(Pasādabahula Brāhmaṇa Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Blessed One spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Chinda sotaṃ," concerning a Brahmin with great faith.

## Special Care Should Be Taken When Receiving Faith

That Brahmin, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, developed a faithful heart and established a regular offering of alms-food for sixteen monks at his house. When the monks arrived, he would take their bowls and say, "May the noble Arahants come; may the noble Arahants sit," always using words related to the title of "Arahant." Among those monks, the worldling (puthujjana) monks thought, "This Brahmin regards us as Arahants." The Arahants thought, "This Brahmin knows our state as Arahants." Thus, all of them, feeling uneasy, stopped going to the Brahmin's house. The Brahmin, being troubled and unhappy, wondered, "Why do the noble ones not come?" He went to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One, and reported the matter.

The Blessed One called the monks and asked, "Monks, what is the reason for not going?" When the monks reported the reason, He asked, "Monks, do you take delight in being called Arahants?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, we do not take delight in it." "If that is so, this manner of speaking by people is due to their faith. Monks, there is no offense (āpatti) in words spoken out of faith. However, the Brahmin's love and faith toward Arahants is extreme. Therefore, you too should cut the stream of craving and it is proper only to reach the fruit of Arahantship." Wishing to teach the Dhamma, He spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(383) Strive and cut the stream, O Brahmin; discard sense desires. Having known the destruction of conditioned things, you are a knower of the Unmade, O Brahmin.

Brahmin, one who has cast away evil. You, striving with effort joined with wisdom, cut the stream of craving.
(The stream of craving cannot be cut with little effort; therefore, it must be cut by striving with great effort joined with wisdom.)
Discard the two types of sense desires: objective (vatthu-kāma) and subjective (kilesa-kāma). Brahmin, one who has cast away evil. You, having known the end of the conditioned things (saṅkhāras), the five aggregates, are one who knows the Unmade (Akata), Nibbāna.
(Because Nibbāna is not made by anything such as gold or silver, it is called "Akata" (the Unmade). One who knows that Unmade Nibbāna is called "Akataññū.")

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people reached the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of the Brahmin with Great Faith ends.
394:
## The Teaching
(384) When in two states, the Brahmin has reached the far shore, then all fetters of that knowing one come to an end.

When: at which time. Brahmin: the Arahat who has cast away evil. In two states: in the two categories of Samatha (tranquillity) and Vipassanā (insight). Reached the far shore: has reached the end of knowledge. Then: at that time. Of that knowing one: of that Arahat who knows. All fetters: all the bonds (saṃyojana) come to an end (extinction).

## 2. The Story of Many Monks
(Sambahulabhikkhu Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this religious teaching, beginning with "Yadā dvayesu," concerning many monks.

## The Question of the Two Teachings
One day, about thirty monks residing in the four directions arrived, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat down. The Venerable Sāriputta, seeing their potential (upanissaya) for attaining Arahatship, approached the Buddha and, while standing, asked this question: "Venerable Sir, it is said 'two teachings' (dve dhammā). What indeed are these two teachings?"

Then the Buddha said to the Venerable Sāriputta, "Dear Sāriputta, Samatha and Vipassanā are called the two teachings," and then spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, all those thirty monks were established in Arahatship.

The Story of Many Monks ends.

## The Teaching
(385) For whom there exists neither the far shore nor the near shore, nor both; him, free from distress and unfettered, I call a Brahmin.

For whom: for which person. The far shore: the six internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana). The near shore: the six external sense bases (bāhirāyatana). Both: both the internal and external sense bases. Does not exist: does not exist because of the absence of grasping as "I" or "mine." Free from distress: free from the heat of defilements. Unfettered: not associated with defilements. Him: that person. I: the Buddha. Brahmin: one who has cast away evil. I call: I so declare.

## 3. The Story of Māra
(Māra Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this religious teaching, beginning with "Yassa pāraṃ," concerning Māra.

## The Question of "Pāra"
One day, that Māra, having disguised himself as a young man, approached the Buddha and asked: "Venerable Sir, it is said 'pāraṃ, pāraṃ' (the far shore). What indeed is this thing called 'pāra'?"
395:
The Buddha, knowing that "This is Māra," said: "Evil Māra, what use is the far shore (pāra) or the near shore (apāra) to you? That which is called the far shore is to be reached only by those who are free from lust (rāga)," and then spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of Māra ends.

## 4. The Story of a Certain Brahmin
(Aññatarabrāhmaṇa Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this religious teaching, beginning with "Jhāyiṃ," concerning a certain Brahmin.

## The Question of a Brahmin
That Brahmin thought: "The Buddha refers to his own disciples as 'Brahmins.' I, too, am a Brahmin by birth and lineage. Is it not proper to address me in this way as well?" He approached the Buddha and asked about this matter. The Buddha said: "I do not call one a Brahmin merely by birth and lineage; I call only that person a Brahmin who has reached the highest goal, Arahatship," and then spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(386) Him who meditates, is free from dust, seated alone, has done what was to be done, is free from taints, and has reached the highest goal—him I call a Brahmin.

Him who meditates: one who habitually meditates with the two kinds of jhāna. Free from dust: free from the dust of sensual desire (kāma). Seated: one who habitually dwells alone in the forest. Has done what was to be done: has completed the sixteen functions of the Path. Free from taints: free from the outflows (āsava) due to their absence. The highest goal: the noble Fruit of Arahatship. Reached: has attained. Him: that person. I: the Buddha. Brahmin: a Brahmin. I call: I so declare.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, that Brahmin was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The religious teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of a Certain Brahmin ends.
396:
## The Teaching

(387) The sun shines by day, the moon glows by night.
The warrior shines when clad in armor, the brahmin shines when meditating.
But the Buddha shines all day and night with his glory.

**Ādicco**, the sun. **Divā**, by day. **Tapati**, shines. **Candimā**, the moon. **Ratti**, by night. **Ābhāti**, glows. **Khattiyo**, the lord of the land, the king. **Sannaddho**, when adorned with all ornaments. **Tapati**, shines. **Brāhmaṇo**, the Arahant. **Jhāyī**, when having abandoned company and entered into meditative absorption. **Tapati**, shines. **Atha**, furthermore. **Buddho**, the Buddha. **Sabbaṃ ahōrattiṃ**, throughout the whole day and night. **Tejasā**, by means of the fivefold power. **Tapati**, shines gloriously.

## 5. The Story of Elder Ānanda
(Ānandattheravatthu)

While staying at the palace of Visākhā, the mother of Migāra, the Teacher spoke this teaching beginning with "Divā tapati" concerning Elder Ānanda.

## The Five Types of Auspicious Radiance

On the day of the Great Pavāraṇā (the end of the rains retreat), King Pasenadi of Kosala, adorned with all his ornaments and carrying perfumes, flowers, and so forth, went to the monastery. At that moment, Elder Kāḷudāyi was seated at the edge of the assembly, having entered into meditative absorption. The body of Elder Kāḷudāyi was pleasing to behold and had a hue like gold. At that same moment, the moon was rising and the sun was setting. Elder Ānanda, looking at the radiance of the setting sun and the rising moon, also observed the radiance of King Kosala's body, the radiance of the Elder's body, and the radiance of the Buddha's body. Among all those radiances, the Buddha alone shone, surpassing all others. 

Elder Ānanda paid homage to the Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, today as I look at these radiances, I delight only in Your radiance. Your body shines, greatly surpassing all other radiances, Venerable Sir." Then the Buddha said to Ānanda, "Ānanda, the sun shines only by day. The moon shines only by night. A king shines only when he is adorned. An Arahant, who has discarded the company of the crowd—that is, the group of thoughts falling upon various objects—shines only while in meditative attainment. 

Buddhas, however, shine both by night and by day with fivefold power," and he spoke this verse:

(The meaning is: The Buddha shines constantly with this fivefold power, having completely overcome the power of the immoral with the power of virtue, the power of the meritless with the power of quality, the power of the unwise with the power of wisdom, the power of the unmeritorious with the power of merit, and the power of the unrighteous with the power of Dhamma.)
397:
The Buddha shines constantly with this fivefold power.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of Elder Ānanda ends.

## The Teaching

(388) Because he has discarded evil, he is called a Brahmin. Because of his calm conduct, he is called a recluse.
Because he has banished his own stains, therefore he is called a renunciant.

**Bāhitapāpo**, one who has discarded evil. **Iti tasmā**, therefore. **Brāhmaṇo ti**, he is called a Brahmin. **Samacariyā**, because of practicing by calming unwholesome states. **Samaṇo ti**, he is called a recluse (Samaṇa). **Yo**, whoever. **Attano**, his own. **Malaṃ**, stains such as lust and so forth. **Pabbājayaṃ/Pabbājayanto**, discards, cleanses, and banishes. **Tasmā**, therefore. **So**, that person. **Pabbajito ti**, is called a renunciant (Pabbajita).

## 6. The Story of an Unnamed Brahmin Ascetic
(Aññatarabrāhmaṇapabbajitavatthu)

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this teaching beginning with "Bāhitapāpo" concerning an unnamed brahmin.

## The Question of the Renunciant

A certain brahmin, having gone forth as an ascetic outside the Buddha's dispensation, thought, "The ascetic Gotama is in the habit of calling his own disciples 'pabbajita' (renunciants). I too am one who has gone forth; it is certainly fitting that I also be called by this name." He then approached the Buddha and asked about this matter. The Buddha said, "I do not call one a 'pabbajita' merely by this much. One is called a 'pabbajita' because of having cleansed and banished the stains of defilements," and he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, that brahmin ascetic was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The story of the unnamed brahmin ascetic ends.
398:
## 7. The Story of Elder Sāriputta
(Sāriputtattheravatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Na brāhmaṇassa," while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, concerning Elder Sāriputta.

## The Brahmin who Struck Elder Sāriputta
In a certain place, many people were praising the virtues of Elder Sāriputta, saying, "Our noble lord is truly endowed with the power of patience. Even when others abuse or strike him, he does not have even a trace of anger." Then, a brahmin of wrong view asked, "Who is this person who does not get angry?" When they replied, "It is our Elder," he said, "Could it be that there is no one who can make him angry?" They replied, "Brahmin, there is no such person." He then said, "In that case, I shall make him angry." They replied, "If you are able, then try to make him angry." The brahmin said, "So be it, I shall see what must be done to him." Seeing Elder Sāriputta entering for alms, he followed from behind and struck him a heavy blow with his hand in the middle of his back.

Elder Sāriputta, without even looking back to see what had happened, continued on his way. A burning sensation arose throughout the brahmin's body. He thought, "Oh, how endowed with virtue is this noble lord!" and prostrating at the Elder's feet, he said, "Venerable sir, please forgive me." When asked, "What is the reason for this?" he replied, "I struck you, venerable sir, in order to test you." The Elder said, "Let it be so, I forgive you." The brahmin then said, "Venerable sir, if you forgive me, please sit and accept alms only at my house." He took the Elder's bowl, and the Elder gave it to him. The brahmin then led the Elder to his house and served him food.

## How Other People and Monks Could Not Tolerate It
The people were very angry and stood at the door of the brahmin's house holding clods of earth, sticks, and so on, saying, "This brahmin struck our innocent teacher, Elder Sāriputta. He should not escape even with punishment; we shall kill him right here." When Elder Sāriputta rose from his seat and was departing, he gave his bowl into the hand of the brahmin. Seeing the brahmin walking together with the Elder, the people said, "Venerable sir, please take your bowl and send the brahmin back." When the Elder asked, "Lay devotees, what is the reason for this?" they replied, "The brahmin struck you, venerable sir. We wish to know what should be done to him."
399:
## The Teaching
(389) One should not strike a Brāhmaṇa, nor should a Brāhmaṇa release (anger) against him.
Woe to the striker of a Brāhmaṇa, and more woe to him who releases (anger) against the striker.
(390) For a Brāhmaṇa, there is no small benefit when the mind is restrained from what is dear (anger).
Whenever the intent to harm subsides,
then suffering is truly stilled.

"Brāhmaṇo" refers to a Brāhmaṇa who is an Arahant. "Brāhmaṇassa" refers to another Arahant Brāhmaṇa or a brahmin by birth. "Na pahareyya" means one should not strike. "Brāhmaṇo" refers to the Arahant Brāhmaṇa who has been struck. "Assa" means against that striker or upon him. "Na muñcetha" means he should not release anger. "Brāhmaṇassa" refers to the Arahant Brāhmaṇa. "Hantāraṃ" means the one who strikes; "Dhī" means I, the Buddha, censure him as loathsome. "Yo" refers to the person who, being struck, "muñcati" releases anger against the striker. "Taṃ" refers to that person who gets angry after being struck; "Dhī" means I, the Buddha, censure him as even more loathsome than the striker.

"Brāhmaṇassa" refers to the Khīṇāsava (Arahant) Brāhmaṇa. "Etaṃ" refers to not abusing in return one who abuses, and not striking in return one who strikes. "Kañci seyyo" means it is not just a small benefit. "Na" means it is not; it means it is a great benefit. "Manaso piyehi" refers to the arising of anger which is dear to the angry mind. "Yadā niseḍho" refers to the restraint from such anger. "Etaṃ" refers to this restraint from anger; it is of no small benefit. "Hiṃsamano" means the mind of anger. "Yato yato" refers to whatever object from which the mind "nivattati" is completely uprooted and sinks away by the Path of Non-Returning (Anāgāmi-magga). "Tato tato" means from those various objects, "dukkhaṃ" the suffering of the round of rebirths "sammati" is truly stilled.

"Lay devotees, how is it? Did this brahmin strike you, or did he strike me?" the Elder asked. They replied, "Venerable sir, he struck you." "This brahmin has already apologized and asked for forgiveness for striking me. You may go," he said, dismissing the people. After sending the brahmin back, Elder Sāriputta went to the monastery.

The monks complained, saying, "What kind of action is this? Elder Sāriputta was struck by a brahmin, yet he sat in that very brahmin's house, accepted alms, and then returned. From the time he struck the Elder until now, whom will that brahmin be ashamed of? He will go around striking the rest of the monks." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what purpose are you sitting here gathered in conversation now?" When they replied, "With such a conversation, venerable sir," he said, "Monks, there is no such thing as a true Brāhmaṇa striking another true Brāhmaṇa. However, a householder brahmin may have struck a true Arahant Brāhmaṇa. This thing called anger is completely eradicated by the Path of Non-Returning." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke these verses.
400:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of the Elder Sāriputta ends.

## The Teaching
(391) He for whom there is no evil deed by body, speech, or mind,
Who is restrained in these three respects—him I call a Brahmin.

(Yassa: to whom. Kāyena vā: by body. Vācāya vā: by speech. Manasā vā: by mind. Dukkaṭaṃ: an evil deed that is blameworthy, leads to suffering, and leads to the lower realms. Natthi: does not exist. Tīhi ဌာနေဟိ: by these three causes. Saṃvutaṃ: the door through which misconduct enters has been restrained and closed. Taṃ: that person. Ahaṃ: I, the Buddha. Brāhmaṇaṃ: as a Brahmin. Brūmi: declare.)

## 8. The Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī
(Mahāpajāpatīgotamī Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, related this religious teaching starting with "Yassa kāyena vācāya," in reference to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.

(The Blessed One had prescribed the eight heavy rules (Garudhammas) before the actual event occurred. Because Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepted them upon her head—just as a man who loves ornaments would accept a fragrant garland of flowers upon his head—she, together with her retinue, received higher ordination (Upasampadā). For this Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, there was no other preceptor (Upajjhāya) or teacher (Ācariya) besides the Buddha. In reference to the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī who had thus obtained ordination, the following discussion arose at a later time.)

## Doubts Regarding the Great Foster-Mother Gotamī
On another occasion, a conversation arose: "The teachers and preceptors of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī are not known; she took the robes with her own hands (and wore them)." Having said this, the nuns became doubtful and would not perform the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā with the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. Those nuns went and reported the matter even to the Tathāgata. The Teacher, having heard the report of those nuns, said: "The eight heavy rules were given by Me to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. I alone am her preceptor; I alone am her teacher. One should not have doubts regarding Arahants (Khīṇāsavas) who are free from bodily misconduct and so forth." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

(The Eight Heavy Rules are:
1. A nun, even if ordained for a hundred years, must pay respect to a monk ordained that very day.
2. A nun must not spend the rainy season in a residence where there are no monks.
3. Every fortnight, a nun must ask the Order of Monks for the date of the Uposatha and the time for exhortation.
4. After the rainy season, a nun must invite Pavāraṇā before both the Order of Monks and the Order of Nuns.
5. A nun who has committed a grave offense (Saṅghādisesa) must undergo the Mānatta discipline for fifteen days before both Sanghas.
6. A female probationer (Sikkhamānā) who has trained in the six rules for two years must seek higher ordination from both Sanghas.
7. A nun must not abuse or revile a monk for any reason.
8. Nuns are forbidden from admonishing monks.
These eight rules must be respected and not transgressed for life; thus they are called 'Garudhamma' meaning 'Heavy Rules'.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī ends.
401:
## 9. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta
(Sāriputtatthera Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, related this religious teaching starting with "Yamhā dhammaṃ," in reference to the Elder Sāriputta.

## Accused of Worshipping the Directions
It is said that from the time the Elder Sāriputta attained the fruit of Stream-entry after hearing the Dhamma from the Elder Assaji, whenever he heard that the Elder Assaji was residing in a certain direction, he would pay homage with joined palms in that direction and sleep with his head turned toward that direction. The monks said, "The Elder Sāriputta has wrong view; even today he wanders about worshipping the directions," and they reported this matter to the Tathāgata. The Teacher had the Elder Sāriputta summoned and asked, "Is it true, Sāriputta, that you wander about worshipping the directions?" When Sāriputta replied, "Venerable Blessed One, only You know whether I worship the directions or not," the Buddha said, "Monks, Sāriputta does not worship the directions. Rather, because he attained the fruit of Stream-entry by hearing the Dhamma from the Elder Assaji, he is paying homage to his teacher. A monk should devotedly revere the teacher through whom he understands the Dhamma, just as a Brahmin reveres the sacrificial fire." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(392) From whomsoever one may learn the Dhamma taught by the Fully Enlightened One,
One should revere him devotedly, as a Brahmin reveres the sacrificial fire.

(Yamhā: from which teacher. Sammāsambuddha-desitaṃ: taught by the Blessed One. Dhammaṃ: the Dhamma. Vijāneyya: if one should know. Taṃ: that teacher. Brāhmaṇo: a Brahmin. Aggihuttaṃ: the sacrificial fire. Sakkaccaṃ namassati iva: just as he reveres devotedly. Evaṃ: in this way. Sakkaccaṃ: devotedly. Namasseyya: one should revere.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of the Elder Sāriputta ends.

## 10. The Story of the Brahmin with Matted Hair
(Jaṭila Brāhmaṇa Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, related this religious teaching starting with "Na jaṭāhi," in reference to a Brahmin with matted hair.
402:
## The Verse
(393) Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a Brahmin.
In whom there is truth and Dhamma, he is pure and he is a Brahmin.

One does not become a Brahmin by matted hair. One does not become a Brahmin by lineage. One does not become a Brahmin by birth. In whom there is the knowledge of the Truth (Sacca-ñāṇa) through the penetration of the Four Truths in sixteen ways, and the ninefold Supramundane Dhamma (Lokuttara Dhamma), he is pure; he alone is called a Brahmin.

## Not a Brahmin Merely by Matted Hair
That Brahmin thought, "I am well-born on both my mother's and father's side, born into a Brahmin family. If the Ascetic Gotama calls his own disciples 'Brahmins', it is fitting that he should call me a Brahmin as well." Thinking thus, he went to the Teacher and asked about the matter. Then the Teacher said to that matted-hair Brahmin, "Brahmin, I do not call one a Brahmin merely because of matted hair or lineage; I call one a Brahmin only if they have penetrated the Truth." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.
The Story of the Matted-hair Brahmin ends.

## 11. The Story of the Deceitful Brahmin
(Kuhaka-brāhmaṇa Vatthu)
While residing at the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgāra-sālā), the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning a deceitful Brahmin who practiced the bat-vow.

## The Brahmin Deceitful with the Bat-Vow
That Brahmin climbed a Kakudha tree near the gate of the city of Vesālī, gripped a branch with his two feet, and hung upside down, saying, "Give me a hundred brindled cows! Give me coins (kahāpaṇas)! Give me a female attendant! If you do not give them, I will fall from this tree and die, and I will turn this city into a non-city (ruin it)!" When the Tathāgata entered the city surrounded by the community of monks, the monks saw that Brahmin, and they saw him still hanging there when they left. The citizens also thought, "This Brahmin has been hanging like this since morning. If he falls and dies, he might ruin the city." Fearing the destruction of the city, they promised, "We will give whatever he asks," and they gave it. He climbed down, took everything, and left. The monks, seeing him walking in the vicinity of the monastery, crying out like a cow, recognized him and asked, "Brahmin, did you get what you desired?" Hearing him reply, "Yes, I got it," they reported the matter to the Teacher inside the monastery. The Teacher said, "Monks, not only now is he a deceitful thief; in the past also, he was a deceitful thief. Now, however, he deceives the foolish; in the past, he was unable to deceive the wise." Being requested by them, he brought forth the past.
403:
Thinking you were an ascetic, I approached you, the unrestrained one.
He struck me with a stick, just as one who is not an ascetic would.
What use is your matted hair, O witless one? What use is your antelope skin?
Your interior is a jungle; you polish the exterior.

O ascetic! Thinking you were a peaceful and noble ascetic who had calmed evil, I approached you. Just as a base person who has not calmed evil strikes, so did you, O ascetic, strike me with a stick.

O witless ascetic! What benefit is there for you in matted hair? What benefit is there for you in the antelope skin worn over one shoulder? Your interior is filled and cluttered with defilements.

Come, O Iguana, return; eat the rice of hill-paddy.
I have oil and salt, and I have plenty of long pepper.

O Iguana King! Come! Please return! Eat the hill-paddy rice. I have oil and salt. I also have plenty of long pepper.

## The Ascetic Who Attempted to Kill the Iguana
In the past, a deceitful ascetic lived near a certain village. A certain man supported that ascetic. From the food and snacks obtained during the day, he would give a portion to the ascetic just as he did for his own children. He would set aside the portion obtained in the evening and give it the next day. Then one day, having obtained iguana meat in the evening and cooking it well, they set aside a portion of that iguana meat and gave it to the ascetic the next day. After eating the meat, the ascetic became bound by craving for the taste and asked, "What meat is this?" Hearing the reply, "It is iguana meat, venerable sir," he went for alms, took ghee, curds, pepper, and other ingredients, went to his leaf-hut, and placed them to one side. Not far from the leaf-hut, an Iguana King lived in an anthill. That Iguana King used to come from time to time to pay respects to the ascetic. On that day, however, thinking "I will kill the Iguana King," the ascetic concealed a stick and sat near the anthill as if he were sleeping. The Iguana King came out of the anthill, and while approaching the ascetic, he noticed his posture and thought, "Today, I do not like the posture of my teacher," and he turned back from that very spot. The ascetic, knowing that the Iguana King was retreating, threw the stick to kill him. The stick missed its mark.

(In this Dhammapada Commentary, it says 'daṇḍa' - a stick; in the Godha-rāja Jātaka of the Catukka Nipāta, it says 'muggara' - a club. It is also mentioned that when he missed, the ascetic said, "I missed," and the Iguana King replied, "You missed me, ascetic, but you did not miss the four woeful states.")

## How the Iguana King Rebuked the Ascetic
The Iguana King entered the anthill, poked his head out, and looking at the path he had come, spoke thus to the ascetic:

(It is like a gourd full of poison, a pit full of excrement, or an anthill full of poisonous snakes.)

The exterior, the body, you polish; it is clean and pure.

(Being rough inside but very smooth outside, it is like the dung of an elephant or a horse.)
404:
I shall enter further into the anthill, a hundred man-lengths deep.
You speak of oil and salt; your long pepper is of no benefit to me.

Tāpasa, O ascetic. Tvaṃ, you ascetic. Telañca, of oil. Loṇañca, and of salt. Kittesi, you speak. Pipphali, your long pepper, which is a pungent commodity. Mayhaṃ, to me. Ahitaṃ, is of no benefit. Or—is unsuitable. Esa - eso ahaṃ, I. Sataporisaṃ, into a hundred man-lengths deep. Vammikaṃ, anthill. Bhiyyo, further. Pavekkhāmi, shall enter.

## The Teaching
(394) What is the use of your matted hair, O witless one? What is the use of your antelope skin? Within you is a tangled jungle, but you polish only the outside.

Dummedha, O witless ascetic. Te, for you. Jaṭāhi, what is the use of these bound matted locks? Te, for you. Ajinasāṭiyā, what is the use of this antelope skin worn with its claws? Or, worn with its pair of claws and hooves. Kiṃ, what benefit is there? Abbhantaraṃ, your interior. Gahanam, is a tangled jungle of defilements such as lust. Bāhiraṃ, your exterior body. Parimajjasi, you polish to be clean and pure.

## The Lizard's Reply to the Ascetic's Enticement
At that time, the ascetic spoke thus for the purpose of enticing the lizard king with his own food and provisions.

(I have various pungent goods such as asafoetida, cumin, ginger, garlic, pepper, and long pepper. Come and eat the rice prepared with these spices.)

Hearing the words of that ascetic, the lizard king said, "In whatever way you speak, in that same way I only desire to flee," and spoke this verse:

(A man's height is called one 'thu'. I will flee into a depth of about six hundred feet.)

Having spoken thus, he said again, "For so long a time, I perceived you as an ascetic whose evils were stilled. Now, you have thrown a stick as one who desires to strike me. At the very moment of that throwing, you were no longer an ascetic. What is the use of matted hair to a witless person like you? What is the use of an antelope skin with its claws? Your inner self is a tangled jungle of defilements; only your exterior is clean and pure." The Teacher, having brought forth this past story, identified the birth: "At that time, this deceitful Brahmin was the ascetic, and I myself was the lizard king." Desiring to show the reason for the wise lizard king's rebuke of the deceitful ascetic, he spoke this verse:

(By saying 'with claws', it is likely that the 'black leopard' [thit-net] is a type of animal with claws like a deer, sambar, or barking deer. However, since the nails and claws are at the tips, they are also called 'claws'. Thus, the Venerable Mahā Sīlavaṃsa composed: "With claws intact, like the Punnaga flower's pattern, beautifully adorned, wearing the skin of a black leopard." It is a type of black leopard.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the deceitful Brahmin ends.

## 12. The Story of Kisāgotamī
(Kisāgotamī Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing on Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Paṃsukūladharaṃ' concerning Kisāgotamī.

## Returning Upon Seeing Sakka
At that time, it is said that Sakka, at the end of the first watch of the night, approached the Teacher with a company of devas, paid homage, and sat listening to the memorable Dhamma talk. At that moment, Kisāgotamī, thinking "I will see the Teacher," came through the air, but seeing Sakka, she turned back. Sakka, seeing Kisāgotamī turning back, asked the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, who is this bhikkhunī who, as soon as she came and saw you, turned back?"
405:
The Teacher said, "Great King, she is Kisāgotamī, my daughter, the foremost among the bhikkhunīs who wear rag-robes," and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(395) The person who wears rag-robes, who is lean, whose veins stand out, who meditates alone in the forest—him I call a Brahmin.

Paṃsukūladharaṃ, one who habitually wears rag-robes. Kisaṃ, one who has a lean body. Dhamanisanthataṃ, one whose body is covered with veins.

(Those who wear rag-robes fulfill the practice suitable for themselves, and thus they have little flesh and blood, and their bodies have protruding veins.)

Ekaṃ, alone. Vanasmiṃ, in a secluded forest. Jhāyantaṃ, one who habitually practices jhāna. Taṃ jantuṃ, that person. Ahaṃ, I, the Buddha. Brāhmaṇaṃ, call one who has put away evil. Brūmi, so I declare.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of Kisāgotamī ends.

## 13. The Story of a Certain Brahmin
(Ekabrāhmaṇa Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Na cāhaṃ' concerning a certain Brahmin.

## Being Born a Brahmin Does Not Make One a Brahmin
That Brahmin thought, "The ascetic Gotama calls his own disciples Brahmins. I too was born in the Brahmin caste. Surely it is fitting to call me so as well." He approached the Teacher and asked about this matter. Then the Teacher said to him, "Brahmin, I do not call one a Brahmin merely because of being born in the Brahmin caste. He who is without anxiety caused by defilements like lust, and who has no firm grasping through attachments—him I call a Brahmin," and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(396) I do not call him a Brahmin because he is born of a [Brahmin] womb or sprung from a [Brahmin] mother. He is merely a 'Bho-sayer' if he has attachments. He who is without anxiety and without grasping—him I call a Brahmin.

Yonijaṃ, one born in the Brahmin caste. Mattisambhavaṃ, a Brahmin conceived in the womb of a Brahmin mother. Brāhmaṇaṃ, as a Brahmin. Ahaṃ, I. Na brūmi, do not call. So, that Brahmin by birth. Sakincano, if he has anxieties such as lust. Sace hoti, if he should be so. Bhovādināma, he is called a 'Bho-sayer'. Hoti, he is. Akiñcanaṃ, one who has no anxiety through lust and so forth. Anādānaṃ, one who has no grasping through the four types of attachment. Taṃ, that person. Ahaṃ, I. Brāhmaṇaṃ, call a Brahmin. Brūmi, so I declare.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, that Brahmin was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry.
406:
The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.
The Story of the Single Brahmin ends.

## The Verse
(397) Having cut every fetter, he who indeed does not tremble,
Who has transcended attachments and is detached, him I call a brahmin.

Whoever, because he has cut all ten fetters (saṃyojana), indeed does not tremble with fear. Him, who has transcended attachments such as lust (rāga) and is detached due to the absence of the four bonds (yoga), I, the Buddha, call a brahmin.

## 14. The Story of Uggasena, the Merchant's Son
(Uggasenaseṭṭhiputtavatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana monastery, the Blessed One spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Sabbasaṃyojanaṃ", concerning the merchant's son named Uggasena.

## Not Fearing when Fetters are Severed
(The story is already detailed in the commentary on the verse "Muñca pure muñca pacchato" in the Taṇhāvagga, the Story of Uggasena.)

At that time, when the monks reported to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, the monk Uggasena says, 'I am not afraid.' We think he is falsely claiming the fruit of Arahatship," the Blessed One said, "Monks, those like my son, whose fetters are severed, are indeed not afraid," and spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and so forth.
The Story of Uggasena, the Merchant's Son, ends.

## 15. The Story of Two Brahmins
(Dvebrāhmaṇavatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Blessed One spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Chetvā naddhiṃ", concerning two brahmins.
407:
## The Verse
(398) Having cut the strap and the thong, the harness with its appurtenances,
Who has lifted the crossbar and is awakened, him I call a brahmin.

Because he has cut the strap that binds, the strong leather thong, and the harness that moves continuously like a cart; who has opened the crossbar of the gate so the enclosure is open; him, the great ox, I, the Buddha, call a noble ox.

## The Need to Sever the Internal Ropes
Among those two brahmins, one had an ox named Cūḷarohita, and the other had an ox named Mahārohita. One day, they argued, "My ox is stronger," "My ox is stronger." They decided, "What is the use of arguing? We shall know after driving them." They filled a cart with sand on the bank of the Aciravatī River, yoked the oxen, and drove them. At that moment, monks had also gone there to bathe. The brahmins drove the oxen. The cart remained motionless, but the binding straps broke. The monks saw this, went to the monastery, and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Monks, those binding straps are external. Anyone can cut them. A monk, however, should cut the internal bond of anger and the strap of craving," and spoke this verse:

(This is the literal meaning concerning the ox, which is not the primary intent.)

Having cut the strap of anger formed by bearing a grudge, and the thong of craving formed by the nature of binding; having destroyed the cart of the sixty-two views along with the sequence of latent tendencies (anusaya); who stands with the crossbar of ignorance (avijjā) lifted away; who has realized the Four Noble Truths; him I, the Buddha, call a brahmin, one who is pure and free from evil.

(This is the spiritual meaning concerning the monk, which is the primary intent.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, five hundred monks were established in the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala). The teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.
The Story of the Two Brahmins ends.

## 16. The Story of Akkosaka Bhāradvāja, the Abuser
(Akkosakabhāradvājavatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana monastery, the Blessed One spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Akkosaṃ", concerning the brahmin named Akkosaka Bhāradvāja because he was abusive.

## Seeking a Quarrel with the Buddha due to Inability to Control His Wife
The wife of Akkosaka Bhāradvāja's brother, a brahmin woman named Dhanañjānī, was a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Whether she sneezed, tripped, or stumbled, she would utter this inspired exclamation: "Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa." One day, while serving a group of brahmins a meal, she stumbled and uttered the exclamation loudly as before. The brahmin became very angry and said, "This wretched woman, whenever and wherever she stumbles, she praises the virtues of that shaven-headed ascetic." He then said, "Wretched woman, now I will go and challenge the doctrine of your teacher, the Great Buddha." Then the woman said to the brahmin, "Go, O Brahmin. I have not yet seen anyone who could challenge the doctrine of that Blessed One. However, go and ask the Blessed One a question." That brahmin went to the presence of the Blessed One, and without paying homage, stood in a suitable place and, wishing to ask a question, spoke this verse:
408:
Having slain what does one sleep soundly? Having slain what does one not sorrow? Of what one thing do you approve the killing, O Gotama?

Bho Gotama, O venerable Gotama. Kiṃsu, having slain what? Sukhaṃ seti, does one live happily? Kiṃsu, having slain what? Na socati, does one not sorrow? Kissassa ekadhammassa, of what kind of single state? Vadhaṃ, the killing? Rocesi, do you approve?

Having slain anger one sleeps soundly; having slain anger one does not sorrow. The killing of anger, with its poisoned root and honeyed tip, O Brahmin, the Noble Ones praise; for having slain it, one does not sorrow.

Brāhmaṇa, O great Brahmin. Kodhaṃ, having slain anger; sukhaṃ seti, one lives happily. Kodhaṃ, having slain anger; na socati, one does not sorrow. Visamūlassa, of that which has a poisonous root (resulting in suffering); madhuraggassa, of that which has a honeyed tip (the satisfaction of revenge). Kodhassa vadhaṃ, the killing of anger; ariyā, the Noble Ones, the Buddhas and Arahants, praise. Hi, indeed that is right. Taṃ, having slain that anger; na socati, one does not sorrow.

## The Teaching

(399) He who, without being angry, endures abuse, beating, and imprisonment, whose strength is patience and whose army is strength—him I call a Brahmin.

Yo, whoever; aduṭṭho, being without anger; akkosañca, endures one who abuses him with the ten grounds of abuse; vadhabandhañca, and one who beats him with hands and so on, or one who binds him with stocks, ropes, and so on; titikkhati, endures them. Khantībalaṃ, who possesses the strength of patience; balānīkaṃ, who has the host of soldiers that is the strength of patience. Taṃ, him; ahaṃ, I, the Buddha; brāhmaṇaṃ, call a Brahmin, one who has put away evil; brūmi, so I declare.

(This verse was asked by the Brahmin who approached thinking: "If he answers that he approves of killing something, I will blame him, saying 'Is this a Buddha who has appeared to kill living beings? What benefit is there?' If he answers that he does not approve of killing anything, I will blame him, saying 'Do you not wish to kill lust, hatred, and so on? Why then do you wander as a monk?'" Thinking that the ascetic Gotama would be unable to spit it out or swallow it and would be confounded by this double-edged problem, he approached and asked this question in verse.)

## Becoming an Arahant through the Buddha's Answer

Then the Blessed One, answering the question for the great Brahmin, spoke this verse. Upon hearing this answer, the great Brahmin was so inspired by the Blessed One that he ordained and attained the fruit of Arahantship.

## Subsequent Brahmins also becoming Arahants

Then the younger brother of the great Brahmin, named Akkosaka Bhāradvāja, heard that his elder brother had ordained. Enraged, he came and abused the Blessed One with unseemly and harsh words. When that Brahmin was made to understand by the Blessed One through the simile of giving food and snacks to a guest, he became deeply inspired by the Blessed One, ordained, and attained the fruit of Arahantship. Furthermore, Asundarika Bhāradvāja and Bilaṅgika Bhāradvāja, the two other younger brothers of the great Brahmin, also abused the Blessed One. When they were disciplined by the Blessed One, they all ordained and attained the fruit of Arahantship. Then one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, how wonderful are the qualities and graces of the Buddha! Even when the four Brahmin brothers abused him, the Blessed One did not say a single word in retaliation and became the very refuge and support for those four." The Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, for what conversation are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a conversation, Bhante," he said, "Monks, because I am endowed with the power of patience, I do not retaliate against those who wrong me, and thus I am indeed the refuge, support, and reliance for many people," and he spoke this verse.

(The simile is: "Do you not occasionally prepare food and snacks for guests who come to you? If the guests do not accept those foods and snacks, for whom are they intended?" The Blessed One asked this, and Bhāradvāja the Brahmin replied, "If those guests do not accept them, they are for me alone." "Bhāradvāja, likewise, you abuse us who do not like abuse. We do not accept that abuse of yours. All of it remains for you alone. To abuse in return is to accept and eat. We do not wish to eat. Let it all be for your portion alone.")

(Akkosa-vatthu = The ten grounds of abuse:
1. By way of birth.
2. By way of name.
3. By way of lineage.
4. By way of occupation.
5. By way of craft.
6. By way of disease.
7. By way of physical appearance...)
409:
8. By way of defilements, such as being very greedy or very angry.
9. By way of major or minor offenses (āpatti).
10. By way of harsh insults using words like dog, pig, mother, or sister; this is what is meant by 'insulting'.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of the Brahmin Akkosakabhāradvāja ends.

## The Teaching
(400) Akkodhanaṃ vatavantaṃ, sīlavantaṃ anussadaṃ.
Dantaṃ antimasārīraṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.

Free from anger (akkodhanaṃ); possessing the practice that sheds defilements (vatavantaṃ); possessing the fourfold purity of virtue (sīlavantaṃ); free from the increase of craving (anussadaṃ); tamed through the restraint of the six sense faculties (dantaṃ); possessing a body that exists in the final birth (antimasārīraṃ); him, I, the Buddha, call a Brahmin.

## 17. The Story of Venerable Sāriputta
(Sāriputtatthera-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, spoke this legal discourse beginning with 'Akkodhanaṃ' concerning Venerable Sāriputta.

## The Abuse by Venerable Sāriputta's Mother
At that time, it is said that while Venerable Sāriputta was wandering for alms together with five hundred monks, he arrived at the door of his mother's house in the village of Nālaka. Then, his mother, the lay devotee, invited him to sit and, while serving the meal, insulted him: 'O eater of leftovers! When you do not get leftover rice and sour gruel, you wander to other houses to eat sour gruel stirred with the back of a ladle. Having abandoned eighty crores of wealth to become a monk, you have ruined us. Now, eat!' While giving alms to the monks, she also said: 'You have made my son your little attendant. Now, eat!' Venerable Sāriputta took the alms and went back to the monastery.

Then, Venerable Rāhula informed the Buddha about the alms-food. The Teacher asked him: 'Dear Rāhula, where did you go?' 'To my grandmother's village, Bhante.' 'What did your grandmother say to your preceptor?' 'Bhante, my grandmother insulted my preceptor.' 'Saying what?' 'She said such and such, Bhante.' 'And what did your preceptor say to her?' 'Nothing at all, Bhante.' Hearing this, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: 'Friends, how wonderful are the virtues of Venerable Sāriputta! Even when his mother insulted him with such words, not even a trace of anger arose in him.'
410:
The Teacher arrived and asked: 'Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?' When they replied: 'For such and such a discussion,' he said: 'Monks, those who have destroyed the taints (arahants) are indeed free from anger,' and spoke this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of Venerable Sāriputta ends.

## The Teaching
(401) Vāri pokkharapatteva, āragge-riva sāsapo.
Yo na limpati kāmesu, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.

Just as water (vāri) does not cling (na limpati) to a lotus leaf (pokkharapatte), and just as a mustard seed (sāsapo) does not remain (na saṇṭhati) on the point of an awl (āragge), so too, he who (yo) does not cling (na limpati) to sensual pleasures (kāmesu)—him, I, the Buddha, call a Brahmin.

## 18. The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā
(Uppalavaṇဏātherī-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, spoke this legal discourse beginning with 'Vāri pokkharapatteva' concerning the elder nun named Uppalavaṇṇā.

## Like Water on a Lotus Leaf, a Mustard Seed on an Awl
(The story has already been detailed in the commentary on the verse 'Madhuvā maññati bālo' in the Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā. Indeed, that is true. In the commentary on that verse, the words 'At another time' and so forth were spoken.)

At another time, a great crowd of people started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: 'I suppose even those who have destroyed the taints (arahants) enjoy sensual pleasures and indulge in them. Why would they not? They are not dry wood, nor are they anthills; they have bodies of moist flesh. Therefore, they too must enjoy the pleasure of the senses.' The Teacher arrived and asked: 'Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?' When they replied: 'For such and such a discussion,' he said:

'Monks, those who have destroyed the taints do not enjoy sensual pleasures, nor do they indulge in them. Just as a drop of water falling on a lotus leaf does not cling or remain, but rolls off and falls away; and just as a mustard seed does not stick or remain on the point of an awl, but rolls off and falls away; even so, in the mind of one who has destroyed the taints, the two kinds of sensual pleasure do not cling or remain.' Having thus connected the sequence, he spoke this verse to teach the Dhamma:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā ends.
411:
## The Teaching

(402) He who knows even here in this life the end of his suffering, who has laid down the burden and is detached—him I call a Brahmin.

He who: that person. Even here: in this very life. Of his own: his own. Suffering: the suffering of the burden of the aggregates. End: Nibbāna, the end of suffering. Knows: knows distinctly. Who has laid down the burden: who has put down the burden of the aggregates. Detached: freed from the four yokes and all defilements. Him: that person. I: the Buddha. Brahmin: as a Brahmin. Call: I declare.

## 19. The Story of an Unnamed Brahmin
(Aññatarabrāhmaṇa Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching starting with "Yo dukkhassa," concerning a certain Brahmin.

## Arresting the Runaway Slave Monk

A slave of that Brahmin, before the training rules were promulgated, ran away and ordained, eventually reaching the fruit of Arahantship. The Brahmin, searching for that slave and not finding him, one day saw him entering for alms with the Teacher at the doorway and firmly grabbed his robe. The Teacher turned back and asked, "Brahmin, what is the reason for this grabbing?" "O Gotama, he is my slave," he replied. "Brahmin, this monk has laid down the burden," the Teacher said. When the Teacher said "He has laid down the burden," the Brahmin understood it to mean he was an Arahant. Therefore, the Brahmin asked again, "O Gotama, is it true that he has laid down the burden?" The Teacher replied, "Yes, Brahmin, he has laid down the burden," and spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the Brahmin who was searching for his lost slave was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience. The story of the unnamed Brahmin ends.

## 20. The Story of the Nun Khemā
(Khemābhikkhunī Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing on Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa), told this Dhamma teaching starting with "Gambhīrapaññaṃ," concerning the nun named Khemā.

## Returning After Seeing Sakka

One day, immediately after the first watch of the night, Sakka, the king of devas, came with his celestial retinue and sat near the Teacher, listening to the delightful Dhamma talk that should be remembered for a lifetime. At that moment, the nun named Khemā came to see the Teacher. Seeing Sakka, she paid homage to the Teacher while remaining in the air and then returned.
412:
## The Teaching

(403) Him of profound wisdom, the sagacious, skilled in the path and the non-path, who has reached the highest goal—him I call a brahmin.

*Gambhīrapaññaṃ*: endowed with wisdom that knows the profound aggregates and so forth. *Medhāviṃ*: endowed with sharp wisdom. *Maggāmaggassa*: in what is the path and what is not the path. *Kovidam*: one who is skilled.

When Sakka, the king of devas, saw that nun named Khemā departing, he asked, "Venerable Sir, who is this nun who, having come and stood in the air, paid homage to the Teacher and then departed?" The Buddha replied, "Great King, this nun is my daughter named Khemā. She possesses great wisdom. She is very skilled in what is the path and what is not the path," and he spoke this verse.

(This means: "This is the path leading to the woeful states. This is the path leading to the heavenly states. This is the path leading to Nibbāna. This is not the path." Thus, she is proficient and skilled in both the path and the non-path.)

*Uttamattham*: the highest goal, known as the fruit of Arahantship. *Anuppattaṃ*: who has reached in due course. *Taṃ*: that person. *Ahaṃ*: I, the Buddha. *Brāhmaṇaṃ*: as a brahmin. *Brūmi*: I declare.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of Khemā Bhikkhunī ends.

## 21. The Story of Elder Pabbhāravāsī Tissa

(Pabbhāravāsītissattheravatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ" concerning Elder Pabbhāravāsī Tissa.

## The Suffering of Deities because of the Monk

That Elder Tissa, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered the forest. While searching for a suitable lodging, he reached a mountain cleft with a cave. At the very moment of arrival, the Elder's mind attained one-pointedness. The Elder thought, "If I live in this cave, I shall be able to accomplish the task of a monk." The deity who resided permanently in the cave thought, "A virtuous monk has arrived. It is difficult to live in the same place with this monk. However, this monk will stay in this cave for only one night and then depart." Thinking thus, the deity took her young sons and daughters and left. 

On the following day, early in the morning, Elder Tissa entered the alms-resort village for alms. Then, as soon as a female lay devotee saw the Elder, she felt a motherly affection for him as if he were her son. She invited him to sit in her house, offered him food, and requested him to stay and observe the three months of the rainy season depending on her. The Elder also thought, "Depending on this lay devotee, I might be able to achieve liberation from the round of rebirth," and having accepted, he returned to that very cave.
413:
When the deity saw Elder Tissa returning, she thought, "Surely he must have been invited by someone; he will depart tomorrow or the day after tomorrow." When half a month had passed in this way, she thought, "This monk, I suppose, will stay in this cave for the entire three months of the rainy season retreat."

## The Deity Making the Monk a Physician

"It is very difficult to live in the same place as a virtuous monk along with young children. It is also not proper to tell this monk to 'leave.' Is there perhaps any lapse in this monk's virtue?" Looking with her divine eye, she examined his virtue starting from the time of his higher ordination platform and saw no lapse. She then thought, "His virtue is perfectly pure. I will say something to him to cause him disgrace." She then possessed the body of the eldest son of the laywoman who was the Elder's supporter and twisted his neck. The son's eyes bulged out, and saliva dripped from his mouth. When the laywoman saw her son in that state, she wailed, "What is this?" Then the deity, remaining invisible, spoke to her:

"I have possessed your son. I have no need for offerings. However, ask your teacher, the Elder, for some licorice, cook it with oil, and give it to this boy as a nasal treatment. If you do this, I will release him." When she said this, the laywoman replied, "Whether my son perishes or dies, I cannot bring myself to ask the Venerable One for licorice." The deity then said, "If you cannot ask for licorice, then tell him to put some asafoetida powder in your son's nose." The laywoman replied, "I cannot say that either." "In that case," the deity said, "take the water used for washing the Elder's feet and pour it over the boy's head." The laywoman said, "This I can do." When the Elder arrived at the time for alms, she had him sit down and offered him gruel and snacks. While the Elder was sitting before his meal, she washed his feet, took the water, and asked, "Venerable Sir, we wish to pour this foot-washing water over the boy's head." When the Elder said, "If so, pour it," she did as he said. The deity released the boy immediately and went to stand at the entrance of the cave.

## Attaining Arahatship upon being Accused of being a Physician

The Elder, having finished his meal, rose from his seat and, because his meditation was never abandoned, departed while reciting the thirty-two parts of the body, such as hair of the head and hair of the body. When he reached the cave entrance, the deity said, "Great physician, do not enter here." The Elder stood right there and asked, "Who are you?" "I am the deity residing in this cave," she replied.
414:
## Expelling the Evil Deity

Pure indeed is my dwelling;
I am a practitioner of austerities, free from stain.
Do not defile me, who am pure;
Depart, you, from this pleasant forest!

O Deity! My dwelling is indeed pure. Do not defile me, who am pure in virtue and a practitioner of the noble practice, free from stain. You, depart from this pleasant forest grove!

## The Teaching

(404) One who does not associate with both,
The householders and the homeless,
Who wanders without a home and has few desires—
That one I call a Brahmin.

One who has no association with both householders and the homeless through the five types of association—namely, association by sight, hearing, conversation, use of requisites, and physical contact—or one who has no clinging conduct; who does not descend into the realm of sensual pleasures; who has few desires—that person, I, the Buddha, call a Brahmin.

When she said this, the Elder thought, "Is there any instance where I have performed the work of a physician?" Looking back from the time of his higher ordination platform, he saw not even a dark spot the size of a sesame seed in his virtue. He then said, "I do not see any place where I have performed medical work. Why do you speak thus?"

"Do you not see it?" she asked. "Indeed, I do not," he replied. "Then I shall tell you." "Very well, tell me." "Let alone what was done in the distant past; only today, did you not have the water used for washing your feet poured over the head of the son of your supporter who was possessed by a spirit?" "Yes, it was poured." "How is it that you do not see this?" "Are you saying this with reference to the pouring of that foot-washing water?" "Yes, I say it with reference to that."

The Elder thought, "Ah, how well-directed is my mind! How truly my conduct is in accordance with the Teaching! Even a deity, finding not even a dark spot the size of a sesame seed in my fourfold purification of virtue, saw only the mere pouring of foot-washing water over a child's head." Reflecting on his virtue, powerful joy (pīti) arose within him. Suppressing that joy and without even taking a step, he attained Arahatship right there. Then, wishing to admonish the deity, he said, "Do not live in this forest grove while insulting a pure monk like me. You yourself must leave!" and he uttered this inspired utterance found in the Subhūti Thera Apadāna.

Elder Tissa stayed there for the three months of the rainy season. Having completed the retreat, he went to the presence of the Teacher. When asked by the monks, "Friend, have you brought the task of a monk to its consummation?" he related the entire event from the day he entered the retreat in that cave. When the monks asked, "Friend, were you not angry when spoken to thus by the deity?" he replied, "I was not angry." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, this monk claims higher attainment. He says he was not angry even when spoken to in such a manner by a deity." Hearing their words, the Teacher said, "Monks, my son does not get angry. For that monk Tissa, there is no association with householders or the homeless; he does not associate. This monk has few desires and is easily contented," and wishing to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse.
415:
## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the Elder Pabbhāravāsī Tissa ends.

## 22. The Story of a Certain Monk

(Aññatarabhikkhu Vatthu)

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha gave this Dhamma teaching starting with 'Nidhāya,' in reference to a certain monk.

## The Monk Beaten for Allegedly Abducting a Woman

That monk, having taken a meditation subject from the Buddha and striving in the forest, attained the fruit of Arahantship. Thinking, 'I will inform the Buddha of the qualities I have attained,' he departed from that forest. At that time, in a certain village, a woman had a quarrel with her husband. While her husband was out, she set out on the road, thinking, 'I will return to my parents' house.' Seeing the Elder on the way, she followed behind him, thinking, 'I will travel by relying on this Elder.' The Elder, however, did not see her following him. Later, when her husband returned home and did not see her, he followed her, thinking, 'She must have gone to her parents' village.' Seeing her, he thought, 'This woman could not have traveled through this forest alone. On whom is she relying?' Looking around, he saw the Elder and thought, 'This monk must have taken this woman and left.' He then threatened and scolded the Elder. At that time, the woman said to her husband, 'This noble one does not see me, nor did he call or speak to me. Do not say anything to that monk.' The husband replied, 'What? Would you tell me that he is taking you away? Therefore, I will do to this monk what is fitting for you!' In his anger and with a grudge against the woman, he beat and struck the Elder and then took the woman back. The Elder's entire body became covered in swellings.

Later, when he arrived at the monastery, the monks, while massaging his body, saw the swellings and asked, 'Venerable sir, why have these swellings occurred?' The Elder told them the reason. Then the monks asked him, 'Friend, while that man was beating you like this, what did you say? How was it?"
416:
"Did anger arise in you, venerable sir?" they asked. When he said, "Friends, anger did not arise in me," the monks went to the Buddha and reported the matter, saying, "Venerable Sir, when this monk was asked, 'Did anger arise in you?', he replied, 'Friends, anger did not arise in me.' He is speaking untruth and claiming the fruit of Arahantship." Hearing the words of those monks, the Buddha said, "Bhikkhus, those who are Arahants have laid down the rod; even when they are beaten, they do not give way to anger." He then spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(405) He who has laid down the rod towards beings, both those who tremble and those who are firm, who neither kills nor causes to kill—him I call a Brahmin.

'He who' (yo): that person. 'Those who tremble' (tasesu): those who have trembling due to the trembling of craving, namely worldlings and learners (sekhas). 'And those who are firm' (thāvaresu ca): those who are stable and firm due to the absence of craving, namely Arahants. 'Laid down the rod' (nidhāya daṇḍaṃ): having abandoned and put down the rod. 'Neither kills' (na hanti): he himself does not kill, torment, or oppress anyone. 'Nor causes to kill' (na ghāteti): nor does he cause others to kill, torment, or oppress. 'Him' (taṃ): that person. 'I' (ahaṃ): I, the Buddha. 'Call a Brahmin' (brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ): declare to be a Brahmin.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the certain monk ends.

## 23. The Story of the Four Novices

(Sāmaṇerānaṃ Vatthu)

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha gave this Dhamma teaching starting with 'Aviruddhaṃ,' in reference to four novices.

## Lack of Faith to Offer Alms Due to Their Young Age

A Brahmin woman, having prepared alms dedicated to four monks, said to the old Brahmin, "Go to the monastery, request four elderly Brahmins, and bring them here." The Brahmin went to the monastery and requested, "Venerable sirs, please assign four Brahmins to me." Four seven-year-old Arahant novices—Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera, Paṇḍita Sāmaṇera, Sopāka Sāmaṇera, and Revata Sāmaṇera—were assigned to him. The Brahmin woman had prepared seats suitable only for noble ones. When she saw the young novices, she became very angry, crackling like salt thrown into a furnace, and said, "You went to the monastery and brought back four young boys who are not even as old as your own grandsons!" She did not allow the young novices to sit on those seats but spread out low stools and said, "Sit on these." Then she said again, "Brahmin, go back and look for elderly Brahmins and bring them here."

## Returning After Inviting the Great Disciples

The Brahmin went to the monastery, and seeing the Elder Sāriputta, he invited him, saying, "Please come, venerable sir, let us go to our house."
417:
Elder Sāriputta arrived and, seeing the novices, asked, "Have these Brahmins received alms-food?" When they replied, "Not yet, venerable sir," he realized that food had been prepared for only four people. He said, "Bring me my bowl," and taking his bowl, he departed. The Brahmin woman asked, "What did this person say?" The Brahmin replied, "He said, 'It is proper for these seated Brahmins to receive it; bring me my bowl,' and then he took his bowl and left." Hearing this, she thought, "He must not wish to eat," and sent him again, saying, "Go quickly, look for another person and invite him." The Brahmin went and, seeing Elder Mahāmoggallāna, invited him in the same way. That Elder also saw the novices, spoke in the same manner, took his bowl, and departed. Then the Brahmin woman said to the Brahmin, "These people do not wish to eat. Go to the monastery and bring a great elderly Brahmin." The novices, having received nothing since early morning, sat there oppressed by hunger.

## Rejoicing at Finding the Old Brahmin
At that time, due to the power of the virtues of the four novices, Sakka’s Paṇḍukambala stone throne showed signs of heat. When Sakka reflected and realized the exhaustion of those four novices who had been sitting since early morning, he thought, "It is proper for me to go there." Disguising himself as a very old, decrepit Brahmin, he went and sat in the noble seat prepared for Brahmins in that Brahmin quarter. When the Brahmin saw the old man, he thought, "Now my wife will be delighted," and invited him, saying, "Come, let us go to the house," and took the old Brahmin (Sakka) to his home. As soon as the Brahmin woman saw the old Brahmin, her heart was filled with joy. She spread a cover on only one of the two seats and said, "Venerable sir, please sit here."

## Dragging Out the Old Brahmin Sakka
Sakka entered the house and, after paying homage to the four young novices with the five-point prostration, sat cross-legged on the ground at the end of the novices' row. Seeing him sitting like that, the Brahmin woman said to the Brahmin, "How strange is this old Brahmin you brought! You have brought an old man who is like a father, yet he goes around bowing to children who are like his own grandchildren. What use is this old Brahmin? Drive him out!" Although they grabbed him by the shoulders, hands, and armpits to drive him out, the old Brahmin Sakka did not even wish to stand up. Then the Brahmin woman said to the Brahmin, "Brahmin, come! You take one hand, and I will take the other." Both of them grabbed his hands, and while striking and pounding him on his back, they dragged him out of the house door. Sakka, however, remained sitting exactly where he had been and released his hands. When the couple turned back and saw the old Brahmin still sitting there, they cried out in terror and let go. At that moment, Sakka revealed his identity as Sakka. Only then did they offer them food.
418:
## The Teaching
(406) He who is friendly among the hostile,
Peaceful among the violent,
And unattached among the attached,
Him I call a Brahmin.

Among the hostile: Among the worldly people who are hostile through resentment. Friendly: Not being hostile because of the absence of resentment. Among the violent (those with sticks): Among people who have sticks and weapons in themselves. Peaceful: Being one who has laid down the stick and is at peace. Among the attached: Among those who grasp the five aggregates as "I" or "mine." Unattached: Being one who does not have such grasping. Him: That person. I: The Buddha. Call a Brahmin: I declare to be a Brahmin.

## The Brahmin's House Becoming Five-Holed
The five of them took the food; one pierced through the circular roof-peak, one through the front of the roof, one through the back, one by sinking into the earth, and Sakka departed through another place; thus the five went in five directions. From that time on, that house was indeed known as the "Five-Holed House." When the novices reached the monastery, the monks asked, "Friends, what was it like?" "Venerable sirs, do not ask us. From the moment she saw us, the Brahmin woman was oppressed by anger and did not even let us sit on the prepared seats, saying 'You must quickly invite a great Brahmin.' Our preceptor, Elder Sāriputta, arrived and seeing us, said 'It is proper for these seated Brahmins to receive alms,' and having his bowl brought, he departed. When she said again 'Invite another great Brahmin,' the Brahmin invited Elder Mahāmoggallāna. That Elder Mahāmoggallāna also saw us and, speaking just like Elder Sāriputta, departed. Then the Brahmin woman said, 'These people do not wish to eat. Go, Brahmin! Invite an old, elderly Brahmin from the place where Brahmins recite.' She sent the Brahmin. That Brahmin went to that place and invited Sakka, who had come in the guise of a Brahmin. Only when that Sakka arrived did they offer us food," they reported. When asked again, "Did you not get angry at that Brahmin couple who did such things?" they replied, "We did not get angry, venerable sirs." The monks, hearing those words, reported to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, these young novices are saying what is not true, declaring the fruit of Arahantship by saying 'We did not get angry'." The Blessed One said, "Monks, those who are Arahants do not conflict even with those who are conflicting," and he preached this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of the four novices ends.
419:
## The Teaching
(407) He who has cast off lust and hatred, pride and detraction, like a mustard seed from the point of an awl—him I call a Brahmin.

From the point of an awl (āragga); like a mustard seed (sāsaporiva). He who (yassa) has cast off (pātito) lust (rāgo ca), hatred (doso ca), the conceit of 'I' (māno ca), and the smearing of others' virtues (makkho ca). Him (taṃ), I (ahaṃ) call (brūmi) a Brahmin (brāhmaṇaṃ).

## 24. The Story of Elder Mahāpanthaka
(Mahāpanthakattheravatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching regarding Elder Mahāpanthaka, starting with "Yassa rāgo ca."

## Elder Mahāpanthaka's Freedom from Anger
The venerable Mahāpanthaka, seeing that the venerable Cūḷapanthaka was unable to master a single verse even in four months, said, "You are not fit for this Dispensation; you have also fallen away from worldly wealth. What is the use of you staying in this Dispensation? Get out of here!" He then drove him out of the monastery and closed the door. The monks started a conversation: "Friends, Elder Mahāpanthaka has done such a thing. It seems even in Arahants, anger can arise." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what subject are you gathered here discussing now?" When they replied, "This subject, Bhante," He said, "Monks, Arahants do not have defilements like lust and so on.
