My son Mahāpanthaka acted solely with a view to the benefit and with a view to the Dhamma." He then spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The story of Elder Mahāpanthaka ends.

## 25. The Story of Elder Pilindavaccha
(Pilindavacchattheravatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching regarding Elder Pilindavaccha, starting with "Akakkasaṃ."

## Habitual Use of 'Outcaste' without Anger
The venerable Pilindavaccha used to address both laypeople and monks with the word 'outcaste' (vasala), saying things like "Come here, outcaste," "Go there, outcaste." Then one day, many monks informed the Teacher: "Bhante, the venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the monks with the word outcaste."
420:
## The Teaching
(408) One should speak words that are gentle, instructive, and true, by which one would not offend anyone—him I call a Brahmin.

By which words (yāya girāya); one would not offend (nābhisaje) or cause anyone (kañci) to be provoked to anger. One should speak (udīraye) those words (taṃ giraṃ) which are gentle (akakkasaṃ), instructive (viññāpaniṃ), and true in nature (saccaṃ). Therefore (tasmā), him (taṃ), I (ahaṃ) call (brūmi) a Brahmin (brāhmaṇaṃ).

The Teacher summoned Elder Pilindavaccha and asked, "Is it true, Pilindavaccha, that you address the monks with the word outcaste?" When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher, reflecting on the past lives of the venerable Pilindavaccha, said, "Monks, do not find fault with the monk Vaccha. Monks, it is not because he has anger in his heart that Vaccha addresses the monks as outcaste. Monks, for five hundred consecutive births, the monk Vaccha was reborn in Brahmin families. This addressing as outcaste has been practiced by him for a long time. In an Arahant, there is no harsh or rough speech that strikes at the vitals of others. It is only through the power of habit that my son Pilindavaccha speaks in this way." He then spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The story of Elder Pilindavaccha ends.

## 26. The Story of an Unknown Elder
(Aññatarattheravatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching regarding an unknown elder, starting with "Yodha dīghaṃ."

## Being Accused of Stealing a Robe
In the city of Sāvatthī, a Brahmin with wrong view, fearing the smell of the body, took off his upper robe and placed it in a suitable spot, then sat facing outward at his door. Then an Arahant, having finished his meal and returning to the monastery, saw the robe. Looking here and there and seeing no one, he thought, "This robe has no owner; it is a refuse-rag (paṃsukūla)," and taking it up with that resolve, he departed. When the Brahmin saw the elder taking it, he approached him while reviling him, saying, "Shaveling ascetic, you are stealing my robe!" When asked, "Brahmin, is this your robe?" he replied, "Yes, ascetic." "I took it with the perception that it was a refuse-rag because I saw no one."
421:
## The Teaching

(409) Whoever in this world takes nothing that is not given, whether long or short, small or large, beautiful or ugly—him I call a brahmin.

"Whoever," that is, any person. "Long or short," whether it be long or short.

"Take your cloth," he said, and having given it to the brahmin, he went to the monastery and told the monks about the matter. Then, hearing the Elder's words, the monks teased him, saying, "Friend, how is it? Is the cloth long or short, coarse and thick, or fine and soft?" He replied, "Friends, whether it be long or short, coarse or fine, I have no attachment to that cloth. I took it with the perception that it was a refuse-rag (paṃsukūla)." Hearing this, the monks reported to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, this monk speaks what is not true and claims the fruit of Arahatship."

The Buddha said, "Monks, this monk speaks the truth. Those who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) do not take what belongs to others," and he spoke this verse:

(Take it as referring to clothes, ornaments, etc.)

"Small or large," whether it be small or large.

(Take it as referring to pearls, gems, etc.)

"Beautiful or ugly," whether it be suitable and good, or unsuitable and not good. "Nothing that is not given," the property of another that is not given by the owner. "In this world," in this world. "Takes nothing," does not take. "Him," that person. "I," the Buddha. "A brahmin," as a brahmin. "I call," I declare.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of an unknown Elder ends.

## 27. The Story of Elder Sāriputta

(Sāriputtattheravatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, spoke this religious teaching beginning with "He whose cravings" (Āsā yassa) in reference to Elder Sāriputta.

## Elder Sāriputta's Freedom from Craving for Requisites

Elder Sāriputta, accompanied by five hundred monks, went to a monastery in the countryside and entered the rains retreat (vassa). When the people saw Elder Sāriputta, they promised many rains-retreat robes (vassāvāsika). After performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, and even before all the rains-retreat robes had arrived, Elder Sāriputta, while departing to the presence of the Buddha, said to the monks: "For the sake of the young monks and for the sake of the novices...
422:
## The Teaching

(410) He whose cravings are no more, in this world or the next, who is free from craving and detached—him I call a brahmin.

"Whose," for which person. "Cravings," the cravings. "Are no more," do not exist. "In this world," in this present world. "Or the next," and in the world beyond. "Free from craving," being without craving. "Detached," being unfettered from the defilements. "Him," that person. "I," the Buddha. "A brahmin," as a brahmin. "I call," I declare.

...when the people bring the rains-retreat robes, take them and send them, or keep them and send word." Having given these instructions, he departed to the presence of the Buddha. At that time, the monks raised a discussion: "Even now, it seems, Elder Sāriputta still has attachment and craving. That is why, when the people offer rains-retreat robes, he instructed the monks to send the robes for his own co-resident pupils, or to keep them and send word, before he left for the Buddha's presence."

The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your discussion as you sit here now?" When they replied, "It is this subject, Venerable Sir," the Buddha said, "Monks, my son Sāriputta has no attachment or craving. He spoke thus only with the thought: 'Let not the people's merit be diminished, and let not the young monks and novices be deprived of their rightful gains (dhammika-lābha).'" Having said this, he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of Elder Sāriputta ends.

## The Teaching

(411) He who has no attachments, who through knowledge is free from doubt, who has reached the depth of the Deathless—him I call a brahmin.

"Whose," for which person. "Attachments," the cravings. "Are no more," do not exist. "Through knowledge," having known thoroughly with the Path-knowledge. "Free from doubt," having no uncertainty or hesitation regarding the eight bases of doubt. "Reached the depth of the Deathless," having entered and reached the Deathless Nibbāna. "Him," that person. "I," the Buddha. "A brahmin," as a brahmin. "I call," I declare.

## 28. The Story of Elder Mahāmoggallāna

(Mahāmoggallānattheravatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, spoke this religious teaching beginning with "He who has no attachments" (Yassālaya) in reference to Elder Mahāmoggallāna.

## Elder Moggallāna's Freedom from Craving

(The story is just the same as the previous story of Elder Sāriputta. In this story, the Buddha spoke of the state of being free from craving of the noble Elder Mahāmoggallāna and spoke this verse.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of Elder Mahāmoggallāna ends.
423:
(412) He who has here passed beyond the attachment to both merit and demerit, who is sorrowless, stainless, and pure—him I call a Brahmin.

Idha, in this Dispensation. Yo puggalo, that person who. Puññañca, merit and. Pāpañca, demerit. Ubho, both types of kamma. Saḍḍhetvā, having abandoned. Saṅgaṃ, the attachment characterized by lust and so forth. Upaccagā, has transcended. Asokaṃ, who is without sorrow. Virajaṃ, who is without the dust of lust. Suddhaṃ, who is purified from defilements. Taṃ puggalaṃ, that person. Ahaṃ, I, the Buddha. Brāhmaṇaṃ, a Brahmin. Brūmi, so I call.

## 29. The Story of Elder Revata (Revatattheravatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Pubbārāma, spoke this Dhamma teaching, "He who has here passed beyond merit..." starting with Elder Revata.

## Arahants Have Neither Merit Nor Demerit

(The story has been detailed in the commentary on the verse "Gāme vā yadi vā raññe" (Dhp. 98). Indeed, in that story, the passage beginning with "Again, one day..." was stated.)

Again, one day, the monks raised a discussion: "Oh, how great are the gains of the novice Revata! Oh, how great is his merit! Though he is but one, he has built five hundred pinnacled houses for the sake of five hundred monks." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now as I have just arrived?" When they replied, "We are gathered for such a discussion," he said, "Monks, my son Revata has neither merit nor demerit; my son Revata has abandoned both merit and demerit," and he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of Elder Revata ends.

## 30. The Story of Elder Candābha (Candābhattheravatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching, "Like the moon..." starting with Elder Candābha.

## The Merchant Seeking Sandalwood

(In this teaching, the following is the sequential narrative.)

In the past, a merchant living in Bārāṇasī, thinking, "I will go to the border regions and bring back sandalwood," took many clothes and ornaments and went to the border regions with five hundred carts. Upon reaching the village gate, he took up residence and asked the cowherd boys in the forest, "Is there any man in this village who works at the foot of the mountain?"
424:
When they said, "He is in such and such a place," the merchant, following the directions given by the cowherd boys, rode in a fine carriage to the door of that man's house. Alighting from the carriage, he entered the house and called the woman, "Mother [Name]!" The woman, thinking, "He must be one of our relatives," came quickly and prepared a seat. The merchant sat on the prepared seat, mentioned his name, and asked, "Where is my friend?" She replied, "Sir, he has gone to the forest." He then asked, mentioning all their names, "Where is my son [Name] and my daughter [Name]?" and gave them gifts, saying, "These clothes and ornaments are for the children." He also gave a gift for his friend, saying, "Give these clothes and ornaments to my friend when he returns from the forest." The woman treated the merchant with great respect. When her husband returned, she said, "Sir, this merchant, from the moment he arrived, called everyone by name and gave these various clothes and ornaments." The man also treated the cart-merchant with appropriate hospitality. Later, in the evening, while sitting on the bed, the merchant asked the mountain-foot worker, "Friend, while wandering at the foot of the mountain, what trees have you seen in abundance?" The man replied, "I have seen no other trees, but I have seen many trees with red branches." The merchant asked, "Are there many such trees?" "Oh, yes, many," he replied. "If so, please show those trees to me," the merchant said. He went with the man, cut down red sandalwood trees, filled five hundred carts, and as he was leaving, he said to the mountain-foot worker, "Friend, my house is in such and such a place in Bārāṇasī. Please come to me from time to time. I do not desire any other gift; just bring me trees with red branches."

## The Past Merit of Elder Candābha

The mountain-foot worker said, "Very well," and whenever he came to the merchant, he brought only red sandalwood. The merchant, in turn, gave him much wealth. Later, after the Parinibbāna of Kassapa the Buddha, when the golden stūpa was being built, that mountain-foot worker took much sandalwood and went to Bārāṇasī. Then his friend, the merchant, had much sandalwood ground into powder, filled a bowl, and said, "Come, friend, while the rice is still cooking, let us go to the place where the stūpa is being built and return." Taking him along, they went there and made an offering of sandalwood. His friend from the border region also made a moon-disk with sandalwood on the inner part of the stūpa. This was the previous deed of that villager from the border region.

## Becoming the Brahmin Candābha with a Moon-like Glow from his Navel

When that villager from the border region passed away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. He spent the interval between the two Buddhas, Kassapa and Gotama, in that celestial realm. When our Buddha Gotama appeared in the world, he was reborn in Rājagaha in a wealthy Brahmin family. From the circle of his navel, a bright light resembling the moon's disk emerged. Therefore, they named him Candābha.
425:
(The radiance like a moon-disc emanating from his navel was the result of the merit of having made an offering in the form of a moon-disc with sandalwood at the stupa of the Buddha Kassapa.)

The Brahmins thought, "We can take this man and deceive the people." They placed him on a vehicle and wandered about, saying, "Whoever touches this Brahmin's body with their hand will obtain such sovereign wealth and prosperity." Those who gave a hundred or a thousand pieces of money were allowed to touch the Brahmin's body. As they wandered in this manner, they reached the city of Sāvatthī and took up residence between the city and the Jetavana monastery.

## Competing in Radiance with the Buddha

In Sāvatthī, about five crores of noble disciples, having given alms in the morning, would go to hear the Dhamma in the afternoon, carrying perfumes, flowers, robes, medicines, and so on. When the Brahmins saw them, they asked, "Where are you going?" When they replied, "We are going to the presence of the Blessed One to hear the Dhamma," the Brahmins said, "Come here! What will you do by going to that Buddha? There is no power equal to the power of our Brahmin named Candābha. Those who touch the body of this Brahmin Candābha obtain such and such wealth and prosperity. Come and see this Brahmin Candābha." The disciples replied, "What is the power of your Brahmin Candābha? Only our Teacher possesses great power." Being unable to convince one another, they said, "Let us go to the monastery and find out the power of either Candābha or our Teacher," and taking Candābha with them, they went to the monastery.

As soon as Candābha approached the presence of the Blessed One, the Buddha caused the radiance to disappear. In the presence of the Teacher, that Brahmin Candābha became as dark as a crow in a charcoal basket. Then they took Candābha to another place, and the radiance returned to its normal state. Again, they brought him to the presence of the Teacher, and the radiance disappeared just as before.

## Asking the Buddha for the Mantra

Having seen the radiance disappear three times in this way, Candābha thought, "This Teacher surely knows the mantra that causes the radiance to disappear." Candābha asked the Blessed One, "How is it, Venerable Sir? Do you know the mantra that causes my radiance to disappear?" When the Buddha replied, "Yes, I know it," Candābha said, "If so, please grant it to me." The Buddha said, "It cannot be given to one who is not ordained." Candābha said to the Brahmins, "Once I have acquired this mantra, I shall be the greatest in the whole of Jambudīpa. You stay right here; I will ordain and learn the mantra in just a few days."
426:
## The Teaching

(413) Spotless like the moon, pure, serene, and undisturbed,
In whom craving for existence is exhausted—him I call a Brahmin.

*Vimalam*: free from impurities such as clouds or mist. *Candamva*: like the full moon. *Suddham*: pure. *Vippasannam*: having an exceptionally clear mind. *Anāvilam*: being free from the defilements and thus undisturbed. *Nandībhavaparikkhīṇam*: having craving exhausted in the three realms of existence. *Tam*: that person. *Aham*: I, the Buddha. *Brāhmaṇam*: call a Brahmin, one who has put away evil. *Brūmi*: so I declare.

"You stay right here; I will ordain and learn the mantra in just two or three days," he told them.

## Attaining Arahantship while Learning the Mantra

Candābha requested the novice ordination from the Blessed One and became a monk. Then, the Blessed One taught the new monk Candābha the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra). The monk Candābha asked, "Venerable Sir, what is this?" The Buddha replied, "This is the preliminary practice (parikamma) for the mantra; it is proper to recite it." The Brahmins also came from time to time and asked, "Have you mastered the mantra?" He replied, "I have not mastered it yet." Within just two or three days, that monk Candābha attained the Fruit of Arahantship. When the Brahmins came and asked him again, he said, "You may go; I have now become one who has no reason to return." The monks reported to the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, this monk Candābha is speaking what is not true and is declaring the Fruit of Arahantship." The Blessed One said, "Monks, my son Candābha has now exhausted the taints (āsavas); he speaks only the truth," and he uttered this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the Elder Candābha ends.

## 31. The Story of Elder Sīvali

(Sīvalitthera-vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing in the forest named Kuṇḍadhāna near the city of Kuṇḍakoliya, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yo imaṃ," concerning the Elder Sīvali.

## The Suffering of Elder Sīvali's Mother

On one occasion, the Koliyan princess named Suppavāsā, having carried a pregnancy for seven years, suffered for seven days from the confusion of the womb, being afflicted by painful, sharp, and bitter sensations. She thought: "The Blessed One is truly the Fully Enlightened One who teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of such suffering. The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is truly practicing well to abandon such suffering. That Nibbāna is truly blissful, where such suffering does not exist."
427:
Thinking, 'In Nibbāna, such a mass of suffering does not exist; how peaceful is that Nibbāna,' she endured those pains with these three thoughts and sent her husband to the presence of the Blessed One. When the husband conveyed the salutation of Princess Suppavāsā to the Blessed One, the Blessed One said: 'May Suppavāsā, the daughter of the Koliyans, be happy. May she, being healthy and free from disease, give birth to a healthy and noble son.' At that very moment, she became happy and healthy, and gave birth to a healthy and noble son. She then invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and offered a great alms-giving for seven days.

## The Boy Who Could Work on the Day He Was Born
From the day he was born, the son of Princess Suppavāsā took a water filter (dhammakaraṇa) and filtered water for the Saṅgha. Later, when that young boy renounced the world and became a monk, he attained the fruit of Arahantship. One day, the monks were discussing in the Dhamma Hall: 'Friends, look! A monk like this, who is endowed with the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for Arahantship, had to endure suffering in his mother's womb for such a long time. What need is there to mention others? Indeed, this monk has crossed over a great mass of suffering.' The Blessed One arrived and asked, 'Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here now?' When they replied, 'With such a subject, Bhante,' the Blessed One said, 'Monks, it is true. My son Sīvali has been released from such suffering and now dwells having realized Nibbāna.' He then spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(414) Yo maṃ palipathaṃ duggaṃ, saṃsāraṃ mohamaccagā.
Tiṇṇo pāraṅgato jhāyī, anejo akathaṃkathī.
Anupādāya nibbuto, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.

*Yo*: that monk. *Imaṃ*: such as this. *Palipathaṃ*: the obstacle of passion (rāga). *Duggañca*: the mire of defilements (kilesa). *Saṃsārañca*: the suffering of the round of rebirths. *Mohañca*: the delusion of not piercing the Four Noble Truths. *Accagā*: has transcended. *Tiṇṇo*: having crossed the four floods (ogha). *Pāraṅgato*: has reached the further shore, which is Nibbāna. *Jhāyī*: is accustomed to meditating with the two kinds of jhāna. *Anejo*: is free from craving (taṇhā). *Akathaṃkathī*: is free from doubt, thinking 'is it this or that?'. *Anupādāya*: without clinging through craving or views. *Nibbuto*: is cooled through the extinguishing of defilements. *Taṃ bhikkhuṃ*: that monk. *Ahaṃ*: I, the Buddha. *Brāhmaṇaṃ*: as one who has put away evil. *Brūmi*: I call.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.
The story of Elder Sīvali ends.
428:
## 32. The Story of Elder Sundarasamudda
(Sundarasamuddattheravatthu)
The Blessed One, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Yo'dha kāme,' concerning the Elder named Sundarasamudda.

## Mother Weeps Because Her Son Became a Monk
In the city of Sāvatthī, a young man named Sundarasamudda was born into a great family with a wealth of four hundred million. One day, in the afternoon, seeing a great crowd of people going to Jetavana Monastery with perfumes and flowers in their hands to listen to the Dhamma, he asked, 'Where are you going?' When they replied, 'We are going to the presence of the Blessed One to listen to the Dhamma,' he said, 'I will go too.' He went along with the crowd and sat at the edge of the assembly. The Blessed One, knowing his inclination, gave a graduated discourse. The young man thought, 'It is not possible for one living the household life to practice the holy life (brahmacariya) which is as pure and polished as a conch shell.' Relying on the Blessed One's Dhamma talk, he felt an urge to ordain. When the assembly had departed, he requested ordination from the Blessed One. Hearing that the Buddhas do not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his parents, he went home. With great effort, like the young man Raṭṭhapāla and others, he obtained his parents' permission and was ordained in the presence of the Blessed One. After receiving higher ordination (upasampadā), he thought, 'What is the use of me staying here?' He left Jetavana in Sāvatthī and went to Rājagaha, where he spent his time wandering for alms. One day, during a festival in Sāvatthī, the Elder's mother and father saw his young friends playing with great splendor and glory. They wept, saying, 'It is difficult for our son to obtain such a collection of splendor and glory.'

(The young man Raṭṭhapāla, when asking for permission to ordain and being refused by his parents, lay down on the bare ground without eating, saying, 'If I get to ordain, let it be; if not, let me die here.' He obtained permission only after seven days. This means Sundarasamudda made a similar effort.)

## The Woman Who Promised to Make Him Disrobe
At that moment, a certain courtesan went to that family's house and, seeing the mother of Elder Sundarasamudda sitting and weeping, asked, 'Mother, for what reason are you weeping?' When she replied, 'I am weeping because I long for my son,' the woman asked, 'Mother, where is that son living?' She said, 'He is living as a monk in the Saṅgha.' The woman asked again, 'Is it not proper to make him disrobe?' The mother replied, 'He has no such desire; he has left Sāvatthī and gone to Rājagaha.' The woman then said, 'If I can make that monk disrobe, what will you do for me?' The mother replied, 'We will make you the mistress of this family's wealth and property.' The woman said, 'If that is so, give me the necessary expenses.' Taking the expenses, she went to Rājagaha with a large retinue. She noted the street where the Elder wandered for alms and took a house on that street. Early in the morning, she prepared excellent food and offered alms when the Elder entered for his alms-round. After a few days had passed, she said, 'Venerable Sir, please sit and take your meal in this house,' and she took his bowl. The Elder gave her the bowl.
429:
## Enticement through Craving for Taste

Then, after serving the Elder with choice food, she said, “Venerable Sir, it is convenient to wander for alms right here in this house.” She had him sit and eat on the veranda for two or three days. She then won over the children by giving them cakes and said, “Come, when the Elder arrives, even if I try to stop you, come here and raise up the dust.” The next day, when the Elder was taking his meal, they raised the dust even though the woman tried to stop them.

The next day, she said, “Venerable Sir, although I tried to stop them, the children did not listen to my words and raised the dust here. Please sit inside the house.” She had him sit inside and served him for two or three days. Again, she won over the children and said, “Even if I try to stop you, make a great noise when the Elder is taking his meal.” The children did as she said. The next day, she said, “Venerable Sir, there is a very great noise in this place. Although I tried to stop them, the children do not listen to my words. Please sit only on the upper floor of the mansion.” When the Elder consented, she led the way and ascended the mansion, closing the doors as she went. Although the Elder Sundarasamudda was an eminent practitioner of the dhutaṅga of uninterrupted alms-gathering (sapadānacārī), because he was bound by the craving for taste (rasa-taṇhā), he ascended the seven-storied mansion at that woman's word. After she had the Elder sit down—

## The Forty Wiles

“Friend Puṇṇamukha, indeed, a woman overcomes and dominates a man through forty wiles. These forty wiles are: ...
8. Dārakaṃ ullaṅghetti: She lifts up a child.
9. Dārakaṃ ullaṅghāpetti: She has a child lifted up.”

## The Battle between the Monk and the Woman

Thus, showing the behavior and the charms of women as mentioned in the Mahākuṇāla Jātaka of the Asītinipāta, she stood before the Elder and recited this verse:

“With feet stained red with lac, and wearing golden sandals,
I am young, and you too are young.
Let us both enjoy life, and later, when we are old
And must lean on staves, we shall both ordain.”

(Alattakakatapādā, pādukāruyha vesiyā...)
With feet stained red with lac, the courtesan, wearing golden sandals, spoke these sweet and enticing words: “Venerable Sir, you also, please be my beloved and youthful husband. I too shall be your beloved and youthful wife. Later, when we have enjoyed full wealth and have become old and aged, leaning on walking staves for support, let us both—the two of us who have fulfilled perfections together—ordain and strive for the immortal state of Nibbāna, with you leading and me following.”

Great spiritual urgency (saṃvega) clearly arose in the Elder Sundarasamudda, thinking, “Alas! I have done a very heavy deed without investigation or reflection.”
430:
## The Teaching

(415) He who has abandoned sensual desires in this world,
Who wanders homeless,
In whom craving for existence is exhausted,
Him I call a Brahmin.

(Yo'dha kāme pahantvāna, anāgāro paribbaje...)
“Whosoever in this world, having abandoned both types of sensual desires and becoming homeless, wanders forth; him, in whom both sensual craving and the craving for existence are exhausted, I call a Brahmin.”

“There is indeed no evil worse than tastes,
Neither dwellings nor intimacies.
The wind-deer (Vātamiga) that dwelt in the thicket,
Sañjaya brought under his power by means of tastes.”

(Na kiratthi rasehi pāpiyo...)
Among the cravings for taste (rasa-taṇhā) that cling to the six flavors—sweet, sour, spicy, salty, astringent, and bitter—there is indeed no quality more wretchedly clinging. This craving for taste is far more wretched than the craving for dwellings or the craving for companions. Sañjaya, the gardener, brought the wild deer known as the Vātamiga, which lived in the deep forest, under his control by using the taste of honey-smeared grass.

At that moment, the Blessed One, staying at the Jetavana monastery forty-five leagues away, saw that matter and manifested a smile. Then the Elder Ānanda asked the Blessed One, “Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for manifesting a smile?” When the Buddha replied, “Ānanda, in the city of Rājagaha, on the upper floor of a seven-storied mansion, a battle is taking place between the monk Sundarasamudda and a courtesan,” Ānanda asked again, “Venerable Sir, who will win and who will lose?” The Blessed One declared the Elder's victory, saying, “Ānanda, the monk Sundarasamudda will win, and the courtesan will lose.” While remaining at the Jetavana monastery, He emitted a radiance and said, “Dear monk, abandon both types of sensual desires—objective sensuality and subjective defilement—without any lingering regard,” and spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the Elder Sundarasamudda attained Arahantship. By the power of his psychic abilities, he flew into the air, passed through the peak of the roof, and arrived while praising the physical body of the Blessed One, then paid homage to the Blessed One.

## The Evil of Craving for Taste

In the Dhamma hall, the monks started a conversation: “Friends, the Elder Sundarasamudda was nearly ruined because of the taste known through tongue-consciousness. However, the Blessed One became his refuge.” When the Blessed One heard this, He said, “Bhikkhus, not only now, but in the past too, I have been the refuge of this monk whose mind was bound by the craving for taste.” Being requested by the monks, He brought forth the past to clarify that matter:
431:
Having expanded this Vātamiga Jātaka of the Ekanipāta, Sīlavagga, the Teacher concluded the Jātaka by saying: "At that time, the monk Sundarasamudda was the flying deer. I myself was the king's great minister who spoke this verse and caused the deer to be released."

The story of Venerable Sundarasamudda Thera ends.

## 33. The Story of Venerable Jaṭila Thera
(Jaṭilattheravatthu)

The Teacher, while staying at Veḷuvana Monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yodha taṇhaṃ..." concerning Venerable Jaṭila.

## The Householder who offered Sugarcane Juice to a Paccekabuddha
(The following is the sequence of the narrative that serves as the biography of Venerable Jaṭila.)

In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, two brothers who were householders cultivated a large sugarcane field. One day, the younger brother went to the sugarcane field and thought, "I will give one stalk of sugarcane to my elder brother, and one will be for me." He then cut and tied the stalks at the ends with leaves or similar materials to prevent the juice from leaking out.

(In those days, there was no need for a machine to crush the sugarcane. When the stalks were cut at the top or the bottom and lifted, the juice would flow out by itself, just like water leaking from a water-strainer [dhammakaraṇa].)

As the younger householder was returning from the field carrying the sugarcane stalks, a Paccekabuddha on Mount Gandhamādana arose from his meditative attainment (samāpatti). Contemplating, "Whom shall I bless today?", he saw the householder carrying the sugarcane stalks entering the net of his knowledge. Knowing that he was capable of being helped, the Paccekabuddha took his bowl and robes, arrived by psychic power, and stood before the householder. As soon as the householder saw the Paccekabuddha, his heart was filled with faith. He spread his upper robe on a high spot of ground and said, "Venerable Sir, please sit here." After inviting the Paccekabuddha to sit, he said, "Please hold out your bowl, Venerable Sir." He then untied the binding of the sugarcane stalk and held it over the bowl. The juice flowed down and filled the bowl. When the Paccekabuddha drank the juice, the householder thought, "How wonderful that the Noble One has drunk my juice! If my elder brother demands the price, I will give him the price. If he demands the share of merit, I will give him the share of merit." He then requested, "Venerable Sir, please hold out your bowl to me again," and untying the second sugarcane stalk, he offered the juice once more.
432:
(The younger householder did not have even a trace of deceitful thought such as, "My elder brother will take and eat another sugarcane from the field.")

The Paccekabuddha, having already drunk the first portion of sugarcane juice, accepted the second portion and remained there, wishing to share it with other Paccekabuddhas.

## The Younger Householder's Aspiration
Knowing the Paccekabuddha's intention, the householder paid homage with the fivefold prostration and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by the result of this offering of the choice juice, may I enjoy prosperity in the realms of gods and humans, and in the end, may I attain the very same Dhamma that you have attained."

The Paccekabuddha said to the householder, "May it be as you have requested," and after giving a blessing of appreciation (anumodanā) with two verses beginning with "Iccitaṃ pattitaṃ...", he performed a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) so that the householder could see him. He then flew through the air to Mount Gandhamādana and gave that juice to five hundred Paccekabuddhas.

## The Elder Householder's Aspiration
When the householder saw that miracle, he went to his elder brother. When asked, "Where did you go?", he replied, "I went to look at the sugarcane field." The elder brother said, "Is that so? Should not someone like you who went to the sugarcane field bring back one or two stalks?"

The younger brother replied, "Yes, brother, I did take two stalks of sugarcane. But seeing a Paccekabuddha, I gave him the juice from my stalk. Then, thinking I would give you the price or the share of merit, I also offered the juice from your stalk. Now, will you take the price of the sugarcane stalk, or will you take the share of the merit?"

When asked, "What did the Paccekabuddha do?", the younger brother said, "After drinking the juice from my stalk, he took the juice from your stalk, flew through the air to Mount Gandhamādana, and gave it to five hundred Paccekabuddhas." While the younger brother was speaking, the elder householder's body was continuously suffused with joy (pīti). He then made an aspiration: "May I realize the very same Dhamma that the Paccekabuddha has realized."

## Becoming Brothers in the Time of Buddha Vipassī
In this way, the younger brother aspired for the three types of prosperity (human, divine, and Nibbāna). The elder brother, however, aspired for the bliss of the Fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala) with a single wish.

(This was the previous meritorious deed of those two householders.)

Those two householders lived out their life span, and after passing away from that life, they were reborn in the celestial realm and spent the interval between two Buddhas there. While they were in the celestial realm, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Vipassī appeared in the world. They passed away from the celestial realm and took rebirth in a certain family in the city of Bandhumatī, where the elder brother was again the elder and the younger brother was the younger. The elder brother was named Sena, and the younger brother was named Aparājita. When the two brothers reached adulthood and were managing their wealth, they heard the proclamation: "The Buddha-treasure has appeared in the world! The Dhamma-treasure and the Saṅgha-treasure have appeared! Therefore, give alms! Perform meritorious deeds! Today is the eighth day, today is the fourteenth day, today is the fifteenth day; observe the Uposatha!"
433:
“Observe the Uposatha! Listen to the Dhamma!” Hearing the announcement of the Dhamma-preacher in the city of Bandhumatī, a great multitude of people gave alms in the morning and went to listen to the Dhamma in the afternoon. Seeing this, the householder named Sena asked, “Where are you going?” When they replied, “We are going to the presence of the Teacher to listen to the Dhamma,” he thought, “I will go too,” and went along with them, sitting at the edge of the assembly.

## The Ordination of the Elder Brother, Sena the Householder

The Blessed One, knowing the householder Sena’s inclination, gave a graduated discourse. Having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma, Sena was filled with enthusiasm for ordination and requested the Teacher for it. Then the Teacher asked the householder, “Do you have any relatives who should be informed?” He replied, “Venerable Sir, I do.” “If that is so, come back after informing them,” said the Teacher.

Sena went to his younger brother and said, “Whatever wealth there is in this family, let all that wealth be for you, my brother.” The brother asked, “But what about you, my lord?” He replied, “I shall ordain in the presence of the Teacher.” The brother pleaded, “What are you saying? When my mother died, I found a mother in you; when my father died, I found a father in you. This family has great wealth. It is possible to perform meritorious deeds while staying at home. Please do not do this.” Sena replied, “I have heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. It is not possible to fulfill that Dhamma while living in the midst of a household. I shall certainly ordain. You stay behind.”

Thus, having made his younger brother stay behind, Sena ordained in the presence of the Teacher. Having received higher ordination, he attained Arahantship before long. The younger brother, thinking, “I will perform an act of honor for my brother’s ordination,” gave alms for seven days to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Then, having paid homage to his elder brother, the Elder, he said, “Venerable Sir, you have achieved your own escape from existence. But I am bound by the five cords of sensual pleasure and am unable to renounce the world and ordain. Please point out a great and suitable meritorious deed for me who remains at home.”

## The Younger Brother Aparājita Builds the Perfumed Chamber

Then the Elder said to the younger brother, “Excellent, excellent, wise brother! Build a Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) for the Teacher.” The householder agreed, saying, “Very well, Bhante.” He had various kinds of wood brought and carved for the purpose of pillars and so on. He made one pillar decorated with gold, one with silver, and one with gems. In this way, he had all the pillars decorated with the seven kinds of jewels. With those pillars, he had the Perfumed Chamber built and covered it with roof tiles also decorated with the seven kinds of jewels. While the Perfumed Chamber was being built, his nephew, also named Aparājita, approached him and said, “Uncle, I also wish to help. Please grant me a share [of the merit].” The uncle replied, “I cannot give it, dear. I wish to make this a deed not shared with others.” Although the nephew pleaded much, he did not receive a share. Therefore, thinking, “It is proper to have an Elephant Hall (Kuñjarasālā) in front of the Perfumed Chamber,” he had an Elephant Hall made of the seven kinds of jewels. In this current Buddha’s era, he (the uncle) was reborn as Meṇḍaka the Treasurer.

Then the Elder said to the younger brother, “Excellent, excellent, wise brother! Build a Perfumed Chamber for the Teacher.” The householder agreed, saying, “Very well, Bhante.” He had various kinds of wood brought and carved for the purpose of pillars and so on. He made one pillar decorated with gold, one with silver, and one with gems. In this way, he had all the pillars decorated with the seven kinds of jewels. With those pillars, he had the Perfumed Chamber built and covered it with roof tiles also decorated with the seven kinds of jewels. At the very time of building the Perfumed Chamber, the nephew, also named Aparājita, approached that householder Aparājita and said, “Uncle, I also wish to help. Please grant me a share [of the merit].” When the uncle said, “I cannot give it, dear. I wish to make this a monastery not shared with others,” the nephew Aparājita, despite pleading much, did not receive a share. Therefore, of the Perfumed Chamber...
434:
Previously, having suggested, "It is fitting to obtain a hall named Kuñjara," he had the Kuñjara hall built with the seven kinds of jewels. This nephew named Aparājita became the great merchant Meṇḍaka when our Buddha appeared. In the Gandhakuti, there were three large windows made of the seven kinds of jewels. In front of those large windows, below, he had three ponds made, finished with plaster, and filled them with water scented with the four kinds of perfumes. The householder Aparājita had flowers of five colors planted so that when the Tathāgata was staying inside, the pollen and dust raised by the force of the wind would sprinkle upon His body. The vessel of the pinnacle of the Gandhakuti was made of red gold; the peaks were made of coral; below, the roofing tiles were made of rubies. Thus, that Gandhakuti stood beautiful like a dancing peacock.

## Scattering the Seven Kinds of Jewels in the Gandhakuti

Among the seven kinds of jewels, he had those that could be broken into pieces cut, and those that could not be broken taken whole. He filled the monastery courtyard, surrounding the Gandhakuti with jewels to the depth of the knees. Having thus completed the Gandhakuti, the householder Aparājita approached his elder brother, the Elder, and said: "Venerable Sir, the Gandhakuti is finished. I only desire its use [by the Buddha]. By its use, great merit will surely accrue." That elder brother approached the Blessed One and said: "Exalted Buddha, this householder has built a Gandhakuti for the sake of the Blessed One; now he desires its use." The Teacher rose from His seat, went towards the Gandhakuti, and stood at the gateway, looking at the heap of jewels surrounding the Gandhakuti. Then the householder said to the Blessed One: "Enter, Exalted Buddha."

The Teacher stood at that very gateway, and when invited for the third time, He looked at the Elder Sena, the elder brother of that householder Aparājita. The Elder, knowing [the reason] just by the manner of His look, said to his younger brother: "Come, dear brother, say to the Teacher: 'The protection [of the jewels] shall be my responsibility alone, Venerable Sir; may the Blessed One stay as He pleases and as comfortably as He wishes.'" Hearing the Elder's words, the householder paid homage to the Blessed One with the fivefold prostration and said: "Venerable Sir, just as people enter the foot of a tree and depart without looking back, or as they cross a river and abandon the raft without looking back, even so, being without concern [for the jewels], may the Blessed One stay."

(Why did the Teacher stand there? It is said that this thought occurred to Him: "Many people come to the presence of the Buddhas both before and after the meal. If they depart taking the jewels, it is not possible for Us to stop them. If the householder should bear a grudge against Me, thinking, 'He does not stop them even when his own attendants take away so many jewels scattered in the courtyard,' he might be headed for a state of misery." For this reason, He stood there.)

## Those Coming to Listen to the Dhamma Being Able to Take [Jewels] by the Handful

When the householder said, "Venerable Sir, the protection shall be my responsibility alone; may the Blessed One enter," He entered. The householder placed guards all around and told those people: "Friends, stop those who go away taking [jewels] in their waist-folds or in baskets and bags. But do not stop the people who go away taking them by hand." In the city also, he had it proclaimed: "I have scattered the seven kinds of jewels in the courtyard of the Gandhakuti. After listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, let the poor people who return take as much as fills both hands. Let the wealthy and prosperous people take with one hand."
435:
(This householder had this thought: "Those who have faith in the Triple Gem and wish to hear the Dhamma will surely come. But those without faith, coming out of greed for wealth, will hear the Dhamma and be released from the mass of suffering in the round of rebirths." Therefore, for the sake of helping the people, he made this announcement.)

The great multitude took the jewels exactly as the householder Aparajita had instructed. When the jewels scattered once were exhausted, he had them scattered again up to three times, to a depth of the knees.

## The Brahmin of Wrong View Taking the Ruby the Size of a Cucumber

Specifically, at the feet of the Blessed One, he placed a priceless ruby the size of a cucumber.

(The householder had this thought: "When people look at the radiance of the ruby together with the golden-hued rays emanating from the Buddha's body, they will never be satisfied." Therefore, he did this. The great multitude also looked on without ever being satisfied.)

Then one day, a brahmin of wrong view thought, "A very precious ruby has been placed at the feet of the Blessed One; I will take it." He went to the monastery and entered among the great crowd who had come to pay homage to the Blessed One. The householder, noticing the manner of his entry, realized, "He wants to take the ruby," and thought, "Oh, if only he would not take it!" That brahmin, as if paying homage to the Blessed One, extended his hand toward the feet, took the ruby, tucked it into his waist-cloth, and departed. The householder was unable to maintain a clear and peaceful mind while the brahmin was taking the ruby. At the conclusion of the Dhamma talk, he approached the Blessed One and said: "Venerable Sir, three times I have scattered the seven kinds of jewels around the Gandhakuṭī to a depth of the knees. I felt no resentment toward those who took those jewels; indeed, my heart became more and more clear. But today, I thought, 'Oh, if only this brahmin would not take the ruby,' and when he took the ruby and left, I was unable to keep my mind clear and peaceful."

## Praying that Enemies Cannot Destroy One's Wealth

When the Blessed One heard the words of the householder Aparajita, He gave him a method, saying, "Lay follower, are you not able to make your own property such that it cannot be taken by others?"
436:
The householder, established in the method given by the Blessed One, paid homage to the Blessed One and made this aspiration: "Starting from today, let no kings or thieves, even if they number in the hundreds, be able to overpower me and take even a single thread of my property. May my property not be burned by fire, nor swept away by water." The Blessed One also gave his blessing, saying, "Lay follower, may it be as you have wished." When that householder performed the celebration for the Gandhakuṭī, he gave a great alms-offering for nine months to six million eight hundred thousand monks within the monastery itself. At the conclusion of the offering, he presented the triple robes to all the monks. The robes received by the most junior monk were worth a thousand pieces.

## Becoming the Treasurer's Son Jotika

Thus, the householder Aparajita performed meritorious deeds throughout his life. When he passed away from that existence, he was reborn in the celestial realm. After wandering through the worlds of gods and humans for this long period, he took rebirth in a treasurer's family in Rājagaha during the time of our Buddha's appearance. He remained in his mother's womb for nine months and a half. On the day he was born, all the weapons in the entire city glowed. The ornaments worn on the bodies of all the people also emitted radiance as if they were ablaze. The entire city became a single mass of light. The Great Treasurer went to attend upon the King early in the morning. Then the King asked him, "Today all the weapons are glowing, and the entire city has become a single mass of light. Do you know the reason for this?"

When he replied, "I know, Your Majesty," the King asked again, "What is it, Treasurer?" "A servant of yours has been born in my house. It is due to the power of that child's merit that this has happened." The King asked, "What? Will he be a thief?" "Your Majesty, there is no reason for him to be a thief. He is a being of great merit who has made past aspirations." The King then said, "If that is so, it is proper to nourish him well. Let this be the price for his milk," and he provided a thousand pieces of money daily.

## The Appearance of the Mansion from the Earth for the Treasurer Jotika

Then, on the day of his naming ceremony, because of the fact that the entire city had become a single mass of light, they gave him the name "Jotika." Later, when Jotika reached the age of maturity, while the ground was being cleared to build a house, the abode of Sakka, King of Gods, showed signs of heat. When Sakka investigated, "What is the reason for this heating of the Paṇḍukambala stone throne?" he realized, "They are taking a site for Jotika's house." Thinking, "This youth Jotika will not live in a house built by these humans; it is proper for me to go there," he went to that place in the guise of a carpenter and asked, "What are you doing?" When they replied, "We are taking a site for the youth Jotika's house," he said, "Move aside. This youth Jotika will not live in a house built by you." He then looked at a piece of land about sixteen karīsas in extent. As soon as Sakka looked at it, the ground became as level as a kasiṇa-maṇḍala. Again, he thought, "Let a seven-storied palace made of the seven kinds of jewels arise here, breaking through the earth," and he looked. At that very moment, such a palace appeared.

## The Appearance of Walls and Wish-fulfilling Trees

Again, he thought, "Let seven walls made of the seven kinds of jewels arise surrounding this palace," and he looked.
437:
Such walls appeared. Then, thinking, "Let wish-fulfilling trees appear at the edges of those seven walls," he looked, and such wish-fulfilling trees appeared. Thinking, "Let four treasure pots appear at the four corners of the mansion," he looked, and everything happened exactly like that. Among the treasure pots, one was a yojana in size, one was three gāvutas, one was half a yojana, and one was one gāvuta in size. As for the treasure pots that appeared for the Bodhisatta, they were the size of a single opening, and their bottoms reached the end of the earth. As for the treasure pots that appeared for Jotika, the size of the opening is not mentioned; they all appeared full, like a cut palmyra fruit. At the four corners of the mansion, four golden sugarcane stalks appeared, the size of young palmyra trunks. Their leaves were made of rubies, and their stalks were made of gold.

(It is said that these sugarcane stalks appeared to manifest the merit of past deeds.)

## Protection by the Yakkhas

At the seven gateways, seven yakkhas took up guard. At the first gateway, the yakkha named Yamakoli took up guard with his retinue of a thousand yakkhas. At the second gateway, the yakkha named Uppala took up guard with two thousand of his retinue yakkhas. At the third gateway, the yakkha named Vajira with three thousand yakkhas; at the fourth gateway, the yakkha named Vajirabāhu with four thousand yakkhas; at the fifth gateway, the yakkha named Kasakanda with five thousand yakkhas; at the sixth gateway, the yakkha named Kaṭattha with six thousand yakkhas; and at the seventh gateway, the yakkha named Disāmukha took up guard with seven thousand yakkhas. Thus, there was firm protection both inside and outside the mansion. Hearing the news that "A seven-storied mansion made of the seven gems has appeared for the youth Jotika, and seven walls, seven gateways, and four treasure pots have also appeared," King Bimbisāra sent the umbrella of a treasurer. He became known as the treasurer Jotika.

## The Treasurer's Wife and Items from the Northern Continent

The woman who had performed meritorious deeds together with the treasurer Jotika was reborn in Uttarakuru. Then, the deities brought her from Uttarakuru and placed her in the auspicious chamber. When she came from Uttarakuru, she brought a single nāḷi of rice and three ruby hearthstones called Jotipāsāṇa. For that couple, Jotika and his wife, their meals were cooked with only that single nāḷi of rice for the rest of their lives. If they wished to fill even a hundred carts with rice, that single nāḷi of rice would remain as a nāḷi [while filling them]. At the time of cooking rice, they would put the rice in the pot and place it...
438:
...place it on top of the stones. At that moment, the stones would ignite, and as soon as the rice was cooked, they would go out. By that sign of the fire going out, they knew the rice was cooked. The same method applied when cooking curries and other dishes. Thus, their food was cooked by the Jotipāsāṇa stones. They lived by the light of gems and did not even know the light of fire or lamps. The fame that "Such is the prosperity of Jotika" spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

## People from All Over Jambudīpa Coming to See

A great multitude of people came to see, harnessing their carts and vehicles. The treasurer Jotika had meals cooked from the Uttarakuru rice and given to all who came. He commanded, "Take clothes from the wish-fulfilling trees; take ornaments." He had the opening of the gāvuta-sized treasure pot opened and commanded, "Take as much wealth as needed for your livelihood." Even though all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa took wealth and left, the treasure pot did not decrease by even a finger's breadth.

(It is said that this was the result of his having spread gems as sand in the precinct of a Gandhakuṭi.)

While the great multitude of people were thus taking clothes, ornaments, and wealth as they pleased and leaving, King Bimbisāra, though wishing to see Jotika's mansion, did not get the opportunity because of the coming of the great multitude.

## King Bimbisāra Sets Out to See

Later, when the people became few because they had taken wealth as they pleased and left, King Bimbisāra said to Jotika's father, "I wish to see your son Jotika's mansion." The father replied, "Very well, your Majesty," and went to tell his son, "Dear son, King Bimbisāra wishes to see your mansion." Jotika said, "Very well, father, let him come." Then King Bimbisāra, with a great retinue, proceeded to Jotika's residence. At the first gateway, a maidservant who was sweeping and discarding the rubbish offered her hand to the King.

## Mistaking the Maidservant for the Treasurer's Wife

King Bimbisāra, thinking "This is the treasurer's wife," felt embarrassed and did not dare to place his hand on the maidservant's arm. In the same way, at the remaining gateways, thinking the maidservants were "the treasurer's wives," he did not dare to place his hand on their arms. Jotika came out, welcomed the King, paid homage, and following behind, said, "Please proceed ahead, your Majesty." To the King, the ruby floor appeared like a chasm a hundred fathoms deep.
439:
## Thinking It Was a Pit to Capture Him
King Bimbisāra thought, "This Jotika the Treasurer has dug a pit to capture me," and thus did not dare to set his foot down. Jotika the Treasurer said, "Great King, this is not a pit. Please follow behind me, treading with your golden feet," and led the way.

Only when Jotika the Treasurer had stepped down did the King tread upon the ground, wandering about and viewing the mansion from the ground floor upwards.

## Ajātasattu’s Reflection
At that time, Prince Ajātasattu, while walking about holding his father’s finger, thought: "How blindly foolish my father the King is! While a mere householder lives in a mansion made of the seven kinds of jewels, my father, though he is the King, lives in a house made of wood. If I were to become King now, I would not allow this Jotika the Treasurer to live in this mansion."

## Partaking of the Morning Meal at Jotika’s House
While King Bimbisāra was ascending to the upper floors, the time for the morning meal arrived. The King called the Treasurer and said, "Great Treasurer, let us have the morning meal right here in this house." The Treasurer replied, "I understand, Your Majesty. Food has already been prepared for Your Majesty."

King Bimbisāra bathed with sixteen jars of scented water and then sat upon the Treasurer’s own throne, which was prepared in the Treasurer’s jeweled pavilion. Then, after giving the King water to wash his hands, they served soft milk-rice in a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [kahāpaṇas] and placed it before him. The King, thinking it was the main meal, began to eat. The Treasurer said, "Your Majesty, this is not the main meal; this is soft milk-rice." Then, they served the main meal in another golden bowl and placed it on top of the first golden bowl.

(It is said that it was pleasant to eat that meal because of the warmth rising from that bowl.)

## Warning Against Overeating
Because the King was partaking of such delicious and flavorful food, he did not know the proper measure of eating. Then the Treasurer paid homage to the King and, with palms joined, said, "Your Majesty, that is enough. Let this much be the meal. If you consume more than this, you will not be able to digest it."

Then the King said to the Treasurer, "Great Treasurer, why is this? Are you speaking thus because you value your own food so highly?"

"Your Majesty, it is not that I value this food. I would serve this very same rice and curry to your entire army. However, I am afraid of ill-repute." When asked, "For what reason?"

[He replied,] "Your Majesty, if you were to experience physical lethargy or sluggishness, I fear people would say, 'Yesterday the King had a meal at the Treasurer’s house; the Treasurer must have done something to him.' I fear such words, Your Majesty." The King then said, "If that is so, take away the food and bring water." At the conclusion of the King's meal, all the royal attendants partook of that same food.

## The Treasurer’s Wife’s Reaction
After resting comfortably, the King called Jotika the Treasurer and asked, "Great Treasurer, how is it? Is there no wife of a treasurer in this house?"

When he replied, "There is, Your Majesty," the King asked again, "Where is she?" He answered, "She is in the auspicious chamber. She does not know of Your Majesty’s arrival."

(This was true; although King Bimbisāra had arrived with his retinue early in the morning, the Treasurer’s wife indeed did not know of the King’s arrival.)

She
440:
Then, Jotika the Treasurer went to his wife and said, "The King wishes to see you." He approached her and said, "The King has arrived. It is proper for you to see him." While still reclining, the Treasurer's wife asked, "My lord, who is this person called a King?" When he replied, "A King is our master," she expressed her displeasure, saying, "Alas, our meritorious deeds must have been poorly performed, for we still have a master. Having performed meritorious deeds without faith, we have attained this prosperity yet are born under the dominion of another. Surely, we must have given gifts without faith; this is the result of that deed performed without faith." She then asked, "My lord, what should I do now?"

## The Treasurer's Wife Sheds Tears

"Take a palmyra fan and fan the King," he said. As the Treasurer's wife took the palmyra fan and fanned the King, the scent from the King's turban struck her eyes. At that moment, a stream of tears began to flow from her eyes. Seeing her weeping, the King said to the Treasurer, "Great Treasurer, women are of little wisdom. I suppose she is weeping out of fear that I might take your wealth. Reassure her, saying, 'I have no need for your prosperity.'" "Your Majesty, she is not weeping," the Treasurer replied. "If that is not so, then what is the reason?" the King asked. "The scent of Your Majesty's turban caused her tears to flow."

(Indeed, this lady never saw the light of lamps or fire; she ate, sat, and slept only by the light of gems.)

When the Treasurer remarked, "Your Majesty must live by the light of lamps," the King replied, "Yes, Treasurer, that is true." "In that case, Your Majesty, from this day forth, live by the light of gems," and he presented a priceless gem the size of a large melon. King Bimbisāra, after looking over Jotika's house, remarked, "How magnificent is the prosperity of Jotika!" and departed.

(This is the account of Jotika's origin.)

## The Treasurer's Daughter and the Vijjādhara

Now, the origin of Jatila should be known in the following way: In the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a treasurer's daughter of great beauty. When she reached the age of fifteen or sixteen, her parents gave her a maidservant for protection and had her live in a magnificent chamber on the top floor of a seven-storied palace. One day, while she was looking out through an open window, a Vijjādhara traveling through the air saw her. Overcome with affection, he entered through the window and had relations with her. Because of this union with the Vijjādhara...
441:
...she soon became pregnant. When the maidservant noticed her condition and asked, "Dear lady, what is this?" the daughter replied, "Let it be so, but do not tell anyone." Out of fear, the maid remained silent. After ten months, she gave birth to a son. She had a new vessel brought, placed the infant inside, closed it, and placed garlands of flowers on top. She then commanded the maid, "Carry this on your head, go to the Ganges River, and set it adrift. If anyone asks, 'What is this?' say, 'It is an offering for my mistress's deity.'" The maid did exactly as she was commanded.

## Two Women Go to Court Over a Pot

Downstream on the Ganges, two women were bathing. Seeing the vessel floating in the water, one woman said, "This vessel is mine." The other said, "Whatever is inside is mine." When the vessel reached them, they took it to the shore and opened it. Seeing the infant, the first woman said, "Since I claimed the vessel, the child is mine." The other said, "Since I claimed whatever was inside, the child is mine." As they were quarreling, they went to the court. When the ministers were unable to decide the matter, they went before the King. Having heard their words, the King decreed, "You take the child, and you take the vessel."

## Receiving the Name Jatila and Meeting Venerable Kaccāna

The woman who received the child was a supporter of the Elder Mahākaccāna. She raised the child, thinking, "I shall have him ordained under the Elder Kaccāna." Because his hair was not washed to remove the impurities of birth on the day he was born, it became matted and tangled. Therefore, they named the boy Jatila. When he was old enough to walk, the Elder entered that house for alms. The female lay follower invited the Elder to sit and offered him food. Seeing the boy, the Elder asked, "Lay follower, have you obtained a child?" "Yes, Bhante. I have raised this boy to be ordained under you. Please ordain him," she replied, handing him over.

## Sending Jatila to Takkasilā

The Elder said, "Very well," and took him away. While departing, he considered, "Does this boy have the merit to enjoy worldly prosperity?" He saw that the boy was a being of great merit who would enjoy immense wealth. Thinking, "He is still young, and his wisdom has not yet matured," he took the boy to the house of a lay supporter in Takkasilā. The supporter prostrated to the Elder and, seeing the boy, asked, "Bhante, have you obtained a child?" "Yes, lay follower. He will be ordained, but he is still young. Let him stay with you for now." The supporter agreed, saying, "Very well, Bhante," and cared for the boy as his own son.
442:
## Jatila’s Success in Trade
In that donor's house, the goods for sale collected over twelve years were very numerous. When that donor went to another village, he brought all those goods to the shop at his house, placed the youth there, and after telling him the prices of the various goods, saying, "Sell such and such a good for this much price," he departed. On that day, the guardian deities of the city assisted by making people who desired even as little as a bit of chili or cumin go directly to the shop of the youth Jatila. The youth Jatila sold all the many goods collected over twelve years in a single day. When the householder returned and saw nothing in the shop, he said, "Dear son, have you destroyed all the goods?" When the youth replied, "I did not destroy them; I sold everything exactly as you instructed. This gold and silver is the price of such and such a good. This gold and silver is the price of such and such a good," the householder was pleased and thought, "This is a man of inestimable value; he is capable of making a living anywhere." He then gave his daughter, who had reached marriageable age, to Jatila and commanded his men, "Build a house for the youth Jatila." When the house was finished, he said, "Go now and live in your own house."

## The Appearance of the Golden Mountain, Becoming a Treasurer, and the Desire to Ordain
Then, at the moment he stepped onto the threshold with one foot to enter the house, a golden mountain eighty cubits high rose up, breaking through the earth at the back of the house. As soon as the King heard the report, "It is said that a golden mountain has risen, breaking through the earth at the youth Jatila's house," he sent the treasurer's parasol to the youth Jatila. He became known as the treasurer Jatila. That treasurer Jatila had three sons. When those three sons reached marriageable age, he conceived the desire to ordain, thinking, "If there is a treasurer's family with wealth equal to ours, they will allow me to ordain. If not, they will not. Is there any family in Jambudīpa with wealth, treasures, gold, and silver equal to ours?" For the purpose of investigating this, he had a brick made of gold, a goad made of gold, and sandals made of gold. Giving them into the hands of his men, he sent them forth, saying, "Go, take these golden bricks and other items, and travel throughout the land of Jambudīpa as if you are looking for something. Find out whether there is a treasurer's family with wealth equal to ours and return."

## Hearing about Meṇḍaka the Treasurer
As those men were traveling, they reached the city of Bhaddiya. Then, when the great treasurer Meṇḍaka saw those men, he asked, "Friends, what are you doing as you travel about?" When they replied, "We are traveling while looking for something," Meṇḍaka realized, "These men have no need to travel looking for something with these golden bricks; they are traveling to investigate the country." He then said, "Friends, enter the back of our house and take a look." In an area of about eight karīsas at the back of that house, those men saw golden rams of the size of elephants, horses, and bulls, which had risen breaking through the earth, standing back to back, as described in the Mala Vagga below.
443:
After walking and looking among those golden rams, they departed. Then the treasurer Meṇḍaka asked them, "Friends, have you seen the object you were looking for?" When they replied, "We have seen it, lord," he dismissed them, saying, "In that case, you may go." They returned from the city of Bhaddiya, and when their own treasurer Jatila asked, "Friends, how is it? Did you see a treasurer's family with wealth equal to ours?" they reported the whole matter, saying, "Lord, what wealth do you have? In the city of Bhaddiya, the great treasurer Meṇḍaka has such fortune as this."

## The Blanket Worth One Hundred Thousand and Jotika’s Maidservant
Upon hearing those words, the treasurer Jatila was very delighted and thought, "One treasurer's family has been found; is there yet another?" He gave them a woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand and sent them again, saying, "Friends, go once more and search for another treasurer's family."

Those men went to the city of Rājagaha, and at a place not far from the great treasurer Jotika's house, they made a pile of wood, set it on fire, and stood there. When asked, "Why are you setting this fire?" they replied, "We wish to sell a single precious blanket, but there is no buyer. As we travel carrying it, we are afraid of thieves. Therefore, we will burn this precious blanket and then depart."

Then, when the treasurer Jotika saw those men, he asked, "What are these people doing?" and upon hearing the reason, he had them summoned and asked, "How much is the blanket worth?" When they said, "It is worth a hundred thousand," he had the hundred thousand paid and sent it by the hands of those same traders, saying, "Give this to the maidservant who sweeps the gatehouse and discards the rubbish." That maidservant took the blanket and went weeping to her master, the treasurer, saying, "Lord, if I have committed a fault, is it not proper to beat me? Why did you send me such a coarse and rough blanket? How could I possibly wear this or wrap myself in it?" When the treasurer said, "I did not send it for you to wear or wrap yourself in. I sent it to you so that you could wrap it and place it near your bed to wipe your feet, which have been washed with scented water, when you go to sleep. What, are you not even able to use it as a foot-wiper?" the maidservant replied, "I can use it as a foot-wiper," and took it away.

When those men saw that incident, they went to their own treasurer and when asked, "Friends, did you see a treasurer's family?" they reported all the prosperity of the house and told the story, saying, "Lord, what wealth do you have? In the city of Rājagaha, the treasurer Jotika has such fortune as this." Upon hearing their words, the treasurer Jatila was joyful in heart and went to the King, saying, "Your Majesty, I wish to ordain." "Very well, Great Treasurer," [the King replied].
444:
## Jatila the Merchant Asks Permission to Ordain

The men sent by Jatila the merchant, upon seeing that display, returned to their master Jatila. When he asked, “Friends, how was it? Did you see a family of equal wealth?”, they replied, “Lord Merchant, how much wealth could you possibly have? In the city of Rājagaha, the merchant Jotika possesses such wealth,” and they described the abundance of his entire house and the matter of the woolen garment. Upon hearing the words of those men, Jatila the merchant felt a sense of clarity and joy, thinking, “Now I shall be able to ordain.” He went to the King and said, “Your Majesty, I wish to ordain.” When the King granted permission, saying, “Merchant, very well, go and ordain,” Jatila the merchant went home and summoned his sons. Placing a diamond-tipped hoe with a golden handle in the hand of his eldest son, he said, “Dear son, go and take a lump of gold from the golden mountain at the back of the house.”

## Giving Inheritance to the Youngest Son

The eldest son took the hoe and went to strike the golden mountain. It was as if he were striking solid rock. Taking the hoe from the eldest son’s hand, the merchant gave it to the middle son and sent him. When the middle son struck the golden mountain, it was also as if he were striking solid rock. Then, he gave the hoe to the youngest son and sent him. When the youngest son took the hoe and struck it to gather gold, it was as if he were striking soft clay. Then Jatila the merchant said to the youngest son, “Dear son, come; this much is suitable for my son.” He then summoned the other two elder brothers and said, “This golden mountain did not arise for your sake; it arose for my sake and for the sake of the youngest son. Live together with this youngest son and enjoy it in common.”

## Past Karma of Being Cast into the Water

If one asks: Why did that golden mountain arise only for the sake of those two? And why was Jatila cast into the water at the time of his birth? It was solely due to his own past deeds. To elaborate on that matter: When the great shrine (cetiya) of the Buddha Kassapa was being built, an Arahant went to the site of the shrine, looked around, and asked, “Lay followers, why has the masonry not yet risen at the northern entrance of the great shrine?” They replied, “Venerable sir, there is not enough gold.” He said, “I will go into the village and exhort the people; you all perform the work with care.” Having said this, the Arahant entered the city and exhorted the multitude, saying, “Mothers and fathers, there is not enough gold for one entrance of your great shrine. Know the need for gold.” Thus exhorting them, he went to the house of a goldsmith. At that moment, the goldsmith was sitting there quarreling with his wife. Then the Elder Arahant exhorted him, saying, “Lay follower, you should know that there is not enough gold for the entrance you have taken responsibility for at the shrine.” Out of anger toward his wife, the goldsmith said, “Throw your Teacher into the water and go!” Then his wife said to him, “You have committed an extremely reckless and evil deed. If you are angry with me, you should only abuse or strike me. Why do you show enmity toward the Buddhas of the past, future, and present?”

## Past Karma for Obtaining the Golden Mountain

The goldsmith immediately became struck with remorse and, saying, “Venerable sir, please forgive me,” he prostrated at the feet of the Elder. The Elder said, “Lay follower, you said nothing to me. Ask forgiveness from our Teacher, the Buddha.” He asked, “Venerable sir, how shall I ask for forgiveness?” The Elder replied, “Lay follower, make three flower pots filled with golden flowers, place them inside the relic chamber, and ask for forgiveness while wearing wet clothes and having wet hair.” The goldsmith replied, “Very well, venerable sir.” While making the golden flowers, he summoned the eldest of his three sons and said, “Dear son, come. I have offended the Buddha with words of enmity. Therefore, I shall make these gold flowers, place them in the relic chamber, and ask for forgiveness. You, too, be my companion.” The eldest son replied, “I did not speak words of enmity toward the Buddha.”
445:
## The Teaching

(416) He who, having given up craving in this world, would wander forth as a homeless one, in whom craving and existence are exhausted, him I call a Brahmin.

Yo puggalo: that person. Idha: in this world. Taṇhaṃ: craving. Pahantvāna: having abandoned.

"You—do it alone," he said, and did not wish to help. He called the middle son and said the same. The middle son also said the same as the eldest and did not wish to help.

## Past Kamma of the Youngest Son Receiving Inheritance

He called the youngest son and spoke to him again. That youngest son said, "Whatever business arises for parents is the responsibility of the children," and thus became his father's helper in making the golden flower clusters and blossoms. The goldsmith completed three flower pots filled with flower clusters and blossoms, each one span in size. He placed them in the relic chamber where the relics are enshrined. Wearing wet clothes and with wet hair, he asked for the Buddha's forgiveness. Because of this past kamma, that Jatila the treasurer was cast into the water (set adrift) seven times at the time of his birth. This present physical body of Jatila the treasurer is his final existence. Even in this final existence, he was cast into the water solely due to the consequence of that unwholesome kamma.

The two elder brothers of Jatila the treasurer did not wish to help when the golden garlands and flowers were being made. For that reason, the golden mountain did not arise for those two elder sons. However, for the youngest son, it arose because of the merit he performed together [with his father].

## Venerable Jatila Becoming an Arahant

In this way, Jatila the treasurer instructed his sons, "Live together with the youngest son and enjoy [the wealth]." He then went to the Buddha and was ordained. Within just two or three days, he attained the Fruit of Arahantship. On another occasion, while the Buddha was wandering for alms with five hundred monks, He arrived at the doorstep of the house of Venerable Jatila's sons. They offered alms-food to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha for half a month. The monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friend Jatila, even today, do you still have craving for the golden mountain, which is eighty cubits in size, and for your sons?" When he replied, "Friends, I have no craving or pride for that golden mountain or for my sons," those monks said, "This Venerable Jatila is speaking a falsehood and is declaring the Fruit of Arahantship." When the Buddha heard the words of those monks, He said, "Monks, my son Jatila has no craving or pride for that golden mountain or for his sons," and desiring to preach the Dhamma, He spoke this verse:
446:
(It means abandoning craving and pride that arise at the six doors.)

Anāgāro: having left the household life and abandoned the home. Paribbaje: practices the life of a monk. Taṇhābhavaparikkhīṇaṃ: in whom craving and existence are exhausted. Taṃ puggalaṃ: that person. Ahaṃ: I, the Buddha. Brāhmaṇaṃ: call a Brahmin, one who has put away evil. Brūmi: I declare.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of Venerable Jatila ends.

## 34. The Story of Venerable Jotika

(Jotikattheravatthu)

The Buddha, while residing at Veḷuvana Monastery, spoke this teaching beginning with "Yo'dha taṇhaṃ" concerning Venerable Jotika.

## Ajātasattu Seizing Jotika’s Mansion

Prince Ajātasattu, having allied with Devadatta and killed his father King Bimbisāra, was established in kingship. He thought, "I will seize the great mansion of Jotika the treasurer." He made preparations for war and departed from the palace. Seeing his own reflection along with his retinue in the gem-wall, he thought, "Jotika the treasurer has made preparations for war and has come out with his army," and he did not dare to approach. Jotika the treasurer, however, was observing the Uposatha on that day. Having eaten his morning meal early, he went to the monastery and was listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha. The Yakkha named Yamakoḷi, who stood guard at the first gatehouse, saw King Ajātasattu coming for war and said, "Where are you going?" He then routed the King and his retinue and pursued them in all directions. The King went only to the monastery. When the treasurer saw the King, he said, "Your Majesty, what is the reason?" and rose from his seat. "Treasurer, what is this? You commanded your men, 'Fight with me,' and then you sit here in this Veḷuvana Monastery as if you are listening to the Dhamma?"

## Ajātasattu Unable to Remove Jotika’s Rings

When the treasurer asked, "Your Majesty, did you go to seize my house?", the King replied, "Yes, I went."
