"Your Majesty, without my consent, even a thousand kings cannot seize my house," the treasurer said. Then King Ajātasattu became angry and asked, "Will you become the king?" "I am not the king. However, without my consent, neither kings nor thieves can seize even a single thread of my property." "What? Shall I take it only with your consent, treasurer?" "Your Majesty, if that is so, on my ten fingers, these twenty rings..."
447:
## The Teaching

(417) He who, having given up craving in this world, would wander forth as a homeless one, in whom craving and existence are exhausted—him I call a brahmin.

*Yo puggalo*: whatever person. *Idha*: in this world. *Taṇhaṃ*: craving. *Pahantvāna*: having given up. *Anāgāro*: having abandoned the household life and become homeless. *Paribbaje*: practices the life of a monk. *Taṇhābhavaparikkhīṇaṃ*: in whom craving and existence are exhausted. *Taṃ puggalaṃ*: that person. *Ahaṃ*: I, the Buddha. *Brāhmaṇaṃ*: as one who has put away evil. *Brūmi*: I declare.

[Jotika said,] "...there are; I do not wish to give these rings to Your Majesty. If you are able, please take them." When he said this, King Ajātasattu, who could leap to a height of eighteen cubits from a crouching position and eighty cubits from a standing position, despite having such great strength, tried repeatedly from this side and that but was unable to pull off even a single ring. Then Jotika the Treasurer said to King Ajātasattu, "Your Majesty, please spread out your royal cloth," and he held his fingers straight. All twenty rings slipped off by themselves. Then Jotika the Treasurer said to King Ajātasattu, "Your Majesty, thus it is not possible to take my property without my consent." Having said this, he felt spiritual urgency due to the King's actions and said, "Your Majesty, please grant me permission to ordain."

## Jotika Ordains and Becomes an Arahant

King Ajātasattu, thinking, "If this Jotika the Treasurer ordains, I shall easily take the palace," granted permission with a single word, saying, "You may ordain." Jotika the Treasurer ordained in the presence of the Teacher and, before long, attained the fruit of Arahantship, becoming known as Elder Jotika. At the very moment he attained Arahantship, all that wealth and prosperity disappeared. Because the Elder had a body as soft as cotton wool, the deities took his wife, named Satulakāyī, back to the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru). 

Later, one day, the monks called Elder Jotika and asked, "Friend Jotika, do you still have craving for that palace or for your wife?" When he replied, "Friends, I have no craving," they informed the Teacher, saying, "Venerable Sir, this Elder Jotika is speaking what is not true and claiming Arahantship." The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, my son Jotika truly has no craving for the palace or for the woman," and he spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of Elder Jotika ends.

## 35. The Story of the Elder who was the Son of a Dancer

(Naṭaputtakattheravatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Veḷuvana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Hitvā mānusakaṃ" concerning a son of a dancer.

## The Arahant's Transcendence of Bonds

While that son of a dancer was traveling around performing a certain dance, he heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, ordained, and attained the fruit of Arahantship.
448:
While that monk was entering for alms together with the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha, the monks saw a dancer performing. They asked the monk who was formerly a dancer, "Friend, this dancer is performing the same dance you used to perform; do you still have any affection for this?" When he replied, "No, venerable sirs," they said, "Venerable Sir, this monk speaks what is not true and claims the realization of Arahantship." Hearing the words of those monks, the Blessed One said, "Monks, my son has transcended all bonds (yogas)," and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(418) Having abandoned human bonds, he has transcended divine bonds; him who is detached from all bonds, I call a Brahmin.

In that verse, 'human bonds' (mānusakaṃ yogaṃ) refers to human life and the five cords of sensual pleasure. The same applies to 'divine bonds' (dibbaṃ yogaṃ). The meaning of 'transcended' (upaccagā) is: I call him a Brahmin who, having abandoned human bonds, has transcended divine bonds and is detached from all four types of bonds.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many reached the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of the Elder Son of a Dancer, the thirty-fifth.

## 36. The Second Story of the Elder Son of a Dancer
(Naṭaputtakattheravatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Blessed One spoke this Dhamma teaching, "Having abandoned delight..." (Hitvā ratiñca), concerning another son of a dancer.
(The story is just like the previous one.)

## The Arahant's Freedom from Delight and Discontent
In this story, the Blessed One said, "Monks, my son has abandoned both delight and discontent," and spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(419) Having abandoned delight and discontent, cooled, without acquisitions, the hero who has conquered all worlds—him I call a Brahmin.

'Delight' (ratiṃ) means delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Discontent' (aratiṃ) means dissatisfaction or boredom with living in the forest. 'Cooled' (sītibhūtaṃ) means extinguished (nibbūtaṃ). 'Without acquisitions' (nirūpadhiṃ) means free from defilements. 'Hero' (vīraṃ) means one who possesses energy and stands having conquered the entire world of the five aggregates. Such a person, I call a Brahmin.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many reached the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Second Story of the Elder Son of a Dancer, the thirty-sixth.
449:
## 37. The Story of Venerable Vaṅgīsa
(Vaṅgīsatthera Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "He who knows the passing away," concerning Venerable Vaṅgīsa.

## Knowing the Place of Rebirth by Tapping the Skull

In the city of Rājagaha, there was a Brahmin named Vaṅgīsa who, by tapping the skulls of deceased humans, could know: "This is the skull of one reborn in hell; this is the skull of one reborn in the animal realm; this is the skull of one reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (petas); this is the skull of one reborn in the human world; this is the skull of one reborn in the celestial world (deva loka)."

Thinking, "We can live off the world by relying on this Vaṅgīsa," the Brahmins had him dress in two red garments and took him around the countryside, saying to the people: "This Brahmin named Vaṅgīsa can know the place of rebirth by tapping the skulls of the deceased. Ask him about the place of rebirth of your relatives."

(The Samyutta Commentary states that he was the son of a female wandering ascetic and had mastered a thousand doctrines—five hundred from his father's side and five hundred from his mother's side. The Aṅguttara Commentary states that upon reaching adulthood, after learning the three Vedas, he learned the "Chavasīsa Mantra" from a teacher. By reciting this mantra and tapping the skull of someone who had died even three years prior with his fingernail, he could know the place of rebirth through the power of the mantra.)

People, according to their means, gave ten, twenty, or a hundred kahāpaṇas and asked about the place of rebirth of their relatives. In due course, those Brahmins reached Sāvatthī and took up residence near the Jetavana Monastery. After eating their morning meal, they saw a great multitude of people carrying perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, going to hear the Dhamma. When asked, "Where are you going?" and being told, "To the monastery to hear the Dhamma," the Brahmins said, "What can you achieve by going there? There is no one like our Brahmin Vaṅgīsa. He can know the place of rebirth by tapping the skulls of the deceased. Ask him about the place of rebirth of your relatives."

## The Skull of an Arahant

Those people replied, "What does Vaṅgīsa know? There is no one like our Teacher." When the other Brahmins insisted, "There is no one like Vaṅgīsa," they argued at length and finally said, "Come, let us now find out who knows more, Vaṅgīsa or our Teacher." They then took the Brahmins and went to the monastery.

The Teacher, knowing of their coming, had five skulls brought and arranged in a row: four skulls of those reborn in hell, the animal realm, the human world, and the celestial world, and the fifth being the skull of an Arahant. When they arrived, the Teacher asked Vaṅgīsa, "Is it true that you can know the place of rebirth of the deceased by tapping their skulls?" "It is true, Venerable Sir," he replied. When asked, "Whose skull is this?" he tapped it and said, "It is the skull of one reborn in hell."

The Teacher then said, "Excellent, excellent!" and gave him praise. He then asked about the other three skulls, and Vaṅgīsa answered correctly without error, receiving praise each time. Then, showing the fifth skull, the skull of an Arahant, the Teacher asked, "Whose skull is this?" Although Vaṅgīsa tapped that skull, he could not know the place of rebirth. Then the Teacher asked, "Vaṅgīsa, what is it? Do you not know?" When he replied, "I do not know, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "I, however, know."
450:
## Attaining Arahantship while Learning the Mantra from the Buddha

Then Vaṅgīsa the Brahmin requested, "Venerable Sir, please give this mantra to me." The Teacher replied, "It cannot be given to one who is not a monk." Vaṅgīsa thought, "If I master this mantra, I will be the greatest and most noble in the entire Jambudīpa island." He then dismissed the other Brahmins, saying, "You all stay here for a few days; I will become a monk." He was ordained in the presence of the Teacher, and after receiving full ordination, he became known as Venerable Vaṅgīsa.

The Teacher then gave him the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body and said, "Recite and practice this preparatory work for the mantra." While Venerable Vaṅgīsa was reciting and practicing this meditation-mantra, his Brahmin companions would occasionally ask, "Have you mastered the mantra?" He would reply, "Wait a while, I am still in the process of learning it." Within a few days, he attained Arahantship. When the Brahmin companions asked him again, he replied, "Friends, I am no longer fit to go with you."

Hearing this, the monks reported to the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, this Venerable Vaṅgīsa is declaring Arahantship falsely." The Teacher said, "Monks, do not say so. Monks, now my son Vaṅgīsa has become skilled in the passing away and rebirth of beings." He then spoke these verses:

(The Aṅguttara Commentary states that after this Elder became an Arahant, whenever he approached the Buddha, he would frequently praise the Buddha's virtues with many verses, comparing him to the sun, the moon, the sky, the ocean, the noble elephant, and the lion. Because of this, he was declared the foremost (etadagga) among those of quick and brilliant wit (paṭibhānavanta).)

## The Teaching

(419) He who knows the passing away and rebirth of beings in every way, who is unattached, well-gone (sugata), and awakened (buddha)—him I call a Brahmin.

(420) He whose destination is unknown to gods, gandhabbas, and humans, who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) and is an Arahant—him I call a Brahmin.

*Yo puggalo*, whichever person; *sattānaṃ*, of beings; *sabbaso*, in every way; *cutiñca*, the passing away; *upapattiñca*, and the rebirth; *vedi*, knows. *Asattaṃ*, who is without attachment; *sugataṃ*, who has gone well through practice; *buddhaṃ*, who has realized the Four Noble Truths; *taṃ*, that person; *ahaṃ*, I the Buddha; *brūmi*, call; *brāhmaṇaṃ*, one who has set aside evil.

*Yassa*, of whichever Arahant; *gatiṃ*, the destination; *devā*, gods; *gandhabbā*, celestial musicians; *mānusā*, and humans; *na jānanti*, do not know. *Khīṇāsavaṃ*, who has exhausted the taints; *arahantaṃ*, who is far removed from defilements; *taṃ*, that Arahant; *ahaṃ*, I the Buddha; *brūmi*, call; *brāhmaṇaṃ*, one who has set aside evil.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other higher paths.

The Story of Venerable Vaṅgīsa ends.
451:
## 38. The Story of Dhammadinnā Therī
(Dhammadinnattherī Vatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Yassa pure ca," concerning the nun named Dhammadinnā.

## Visākha the Lay Devotee Handing Over Wealth to His Wife
One day, during the time when the nun Dhammadinnā was still a laywoman, her former husband, a lay devotee named Visākha, heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and attained the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). He thought, "It is proper for me to hand over all my wealth to Dhammadinnā." Before attaining this Fruit of Non-returning, whenever Visākha returned home, he used to smile when he saw Dhammadinnā looking out from the window. On that day, however, he went along without even looking at Dhammadinnā, who was standing at the window. Dhammadinnā thought, "What could this mean?" and then reflected, "Let it be; I will know at mealtime." At the time of the meal, she brought the food to him. On other days, Visākha used to say, "Come, let us eat together." But on that day, he ate in silence. Dhammadinnā thought, "He must be angry for some reason." Later, when Visākha was sitting comfortably, he called Dhammadinnā and said, "Dhammadinnā, please take over and manage all the wealth and property in this house."

Dhammadinnā thought, "Those who are angry do not give or hand over their wealth. What could be the reason for this gift?" She then said, "My lord, will you not be here?"

(Visākha was one of the one hundred and ten thousand people who attained Stream-entry along with King Bimbisāra when the Buddha first arrived in Rājagaha. Later, he attained the stage of Once-returner, and then the stage of Non-returner.)

## Dhammadinnā Refusing the Wealth
When he said, "From this day forward, I shall no longer manage any worldly affairs," she pleaded, "Who would accept the spit that you have cast out? In that case, please grant me permission to ordain as a nun." Visākha agreed, saying, "Very well, dear sister," and after making great offerings, he escorted her to the nunnery and had her ordained. Once she received her higher ordination, she became known as Dhammadinnā Therī. Desiring seclusion, Dhammadinnā Therī went to the countryside with other nuns. While staying there, she attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) before long. Thinking, "Now, depending on me, my relatives will perform many meritorious deeds with great devotion," she returned to Rājagaha.

## The Woman Worthy of Worship by her Non-returner Husband
When the lay devotee Visākha heard of the nun Dhammadinnā's return, he wondered, "For what reason has she come back?" He went to the nunnery, and upon seeing Dhammadinnā Therī, he paid homage to her and sat in a suitable place. Thinking, "It is not appropriate to ask, 'Noble Lady, are you weary or bored?' I will instead ask her a question," he inquired about the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga). Dhammadinnā Therī answered the question.
452:
## The Teaching
(422) Yassa pure ca pacchā ca, majjhe ca natthi kiñcanaṃ.
Akiñcanaṃ anādānaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.
For whom there is no longing for the past, the future, or the present. Him who is without longing and without attachment, I call a Brahmin (one who has cast out evil).

Visākha the lay devotee, in this same manner, asked questions about the remaining Paths. When he went beyond his range in asking, Dhammadinnā Therī said, "Lay devotee Visākha, the questions have gone too far," and added, "If you wish, approach the Blessed One and ask Him this question." Having paid homage to the Therī, he rose from his seat, went to the presence of the Blessed One, and reported the entire conversation to Him. The Blessed One said, "My daughter Dhammadinnā has spoken well. If I were asked the same question, I would answer it in exactly the same way," and He then spoke this verse:

(Since she had many gains and offerings from the time she ordained, she did not get the chance to practice meditation. Therefore, she went to the countryside. In the time of Padumuttara Buddha, when she was a house-slave, she had sold her hair to make an offering to the Chief Disciple Sujāta Thera and made a wish. Because of that past merit, she became an Arahant within just two or three days and then returned.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of Dhammadinnā Therī ends.

## The Teaching
(423) Usabhaṃ pavaraṃ vīraṃ, mahesiṃ vijitāvinaṃ.
Anejaṃ nhātakaṃ buddhaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.
The noble one who is like a bull, free from fear and trembling; the excellent, the heroic, the great seeker who has sought the highest virtues such as the aggregate of virtue; the conqueror who has defeated the three Māras; the one free from craving; the one who has washed away defilements; the one who has realized the Four Noble Truths—him I call a Brahmin.

## 39. The Story of Angulimāla Thera
(Angulimālatthera Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Usabhaṃ," concerning the Elder Angulimāla.

## The Arahant Does Not Fear the Fierce Elephant
(The story is already told in the commentary on the verse "Na ve kadariyā devalokaṃ vajanti" in the Lokavagga, specifically in the Story of the Incomparable Almsgiving. Indeed, in the commentary on that verse, the words "The monks asked..." were spoken.)
The monks asked the Elder Angulimāla, "Friend Angulimāla, how is it? Were you afraid when you saw the fierce elephant standing there with a parasol held over it?" When he replied, "Friends, I was not afraid," the monks reported to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, the Elder Angulimāla is claiming the Fruit of Arahantship."
453:
The Blessed One said, "Monks, my son Aṅgulimāla is not afraid. Monks like my son, who are the greatest and noblest bulls among the bulls of Arahants, are not afraid." Having said this, he preached this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other fruits.

The Story of Elder Aṅgulimāla ends.

## 40. The Story of Devahita the Brahmin
(Devahitabrāhmaṇavatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher preached this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Pubbenivāsaṃ,' concerning the question of a Brahmin named Devahita.

## The Buddha's Ailment and the Offering of Hot Water
On one occasion, the Blessed One was severely afflicted by a wind ailment and sent Elder Upavāṇa to the Brahmin named Devahita to obtain hot water. The Elder went and informed the Brahmin of the Blessed One's severe affliction and requested hot water. Upon hearing this, the Brahmin was greatly delighted in heart and thought, "What a gain for me! The Fully Enlightened One has sent a disciple to me for hot water." He had a man carry a load of hot water and offered a jar of molasses to Elder Upavāṇa. The Elder had the molasses taken, went to the monastery, bathed the Blessed One with the hot water, and then, mixing the molasses with hot water, offered it to the Blessed One. At that very moment, the Blessed One's ailment subsided.
454:
## The Teaching
(424) He who knows his former lives, who sees heaven and the states of woe,
Who has reached the end of births, a sage perfected by higher knowledge,
Who has completed all completions—him I call a Brahmin.

'He who' (yo): That person. 'Former lives' (pubbenivāsaṃ): Knows clearly the sequence of aggregates lived in the past. 'Heaven and the states of woe' (saggāpāyañca): Sees with the divine eye the twenty-six heavenly realms and the four states of woe. 'Furthermore' (atho): Besides that. 'End of births' (jātikkhayaṃ): Reached the Fruit of Arahantship, which is the end of birth. 'By higher knowledge' (abhiññā): Knowing with special wisdom. 'Perfected' (vositော): Reached Nibbāna.

Devahita the Brahmin thought, "I will ask the Blessed One to which person a gift given yields great fruit." That Brahmin went to the presence of the Blessed One and, wishing to inquire about that matter, addressed him with this verse:

Where should one give a gift? Where given does it yield great fruit?
How for the one making the sacrifice? How does the offering succeed?

"Venerable Sir, in whom (kattha) should a gift (deyyadhammaṃ) be given (dajjā)? To whom (kattha) given (dinnaṃ) does the merit yield great fruit (mahapphalaṃ)? How (kathaṃ hi) should the sacrifice (yajamānaṃ) be for him (assa)? How (kathaṃ) does the noble offering (dakkhiṇā) succeed (ijjhati)?"

Then the Blessed One, saying to the Brahmin, "A gift given to such a person who has discarded evil yields great fruit," and wishing to make it clear to the Brahmin, preached this verse:
455:
(It means: He is one who has reached Nibbāna, having known with higher knowledge what should be known, having fully understood what should be understood, having abandoned what should be abandoned, and having realized what should be realized.)

'Sage' (muni): He is a sage because he has reached the state of sagehood (mona) through the knowledge of the destruction of taints. 'Who has completed all completions' (sabbavositavosānaṃ): One who has practiced the path of Arahantship, which is the end of all defilements. 'Him' (taṃ): That person. 'I' (ahaṃ): I, the Buddha. 'Call a Brahmin' (brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ): Call a person who has discarded evil a Brahmin.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other fruits. Devahita the Brahmin, with a heart full of faith, established himself in the Three Refuges and declared his status as a lay follower (upāsaka).
456:
The Story of Devahita the Brahmin ends.

The Chapter on the Brahmin (Brāhmaṇavagga) ends.

The Commentary on the Dhammapada, adorned with three hundred and five stories and four hundred and twenty-three verses, consisting of twenty-six chapters, is completed in all its aspects.
